title: Interesting Facts About Nollywood Legend Pete Edochie
description: Veteran actor and broadcaster, Chief Pete Edochie, who died on Wednesday at the age of 79, was one of Nollywood’s most celebrated and respected for his distinctive voice and commanding screen presence.According to a statement signed by his son, Leo Pete Edochie, on behalf of the family, the ac
content:
Veteran actor and broadcaster, Chief Pete Edochie, who died on Wednesday at the age of 79, was one of Nollywood’s most celebrated and respected for his distinctive voice and commanding screen presence.

According to a statement signed by his son, Leo Pete Edochie, on behalf of the family, the actor died at 12:30 am in Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

Edochie’s rich repertoire of African proverbs and portrayal of traditional rulers and family patriarchs endeared him to many hearts.

Early Life And Education

Born on March 7, 1947, in Zaria, Kaduna State, Edochie hailed from Akamnato, Ifite Nteje, in Anambra State.

He attended St Patrick’s and St James Primary Schools in Zaria before proceeding to St John’s College, Kaduna. He also studied journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in England.

His Broadcasting Career

Before becoming a household name in the Nigerian film industry, Edochie built a career in broadcasting.

He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967 as a junior programmes assistant and gradually rose through the ranks.

He eventually became Director of Programmes at the Anambra Broadcasting Service, where he also served as Deputy Managing Director and occasionally acted as Managing Director.

During his years in broadcasting, Edochie was also known for presenting a classical music programme titled Music from the Masters.

Marriage And Family

He was married to Barrister Josephine Edochie, with whom he had six children, including actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

His family life occasionally attracted public attention, particularly following controversies surrounding his son Yul’s marriage to actress Judy Austin and the resulting public disagreements involving his first wife, May Edochie.

Things Fall Apart

Edochie’s breakthrough as an actor came through his portrayal of Okonkwo in the Nigerian Television Authority’s adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s acclaimed novel, Things Fall Apart.

His performance as the respected but deeply troubled Igbo warrior earned him widespread recognition and established him as one of Nigeria’s leading television actors.

The role attracted international attention, with the British Broadcasting Corporation sending a delegation to interview him about his portrayal.

In a 2023 interview with The Nation, Edochie recalled that his performance had received international recognition even before the Nigerian movie industry became widely known as Nollywood.

Films And Acting Career

Following his success in Things Fall Apart, Edochie featured in numerous Nigerian films and television productions.

Some of his notable works include Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire’s Club and Genevieve Nnaji’s 2018 film Lionheart, in which he played Chief Ernest Obiagu.

He became particularly associated with roles as traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and authoritative family patriarchs.

His deep voice, measured delivery and frequent use of traditional expressions and proverbs became distinctive features of his performances.

Awards And Recognition

Edochie’s contributions to Nigerian entertainment earned him several honours during his career.

In 2003, he received the national honour of Member of the Order of the Niger (MON) from former President Olusegun Obasanjo.

He also received the Industry Merit Award from Africa Magic and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Africa Film Academy.

In 2020, he was honoured with the African Film Legend Award at the African Film Festival.

Legacy

With a career spanning broadcasting, television and film, Edochie remained one of the most recognisable veteran actors in Nigeria.

His portrayal of Okonkwo in Things Fall Apart remains among his most memorable performances, while his subsequent roles helped establish him as a defining presence in Nollywood

title: “We’ve lost a titan, legend, an icon,” Gov Mbah mourns Pete Edochie
description:

Mbah further described it as a personal loss to Enugu State, recalling that although the reno
content:
Governor of Enugu State, Dr. Peter Mbah, has expressed deep grief over the passing on of one of Nollywood’s greatest, Chief Pete Edochie, describing it as the departure of a giant, icon, and patriot.

Mbah further described it as a personal loss to Enugu State, recalling that although the renown thespian hailed from Nteje in Anambra State, he had unequivocally acknowledged his life-long ties with Enugu State, which he had often described as his birth place, his “first port of call,” and a home away from home.

The Governor, in his personal tribute to Edochie in the early hours of Wednesday, following the announcement of the actor’s demise, aged 79, by his son, Leo Pete Edochie, further explained that the deceased was a great ambassador of Enugu State and fan of his administration.

“I am deeply saddened by the passing of Chief Pete Edochie, one of Nigeria’s most iconic actors and titans, and one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood and Africa’s creative industry across the world.

“The pain of this loss is further deepened by its timing. It comes at a particularly poignant moment when Enugu, a city whose history and identity are deeply intertwined with the arts, is hosting the National Festival of Arts and Culture (NAFEST).

“At a time when we are celebrating the richness of our cultural heritage and the creative talents that give it expression, we are confronted with the loss of one of its most distinguished ambassadors. It is a sobering reminder that while we celebrate the enduring power of our arts and culture, we must also mourn those who gave them life and brought them global recognition.

“Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor; he was an institution. With his commanding screen presence, unmistakable voice, remarkable mastery of dialogue and profound understanding of his craft, he helped shape the identity of Nigerian cinema and took the stories, values and cultural expressions of our people to audiences across the world.

As an illustrious son of the South East, and dating back to his role as a tragic protagonist in the dramatization of Chinua Achebe’s 1958 novel, ‘Things Fall Apart,’ Edochie eloquently interpreted the society to the world. He wore his Igbo identity with pride, bringing its language, wisdom, proverbs and rich cultural heritage to life in ways that resonated far beyond our shores.

“His performances transcended entertainment, preserving aspects of our cultural heritage and inspiring generations of actors and storytellers.

“His was a career defined not merely by longevity but by excellence, distinction and enduring influence and uncommon social grace.

“Even as the curtain falls on this remarkable life, his legacy as a fine broadcaster, thespian, cultural ambassador, and super star will continue to live on in the countless lives he touched and the generations of performers he inspired.

“Although this is a personal loss to us as Ndi Enugu, my heart, nevertheless, particularly goes out to his immediate household. On behalf of the Government and people of Enugu State, I extend my heartfelt condolences to his family, the Nollywood community, the Government and people of Anambra State, and all Nigerians and his global fans, who mourn this monumental loss.

May God grant his family the strength to bear this irreparable loss and grant his gentle soul eternal rest.

Adieu, Chief Pete Edochie, MON. Adieu Ononenyi, Ebubedike, Gaga n’ ogwu, Ogadagidi, Nwoke ka Ibe Ya, Okara Mmadu Okara Mmuo, a legend, fine gentleman, veteran broadcaster and actor.

“Your voice may have gone silent, but your legacy will speak for generations,” the governor mourned.

content:
By Henry Umoru

ABUJA – THE Nigeria Governors’ Forum, the umbrella body of the 36 state governors has denied having transactions with regard to the N135.5 billion paid to the forum as stakeholder in the Paris Club refunds dispute.

Read Also: Paris Club Refunds: Court freezes N135.5bn linked to Governors’ Forum

The NGF said it did not engage any party thereto, nor held any such monies in its custody at any time.

The governors made the clarification in a statement signed very late yesterday night by Director Media and Strategic Communications NGF, Yunusa Tanko Abdullahi. It was in reaction to reports on the Federal Capital Territory Court interim order freezing N135.5 billion linked to Governors’ Forum and restraining 29 banks.

The Forum said: “The Nigeria Governors’ Forum (NGF) is aware of recent media reports regarding the November 19, 2026 interim order, obtained exparte, issued by the Federal High Court of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Abuja in the Paris Club refund suit filed by Dr. Ted Iseghohi-Edwards from events that happened in 2016.

“Please note that this issue emanated from allegations of transactions between the plaintiff and the Association of Local Government of Nigeria, ALGON. The Nigeria Governors Forum has no hand in that transaction and did not engage any party thereto, nor held any such monies in its custody at any time.

“Meanwhile, the NGF’s legal team is currently reviewing the court processes and will respond accordingly. The Forum reiterates its unwavering commitment to the rule of law, transparency and accountability.”

Abuja High Court order

Justice O. C. Agbaza granted the interim Mareva injunction following an ex-parte application brought by Dr. Ted Iseghohi-Edwards.

The order restrained the Incorporated Trustees of the NGF from withdrawing, transferring, dissipating or otherwise dealing with the funds.

The order also restrained 29 commercial banks from releasing, transferring, converting or otherwise dealing with funds belonging to the NGF within their custody.

The judge further directed the banks to disclose, within 48 hours of service, whether the NGF maintains accounts containing the disputed funds.

The banks are required to identify such accounts, their currencies, available balances and amounts preserved under the court’s order.

The amount represents 100 million dollar, equivalent to the N135.55 billion, calculated at the exchange rate of N1,355.80 to the dollar.

Justice Agbaza made the orders on November 19, following the ex parte application and submissions by the claimant’s Counsel, Emonye Adekwu, SAN, alongside Damilola Odesola, from Ade Okeaya-Inneh & Co. Law Firm.

According to the report, Iseghohi-Edwards, who carries on business as Edwards and Partners Law Firm, had sought the recovery of the money pursuant to an indemnity issued by the NGF.

The claimant’s case is that the money belongs to him under an indemnity dated December 20, 2018, issued by the NGF.

The indemnity reportedly arose from an arrangement under which the Federal Government paid 100 million dollar to the NGF as stakeholder.

The money was to be held pending the determination of the Federal Government’s liability to Iseghohi-Edwards over legal and consultancy fees, just it arose from services allegedly rendered in connection with the London and Paris Club loan transaction.

Iseghohi-Edwards claimed he was retained by the Incorporated Trustees of the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria (ALGON) to represent the 774 local government councils in the London and Paris Clubs refunds matters.

The first respondent in the suit is the Incorporated Trustees of the Nigerian Governors’ Forum. The 29 banks are joined as co- respondents.

title: Pete Edochie, Olu Jacobs, Sam Loco: Remembering Nollywood’s fallen legends
description:
The death of veteran actor Pete Edochie has added another painful chapter to the history of Nollywood’s older generation, whose performances helped shape Nigeria’s film and television industry over several decades.
Edochie, who died on Wednesday at the age of 79 after a prolonged battle with prostat
content:
The death of veteran actor Pete Edochie has added another painful chapter to the history of Nollywood’s older generation, whose performances helped shape Nigeria’s film and television industry over several decades.

Edochie, who died on Wednesday at the age of 79 after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer, was among the actors whose commanding screen presence, distinctive delivery and memorable characters made them household names across the country.

His death comes barely two months after the demise of another veteran actor, Olu Jacobs, who died at the age of 84 on September 16, 2026. Both actors were widely recognised for their contributions to Nigerian theatre, television and film.

From traditional rulers and wealthy patriarchs to comic characters and village elders, their performances became familiar features of Nigerian home videos and television productions.

Pete Edochie

Edochie was one of Nollywood’s most recognisable faces, particularly for his portrayal of traditional rulers, wealthy men and authoritative family heads.

He gained widespread recognition for playing Okonkwo in the Nigerian Television Authority’s adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s classic novel, Things Fall Apart. His performance in the production established him as one of Nigeria’s leading actors.

Over the years, his deep voice, expressive delivery and use of proverbs became defining features of his performances.

His contributions to Nigerian entertainment also earned him the national honour of Member of the Order of the Niger.

Olu Jacobs

Jacobs was another towering figure whose career spanned theatre, television, international cinema and Nollywood.

Born on July 11, 1942, in Kano, the actor developed an interest in performing arts at a young age before travelling to the United Kingdom to study at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London.

He subsequently worked with repertory theatres in Britain and appeared in several television productions, including The Goodies, Till Death Us Do Part and The Professionals.

His international film credits also included The Dogs of War, Baby: Secret of the Lost Legend and Pirates. After returning to Nigeria, he became a prominent figure in the country’s growing film industry.

In Nollywood, Jacobs became particularly known for playing traditional rulers, wealthy patriarchs and influential men.

His commanding performances and theatrical training made him one of the industry’s most respected actors.

He won the Africa Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role in 2007 and received the Industry Merit Award at the 2013 Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards.

He was also conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic in 2011.

Jacobs was married to fellow veteran actress Joke Silva. Together, they founded the Lufodo Group, with interests in film production, distribution and performing arts education.

Sam Loco Efe

Unlike Edochie and Jacobs, Sam Loco Efe was particularly celebrated for his comic performances and ability to bring humour to Nigerian films.

The actor, who died in 2011, was one of the most recognisable comic actors of his generation.

His performances, often characterised by expressive facial gestures, distinctive delivery and comic timing, made him a favourite among audiences.

In a 2018 interview with PUNCH, his son, Omoruyi, described him as a playful but strict father who made the home lively.

He also recalled how his father combined his acting career with family life despite spending much of his time on film locations.

Dad and Osuofia were a dangerous combination in any movie — Sam Loco-Efe’s son

Fabian Adibe

Adibe was another veteran actor whose contribution to Nigerian television and film spanned several decades.

He was particularly remembered for his role as Ogbuefi Uzowulu in the television adaptation of Things Fall Apart, where he acted alongside Edochie, who played Okonkwo.

In a 2022 interview with PUNCH, Adibe recalled that the audition process for the production lasted almost a year.

He also spoke about his childhood, acting career and experiences in the Nigerian movie industry.

Adibe said he featured in the 1985 production and also worked as its art director.

He later featured in other productions, including Living in Bondage. He died on August 20, 2025, at the age of 81.

Justus Esiri, Enebeli Elebuwa and Dejumo Lewis

The television series The Village Headmaster also produced some of the most recognisable faces in Nigerian entertainment, including Justus Esiri, Enebeli Elebuwa and Dejumo Lewis.

Esiri became widely known for playing the headmaster in the popular television drama, which began airing in 1968 and ran until 1988.

Elebuwa was remembered for his role as a police officer, while Lewis played Kabiyesi.

The series was among Nigeria’s influential television productions and featured actors whose work became part of the country’s entertainment history.

In a retrospective on the programme, a column by PUNCH noted that several of its notable cast members, including Esiri and Elebuwa, had died, while Lewis remained one of the surviving figures associated with the production then.

A generation that shaped Nollywood

Beyond their individual achievements, the contributions of these actors helped create the foundation upon which contemporary Nollywood has continued to grow.

Their performances introduced audiences to memorable characters and storytelling styles that remain influential in Nigerian entertainment.

The Village Headmaster, for instance, connected generations of television viewers to a cast of performers whose work became part of the country’s entertainment history. Several of its notable actors have since died.

Similarly, Edochie, Adibe and Jacobs represented a generation of actors whose careers connected traditional theatre and television with the development of modern Nigerian cinema.

Their performances in productions that became household favourites helped establish Nigerian actors and stories before the expansion of the home-video industry.

While the industry has evolved with new production techniques, streaming platforms and younger performers, the works of the older generation remain an important part of its history.

For many Nigerians, their films and television appearances provided some of the most memorable entertainment experiences of their childhood and helped establish Nigerian productions as a major part of popular culture.

With Edochie’s death, Nollywood has lost another prominent figure from a generation whose influence continues to be felt in the industry.

The post Pete Edochie, Olu Jacobs, Sam Loco: Remembering Nollywood’s fallen legends appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

His death was announced on Wednesday by his son, Chief Leo Pete Edochie, in a statement shared on Instagram on behalf of the family.

According to the announcement, the actor died at 12:30 am on November 25, 2026, in Enugu, Nigeria.

The family expressed its grief over his death, describing him as a beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman.

“An Iroko Has Fallen. With profound sadness and hearts bowed in total submission to the will of Almighty God, we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman, Chief Dr Pete Edochie, MON (Ononenyi),” the statement read.

The family said the “retired broadcaster and veteran actor” died after “battling prostate cancer” for an extended period.

Announcing the death, the family also appealed for prayers and strength as they come to terms with the loss.

“As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss,” the statement added.

The family said arrangements for his funeral would be communicated in due course.

Edochie hailed from Akamnato, Ifite Nteje, Anambra State. He is survived by his wife, Josephine Edochie, his children, siblings and other relatives.

He began his professional career in broadcasting in 1967 with the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation, where he worked for several years and rose to senior management positions, including Director of Programmes and Deputy Managing Director.

His transition into acting brought him national prominence in the 1980s when he portrayed Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s novel, Things Fall Apart.

The performance established him as a formidable screen presence and opened the door to a long career in Nigerian cinema.

Over the years, he became particularly associated with roles as traditional rulers, community leaders and family patriarchs, with his deep voice, commanding delivery and frequent use of proverbs becoming defining features of his performances.

His film credits include Igodo, Rituals and Lionheart, the 2018 film directed by Genevieve Nnaji.

In recognition of his contributions to the entertainment industry, he received the national honour of Member of the Order of the Niger (MON) in 2003. He also received the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards Industry Merit Award and other lifetime achievement honours.

title: Kwara unveils five-year strategy to tackle malnutrition
description:
The Kwara State Government has unveiled a five-year nutrition strategy aimed at tackling the social, cultural and behavioural factors contributing to malnutrition, particularly among women and children.
The development was contained in a statement issued on Tuesday by the Assistant Press Secretary,
content:
The Kwara State Government has unveiled a five-year nutrition strategy aimed at tackling the social, cultural and behavioural factors contributing to malnutrition, particularly among women and children.

The development was contained in a statement issued on Tuesday by the Assistant Press Secretary, Ministry of Health, Funke Olutemilehin, following the unveiling of the strategy by the Commissioner for Health, Amina El-Imam.

The State Social and Behavioural Change Strategy for Nutrition Across the Life Cycle was unveiled at a dissemination meeting held at the ministry’s headquarters on Monday, with representatives of the United Nations Children’s Fund, government ministries, departments and agencies, religious organisations and civil society groups in attendance.

Speaking at the meeting, El-Imam said addressing malnutrition required interventions beyond the provision of healthcare services and nutrition commodities.

“Poor nutritional knowledge, harmful traditional beliefs, inadequate dietary practices, gender norms, poor health-seeking behaviour and weak community engagement remain major contributors to malnutrition,” the commissioner said.

El-Imam explained that the ministry, with financial and technical support from UNICEF, had successfully domesticated, costed and validated the National Social and Behavioural Change Strategy for Nutrition Across the Life Cycle.

“The framework will promote positive nutrition practices through strategic communication, advocacy, community mobilisation, social norm transformation and stronger intersectoral collaboration,” she added.

Highlighting the state’s progress, the commissioner disclosed that findings from the Mini Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey 2025/26 showed that stunting prevalence in Kwara had declined from 40.8 per cent to 35.5 per cent.

“Stunting prevalence has reduced from 40.8 per cent to 35.5 per cent, wasting from 6.1 per cent to 3.5 per cent and underweight from 24.5 per cent to 14.8 per cent,” she said.

El-Imam attributed the improvements to sustained government commitment and interventions, including Accelerating Nutrition Results in Nigeria 1.0, nutrition promotion campaigns, dietary diversification and micronutrient supplementation.

She also listed the distribution of oral rehydration salts and zinc at primary healthcare facilities and community levels among the interventions contributing to the progress recorded.

The commissioner called on ministries, departments and agencies, development partners, traditional and religious institutions, the media and community structures to support the transition to ANRiN 2.0.

She urged stakeholders to ensure effective implementation of the strategy, stressing the importance of collective action in addressing the factors responsible for malnutrition.

In his remarks, the Acting Chairman of the State Committee on Food and Nutrition, Mohammed Ibrahim, representing the Ministry of Planning and Economic Development, reaffirmed the state government’s commitment to improving nutrition outcomes.

Ibrahim disclosed that the government had contributed N100m to the Child Nutrition Fund, which UNICEF leveraged at a one-to-one ratio to procure 3,964 cartons of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food.

He also highlighted advocacy for six-month paid maternity leave and sustained investments in primary healthcare as part of the state’s efforts to improve maternal and child nutrition.

The acting chairman said, “We need adequate budgetary provisions and stronger multisectoral collaboration to further accelerate improvements in the nutrition indices of the state.”

Earlier, the Nutrition Focal Person in the Ministry of Health, Dr Habib Abayomi Lawal, commended members of the multisectoral committee for their contributions towards improving nutrition outcomes.

Lawal urged stakeholders to sustain their collaboration and demonstrate continued commitment to the successful implementation of the strategy.

title: Kwankwasiyya supporters carry sticks but harm no one – Obi
description:
Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, Peter Obi has defended supporters of his running mate, Rabiu Kwankwaso, over allegations that they carry sticks to political campaigns, saying the items have not been used to harm anyone.
Obi said members of the Kwankwasiyya movement were kn
content:
Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, Peter Obi has defended supporters of his running mate, Rabiu Kwankwaso, over allegations that they carry sticks to political campaigns, saying the items have not been used to harm anyone.

Obi said members of the Kwankwasiyya movement were known for carrying such items during political gatherings but insisted that he had not witnessed anyone being attacked with them.

He spoke in an interview with Channels Television on Tuesday evening in Jalingo, Taraba State, after an Obi-Kwankwaso town hall meeting held at The Crest Hall.

Addressing concerns over the presence of weapons at political gatherings, Obi said the public had misunderstood calls against electoral malpractice as opposition to political campaigns.

“They said we said ‘rig and die.’
We didn’t say ‘campaign and die.’ What we, people said is that they don’t want rigging this time. They didn’t say they don’t want campaign this time. If anything, they want campaign this time,” he said.

Obi explained that the Kwankwasiyya movement, led by Kwankwaso, had a longstanding tradition of supporters appearing at political gatherings with sticks and similar items.

He said, “Everybody who had followed the Kwankwansiyah group in Kano know that they come out with such sticks and everything, but they’ve never used it to harm anybody.

title: AEDC seeks partnership with developers to boost electricity supply
description:
Residential buildings and real estate developments account for more than 80 per cent of electricity infrastructure utilisation by the Abuja Electricity Distribution Company, highlighting the growing pressure housing developments are placing on power networks across its franchise areas.
The company s
content:
Residential buildings and real estate developments account for more than 80 per cent of electricity infrastructure utilisation by the Abuja Electricity Distribution Company, highlighting the growing pressure housing developments are placing on power networks across its franchise areas.

The company said nearly 85 per cent of its electricity customers in the Federal Capital Territory were residential consumers, underscoring the need for closer collaboration with property developers to ensure electricity infrastructure keeps pace with the expansion of estates and new housing communities.

The Chief Operating Officer of AEDC, Blessing Ogbe, disclosed this on Tuesday at the company’s Real Estate Developers’ Stakeholder Forum in Abuja, where electricity distribution and property industry stakeholders discussed ways to improve power supply to residential developments.

Ogbe said the high concentration of residential buildings on the company’s network made real estate developers critical partners in electricity infrastructure planning, particularly as new estates continued to emerge across Abuja and neighbouring states.

“Today, I can clearly state that over 80 per cent of our infrastructure are currently utilised by residential buildings. Most of them are real estates. We know the value of a structure when it comes to residents, you need it,” he said.

The forum, themed ‘Powering Sustainable Real Estate Development: Building Better Communities Through Reliable Electricity’, focused on integrating electricity infrastructure into property development from the planning and design stages rather than waiting until construction had been completed.

AEDC said it wanted developers to engage with the distribution company before embarking on projects so that electricity demand, network capacity, transformer requirements and other infrastructure needs could be assessed in advance.

The company warned that failure to coordinate estate development with electricity distribution planning could result in delayed connections, inadequate transformer capacity, additional construction costs and disagreements between developers and electricity providers.

Ogbe said reliable electricity was central to the commercial value of properties, noting that adequate power supply could improve residents’ experience, strengthen property values and make estates more attractive to buyers and tenants.

He said, “Reliability is real estate value. How we understand that challenges are real, but they are manageable.”

According to him, AEDC was seeking partnerships that would allow it to understand developers’ investment plans and anticipate electricity demand in emerging residential corridors.

He urged property developers to register their estates with the company and provide information about projects expected to be developed over the next 12 months to enable the distributor to plan its network expansion.

“If we can collaborate, we will be able to solve these problems from the very best. And how do we do this? We are expecting that you will register your estate with us so we can plan for it and plan the estate in the future. Let us know within the next 12 months where we are heading towards so we will be able to plan around you,” Ogbe said.

He added that the company was also interested in working with developers on joint infrastructure development, embedded electricity generation, renewable energy partnerships, smart metering and digital energy management.

AEDC operates electricity distribution networks across the FCT, Nasarawa, Niger and Kogi states, serving residential, commercial and industrial customers.

The company said it had more than 1.3 million customers across the four states, including about one million in the FCT. Its figures showed that more than 1.13 million customers were metered, compared with approximately 650,000 in 2023.

The distributor also reported audited revenue of N699.48bn in 2025 and 4,749 gigawatt-hours of energy traded during the year.

title: Greenwich Bank opens Warri, Uyo branches, targets five more cities
description:
By Peter Egwuatu







Greenwich Bank Limited has opened branches in Warri, Delta State, and Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, as it targets five additional cities in its nationwide expansion drive.







The new outlets bring its physical network to seven, following the opening of five branches in Lagos, Ond
content:
By Peter Egwuatu

Greenwich Bank Limited has opened branches in Warri, Delta State, and Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, as it targets five additional cities in its nationwide expansion drive.

The new outlets bring its physical network to seven, following the opening of five branches in Lagos, Ondo and Ekiti states in October. The Bank plans to extend its operations to Asaba, Port Harcourt, Abuja, Benin and Ibadan in the coming months. Speaking at the commissioning of the Warri branch, Group Chairman of Greenwich Holdings, Kayode Falowo, described the Niger Delta as a strategic market, citing its economic importance and entrepreneurial potential, particularly in oil and gas, maritime services and logistics.

He said: “Warri’s economic prospects extend beyond its natural resources to the entrepreneurs, traders, contractors, service providers and other businesses driving commercial activities in the region.”

At the Uyo branch commissioning, Chairman of Greenwich Bank, Segun Oloketuyi, said the commercial banking licence would enable the institution to extend its 32 years of financial services experience to farmers, traders, civil servants, students and entrepreneurs.

He identified credit facilities, agricultural and SME financing, trade and treasury services, salary solutions and digital banking as key offerings.

Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, represented by Commissioner for Finance, Fidelis Telije, urged residents, particularly small businesses, young entrepreneurs and women-owned enterprises, to take advantage of the Bank’s services.

Similarly, Akwa Ibom State Governor, Umo Eno, represented by Commissioner for Finance, Emem Almond Bob, said the Uyo branch would improve access to banking services and credit, support business growth and potentially boost the state’s internally generated revenue.

Managing Director of Greenwich Bank, Benson Ogundeji, said the branches would deepen customer engagement and bring financial solutions closer to businesses and individuals.

He identified oil and gas, maritime services, agriculture, manufacturing, trade, logistics and SMEs as priority sectors, adding that the Bank would combine physical branches with technology-driven solutions to promote enterprise growth and financial inclusion.

Greenwich Holdings has over three decades of financial services experience, with interests in commercial banking, capital markets, asset management and securities.

title: Political Violence: Dying for nothing as a Nigerian politician?
description:
By Jide Ajani



From the First Republic to the Fourth, politicians have been murdered, opposition figures silenced and political supporters killed. Yet, beyond the initial outrage, Nigeria has perfected the art of forgetting its dead. What, then, is the value of dying for a political cause in a cou
content:
By Jide Ajani

From the First Republic to the Fourth, politicians have been murdered, opposition figures silenced and political supporters killed. Yet, beyond the initial outrage, Nigeria has perfected the art of forgetting its dead. What, then, is the value of dying for a political cause in a country that cannot even preserve the memory of its political martyrs? The alleged assassination attempt on the former Deputy Senate President, Ovie Omo-Agege, two days ago, in Uduere community of Ughelli North LGA of Delta State, brings this odd reality into focus once again. Worse, many innocent, ordinary Nigerians have lost their lives while supporting or opposing politicians, only becoming part of an unidentified statistical figure.

There is something inescapably tragic about dying while politicking in Nigeria. You could spend a lifetime building a political movement, challenging an unjust system, defending an electoral mandate, or fighting for an idea about your country’s future – or just being loud for nothing like a former, two-time state governor from the South West, or a former Rep and Senator from the North Central. You could become a household name, command enormous political influence and acquire a place in the nation’s history. Then, one morning, gunmen arrive, bullets are fired, and your life is terminated.

There will be outrage. Condemnations will pour in. Politicians will issue statements, newspapers will publish editorials (like this), civil society organisations will demand justice, and the police will announce investigations.

And then, Nigeria happens, and the people move on.

The murder will become another entry in the country’s expanding archive of unresolved political crimes. The victim’s name will gradually disappear from public conversations, except when anniversary commemorations provide an opportunity for political speeches. Even the circumstances of the death may eventually become blurred by competing narratives, political expediency and the convenient amnesia of a nation.

Is it, therefore, worth dying for Nigeria’s politics?

The question intends to interrogate a society that celebrates political martyrs without demonstrating a corresponding commitment to preserving their legacies or establishing the truth about their deaths.

On Monday, November 23, 2026, four persons were killed during an alleged assassination attempt on the former Deputy Senate President, Ovie Omo-Agege, two days ago, in Uduere Community of Ughelli North LGA of Delta State. Over a dozen were said to have been injured. Mind you, in an outburst of emotive frustration about happenings inthe political sphere, the self-same Omo-Agege had used the phrase ‘ ig and die’. He was to later clarify that he was merely drawing attention to the need for credible elections.

A bloody inheritance

Political violence has accompanied Nigeria’s political evolution almost from independence.

The January 15, 1966 military coup was a defining bloodbath. Among the prominent political victims were Prime Minister Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Northern Premier Sir Ahmadu Bello, Western Premier Chief Samuel Ladoke Akintola and Federal Finance Minister Chief Festus Okotie-Eboh.

They were not anonymous casualties. They occupied the commanding heights of the First Republic and represented competing political interests and constituencies. Their assassination, alongside the killing of senior military officers, fundamentally altered Nigeria’s political trajectory.

The July 1966 counter-coup brought another round of killings, including Head of State Major-General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi and Western Region Governor Colonel Adekunle Fajuyi.

Although these were killings arising from military coups and counter-coups rather than conventional electoral assassinations, they established a dangerous precedent: political disagreements and struggles for power could be settled through the elimination of human beings.

On February 13, 1976, another military coup attempt claimed the life of Head of State General Murtala Mohammed. He was assassinated in Lagos by officers involved in the unsuccessful coup led by Lieutenant-Colonel Buka Suka Dimka.

The military era also saw attacks on prominent government opponents.

In October 1995, Chief Alfred Rewane, businessman, political financier and prominent supporter of the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), was murdered in his Ikeja residence. The killing occurred during General Sani Abacha’s military dictatorship. The circumstances generated widespread suspicions of political motivation, but no satisfactory public resolution followed.

The following year, on June 4, 1996, Kudirat Abiola was assassinated by unknown gunmen while travelling along the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway. She had become a prominent campaigner for the validation of her husband Moshood Abiola’s June 12, 1993 presidential mandate.

Her murder was widely perceived as an attempt to silence the pro-democracy movement. Subsequent proceedings produced a conviction of Major Hamza al-Mustapha and another accused person, but the Court of Appeal overturned the convictions. The circumstances and ultimate accountability for her killing have remained contested.

There were other disturbing incidents. Alex Ibru, publisher of The Guardian and a former minister, survived an assassination attempt in February 1996 after being shot in Lagos. Gani Fawehinmi, the human rights lawyer, was also the subject of a reported attack on the prison facility where he was detained, although he was not there at the time.

The Fourth Republic: democracy and its dead

The return to civilian government in 1999 raised expectations that constitutional politics would make political violence less attractive. Those expectations were soon tested.

On December 19, 2001, Osun State legislator Odunayo Olagbaju was stabbed to death in Ile-Ife. Four days later, on December 23, Chief Bola Ige, the serving Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, was shot dead in his Bodija residence in Ibadan.

Ige was a formidable politician, former governor of Oyo State, intellectual and prominent member of the Alliance for Democracy. His murder, against the background of the political crisis involving the governor and deputy governor of Osun State, sent shockwaves through the country.

Several suspects were arrested and prosecuted, but the accused were discharged and acquitted in June 2004. The actual perpetrators have not been established through a successful prosecution.

What happened to the national outrage that followed the murder of a sitting Attorney-General?

On March 5, 2003, Harry Marshall, a senior opposition politician and national vice-chairman of the All Nigeria Peoples Party (ANPP), was murdered in his Abuja residence. Armed men reportedly forced their way into his home at about 3 a.m., tied up his security guard, and shot him in his bedroom. His killing occurred days before the commencement of the party’s presidential campaign.

The police initially investigated extensively, but the motive was never conclusively established. Some suspected political connections; the authorities also considered armed robbery.

In February 2004, Chief Aminasoari Dikibo, a prominent PDP national vice-chairman, was murdered while travelling in Delta State. His death generated allegations of political conspiracy, but no definitive public resolution emerged.

Then came July 27, 2006. Engineer Funsho Williams, a prominent Lagos politician and governorship aspirant, was found murdered in his Ikoyi residence. His hands were reportedly tied, and the post-mortem evidence presented during the subsequent proceedings indicated death by strangulation.

Several people were prosecuted. In 2014, however, a Lagos High Court discharged and acquitted the defendants after finding that the prosecution had failed to establish a sufficient connection between them and the murder.

Another aspirant, Dr Ayo Daramola, was murdered at his home in Ekiti State in August 2006.

The catalogue does not end there. Ogbonnaya Uche was killed in Owerri in 2003; Barnabas and Abigail Igwe, a lawyer and his wife, were murdered in Onitsha in September 2002; and Dipo Dina, an Ogun State governorship candidate in the 2007 election, was shot dead in January 2010.

These are unfinished investigations, abandoned questions and families left without satisfactory answers.

Other election-related attacks have included the killing of candidates, party officials and campaign workers. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have documented the wider pattern of electoral violence, including attacks that never attracted the national attention accorded to the deaths of prominent politicians.

The national habit of forgetting

What is perhaps more disturbing than the killings is the country’s relationship with the memory of those killed.

Nigeria has become remarkably efficient at converting tragedy into political folklore and then consigning the folklore to oblivion.

The murder of Bola Ige should have become an enduring national lesson about the vulnerability of public institutions. Instead, the country largely returned to its political routines.

Funsho Williams should have remained a reference point in conversations about the safety of political aspirants. Harry Marshall should have become a symbol of the dangers confronting opposition politics. Alfred Rewane and Kudirat Abiola should occupy permanent places in the country’s democratic memory.

Yet, their names are invoked intermittently, often by politicians seeking temporary moral authority.

The philosopher George Santayana famously warned: “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.”

The warning is particularly relevant to Nigeria. Forgetting is not necessarily an innocent failure of memory. When a society fails to demand answers, preserve records and sustain public attention, it creates the conditions in which impunity can flourish.

Cicero’s observation that “the life of the dead is placed in the memory of the living” offers another uncomfortable reflection. What kind of afterlife does a nation confer on those whose sacrifices it cannot remember?

Others have learned to remember

Nigeria is not the only country with unresolved political assassinations.

Sweden has never conclusively established who murdered Prime Minister Olof Palme, who was shot dead on a Stockholm street on February 28, 1986. Although investigators identified a likely suspect in 2020, he was dead and could not be prosecuted. Swedish prosecutors subsequently maintained that there was insufficient evidence to reopen the investigation.

Pakistan continues to wrestle with the circumstances surrounding the December 27, 2007 assassination of former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto. A United Nations Commission of Inquiry examined the circumstances of her death but did not identify the individuals ultimately responsible for the assassination.

Lebanon’s former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri was killed in a massive bomb explosion in Beirut on February 14, 2005, alongside other victims. The subsequent United Nations-backed investigation and Special Tribunal produced important findings and convictions, although questions about the full chain of responsibility and political accountability have persisted.

The difference is not that these countries have solved every political murder. It is that their investigations, public inquiries, official records and continuing debates demonstrate that the death of a political leader need not become a forgotten footnote.

There are also examples of murdered leaders whose deaths did not extinguish their causes. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 4, 1968. He was 39 years old. He had spent his life fighting racial discrimination through non-violent resistance and civil rights activism.

His death was a devastating blow, but it did not terminate the movement. His words, philosophy and political struggle became enduring reference points in American public life. His legacy was institutionalised through memorials, national commemorations and continuing civil rights advocacy.

The United States did not simply mourn King and move on. It preserved his memory as part of its national identity.

King’s legacy illustrates something important: a political assassination can destroy a human life, but it need not destroy the cause that gave the life meaning.

And what of MKO Abiola?

Perhaps the most troubling example of Nigeria’s complicated relationship with political memory is Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola.

He died in detention on July 7, 1998, while the struggle to reclaim his mandate from the annulled June 12, 1993 presidential election remained unresolved.

Abiola’s death did not end the controversy surrounding his mandate. Indeed, more than two decades after his death, the political interpretation of June 12, his democratic credentials and his place in history continue to be contested and appropriated by different political interests.

The declaration of June 12 as Democracy Day was an important official recognition. But recognition must mean more than appropriating a dead man’s political capital. His historical significance should be examined honestly, including the political compromises, convictions and sacrifices that defined his life.

There is something deeply ironic about a country that celebrates a man for the mandate he fought to reclaim but cannot protect the historical integrity of his struggle from partisan manipulation.

Is it worth dying for?

This brings us back to the original question: Is it worth allowing yourself to be killed for Nigerian politics?

There is no universal answer. People have a right to stand for their convictions, defend democracy and challenge injustice. A society without courageous people willing to confront abuse of power would be a society without meaningful political progress.

But courage must not be confused with recklessness, and martyrdom must not become an excuse for national irresponsibility.

Albert Camus, in The Myth of Sisyphus, wrote: “The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart.”

Perhaps the meaning of political life lies not in the eventual reward of public recognition but in the principles one defends and the institutions one helps to build.

Yet, a nation also has obligations to its dead. It must investigate their murders, prosecute offenders where evidence permits, preserve historical records and resist the temptation to turn their sacrifices into disposable political slogans.

A politician’s life should not be measured exclusively by the office he occupied, the money he accumulated or the number of followers who attended his funeral. It should also be measured by the ideas he advanced, the institutions he strengthened and the generations he inspired.

The tragedy of Nigeria is not simply that Bola Ige, Harry Marshall, Funsho Williams, Kudirat Abiola, Alfred Rewane and so many others died violently. It is that we have not demonstrated sufficient determination to establish the truth about their deaths and protect the historical meaning of their lives.

A country that forgets its murdered leaders diminishes the value of public service and discourages the next generation from believing that political conviction is worth defending.

Perhaps the most painful question is not whether these men and women died for nothing; it is whether Nigeria, by its persistent refusal to remember, investigate and learn, has ensured that they did.

title: FirstBank redefines personal lending experience with mApply, mServe
description:
FirstBank has launched mApply and mServe, two digital solutions that are transforming how customers access and manage Personal Loan Against Salary (PLAS) facilities.







The launch marks a significant milestone in FirstBank’s personal lending journey as, for the first time in the Bank’s history,
content:
FirstBank has launched mApply and mServe, two digital solutions that are transforming how customers access and manage Personal Loan Against Salary (PLAS) facilities.

The launch marks a significant milestone in FirstBank’s personal lending journey as, for the first time in the Bank’s history, eligible customers can initiate a personal loan application digitally without having to visit a branch to begin the process.

Previously, accessing a PLAS facility required customers to engage the Bank through the branch or their Relationship Manager. With mApply, FirstBank has digitised the application journey, giving eligible customers the convenience of applying through the Bank’s digital channels from wherever they are.

Through mApply, customers can initiate their PLAS application, provide the required document, select their employer and preferred branch for processing, and submit their request digitally. The solution significantly reduces the reliance on physical documentation and branch visits at the application stage, creating a simpler and more convenient route to accessing personal credit.

PLAS is available to eligible salary account holders domiciled with FirstBank, as well as employees of eligible organisations seeking to move their salary accounts to the Bank. Customers can access up to N150 million, with repayment tenors of up to 72 months, subject to applicable terms and conditions.

FirstBank is also extending the digital experience beyond loan application through mServe, its self-service solution for customers with existing PLAS facilities. With mServe, customers can view their loan details and outstanding balances, monitor their facilities and update relevant information, providing greater visibility and control over their loans without having to rely solely on branch-based servicing.

Together, mApply and mServe create a more connected digital experience across the PLAS journey. While mApply simplifies how customers initiate and submit new loan requests, mServe provides existing borrowers with a convenient way to manage and monitor their facilities. Both solutions are accessible through FirstMobile and Lit App, bringing personal lending into the same digital environment customers already use for their everyday banking needs.

title: NRS seeks simpler tax rules for creative sector
description:
By Godwin Oritse







The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) has called for simpler, clearer and business-friendly tax rules to unlock investment opportunities in Nigeria’s creative economy, stressing the need for a tax system that supports innovation, enterprise growth and wealth creation.



The Serv
content:
By Godwin Oritse

The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) has called for simpler, clearer and business-friendly tax rules to unlock investment opportunities in Nigeria’s creative economy, stressing the need for a tax system that supports innovation, enterprise growth and wealth creation.

The Service noted that the emergence of digital business models, intellectual property-driven enterprises and cross-border transactions required regulations that creators, entrepreneurs and investors could easily understand and navigate.

Speaking at the just concluded high-level dialogue on taxation and investment in the creative economy during the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) event in Lagos, Executive Chairman of the NRS, Dr. Zacch Adedeji, described the creative economy as one of Nigeria’s most promising economic assets, noting that it had evolved beyond entertainment into a major source of employment, foreign exchange earnings, investment and economic opportunities.

Adedeji who was represented by the Executive Director, People, Stakeholders and Communication, Mr. Obinna Ihedioha, also said that digital platforms had transformed how creative value was produced and commercialised, with entrepreneurs building businesses around copyrights, designs, brands and digital products.

He reiterated that tax administration must evolve to accommodate these developments without discouraging innovation or business expansion.

“The government needs sustainable revenue to invest in education, security, technology and infrastructure. But how we tax matters as much as what we collect. It shapes whether businesses start, whether investors come, and whether enterprises grow or stay small,” he said.

Adedeji added that the new tax laws offered an opportunity to establish a more efficient system through clearer regulations, reduced compliance burdens for small businesses and improved taxpayer support. He identified clarity, understanding and value as essential to effective taxation, stressing that formalisation should provide creative businesses with tangible benefits, including access to finance, contracts, investment, wider markets and legal protection.

The NRS, he said, participated in CANEX through a high-level dialogue, an Investment and Tax Advisory Hub for creators and investors, and the Creative Economy Tax and Investment Initiative (CETII), designed to sustain engagement beyond the event.

The Command’s spokesperson, Eno Ikoedem, disclosed this while parading 16
content:
By Ozioruva Aliu

BENIN CITY — THE Edo State Police Command said four members of the Edo State Security Corps, ESSC, have been arrested for allegedly leaking information to suspected cultists to enable them evade arrests.

The Command’s spokesperson, Eno Ikoedem, disclosed this while parading 16 suspects arrested across the state in connection with various criminal activities.

The suspects, Isaac Irú we, Ashem Gideon, Tony Okhiale and Venture Uzu were arrested at Evbhomore community, in Ovia North-East Local Government Area of the state.

They were accused of leaking information on police movements to cultists, enabling them to escape arrest.

According to the Command, operatives of the Anti-Cultism Unit acted on intelligence on cult initiation activities in Benin City and immediately swung into action.

“Upon getting there, we discovered that someone was giving out information on our movement to these cultists who escaped arrest.

“Further investigation revealed that these men are members of the Edo State Security Corps, and four of them have been arrested and they are in our custody.”

The command said investigation was still ongoing to ascertain their roles in the secret cult organisation.

content:
By Godwin Oritse

Imports of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), also known as petrol, through Lagos ports plunged by 52.23 per cent in November, while crude oil and bulk wheat ranked among the leading commodities imported through the ports in October and November.

According to the Shipping Position document obtained from the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), PMS imports fell to 73,895 metric tonnes in November from 328,231 metric tonnes recorded in October.

Crude oil imports through Lagos ports also dropped sharply, with 702,254 metric tonnes recorded in October, while no crude oil import was recorded in November.

Bulk wheat ranked among the major commodities imported through Lagos ports during the period, with a combined 461,190 metric tonnes recorded in September, October and November.

The breakdown showed that wheat imports rose to 252,348 metric tonnes in October and declined by 17.24 per cent to 208,842 metric tonnes in November.

Other commodities on the import chart included 402,126 metric tonnes of PMS, 209,000 metric tonnes of Automotive Gas Oil (AGO), or diesel, 212,700 metric tonnes of bulk sugar, 150,000 metric tonnes of aviation fuel and 114,263 metric tonnes of bulk salt.

Bulk sugar imports stood at 109,350 metric tonnes in October and 103,400 metric tonnes in November, while bulk salt imports rose from 33,000 metric tonnes to 81,263 metric tonnes over the same period.

The document also showed that 624 trucks, 157 transformers and three Rubber-Tyred Gantry (RTG) cranes were received through Lagos ports during the period under review.

description: FCMB Group Plc reported pretax profit of N272.8 billion for the nine months ended September 30, up 103% from N134.5 billion a year earlier, driven by improved interest margins and a lower cost-to-income ratio. Annualised return on average equity rose to 30.1% from 22.4% a year earlier, while annuali
content:
FCMB Group Plc reported pretax profit of N272.8 billion for the nine months ended September 30, up 103% from N134.5 billion a year earlier, driven by improved interest margins and a lower cost-to-income ratio. Annualised return on average equity rose to 30.1% from 22.4% a year earlier, while annualised return on average assets rose to 3.9% from 2.3%.

Gross earnings for the same nine-month period rose 21% from a year earlier to N1 trillion, while after-tax profit increased 85.7% to N232.9 billion from N125.5 billion. Annualised earnings per share rose to N4.59, up 15% from N3.99 for full-year 2025, despite the expanded share base post-recapitalisation.

The group’s unaudited results include the audited results of its Nigerian banking subsidiary – First City Monument Bank Limited.

Commenting, FCMB Group’s Chief Executive Officer, Mr. Ladi Balogun, said he expects fourth-quarter earnings to benefit from a seasonal increase in digital lending and payments and lower operating expenses after the group recognised the full 2026 Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria levy in the first nine months.

“With nine-month RoE at 30%, we expect full-year RoE to be materially above an earlier guidance of 25%, providing a strong foundation for further profitable growth and sustained shareholder value creation,” Balogun said.

FCMB Group’s interest income rose 23.4%, while interest expense fell 3% as low-cost deposits made up a larger share of customer deposits. Net interest income rose 52.3% to N534.2 billion from N350.8 billion a year earlier, and net interest margin rose to 12.3% from 10.1%. Operating expenses rose 12.5% to N268.9 billion from N239 billion a year earlier, while the cost-to-income ratio fell to 43.5% from 55.5%.

content:
By Shina Abubakar

Osogbo —The Osun State Police Command has said it arrested a 48-year-old man, Ogunniran Kayode over alleged murder of his son, Raphael, at Faaji, Odo-Otin Local Government Area of the state.

A statement by the command’s Public Relations Officer,  Abiodun Ojelabi, yesterday, stated that the police received intelligence on October 19, 2026, that the suspect tortured his 21-year-old son to death. Then he buried his body in a shallow grave.

Following the intel, the statement disclosed that the operatives of the command swung into action and arrested the suspect as he confessed to the killing of his son.

“During the interrogation, he stated that his son stole a sum of N75,000 and absconded with one android phone he bought for him on easy buy to an unknown place.

“And being a member of Iru-Ekun Security Network, he was able to get the son arrested through the help of his colleague.”

“The case was then transferred to Homicide Section for further investigation”, the statement added.

Meanwhile, operatives of the homicide unit visisted the crime scene and the shallow grave, where details and pictorial evidence of the torture were retrieved.

The state Police Commissioner, Ibrahim Zungura, therefore, warned individuals with criminal intent to desist from the act or face full wrath of the law.

content:
By Efe Onodjae & Jacintha Ezugwu

Access Bank has urged small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to embrace sustainable business practices to ensure their survival and growth beyond their first five years.

The Head of SME Banking Group at Access Bank Plc, Mrs Abiodun Olubitan, gave the advice at the three-day Access Bank SME Academy 2.0, organised in partnership with Deloitte to equip business owners with skills to improve their operations and sustainability.

The programme, which ended on Friday in Lagos, attracted about 100 SME owners physically, with others participating virtually. It targeted businesses that had operated for between two and five years.

Olubitan said SMEs were critical to economic development, noting that their survival and expansion were necessary for job creation and national growth.

She urged participants to apply the knowledge acquired, particularly in separating personal finances from business accounts and understanding the difference between turnover and profit.

According to her, the bank introduced the academy to support businesses at different stages of growth and help them overcome challenges that often threaten their survival. In her part, Team Lead, SME Banking Products at Access Bank and coordinator of the academy, Adesola Oyedipe, said the initiative was designed to address gaps in access to finance and capacity building among SMEs.

Oyedipe said the three-day programme provided participants with more extensive training than the bank’s usual short workshops and business clinics.

She explained that the partnership with Deloitte was aimed at giving business owners access to professional advisory services they might otherwise be unable to afford.

title: No missing funds in $2.04bn Duke Oil crude cargoes — NNPC
description:
By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja







The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) has dismissed reports alleging that $2.04 billion realised from crude oil cargoes lifted by Duke Oil Company Incorporated, now NNPC Trading S.A., was unaccounted for, insisting that all transactions were fully reco
content:
By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja

The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) has dismissed reports alleging that $2.04 billion realised from crude oil cargoes lifted by Duke Oil Company Incorporated, now NNPC Trading S.A., was unaccounted for, insisting that all transactions were fully reconciled.

The company said the $2.04 billion represented the gross value of 29 cargoes whose proceeds were set off against the cost of refined petroleum products supplied to Nigeria under the Direct Sale Direct Purchase (DSDP) programme.

In a statement by its Chief Corporate Communications Officer, Andy Odeh, NNPC said the absence of separate dollar receipts for some cargoes did not indicate missing funds.

“No separate receipt appears because the crude sale proceeds were set off against the product purchase price, as the contracts provide,” it stated.

Under the DSDP programme, participating traders lifted crude oil in exchange for refined petroleum products, including petrol, for the Nigerian market. NNPC explained that while crude was priced in dollars, products supplied were sold in naira, with transactions reconciled and captured in the audited financial statements of the relevant entities.

The company said all 59 cargoes referenced in the reports were accounted for, adding that 30 were paid for in dollars, while proceeds from 28 cargoes, valued at approximately $1.96 billion, were remitted in naira to the NNPC Group Treasury or NNPC Upstream Investment Management Services accounts.

The remaining cargo, a February 2023 Bonga tax-oil lifting valued at about $75.9 million, was paid into the then designated Federal Inland Revenue Service dollar account.

On Duke Oil’s ownership, NNPC said it was incorporated in 1989 as its wholly owned trading subsidiary, adding that the relationship was documented in its corporate history, audited financial statements and NEITI’s 2023 industry report.

It maintained that transactions between the company and its subsidiaries were disclosed as related-party transactions under International Financial Reporting Standards.

NNPC reaffirmed its commitment to transparency and accountability, but warned that it reserved the right to take legal action against publications it considered false or misleading.

The post No missing funds in $2.04bn Duke Oil crude cargoes — NNPC appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: CBN holds MPR at 23%, says external  reserves drop  temporary
description:
By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief







The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has retained its Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) at 23 per cent, dismissing concerns over a decline of over $300 million in external reserves as a temporary, seasonal movement.







Governor of the CBN, Mr. Olayemi Cardoso, discl
content:
By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has retained its Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) at 23 per cent, dismissing concerns over a decline of over $300 million in external reserves as a temporary, seasonal movement.

Governor of the CBN, Mr. Olayemi Cardoso, disclosed this yesterday at a press conference announcing the outcome of the 308th meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in Abuja.

The bank also retained the standing facilities corridor at +50/-300 basis points around the MPR, Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) for Deposit Money Banks at 45 per cent, Merchant Banks at 16 per cent and Non-TSA public sector deposits at 75 per cent.

Explaining the decision to retain the policy rate, Cardoso said: “In reaching its decision, the committee acknowledged the continued decline in headline inflation, but remained mindful of lingering upside risks, particularly those arising from the ongoing Middle East conflict, which could sustain pressure on energy prices.

“In addition, the MPC observed that the anticipated increase in spending from the end-of-year festive season and election-related activities could impact aggregate demand with likely upward pressure on prices.

“Nevertheless, the committee judged that maintaining the current policy stance is appropriate to safeguard the gains of disinflation so far achieved, while remaining data-dependent and vigilant in taking further appropriate measures.”

He added that continued exchange rate stability and improved food supply associated with the harvest season would further strengthen the disinflation process.

Cardoso said headline inflation had moderated for five consecutive months, reflecting sustained exchange rate stability and improved monetary policy transmission.

“However, given the prevailing headwinds, which have slowed the pace of moderation in price pressures, members were of the view that maintaining the current policy stance would further anchor inflation expectations and support the disinflation process,” he said.

On concerns over the decline in external reserves by over $300 million, Cardoso said the movement was not a source of worry, describing it as seasonal.

“Our reserves is in a very strong position. So, that, I want to say, has not changed. And in actual fact, I believe it will continue to improve. What you mention is something that is transient,” he said.

He explained that portfolio investors tend to recalibrate their positions towards year-end, while domestic users also increase demand for foreign exchange to hedge against future uncertainties.

“These are all seasonal issues. And of course, with the elections coming, there’s more spending that is going on. These are all seasonal. And we believe very strongly that as we go into the next year, we will find a major moderation in the volatility that you have seen,” he said.

Cardoso disclosed that gross external reserves stood at $54.02 billion as of November 17, 2026, sufficient to cover 10.26 months of imports of goods and services.

He also cited a current account surplus and diaspora remittances of over $900 million in the latest month as supporting external buffers.

“I want to assure all Nigerians that the Central Bank of Nigeria will do everything that is possible to ensure that that stability, that hard-earned stability, will continue,” he said.

The post CBN holds MPR at 23%, says external  reserves drop  temporary appeared first on Vanguard News.

content:
By Emem Idio

YENAGOA — It was tears and wailing at the Azikoro Cemetery in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, yesterday, as victims of Friday’s boat mishap in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area of the state, were laid to rest in a mass burial.

The burial, which commenced at about 11am, ended at 4pm, when the last batch of bodies, wrapped in black plastic bags, were brought to the cemetery in ambulances.

The exercise was supervised by the Secretary to the State Government, Prof. Nimibofa Ayawei, and the Commissioner for Environment, Mr. Ebi Ololo, alongside other government officials.

The cemetery was enveloped by a foul stench from the bodies, some of which had begun to decompose, as grieving relatives, friends and sympathisers gathered to witness the burial.

Many mourners broke down in tears, while others stood in groups, speaking in hushed tones as the remains of their loved ones were lowered into shallow graves.

One of the bereaved relatives, Timipreye Diepreye, who said she lost seven family members in the tragedy, faulted the manner in which relatives were informed about the mass burial.

She said the family would have made arrangements for coffins for their deceased relatives, particularly those whose bodies were recovered on Friday, if they had been adequately informed ahead of the exercise.

Also speaking, the Chairman of the Community Development Committee, CDC, of Ukubie community, Mr. Ruben Kemelate, said the tragedy had plunged the entire community into mourning, with hardly any family left untouched by the loss.

Kemelate, who disclosed that his elder sister also died at the Federal Medical Centre, said the scale of the tragedy had left the community devastated.

He said: “We are in a very sad mood. Every family is affected. There is no family that is not affected. Like me particularly, my elder sister died in the FMC. So, every family is in a sad mood. We are in a very sad mood as a community.

“So far so good, we have recovered 35 bodies and we have buried 29. We buried one on the first day, one seven-year-old boy. And today (yesterday) we have buried 28 corpses.

title: Campaign Violence: INEC awaits police case files to prosecute offenders
description:
By Omeiza Ajayi



ABUJA — The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, has asked the Nigeria Police Force to speed up the arrest, investigation and transmission of case files against perpetrators of campaign violence, so the Commission can prosecute them directly.



The INEC Chairman, Prof
content:
By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA — The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, has asked the Nigeria Police Force to speed up the arrest, investigation and transmission of case files against perpetrators of campaign violence, so the Commission can prosecute them directly.

The INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, SAN, said swift action was necessary so that “impunity is decisively checked before January.”

He spoke on Tuesday in Abuja at the Inspector General of Police’s Interactive Session with Chairmen and Secretaries of Political Parties on a peaceful electoral process before, during and after the 2027 General Elections.

The session held at the Goodluck Ebele Jonathan Peace Conference Hall, Force Headquarters.

According to a statement by the commission, last night, Amupitan said INEC was “deeply concerned by isolated incidents of campaign violence, intimidation, and attacks on political rivals, journalists, and electoral facilities.”

No election, office, or partisan interest is worth the loss of a single Nigerian life. Achieving a peaceful political environment is a collective national responsibility, not the duty of a single institution”, he added.

He said the Electoral Act 2026 had “significantly strengthened legal deterrence,” adding that Sections 96 and 97 prohibit inciting campaign rhetoric and ban the use of thugs, private armed guards or masquerades at political rallies.

According to him, the Act prescribes penalties of up to ₦5 million or twelve months’ imprisonment for individuals, and up to ₦10 million for political parties, on initial breaches.

“Under Section 148, INEC is empowered to prosecute electoral offenders directly upon receipt of completed case files,” he said, explaining the Commission’s request for prompt transmission of the files by the Police.

The INEC chairman stressed that the Commission remained distinct from security agencies. “INEC is not a security agency; it lacks both the constitutional mandate and operational capacity to maintain public order, arrest offenders, or provide armed security,” he said.

He said Section 95 of the Electoral Act assigns the duty of securing political rallies to the Police. The Section also mandates the Commissioner of Police in each state and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) to provide adequate security for rallies and processions, with support from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, and other federal security agencies.

Amupitan reminded political parties that INEC guidelines required them to notify the commissioner of police in writing of rally venues and times, and to submit the details to the Commission at least ten days in advance.

He appealed to political leaders “to refrain from seeking political support by creating fear,” urging them instead to “earn public confidence through integrity and transparency.”

In his remarks, the Inspector General of Police IGP, Olatunji Rilwan Disu, said recent violent clashes among political supporters, attacks on campaign venues and convoys, and the use of dangerous weapons had become matters of serious concern.

He described these developments as “warning signs that must be addressed decisively before they escalate into a broader threat to national security.”

The IGP declared that the Police have “zero tolerance for political violence, irrespective of the political party, candidate, personality or interest involved,” adding that the Force’s neutrality in the political process “is non-negotiable.”

Disu said those who sponsor, finance or direct political violence “will be treated with the same seriousness as those who carry them out.”

He assured participants that the Police would “protect the rights of all lawful political actors to organise rallies, hold meetings and participate in the democratic process.”

The IGP, however, that the Force would “not hesitate to take lawful and decisive action against anyone who engages in thuggery, intimidation, assault, the use of offensive weapons or any conduct capable of disrupting public peace.”
