title: Veteran actor Pete Edochie dies at 79
description:
Veteran Nigerian actor and broadcaster, Chief Pete Edochie, has died at the age of 79.
Edochie died at 12:30am on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, in Enugu, after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
His death was announced in a statement signed by his son, Leo Pete Edochie, on behalf of the family
content:
Veteran Nigerian actor and broadcaster, Chief Pete Edochie, has died at the age of 79.

Edochie died at 12:30am on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, in Enugu, after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

His death was announced in a statement signed by his son, Leo Pete Edochie, on behalf of the family and shared on Instagram on Wednesday.

The statement described the deceased as a beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman, adding that he hailed from Akamnato, Ifite Nteje, Anambra State.

The statement read, “With profound sadness and hearts bowed in total submission to the will of Almighty God,we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman, Chief Dr Pete EDOCHIE, MON (Ononenyi) a retired broadcaster and veteran sctor, who departed this life on Wednesday,25th November 2026 at 12.30am after a protracted battle with prostate cancer in Enugu, Nigeria. He was aged 79 years.

“Chief Dr Pete EDOCHIE hailed from Akamnato Ifite Nteje and is survived by his beloved wife, Barrister Mrs Josephine Edochie, his children, siblings and numerous other relations.

“Funeral arrangements will be announced in due course.

“As we mourn this painful loss,we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss.May God be with us all at this trying time.Amen. Chief Leo Pete EDOCHIE For the Family”

Edochie was one of Nigeria’s most recognisable actors, renowned for his commanding screen presence and portrayal of traditional patriarchal figures.

He rose to national and international prominence for his role as Okonkwo in the 1987 Nigerian Television Authority adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s novel, Things Fall Apart.

His performance in the television adaptation established him as a prominent figure in Nigerian acting and helped introduce his work to audiences beyond the country.

Before becoming widely known as an actor, Edochie had a career in broadcasting.

He began working as a broadcaster in 1967 before transitioning into acting, where he built a career spanning several decades and featured in numerous Nigerian films.

His contributions to the entertainment industry earned him the national honour of Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

title: Ebonyi govt approves 933.777 hectares for smart city, dredging of 3.3km Ebonyi River against flooding
description:
By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki



The Ebonyi State Government has approved the establishment of a 933.777-hectare of new city called FON Smart City in Abakaliki, alongside the dredging of 3,305.61 metres of the Ebonyi River as part of measures to expand the state capital and mitigate potential flooding.
content:
By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki

The Ebonyi State Government has approved the establishment of a 933.777-hectare of new city called FON Smart City in Abakaliki, alongside the dredging of 3,305.61 metres of the Ebonyi River as part of measures to expand the state capital and mitigate potential flooding.

The approvals were granted by the State Executive Council (EXCO), presided over by Governor Francis Ogbonna Nwifuru, during its meeting.

The Commissioner for Information and State Orientation, Chief Ikeuwa Omebeh ehike briefing journalists on the outcome of the Exco meeting, said the proposed smart city would be developed on an additional 933.777 hectares of land acquired from the former Army land within Abakaliki capital.

Omebeh explained that the council had approved the designation of the newly acquired territory and its entire development layout as FON Smart City, Abakaliki.

He said the initiative was part of the Nwifuru administration’s strategic urban development agenda aimed at expanding the territorial boundaries of the state capital, attracting private-sector investments and stimulating economic activities.

According to him, the proposed smart city has been designed with clearly defined land-use zones to accommodate the state’s growing residential, commercial, institutional and developmental requirements.

He listed the components of the master plan to include residential neighbourhoods, institutional zones, commercial districts, a Central Business District, green verges, agricultural and farming zones, community resettlement areas and special provision areas.

The commissioner said the carefully structured development framework was intended to create a modern urban environment capable of accommodating future population growth while improving the infrastructural capacity, aesthetics and economic outlook of Abakaliki.

He added that the project would open up new investment opportunities, expand economic activities and strengthen Ebonyi State’s position as an emerging investment destination in the South-East.

Also, the State Executive Council approved the dredging of approximately 3,305.61 metres (3.3 kilometres) of the Ebonyi River to address potential flooding threats within sections of the proposed smart city.

Omebeh said the decision followed the identification of flood-prone areas within the proposed development corridor, necessitating proactive environmental intervention to safeguard the planned urban infrastructure.

He explained that the dredging exercise would improve water flow, reduce flooding risks and provide the necessary environmental protection for the sustainable development of the new city.

The commissioner stressed that the government’s decision to incorporate flood-control measures into the smart city project underscored its commitment to sustainable urban planning and the protection of public infrastructure against environmental hazards.

The FON Smart City project represents a major component of the Nwifuru administration’s urban renewal and expansion agenda, with the potential to transform Abakaliki’s development landscape through the provision of planned residential, commercial and institutional infrastructure.

The government maintained that the initiative would expand the economic frontiers of the state capital, attract investments and position Abakaliki to meet the demands of future urban growth.

title: 20% HIV diagnosis gap threatens Nigeria’s 2030 AIDS target — NACA

By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja

The agency said the count
content:
By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja

The National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA) has warned that about 20 per cent of Nigerians living with HIV are unaware of their status, a gap that could undermine the country’s efforts to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

The agency said the country was yet to achieve the first of the UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets, which seeks to ensure that 95 per cent of people living with HIV know their status, 95 per cent of those diagnosed receive antiretroviral treatment and 95 per cent of those on treatment achieve viral suppression.

NACA Director-General, Dr Temitope Ilori, disclosed this at a press briefing in Abuja ahead of the 2026 World AIDS Day, observed annually on December 1.

Ilori said although Nigeria had recorded progress in HIV treatment and viral suppression, more efforts were needed to close the gap in diagnosis.

According to her, 80 per cent of Nigerians living with HIV know their status, while 98 per cent of those diagnosed are receiving antiretroviral treatment. Of those on treatment, 94 per cent have achieved viral suppression.

She stressed that identifying people who were unaware of their HIV status was critical to linking them to treatment and care.

Ilori called for expanded HIV testing services, uninterrupted access to antiretroviral medicines and stronger community-based interventions to reach people who had yet to access healthcare services.

The NACA director-general identified stigma and discrimination as major barriers to HIV testing and treatment, noting that fear of rejection and discrimination continued to discourage people from knowing their status and seeking medical care.

She urged relevant authorities to strengthen enforcement of the HIV and AIDS (Anti-Discrimination) Act to protect people living with the virus and ensure that discrimination did not prevent them from accessing essential services.

Ilori also called on federal, state and local governments to assume greater responsibility for financing and implementing HIV programmes, stressing that sustainable domestic funding, political commitment and stronger health systems were essential to sustaining progress.

On efforts to prevent mother-to-child transmission, she disclosed that early infant diagnosis coverage among HIV-exposed babies increased from 15 per cent in 2022 to 66 per cent in 2025.

She described the improvement as encouraging but said further efforts were required to ensure that all HIV-exposed infants received timely testing and appropriate care.

Providing an overview of the country’s HIV response, Ilori said annual AIDS-related deaths declined from 80,000 in 2010 to 32,000 in 2025, representing a reduction of about 60 per cent.

She added that new HIV infections fell from 130,000 in 2010 to 64,000 in 2025, while national HIV prevalence declined from 5.8 per cent in 2001 to 1.3 per cent in 2025.

Reviewing the agency’s activities in 2026, Ilori listed the development and launch of the National HIV Prevention Plan, progress on the National Strategic Plan and preparations for the National HIV Domestic Resource Mobilisation and Sustainability Strategy 2026–2030.

She said the sustainability strategy, scheduled for unveiling on December 1, would strengthen domestic financing, promote national ownership of HIV programmes and reduce Nigeria’s dependence on external funding.

The agency, she added, had also advanced preparations for the 2026 Integrated Biological and Behavioural Surveillance Survey and coordinated Nigeria’s proposal development for the Global Fund Grant Cycle 8.

Ilori further disclosed plans to convene a National Prevention Conference themed, “Reimagining HIV Prevention Strategies in Nigeria”, to explore more effective approaches to reducing new infections.

She called for wider access to HIV self-testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and community-led prevention services, particularly for populations facing barriers to conventional healthcare.

The 2026 World AIDS Day will be commemorated under the theme, “Ending AIDS Starts with Access: Equity, Ownership and Sustainability.”

NCAA, which lamented that the situation had become an embarrassment, sa
content:
By Dickson Omobola

Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority, NCAA, Monday, disclosed that it is designing an advisory to educate passengers on how to navigate the menace of begging and extortion at airports across the country.

NCAA, which lamented that the situation had become an embarrassment, said some passengers had missed flights after passing through screening because of the vindictive behaviour of personnel involved in the practice.

Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection at the NCAA, Mike Achimugu, made this known on X, formerly Twitter, following an incident in which he was allegedly harassed at one of the country’s airports on his return from Canada a few days ago.

He also urged airlines and service providers to develop systems that would enable them to identify personnel involved in the practice and have them removed from the airports.

He stated: “A student is travelling and has successfully passed through all screenings. Airline staff at the boarding gate verify their ticket and pass them through.

“The last bag check, and then the staff demand money from the student. The student says: ‘Sorry, I have no cash on me.’ This bag-check official replies: ‘I have an Opay account, you can send it there.’ The student puts a call across, seriously confused and afraid they would not be allowed through to the boarding gate because the official has delayed the bag check, keeping the passenger standing unnecessarily.

“This behaviour must stop. Begging is becoming institutionalised, and all airlines and service providers are advised to develop a system that allows them to identify these personnel and remove them from our airports.

“This menace has become too much. It is a bad image. It is harassment. It is inconvenient. This has nothing to do with poverty or salary; it is fast becoming a cultural trend and must be rejected.

“I get harassed on almost every trip. On my return from Canada a few days ago, it happened again. I told this personnel (a uniformed officer in this case): ‘I am the one passengers report you to when you do things like this. Who may I report you to when you do it to me? This is not a great look. You are wearing a uniform.’

“She looked at me, uncovered, and said: ‘Okay, do am as oyoyo (gift) for us na. You are a big man.’ I sighed and left.

“At the NCAA, we are designing an advisory to educate passengers on how to navigate this challenge. If this challenge were random, one could excuse it. But how can you defend something so rampant that it respects nobody, not even the image of the country we serve, or feels shame in the presence of strangers?

“This is embarrassing. Some passengers have actually missed flights after passing screening because of the vindictiveness of some of these horrible personnel. At the risk of sounding self-righteous, we will not allow this to fester beyond this point.

“We will engage the employers of these service providers and demand more from them! Enough, please.

“People travel for different reasons. Some travel for medical reasons. Some are running away from abusive partners and have barely enough to pay for a taxi on arrival at their destination. Others came in a hurry and had no cash on them. Some are struggling with infants while you harass them. For many others, their organisations purchased their tickets. They even had to borrow money for upkeep while abroad because their estacode had not been paid before their departure.

“These are the people you harass for money? Why won’t they lay curses on you? Do you think every traveller is financially comfortable? Even if they were, why not offer such professional service that they choose to tip you voluntarily?

“Why are we never focused on providing world-class service before reward? Why do we want to be given money for doing nothing? Why are you not afraid to offer a stranger your account details for such harassment? Are you not afraid of being sacked?

“Every time, it is ‘saner climes’. Is it only governments that are responsible for what you admire about them? Isn’t it a collective responsibility?

“Well, this must begin to change. Passengers are advised to report every single case of such harassment. This is not a campaign against people’s livelihoods. It is a battle for the soul and image of our country. The airport is the first impression that the world has of us. We will not lose that space. There is no argument that makes this menace okay.”

The post NCAA plans crackdown on airport extortion, seeks employers’ support appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Surgeons offer free knee replacements as orthopaedic association begins AGM
description:
… Over 100 patients receive free treatment in Abuja outreachBy Ruth Onyekachi



No fewer than 100 people living with disabling bone and joint conditions received free medical attention on Monday as Nigerian orthopaedic surgeons began a three-day surgical outreach in Abuja, offering procedures, incl
content:
… Over 100 patients receive free treatment in Abuja outreach
By Ruth Onyekachi

No fewer than 100 people living with disabling bone and joint conditions received free medical attention on Monday as Nigerian orthopaedic surgeons began a three-day surgical outreach in Abuja, offering procedures, including costly knee replacements, to patients who cannot afford them.


The outreach, organised by the Nigerian Orthopaedic Association (NOA) as part of activities marking its 49th Annual General Meeting (AGM) and Scientific Conference, will run until Wednesday across five hospitals in the Federal Capital Territory.


The participating facilities are Wuse District Hospital, Garki Hospital, Federal Medical Centre, Abuja, Cedarcrest Hospital and Alliance Hospital, where orthopaedic surgeons drawn from across the country are providing consultations, surgeries and post-operative care at no cost to beneficiaries.


For many of the patients, the intervention represents an opportunity to access procedures that would ordinarily cost millions of naira, particularly knee replacement surgeries that remain beyond the reach of low-income Nigerians.
Vice President of the association, Dr Christian Madubueze, who represented its President, Dr E.A. Orimolade, said the outreach was part of NOA’s commitment to making specialised orthopaedic care accessible to underserved Nigerians.
“This is not the first time we have done an outreach with the FCT — we did one during our 2023 AGM that was hosted here, and we were very happy, we were well treated, and we were able to serve patients,” he said.
He disclosed that the association would undertake a significant number of knee replacement operations free of charge.
“We are doing a significant number of knee replacement surgeries which normally would have cost these patients millions of naira, but we as an association are going to do them here,” he explained.
Madubueze said the choice of established hospitals was deliberate because complex procedures such as joint replacement require standard operating theatres and specialised facilities.
“It is actually not possible for us to be doing this in the villages unless we are going to set up a makeshift hospital there, which will dramatically increase the cost,” he said, adding that “Wuse District Hospital is very important to us.”
The FCT administration also welcomed the initiative, describing it as an important intervention for residents who struggle to access specialised medical services.
Director of Clinical Services, Dr Osayande Osagie, who represented the Mandate Secretary for Health Services and Environment, Dr Adedolapo Fasawe, said the administration appreciated the association for bringing the services closer to the people.
“Orthopaedic surgery or consultations are not things that are cheap to find, especially in a town like Abuja,” Osagie said.
“This corporate social responsibility that you brought to the people of Abuja, we really appreciate it, and on their behalf I want to say a big thank you.”
She also defended the decision to hold the outreach in established hospitals rather than rural communities, stressing that patients undergoing surgery would require continued medical attention after the visiting surgeons had departed.
“It’s better this thing is done where there are orthopaedic surgeons,” she said.

Chairman of the Local Organising Committee, Dr Aker Kenneth Ityo, said the FCT Mandate Secretary had promptly approved the use of district hospitals and their facilities after the association approached her office.

He said the hospitals provided theatres, medical personnel, laboratories, imaging services and beds, while NOA supplied the surgeons, some consumables and medicines.

According to him, the arrangement would enable indigent residents to access specialised treatment without bearing the financial burden.

“Many of the patients we will see today have lived with deformities, neglected injuries and disabling joint disease for years, simply because they could not afford treatment,” Ityo said.

“For them, this outreach is not charity. It is a chance to walk again, work again and live with dignity.”

Among the beneficiaries is Miss Vanessa Adamu, who was born with bowlegs and experiences pain when standing for long periods or walking any distance. Although surgery offers a solution to her condition, the cost had remained beyond her reach until she learnt about the outreach through a TikTok post.

Another beneficiary, Mrs Abdusalam, brought her toddler daughter, who was also born with bowlegs that affect her ability to walk properly. She learnt about the intervention through a relative.

Mr Godswill James, who suffers from knee bursitis, an inflammation of the bursa in the knee, following football injuries, also turned up for treatment after a friend informed him about the programme.

The outreach forms part of the NOA’s broader effort to address barriers to orthopaedic care in Nigeria.

The association, which has about 600 members, is the country’s umbrella body for orthopaedic surgeons and is using its 49th AGM to examine challenges affecting access to specialised care.

The conference, themed around access to orthopaedic care in Nigeria, will also explore the application of artificial intelligence and robotics in orthopaedic practice, as well as the future of group practice in private orthopaedic healthcare.

Pre-conference activities include hands-on training in complex primary and revision knee arthroplasty, including unicondylar knee replacement, and knee arthroscopy, using dry laboratory facilities and artificial joints.

The main scientific conference and a two-day trade exhibition are scheduled to hold from Thursday to Friday.

title: Nigerian children: Millions still face barriers to education, protection
description:
…Demand free education, stronger safeguards, greater voice in decisionsBy Chioma Obinna



For millions of Nigerian children, the promise of a safe childhood, quality education and a future shaped by their dreams remains a daily struggle. From access to basic education and healthcare to protection f
content:
…Demand free education, stronger safeguards, greater voice in decisions
By Chioma Obinna

For millions of Nigerian children, the promise of a safe childhood, quality education and a future shaped by their dreams remains a daily struggle. From access to basic education and healthcare to protection from abuse and poverty, the gap between children’s rights and their lived realities continues to raise concerns about the country’s commitment to its youngest population.

The challenge came into focus on Friday as the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the Lagos State Government marked the 2026 World Children’s Day, calling for stronger protection of children’s rights and concrete government action to secure their future.

At the celebration, held at the UNICEF Lagos Office under the theme, “My Day. My Rights. My Future,” children demanded free education, greater protection and a stronger voice in decisions affecting their lives.

UNICEF Chief of Field Office, Lagos, Celine Lafoucriere, warned that children’s rights were increasingly under threat globally, stressing that governments and other stakeholders must do more to guarantee access to education, healthcare, good nutrition, clean water, sanitation and social protection.

“Children’s rights are under pressure, they’re under threat, they’re being increasingly threatened throughout the world,” she said.

She noted that recognising children’s rights was not enough if families and communities lacked the resources to make those rights meaningful.

Lafoucriere explained that social protection programmes were essential to helping vulnerable children access basic services, particularly education, healthcare and adequate nutrition.

“Having a right is one thing, but it’s not going to put food on the table,” she said.

She stressed that UNICEF was working with the Lagos State Government to ensure that children’s rights were respected and accessible to every child, particularly those from vulnerable backgrounds.

“The child is the future, and the future of Nigeria is today,” she declared, urging society to recognise that investment in children could not be postponed.

Children want more than promises

Beyond the concerns raised by development partners and government officials, the celebration provided an opportunity for children to articulate their expectations of those responsible for protecting their rights.

The Speaker of the Lagos State Children’s Parliament, Rt. Hon. Abdulsalam Anjola, called for greater involvement of children in decisions affecting their welfare, insisting that their experiences and opinions must count when policies concerning them are formulated.

He said children were often better positioned to explain the challenges they faced, particularly cases of abuse and other threats to their safety.

Anjola also urged the government to increase investment in education and create opportunities for children who were out of school.

“Education is the weapon that can instigate war,” he said, calling for effective implementation of education policies to ensure that every child had access to opportunities to realise their potential.

His appeal highlighted the need to move beyond policy declarations to practical interventions that would keep children in school and provide them with the skills and opportunities required to build meaningful futures.

A 14-year-old student of Ikeja Senior High School, Ishola Moyinoluwa, also called for stronger protection of children’s rights, particularly access to basic and free education.

She said every child deserved an opportunity to be heard, educated and equipped to pursue their dreams.

Using her artwork depicting a young boy aspiring to become an astronaut, Moyinoluwa illustrated how children’s ambitions could become achievable when parents provided guidance and the government created the necessary opportunities.

She urged parents to guide their children educationally, morally and socially, while calling on the government to establish platforms where young people could express their views on issues affecting their rights and future.

Government promises action

The Lagos State Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, Mr Mobolaji Ogunlende, acknowledged that protecting and promoting children’s welfare required collective responsibility involving government, parents, schools, communities and development partners.

He said the government remained committed to creating an environment where every child felt safe, valued and heard.

“We must translate what we hear today into meaningful action and commitment,” Ogunlende said.

He assured the children that their concerns and contributions during the celebration would not end with the event but would inform policies and practical interventions.

The Permanent Secretary of the ministry, Pharm. (Mrs.) Toyin Oke-Osanyintolu, encouraged children to speak out whenever their rights were threatened and urged them to remain confident in their aspirations.

“If you can dream it, you can do it,” she said, commending UNICEF for its partnership with the state government in advancing children’s welfare.

As part of the celebration, 80 children, divided into eight groups, participated in an art project titled “80 Children, One Future”, presenting their visions of the Nigeria they hoped to see.

The exercise provided a creative platform for children to communicate their expectations and aspirations, while UNICEF urged adults to listen to their concerns and make practical commitments to address them.

Beyond the speeches, artworks and assurances, the central message of the 2026 World Children’s Day celebration was clear: children’s rights must be reflected in their everyday experiences, not merely recognised during annual commemorations.

For Nigerian children, the future they envision will depend largely on whether the government and society can translate commitments into accessible education, adequate healthcare, protection from abuse, social support and meaningful participation in decisions that shape their lives.

The post Nigerian children: Millions still face barriers to education, protection appeared first on Vanguard News.

content:
George Ilenikhena marked his return from injury with a goal as Al-Ittihad defeated Pakhtakor 2-0 in the AFC Champions League in Jeddah on Tuesday.

The Nigerian forward started the encounter at King Abdullah Sports City and opened the scoring shortly after the restart, reacting quickest to the rebound after an effort from the edge of the penalty area struck the woodwork.

The strike marked a welcome return to action for the 19-year-old, who had been sidelined by injury shortly before the international break, thereby missing Nigeria’s double-header against Tanzania in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

Ilenikhena was replaced with 17 minutes remaining, making way for former Sevilla striker Youssef En-Nesyri as Al-Ittihad sought to protect their advantage.

The goal takes his tally to nine goals and three assists in 16 appearances across all competitions this season

The former Monaco striker will now hope to build on the performance and maintain his fitness as Al-Ittihad pursue domestic and continental honours.

His return also provides a boost to Nigeria’s attacking options ahead of their next international engagements.

title: N’Assembly demands nationwide boat safety audit
description:
The Senate and House of Representatives have called for a nationwide audit of boats and ferries operating on Nigeria’s waterways, alongside stricter enforcement of safety regulations, following a boat accident in Bayelsa State that claimed 29 lives, including two children.
The lawmakers blamed the N
content:
The Senate and House of Representatives have called for a nationwide audit of boats and ferries operating on Nigeria’s waterways, alongside stricter enforcement of safety regulations, following a boat accident in Bayelsa State that claimed 29 lives, including two children.

The lawmakers blamed the November 20, 2026, disaster on overloading, poor safety standards and the use of unserviceable vessels, urging regulatory agencies to ensure compulsory use of life jackets and other safety equipment to prevent further accidents.

The resolutions followed separate motions moved at plenary on Tuesday by Senator Benson Konbowei, representing Bayelsa Central, and Rodney Ambaiowei, representing Southern Ijaw Federal Constituency.

Leading the debate in the Senate, Konbowei described the incident as shocking and unfortunate, saying the ill-fated boat was carrying more than 300 passengers, far above its capacity, before its weak structure broke apart and capsized.

He said, “The boat had more than three hundred passengers on board, which was more than its old and weak frame could comfortably carry, and it broke apart, capsized and threw the passengers into the river.”

Konbowei disclosed that 29 bodies had been recovered, while divers and rescue workers continued searching for missing passengers. Several survivors had also been taken to hospitals for treatment.

In the House, Ambaiowei said more than 150 people, mostly indigenes of Southern Ijaw, were involved in the accident while travelling from Ayama Community to Ukubie for a condolence visit.

He said the boat capsized at the river junction between Oweikorogha and Otuan, throwing its occupants into the water.

According to him, 51 people had been rescued alive with varying degrees of injuries and discomfort as of November 22, while 29 others, including two children, had been confirmed dead.

The rescued victims were taken to medical facilities in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area and government hospitals in Yenagoa, while search operations continued for missing persons and possible survivors.

Both lawmakers attributed the vulnerability of riverine communities to inadequate road networks and dependence on poorly maintained boats, many of which were old, overworked and frequently overloaded.

Konbowei called on the Federal Government to support critical road projects, particularly the proposed Yenagoa-Oporoma Road, which he said was recommended in the 1958 Willink Commission Report.

He also commended Governor Douye Diri for his response to the disaster and President Bola Tinubu for sending Vice-President Kashim Shettima to the state. Shettima had announced a donation of N250m to support the state government’s disaster management efforts and affected families.

Contributing to the Senate debate, Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin urged regulatory agencies to conduct routine inspections of boats and ferries to ensure compliance with safety standards.

He said, “I think if that was the case, if there were routine checks, I’m sure this kind of calamity will not be occurring at the rate they are occurring in our country.”

Similarly, Senator Sunday Marshall Katung, representing Kaduna South, called for a comprehensive investigation into the accident and an audit of vessels operating in the country’s territorial waters.

He said, “There are gaps in the regulatory framework that have given rise to situations such as this, and I want to urge that the relevant committee of the Senate needs to step in and conduct investigations.”

In the House, Minority Leader Fred Agbedi called for subsidised modern boats for riverine communities, similar to the Federal Government’s intervention in road transportation through Compressed Natural Gas buses.

He said, “I’m aware that the federal government is providing CNG buses, you know, that are more economical. But each time we talk about mass transit and all that, there is no river craft provision.”

Agbedi argued that government transportation interventions should also accommodate communities with limited access to roads, adding that modern boats should be provided at subsidised rates.

Also contributing, Shina Oyedeji urged the government to strengthen safety regulations, particularly the training and certification of boat operators.

He questioned the standards used in certifying operators and inspecting vessels, insisting that safety requirements must be properly established and enforced.

The Deputy Majority Whip, Isiaka Ibrahim, said responsibility for safety on inland waterways rested with both federal and state governments, noting that creeks and offshore waters were on the concurrent legislative list.

He called for an investigation into the accident, arguing that safety measures observed by multinational companies operating in Nigeria’s offshore waters should guide improvements in local water transportation.

Ibrahim also cautioned against relying on swimming ability as a substitute for basic safety precautions.

“Life vests, life jackets, we ignore it. And then we are not talking about mishap. Definitely, it’s a hazard,” he said.

However, the House Leader, Prof Julius Ihonvbere, said communities, maritime associations, local governments and state authorities must also be held accountable for safety failures.

He said television footage of the accident showed passengers boarding boats without life jackets, describing the practice as unacceptable and calling for tougher penalties against violators.

“Soldiers that die in war also know how to shoot. They know how to deploy grenades. So the fact that I was born in the riverside, I was thrown into the river, I was a baby, I have been swimming for 20, 35 years, is not an excuse to board a boat without the appropriate life vest,” he said.

The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, blamed the accident on overloading and urged boat operators to observe approved passenger limits.

“This clearly was as a result of overloading, and if we do not carry overload and we restrict to the capacity of the boat, this would never have happened,” he said.

The Senate unanimously adopted seven prayers contained in its motion, including a minute’s silence for the victims, a nationwide audit of vessels and stronger enforcement of water transportation regulations.

The lawmakers also urged the Federal Government to support the construction of the Yenagoa-Oporoma Road and other critical roads in Bayelsa State, while calling on the Nigerian Inland Waterways Authority and other regulatory agencies to enforce safety standards.

The House also unanimously adopted its motion and mandated its Committee on Emergency and Disaster Management to work with the National Emergency Management Agency and the Bayelsa State Government to investigate the immediate and remote causes of the accident and recommend measures to prevent future occurrences.

It further urged NEMA, the Niger Delta Development Commission, the Nigerian Inland Waterways Authority and the South-South Development Agency to provide relief materials to affected communities.

The lawmakers also called for the urgent provision of safer boats, life jackets, floaters and other water transportation safety equipment to riverine communities, with measures to ensure their compulsory use.

The Senate subsequently observed a minute’s silence in honour of those who died in the accident.

title: ‘Tinubu risked political future to return from exile’
description: President Bola Tinubu risked his life and political future by returning to Nigeria shortly after the death of military dictator General Sani Abacha in 1998, overruling the caution of fellow pro-democracy exiles just The disclosure is contained in Chapter 11, pages 185–187, of From AD to APC: The Evo
content:
President Bola Tinubu risked his life and political future by returning to Nigeria shortly after the death of military dictator General Sani Abacha in 1998, overruling the caution of fellow pro-democracy exiles just The disclosure is contained in Chapter 11, pages 185–187, of From AD to APC: The Evolution of Nigerian Political Parties and the Exploits of One Man (1998–2015), a new book by veteran journalist Sam Omatseye.

The excerpt was contained in the programme of events for the book’s public presentation on Tuesday at the State House Conference Centre, Abuja, which the President is expected to attend.

Only the programme was made available to our correspondent, as the book had yet to be formally presented at the time of this report.

According to the book, Tinubu, who was in exile, expressed a desire to see his mother during an emergency meeting in London convened by NADECO Abroad following Abacha’s sudden death in June 1998.

“It was in a room in London, and members of the NADECO Abroad had convened.

“The meeting was tense. An earthquake had happened at home, and the consequence was one for the ages. The dictator Sani Abacha had died,” the excerpt read.

According to Omatseye, although the new military Head of State, General Abdulsalami Abubakar, had conveyed a conciliatory tone to civil society organisations, suspicions ran deep.

Present at the London meeting were former Foreign Affairs Minister, Professor Bolaji Akinyemi, retired General Alani Akinrinade and Prince Iludoyin, all of whom had suffered exile and deprivation, with the constant fear of being captured by the regime.

He wrote, “Most did not want to return just yet. They still wanted to watch the direction of affairs. There was a sense in which caution made sense.

“The military from the times of Babangida had laid ambush against the political society.”

However, Tinubu, described in the book as the face of NADECO Abroad, argued for an immediate return.

He warned that any delay would hand the political space to those who had propped up military rule.

“If they delayed and stayed back, they would surrender the country to the apologists of the military.

“They were the members of the five leprous fingers, and they could execute a pirouette and style themselves as democrats.

“It would turn the work of all of them, who had lost lives and resources, into a waste. He did not want that,” it read.

Omatseye added, “Tinubu tried to persuade them to take the plunge, and that the death of Abacha meant the decapitation of an era.”

Nonetheless, his fellow exiles hesitated, as those unwilling to return argued that it made sense to visit Nigeria first and assess the situation rather than commit to a full return.

Addressing his unwilling comrades, Omatseye wrote that Tinubu revealed his real reason for returning to the country was to see his mother again.

“So, in order to provide an excuse, he brought in a sense of domestic humour to disarm his fellows. He burst out in Yoruba, ‘Mo fe lo ri maami.’ (I want to see my mother.) They were amused, but they had no counterpoint to his cheerful alibi,” the book stated.

The 1998 meeting followed the death of Abacha, who seized power from the Ernest Shonekan-led interim government several months after the annulled June 12, 1993, presidential election won by Chief M.K.O. Abiola.

Abiola died in custody on July 7, 1998.

General Abdulsalami subsequently oversaw a transition programme that produced the 1999 Constitution and handed power to civilian rule on May 29, 1999.

Tinubu, a former senator who had run on the Social Democratic Party platform in the 1992 senatorial elections, returned from exile and contested the Lagos governorship under the Alliance for Democracy, winning in 1999 and beginning the political journey that would eventually take him to the presidency in 2023.

The book, which covers the period from 1998 to 2015, from Nigeria’s return to civilian rule through the collapse of the Peoples Democratic Party’s 16-year grip on federal power, is Omatseye’s second major political work.

His first, Beating All Odds: How Bola Tinubu Became President, was published in 2024.

An award-winning journalist, author, poet and playwright, Omatseye is Chairman of the Editorial Board of The Nation newspaper, where his weekly column, In Touch, has run for two decades.

Born on June 15, 1961, he studied History at the University of Ife, now Obafemi Awolowo University, and began his career at Newswatch magazine before rising to deputy political editor at Concord Newspapers during the June 12 crisis.

He was beaten by soldiers while covering the 1992 Ejigbo air crash. He went on to win the Nigerian Media Merit Award for Reporter of the Year.

Omatseye has won three additional NMMAs as Columnist of the Year and four Diamond Awards for Media Excellence.

He is also a recipient of the Association of Black Journalists’ Features Prize, the Scripps Howard Award for deadline reporting, and was the inaugural recipient of the Gordon N. Fisher Commonwealth Fellowship for Journalists.

He was among 51 persons granted National Honours by the President in his 2026 Democracy Day speech on June 12.

According to the programme of events, the gathering will receive goodwill messages from the governors of Lagos, Delta and Kaduna states, as well as former Zamfara Governor Abdulaziz Yari, former APC National Chairman Adams Oshiomhole, Minister of Environment Tunji Bello, media executive Dapo Olorunyomi and Alex Kabba.

The book is to be reviewed by Louis Odion, with excerpts to be read by Ohi Alegbe, Stella Din Jacobs and Yomi Odunuga.

The post ‘Tinubu risked political future to return from exile’ appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: DSS asks court to close Sowore’s defence
description:
The Department of State Services has asked the Federal High Court in Abuja to foreclose the defence of the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress, Omoyele Sowore, over alleged delays in his ongoing cyberbullying trial.
The DSS, through its counsel, Akinlolu Kehinde (SAN), on Tuesday u
content:
The Department of State Services has asked the Federal High Court in Abuja to foreclose the defence of the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress, Omoyele Sowore, over alleged delays in his ongoing cyberbullying trial.

The DSS, through its counsel, Akinlolu Kehinde (SAN), on Tuesday urged Justice Mohammed Umar to grant an application seeking to close the defendant’s case, alleging that he had exceeded the number of adjournments permitted under the law.

Kehinde told the court that the application, filed on November 23, had been served on Sowore’s legal team, adding that the defendant had sought or procured adjournments on at least 14 occasions since the commencement of the trial.

He argued that the number was far beyond the five adjournments permitted under Section 396(4) of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act, 2015.

“Before we finally draw the curtain on the proceedings, I want to bring to your lordship’s notice the application we filed and served on the defendant.

“The application is that there must be an end to all these. The defendant has since exceeded the number of adjournments as required by law,” he said.

In the motion on notice, the DSS sought an order closing the defence’s case and directing the parties to file and exchange their final written addresses within a period to be determined by the court, ahead of a date for their adoption.

Giving nine grounds in support of the application, Kehinde said Sowore was re-arraigned on a two-count charge on January 19, 2026, to which he pleaded not guilty, after which the trial commenced.

He said the prosecution called its witness and closed its case in March 2026, while the court dismissed Sowore’s no-case submission on May 8, 2026, and directed him to enter his defence.

According to the prosecution, Sowore subsequently sought or procured adjournments on at least 14 occasions, eight of which occurred after he was called upon to open his defence.

Kehinde said the trial had made little progress since Sowore opened his defence on July 6, 2026, with only two defence witnesses having testified.

“Since the defendant/respondent opened his defence on 6th July 2026, the trial has not progressed beyond the evidence of two defence witnesses,” he said.

The senior lawyer further accused Sowore of repeatedly filing applications and court processes that allegedly stalled the proceedings, including the subpoena issued against the lead counsel to the complainant.

He said the court had, on several occasions, cautioned the defendant against delaying the trial.

Kehinde argued that the constitutional right to a fair hearing did not confer an unlimited right to adjournments, stressing that a defendant who had been given sufficient opportunity to present his case could not complain of a breach of that right.

“Section 36(4) of the Constitution guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and the Administration of Criminal Justice Act, 2015 requires that criminal trials proceed from day to day or, where that is impracticable, within the strict limits on adjournments prescribed by Section 396 of the ACJA.”

He urged the court to grant the application in the interest of justice.

However, Sowore’s counsel, Reuben Adakole, opposed the timing of the application, arguing that the court should first determine pending applications relating to the subpoena issued against the Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Prof. Joash Amupitan (SAN).

Adakole acknowledged receiving the DSS application but maintained that the court needed to deliver its ruling on Amupitan’s application to set aside the subpoena, as well as the defence’s preliminary objection and ex-parte motion, before considering the prosecution’s request.

“Inasmuch as the application tends to foreclose us, there is our application which the court ought to pronounce on first. Until after the ruling, we can look at it. The application is unripe, my lord,” he said.

Meanwhile, Alex Iziyon (SAN), who represented Amupitan, informed the court that the matter had previously been adjourned because the defence had yet to file its counter-affidavit.

He, however, confirmed that the defence had subsequently filed the process and that he had responded, urging the parties to adopt their respective processes.

Adakole confirmed that the processes had been exchanged but clarified that the subpoena issued to the INEC chairman was strictly a subpoena duces tecum, requiring him to produce documents rather than appear as a witness to give oral evidence.

“It is just strictly to come and tender the documents, and that was why we filed a motion to amend the application.

“We ask that we be allowed to move our motion ex parte, so that it will lay to rest all these issues.

“So the intent was just for the INEC chairman to tender the documents and not to testify,” he said.

Iziyon disagreed, accusing the defence of attempting to circumvent the court’s earlier directive.

“The defendant cannot take this court for a ride. I submit with all sense of responsibility,” he said.

He reminded the court that it had directed the defence to file a formal application on notice to enable the opposing parties to respond.

In response, Justice Umar told Adakole that the defence was required to comply with the court’s directive since the parties had already joined issues on the matter.

“Before the last adjourned date, I told you that since you have issued that subpoena and they have been joined, anything you want to do now will be by motion on notice; serve them, and they will respond,” the judge said.

The court subsequently heard the applications, with Iziyon adopting three processes filed on behalf of Amupitan and urging the court to set aside the subpoena.

He relied on an earlier ruling by Justice Umar on the court’s power to set aside a subpoena and cited a previous case in which a subpoena was set aside because the person sought to be summoned had no connection with the subject matter of the proceedings.

Adakole, in his response, adopted the defence processes and urged the court to dismiss Amupitan’s application.

He also moved an ex parte application filed on November 11, seeking four reliefs, arguing that the documents requested were public records in the custody of a public officer and were necessary for Sowore’s defence.

He maintained that their relevance could only be determined by the court after they had been produced.

“It is not for the applicant to say so. That will be preemptive,” he said.

After listening to the parties, Justice Umar adjourned the case until December 7 for ruling on Amupitan’s application to set aside the subpoena.

The judge also fixed the date for the hearing of the DSS application seeking to foreclose Sowore’s defence and other pending applications.

title: Nigeria’s oil revenue safe as crude prices fall to 3-month low
description:
Nigeria’s oil revenue outlook remains relatively secure despite the fall in global crude prices to a three-month low.
Oil prices fell for a second consecutive day on Tuesday as rising global supplies and fears of a possible glut outweighed concerns over disruptions to crude shipments in the Middle E
content:
Nigeria’s oil revenue outlook remains relatively secure despite the fall in global crude prices to a three-month low.

Oil prices fell for a second consecutive day on Tuesday as rising global supplies and fears of a possible glut outweighed concerns over disruptions to crude shipments in the Middle East.

Brent crude futures dropped 75 cents, or 0.8 per cent, to $88.62 per barrel by 9:15 GMT, after hitting their lowest level since August 27.

Similarly, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell 64 cents, or 0.8 per cent, to $79.53 per barrel, after sliding to its weakest level since August 10.

The price is above the Federal Government’s 2026 budget benchmark of $64.85 per barrel.

The price cushion offers some relief to the government amid concerns over falling oil prices, although the country’s ability to meet its production target remains critical to maximising earnings from crude exports and supporting the nation’s finances.

The decline in global prices came despite continued tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, a major global oil shipping route, where Iran’s Revolutionary Guards navy said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on Monday.

The United States is also investigating possible Iranian involvement in cyberattacks targeting as many as 50 energy tankers, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.

However, improving supply conditions have put pressure on prices, with Libya’s Sharara oil pipeline reopening after a disruption, allowing crude to flow into storage facilities.

China and India are also increasing their purchases of Russian oil, helping to make up for supply disruptions caused by the conflict involving Iran.

Analysts said the combination of rising supplies, strategic oil reserve releases and expectations of increased global production had weakened the support that geopolitical tensions previously provided for oil prices.

UBS analyst, Giovanni Staunovo, said oil prices were facing downward pressure as markets reduced their concerns about immediate geopolitical risks, while releases from strategic reserves were helping to keep supplies adequate despite lower exports from the Middle East.

He said the market was also weighing the possibility of excess supply against continuing tensions and shipping disruptions in the region.

Deutsche Bank said global oil and liquid fuel inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October, suggesting that supply exceeded demand by about 1.7 million barrels per day.

The bank said growing evidence showed that the global oil market was moving towards a surplus, although further disruptions could delay the trend.

Meanwhile, a preliminary Reuters poll indicated that US crude oil and petroleum product inventories were likely to have increased in the previous week, adding to concerns about oversupply.

However, analysts warned that the market remained vulnerable to fresh disruptions.

Daniel Hynes, senior commodity strategist at ANZ, said oil prices and other market indicators suggested that investors were increasingly expecting supply conditions to return to normal.

He, however, warned that shipping constraints and limited inventory buffers meant the market remained exposed to further shocks.

Suvro Sarkar, head of energy research at DBS Bank, also warned that oil prices could rise again depending on the outcome of talks between the United States and Iran and possible moves by both sides over the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

The post Nigeria’s oil revenue safe as crude prices fall to 3-month low appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Disu targets schools to revive Nigerian judo
description:
Nigeria Judo Federation president Olatunji Disu has unveiled plans to revive the sport’s grassroots structure through secondary schools, universities and polytechnics, identifying educational institutions as the foundation for discovering and developing the next generation of judokas.
Disu said his
content:
Nigeria Judo Federation president Olatunji Disu has unveiled plans to revive the sport’s grassroots structure through secondary schools, universities and polytechnics, identifying educational institutions as the foundation for discovering and developing the next generation of judokas.

Disu said his administration would return attention to schools, which he believes played an important role in developing Nigerian judo in the past.

The Inspector-General of Police said attracting young people to the sport would be central to efforts to increase participation and create a stronger pool of athletes for future national and international competitions.

“I’m going to concentrate on the grassroots, starting from all secondary schools and universities because, in the past, this was where we got people to populate the sport of judo,” Disu said.

He also pledged to extend the initiative to polytechnics and embark on campaigns to make the martial art more accessible and attractive to young Nigerians.

The former chairman of the Lagos State Judo Association said reconnecting stakeholders and Nigerian judokas living abroad would also form part of his administration’s efforts to reposition the sport.

His emergence followed a period of divisions within the judo community, with reconciliation identified as an immediate priority.

Disu, a third-dan black belt, has been involved in the sport for decades and previously won silver in the veterans’ under-100kg category at the 2022 US Open Judo Championship.

His grassroots plan will require collaboration with schools, state associations and other stakeholders to turn the proposed expansion into regular participation and a pathway for young athletes.

The new administration is expected to face the task of translating its promises into a sustainable development structure for Nigerian judo.
