title: 2027: N’Central battles  violence, thuggery
description:
By Romanus Ugwu, Okwe Obi, Abuja; Scholastica Hir, Makurdi; John Adams, Minna; Emmanuel Adeyemi, Lokoja; Jude Owuamanam, Jos
The dark side of the build-up to the forthcoming 2027 general election is certainly the escalating spate of senseless violent attacks at political campaign rallies and the oth
content:
By Romanus Ugwu, Okwe Obi, Abuja; Scholastica Hir, Makurdi; John Adams, Minna; Emmanuel Adeyemi, Lokoja; Jude Owuamanam, Jos

The dark side of the build-up to the forthcoming 2027 general election is certainly the escalating spate of senseless violent attacks at political campaign rallies and the other hostilities that political thugs are unleashing on Nigerians across every part of the country ahead of next year’s polls.

The violence has taken the forms of killings, attacks on President Bola Tinubu and the convoys of other notable opposition candidates, invasion of the venues of rallies and town hall meetings, intolerance, destruction of billboards and posters, verbal abuse, coordinated cyberbullying, denial of access to public assets for campaigns and mayhem unleashed on innocent Nigerians by thugs.

The series of incidents recorded in Benue, Kogi, Nasarawa, Niger, Kwara and Plateau states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, is a glaring confirmation that the North Central geopolitical zone is not immune to the pestilence destabilising the country and posing a threat to the forthcoming general election.

What paints an even more disturbing and uglier picture is that the menace has now become a bug spreading across all political parties, with both the ruling and opposition parties bearing the brunt in equal measure.

Perhaps, never in the history of general election build-ups in Nigeria’s democratic journey has the country witnessed such widespread attacks as in the forthcoming polls.

To underscore the veracity and magnitude of the trend, the national leadership of the All Progressives Congress (APC), through its National Working Committee (NWC), while decrying the ugly circumstances only recently, issued a reprisal threat indicating the readiness of the ruling party’s youths to crush what it described as a deliberate, sustained campaign of calumny and targeted hate against its supporters.

APC National Youth Leader, Dayo Israel, who read the riot act in a statement he personally signed and issued recently, expressed fury over the disturbing menace encapsulated in the targeted hate against President Tinubu, his family and every Nigerian who openly stands with him.

Israel, while lamenting the attacks, claimed that a section of the opposition, particularly elements within the Obidient Movement, had made it a full-time occupation to attack, insult, threaten and attempt to silence anyone associated with the President, from online mobs to physical confrontations.

Enumerating documented incidents, such as the London attack on the chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Prof. Joash Amupitan, and the labelling of the commission as a “criminal organisation”, as well as the dastardly attack on the convoy of President Tinubu at a mosque in Abuja, he warned: “Any further attack on the person or the convoy of President Tinubu will not be condoned. Nigeria is a country governed by the rule of law, not the law of the mob. These attacks extend to the First Lady, Oluremi Tinubu.

“What we are witnessing is no longer ordinary political disagreement. It is a deliberate, sustained campaign of targeted hate against President Tinubu, his family and every Nigerian who openly stands with him. From online mobs to physical confrontations, a section of the opposition, particularly elements within the Obidient Movement, has made it a full-time occupation to attack, insult, threaten, and attempt to silence anyone associated with the President.

“Comedians, entertainers, creative professionals, ordinary supporters and even public officials are routinely marked for destruction the moment they defend the administration or celebrate its achievements. Many in the creative industry have grown afraid to publicly identify with the President, not because they disagree with him but because they know the personal cost of doing so.

“Families have been dragged into the fray. This is not politics. It is persecution. Democracy is not the exclusive preserve of those who hate the President. Supporters of Tinubu will not be intimidated… Their intimidation, both virtually and physically, must stop, henceforth. Attempts to cow us online or on the streets will fail. We live under a Constitution that protects the right of every citizen to associate with, defend and vote for candidates of their choice. Nobody is rigging the future.

“Any further attack on the President, the First Lady, their convoy or their supporters will be met with the full force of lawful resistance and the unbreakable resolve of those who believe Nigeria is worth the effort. Let the opposition be warned: we will not be intimidated,” he cautioned.

Unfortunately, the attacks are not restricted to Abuja alone. As political activities gather momentum in Benue State ahead of the 2027 elections, there are growing concerns over the destruction of campaign materials and the denial of equal access to public facilities for all political parties to canvass for votes.

Although political parties said there had been no physical attacks on their members, apart from the harassment of some people, including the convoy of the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, the state chapter of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) has raised concerns over the alleged destruction of its campaign billboards and banners in some parts of the state.

While describing the incidents as attempts to intimidate opposition parties ahead of the elections, the party specifically cited the destruction of campaign billboards belonging to its Benue North West senatorial candidate, Dr. Eunice Ortom, at Naka, in Gwer West Local Government Area, and another at Ajio in Ishangev Ya, Kwande West State Constituency.

In separate statements issued recently, the PDP State Publicity Secretary, Bright Antyo, condemned the incidents, describing them as attacks on democratic rights and political expression, and urged security agencies to investigate the alleged vandalism and bring those responsible to justice, irrespective of their political affiliations and status.

Speaking to the Daily Sun in Makurdi on the incidents, PDP Secretary, Fan Nyikwagh, said: “Yes. Recently, our Benue North East senatorial candidate, Hon. Thomas Tyolumun Unongo, was reportedly attacked and harassed by APC loyalists. They attempted to prevent his convoy from accessing the burial ceremony of a deceased traditional ruler in Vandeikya. This is a disturbing demonstration of the growing political intolerance in our state.

“Even more disturbing, some LGA chairmen have reportedly gone as far as attacking places of worship where members and supporters of our party gather for thanksgiving services. Unfortunately, political intolerance has degenerated to the point where even places of worship and religious activities are being subjected to political hostility.

“Verbal attacks have practically become the operational culture of the current APC-led administration and now appear to be part of its campaign strategy. We have witnessed coordinated cyberbullying and harassment of opposition figures by individuals seemingly on the ruling party’s payroll. They go as far as manufacturing and circulating fabricated stories to damage the reputations of our leaders and candidates.

“The PDP has been denied access to public spaces and government institutions on several occasions. The situation has become so predictable that we have resolved not to continue embarrassing ourselves by seeking approvals that we already know will be denied. Public facilities belong to the people, not the ruling party.

“We have witnessed several cases of defacement and destruction of our posters, billboards and other campaign materials. More recently, the APC-led administration introduced a billboard and outdoor advertising policy which, in our assessment, places opposition parties at a considerable disadvantage. Government regulations must not become instruments of political exclusion,” he lamented.

He further explained: “To avoid unnecessary confrontations and possible denial of access, the PDP has increasingly resorted to using facilities and event centres belonging to its members and sympathisers, just as it has done with public institutions. We should not have to operate under such constraints in a democracy.”

Similarly, the Benue State chapter of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) has raised concerns over difficulties in securing public venues for its political activities, alleging that its request to use facilities in Buruku Local Government Area was turned down by the council chairman.

The party’s Publicity Secretary, Michael Inyaregh, who lamented the denial of access to Buruku Youth Centre to organise a consultation meeting with stakeholders from the area, explained that the party subsequently approached the management of Tombo Community Secondary School for an alternative venue, but was also denied permission.

Inyaregh explained that the council chairman hid behind the excuse that the Youth Centre was due for renovation, while the use of the secondary school could generate political tension. He added that the party is still awaiting approval to use IBB Square, Aper Aku Stadium and Machathy Stadium in Wadata, Makurdi, the state capital, for its presidential campaign launch scheduled for 7 December 2026.

Expressing optimism that the state government would grant its request to use one of the proposed venues, Inyaregh said: “The incident of the government’s denial of our request to use a public venue was in Buruku LG when we wanted to hold a consultation meeting with stakeholders from that part of the state.

When the Buruku Youth Centre was denied, we opted for Tombo Community Secondary School, which was denied again by the same chairman, whose reason was wanting to renovate the Youth Centre and avoiding political tension.

“We have currently applied for approval to use the following facilities, in order of preference: IBB Square, Aper Aku Stadium and Machathy Stadium in Wadata, directly to Governor Hyacinth Alia, and are waiting for approval. We have high hopes that a venue will be approved for us to launch our presidential campaign on 7 December in Makurdi,” he explained.

However, the Labour Party (LP) State Publicity Secretary, Ephraim Iyorhe, who argued that attacks were synonymous with the Nigerian political climate, said that since campaigns had not been fully flagged off, there had been few occasions for party members to cross paths.

He, however, admitted that there had been verbal attacks on social media, citing claims that the LP is in a coalition or some sort of strategic alliance.

“We have written a strong response to say we are not in any coalition or strategic alliance. Those are some of the subtle tactics used to shape the political landscape, disenfranchise people who are in love with the party, or create a narrative that will make people feel their candidates have sold out.

“The LP has categorically stated that it is not in any coalition or strategic alliance of any sort. If such an arrangement is to be considered, the national leadership of the party, together with the State Working Committee, which is the highest organ of the party, and all other relevant stakeholders, will be involved,” he said.

Stating that the party has not rolled out a campaign and has not been accosted or attacked in any form, he said: “At least, we have not visited any ward or LGA or even launched our campaign council. We have our campaign secretariat, and nothing has happened officially outside our secretariat. There have been no attacks, and I have not been told of any.”

Weighing in on the issues, the Benue State Police Command had earlier convened a meeting with political party chairmen, candidates, security agencies and other stakeholders in Makurdi, where they all signed a peace accord ahead of the elections.

The Commissioner of Police, CP Cletus Nwadiogbu, had urged political parties to discourage violence, political thuggery and the recruitment of criminal elements to intimidate opponents, assuring political actors that the command would remain professional and impartial in providing security for all lawful political activities.

On his part, the state governor, Rev. Fr. Hyacinth Alia, had cautioned politicians and their supporters against violence, bitterness and inflammatory rhetoric, urging them to embrace issue-based campaigns.

Governor Alia maintained that political differences should not threaten peace and security, stressing that elections should be contests of ideas and development alternatives.

He advised that political campaigns should be conducted with maturity, mutual respect and a sense of responsibility, urging the people to reject violence and be guided by issues that directly affect their welfare and the future of the state when making decisions.

Interestingly, the situation is almost the same, if not worse, in Niger State, where stakeholders are raising the alarm over political violence. The recent arrest of six youths by the Niger State Police Command for allegedly engaging in political violence in Minna, the state capital, confirmed the enormity of the political violence that has characterised the build-up to the elections in the state.

Only recently, youths in large numbers invaded the State Trade Fair Complex in the Shango area of Minna, armed with dangerous weapons, with the motive of disrupting the governorship campaign flag-off of the incumbent governor, Umaru Mohammed Bago, of the ruling APC.

However, while the heavy security presence at the venue prevented them from unleashing terror, the youths broke loose immediately after the national anthem signalled the end of the event, and hurled stones and other dangerous weapons at the crowd, chanting “ba ma so”, literally meaning “we don’t want”, as party supporters scampered for safety.

Dangerous weapons were freely used by the suspected political thugs, and before the police anti-riot squad stepped in to bring the situation under control, several people had sustained various degrees of injuries and were treated at different government medical facilities in Minna.

In a statement by its Public Relations Officer, SP Wasiu Abiodun, the state police command confirmed the arrest of six suspects in connection with the political violence.

“Police operatives of the anti-thuggery unit of the command arrested six suspects at Trade Fair Complex, Shango, who were found engaging in thuggery activities during a political campaign activity. The suspects were arrested with two cutlasses, four knives, scissors, and other dangerous weapons,” he said.

Before the violence at the APC governorship campaign flag-off, some suspected political thugs had accosted campaign vehicles belonging to the ADC in the state, heading to the party office, and damaged the entire windscreens of the three vehicles attacked.

The gang leader, popularly known as “Anasho”, was arrested by the police in connection with the alleged attack and, according to the state police command, “the suspect arrested with a cutlass is in custody for further investigation.”

The political violence is not restricted to the state capital alone. In October, supporters of the PDP governorship candidate in the state, Mohammed Nami, and of the incumbent governor, Umaru Bago, engaged each other in a fierce battle in Lapai, the headquarters of Lapai Local Government Area, leaving several supporters hospitalised with injuries.

That particular incident raised serious concern among political watchers and critical stakeholders in the area about whether political violence and intimidation are becoming part of the political atmosphere, particularly when opposition parties seek to exercise their democratic rights.

A political stakeholder in the area and former Chief Press Secretary to the late Governor Abdulkadir Kure, Mahmoud Abdullahi, while condemning the spate of political violence in an interview with the Daily Sun, argued that the new trend poses a great danger to democracy in the country.

According to him: “If the reports of violence and intimidation are confirmed, such actions must be condemned by all well-meaning citizens, regardless of their political affiliations. Democracy is built on the freedom to express opinions, support different candidates, organise political activities, and disagree peacefully without fear of attacks or intimidation.”

In his reaction, the spokesperson of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) governorship campaign council in the state, Hon. Jonathan Vatsa, blamed the desperation of political leaders to impose themselves on the people at all costs as the root cause of the rising political violence across the country, describing the development as unfortunate.

“The people, not only in Niger State, deserve a political environment where every political party can operate freely, and every citizen participates in the democratic process without feeling threatened. Political differences should never become a reason for violence, hostility, or denial of another person’s fundamental rights,” he noted.

Vatsa, who was formerly the State Publicity Secretary of the APC, nonetheless faulted his former party for the political violence experienced across the country, asking: “Is this the kind of politics APC wants to promote in Niger State? If political disagreements are answered with violence rather than dialogue, it raises serious concerns about the future of democracy and peaceful political participation in our state. No political party owns Niger State, and no individual has the right to intimidate others simply because they belong to a different political camp.”

He further pointed out that the state belongs to all its citizens, regardless of party affiliation, adding: “We, therefore, call on the relevant security agencies to investigate all these incidents and identify anyone responsible for any confirmed acts of violence, and ensure that culprits are held accountable in accordance with the law.”

While advising political leaders across party lines to always caution their supporters against violence and encourage peaceful engagement, he noted: “As we approach the 2027 general elections, Niger State and the country in general need peace, tolerance, responsible leadership, and respect for the rule of law.”

It is the same sad tale in Kogi State, where there are reported cases of attacks on opposition parties and even on ruling party factions led by former Governor Yahaya Bello and Hon. James Faleke, said not to be in the good books of the authorities in the state.

The volatility of the state has been stretched beyond limits as Bello’s faction, bent on Governor Usman Ododo’s re-election bid, battles with Faleke’s group, which is agitating for a power shift to the western senatorial district, which has not tasted power since the creation of the state 35 years ago.

The sharp division within the ruling party has led to serious friction, such that anything associated with Faleke or Senator Sunday Karimi, regarded as the mouthpiece of the power shift in the state, is treated with disdain by the other faction.

Karimi himself, who currently represents Kogi West senatorial district, has been variously attacked and booed at public rallies and functions, while a senatorial candidate outside the ruling party is said to be secretly supported to take over from him at the general elections.

In fact, an aspirant, Samuel Bamidele Aro, who allegedly withdrew from the party’s primary, is now said to be the sudden APC candidate. The case is still under litigation.

The recent vandalisation of Tinubu’s campaign office, where his pictures and those of the national chairman of the party were pulled down by unknown persons, has added another dimension to the political harassment in the Confluence State.

Although Governor Ododo immediately condemned the dastardly act and ordered security agencies to unmask those behind it, close to one month after, no one has been arrested over the incident.

The campaign secretariat, tagged Tinubu Support Group (TSG), located opposite Phase Two Gate in Lokoja, has also been vandalised, with air conditioners and other valuables reportedly stolen.

The State Administrative Secretary of the TSG, Hon. Musa Bakare, who spoke to the Daily Sun, lamented that photographs, banners and posters of President Bola Tinubu, the APC National Chairman and Hon. James Faleke were pulled down and destroyed during the attack.

Bakare, who expressed disappointment, wondering how some individuals could resort to destroying political campaign materials, noted that banners and posters cannot win elections, only the performance of individuals can.

Beyond the factional battle, the huge levies the state government imposed on campaign banners and billboards have made it almost impossible for opposition parties to campaign seamlessly in the state.

Speaking on behalf of the opposition parties, the PDP chairman, Mohammed Gambo, who expressed grave concern and complained of the exorbitant signage fees introduced by the APC-led government in the state, argued that the fees were targeted at opposition parties to weaken their campaigns and popularity.

He lamented that the Kogi State Government had announced fees of N150 million for presidential candidates, N50 million for senatorial candidates, N30 million for House of Representatives candidates and N5 million for State Assembly candidates, stressing that the fees had really hampered their campaigns.

Similarly, around July, in Ejule community of Ofu Local Government Area of the state, political thugs were said to have disrupted meetings of ADC members, which almost resulted in a breakdown of law and order in the community, reputed to be a hotbed of violence.

A similar incident happened in Gegu community in Koton Karfe Local Government Area at the same time, where a group of political thugs also attacked the campaign train of another political party. However, a more worrisome scenario was the recent incident at Dekina, where the ADC office was destroyed and set ablaze, and thugs allegedly loyal to the APC threatened members of the opposition party.

In a statement, the State Coordinator of the ADC Coalition Support Network, Hon. Ajodo Onuh, noted that the destruction of property and the threats to lives were clear indications of the thugs’ desperation to impose a one-party system on the people of Dekina.

“The ADC office in Dekina town was viciously attacked by thugs who claim to be loyal to the APC. These hoodlums, in a brazen display of intolerance, declared that they would not tolerate the presence of any other political party besides the APC in the area.

“They went further to threaten the lives of pioneers of the ADC Coalition party in Dekina town, vowing to eliminate anyone who dares to support or participate in the party’s activities. We, the ADC Coalition Support Network, condemn this attack in the strongest possible terms.

“The destruction of property and the threats to lives are clear indications of the APC-backed thugs’ desperation to impose a one-party system on the people of Dekina. This is unacceptable in a democracy, where every citizen has the right to belong to a political party of their choice,” he warned.

However, the ruling party, through its campaign spokesperson, Kingsley Fanwo, has consistently denied any attack associated with the party, insisting that Kogi is an APC state and that there is no reason to lose sleep over any opposition threats.

On his part, the State Commissioner of Police, Naziru Bello Kankarofi, has warned political parties and their candidates against violence, intimidation and destruction of campaign materials, urging them to ensure peaceful, issue-based campaigns and restrain their supporters from acts capable of disrupting public order.

The CP stressed that the police and other security agencies under the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security in the state had identified and analysed threats and black spots, and were ready to ensure a peaceful election.

In Plateau State, where there was also a display of intolerance of political opposition, exemplified by the rampant destruction of billboards and other campaign materials, the ruling APC opted to downplay the gravity, stressing that it does not imply the rejection of President Tinubu.

Although no politically motivated killings have been recorded in the state, the people have exhibited political resentment through low-level incidents of destruction of campaign materials, especially posters and billboards.

The trend became more noticeable during the recent North Central APC campaign rally. While two major political parties, the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), held town hall meetings in Jos without any incident, practically all billboards bearing the messages of both President Tinubu and Governor Caleb Mutfwang, located in strategic places in Jos metropolis, were pulled down before the recent mega rally in the state.

Even after they were replaced on the eve of the rally, the posters were removed a few hours after it. At the Zaria Road Stadium, venue of the rally, not a single campaign poster was left an hour after the rally. What remained scattered all over the venue were planks and boards used in mounting them. Even then, people scavenged what they could use as firewood from the planks and boards.

Speaking on the development, the APC Public Relations Officer in Plateau, Bako Wumanna, condemned the incidents, describing them as unfortunate. He, however, said that the destruction of the billboards did not mean that the people of Plateau had rejected Tinubu in 2027.

While describing the perpetrators as disgruntled elements who take advantage of every situation to cause chaos, he said: “Though we in the APC condemn, in strong terms, the destruction of billboards of our party or any other political party for that matter, that does not, in any way, represent the fact that the people of Plateau have rejected the President or our party.

“Let me tell you, people should not be deceived that Plateau people have rejected our party and our candidates. We will win Plateau at all levels with a higher margin than in the 2023 election,” he said, exuding confidence.

Also speaking on the trend, the PDP governorship candidate, Sunday Biggs, appealed to the electorate to stop the destruction of billboards, as posters alone do not win elections, and urged them to listen to the programmes and promises put forward by political parties in deciding who to vote for. He, however, called on the government not to shrink the political space by fixing the prices of campaign billboards far above what ordinary politicians could afford.

Biggs, who is contesting under the Saminu Turaki-led PDP, urged security agencies to apprehend and prosecute those involved in the destruction of campaign materials, stressing: “I don’t support violence in any form, but people must understand that posters alone do not win elections. If it were so, Caleb Mutfwang wouldn’t have won in 2023 because he had no posters anywhere.

What people should do is listen to the campaign promises of politicians and decide where to cast their ballot.”

In its reaction, the Police Command in Jos, however, said it had yet to receive any report of violence by any politician or political party. The Police Public Relations Officer, SP Alfred Alabo, appealed to political parties to play by the rules of the game, warning that the police would not tolerate any distractions during the election.

“We, in the Plateau State Police Command, haven’t received any official complaints about any form of political violence from anybody. Though we have seen reports of destruction of billboards on social media, we can’t take such reports as official complaints. However, we appeal to political parties to restrain their supporters from engaging in any form of violence, including destruction of billboards,” he said.

Meanwhile, both the SDP and the Action Democratic Party (ADP) have accused the APC of shrinking the political space, following the dangerous dimension that political activities have taken in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, ahead of next year’s polls.

The opposition parties lamented that they can hardly find spaces to campaign and even showcase their candidates because of the anti-democratic shenanigans deployed by the APC.

SDP spokesperson, Rufus Aiyenigba, who claimed that opposition parties were asked to pay as much as N250 million before using billboards, noted: “I was a panellist, including Bolaji Abdullahi of the ADC, the LP and the NDC, and we spoke on these issues generally: that the ruling party is undeniably stifling opposition parties and suppressing the democratic space, which is anti-democratic.

“It is not good for our democratic consolidation; it is not good for trust building. Just imagine opposition parties being asked to pay as much as N250 million per billboard. Where is the money going to come from?” Aiyenigba asked.

He stated that billboards from the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport, Abuja, to the city centre had been taken over by the APC, emphasising: “From Abuja Airport to the city centre, the whole corridor is littered with APC billboards and so on.

The question is: is this the democracy we are practising? We have condemned it.

“Nigerians should wake up because this is not the democracy we laboured for. The democratic space is strangulated, boxed out of the system, and it is not good for our democracy,” Aiyenigba noted, stressing that even without the billboards and restrictions, the SDP would continue to preach its message of hope to Nigerians through other means.

“Well, billboard or no billboard, SDP is everywhere. We are connecting with the people and taking the message of hope and farewell to poverty and insecurity across Nigeria. And people are connecting with our messages of true national retrieval,” the spokesperson said.

In terms of police restrictions and permission, he said: “There is nowhere in our law that says we have to seek permission from the police to carry out campaigns. It is just part of the shenanigans of the government in power to suppress the opposition. We are not bothered by that. We have not broken any law when we move around to campaign. The FCT is the capital city of Nigeria, and all Nigerians are entitled to use the space.”

His ADP counterpart, Sani Dawop, corroborated the concerns of opposition parties, stressing: “Most of the opposition parties cannot afford to pay for the billboards, and even when they can afford it, they will tell you that space is not available.

“Even with venues for political rallies or functions, opposition parties have difficulties even when you have your money to pay for it. In most cases, they disrupt the venue and disturb the landlords, forcing them to refund your money.

“This is done by the ruling party to emasculate the opposition parties out of existence. So, it is very unfortunate. And it is not healthy for democracy. At least the ruling party should allow people to air their opinions, and then you can go ahead and look for support from the masses.

“The cost is too high. Before they came into office, it was like. Why should it happen now? If they were denied opportunities, or if the authorities in power then denied them the opportunity or carried out undemocratic policies, would they have been in power?

“For you too, campaigning should be a privilege for every political party to enjoy. At least, they should allow the democratic space to exist for political parties to exercise their rights and carry out their programmes,” he lamented.

The post 2027: N’Central battles violence, thuggery appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: MPR: Why CBN chose stability over cheaper loan
description: For millions of Nigerians struggling with the cost of living and businesses battling expensive loans, the decision by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) on Tuesday to retain its benchmark interest rate at 23 per cent may appear difficult to understand, particularly as inflation has declined for five
content:
For millions of Nigerians struggling with the cost of living and businesses battling expensive loans, the decision by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) on Tuesday to retain its benchmark interest rate at 23 per cent may appear difficult to understand, particularly as inflation has declined for five consecutive months.

With headline inflation dropping to 14.06 per cent in October from 14.63 per cent in September, food inflation easing to 19.13 per cent and foreign reserves rising to $54.02 billion, there are signs that some of the country’s economic pressures are moderating.

Ordinarily, such improvements might encourage expectations of lower interest rates, cheaper bank loans and increased economic activity. But the CBN has chosen a different path.

At its November 23 and 24, 2026 meeting, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) retained the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) at 23 per cent, maintaining the tight monetary policy stance it believes is necessary to protect the gains recorded in the fight against inflation.

The decision raises an important question of why the CBN would keep interest rates high when inflation is falling and the economy is showing signs of improvement?

For analysts, the answer lies in the nature of Nigeria’s economic challenges, the dangers of relaxing monetary policy too early and the determination of policymakers to ensure that the current improvement in prices becomes sustainable.

Understanding the 23% interest rate

The Monetary Policy Rate is the benchmark interest rate set by the CBN to influence the cost and availability of money in the banking system.

It is one of the major instruments through which the apex bank manages inflation and other economic pressures.

When the CBN raises or maintains the benchmark rate at a high level, borrowing generally becomes more expensive for financial institutions, businesses and individuals.

The intention is to discourage excessive borrowing and spending, thereby reducing the pressure on demand for goods and services.

For instance, when businesses find it more expensive to obtain loans, they may reconsider expansion plans, reduce borrowing or postpone some investments. Individuals may equally become more cautious about taking loans to finance consumption.

The expectation is that moderating spending and demand will help slow the rate at which prices increase.

On the other hand, when inflation is sufficiently under control, the CBN can reduce interest rates to encourage borrowing, investment and economic activities.

However, the challenge is determining when it is safe to make that adjustment.

For the CBN, the latest improvement in inflation is encouraging but not enough to justify an immediate reduction in interest rates.

The committee believes that maintaining the existing rate will help anchor inflation expectations and prevent a reversal of the progress recorded so far.

Why falling inflation does not mean cheaper goods

One of the biggest misunderstandings about inflation is the belief that a decline in the inflation rate automatically means that the prices of goods and services are falling. That is not necessarily the case.

Inflation measures the rate at which the general prices of goods and services increase over a period.

When inflation falls from 14.63 per cent to 14.06 per cent, as recorded between September and October, it means prices are rising at a slower rate compared with the previous period. It does not mean that the prices of rice, bread, transport fares, rent, school fees and other household essentials have returned to their previous levels.

For example, if a household item previously sold for N10,000 increases to N12,000, a subsequent slowdown in inflation does not automatically bring its price back to N10,000.

The price may continue increasing, but at a slower pace.

This explains why many Nigerians may still feel the pressure of the high cost of living even when official inflation figures are declining.

The CBN is, therefore, concerned about ensuring that the slowdown in inflation continues until price stability becomes more firmly established.

Why CBN fears an early rate cut

The committee’s position is that reducing interest rates too early could weaken the progress made in controlling inflation.

A reduction in the benchmark rate could encourage banks to lend more, while businesses and consumers may become more willing to borrow and spend.

Although increased lending can stimulate production, investment and consumption, excessive demand without a corresponding increase in the supply of goods and services could put pressure on prices.

This is important in an economy where food supply, transportation costs, energy prices and foreign exchange conditions continue to influence the cost of doing business.

The CBN is also concerned that expectations of lower interest rates could encourage spending at a time when seasonal and election-related activities are expected to increase demand.

The MPC specifically identified the anticipated rise in spending during the end-of-year festive season and election-related activities as potential sources of inflationary pressure. Its concern is that if demand rises faster than the available supply of goods and services, businesses could increase prices, reversing some of the recent gains.

The committee, therefore, considers it necessary to maintain its current policy position until it is more confident that inflation can continue declining without additional pressure.

What the 23% rate means for businesses

While the CBN’s decision is aimed at maintaining price stability, its implications for businesses cannot be ignored.

For manufacturers, traders, small businesses and other private sector operators, the cost of obtaining loans remains an important consideration.

Businesses require financing to purchase equipment, pay workers, acquire raw materials, maintain inventory and expand operations.

When borrowing costs are high, companies may find it difficult to obtain affordable credit, while some may postpone expansion plans or depend more heavily on internally generated funds.

Small and medium-sized enterprises, which often have limited access to alternative sources of financing, can be particularly affected.

However, the CBN’s position is that controlling inflation and maintaining exchange rate stability are also important to the survival of businesses.

When prices rise rapidly, companies face uncertainty over the cost of raw materials, transportation, imported equipment and other production inputs.

Frequent exchange rate movements can equally make business planning difficult, particularly for companies that depend on imported materials.

The CBN is seeking to create a more stable economic environment in which businesses can plan and operate with greater certainty.

The difficult part is balancing the benefits of price stability against the immediate burden of expensive credit.

Why the naira and foreign reserves matter

Another important consideration behind the MPC’s decision is the need to sustain stability in the foreign exchange market.

The CBN reported that Nigeria’s gross external reserves stood at $54.02 billion as of November 17, 2026, enough to cover 10.26 months of imports of goods and services. This represents an important buffer for the economy.

Foreign reserves are the country’s stock of foreign currency and other external assets held to support international transactions and meet external obligations.

They are important because Nigeria depends on foreign exchange to pay for imported machinery, raw materials, medicines, industrial equipment and other goods.

A stronger reserve position can improve confidence in the country’s ability to meet its external obligations and withstand pressure on the foreign exchange market.

The MPC acknowledged that the improved reserve position and stronger remittance inflows would enhance the economy’s capacity to withstand external shocks.

It also expressed confidence that sustained exchange rate stability would support the fight against inflation.

The relationship between the naira and inflation is particularly important because exchange rate movements can affect the prices of imported goods and production inputs.

When the naira weakens significantly, importers may require more money to purchase the same quantity of foreign goods.

These additional costs can eventually be transferred to consumers through higher prices.

By maintaining a tight monetary policy, the CBN hopes to protect the stability achieved in the foreign exchange market and prevent developments that could trigger another round of price increases.

The importance of the CBN-NNPC agreement

The MPC also welcomed the Memorandum of Understanding between the CBN and the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC).

The agreement is designed to improve foreign exchange inflows, support financing for energy projects and strengthen macroeconomic stability.

Its successful implementation could increase the supply of foreign exchange, improve liquidity in the market and support further growth in external reserves.

The committee believes these developments could also strengthen investor confidence in the Nigerian economy.

The importance of the agreement lies in the need to strengthen foreign exchange supply through improved inflows rather than relying solely on monetary policy measures.

For Nigeria, stronger foreign exchange inflows could help reduce pressure on the market and support businesses that require foreign currency to finance imports and other international transactions.

However, the MPC stressed that effective implementation would be necessary to achieve the expected benefits.

Food supply: Another reason for optimism

Beyond interest rates and foreign reserves, the CBN is also counting on improved food supply to sustain the decline in inflation.

Food inflation fell to 19.13 per cent in October from 19.59 per cent in September, following moderation in the prices of processed food and farm produce.

The committee attributed the improvement partly to the commencement of the harvest season.

This is significant because food prices have a direct impact on household budgets and the general cost of living.

When farmers produce more food and supplies reach markets in sufficient quantities, shortages can ease and price pressures may moderate.

The CBN expects improved food supply to support the disinflation process over the short to medium term.

However, it also identified adverse weather conditions as a potential threat to the inflation outlook.

This means that maintaining the improvement will require sustained agricultural production and the avoidance of disruptions that could reduce food availability.

Are businesses growing despite tight monetary policy?

Interestingly, the CBN’s latest assessment suggests that economic activities are expanding despite the high interest rate environment.

The committee reported that Nigeria’s composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) increased to 53.2 points in October from 53.0 points in September.

The PMI is an indicator of the direction of business activities across different sectors.

A reading above 50 points generally indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 points signals contraction.

Nigeria’s October reading therefore indicates that industrial, agricultural and services activities continued to expand.

The CBN also expressed optimism about the domestic economic outlook for the rest of 2026 and into 2027.

It attributed this outlook to improved crude oil production and sustained expansion in agriculture, services and industrial activities.

For monetary authorities, the continued expansion of business activities provides some reassurance that the economy is maintaining growth momentum despite restrictive monetary conditions.

However, sustaining this expansion will require businesses to remain productive and competitive, particularly as high financing costs continue to pose challenges.

Global developments could upset calculations

The CBN is also looking beyond Nigeria’s borders in assessing the risks to price stability.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East is one of the major developments worrying the committee because of its potential impact on global energy prices.

Higher energy prices can increase production and transportation costs, putting pressure on the prices of goods and services.

Supply chain disruptions, expensive freight and rising commodity prices could equally make imported inputs more costly.

The MPC noted that global economic growth was expected to moderate in 2026 before recovering in 2027.

It also identified persistent energy price pressures, trade policy uncertainty and supply chain disruptions as risks to the global economic outlook.

For Nigeria, these developments could complicate efforts to sustain falling inflation, particularly if they lead to higher import and production costs.

What Nigerians should expect

The immediate implication of the MPC’s decision is that the CBN is not yet ready to ease its restrictive monetary policy.

The benchmark rate remains at 23 per cent, while the Cash Reserve Requirement for deposit money banks stays at 45 per cent, merchant banks at 16 per cent and non-Treasury Single Account public sector deposits at 75 per cent.

The Standing Facilities Corridor also remains at +50/-300 basis points around the MPR.

These measures reinforce the committee’s decision to maintain its current monetary policy direction.

For households, the decline in inflation offers some relief, but it does not mean that the cost of living will immediately return to previous levels. For businesses, the high interest rate environment means that access to affordable credit may remain difficult, even as improving price stability and foreign exchange conditions offer some opportunities. For investors, the stronger external reserve position and continued expansion in business activities provide encouraging signals about the economy.

Ultimately, the CBN’s November decision reflects its belief that sustaining economic stability requires patience and consistency.

The committee is betting that protecting the gains already achieved against inflation will provide a stronger foundation for sustainable economic growth than an early reduction in interest rates.

The real test, however, will be whether the country can sustain falling inflation, improve food supply, strengthen foreign exchange stability and maintain business expansion without keeping the cost of borrowing excessively high for too long.

The next MPC meeting, scheduled for February 22 and 23, 2027, will provide another opportunity to assess whether the current policy stance remains appropriate.

For now, the CBN’s message, analysts note, is that falling inflation is encouraging, but the battle for lasting price stability is not yet over.

title: Glo woos Nigerian businesses with cost-effective enterprise solutions
description:
As operating costs continue to rise across Nigeria, digital solutions provider,  Globacom has positioned its Enterprise Business arm as a vital partner for organizations seeking cost-effective digital and telecom solutions to drive growth.
Glo Enterprise delivers end-to-end ICT, telecom, and digital
content:
As operating costs continue to rise across Nigeria, digital solutions provider,  Globacom has positioned its Enterprise Business arm as a vital partner for organizations seeking cost-effective digital and telecom solutions to drive growth.

Glo Enterprise delivers end-to-end ICT, telecom, and digital services tailored for large corporations, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), and public sector institutions.

According to a Globacom statement in Lagos, Glo Enterprise is a purpose-built service department designed not just as a connectivity provider, but as a comprehensive ICT and business solutions partner that helps organisations connect better, operate smarter, optimize costs and grow faster.

The company said Glo Enterprise also powers public sector digitalization, making it ideal for government ministries and state agencies that require large-scale broadband deployment for e-governance and smart city projects.

“Glo Enterprise improves business efficiency and productivity by providing reliable and integrated telecommunications solutions that enable organisations to communicate, collaborate and operate seamlessly. With dependable voice and data services, businesses can connect employees, offices, customers and business partners more effectively, reducing communication delays and ensuring that important decisions are carried out promptly,” the statement said.

It added that its digital and cloud-enabled solutions support remote work, secure data management and the smooth running of critical business operations, while also delivering connectivity and cost optimization for banks, oil and gas firms, logistics firms and manufacturing companies.

For the financial sector, Glo Enterprise supports banking operations through dedicated internet, leased lines and data centre solutions, while in oil and gas it provides dependable connectivity across remote locations.

It also offers fleet management, vehicle tracking and delivery coordination for logistics firms, and helps manufacturers coordinate production, inventory, suppliers and distribution between factories and warehouses.

content:
From Stanley Uzoaru, Owerri Onitsha Enugu

They  were supposed to be in the lecture halls, laboratories, and libraries, shaping the next generation of doctors, lawyers, engineers, teachers, and other professionals.

But, on Thursday, November 19, the academic staff of the Imo State University (IMSU), led by professors, took to the streets of Owerri, carrying placards, chanting, and begging to be paid.

For over 102 days, lecturers at IMSU have been on strike. No lectures. No exams. No graduation. No NYSC mobilisation. Just silence on the campus that used to buzz with over 20,000 students. The strike began on August 10, 2026. Three months later, it has become a waiting game, and everyone is losing.

“Over three months at home, no lectures, no exams!” That was the cry that echoed through the streets in Owerri as lecturers under the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU), IMSU chapter, marched through the city of the Imo State capital.

They were not asking for luxury. They were asking for what they described as their rights: unpaid salaries and arrears, implementation of the new salary structure, earned academic allowances, promotion arrears, and withheld check-off dues.

At the heart of the dispute is the 2025 Federal Government-ASUU agreement, which ASUU-IMSU said the state government and university authorities have failed to implement.

The branch chairman, Stephen Oguji, had earlier disclosed that several letters and meetings with university authorities and the governing council had failed to produce a satisfactory solution. One lecturer, speaking during the protest, captured the frustration of his colleagues and their students.

“We have spent more than three months at home without lectures or examinations,” he said.

The union also kicked against conducting examinations while the strike remained unresolved, insisting that normal academic activities should not continue under the present circumstances.

The big question hanging over Owerri is simple: Who is really paying the price for this prolonged dispute? Is it the government, the university management, or the students whose future is on hold?

For the students, the answer is clear. They cannot graduate. Graduates cannot proceed to their compulsory NYSC programme. Final-year students cannot defend projects. Fresh students have no idea when they will resume.

IMSU has contributed immensely to the development of Imo State, producing graduates who now occupy important positions across government and society. It is, therefore, disappointing to many that an institution of such importance is being neglected.

A prolonged university strike goes beyond lecturers and government disagreements. It affects students, parents, families, the economy, and the future of our youth.

Across the country, the IMSU strike has sparked anger, sympathy, and frustration:

Chinagorom, a student, said Owerri, “Three months at home is no joke. The government and lecturers should find a way to settle this.”

Chiwendu on her own part said, “Students are the ones suffering while those in authority keep exchanging accusations.”

Also, Mrs Amaka, not happy about the development, said, “How can students plan their future when they don’t even know when school will reopen?”

Another parent urged the government to settle whatever the case may be.

“Government should treat education as a priority. As of the November 19 protest, the Imo State government had not issued a formal response to the specific demands raised by the protesting lecturers. The lecturers are now asking Governor Hope Uzodimma to intervene personally and ensure negotiations produce a lasting solution.

How long must the students continue to suffer for a problem they did not create?

That is the question now echoing from Owerri to Abuja. The lecturers say they want to return to class, but not on empty stomachs and broken promises. The students say they want to return to the classrooms.

Until the government, the university management, and the ASUU find a common ground, IMSU will remain a ghost town, with empty lecture halls and the professors on the streets. The government must act fast and pay the lecturers, resolve the disputes, and reopen the institution.

The post IMSU strike: Day professors took to the streets over unpaid salaries appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Greenwich Bank opens Warri, Uyo branches, eyes 5 more cities
description:
Greenwich Bank Limited has intensified its national expansion drive with the opening of branches in Warri, Delta State, and Uyo, Akwa Ibom State.
It also targets five additional cities in its quest to establish a stronger presence in Nigeria’s commercial banking sector.
In a statement signed by Ozen
content:
Greenwich Bank Limited has intensified its national expansion drive with the opening of branches in Warri, Delta State, and Uyo, Akwa Ibom State.

It also targets five additional cities in its quest to establish a stronger presence in Nigeria’s commercial banking sector.

In a statement signed by Ozena Utulu, Head, Corporate Communications of Greenwich Holdings, the new outlets bring the Bank’s physical network to seven, following the opening of five branches in Lagos, Ondo and Ekiti States in October.

The Bank plans to extend its operations to Asaba, Port Harcourt, Abuja, Benin and Ibadan in the coming months.

Speaking at the commissioning of the Warri branch, Group Chairman of Greenwich Holdings, Kayode Falowo, described the Niger Delta as a strategic market, citing its economic importance, entrepreneurial potential and concentration of business activities across oil and gas, maritime services and logistics.

He said Warri’s economic prospects extended beyond its natural resources to the entrepreneurs, traders, contractors, service providers and other businesses driving commercial activities in the region.

According to Falowo, Greenwich’s more than three decades of financial services experience, combined with its commercial banking mandate, positions it to provide a wider range of financial solutions to individuals, small businesses and corporate customers.

At the Uyo branch commissioning, Chairman of Greenwich Bank, Segun Oloketuyi, said the commercial banking licence would enable the institution to extend its 32 years of financial services expertise to a broader customer base, including farmers, traders, civil servants, students and entrepreneurs.

He identified credit facilities, agricultural and SME financing, trade and treasury services, salary solutions and digital banking as some of the services through which the Bank intends to support businesses and individuals.

Oloketuyi added that the Bank would leverage the resources and expertise of the Greenwich Group to help local enterprises access financial services beyond conventional lending.

Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, represented by the Commissioner for Finance, Hon. Fidelis Telije, who commissioned the Warri branch, welcomed the Bank’s entry into the state, describing it as an opportunity to strengthen financial services and support economic development.

He urged residents and businesses to take advantage of the new outlet, particularly small businesses, young entrepreneurs and women-owned enterprises that require financial support to expand operations and create jobs.

Similarly, Akwa Ibom State Governor, Pastor Umo Eno, represented by the Commissioner for Finance, Emem Almond Bob, described the Uyo branch as a significant development that would improve access to banking services and credit, support business growth and potentially enhance the state’s internally generated revenue.

The Oruesen of Okere-Urhobo, Warri, His Royal Majesty (Dr.) Ogheneochuko Morris, also welcomed the Bank’s establishment in the community, expressing confidence that its presence would create opportunities for businesses and residents.

Group Managing Director of Greenwich Holdings, Oyewale Ariyibi, said the Bank’s entry into the region would support the emergence of new businesses and strengthen existing enterprises through specialised financial services.

He noted that the Group’s long-standing experience in the financial services industry had provided valuable insights into regional business dynamics, which would inform its approach to supporting enterprises across different sectors.

Managing Director of Greenwich Bank, Benson Ogundeji, said the Warri and Uyo branches would deepen customer engagement and bring financial solutions closer to businesses and individuals in the South-South.

He identified oil and gas, maritime services, agriculture, manufacturing, trade, logistics and small and medium-sized enterprises as priority sectors requiring responsive financial support.

Ogundeji stressed that the Bank’s expansion strategy went beyond physical branch openings to building lasting customer relationships and deploying technology-driven solutions that promote enterprise growth and financial inclusion.

Other dignitaries at the commissioning ceremonies included Greenwich Bank Directors Olutoyin Okeowo, Anthony Uponi, Daisy Ekineh and Anselm Orazulike, alongside senior Greenwich executives and guests from the business community.

Greenwich Holdings, the Bank’s parent company, has more than three decades of experience in financial services, with interests spanning commercial banking, capital markets, asset management and securities.

The post Greenwich Bank opens Warri, Uyo branches, eyes 5 more cities appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: The powerful trio, CHOGM, OIF and the world
description:
ByVictor C. Ariole
New world order is taking shape and Africa seems to be left out. The world order that ushered in United Nations Organisation that has steered the world away from another global conflagration for 80 years is about to be rested as the most powerful trio — USA, China and Russia — put
content:
ByVictor C. Ariole

New world order is taking shape and Africa seems to be left out. The world order that ushered in United Nations Organisation that has steered the world away from another global conflagration for 80 years is about to be rested as the most powerful trio — USA, China and Russia — put heads together (16–19th November, 2026) in Shenzhen, China. They claim it is about the reduction of nuclear warheads, which three of them have in quantum and capable of using them for evil ends like Hitler contemplated before USA finally used it in Japan in the Second World War.

For Hitler, scientists advised him to first invade Norway and secure the provision of heavy water that serves for coolant for them to really make it possible, as Norway was in lead in production of heavy water. So, between a Nazi or Fascist-led world order and USA-NATO liberal-led world order, the latter prevailed. It was a function of head-headed force, albeit acceptable between two evils. Head-headed in the sense that colonial masters — Britain and France who are in control of Africa — joined forces with USA to prevail.

Today the most powerful trio are not colonial masters but are military occupiers of both terrestrial spaces and celestial spaces with over 10,000 satellites in the celestial space, and concentrated on Africa’s sphere as the most effective and efficient sphere to cluster satellites. The fact is that the efficiency and effectiveness of Africa, not yet explored by its scientists, is that while Africa sees the Sun and the Moon all year round, China, Russia and to some extent USA do not see them all year round; a great blessing Africa is not capitalising on, and the reason why Africa, to them, must be marginalised and be used for their own interest — terrestrial and celestial-wise.

Like Hitler wanted to occupy Norway to actualise his own world order, the trio are seeking cooperation from one another to take hold of Greenland and its natural resources (USA), to take hold of Ukraine and its great resources (Russia), and to take hold of Taiwan and its great chip production (China). For them, Africa is taken for granted as a shareable space like it was done in Berlin in 1884-1885. Unfortunately, the Germany of Otto von Bismarck, who chaired the sharing of Africa, has no space in Africa today to call his own. Hopefully, China could learn to chair and not lose.

Today, both terrestrial and celestial spread, China is the least spread among the trio of most powerful as it chairs their interests for further occupation of spaces — terrestrial and celestial. Even when USA freed itself from British occupation on 4th July, 1776, it was not invited for the Bismarck conference of 1884–1885.

So, no European country among the trio; Russia is Eurasia. The most powerful trio are heralding a new world order, as UN continues warning them on how they are breaching the peace of the world by disregarding international laws — China breaching Human Rights and International Labour Laws, Russia and USA breaching Sanctity of Sovereignty and Rules of Engagement Laws and condemning International Court of Justice.

Britain andFrance are under Left-Party regimes and are greatly associated with UN warnings; and they are leading members, if not the leaders, of Commonwealth of Nations, and Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), respectively. The Commonwealth, under CHOGM (Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting), held their meeting in the Caribbean Islands of Antigua and Barbuda on 1st–4th, November, 2026. The OIF held their meeting in Phnom Penh in Cambodia 15–16, November, 2026.

Coincidentally, the three meetings in November are unknowingly forming a quadratic assembling for a quadratic equation that the world mathematicians should be interested in unravelling, the way Newton, Descartes and Copernicus led in calculus that determines differentials, limits and integration of the observable cosmos, leading to systematic approach of subduing spaces, and exploration-cum-expansion conquest.

In all their considerations, someone should tell them that Africa is the mid-point without which other extensions and differentials could be meaningless as exemplified by OIF meeting.

CHOGM, with 56 members, still sees the king of United Kingdom as the mid-point, and he is the Head of State of about 15 of them, including Canada and Australia.

In OIF, 53 members, five associates and 32 observers, grouping almost half of the world’s recognised 193 countries in the UN, the African presence is highly appreciated to an extent that President Macron’s wish to impose a Romanian leader as a consensus leader against an African leader of either Rwandan or Congolese candidate failed woefully. Since inception on March 20, 1970, its founding fathers — Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal, Habib Bourguiba of Tunisia, Hamani Diori of Niger, Norodom Sihanouk of Cambodia — expect it to be of non-colonial imposition and it has been headed mostly by a Secretary General, and mostly Africans or Africans in the Diaspora like Michaëlle Jean—also former Governor General of Canada.

Currently, a Rwandan lady, Louise Mushikiwabo, is the head. Greater number of African countries are involved in OIF than in Commonwealth, even as France holds on to its overseas collectivity like Réunion and Mayotte in Africa; Guadeloupe, Martinique and French Guiana in the Caribbean; French Polynesia, Melanesia, New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna and Clipperton Island in the Pacific; they are not subjects of any king or maximum ruler. It also shows that OIF is greatly a composite alternative with Commonwealth — all having a great number of African countries and African Diaspora — to exert a worthy lobby group in dousing the seemingly destructive and UN centrifugal positions of USA, Russia and China.

Africa suffers in their warmongering attitudes, and Europe that leads in both CHOGM and OIF, having been the master exploiter of Africa, shows a better sympathy for Africa than the new exploiters, who already are posing great threat to Africa’s integration process as they create exploitation matrix in Africa — West Africa scrambled by Russia and China; East Africa scrambled by USA and China; Central Africa scrambled by Russia and China; Islands in Indian Ocean scrambled by USA; and Maghreb (North) scrambled by Russia and USA. Africa should use CHOGM and OIF to arrest, further, its terrestrial and celestial degradation. Africa must interrogate the brewing new economic order that is bent on seeing a more transhumanistic economic order;and using mostly African resources; ‘Agenda 2063’, the year the powerful ones programmed for Africa to reach a threshold of economic sustainability must be jettisoned and better Agenda, reducing the year, be activated.

• Ariole, PhD, Professor of French and Francophone Studies, University of Lagos

title: Who polices the governors?
description:
By Pat Onukwuli

Nigeria stands at the threshold of a consequential constitutional transformation. The National Assembly’s passage of the State Police Bill, endorsed by all 36 state Houses of Assembly, signals a departure from decades of centralised policing. Conceived in response to the grim realit
content:
By Pat Onukwuli

Nigeria stands at the threshold of a consequential constitutional transformation. The National Assembly’s passage of the State Police Bill, endorsed by all 36 state Houses of Assembly, signals a departure from decades of centralised policing. Conceived in response to the grim realities of banditry, kidnapping, terrorism and communal violence, the reform promises to bring security closer to the people. Yet beneath this laudable ambition lies a troubling contradiction: will decentralising policing decentralise security or merely decentralise the instruments of coercion?

The argument for state police is compelling. Nigeria’s vast geography, diverse communities and increasingly complex security challenges have exposed the limitations of policing a federation of over 200 million people predominantly from Abuja. Officers familiar with local languages, terrain and social dynamics possess advantages that distant command structures cannot easily replicate. Security, after all, is most effective when intelligence travels faster than insecurity.

The proposed constitutional framework recognises this reality without abolishing federal policing. Section 214 envisages complementary Federal and State Police Services, with the former retaining responsibility for federal crimes, terrorism, interstate security and national interests. Importantly, State Police Services cannot commence operations without meeting prescribed national standards. Thus, decentralisation is intended to complement, rather than displace, federal authority.

Herein lies the catch. Nigeria’s governors, frequently described as the chief security officers of their states, have long complained of responsibility without corresponding operational authority. State policing promises to correct that imbalance. Yet authority without restraint can transform today’s protector into tomorrow’s persecutor. The same institution established to apprehend kidnappers could conceivably intimidate political opponents, suppress dissent, manipulate elections or enforce questionable land acquisitions.

Greek mythology offers an instructive parallel in Talos, the bronze giant entrusted with protecting Crete. Patrolling its shores against intruders, his formidable protective powers could also become instruments of destruction against perceived enemies. Yet his vulnerability lay not in any lack of strength but in the fragility of the mechanism controlling him. Nigeria’s emerging state police must avoid becoming modern-day Taloses: powerful enough to confront criminals yet insufficiently restrained from turning against the very citizens they were established to protect.

Significantly, the Bill anticipates these dangers. Section 215(8) prohibits unlawful or partisan policing directives, while subsection (9) permits police commanders to challenge questionable instructions. Subsection (11) further protects State Police Commanders against arbitrary removal through requirements for due process, a recommendation from the National Police Council, and legislative approval. These provisions acknowledge that executive authority must remain subordinate to constitutional restraint.

Nevertheless, safeguards on paper do not necessarily translate into safeguards in practice. State Police Service Commissions must be genuinely independent, ensuring that recruitment, promotion and discipline reflect professionalism rather than political loyalty. Section 204(1A), as proposed, protects their procedural autonomy from gubernatorial control, while Section 216 establishes national minimum standards for training, conduct, use of force and accountability. Their effectiveness, however, will depend on institutional integrity and enforceable oversight.

Equally important is the relationship between federal and state police. Jurisdictions must be clearly delineated, intelligence shared, and operations coordinated to avoid competing commands. Section 214(10) permits exceptional federal intervention where state policing collapses or becomes an instrument of systematic rights violations or political intimidation. Such intervention must remain proportionate, temporary and subject to judicial review, lest federal oversight become another instrument of political interference.

Funding presents another formidable challenge. Policing is a continuous public obligation, not a ceremonial project inaugurated with fanfare. Remuneration, training, communications, forensic facilities and operational mobility demand sustainable financing. In states already struggling with recurrent expenditure, inadequately funded police formations risk becoming vulnerable to corruption, patronage and predatory enforcement. An officer uncertain of tomorrow’s salary may struggle to resist today’s inducement.

Ultimately, genuine federalism requires more than relocating uniforms and command headquarters. It demands institutional independence, fiscal responsibility, legislative scrutiny and respect for fundamental rights. Without these foundations, Nigeria risks exchanging the inefficiencies of centralised policing for the excesses of localised repression.

Above all, success must be measured against tangible outcomes: fewer kidnappings, safer highways, protected communities, improved emergency responses, credible investigations and restored public confidence. The number of state police commands inaugurated, officers recruited or vehicles commissioned cannot substitute for these results.

The passage of the Bill and presidential assent would therefore mark the beginning, not the accomplishment, of reform. Nigeria does not merely need more police; it needs better policing. The objective must be security without oppression, authority without arbitrariness, and decentralisation without tyranny. The primary question is not whether governors should have police but whether citizens will be protected from both criminals and the possible excesses of those empowered to police them.

•Dr Onukwuli is a legal scholar and public affairs analyst. Email: patonukwuli2003@yahoo.co.uk

The post Who polices the governors? appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Tompolo mobilises Rivers for Tinubu, donates 30 campaign vehicles
description:
From Fred Itua
Grand Patron of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, High Chief Oweizidei Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, has inaugurated the Rivers State chapter of the movement as part of efforts to mobilise grassroots support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ahead of the 2027 general elections.
content:
From Fred Itua

Grand Patron of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, High Chief Oweizidei Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, has inaugurated the Rivers State chapter of the movement as part of efforts to mobilise grassroots support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Represented by Chief Kestine Pondi, Managing Director, Tantita Security Services, he said the movement was established to take the President’s campaign directly to the people through door-to-door engagement, persuasion and mobilisation.

Tompolo disclosed that Rivers State was the 32nd state being visited by the movement and announced the provision of 30 campaign vehicles equipped with speakers, generators, amplifiers and microphones to facilitate its operations across the state.

He urged members to take the campaign to their homes, families, neighbours and communities, stressing the need to convince voters through constructive engagement rather than confrontation.

He expressed confidence in the movement’s ability to secure support for Tinubu in Rivers State.

Tompolo further called on members of the newly inaugurated chapter to work with the APC structure in the state, adding that the movement was seeking another four-year mandate for the President to consolidate on his administration’s policies.

Earlier, the National Coordinator of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, Comr. Sunday Adekanbi, said the movement was in Rivers State to engage residents on the policies and achievements of the Tinubu administration and the need to support the President for a second term.

Adekanbi cited the removal of fuel subsidy, increased revenue allocation to states and local governments, the student loan scheme, local government autonomy and economic reforms as reasons Nigerians should support the administration.

He urged members to educate voters on the policies without engaging in unnecessary arguments.

The National Coordinator also called on Rivers residents to support the APC governorship candidate, Hon. Kingsley Ogundu Chinda, describing him as a candidate with the interest of the state at heart, urging eligible voters to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) and participate actively in the 2027 elections.

Similarly, the Rivers State APC governorship candidate, Kingsley Chinda, tasked members of the movement to take the campaign to every household and community, noting that his 15 years in the National Assembly had given him considerable experience in the country’s economic and political affairs.

Chinda defended the removal of fuel subsidy and other economic reforms, arguing that they were necessary to address the country’s financial challenges.

He further urged campaigners to explain the policies to residents and encourage them to understand the administration’s approach to economic recovery.

In the same vein, the Governor of Rivers State, Siminalayi Fubara, who was represented by the Deputy Governor, Prof. Ngozi Nma Odu, commended Tompolo for initiating the movement, describing the inauguration as an important step towards strengthening grassroots political participation, unity and democratic engagement.

Fubara urged the newly appointed coordinators and members to demonstrate commitment, discipline, integrity and dedication to service, stressing that the movement must establish its presence in every ward, local government and community through peaceful and inclusive mobilisation.

The post Tompolo mobilises Rivers for Tinubu, donates 30 campaign vehicles appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.
