title: 2027: Group seeks church backing for Tinubu, Hamzat
description: The Lagos State Directorate of Christian Affairs of the Renewed Hope Ambassadors has begun mobilising Christian leaders, traditional rulers and community stakeholders for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election and the governorship ambition of former Deputy Governor, Kadri Hamzat, ahead of the 2027 gene
content:
The Lagos State Directorate of Christian Affairs of the Renewed Hope Ambassadors has begun mobilising Christian leaders, traditional rulers and community stakeholders for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election and the governorship ambition of former Deputy Governor, Kadri Hamzat, ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The directorate called for stronger grassroots support across Lagos’ three senatorial districts, local government areas and wards, urging religious and traditional institutions to lend their influence to the political campaigns.

The mobilisation was announced at an event tagged ‘Evening with Change Agents’, held in Lagos on Sunday, where the group also solicited financial and logistical support for its political outreach and proposed distribution of educational materials and food assistance to vulnerable residents.

In his address, the Director of the Directorate, Rev. Dr Sam Ogedengbe, said the organisation was committed to taking the Renewed Hope message to communities through sustained engagement and interventions aimed at improving people’s lives.

He urged Nigerians to support Tinubu’s second-term ambition, arguing that continuity was necessary for the administration’s economic reforms and other policy initiatives to achieve their intended objectives.

Ogedengbe also declared the directorate’s support for Hamzat’s governorship ambition, describing the former deputy governor as an experienced administrator with the leadership capacity to sustain Lagos’ development.

He appealed to Christian leaders, traditional rulers, political stakeholders and community influencers to strengthen mobilisation efforts ahead of the elections.

The Royal Father of the Day, the Alara of Ilara, Epe, Oba Olufolarin Ogunsanwo, also urged Christian faithful to pray for Tinubu, Vice-President Kashim Shettima and Hamzat, while calling for peaceful and credible elections in 2027.

The monarch described the political office holders being celebrated at the gathering as worthy ambassadors who had performed creditably in their respective positions.

He also encouraged religious and grassroots political leaders to sustain their contributions, saying the recognition of their efforts should spur them to greater service.

Beyond the political campaign, the directorate announced plans to distribute exercise books to schoolchildren and provide palliatives to elderly and vulnerable residents.

Ogedengbe described the educational intervention as an investment in children’s future, noting that access to basic learning materials could ease the financial burden on parents and support pupils’ participation in school.

He said elderly citizens also deserved practical assistance and recognition for their contributions to society.

The gathering featured the presentation of awards to individuals recognised for their contributions to humanitarian activities, community development and social impact.

Among the dignitaries were the Chairman of the Occasion, Prince Tajudeen Oluyole Olusi; the Lagos State Ambassador of the directorate, Tayo Akinmade Ayinde; and industrialist and philanthropist, Razak Akanni Okoya, who attended with his wife, Folashade Noimot Okoya.

Ogedengbe acknowledged Ayinde’s financial assistance and provision of a branded vehicle to support the directorate’s mobilisation activities.

He also appealed to the Okoya family, corporate organisations and other Nigerians to provide additional vehicles to facilitate outreach across the state’s three senatorial districts.

According to him, the directorate requires more financial and logistical support to expand its political engagement and humanitarian programmes, including the distribution of exercise books, food items and youth empowerment initiatives.

He called for donations of educational materials, food supplies, vehicles, professional services and financial assistance, saying available resources were insufficient to meet the demands of the proposed interventions.

The directorate also commended its coordinators and volunteers, particularly the Lagos Central Senatorial Director, Rev. Dr Michael Akintola, and other senatorial, local government and ward coordinators.

Ogedengbe urged members to remain united and committed to peaceful democratic participation, while encouraging eligible Nigerians to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards and mobilise their communities to participate in the electoral process.

The post 2027: Group seeks church backing for Tinubu, Hamzat appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: ‘Banks must turn N4.65tn capital boost into more loans’
description:
ENY Consulting Inc. CEO and Business Analysis School Founder, Eno Eka, tells JUSTICE OKAMGBA how banks can leverage technology to boost efficiency, SME lending, customer experience and employment

Nigerian banks raised N4.65tn through the recapitalisation exercise. What tangible benefits should Nige
content:
ENY Consulting Inc. CEO and Business Analysis School Founder, Eno Eka, tells JUSTICE OKAMGBA how banks can leverage technology to boost efficiency, SME lending, customer experience and employment

Nigerian banks raised N4.65tn through the recapitalisation exercise. What tangible benefits should Nigerians expect from this capital injection?

Nigerians should expect that the capital will lead to increased access to financial services. Recapitalisation is not the finish line; it is the starting point. A stronger balance sheet should mean more lending to businesses and households, more reliable digital services, and banks able to finance bigger projects. The real test is simple: are more small businesses getting loans, are more young people getting hired, and is banking getting faster and cheaper for the ordinary customer? If the capital simply sits in safe government securities, Nigerians will have paid for strength they never feel.

What strategies can banks adopt to deploy their new capital towards expanding credit access for small businesses, especially the estimated 80 per cent of MSMEs that remain excluded from formal lending?

This is the most urgent question. In 2025, Nigeria’s biggest banking groups recorded the five lowest loan-to-deposit ratios among leading African lenders, as recapitalisation requirements and balance-sheet pressures held back lending.

Most MSMEs are not excluded due to poor risk assessment. They are excluded because banks cannot see them. Their sales run through POS terminals, transfers and mobile wallets, not audited accounts. Banks should use the new capital to build credit models on that transaction data instead of demanding collateral most small businesses do not have.

They should design products around how MSMEs actually earn: short-cycle working capital, invoice financing and seasonal facilities. And they should partner with fintechs and co-operatives that already know these businesses. Lending to MSMEs is a data and process problem before it is a capital problem.

Beyond raising capital, what operational weaknesses must Nigerian banks address to improve lending, reduce costs and serve customers more efficiently?

There are three. First, manual and fragmented processes: a loan application that touches too many hands and systems is slow, expensive and error-prone. Second, legacy technology cannot share data across departments, so the bank does not have one view of its customer. Third, a skills gap between the people who understand the business and the people who build the technology.

When I led a $6bn-plus core banking transformation in Canada, the technology was rarely the hardest part. Redesigning processes and getting people to work differently was. Banks that fix the process first will get far more from every naira they invest.

You have stressed the need for banks to upgrade their core banking infrastructure. What financial and operational losses do outdated systems impose on Nigerian banks, and what tangible improvements should customers expect from modernisation?

The clearest signal of the cost is what banks are already paying to fix the problem. Six major Nigerian banks spent N268.7bn on technology in 2024, largely on core banking upgrades, and much of that software is priced in dollars, so its cost has nearly doubled with the naira’s devaluation. Ten banks spent another N177.91bn on technology in the first quarter of 2026 alone.

The hidden cost shows up elsewhere: failed and reversed transactions, downtime, slow loan decisions, and staff doing manually what a modern system does in seconds. You can see it in efficiency. Across ten leading banks, the average cost-to-income ratio is close to 50 per cent, while the most efficient bank runs at 28 per cent. Much of that gap comes down to process and technology.

For customers, modernisation should mean real-time transactions that do not fail, faster account opening and loan decisions, fewer branch visits, and products designed around how people actually earn. But a core banking replacement is not an IT project. It is a business transformation, and banks that redesign their processes first get far more from every naira they spend on technology.

As banks expand their use of artificial intelligence and automation, which job categories are most likely to face displacement, and what emerging career opportunities could these technologies create for Nigerian professionals?

The most exposed roles are built on repetitive, rules-based work: data entry, routine reconciliations, basic customer enquiries, document checks and parts of back-office operations.

But AI does not remove the need for people; it changes what people do. The growing roles are business analysts, process improvement specialists, data analysts, AI operations and governance professionals, risk and compliance experts who understand technology, and relationship managers who advise rather than just process.

I run my own business with more than 50 AI agents, and every one of them still needs a human owner who decides what it should do and checks the results. That ownership is where the new jobs are.

You have emphasised the need for banks to invest in business analysts and transformation specialists. Does Nigeria have an adequate pool of skilled professionals to drive the banking industry’s digital transformation?

Not yet at the scale the industry needs. The talent is there, but demand is moving faster than the pipeline. I started as an accountant in Nigeria who felt stuck, and business analysis changed my career.

Through Business Analysis School, we have trained more than 100,000 professionals across over 90 countries, including at our training centre in Victoria Island, Lagos. Many Nigerians who build these skills are hired by global employers, which is good for them but widens the local gap.

Banks should stop competing only for finished talent and start building it: reskill existing staff, partner with training providers, and create clear career paths so skilled people stay.

How can banks harness AI and automation to boost productivity while safeguarding jobs, particularly for young Nigerians seeking to enter the labour market?

It comes down to planning. First, map every role before automating it, and decide in advance where affected staff will be redeployed. Second, reskill before you replace: an operations officer who understands the bank’s processes is an excellent candidate to become a business analyst or AI operations.

The post ‘Banks must turn N4.65tn capital boost into more loans’ appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Daura emir suspended, faces sexual assault probe
description:
The Katsina State Government has constituted a committee to investigate the sexual assault allegation made by a Polish tourist, Mirka Czee, against the Emir of Daura, Alhaji Umar Farouk Umar.
The government also announced the suspension of all official engagements and travel by the monarch pending t
content:
The Katsina State Government has constituted a committee to investigate the sexual assault allegation made by a Polish tourist, Mirka Czee, against the Emir of Daura, Alhaji Umar Farouk Umar.

The government also announced the suspension of all official engagements and travel by the monarch pending the outcome of the investigation.

The decision was contained in a press release issued on Tuesday by the state Commissioner for Information, Culture and Tourism, Dr Bala Zango.

According to the statement, Governor Dikko Radda directed the establishment of the committee to investigate the allegations and advise the government on the appropriate course of action.

“The Katsina State Government, under the leadership of His Excellency, Governor Malam Dikko Umaru Radda, has expressed significant displeasure and concern over the purported viral allegations of sexual assault involving the Emir of Daura, Alhaji Umar Farouk Umar, and a foreign tourist,” the statement said.

The government said it was taking the allegations seriously, adding that the committee would examine the matter and submit its findings and recommendations.

It further assured residents that the outcome of the investigation would be implemented.

“The government wishes to assure the public that justice will be served and that the outcome of the committee’s findings and recommendations will be fully implemented,” the statement added.

The state government, however, urged members of the public to remain calm, law-abiding and continue with their normal activities while the investigation was ongoing.

The development follows the circulation of a video in which Czee accused the traditional ruler of sexually assaulting her during a visit to his palace.

The Polish tourist, who was born in the Czech Republic, had said she was left alone with the Emir after being shown around the palace and its surroundings.

She alleged that he held her hand, hugged and kissed her on the cheek before touching her breasts without her consent.

Czee said she recorded part of the encounter using Meta smart glasses and later shared the footage on social media, explaining that she wanted to speak out about her experience and raise awareness about unwanted touching.

The Daura Emirate Council had earlier said it was reviewing the video to establish its authenticity and determine whether it had been manipulated or artificially generated.

The council, through its spokesperson, Ibrahim Daura, said it would examine the footage before making a formal pronouncement.

An unnamed source in the Emir’s palace had also denied the allegation, saying there was nothing of the sort during the tourist’s visit.

Meanwhile, Amnesty International Nigeria called on the Katsina State Government and the police to conduct a transparent and independent investigation into the allegation.

As of the time the government issued its statement, it had not disclosed the composition of the investigative committee or the timeline for submitting its report.

The post Daura emir suspended, faces sexual assault probe appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Umza Air deploys standby aircraft to curb flight disruptions
description:
Umza Air has deployed a backup aircraft to reduce flight disruptions and ensure passengers are not stranded when unexpected operational difficulties disrupt its scheduled services.
The airline said the initiative was part of its commitment to delivering reliable, affordable and efficient air travel,
content:
Umza Air has deployed a backup aircraft to reduce flight disruptions and ensure passengers are not stranded when unexpected operational difficulties disrupt its scheduled services.

The airline said the initiative was part of its commitment to delivering reliable, affordable and efficient air travel, stressing that passengers should not bear the full brunt of operational difficulties when they choose to fly.

Head of Commercial, Umza Aviation Services Limited, Awotunde Adedeji, disclosed this during an engagement with aviation journalists, where he outlined the airline’s operational philosophy, commercial strategy and expansion plans.

Adedeji said the decision to maintain a standby aircraft was a deliberate move by the airline’s chairman to address one of the recurring frustrations of air travellers: flight disruptions and the uncertainty that often follows.

He said, “Our chairman was very clear about his vision. He wants to be able to transport people from one place to another quickly and affordably. That is the vision guiding what we do as an airline.

“One of the things we are doing differently is that we have a standby aircraft in case anything happens. We understand that aircraft can develop technical issues or operational challenges, but our passengers should not always have to suffer the consequences through prolonged disruptions.”

According to him, the standby arrangement is designed to provide an operational alternative whenever unforeseen circumstances affect scheduled flights, reinforcing the airline’s emphasis on reliability.

“Air travel is not just about selling tickets and moving passengers. It is about the confidence people have when they book a flight. They want to know that they can plan their journeys, attend to their businesses, meet family obligations and get to their destinations without unnecessary uncertainty,” Adedeji said.

He explained that Umza Air’s commercial strategy revolves around three major priorities: affordability, connectivity and operational reliability.

“We know the realities of the Nigerian aviation market. Passengers are becoming increasingly sensitive to ticket prices, delays and the overall value they get for their money. Our responsibility is to make flying accessible without losing sight of the standards required to run a safe and sustainable airline,” he stated.

Adedeji maintained that the airline was determined to offer competitive fares despite mounting operational pressures, adding that affordability remained central to the chairman’s vision.

“Our objective is to ensure that ordinary Nigerians can also enjoy the benefits of air transportation. We do not want flying to become something that is completely beyond the reach of the average traveller. We have to be commercially responsible, but we also want passengers to feel that they are getting value for their money,” he said.

Speaking on network expansion, the commercial chief said Umza Air currently serves nine domestic destinations: Abuja, Kano, Birnin Kebbi, Maiduguri, Yola, Sokoto, Lagos, Ilorin and Gombe.

He said the airline was deliberately developing its network around important commercial and regional centres, with particular attention to improving connections between Lagos and major northern cities.

He said, “People travel for different reasons. Some are going for business, others for family engagements, government activities and other economic purposes. We want to make those journeys easier and provide alternatives to the long and often stressful road trips between these destinations.

“We are not interested in opening routes just for the sake of announcing new destinations. We must understand passenger demand, identify markets that can sustain operations and provide frequencies that respond to the actual needs of travellers.”

On fleet expansion, he disclosed that the airline had finalised an acquisition deal for Airbus A320-200 and A340-600 aircraft, describing the move as a significant boost to its operational capacity and growth plans.

He explained that the A320-200 would be deployed for regular commercial flights, while the A340-600 would serve the airline’s 2027 Hajj operations and future pilgrimage exercises.

“The acquisition is an important part of our long-term growth strategy. The A320-200 will support our scheduled commercial operations, while the A340-600 is intended for our Hajj operations in 2027 and subsequent seasons,” he said.

According to him, the planned fleet expansion would enable the airline to increase its operational capacity, diversify its services and explore opportunities in the international aviation market.

Adedeji, however, cautioned that sustainable growth required more than acquiring aircraft, noting that investments must be supported by careful planning, strong partnerships and sound commercial decisions.

He also identified rising operating costs, foreign exchange pressures, aircraft maintenance expenses, infrastructure limitations and increasing aviation service charges as some of the major challenges confronting Nigerian airlines.

“These are realities that affect operators across the industry. The cost of running an airline is enormous, and these pressures eventually have implications for ticket prices and the overall experience of passengers,” he said.

He assured journalists that Umza Air would maintain an open communication channel with the media, insisting that the airline had no expectation of receiving only favourable coverage.

He stated, “We do not expect every report about Umza Air to be complimentary. Constructive criticism is necessary because it helps us identify areas where we need to improve. What we value is accuracy, fairness and balanced reporting.

“Where there are concerns about our operations, services or commercial decisions, we encourage journalists to reach out to us so that the relevant facts can be established. We believe that engagement is better than allowing misinformation or unanswered questions to shape public perception.”

The post Umza Air deploys standby aircraft to curb flight disruptions appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: CAPPA to Nigeria, Africa: Reject climate loans, demand rich nations’ accountability
description:
… Says Africa bears climate burden despite contributing less than 4% of global emissionsBy Chioma Obinna



Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) has urged Nigeria and other African governments to reject climate finance agreements that deepen their debt burdens, calling on
content:
… Says Africa bears climate burden despite contributing less than 4% of global emissions
By Chioma Obinna

Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) has urged Nigeria and other African governments to reject climate finance agreements that deepen their debt burdens, calling on wealthy industrialised nations to take responsibility for the climate crisis they largely created.

The organisation also urged African leaders to unite ahead of next year’s 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32) in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and demand measurable financial commitments from developed countries to support climate adaptation, mitigation and recovery from climate-related disasters.

CAPPA made the call in a statement on Tuesday, November 24, following what it described as disappointing outcomes from COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, which ended on Sunday, November 22.

It said the conference exposed the widening divide between wealthy industrialised countries and climate-vulnerable nations, particularly across Africa and the Global South.

According to the organisation, the summit’s emphasis on investment announcements, energy transition partnerships and implementation rhetoric failed to address the fundamental injustice of developed countries evading their historical climate responsibilities while developing nations struggle to finance their response to the crisis.

CAPPA’s Associate Director and Climate and Environment Programme Manager, Olamide Martins Ogunlade, said it was unacceptable for wealthy nations to pursue their industrial and energy interests while shifting the financial burden of decarbonisation to countries that contributed least to global warming.

“Climate finance that comes in the form of commercial loans is not solidarity. It is another debt burden imposed on countries already paying an enormous price for a crisis they did little to create.

“African governments should not have to borrow their way out of a climate emergency largely driven by the industrialisation and fossil fuel dependence of wealthy nations,” Ogunlade said.

The organisation noted that Africa contributes less than four per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions but suffers disproportionately from the consequences of climate change, losing an estimated two to five per cent of its Gross Domestic Product annually to climate extremes.

Despite this vulnerability, it said the continent receives only about three per cent of global climate finance, much of which comes in the form of loans rather than grants.

It warned that the financing arrangement was particularly damaging to countries such as Nigeria, where mounting public debt, competing development priorities and limited fiscal space already constrain government investment in essential services and infrastructure.

CAPPA also expressed concern over what it described as the weakening of developed countries’ financial obligations under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which requires wealthy nations to provide financial resources to support climate mitigation and adaptation in developing countries.

It cautioned that the proposed Antalya-to-Addis Ababa Roadmap must not become another diplomatic instrument for postponing these obligations or replacing legally grounded responsibilities with voluntary funding announcements.

The organisation cited the United Nations Environment Programme’s Adaptation Gap Report 2026, which estimates that developing countries will require $305 billion annually for climate adaptation by 2035.

It said the persistent shortfall in climate finance posed a serious threat to the survival, livelihoods and development prospects of vulnerable communities.

Highlighting the disparity between fossil fuel industry profits and resources available to countries suffering climate-related losses, CAPPA cited figures referenced by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres at COP31.

According to the organisation, nine major oil companies reportedly earned $95 billion in a single quarter, while the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage had received only about $600 million.

CAPPA described the disparity as evidence of the injustice in the current global economic arrangement, arguing that corporations generating enormous profits from fossil fuels should contribute more meaningfully to addressing the consequences of climate change.

Ahead of COP32, it urged African governments and negotiators to turn the period leading to the summit into a coordinated campaign for climate justice and corporate accountability.

It called on Africa to leverage its position as host continent, working with the G77+China, small island developing states and other climate-vulnerable countries, to secure measurable financing commitments, transparent implementation milestones and regular public reporting under the Antalya-to-Addis Ababa Roadmap.

The organisation identified accessible, grant-based climate finance as a major priority, insisting that commercial loans must not be presented as climate assistance.

It also advocated innovative funding mechanisms, including levies on fossil fuel profits, international shipping and aviation, to generate predictable resources without worsening the debt crisis of developing countries.

On Africa’s energy future, CAPPA called for stronger regional cooperation through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), urging governments to prioritise local mineral processing, regional manufacturing, technology transfer and South-South partnerships.

It said the continent must move beyond exporting raw materials to developing and owning the technologies needed for its energy transition.

The organisation further urged African leaders to defend the 1.5°C global temperature limit and resist attempts to normalise temperature overshoot.

It warned that every additional fraction of global warming would heighten risks to African communities, ecosystems, food systems and economies.

CAPPA said COP32 must provide an opportunity for African countries to move beyond diplomatic declarations and secure concrete commitments that recognise their vulnerability and the historical responsibility of wealthy nations for the climate crisis.

The post CAPPA to Nigeria, Africa: Reject climate loans, demand rich nations’ accountability appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Haulage operators seek reforms to boost efficiency, cut costs
description:
Stakeholders in Nigeria’s haulage and logistics sector have called for stronger industry collaboration, technology adoption and return cargo systems to reduce transportation costs and improve operational efficiency.
They made the call at the 12th Haulage and Logistics Magazines Annual Conference and
content:
Stakeholders in Nigeria’s haulage and logistics sector have called for stronger industry collaboration, technology adoption and return cargo systems to reduce transportation costs and improve operational efficiency.

They made the call at the 12th Haulage and Logistics Magazines Annual Conference and Exhibition, held recently in Lagos, with the theme, ‘Technology as an Enabler for More Efficient Haulage Operations: The Need for Industry Collaboration’.

Speaking at the event, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Lori Systems, Mr Jean-Claude Homawoo, said collaboration among manufacturers, transporters and financial institutions would reduce empty truck journeys and ease logistics expenses.

He identified inefficient truck operations, prolonged waiting periods and poor cargo coordination as major drivers of rising transportation costs.

Homawoo noted that about 90 per cent of goods transportation in Nigeria depended on road networks, making efficient trucking operations essential to economic growth.

“Trucks frequently returned empty after deliveries because of unequal cargo distribution, seasonal demand and limited trust among industry stakeholders,” he said.

Citing a 2024 World Bank study, Homawoo said about 29 per cent of truck kilometres travelled globally were empty, with developing countries recording higher figures.

He disclosed that only about two per cent of trips in his company’s Nigerian network initially involved return cargo carried by the same trucks.

To address the challenge, he advocated technology-driven platforms that connect manufacturers with verified transporters, improve cargo coordination and provide reliable information on available shipments.

He added that digital proof of delivery could shorten payment processing by up to one week, easing financial pressure on transport operators.

Homawoo also identified compressed natural gas and electric trucks as opportunities to reduce fuel and maintenance costs, but warned that inadequate infrastructure and financing could exclude small-scale operators from the transition.

Similarly, Chief Operating Officer of Dukeridges, Mr Aanuoluwapo Agboola, said technology should support intelligence gathering, informed decision-making and cost reduction.

He also called for improved rail infrastructure to facilitate seamless cargo movement.

Head of Logistics at Promasidor Nigeria Ltd, Mr Ibikunle Sodipo, stressed that timely delivery and improved truck turnaround remained critical, urging companies to partner in securing return cargoes.

Managing Director of Trucksoft Logistics Telematics Services, Mr Oluwafemi Oladokun, identified driver management as a major industry challenge, while Chief Executive Officer of Triple A Logistics, Mrs Omotunde Ogunbowale, emphasised teamwork, driver welfare and technology-driven monitoring.

Earlier, HAULMACE Convener, Mr Alfred Okugbeni, said technology alone could not transform the sector without trust and collaboration among manufacturers, transporters, financiers, insurers, technology providers and government agencies.

The post Haulage operators seek reforms to boost efficiency, cut costs appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: 2027 election: Delta killings heighten fears of poll violence
description:
The Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, on Tuesday warned politicians against turning the 2027 general elections into a theatre of violence, vowing to arrest and prosecute anyone involved in attacks on political opponents, destruction of campaign venues and the use of dangerous weapons.
But opp
content:
The Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, on Tuesday warned politicians against turning the 2027 general elections into a theatre of violence, vowing to arrest and prosecute anyone involved in attacks on political opponents, destruction of campaign venues and the use of dangerous weapons.

But opposition parties cautioned that continued attacks on their candidates and supporters could force them to resort to self-defence, raising fresh concerns over the security of political campaigns ahead of the January 16, 2027 presidential election.

While the African Democratic Congress said it would not deny its members the right to defend themselves, the Allied Peoples Movement warned that no political party had a monopoly on violence. The Nigeria Democratic Congress and Labour Party also called for stronger security protection for political actors.

The Peoples Democratic Party, however, urged its members not to take the law into their hands, proposing the establishment of special courts to ensure speedy prosecution of electoral violence offenders.

The ruling All Progressives Congress rejected reprisal attacks and self-help, insisting that political disagreements must be resolved through lawful means.

The differing positions emerged amid a spate of attacks on political rallies, campaign convoys and supporters across the country, including the killing of six persons during an attack on the campaign entourage of former Deputy Senate President, Ovie Omo-Agege, in Delta State on Monday.

Speaking at a high-level security meeting in Abuja with the Independent National Electoral Commission, political party leaders, civil society organisations and other stakeholders, Disu described the growing incidents of political violence as a serious threat to public peace and democratic participation.

He cited attacks on campaign venues, violent clashes among supporters, intimidation of opponents and the use of dangerous weapons as developments that required urgent intervention.

“Political competition must never become justification for violence. Democracy gives citizens an opportunity to freely express their political preferences, support candidates of their choice, and hold differing opinions without fear of intimidation.

“It must never become a contest of who can mobilise more thugs, deploy more weapons or inflict greater harm on political opponents,” the IG said.

Disu declared that the police would remain neutral in the political process, warning that party affiliation, political office or personal influence would not protect offenders from prosecution.

“The position of the Nigeria Police Force is clear. Our neutrality in the political process is non-negotiable. We owe allegiance to the Constitution, the law and the Nigerian people, not to any political party or individual. We will not protect political interests; we will protect the Nigerian people,” he said.

He urged party leaders to take responsibility for their candidates, officials and supporters, warning against inflammatory statements, intimidation and the mobilisation of armed groups.

The police chief also condemned Monday’s killing of six persons in Uduere community, Ughelli North Local Government Area of Delta State, describing the incident as unacceptable.

The Chairman of INEC, Prof. Joash Amupitan, also expressed concern over the growing violence, warning that attacks on political actors could undermine the credibility of the elections even before voting begins.

He urged politicians to see elections as an opportunity to present their programmes to Nigerians rather than engage in intimidation and attacks.

“You will recall during my address to the leaders of political parties and members of the National Peace Committee on August 18, 2026, I emphasised one very key point: that we should not turn our election into a battlefield,” he said.

Amupitan warned that violence could prevent citizens from freely participating in political activities, thereby compromising the electoral process.

“When participants cannot assemble, campaign or organise themselves, express their views freely, the political process is compromised long before election day.

“And that is what this violence is meant to be, to scare the people so that the people will not turn out to vote,” he said.

He urged the police to arrest and prosecute perpetrators, particularly those responsible for inflammatory campaign statements and the deployment of armed groups.

Citing sections 95, 96 and 97 of the Electoral Act 2026, the INEC chairman reminded political parties of their obligations to conduct peaceful campaigns and warned against organising or retaining security groups and political vanguards.

He also disclosed that INEC would hold a security conference on Thursday, November 26, with service chiefs, the police and other members of the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security to address emerging threats.

The Nigeria Democratic Congress disclosed that it boycotted the meeting with the IG, citing alleged police bias and failure to protect its members from attacks by suspected political thugs.

The opposition party said it no longer had confidence in the Nigeria Police Force, accusing security operatives of failing to prevent violence against its members allegedly perpetrated by supporters of the ruling All Progressives Congress.

The decision followed a series of reported attacks on NDC members and campaign activities in different parts of the country, including Benue, Edo, Cross River, Enugu and Delta states.

In a statement by its National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director, the party condemned what it described as a growing pattern of politically motivated violence against its members and accused the police of failing to investigate the incidents and prosecute those responsible.

He said, “The NDC has decided to boycott the security meeting called by the Inspector-General of Police. We no longer feel safe and protected by a Police Force that watches helplessly the slaughter of our members across the country by hired thugs of the ruling APC. We will not lend legitimacy to a process that has failed to protect us.”

Director specifically recalled an incident in Benue State, where he said their presidential candidate, Peter Obi, was prevented from entering the state by thugs loyal to the APC government.

He said, “Politics and campaigns are not supposed to be war. However, the APC government has turned the campaign into a battlefield, where lives have become nasty, brutish and uncertain.”

The NDC further raised concerns that the police and other security agencies failed to intervene during the killing of four of its members in Delta State, describing the incident as evidence of the alleged compromise of security institutions.

“The situation is compounded by the complicity of the Police and security forces. The killing of four members of the NDC in Delta State was done in the full glare of the Police and security forces who were supposed to protect all Nigerians,” it added.

Director said the party’s decision to shun the meeting was informed by what he described as the failure of security agencies to conduct credible investigations into attacks on its members and bring the perpetrators to justice.

The NDC called on the international community to prevail on President Bola Tinubu and the APC-led Federal Government to uphold democratic standards and guarantee the safety of opposition politicians.

“We call on the international community to compel President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the APC government to play by internationally accepted democratic standards.’’

Meanwhile, opposition parties expressed frustration over what they described as inadequate protection for their candidates and supporters.

The National Publicity Secretary of the ADC, Bolaji Abdullahi, said the party had repeatedly raised concerns about attacks on opposition figures but had yet to see sufficient action from security agencies.

He warned that failure by the government to protect citizens could push them towards self-help, with dangerous consequences for national security.

“We believe security agencies need to wake up and protect citizens. If people feel that the state can no longer protect them, they may naturally resort to self-help, which could only result in anarchy.

“Our party is committed to non-violence, but we cannot continue to tell people to forgo their right to self-defence simply because they are our members,” Abdullahi said.

The NDC presidential candidate, Peter Obi, through his spokesman, Idris Zekeri, also called on the Federal Government to strengthen security around presidential candidates, warning that the state must not wait for candidates to formally request protection before discharging its responsibility.

Zekeri condemned the reported attack on the campaign convoy of the party’s vice-presidential candidate, Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso, in Bichi, Kano State, and urged President Bola Tinubu to ensure that members of his party complied with his call for peaceful campaigns.

He said the government should double the security attached to Obi and other leading political figures.

According to him, the responsibility for protecting candidates and their supporters rests primarily with the government and security agencies.

He said, “We don’t have to start protecting ourselves. We want a situation where agencies of government and law enforcement protect everybody, including the APC from itself.

“So we don’t have to do it because it amounts to nearly taking laws into our hands, and that is not in our character.”

Zekeri recalled that Obi’s supporters had resisted attempts by suspected thugs to disrupt a town hall meeting in Lagos, maintaining that political campaigns must be protected from intimidation.

The NDC had earlier accused security operatives of failing to prevent attacks allegedly carried out by APC supporters against its members in Benue, Edo, Cross River, Enugu and Delta States. It also alleged that four of its members were killed in Delta, demanding investigations and prosecution of those responsible.

The PDP National Publicity Secretary, Jungudo Muhammad, took a different position, warning that asking supporters to defend themselves could escalate tensions and lead to further bloodshed.

He urged political leaders to draw lessons from former President Goodluck Jonathan’s declaration that his ambition was not worth the blood of any Nigerian.

Muhammad stated, “We are a political party, and we have confidence in the country’s security system. We will continue to preach peace and urge our members not to take the law into their own hands. Instead, they should report any incident to the relevant security agencies.”

He called for specialised courts to try electoral violence offenders, arguing that speedy trials and punishment would discourage others from engaging in political violence.

“Once offenders are brought to justice within the shortest possible time, it will serve as a deterrent to others and discourage them from engaging in electoral violence,” he added.

The APM National Publicity Secretary, Abubakar Yusuf, accused the APC-led Federal Government of using intimidation to weaken opposition parties, but said his party would not encourage members to take the law into their hands.

He warned, however, that the party would not remain indifferent to attacks on its supporters.

“We will match action for action because no one has a monopoly on violence,” Yusuf said.

He added that the party would continue to conduct its campaigns within the law, urging security agencies to intervene promptly to prevent political disagreements from escalating.

Similarly, the Labour Party National Publicity Secretary, Ken Asogwa, called on political parties to take reasonable steps to protect themselves against attacks while insisting that security agencies must provide equal protection to all political groups.

He said the law recognised the right to self-defence but cautioned against anarchy.

“The law does not expect someone confronted with an attack by non-state actors to simply fold their arms and allow themselves to be killed,” he said.

Asogwa urged the police to ensure that security at political rallies was not the exclusive preserve of the ruling party.

However, the APC National Chairman, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, through his media aide, Abimbola Tooki, said the ruling party would not support self-help, reprisal attacks or the use of violence to settle political disagreements.

He pledged that the APC would work with security agencies and other stakeholders to protect its members and supporters while urging them to report threats and attacks to the appropriate authorities.

“The APC will always defend the rights, safety and legitimate interests of its members and supporters, but we will not encourage self-help, reprisal attacks or the taking of the law into one’s hands,” he said.

Yilwatda added that the right to protect one’s life in the face of immediate danger must not be interpreted as a licence to organise retaliation, carry illegal weapons or engage in violence.

The SDP National Chairman, Prof. Sadiq Gombe, also called for equal security protection for all political parties, warning that any perception of police bias could erode public confidence in the electoral process.

He urged security agencies to investigate reported attacks promptly and prosecute offenders regardless of their political affiliations.

The growing tension has been accompanied by a series of attacks on political activities in different parts of the country.

On November 23, six persons were reportedly killed when gunmen attacked the campaign entourage of Omo-Agege in Uduere community, Delta State. The police confirmed six deaths, against the four earlier reported by the former deputy Senate president’s campaign organisation.

On November 13, the convoy of President Tinubu was reportedly attacked in Abuja after he observed Jumu’ah prayers at a mosque in Garki, with some individuals said to have thrown stones and other objects at the vehicles.

In Kano, suspected thugs reportedly attacked the campaign convoy of Kwankwaso and the NDC governorship candidate, Aminu Abdussalam Gwarzo, in Bichi, vandalising several vehicles and injuring supporters. The party’s campaign organisation alleged that about seven vehicles were damaged.

Earlier in November, Obi’s convoy was attacked in Calabar, Cross River State, while some of his supporters were reportedly assaulted during a town hall meeting in Lagos.

Supporters of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, the ADC presidential candidate, have also reportedly faced attacks in Benin, Edo State, Kaduna and Cross River State.

On October 30, the African Action Congress presidential candidate, Omoyele Sowore, and members of his entourage were attacked at a restaurant in Ado-Ekiti, Ekiti State. Their vehicles were vandalised, while Sowore and some members of his team sustained injuries.

The National Peace Committee’s monitoring report, published by The PUNCH on November 11, further highlighted the scale of the problem.

The report, covering August 19 to October 27, documented 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord in 26 states and the Federal Capital Territory. Political violence and thuggery accounted for 33 incidents, while misinformation and disinformation recorded 29.

Kaduna had the highest number of breaches, with nine, while the FCT recorded seven. The committee also identified Kaduna, Edo and Enugu as electoral flashpoints.

In a related development, former Chief Justice of Nigeria, Justice Olukayode Ariwoola (retd.), on Tuesday warned against a repeat of the violence that followed the 2011 general elections, when more than 800 people were killed, according to Human Rights Watch.

Speaking in Abuja, Ariwoola, who chairs the Council of the Wise of the Savannah Centre for Diplomacy, Democracy and Development, expressed concern over attacks on political convoys, rallies and gatherings in several states.

He called on security agencies to deploy adequate personnel to campaign venues, arrest and prosecute perpetrators, and confiscate dangerous weapons.

He also urged political parties to discipline members involved in violence and called on INEC to enforce electoral laws impartially.

Ariwoola said, “Democracy thrives on the peaceful contestation of ideas and visions, not on bloodshed or coercion.

“It will be an unfortunate national shame if Nigerians collectively allow a repeat of what happened after the 2011 elections. The 2027 elections must be won at the ballot boxes, not on the streets through intimidation and bloodshed.”

President Tinubu recently condemned political violence and directed security agencies to act firmly against those threatening public order.

“Every form of violence stands condemned. Violence should never have a place in our political campaigns as we move towards the 2027 general elections,” the President said, urging politicians to focus on issues and the contestation of ideas.

The post 2027 election: Delta killings heighten fears of poll violence appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: NAMA pensioners protest today over 20-year arrears
description: The Contributory Pensioners Union of Nigeria, Nigerian Airspace Management Agency branch, has threatened to embark on a two-day peaceful protest from 25 November to demand payment of 20 years of accumulated pension increases and arrears approved by the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission
content:
The Contributory Pensioners Union of Nigeria, Nigerian Airspace Management Agency branch, has threatened to embark on a two-day peaceful protest from 25 November to demand payment of 20 years of accumulated pension increases and arrears approved by the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission.

In a statement on Tuesday, the branch Chairman, Stephen Olopha, and the Secretary, Wasiu Lawal, said that the action was provoked by the refusal of NAMA management to respond to its letters dated 30 September, 12 October and 17 November this year.

CPUN said that the protest will commence at the NAMA pension office in Lagos and the agency’s Abuja headquarters by 9 am.

The protest notice was addressed to the of NAMA’s Managing Director and copied to the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, the Director of State Security Services, the Divisional Police Officers of the Nigeria Police Force in Lugbe-Abuja and Ikeja Airport, the Chairman of the Joint Aviation Workers Union and the President of the CPUN.

Last month, the NAMA branch of CPUN said that N2.5bn had been released in April 2026 for the payment of the increases and arrears, but the affected pensioners were yet to receive their outstanding entitlements.

The NAMA branch of the union said it had rejected a meeting proposed by the agency for next Tuesday, insisting that management should settle the arrears before the end of the month.

In a message to pensioners, Lawal said NAMA had responded to the union’s planned industrial action with a letter dated 19 October, which he alleged was intended to mislead retirees.

According to Lawal, the letter was addressed to NAMA contributory pension scheme retirees, rather than CPUN, which he described as the recognised organisation representing the affected pensioners.

“The purported letter was rejected,” he said.

Lawal accused NAMA management of failing to communicate with the union since a meeting held on 10 June 2026, while continuing to engage with an elders’ forum.

“NAMA management has deliberately failed to respond or communicate with the union since the 10 June 2026 meeting, but has been meeting with the elders’ forum and deceiving the gullible retirees as confessed in the letter,” he alleged.

He contrasted the situation of the retirees with that of serving and contract staff, whom he said were receiving their salaries and other payments.

“As we speak, NAMA staff and contract staff are collecting two months’ salary, 13th month, and the October salary, while we have nothing to collect except the peanuts we have been collecting for over 10 years of retirement, which have no increments,” he said.

In a demand letter addressed to NAMA’s Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, CPUN urged the agency to provide a clear and definite timetable for implementing the outstanding pension increases and paying the arrears.

The union also called on management to handle the matter urgently, citing the advanced age, financial circumstances and welfare of the affected retirees.

The letter, signed by Olopha and Lawal, stated that the outstanding pension adjustments and arrears related to entitlements that had remained unpaid for more than two decades.

“Many of the affected pensioners are now over 70 years of age, while some have been retired since 2008 or earlier. A significant number are elderly, financially vulnerable and dependent on their pension income to meet basic necessities, including food, accommodation, medical treatment and other essential family obligations,” the letter stated.

It added that some retirees had died while waiting for the benefits and pension adjustments due to them.

“It is therefore deeply distressing that, after waiting for more than 20 years, these elderly pensioners should continue to face uncertainty over payments that have already been subjected to the relevant computation process,” the union said.

CPUN maintained that further delays were unacceptable, particularly as the pensioners had waited for more than two decades and the relevant calculations had already been submitted to the agency.

The union urged NAMA to resolve the matter before the end of October, warning that failure to meet its demands could lead to protest action.

title: Digital healthcare platform targets ageing parents
description:
A Nigerian health-technology startup, Sporaa Health Hub, is targeting families living abroad who need to coordinate medical care for ageing parents and other relatives in Nigeria, as it seeks to address the challenges of managing healthcare across geographical boundaries.
The company has introduced
content:
A Nigerian health-technology startup, Sporaa Health Hub, is targeting families living abroad who need to coordinate medical care for ageing parents and other relatives in Nigeria, as it seeks to address the challenges of managing healthcare across geographical boundaries.

The company has introduced a digital platform that connects family members abroad with elderly relatives at home, healthcare professionals and care coordinators, allowing subscribers to monitor medical needs, arrange consultations and organise home-based healthcare services remotely.

The platform comes as migration continues to separate many Nigerian families, leaving relatives abroad to depend on phone calls, family members and informal caregivers to monitor the health of ageing parents. Such arrangements can make it difficult to track medication, arrange routine medical appointments, and respond promptly to emerging health concerns.

Sporaa’s Family Plan combines an artificial intelligence-enabled dashboard with access to physicians, medication management, health monitoring and emergency care coordination. The service is designed to give registered family members access to relevant medical information and updates while allowing healthcare professionals to coordinate care.

The Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Sporaa Health Hub, Dr Ogheneochuko Ibe, told The PUNCH in an email that the platform was created to ease the challenges families face in coordinating the healthcare of relatives living in different locations.

“Sporaa is designed to address the growing challenges faced by families separated by distance, particularly those with ageing parents or dependent relatives in Nigeria,” Ibe said.

He said the platform provides a shared system through which families can monitor medical appointments, medication schedules and changes in the health conditions of their relatives while accessing professional healthcare services when required.

“It gives families a shared place to see how a parent or loved one is doing, keep track of medications and appointments, share caring responsibilities, and act early when something changes,” he said.

The platform also connects subscribers to licensed healthcare professionals for home visits, diagnostic tests and medication delivery, with medical results and updates made available through the application.

Its features include shared health records, a family dashboard, health scores, medication reminders and appointment tracking. The system also allows authorised family members to access medical information, including doctors’ notes, laboratory reports and prescriptions.

Through its Family Circle feature, relatives in different locations can participate in coordinating care, while the health overview function brings together vital signs, medical check-up results and other health indicators.

The company said users could also incorporate readings from smartphones and smartwatches, including blood pressure, heart rate and activity levels, to support regular health monitoring.

Beyond its digital services, Sporaa offers access to assigned family doctors, virtual medical consultations, home doctor visits, a 24-hour virtual care coordinator, medication delivery and emergency care coordination.

Ibe said the objective was to move families away from fragmented caregiving arrangements towards more structured healthcare monitoring and professional support.

“The goal is simple, catch problems early, prevent costly emergencies, and give families peace of mind wherever they are,” he said.

The start-up’s model combines digital health management with physical healthcare delivery, placing it within a growing segment of health technology focused on connecting patients, medical professionals and caregivers through digital platforms.

However, the company’s ability to expand would depend partly on the availability of healthcare professionals, the reliability of its service network, and the protection of sensitive medical information shared among family members and care providers.

The post Digital healthcare platform targets ageing parents appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Accountants warn against professional misconduct
description:
The Association of Chartered Certified Accountants has warned members that professional misconduct and ethical breaches could lead to the withdrawal of their qualifications, reinforcing its disciplinary measures as scrutiny of accountability in the accounting profession grows.
The professional body
content:
The Association of Chartered Certified Accountants has warned members that professional misconduct and ethical breaches could lead to the withdrawal of their qualifications, reinforcing its disciplinary measures as scrutiny of accountability in the accounting profession grows.

The professional body said members found guilty of unethical practices or violations of its code of conduct could face sanctions, including the loss of their professional certifications.

The Country Head of ACCA Nigeria, Tom Isibor, disclosed this at the organisation’s recognition ceremony in Lagos, according to a news release issued on Tuesday. He said the association operated a disciplinary framework to ensure that members upheld professional integrity, competence and accountability.

“The professional body operated a robust disciplinary framework designed to uphold ethical standards, professional integrity and accountability among its members,” Isibor said.

He explained that the framework was intended to hold accountants responsible for their conduct and protect the standards expected of professionals working in finance and accounting.

The warning comes as ethical conduct remains a critical issue in the accounting profession, where financial reporting, audit practices and professional judgement influence business decisions, investment confidence and public trust.

Speaking at the ceremony, Dr Ije Jidenma, a partner at Kestria Global and past president of the Chartered Institute of Directors Nigeria, said integrity was fundamental to the profession because of its influence on business decisions and confidence in institutions.

She urged accountants to look beyond professional qualifications and career progression, encouraging them to contribute to mentorship, institutional development and ethical leadership.

The event also honoured 20 individuals and organisations for their contributions to the accountancy profession, particularly in promoting professional excellence, nurturing talent and fostering institutional collaborations.

Isibor said the annual programme, which has run for more than a decade, had expanded its recognition beyond ACCA members and prospective members to include employers, educational institutions and other organisations supporting the profession.

He said the broader recognition was intended to encourage professionals and institutions to contribute to economic development, promote excellence and mentor younger practitioners.

One of the recipients, Nana Ibrahim, a fellow of ACCA and Group Director at the Nigeria Revenue Service, said her recognition reflected more than 15 years of professional development and personal sacrifice.

Ibrahim recalled changing her work shift as a call centre employee at IT Salat to sit her first ACCA examination, adding that the discipline required to complete the programme continued to influence her professional responsibilities.

“The rigours of the examinations and the journey through it are what we carry into the workplace. It is always about service, hard work and dedication,” she said.

title: Discos’ Band A of sorrow
description:
By SUNNY IKHIOYA



The time for another round of elections is drawing close. The people seem to be unaware of where to hold the government responsible. Politicians are only concerned about personal insults and vain things. But in recent times, they have upped the tempo to begin to talk about petrol
content:
By SUNNY IKHIOYA

The time for another round of elections is drawing close. The people seem to be unaware of where to hold the government responsible. Politicians are only concerned about personal insults and vain things. But in recent times, they have upped the tempo to begin to talk about petroleum subsidy and palliatives for the common man. One thing that the people have not been sensitive about is the fraudulent manner in which the electricity distribution companies are taking advantage of the government’s inability to monitor their activities properly.

The NERC, the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission, is there, invisible to consumers. We have also been informed that some states have established their own regulatory commissions, like Lagos, Enugu and others. They, too, do not seem to be making their presence felt. Just like petrol, electricity is also at the centre of a people’s development. A country that cannot independently generate its own electricity is as good as staying dead at the bottom. Manufacturers cannot produce, skilled and small businesses will not grow, and the people will remain unhappy.

Presently, the high-handedness of the electricity distribution companies is a principal cause of the downward drop in our poverty ratings. The middle class has been completely wiped out, businesses are dying, and no one seems to care. You know why our situation is so despicable: the state of Iran has been at war with the US and Israel for close to a year now, with critical infrastructure badly destroyed. In the midst of all these disruptions, it is still able to supply vital electricity to its people and businesses. The same thing is happening to Ukraine against Russia.

Without light, the people are finished. It is a basic principle and also has some spiritual undertone. When you have light, you prevail over challenges and adversaries. That is why our situation is so pathetic. And so they came up with the structuring of the billing system, arguing that with a cost-reflective—no subsidy—tariff system in place, the power companies could be motivated to produce satisfactory power supply to the people and businesses. They embarked on classifying consumers into Classes A–D categories. Although this did not go well with the people, because it clearly was discriminatory and assumed to favour only the wealthy class, it has all turned out to be a scam on the consumers in that category. The Discos have used the monopoly they possess to fleece innocent consumers and businesses of their hard-earned income, with many of them finding it difficult to cope. Yet, on a monthly basis, the bills will arrive.

In announcing the cost-reflective tariffs, the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission emphasised that Band A customers will enjoy a minimum of 20 hours of uninterrupted power supply in a day. They went further to say that, if the Discos are unable to meet up with the terms and conditions of the Band A category, the tariffs must be adjusted downward. What this means is that you enjoy a minimum of 20 uninterrupted hours of power supply, you pay the rate; and if you do not get that service, you do not pay. For serious businesses, they were willing to take the hard route, assuming that their use of alternative power supply, like diesel, will be reduced to the barest minimum. It was assumed also that the power supply will be predictable, therefore allowing for proper operational planning. But what are we seeing? Intermittent power outages without any prior notification. They even go without supply for days, without any notification or apologies from the operators, and they still bring up the outrageous Band A bills.

Businesses are dying, investors are suffering, and so many people are becoming jobless because of the inefficient operational methods of these distribution companies. They say you should report to NERC. Where is NERC? Try to get to them, either by phone or email, and see what their reaction will be. They are overseeing nothing. Recently, staff of BEDC regulators, who cover Ekiti, Edo and Delta states, went on strike over poor welfare conditions and shut down the control rooms for a whole week. When they returned, it was business as usual. A week after resumption, they brought their bills. You will not believe that the one-week work stoppage did not reflect on the tariff. They have again passed the burden to the consumers. Under normal circumstances, they are expected to apologise for the lengthy supply disruptions and follow that up with a discount, in the form of not using the Band A calculation during this period.

The Nigerian operator has failed to realise this; they are wont to shift blame from grid collapse to transmission failures. Even if we accept all of these failures, why should consumers be made to pay the price of their failure? The people are suffering. Band A is killing businesses, and the authorities must do something about it. This is why the people must be sensitive as we approach another election cycle.

The people of a local government in Isoko, Delta State, recently came out to protest the electricity situation in their villages. The chant was, “No light, no voting in Isoko land.” I do not know how far the government has gone in pacifying them, but the governor recently undertook a successful campaign tour in that region. Sometimes, you have to cry and protest loudly for your situation to be addressed.

Former Lagos State Governor Raji Fashola, while trying to defend this government’s performance, touched on the challenges of policy formulation and implementation. It is a big gap in bringing intentions to reality. We have had so many good policies recorded in our files and archives, and the Band A policy was supposed to work hitch-free, allow manufacturers and big businesses to enjoy a free flow of electricity supply and bring about growth and development, but it has become a nightmare for everyone. If you cannot improve on a situation, do not attempt to change it. We have failed with many good policies because we have left room for excuses. Even the government is not left out in this blame game; the money they are owing the electricity companies is enough to cause a significant shift in the electricity supply performance, but again, there is always a reason for their failure.

The people must push for a reversal of the Band A policy. It has failed woefully.

On a final note, given the manner in which the national grid is crumbling at regular intervals, it is now time for the federal government to totally decentralise grid management. Even suspected terrorists are now exploiting its fragility to sabotage government efforts. Diversity does not mean that all should be one and develop at the same pace. Once a little healthy competition is brought into it, the various regions will sit up and confront their own challenges head-on. We must give serious thought to this option.

•Ikhioya writes from Lagos.

The post Discos’ Band A of sorrow appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: 2027: Shunning ethnicity and religion
description: As Nigerians prepare for next year’s general elections, they must move beyond the unhealthy politics of ethnicity and religion in the campaigns and choice of leaders. While diversity and equitable representation deserve recognition, they must not take precedence over competence, accountability and p
content:
As Nigerians prepare for next year’s general elections, they must move beyond the unhealthy politics of ethnicity and religion in the campaigns and choice of leaders. While diversity and equitable representation deserve recognition, they must not take precedence over competence, accountability and proven track records of service delivery. Nigeria cannot build a united democracy on religious intolerance, ethnic suspicion and political exclusion.

The country’s numerous ethnic nationalities, languages, cultures and religious traditions should be sources of strength. Sadly, politicians and influential interest groups increasingly manipulate these identities to deepen divisions, promote intolerance and weaken national unity. The emerging political atmosphere is reminiscent of the 2023 general elections, when ethnic and religious considerations dominated campaigns and public discourse.

The European Union Election Observation Mission (EU-EOM), in its final report, expressed concern over divisive language and the mobilisation of ethnic and religious sentiments during the elections. It is particularly disturbing that candidates are increasingly judged not by their competence, records and policy proposals but by their faith, language or geographical origin. Political differences or disagreements are sinisterly framed as grievances against entire ethnic or religious communities. Such tendencies undermine democratic competition and threaten peaceful coexistence.

The Constitution (1999, as amended) provides clear safeguards against this divisive politics. Section 10 prohibits the adoption of any religion as a state religion, while Section 15 promotes national integration and prohibits discrimination based on place of origin, religion, ethnic or linguistic association. Section 42 further guarantees protection against discrimination on these grounds. These provisions must translate into political practice. No Nigerian should be denied the opportunity to aspire to public office because of religious belief or ethnic origin.

Equally, political appointments and access to public opportunities must be guided by fairness, merit and competence rather than narrow identity considerations. Religious leaders must also recognise their responsibility to promote peace, tolerance and mutual respect. Pulpits and religious platforms should never become instruments for spreading political hatred or hostility against people of other faiths.

Traditional rulers, community leaders and ethnic associations must similarly resist manipulation by partisan interests. Cultural pride should never become an excuse for intolerance. Politicians who exploit religious and ethnic sentiments for electoral advantage must understand that the divisions they create often outlive their political ambitions. The consequences can undermine national cohesion long after elections have ended.

As the general elections approach, political parties and candidates must be challenged to focus on issues that affect all Nigerians, such as insecurity, unemployment, poverty, education, healthcare and economic recovery. These are the issues that should define electoral choices, not religious or ethnic affiliations.

Nigeria’s diversity should enrich its democracy, not undermine it. The Nigerian state belongs to all citizens, and its leadership must remain open to every qualified Nigerian. The time has come to put competence above identity, citizenship above religious affiliation and national interest above ethnic loyalty. That is the path to a united, inclusive and sustainable democracy.

The post 2027: Shunning ethnicity and religion appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Foundation raises alarm over youths’ role in gender violence
description:
The Innocent Chukwuemeka Chukwuma Empowerment Foundation has called on youths, governments and community leaders to intensify efforts to end gender-based violence against women and girls.
The foundation’s Executive Chair, Josephine Effah-Chukwuma, also raised concerns over the increasing involvement
content:
The Innocent Chukwuemeka Chukwuma Empowerment Foundation has called on youths, governments and community leaders to intensify efforts to end gender-based violence against women and girls.

The foundation’s Executive Chair, Josephine Effah-Chukwuma, also raised concerns over the increasing involvement of young people as both victims and perpetrators of gender-based violence, including technology-facilitated abuse.

Effah-Chukwuma made the call in a statement on Tuesday ahead of the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, which begins on Wednesday, November 25, and ends on December 10.

She stated that this year’s campaign, themed “Unite to End Violence Against Women and Girls: Ensure Justice, Protect Survivors, End Impunity,” required commitment from individuals, organisations, religious and traditional institutions, and governments to protect women and girls and ensure access to justice for survivors.

The ICCEF chair noted that, despite the existence of laws and policies against gender-based violence and discrimination in Nigeria, the problem remained widespread, particularly among young people.

Effah-Chukwuma listed battering, rape, femicide, online sexual abuse, cyberbullying, doxxing, deepfake abuse, sextortion and digital blackmail among the forms of violence affecting women and girls.

She urged young men and boys to challenge peer pressure, misogyny, victim-blaming and attitudes that normalise violence against women.

The foundation’s chair also called on young people to reject the non-consensual sharing of intimate images and report harmful online content rather than ridicule or shame survivors.

“Rather than embark on secondary victimisation (ridiculing and shaming) of survivors, young people should provide support,” she added.

Effah-Chukwuma urged federal, state and local governments to strengthen the implementation of laws addressing gender-based violence and provide adequate funding for institutions responsible for protecting women and girls.

She also called on the police, courts and correctional institutions to handle reports professionally, investigate cases thoroughly and ensure that perpetrators are held accountable while protecting survivors from further trauma.

The ICCEF chair urged businesses and organisations to establish workplace policies and safe reporting channels for victims, while asking families, traditional and religious institutions to reject harmful cultural practices and the manipulation of religious doctrines to justify abuse.

She further urged media organisations and digital platforms to challenge narratives that justify violence and use their platforms to protect survivors and hold perpetrators accountable.

As part of the foundation’s activities for the campaign, Effah-Chukwuma said ICCEF would partner with Project Alert on Violence Against Women to organise a webinar titled “When Laws Are Not Enough: Closing the Justice Gap for Women and Girls” on December 10, International Human Rights Day.

She noted that the discussion would bring together young people, women’s rights organisations, legal professionals, justice-sector representatives and members of the public.

She added, “Commemorating the 16 Days of Activism must go beyond symbolic press statements and releases to concrete actions that require institutions to be accountable for actions to address gender-based violence, and provision of support to survivors.”

The post Foundation raises alarm over youths’ role in gender violence appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
