title: CeBIH, NIMC forge strategic alliance on digital identity
description:
The Committee of e-Business Industry Heads has announced a strategic partnership with the National Identity Management Commission to deepen Nigeria’s digital economy and accelerate financial inclusion.
The alliance, unveiled during a press conference in Lagos on Tuesday, will serve as the cornerston
content:
The Committee of e-Business Industry Heads has announced a strategic partnership with the National Identity Management Commission to deepen Nigeria’s digital economy and accelerate financial inclusion.

The alliance, unveiled during a press conference in Lagos on Tuesday, will serve as the cornerstone for the upcoming 2026 CeBIH Annual Conference, themed ‘Digital Identity: A Catalyst for Financial Inclusion, Trust and Growth.’

Speaking at the briefing, the Chairman of CeBIH, Mrs Abidemi Asunmo, stressed the necessity of the collaboration in light of Nigeria’s rapidly evolving financial landscape. She noted that while digital payments and fintech innovations had expanded access to financial services, reliably establishing and verifying identities remained a persistent challenge.

“Our partnership with NIMC is designed to promote dialogue, knowledge exchange and stronger institutional collaboration around the practical integration of trusted digital identity into financial services.

“A trusted digital identity ecosystem can help address some of the structural barriers to financial inclusion, bridging gaps and bringing more people into the formal financial system,” she said.

According to the committee, the urgency of the collaboration has been heightened by the recent signing of the NIMC Act 2026 by President Bola Tinubu, which reinforces the National Identification Number as Nigeria’s foundational identity credential and strengthens data protection frameworks.

Asunmo added, “This represents an important opportunity to build more reliable identity verification and authentication systems, simplify customer onboarding, strengthen trust in digital transactions and expand access to financial services.”

Scheduled for 1 and 2 December, 2026, in Lagos, the conference will examine the critical role of secure and accessible digital identity infrastructure in driving the next phase of financial services and the broader digital economy.

Representing the Director-General and Chief Executive Officer of NIMC, Abisoye Coker-Odusote, the NIMC Lagos State Coordinator, Mr Gbolahan Oluwatobiloba, affirmed the commission’s commitment to the partnership, stressing that a robust identity framework remained the bedrock of economic stability and national security.

“Identity system is the foundation of everything, not just the financial sector, not just the security sector, not just identity ecosystem. When you remove identity, your security will be affected, because how do you secure people you don’t know?” Oluwatobiloba stated.

He further highlighted NIMC’s expanded statutory mandate under the new Act as Nigeria’s Certificate Authority, placing the nation’s public key infrastructure and digital public infrastructure under the commission’s custodianship to bolster public confidence.

“That’s a major role for NIMC, and that gives the average public person the confidence, the trust that whatever you do within the digital space, your information is secured, your information is well protected,” he added.

title: Apapa-Iganmu sets May deadline for road completion
description:
The Apapa-Iganmu Local Council Development Area of Lagos State has commenced construction of the Mosadolorun/Onigemo Road in Oke-Oja, promising completion by May 2027.
The Executive Chairman of the council, Jimoh Saliu, gave this promise on Tuesday during the groundbreaking ceremony.
He said the pro
content:
The Apapa-Iganmu Local Council Development Area of Lagos State has commenced construction of the Mosadolorun/Onigemo Road in Oke-Oja, promising completion by May 2027.

The Executive Chairman of the council, Jimoh Saliu, gave this promise on Tuesday during the groundbreaking ceremony.

He said the project, which spans more than one kilometre, would feature drainage channels on both sides, pedestrian walkways and solar-powered streetlights.

He said the contractor had received more than 30 per cent of the project cost as mobilisation and was expected to complete the construction within six months.

Saliu described the road as a major route that had suffered years of neglect, adding that its reconstruction was intended to improve access and ease transportation for residents of the Oke-Oja community.

“By God’s grace, if we come back in the next six months, we will see another express road within the local government,” he said.

The chairman said the project was part of a broader road infrastructure initiative involving the 57 local government areas and local council development areas in Lagos State, under which each council was expected to execute major road projects.

He said the Mosadolorun/Onigemo Road would bring to nine the number of road projects undertaken by his administration since assuming office about 17 months ago.

Among the roads he identified as completed or rehabilitated were Amosu Street in Badia, Akinola Street in Ward B, Sari-Iganmu, and Makanjuola Street Phases I and II, which he said spanned more than one kilometre.

He also listed another Makanjuola Street project in Oke-Oja.

Other projects, according to him, include Agbebi Street in Marine Beach, Olaiton Street in Ward B, Oniyide Street in Abete, Ireti Owoseni Street and Kadri Street, which are at various stages of construction.

Beyond road infrastructure, Saliu said the council had secured private-sector support for the rehabilitation and equipping of primary healthcare centres in the area, with two facilities benefiting from corporate social responsibility interventions.

He said APM Terminals supported the renovation and provision of medical equipment at the Ojora Olugbode Primary Health Centre, while 7up Bottling Company Plc had supported the refurbishment of the Sari Primary Health Centre.

The chairman also said work on the rehabilitation of the Olojomo Primary Health Centre was nearing completion and that the facility would be commissioned soon.

On education, Saliu disclosed that about 80 students had benefited from the council’s educational support programme, which covers General Certificate of Education examination fees, assistance with university admission and first-year tuition fees.

He said the programme was designed to support students from financially disadvantaged backgrounds who had the academic qualifications to pursue higher education but lacked the resources to do so.

According to him, beneficiaries would subsequently be encouraged to access the Nigerian Education Loan Fund to finance the remainder of their university education.

The council chairman also said his administration had distributed school uniforms, bags, exercise books and other writing materials to pupils in public primary schools across the LCDA.

He said the interventions were part of efforts to cushion the effects of the removal of the petrol subsidy on families, particularly those struggling with the rising cost of education.

In another development, Saliu said the Lagos State Government has approved the construction of a secondary school in Apapa-Iganmu.

He described the approval as significant for the council area which, he said, stood to benefit from additional public secondary school infrastructure.

The chairman also disclosed that a commercial bank was expected to commence operations in the LCDA in the coming days, expressing optimism that its presence would improve access to financial services and support commercial activities in the area.

The Mosadolorun/Onigemo project adds to a series of infrastructure interventions the council says it has undertaken since Saliu assumed office.

The chairman said the administration intended to continue investing in infrastructure and social services across the council area.

The post Apapa-Iganmu sets May deadline for road completion appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Broadcasting, an industry in search of peace and little details, by Okoh Aihe
description: I am sure that Section 6 of the National Broadcasting Commission Act was created for Ministers like Mohammed Idris who will not take advantage of the overwhelming power at their disposal but, at all times, manage such power to meet stakeholder and public expectations from the broadcast industry.
content:
I am sure that Section 6 of the National Broadcasting Commission Act was created for Ministers like Mohammed Idris who will not take advantage of the overwhelming power at their disposal but, at all times, manage such power to meet stakeholder and public expectations from the broadcast industry.

Section 6 states that “Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Minister may give the Commission directives of a general character relating generally to particular matters with regard to the exercise by the Commission of its functions under this Act and it shall be the duty of the Commission to comply with such directives.”

Looking at it closely, the Section gives the Minister the yam and the knife, leaving at his discretion whoever may get a piece of the yam. More like the sword of Damocles, it can come down anytime, dear friend.

I have been against that Section of the Act and have actively canvassed for it to be amended. Reason being that it has been abused serially and is responsible for most of the failures in the broadcast ecosystem, including a number of cases in the court whose outcomes may continue to invalidate the authority of the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC), who is the regulator of the broadcast industry.

But life is full of contradictions. It doesn’t mean however that such contradiction, which could be arbitrary, should be accepted as reality irrespective of brilliant intention and outcome. Idris has managed all the arbitrariness of Section 6 quite different from the reality visited upon us not too long ago, and he continues to bear the elements of a good man who has control over his environment.

Receiving a delegation of the Broadcasting Organisation of Nigeria (BON), which visited him in his office in Abuja recently, Idris directed that all talks about increasing broadcast license fees be suspended following fears raised by broadcast operators that the escalating cost of operations is almost running them out of business.

It means there were simmering discontents and disagreements in the broadcast ecosystem threatening to burst into the open which the public never noticed but the minister has moved swiftly to nip those issues in the bud, as they say.

“Any increase in license fees is hereby put on hold. All reviews relating to licenses are suspended until further notice. I am directing the NBC to ensure strict compliance while we review the situation,” Idris was quoted to have said.

He called the suspension part of the effort of the Nigerian government to create a more conducive environment for broadcasters.

Only if for selfish reasons, Idris needs the broadcast operators to be at the top of their game especially as we approach the 2027 elections. Unfortunately for Nigerian broadcasters, they are hardly prepared for such challenging undertaking, not because of capacity and competence in the profession, but more because of the business environment that has been shrinking.

This point was registered vehemently by BON Chairman, Tony Akiotu, when he painted a dreary picture of the industry, saying that “today, it is difficult if not impossible to count stations that operate up to 12 hours daily. This portends danger as information is the lifeblood of a functioning democracy acting as the foundation for civic participation, transparency and accountability.”

Akiotu made an appeal for the government to grant access to affordable financing to save broadcasting, beside another major concern, for the minister to encourage political parties to present their candidates for Political Debate which is traditionally put together by the gathering of broadcasters before the Presidential Election.

It is possible to see the razzle dazzle of a few flagship programmes on television and get to the erroneous conclusion that the broadcast industry is having a good ride. No. The sector is more like the metaphor of the monkey which sweats profusely but for the hair on its back.

There were two other directives also given by the minister. One. The NBC to expedite the review of the Nigeria Broadcasting Code to ensure that its provisions reflect current developments and emerging realities in the industry; and Two: the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON) to ensure full enforcement of the 45-day payment period for advertising services.

However, there is a third issue which remains troubling, but the minister has promised to handle it by himself – to convene a stakeholders’ meeting to address outstanding concerns on the Digital Switch-Over (DSO). Although Nigeria opted for the satellite option to launch a concluding variant version of the DSO on June 17, there remains a number of sensitive issues awaiting urgent attention of stakeholders, including NBC and BON members, among others.

This writer gathered that the minister was very unhappy with the regulator after receiving complaints from BON that 147 days after his personal intervention pre-DSO launch, it was yet to be involved in any process or meeting to ensure seamless implementation of the resolutions. The simple conclusion is that the DSO has slipped into hibernation and that doesn’t deodorize this government that needs a lot of sprucing up.

On this matter, BON reiterated its belief in the principle of dialogue, consultation and mediation to avert breakdown of Industrial harmony, particularly between licensees and the regulator. Even sources within NBC confessed they have not carried out any appreciable consultation with stakeholders. The minister doesn’t want that either and has urged that something be done urgently by the NBC.

The DSO is a significant development globally and there is no need flogging a dead horse anymore that Nigeria has been sluggish in implementation with the June action shrouded in more uncertain hue and a halo of suspicion. This writer is of the opinion that a resolution of the entire process is much closer and quite easily affordable now only if the regulator can build a coalition of relationships with concerned stakeholders.

In all this however, the minister deserves some commendation for choosing not to flaunt the overwhelming power of Section 6 of the Broadcasting Act but has instead chosen the path of peace in working with the various stakeholders to achieve results that bring common good to the industry in particular and the country in general.

I corrected only clear grammatical and punctuation errors, including spacing after punctuation, capitalization of “Industrial harmony,” and a few minor phrasing adjustments. I preserved the author’s style, sentence structure, and intended meaning.

title: CBN holds rate at 23%, warns of election spending
description:
The Monetary Policy Committee of the Central Bank of Nigeria has retained the benchmark interest rate at 23 per cent, citing inflationary risks arising from anticipated election-related spending, increased festive season expenditure and disruptions to global energy supplies.
The CBN Governor, Olayem
content:
The Monetary Policy Committee of the Central Bank of Nigeria has retained the benchmark interest rate at 23 per cent, citing inflationary risks arising from anticipated election-related spending, increased festive season expenditure and disruptions to global energy supplies.

The CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso, announced the decision on Tuesday at the end of the committee’s 308th meeting, held on 23 and 24 November, 2026, in Abuja, with 10 members in attendance.

Cardoso said the committee retained the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) at 23 per cent.

The committee also maintained the Standing Facilities Corridor at +50 and -300 basis points around the MPR. The Cash Reserve Requirement was retained at 45 per cent for deposit money banks, 16 per cent for merchant banks and 75 per cent for non-Treasury Single Account public sector deposits.

The decision follows the 350-basis-point reduction in the benchmark interest rate from 26.5 per cent to 23 per cent in September 2026.

Cardoso explained that although headline inflation had moderated for five consecutive months, prevailing economic risks necessitated maintaining the current monetary policy stance to consolidate the gains recorded in price stability.

He said, “The MPC observed that the anticipated increase in spending from the end-of-year festive season and election-related activities could impact aggregate demand with likely upward pressure on prices.”

The committee also expressed concern over the ongoing Middle East conflict, which could sustain pressure on energy prices, and adverse weather conditions that could undermine food supply.

Nigeria’s headline inflation declined to 14.06 per cent in October from 14.63 per cent in September, while core inflation fell to 10.78 per cent from 12.95 per cent.

Food inflation also moderated to 19.13 per cent from 19.59 per cent, reflecting easing price pressures on processed food and farm produce following the commencement of the harvest season.

Cardoso attributed the sustained moderation in inflation to exchange rate stability, improved monetary policy transmission and the restrictive monetary policy stance.

He added that the Composite Purchasing Managers’ Index rose from 53 points in September to 53.2 points in October, reflecting improved activities across the industrial, agricultural and services sectors.

Responding to questions from journalists, Cardoso disclosed that the September interest rate adjustment was yielding the intended results, with interbank lending rates moving closer to the lower band of the Standing Facilities Corridor.

“What we’re finding is that the interbank rates are moving closer to the lower band of the corridor, and that’s exactly where we want to be,” he said.

The governor added that rates on Open Market Operations instruments and Treasury bills had moderated, while the gap between the benchmark interest rate and prevailing market rates had narrowed considerably.

He also disclosed that credit to the private sector was gradually recovering, adding that the apex bank would continue to monitor borrowing costs.

“We are very pleased that, really, the amount of credit going out to the private sector has gradually begun to come up,” Cardoso said.

He maintained that the September adjustment was intended to align the benchmark rate with market realities rather than signal a departure from the restrictive monetary policy stance.

On recent pressure on the naira and declining external reserves, Cardoso dismissed concerns over the sustainability of exchange rate stability, describing the developments as temporary and largely seasonal.

Nigeria’s gross external reserves stood at $54.02bn as of 17 November, 2026, sufficient to cover 10.26 months of imports of goods and services.

The governor attributed the recent volatility to year-end portfolio adjustments by foreign investors, increased foreign exchange demand by domestic businesses seeking to hedge against future risks and rising election-related expenditure.

“These are all seasonal. And we believe very strongly that as we go into the next year, we will find a major moderation in the volatility that you have seen,” he said.

Cardoso also disclosed that diaspora remittances exceeded $900m in the preceding month, adding that Nigeria’s current account surplus and sustained remittance inflows would strengthen external buffers.

He assured Nigerians that the apex bank would do everything possible to preserve exchange rate stability.

Speaking on the recently signed Memorandum of Understanding between the CBN and the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited, Cardoso said the agreement followed months of consultations between both institutions.

He explained that the partnership would improve transparency in the management of oil-related FX inflows, deepen the FX market, strengthen external reserves and support energy project financing.

The governor added that the CBN would deploy its advisory expertise and convening power to support the national oil company’s operations.

On the outlook for 2027, Cardoso promised policy consistency, stronger coordination between fiscal and monetary authorities, sustained banking sector stability and further improvements in monetary policy transmission.

“Our goal is single-digit inflation, and we will not stop until we get there. We will continue to ensure that we do everything possible to move inflation to single digits,” he said.

The post CBN holds rate at 23%, warns of election spending appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: FG corrects N330bn promissory note request, blames clerical error
description:
The Federal Government has clarified its request to the House of Representatives for approval of a N330.08bn promissory note, explaining that an earlier communication inadvertently omitted N60.64bn already covered by presidential approval.
In an addendum transmitted to the Speaker of the House of Re
content:
The Federal Government has clarified its request to the House of Representatives for approval of a N330.08bn promissory note, explaining that an earlier communication inadvertently omitted N60.64bn already covered by presidential approval.

In an addendum transmitted to the Speaker of the House of Representatives, the government said an internal review of its records revealed that the omission was caused by an isolated clerical oversight.

The clarification brings the total liabilities covered by the presidential approval to N330.081bn, comprising N269.446bn and an additional N60.635bn.

The original request, conveyed in a letter dated 18 August, 2026, by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Senator George Akume, sought the National Assembly’s approval for the establishment and expansion of the Promissory Note Programme to settle verified outstanding contractual, project-related and other financial obligations owed by the Federal Government.

However, the initial correspondence put the liabilities at N269.45bn, leaving out the additional N60.64bn now covered by the addendum.

The addendum, signed by the Permanent Secretary, General Services Office, Office of the SGF, Dr Ibrahim Kana, on behalf of Akume, attributed the discrepancy to an oversight in the earlier communication.

The letter read, “Our attention was drawn to the non-inclusion, and upon reviewing our internal documentation discovered that an isolated clerical oversight excluded a portion of the Presidential approval.”

It further explained that the presidential approval attached to the addendum covered both liability components, bringing the total proposed issuance to N330.08bn.

Consequently, the government requested an amendment to paragraph 7(b) on page two of its earlier letter to reflect the full amount.

The government stressed that the addendum should be treated as an integral part of the original correspondence, referenced 58775/A/183 and dated 18 August, 2026, rather than as a fresh request.

The clarification establishes that the additional N60.64bn was already covered by the president’s approval and was not a new liability introduced through the addendum.

However, the presidential approval does not dispense with the need for legislative authorisation. The government is still required to secure the National Assembly’s approval for the proposed programme, with the revised request expressly allowing lawmakers to approve the aggregate amount or such other figure as they consider appropriate.

The Promissory Note Programme provides a framework for settling verified government obligations by converting outstanding claims into formal debt instruments, allowing repayment over an agreed period instead of immediate cash settlement.

It has been used by successive administrations to address inherited domestic obligations, including outstanding payments to contractors, suppliers and other creditors arising from government contracts and projects.

title: A campaign of violence, by Rotimi Fasan
description: With more cases of political violence across the country, our politicians are not about to tread the path of peace. They say one thing in the morning and do another in the night. What they say before the cameras is not what you hear from their mouths when the cameras are turned off. The cameras are
content:
With more cases of political violence across the country, our politicians are not about to tread the path of peace. They say one thing in the morning and do another in the night. What they say before the cameras is not what you hear from their mouths when the cameras are turned off. The cameras are becoming more of an energiser than a discourager of violence. Not a few of them have been caught inciting violence before the cameras. What happened in Ughelli North yesterday is sad.

In this game, nobody is left out, from the most educated technocrat and intellectual to the career scoundrels and thugs that kill and maim for a living. Some Nigerians have been losing their humanity as a demonstration of faith in the power mongers they support in the name of politics.

It is no longer sufficient to call for peace. What is needed is to impose heavy sanctions on perpetrators of violence and their promoters. The ruling APC-led government must understand that the greater responsibility lies with it to ensure that the next election and the period thereafter are violence-free. The opposition has less to lose under this climate of fear. It is good that President Bola Tinubu is suing for peace, both in his party and in the country as a whole. But that is not sufficient. He has to go beyond the rhetoric of politicking to actual action, making an example of people, including members of his own party, who are seen as or known to be promoting violence.

It is bad enough that his own comment that all is fair in politics has been turned into a cudgel that is not only being used to beat him. It is the justification some have for promoting violence. Even if what he said is not a direct endorsement of violence, he left room for the narrow interpretation that has been given to it. He should have made a full-throated condemnation of some members of his own party who have been found to be violence-prone. Just as he would not give his opponents a quarter, he cannot expect them to give him one. Last week, he encouraged his supporters to drown his opponents with votes. How does he expect them to respond? They would drown him in and with whatever is at their disposal. He must now draw a firm line between rhetoric and action; between making remarks he might well mean to be light-hearted and saying something open-ended that his opponents can seize upon for their own sinister purposes. He should not be seen to be encouraging Machiavellian schemes in the pursuit of power.

Contrary to the claims of his opponents, who made a meal of his initial campaign itinerary that limited his visits to twelve states, Nigerians can see that he has been doing the work. Not just him but also members of his immediate family have been on the road. All of this while his opponents are the ones whose campaigns have been limited to the few states and places they could manage. Rather than see the President’s decision to restrict his campaign to less than half of the states in the country as their own opportunity to expand the latitude of their message to Nigerians, they draped themselves in sackcloth and ashes, crying themselves blind that the President was too weak to campaign. A few weeks on, the President has changed his itinerary and increased the number of states he will cover before January 16, 2027. He is clearly making good progress.

This would all count for nothing if the ruling APC or the government of President Bola Tinubu allows things to slide out of its control and the country plunges into violence. Nobody would be exonerated. There is hardly any political party, major or minor, that can be given a clean bill as far as its involvement in the violence of this season is concerned. Certainly not any of the leading parties. Which brings me to the ADC and the NDC and other parties that some people tend to see as innocent victims of the intolerant politics of the APC. Nothing could be further from the truth. They are as much perpetrators of violence against others, including the APC and weaker elements within their own parties, as they are victims of violence from the APC and other parties. Their hands, too, are covered in blood. The presidential candidate of the ADC, Atiku Abubakar, has been doing all within his power, for instance, to fish in troubled waters. For very good reasons, he sees Bola Tinubu as the only obstacle to his lifelong dream of becoming a tenant in Aso Villa.

While Peter Obi and his supporters can deceive themselves as they like, Atiku Abubakar knows where his problem lies, and it is right now in Abuja and specifically in Aso Villa. Not Onitsha, Agulu or anywhere else Obi calls home. It is why he has been throwing all the barbs in his arsenal at Tinubu, from name-calling to tantrums, insults to rage-baiting and the commissioning of lobbyists and investigators to dig up all the dirt they can on him. In all of this, Peter Obi only comes into the conversation when Atiku is looking to persuade him to drop his ambition for 2027. His attacks on Tinubu have not had the desired effect. They are not hurting the man who has been teaching the Waziri advanced lessons in politics and strategy. Atiku’s last refuge is now the bare-faced promotion of ethnicity, regional and religious separatism.

It is clear that Atiku is a wounded politician whose desperation to be president knows no limit. His situation has grown more desperate and testier since Justice Peter Lifu booted out his side of the faction involved in the ADC’s leadership crisis. Since then, he has only come short of calling for civil disorder. Which is what appears to be the strategy of Peter Obi and his followers. Their behaviour, as that of Atiku and his followers, suggests an acceptance of defeat and the idea that the only way to stop a Tinubu victory next year is to plunge the country into civil disorder. It is why Peter Obi would be encouraging his supporters to sing the old national anthem at the official campaign of a supposed national party that promotes someone who hopes to lead Nigeria.

The post A campaign of violence, by Rotimi Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Taxation or imposition: The state, economy and citizenship in Nigeria (2), by Usman Sarki
description:
“We cannot demand twenty-first-century compliance with twentieth-century communication.” — Mohammed Idris Bultu



The first part of this article examined taxation as a relationship between the state and the citizen and ended with a fundamental question: what does the state owe the citizen after col
content:
“We cannot demand twenty-first-century compliance with twentieth-century communication.” — Mohammed Idris Bultu

The first part of this article examined taxation as a relationship between the state and the citizen and ended with a fundamental question: what does the state owe the citizen after collecting his money? Two thoughtful responses to that article have since helped to sharpen the inquiry considerably.

Barrister Muhammad Betara, an Abuja-based lawyer, approached the subject mainly from the standpoint of law and public administration, while Mohammed Idris Bultu, a Tax Controller with the Nigeria Revenue Service in Kano, responded from the practical experience of a tax administrator who encounters taxpayers, assessments, compliance and collection in the field.

Taken together, their observations provide an important bridge between theory, law and administrative practice. Barrister Betara’s central point is that Nigeria is not without a legal framework for taxation. On the contrary, the Constitution and the recent tax reforms impose clear duties upon citizens and create elaborate machinery for assessment, collection and administration.

According to him, Section 24(f) of the 1999 Constitution places upon every citizen the duty to declare his income honestly and pay his tax promptly. That obligation is direct and enforceable. At the same time, the Constitution declares that the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government and places upon the state broad responsibilities relating to economic welfare, justice and social order.

Betara’s important observation is that an imbalance exists between these two sides of the constitutional bargain. The citizen’s obligation to pay tax is concrete and enforceable, while many of the wider welfare obligations of government cannot be enforced by the citizen in quite the same manner. This immediately raises the problem of reciprocity.

If the state possesses machinery to compel compliance from the citizen, what equivalent machinery exists which enables the citizen to compel transparency, accountability and adequate service delivery from the state? This lies very close to the heart of the distinction between taxation and imposition.

The recent tax reforms have sought to strengthen and modernise the administrative capacity of government. They aim to harmonise tax administration, rationalise procedures, improve taxpayer identification, expand the tax base and provide mechanisms for objection and appeal.

Barrister Betara therefore makes the important point that the Nigerian problem is not simply the absence of laws. The problem is that the machinery of collection often appears stronger, more visible and more immediate than the machinery of public accountability.

Tax Officer Mohammed Bultu’s practical observations reinforce this point from another direction. His first proposition is simple but profound: legitimacy makes collection possible. A tax may be perfectly lawful, but if taxpayers do not understand why they are paying, under what authority, or what purpose the revenue is intended to serve, resistance increases and enforcement becomes more difficult.

This is particularly striking because it comes from a practising tax administrator. What might appear to an academic as a question of legitimacy is, to the tax officer, an operational reality that could become an impediment. Taxation with understanding is therefore not merely a philosophical ideal but an administrative necessity.

This takes us back to the historical reflections in the first part of this series. From Buchan and Morel to the present day, governments have repeatedly confronted the same question: how can taxation be made legitimate in the eyes of those who are compelled by law to pay? Legality is indispensable, but legitimacy requires something more.

Bultu’s second observation concerns the effect of the oil era on the Nigerian fiscal relationship. For decades, governments relied heavily upon petroleum revenues rather than upon the direct contributions of citizens. This relaxed the psychological link between taxation and citizenship.

The citizen did not always feel that government depended financially upon him, and government did not always feel compelled to explain itself to the citizen in the manner that a truly tax-dependent state might have required. That era is now changing.

As taxation becomes increasingly central to financing government, the psychology of government and citizenship must change with it. Citizens will naturally demand greater explanation of what government costs, what it collects and what it delivers. Bultu’s third point is equally important: law alone does not create trust.

A modern tax regime may expand the tax base and improve collection, but if implementation is perceived as aggressive, rushed or overly focused on targets and penalties, citizens may experience reform not as a social contract but as an imposition. This is why taxpayer education becomes crucial.

His memorable observation that Nigeria cannot demand twenty-first-century compliance with twentieth-century communication deserves to be deeply understood and taken seriously. A taxpayer who understands his obligations, his rights and the procedures available to him is more valuable to the state than one who complies merely out of fear and with resentment.

Taxation should therefore not be organised simply around collection targets. It must also be organised around explanation, simplicity, fairness and confidence.

Barrister Betara similarly draws attention to rights already available to taxpayers, such as rights to proper assessment, objection, appeal and protection from unlawful or multiple taxation. But rights are of little practical value where citizens do not know that these exist or cannot exercise them without excessive cost and difficulty.

Both responses therefore converge on one principle: the state must not only collect efficiently; it must also communicate efficiently, account efficiently and protect the taxpayer efficiently. A second area of convergence concerns taxable capacity. The law may identify income and calculate liability according to established rules, but this does not necessarily reveal the citizen’s real economic condition.

A Nigerian may earn what appears on paper to be a taxable income, while much of that income may already be committed to privately providing electricity, water, transportation, healthcare, education and security. This affects not only personal welfare but the capacity to save, accumulate assets, invest and achieve long-term financial security.

The Nigerian who appears reasonably comfortable on paper may, in reality, possess very little disposable income after meeting expenses that, in other societies, are substantially supported by public services. The same problem confronts businesses even more starkly.

An enterprise may pay taxes and levies while still providing its own electricity, water, security, communications and sometimes access roads, in addition to absorbing transportation costs created by deficient infrastructure and meeting minimum wage requirements for its employees.

This creates what might be described as a double fiscal burden, under which the citizen finances the state and then privately finances the substitutes for services the state has failed adequately to provide. This raises a question that deserves greater attention in Nigerian fiscal policy: should taxable capacity be considered simply in terms of nominal income, or should government become more sensitive to the total economic burden already borne by citizens and businesses?

Both Betara and Bultu also emphasise accountability. If the taxpayer must keep records, disclose income, file returns and prove compliance, then government should be equally capable of showing what it collected, where the money went, who authorised the expenditure and what public value resulted. This symmetry is indispensable. The taxpayer should not be transparent to the state while the state remains opaque to the taxpayer.

There should therefore be a traceable public chain of collection, receipt, appropriation, expenditure, delivery, audit and reporting. Citizens should be able to understand, in reasonably simple language, how public revenue moves from their pockets into the treasury and from the treasury into roads, schools, hospitals, water systems, security and other public services.

This need not require every Nigerian to become an accountant or forensic auditor. Governments themselves should make fiscal information intelligible and accessible in this digitally connected world.

Imagine if every tier of government periodically told citizens, in plain language: this is what we collected; this is what we received; this is what we spent; these are the projects completed; this is what remains; and this is what the auditors found. Such a practice would not weaken government but would strengthen it considerably and grant it legitimacy.

For taxation does more than raise revenue. Properly organised, it strengthens democratic governance and creates a citizen who asks questions, scrutinises expenditure and recognises public money as partly his own contribution to the commonwealth. Nigeria therefore needs more than a tax-paying culture. It needs a tax-accountability culture.

The true reform is not simply a new tax rate or collection mechanism but a new fiscal bargain. The citizen should be able to say: “I will declare honestly, comply with the law willingly and pay what is lawfully due diligently.” The state must also be able to answer: “We will make the system fair, simple, transparent and accountable, and we will show you what your contribution has achieved.”

Until both sides of that bargain are visible and credible, the Nigerian taxpayer will continue to ask the question around which this series revolves: Is this taxation, or is it merely collection? And when does collection become imposition? That question leads naturally to the third and final part, which concludes with the profound issues that Betara and Bultu raised.

The post Taxation or imposition: The state, economy and citizenship in Nigeria (2), by Usman Sarki appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Duke Oil: NNPC explains $2bn crude-for-petrol transactions
description: The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited has denied claims that $2.04bn in crude oil proceeds involving its trading subsidiary, Duke Oil Company Incorporated, now NNPC Trading S.A., is missing, insisting that all transactions under the Direct Sale Direct Purchase programme were fully accounte
content:
The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited has denied claims that $2.04bn in crude oil proceeds involving its trading subsidiary, Duke Oil Company Incorporated, now NNPC Trading S.A., is missing, insisting that all transactions under the Direct Sale Direct Purchase programme were fully accounted for.

The national oil company said the apparent gaps in dollar receipts cited in recent media reports arose from the settlement arrangement under the programme, through which the value of crude supplied was offset against the cost of refined petroleum products delivered to Nigeria.

In a statement issued on Tuesday by its Chief Corporate Communications Officer, Andy Odeh, titled ‘Duke Oil Cargoes Are Fully Accounted For’, the company said the $2.04bn represented the gross value of 29 crude cargoes and did not constitute missing or unpaid revenue.

NNPC said the absence of separate dollar payments for the cargoes was consistent with the contractual terms of the DSDP arrangement, under which crude oil was exchanged for refined products.

“NNPC Limited states categorically that no sum is missing, unaccounted for, or unpaid, in respect of crude cargoes lifted by Duke Oil Company Incorporated, now NNPC Trading S.A., under the Direct Sale Direct Purchase programme.

“No separate receipt appears because the crude sale proceeds were set off against the product purchase price, as the contracts provide,” the company stated.

It added that the reports in question acknowledged that the records pointed to reconciliation of transactions within the NNPC Group rather than any financial loss.

Under the DSDP programme, Duke Oil and other participating traders lifted Nigerian crude oil and supplied refined petroleum products, including petrol, for the domestic market.

While crude oil was priced in dollars, the petroleum products supplied were sold in naira. The value of the products delivered was subsequently reconciled against the corresponding crude oil value, with the transactions reflected in the audited financial statements of the relevant entities.

NNPC further argued that the reports had acknowledged that all 59 crude cargoes were accounted for and reconciled with their respective beneficiaries.

Providing a breakdown, the company said 30 cargoes were paid for in dollars, while proceeds from 28 cargoes, valued at approximately $1.96bn, were remitted in naira into the NNPC Group Treasury or NNPC Upstream Investment Management Services accounts.

It said the remaining cargo, a February 2023 Bonga tax-oil lifting valued at approximately $75.9m, was paid directly into the then-designated dollar account of the Federal Inland Revenue Service.

The company maintained that the transactions were properly documented and that the absence of separate dollar receipts for some cargoes should not be interpreted as evidence of missing funds.

NNPC also defended the role of Duke Oil, following reports, describing the company as NNPC operating under another name.

It said Duke Oil was incorporated in 1989 as a wholly owned trading subsidiary of NNPC, adding that its ownership had been disclosed in the national oil company’s corporate history, audited financial statements and the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative’s 2023 industry report.

“Characterising Duke Oil as ‘NNPC wearing another name’ frames a long-disclosed fact as a revelation,” the company said.

The post Duke Oil: NNPC explains $2bn crude-for-petrol transactions appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: UCL: Dortmund end Arsenal’s perfect home record with 1-1 Emirates draw
description:
Borussia Dortmund ended Arsenal’s perfect home record in this season’s UEFA Champions League league phase after fighting back to secure a 1-1 draw at the Emirates Stadium on Tuesday.
Viktor Gyökeres gave the Gunners an early lead with a stunning long-range effort in the 10th minute, but Maximilian B
content:
Borussia Dortmund ended Arsenal’s perfect home record in this season’s UEFA Champions League league phase after fighting back to secure a 1-1 draw at the Emirates Stadium on Tuesday.

Viktor Gyökeres gave the Gunners an early lead with a stunning long-range effort in the 10th minute, but Maximilian Beier equalised 10 minutes into the second half to earn the German side a valuable point.

Arsenal dominated much of the opening period and created several opportunities to increase their advantage but failed to convert their chances, allowing Dortmund to grow into the contest.

The hosts started brightly, with Noni Madueke creating an early opportunity for Christos Tzolis, whose volley went over the crossbar in the second minute.

Madueke continued to trouble Dortmund down the right flank, while Gyökeres also tested goalkeeper Gregor Kobel with a long-range attempt.

Arsenal eventually broke the deadlock in the 10th minute when Madueke laid the ball back for Gyökeres, who unleashed a powerful, dipping strike from about 25 yards that flew beyond Kobel and into the net.

The goal marked Arsenal’s 400th in Champions League history.

Mikel Arteta’s men continued to push for a second goal, with Tzolis forcing a save from Kobel before Madueke failed to convert the rebound.

Declan Rice also threatened, sending one long-range effort over the crossbar before Dortmund defender Nico Schlotterbeck blocked another attempt after Martin Ødegaard had set him up with a clever touch.

Arsenal maintained the pressure, but Piero Hincapié’s attempted cutback to Gyökeres was intercepted, while the Swedish striker fired over from an Ødegaard pass shortly before half-time.

Dortmund, who had struggled to create clear chances before the break, nearly punished Arsenal immediately after the restart when Beier failed to make proper contact with a low cross inside the penalty area.

Madueke then went close at the other end, cutting inside before sending a low effort narrowly wide.

However, Dortmund gradually found their rhythm and equalised in the 55th minute through Beier.

Joane Gadou drove forward through the middle before picking out Beier inside the penalty area. The forward evaded Gabriel Magalhães before calmly slotting the ball past Kepa Arrizabalaga to make it 1-1.

Arsenal responded with renewed attacking pressure, but Kobel denied Hincapié with a save from a header at a tight angle. Ben White also missed an opportunity, firing over after good work from Gyökeres.

Dortmund thought they had completed the comeback when Jobe Bellingham turned in a rebound, but the goal was ruled out for offside.

Arteta introduced Eberechi Eze and other substitutes as Arsenal searched for a late winner. Madueke, Gyökeres and Ødegaard continued to combine in attack, but the Gunners struggled to find a way past Dortmund’s defence.

Gyökeres missed a chance to restore Arsenal’s lead when he headed an Ødegaard cross wide, while Madueke also failed to hit the target.

The hosts came particularly close in the closing stages. Serhou Guirassy struck his own post while attempting to deal with a dangerous low free-kick from Ødegaard, before Rice hit the opposite upright following a pass from Eze.

Despite registering 29 attempts on goal, Arsenal could not find a winner as Dortmund held firm to secure the draw.

The result ended Arsenal’s 100 per cent home record in the Champions League league phase, although Arteta’s side maintained their unbeaten run in the competition.

Arsenal will turn their attention to the Premier League on Sunday when they host Manchester City at the Emirates Stadium. They will then welcome Real Madrid in their next Champions League fixture on December 9.

The post UCL: Dortmund end Arsenal’s perfect home record with 1-1 Emirates draw appeared first on Very Nigerian.

title: Saving Enyimba FC from relegation, by Ochereome Nnanna
description: This article is not about football per se. It is about Enyimba International Football Club of Aba, Abia State. Before the coming of our phenomenal and algorithmic Governor, Dr Alex C. Otti, to the saddle, Enyimba FC was about the only thing that made us Abians proud of our state. We were like the ea
content:
This article is not about football per se. It is about Enyimba International Football Club of Aba, Abia State. Before the coming of our phenomenal and algorithmic Governor, Dr Alex C. Otti, to the saddle, Enyimba FC was about the only thing that made us Abians proud of our state. We were like the eagle chained by bad governance for so long that we forgot to fly. Enyimba is the most prestigious and dominant force in Nigerian football.

Three football clubs have historically personified the irrepressible, resilient, successful and enterprising spirit for which the Igbo nation is famous all over the world. The Enugu Rangers International served notice that though we lost the Biafra War, we were not a defeated people. However, though the Rangers dominated Nigerian football and the Green Eagles in the 1970s, their Ibadan rivals, IICC Shooting Stars, beat them to the first achievement of winning the African Winners Cup in 1976. The following year, Rangers achieved the same feat, but IICC fans retain the bragging rights of being there first.

Later on, the Spartans FC of Owerri, which was formed around the same time as Enyimba in 1976, became Iwuanyanwu Nationale and dominated the so-called “professional” era. The Owerri club was renamed Heartland FC, a name it wore until it was relegated for the fourth time to the Nigeria National League (NNL) on 25th May 2025 under the hand of Governor Hope Uzodimma. Its first relegation took place in 2016. Imo has seemingly ceased to be a notable footballing state despite an abundance of talents.

Enyimba FC of Aba is the real “agba baller” of Nigerian football. It is to Nigeria what Real Madrid is to Spain. It also compares only to Liverpool FC in England in terms of comprehensive domestic dominance and continental conquests. Enyimba remains the only Nigerian club to win the CAF Champions League – back-to-back in 2003 and 2004 – with two African Super Cups. This is apart from dominating in the local league and sharing top prizes in the FA Cup series. If there is any one lasting legacy for which Senator Orji Uzor Kalu will be forever remembered, it is the Enyimba CAF Champions League achievements, which happened under his watch as Governor of Abia State.

If you check how our mighty Enyimba FC is doing in the 14th week of the current NPFL season, you will be shocked to see it slumbering in the 18th position – topping the relegation zone! That was how Heartland started before it became a regular customer in the second-class NNL. God forbid that Enyimba will suffer this fate. It will be so abominable, a taboo! Experience has shown that once a mighty club tastes relegation, it always goes back for more. Enyimba must NEVER be relegated! It must return to its pride of place – at the top currently occupied by its elder brother, Rangers.

In truth, Enyimba has been suffering since 2015 when Dr Okezie Ikpeazu took over as governor. When Otti assumed office, one of the steps he took to revive the fortunes of the club was the appointment of Nigeria’s international star and most decorated hero, Nwankwo Kanu, as Chairman in July 2023. The reasoning behind this was impeccable. Kanu, with his wealth of professional experience, influence and network, should bring back the days of glory. In football circles, there is always this argument that former top players are the natural choices to inherit football coaching and management because they know where the shoe pinches.

The stupendous successes recorded by superstar Zinedine Zidane at his former club, Real Madrid, made this case for ex-players. During his 2016–2018 and 2019–2021 tenures as Madrid manager, Zidane won eleven major trophies, including the historic three consecutive Champions League victories. By contrast, Enyimba FC did not win anything under Kanu’s reign. It only managed to place 3rd in 2023/2024, sixth in 2024/2025 and 18th in the current season before the board was dissolved recently. Another former Eagles star, Finidi George, managed to win an NPFL trophy as Enyimba coach but could not subsequently maintain a strong standing in the league, hence the change.

So, being a former intercontinental star and national hero alone isn’t automatic credentials to be a successful coach or manager. Orji Kalu is widely acclaimed to have personally provided the leadership for Enyimba’s success, though he was never a footballer. He loved the game, followed it and learned all the tricks around it. Kalu attended Enyimba training sessions and engaged in football politics. He understood the off-the-pitch intrigues that often resonate in on-pitch victories. He also had in Victor Agwu Anyansi a club Chairman in the same mould, though Anyansi, like me, never played football except as a hobby. OUK would have been more useful to Nigeria as a football administrator, not a lawmaker.

The lesson here is that a person does not have to be an ex-player to be a good club chairman whose job is political and managerial. It requires a person who understands the game, player psychology, referee intrigues and the gamut of politics around football. It also requires a person with a rugged character and a “killer instinct”, who will not back down from anything required for victory. Nwankwo Kanu is a jolly good fellow, a gentleman who would probably refuse to break a head. Governor Otti did well to intervene. Thank God, the season is still young. Enyimba still stands an excellent chance to bounce back up if the right hands are found to steer the Board and Bench.

I hope Governor Otti brings his usual savvy in team selection for effective governance to bear in the search for Kanu’s successor. The person must “know” football, its political intrigues, inner games and the ability to motivate action. Enyimba FC is more than a football club.

It is the spirit of our people.

The post Saving Enyimba FC from relegation, by Ochereome Nnanna appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: COP31 president apologises to Africa after interrupting minister
description: The President of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, Murat Kurum, has apologised to Ghana’s Minister for Environment, Science and Technology, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, and the African Group of Negotiators after interrupting her while delivering Africa’s closing statement at the summit
content:
The President of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, Murat Kurum, has apologised to Ghana’s Minister for Environment, Science and Technology, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, and the African Group of Negotiators after interrupting her while delivering Africa’s closing statement at the summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

Kurum’s apology followed an angry protest by African negotiators, who accused him of disrespecting the continent by cutting short the minister’s presentation at the closing plenary on Sunday.

The incident, which unfolded during the final hours of the contentious climate negotiations, added to the tension surrounding a summit that ended without consensus on its overarching political agreement after nearly 50 hours of overtime discussions.

A video of the apology, shared by Ghanaian broadcaster Citi FM and obtained by our correspondent on Tuesday, showed Kurum holding Agyeman-Rawlings’ hand as he addressed her through an interpreter, insisting that he had never intended to undermine her or the African continent.

“There is no way for us to accept any attempt to interrupt you or anyone from your continent, let alone a valuable lady like you. It never crossed my mind.

“We were only trying to seek ways to engage with you and amass the points towards a common decision and advance a grant and concession decision.

“So, in order for us to be able to manage the plenary, I knew you wanted to object even before I finished. I am sure your brother was aware of the discussion we had on the texts.

“Please always remember that we are brothers here. Please don’t see this as disrespect. It was never like that. We would like to convey our apologies for this misunderstanding,” Kurum said.

Agyeman-Rawlings accepted the apology, saying disagreements were inevitable in international climate negotiations but should not undermine the spirit of cooperation among participating countries.

“I think that at forums like this, it is easy to get frustrated during the process, and I understand that it can be something else when there is no consensus around issues.

“We are all here as representatives. We are here for one another. Thank you very much. I wish everyone well as you travel back,” she said.

The exchange attracted applause from officials who witnessed the reconciliation, with the Chair of the African Group of Negotiators, Antwi-Boasiako Amoah also present.

However, the apology came after a tense confrontation during which the Ghanaian environment minister openly challenged the COP31 presidency over what they described as unequal treatment of African countries.

Agyeman-Rawlings was about a minute into reading the African Group’s closing statement when Kurum interrupted her.

The interruption immediately drew an objection from Amoah, who reminded the COP31 president that other delegations had been allowed to express their positions on the proposed agreement without being stopped.

“With all due respect, Mr President, you’ve not shown respect to a group of 54 countries and my country, for that matter,” he said.

“We were just making a short intervention and you cut us in the middle of the conversation. This is not acceptable, Mr President.”

When she was allowed to speak again, Agyeman-Rawlings made it clear that she considered the interruption an affront to the African delegation and the continent’s participation in the negotiations.

“I was rudely cut off during my delivery by your good self,” she told Kurum.

“This, Excellency, is an example of the levels of disrespect that we have endured.”

She also questioned the conduct of the plenary, insisting that the established rules of multilateral negotiations required every delegation to be given a fair opportunity to express its position.

“There is a code of conduct during our deliberations, and yours towards me was unacceptable,” she said.

The minister further disclosed that she had changed her flight arrangements twice and extended her stay by several days to participate in the closing session, which had continued beyond the summit’s scheduled conclusion.

She subsequently restarted the African Group’s statement from the beginning, restating the continent’s concerns about the proposed outcome of the negotiations.

Ghana’s Ministry of Environment, Science and Technology later said the incident underscored the right of every country, regardless of its size or influence, to be heard in international climate negotiations.

The African delegation used its closing intervention to highlight what it considered major shortcomings in the proposed Antalya Pact, particularly the absence of a clear financial commitment to help vulnerable countries adapt to climate change.

Agyeman-Rawlings said African countries had arrived in Türkiye expecting governments to translate the commitment made at the previous climate summit in Belém, Brazil, into a concrete financing arrangement to triple adaptation finance by 2035.

However, she complained that the proposed text repeated the ambition without specifying the existing funding baseline, the amount governments would provide or a clear pathway for achieving the target.

title: FG job freeze: Empower private sector-led jobs
description: AT an official rate of 4.3 per cent, unemployment should not be a pressing concern in Africa’s third-largest economy, with a GDP of $386.67 billion, according to Worldometer. Yet, thousands of young Nigerians roam the streets in desperate search of jobs that do not exist. The disconnect is partly ex
content:
AT an official rate of 4.3 per cent, unemployment should not be a pressing concern in Africa’s third-largest economy, with a GDP of $386.67 billion, according to Worldometer. Yet, thousands of young Nigerians roam the streets in desperate search of jobs that do not exist. The disconnect is partly explained by the fact that more than 90 per cent of working Nigerians are reportedly engaged in the informal sector, where employment is largely precarious, poorly remunerated and devoid of social protection.

The December 2025 State of the Nigerian Youth report by ActionAid Nigeria puts the estimated number of unemployed youths at a staggering 80 million.

Whether this figure captures the full scale of youth unemployment or not, it is undeniable that Nigeria faces a jobs crisis that government employment alone cannot resolve.

Indeed, it is naïve to imagine that an already bloated and inefficient public service can absorb this army of job seekers.

Even the Federal Civil Service, which ought to offer opportunities based on merit and competence, has become a difficult destination for qualified graduates. Recruitment is often perceived to be influenced more by political connections and patronage than by ability, while remuneration at the lower cadres is hardly attractive.

Worse, the proliferation of questionable agencies, unauthorised appointments and payroll irregularities further constricts opportunities for genuine applicants.

The disturbing revelations surrounding the alleged Presidential Foreign Intervention Promotion Council illustrate the rot. Its Director-General, Adeniyi Adeyemi, is standing trial over allegations that he operated a fake federal agency.

How such an outfit allegedly secured office accommodation at the Federal Secretariat in Abuja, opened bank accounts, operated a website presenting itself as a federal institution and purportedly attracted more than N27 billion for its establishment raises fundamental questions about oversight and accountability in the public service. The court will determine the allegations, but the circumstances demand serious scrutiny.

Similarly, the National Brands Development and Made-in-Nigeria Special Project Office reportedly operated within the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation without presidential authorisation.

These revelations expose the absurdity of a public service in which questionable structures can emerge and thrive while qualified young Nigerians struggle to secure legitimate employment.

Against this background, the Federal Government’s decision to rein in recruitment and tighten personnel management is commendable. It has directed MDAs to freeze workforce expansion and maintain their existing personnel levels through 2027.

The directive, issued by the Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, prohibits MDAs from expanding their workforce or creating new units, departments and senior-level positions on Salary Grade Levels 15 to 17 without explicit clearance.

They are required to submit updated nominal rolls showing their personnel strength as of October 31, 2026, alongside their 2027 budget proposals. Agencies that fail to comply risk forfeiting their 2027 personnel allocations and authorised establishments.

The policy is intended to curb escalating personnel costs, eliminate unauthorised positions and ensure that all employees are properly captured on official financial platforms, including the Integrated Personnel and Payroll Information System and the Government Integrated Financial Management Information System.

There is little to quarrel with in a policy designed to stop the public service from becoming an endless drain on public resources.

However, a recruitment freeze, by itself, is no substitute for the more fundamental restructuring that Nigeria’s unwieldy bureaucracy desperately requires. Freezing employment without dismantling redundant institutions, eliminating ghost workers and plugging payroll leakages would amount to treating the symptoms while leaving the disease untouched.

The Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission reportedly assessed 344 MDAs in its 2025 Ethics and Integrity Compliance Scorecard, while the Federal Civil Service Commission’s website lists more than 1,000 MDAs.

Such institutional proliferation is indefensible in a country struggling to finance basic infrastructure, education, healthcare and security.

If the Federal Government is genuinely committed to reducing waste and improving efficiency, it must finally confront the elephant in the room and implement the Stephen Oronsaye Report of 2012.

The report recommended reducing 263 statutory agencies to 161 through the abolition of 38, merger of 52 and conversion of 14 into ministerial departments. Fourteen years later, the continued failure to fully implement these recommendations speaks volumes about the political unwillingness to dismantle structures that serve entrenched interests.

More importantly, Nigeria must abandon the dangerous assumption that government is the country’s principal employer or can somehow manufacture jobs by creating more agencies and expanding payrolls.

The private sector, particularly SMEs, is the real engine of sustainable employment. It is businesses that produce goods, provide services, innovate, generate wealth and create jobs beyond the narrow confines of government offices.

The experience of China demonstrates what is possible. According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, SMEs contribute approximately 50 per cent of the country’s tax revenue, 60 per cent of its GDP, 70 per cent of technological innovation and 80 per cent of urban employment. These figures demonstrate the enormous economic value of cultivating an environment in which businesses can grow, innovate and employ millions.

Nigeria has enormous opportunities in agriculture, telecommunications, hospitality, textiles, manufacturing and aviation. These sectors have the capacity to absorb substantial numbers of workers if properly supported.

Yet, successive governments have paid lip service to industrialisation while presiding over an environment characterised by erratic electricity, poor transport infrastructure, multiple taxation, policy inconsistency, insecurity and prohibitively expensive credit.

The consequences are evident in the exodus of multinational companies that have either shut down operations or scaled back their presence in Nigeria.

Many of these businesses were driven out by foreign-exchange instability, rising operating costs, infrastructure deficits and an unpredictable regulatory environment.

It is self-defeating for a government to lament unemployment while pursuing policies or tolerating conditions that make it increasingly difficult for existing businesses to survive, let alone attract new investments.

Singapore, despite producing only about 20,538 barrels of crude oil daily, the Asian country has developed into a major refining and petrochemical hub, with refining capacity estimated at between 1.38 million and 1.5 million bpd.

Its success underscores the importance of industrial policy, infrastructure, investment and value addition rather than dependence on crude oil exports. Nigeria, with its vastly greater resource endowment, has little excuse for failing to build industries capable of generating millions of jobs.

For SMEs, survival itself has become a struggle. The high cost of borrowing, with the Central Bank of Nigeria’s monetary policy rate at 23 per cent, effectively shuts many small businesses out of formal credit.

Government intervention funds, specialised credit facilities and targeted tax relief are therefore essential.

Small businesses cannot expand their workforce when much of their earnings go into servicing expensive loans, purchasing generators, paying multiple levies and meeting rising operating costs.

The Federal Government must invest deliberately in industrial clusters, accessible markets, vocational training and reliable infrastructure.

Affordable and dependable electricity, efficient ports, functional roads, modern rail networks and affordable digital connectivity are not luxuries; they are prerequisites for productive enterprise.

Public investment should be directed towards removing the obstacles that prevent businesses from expanding and employing more people.

Ultimately, the federal job freeze should be more than an exercise in controlling personnel expenditure.

It should mark a decisive shift in economic thinking: from an overbearing government that creates bureaucratic positions to a developmental state that creates the conditions for productive businesses to flourish.

The government cannot employ every Nigerian, nor should it try. Its responsibility is to provide security, infrastructure, stable policies, affordable financing and an efficient regulatory environment in which the private sector can thrive.

Until Nigeria makes this fundamental shift, millions of young people will continue to chase scarce government appointments while the country’s enormous job-creating potential remains untapped.

The post FG job freeze: Empower private sector-led jobs appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Ecobank announces exit of three directors
description:
Ecobank Transnational Incorporated, the parent company of Ecobank Group, has announced the departure of three members of its board of directors, including representatives nominated by Qatar National Bank and South Africa’s Public Investment Corporation.
The departures involve David O’Sullivan and Za
content:
Ecobank Transnational Incorporated, the parent company of Ecobank Group, has announced the departure of three members of its board of directors, including representatives nominated by Qatar National Bank and South Africa’s Public Investment Corporation.

The departures involve David O’Sullivan and Zanele Monnakgotla, both Non-Executive Directors nominated by the two financial institutions, and Esther Chibesa, an Independent Director who resigned from the board.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, 24 November, 2026, in Lomé, Togo, the bank said O’Sullivan and Monnakgotla retired following the expiration of their respective board tenures, while Chibesa stepped down to pursue other interests.

O’Sullivan represented Qatar National Bank on the board, while Monnakgotla was nominated by the Public Investment Corporation, South Africa’s state-owned investment manager.

The announcement did not disclose the circumstances surrounding Chibesa’s resignation or indicate whether the two institutions would nominate replacements for their outgoing representatives.

The changes come at the board level of the pan-African banking group, which operates across 34 sub-Saharan African countries and maintains additional international operations in France, the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates and China.

Ecobank said its board, management and employees appreciated the contributions of the three departing directors to the group’s development.

The bank also acknowledged their continued willingness to support the organisation whenever called upon.

Ecobank Group employs more than 14,000 people and provides consumer, commercial, corporate and investment banking services to over 30 million customers across its markets.

Its operations span payments, cash management, trade finance and investment banking, supported by digital and other distribution channels.

The post Ecobank announces exit of three directors appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: UCL: Mbappé scores twice as Real Madrid crush PSV 5-1
description:
Real Madrid produced a stunning second-half performance to thrash PSV Eindhoven 5-1 in their UEFA Champions League encounter, recording their fifth consecutive victory in the competition.
The victory temporarily moved Madrid to the top of the league-phase standings and extended their winning streak
content:
Real Madrid produced a stunning second-half performance to thrash PSV Eindhoven 5-1 in their UEFA Champions League encounter, recording their fifth consecutive victory in the competition.

The victory temporarily moved Madrid to the top of the league-phase standings and extended their winning streak across all competitions to 10 matches.

PSV gave the Spanish giants a difficult contest in the first half but were overwhelmed after the break, with England midfielder Jude Bellingham inspiring Madrid’s impressive turnaround.

Bellingham started the match on the bench after manager José Mourinho disclosed that the midfielder had a minor fitness concern. However, with Madrid trailing at half-time, Mourinho introduced him as part of a triple substitution.

PSV had threatened early through Ruben van Bommel, who fired wide, while Vinícius Júnior struck the crossbar at the other end.

The Dutch champions eventually took the lead after Aurélien Tchouaméni fouled Sven Mijnans in the penalty area. Ivan Perišić stepped forward and converted the resulting spot-kick.

Madrid returned from the break with renewed intensity and restored parity five minutes into the second half through Federico Valverde.

A well-worked attacking move involving Vinícius, Yan Diomande and Arda Güler ended with the Turkish midfielder providing a backheel flick for Valverde, who drove the ball into the net.

The hosts continued to dominate, and Bellingham put Madrid ahead with a spectacular volley. The midfielder controlled a loose ball near the edge of the penalty area before flicking it up and sending a superb strike beyond PSV goalkeeper Matej Kovář.

Vinícius was subsequently denied in a one-on-one situation before Kylian Mbappé extended Madrid’s advantage with a clinical finish after receiving a pass from Güler.

Mbappé, who had scored in each of Madrid’s previous Champions League matches this season, added another goal after rounding Kovář to make it 4-1.

Vinícius completed the scoring with Madrid’s fifth goal, ending his wait for a goal since August. Bellingham provided the pass that sent the Brazilian through PSV’s defence before he finished from close range.

Mourinho celebrated enthusiastically after Vinícius found the net, as the Brazilian forward looked to rediscover his best form.

The emphatic victory underlined Madrid’s strength in Europe and extended their remarkable run of results under Mourinho.

The post UCL: Mbappé scores twice as Real Madrid crush PSV 5-1 appeared first on Very Nigerian.
