title: Binnari: Can Taraba community shed its Special Security Concern tag?
description:
As grief grips Binnari after a deadly massacre, residents of Karim-Lamido seek lasting peace amid persistent insecurity and questions about the effectiveness of the area’s Special Security Concern designation, TERVER DOOMGA writes
For the people of Binnari, a community in Karim-Lamido Local Governme
content:
As grief grips Binnari after a deadly massacre, residents of Karim-Lamido seek lasting peace amid persistent insecurity and questions about the effectiveness of the area’s Special Security Concern designation, TERVER DOOMGA writes

For the people of Binnari, a community in Karim-Lamido Local Government Area of Taraba State, October 23, 2026, will remain a date associated with grief, bloodshed and the collapse of the fragile sense of security they had struggled to maintain.

It was a Friday, a market day when residents and traders from neighbouring settlements converged on the community to buy and sell farm produce, food and other necessities. The market, ordinarily a centre of commercial and social interaction, became a scene of horror when armed men invaded the community, shooting residents, looting shops and setting properties ablaze.

For hours, the attackers operated with little resistance, sending residents fleeing in different directions for safety. Some ran towards nearby bushes, while others headed for the Benue River. In the desperate attempt to escape, several people drowned.

By the time the attackers withdrew, families were searching for missing relatives, traders were counting their losses and survivors were struggling to comprehend the scale of the tragedy.

The Taraba State Emergency Management Agency subsequently reported at least 62 deaths and 52 injuries, while thousands of residents were displaced. The police initially reported a lower casualty figure as recovery operations continued. The Senate, in a motion seeking urgent security intervention, cited approximately 80 people killed.

Although the final death toll remains subject to reconciliation, the figures tell a disturbing story of a community that suffered one of the deadliest attacks in Taraba’s recent history.

The tragedy also renewed questions about the government’s capacity to protect rural communities, particularly those located along difficult terrain and state boundaries where criminal groups can exploit inadequate infrastructure and weak security coverage.

For Karim-Lamido, however, Binnari was not the beginning of the crisis. It was another painful chapter in a prolonged security challenge.

A troubled security corridor

Karim-Lamido occupies a strategic position in Taraba, sharing boundaries with parts of Plateau, Bauchi and Gombe states. Its geographical location, extensive rural settlements, farming communities and difficult terrain have created security and administrative challenges over the years.

The local government has experienced recurring communal clashes, farmer-herder conflicts, banditry, kidnapping and attacks on rural settlements.

An assessment by the European Union Agency for Asylum, drawing on conflict-monitoring data, identified Karim-Lamido as the local government area with the highest number of recorded security incidents in Taraba between January 2024 and August 2025.

The assessment recorded 26 incidents in Karim-Lamido, compared with 24 in Wukari and 23 in Takum.

The figures illustrate the extent to which insecurity has affected the state beyond isolated attacks. They also demonstrate that the problem confronting Karim-Lamido predates the recent massacre.

In May 2025, violence escalated in Munga Dosso and surrounding communities, where armed attacks reportedly claimed several lives and forced residents to flee their homes.

The attacks affected farming activities, destroyed property and increased the number of displaced households.

For rural residents, insecurity is not measured only by the number of people killed. It is also reflected in abandoned farms, deserted settlements, disrupted markets, missing livestock and the inability of families to travel freely between communities.

The economic implications are particularly serious in a local government where agriculture remains a major source of livelihood.

When farmers cannot safely access their fields, food production suffers. When traders cannot attend markets, rural commerce declines. When families flee their homes, their ability to earn an income and educate their children is also affected.

It was against this background of recurring violence that the Taraba State Government introduced a special security intervention in January 2026.

On January 2, 2026, Governor Agbu Kefas signed Executive Order No. 1, declaring Karim-Lamido a “Special Area of Security Concern.”

The measure followed consultations and security assessments arising from repeated communal clashes, bandit-related attacks and violent farmer-herder conflicts in the local government.

According to the government, the declaration was intended to strengthen security coordination, protect lives and property, restore peaceful coexistence and create an enabling environment for economic and social activities.

The designation was a recognition that Karim-Lamido required sustained security attention rather than occasional responses to individual attacks.

However, the Binnari massacre exposed the continuing vulnerability of communities within the designated area.

Following the October 23 attack, Kefas convened an emergency security meeting at the T.Y. Danjuma House in Jalingo and announced a further six-month extension of the designation, effective October 26.

At the meeting, the governor acknowledged the loss of lives and the trauma suffered by affected families.

“We have gathered to mourn those we have lost, support those affected, and agree on the actions required to protect our people,” he said.

He also assured residents that the government was determined to identify and apprehend those responsible for the violence.

“Our long-standing peace must not be disrupted by those who seek to destroy it. We are on track to identify and apprehend the criminals who have vowed to threaten our peace and security,” Kefas stated.

The governor directed relevant authorities to account for missing persons, establish their whereabouts and provide support to affected families.

He also tasked security agencies with investigating the movement of the attackers, their possible motives and any links to other criminal activities.

The renewed designation was accompanied by instructions for a coordinated security response involving security agencies, traditional institutions, community leaders and residents.

Yet, for communities that have experienced repeated attacks, the central question is whether the renewed declaration will translate into a security arrangement capable of preventing another massacre.

The road to security

Perhaps one of the most significant lessons from the Binnari tragedy is the relationship between poor road access and the ability of security agencies to respond to emergencies.

The challenge was highlighted during deliberations in the House of Representatives following the attack.

A motion moved by Mohammed Lauya representing Karim-Lamido, Lau, Ardo-Kola Federal constituency, called for urgent federal security and humanitarian intervention.

The lawmaker argued that the absence of adequate access roads had compounded the vulnerability of communities in Karim-Lamido and made it difficult for security personnel to reach affected settlements quickly.

He also urged the Federal Government to complete the abandoned Wase-Karim-Lamido road project to improve security operations and facilitate the rapid deployment of personnel.

“This type of deadly attack has never taken place in Karim Lamido Local Government; the people of Karim Lamido have suffered a lot. No access road leading to all these areas,” Lauya said.

The lawmakers consequently called for additional security camps, improved surveillance and intelligence sharing among security agencies in Taraba, Plateau and Bauchi states.

The road question has since become a major component of the state government’s response.

Following further assessments of the affected communities, the Kefas administration approved six emergency road projects intended to open up vulnerable settlements and improve access for security agencies and rural residents.

The people have mourned their dead. Families are still nursing their wounds, and many displaced residents are hoping that life will soon return to normal.

Yet, beneath the grief, there remains a desire to reclaim the farms, reopen the markets, rebuild homes and restore the relationships that once made their communities places of belonging.

For them, lasting peace will not be measured by official declarations or the number of security meetings held, but by the freedom to live, work, worship and raise their children without fear.

And that is the hope Binnari is holding on to: that the tragedy of October 23 will become a turning point in the collective determination to secure, rebuild and restore the communities of Karim-Lamido.

The post Binnari: Can Taraba community shed its Special Security Concern tag? appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: UNILAG students take Lassa fever campaign to Surulere
description:
The Association of Medical Students, University of Lagos, has taken its Lassa fever prevention campaign to Surulere, Lagos, warning residents about the risks of poor food storage and sanitation, while providing free medical services to more than 1,000 people during a community outreach.
The awarenes
content:
The Association of Medical Students, University of Lagos, has taken its Lassa fever prevention campaign to Surulere, Lagos, warning residents about the risks of poor food storage and sanitation, while providing free medical services to more than 1,000 people during a community outreach.

The awareness walk, organised in partnership with the Lukmon Oyewole-Lawal Foundation as part of activities marking the association’s 60th anniversary, started at the entrance of the Lagos University Teaching Hospital, Idi-Araba, and ended at Sam Shonibare Mini-Stadium, Surulere.

The students urged residents to maintain clean surroundings, observe personal hygiene and store food properly to prevent rodents from contaminating food items and spreading Lassa fever.

The AMSUL President, Adedeji Adeleke, said the walk, themed “Stop the Spread: Stride Against Lassa Fever”, was designed to educate the public on the disease and encourage practical steps to prevent infection.

He urged residents to keep food away from rodents, wash their hands regularly and maintain a clean environment, stressing that prevention remained the most effective way to reduce the spread of communicable diseases.

At the end of the walk, the students and their partners held a free medical outreach at the mini-stadium, where residents from Surulere and neighbouring communities received medical examinations, basic medications and eyeglasses.

The outreach, themed “Healthy Mothers, Healthy Future”, included screening for hypertension, diabetes and obesity, as well as awareness programmes on breast and cervical cancer.

The founder of the Lukmon Oyewole-Lawal Foundation and Special Adviser to the Speaker of the House of Representatives on Budget and Finance, Lukmon Oyewole-Lawal, said the intervention was intended to make basic healthcare more accessible to residents.

He urged beneficiaries to take their health seriously, saying community medical outreaches provided an opportunity for people to know their health status and seek medical attention before illnesses became severe.

Oyewole-Lawal also assured residents that the medical team would follow up on beneficiaries suspected of having health conditions to ensure they received further diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

Describing the Lassa fever campaign as timely, he said cases of the disease were more prevalent between December and March because of dry environmental conditions.

The Chairman of Surulere Local Government Area, Bamidele Yusuf, commended the partnership, saying it had brought medical services closer to residents.

He said his administration was upgrading and equipping primary healthcare centres across the council area to improve service delivery, while urging residents to undergo regular medical examinations to detect health conditions early.

Yusuf also acknowledged the contributions of the Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, to the development of Surulere, saying those who had worked with him had continued to bring the dividends of democracy to the people.

The outreach formed part of AMSUL’s 60th anniversary activities, through which the association said it was reaffirming its commitment to public health education, community service and improved access to healthcare.

title: Stablecoins can’t fix Nigeria’s FX liquidity crisis – Operator
description:
CEO of Luno Nigeria, Ayotunde Alabi, speaks to FELIX OLOYEDE on how Africa can leverage blockchain technology to tackle cross-border payments challenges
For years, cryptocurrency discussions across Africa have largely focused on trading and speculation. What has changed to suggest that the greater o
content:
CEO of Luno Nigeria, Ayotunde Alabi, speaks to FELIX OLOYEDE on how Africa can leverage blockchain technology to tackle cross-border payments challenges

For years, cryptocurrency discussions across Africa have largely focused on trading and speculation. What has changed to suggest that the greater opportunity now lies in the underlying infrastructure supporting financial transactions?

I think what has changed is that we are beginning to understand where the real economic value of digital assets lies.

For much of the last decade, the conversation was understandably dominated by cryptocurrency prices, trading activity and investment returns. But while that conversation was happening, the underlying technology was quietly demonstrating something potentially more significant: the ability to transfer and settle value across different markets without relying on the traditional chain of intermediaries.

For Africa, that is particularly relevant. We have significant trade, remittance and capital flows across borders, yet the infrastructure supporting these transactions remains fragmented, expensive and, in many cases, inefficient.

What excites me is that we are moving beyond asking whether people should buy cryptocurrencies to asking how this technology can help banks, payment companies and businesses move money more efficiently.

At Luno, we increasingly see digital assets not simply as an investment category, but as an additional layer of financial infrastructure. I believe the long-term opportunity is considerably bigger than trading alone.

Nigeria already has a sophisticated payments ecosystem, with banks, fintechs and payment companies moving money at scale. What specific problems in that existing infrastructure do you believe blockchain and stablecoin technology can realistically solve?

Nigeria has built one of Africa’s most sophisticated domestic payment ecosystems. We can move naira between bank accounts almost instantaneously, and that is an achievement we should be proud of.

However, the experience changes considerably when that same transaction needs to cross an international border.

A Nigerian business paying a supplier in another African country may have to navigate multiple banks, currency conversions, correspondent banking relationships and different settlement arrangements.

Blockchain infrastructure can help simplify the movement and settlement of value between financial institutions. Stablecoins, particularly those backed by credible and liquid currencies, can provide a common settlement instrument across otherwise disconnected markets.

There are also opportunities around treasury management, transaction transparency and the ability to operate beyond conventional banking hours.

The important distinction is that we are not suggesting blockchain should replace Nigeria’s existing payment infrastructure. In fact, the greatest value may come from connecting it to global financial networks more efficiently.

Nigeria has already solved a significant part of the domestic payments problem. The next opportunity is improving how our financial system interacts with the rest of the world.

Cross-border transactions remain costly and sometimes time-consuming. Where do you see stablecoins making the most practical impact on Nigeria’s international financial flows, whether through remittances, business payments, trade, treasury management or other areas?

I see the most immediate opportunity in business payments, trade settlement and institutional treasury operations.

Consider a Nigerian importer who needs to settle an invoice with an overseas supplier. Beyond finding the necessary foreign currency, the business must manage settlement timelines, intermediary costs and uncertainty around when the beneficiary will receive the funds.

A properly structured stablecoin settlement arrangement can potentially reduce some of that friction, particularly where the participating financial institutions have access to reliable liquidity and compliant conversion channels.

There is also a compelling opportunity for fintechs, international money transfer operators and payment companies that need to manage liquidity across multiple markets.

Remittances are another important use case, but I believe institutional adoption will be particularly consequential because of the transaction volumes involved and the potential efficiency gains.

At Luno, this informs our increasing focus on businesses and financial institutions. Rather than expecting every consumer to understand stablecoins, we can provide infrastructure that enables regulated businesses to deliver better financial services to their customers.

Ultimately, the customer may not even know that blockchain technology is involved. They will simply experience a faster, more predictable transaction.

New financial technologies often fall short of their promises when deployed on a large scale. What specific challenges in cross-border payments can stablecoins realistically address, and which obstacles are likely to persist regardless of technological advances?

This is an important distinction because I think the industry sometimes overstates what technology alone can achieve.

Stablecoins can materially improve the speed and availability of the settlement leg of a transaction. They can reduce dependence on multiple correspondent banking intermediaries and facilitate the transfer of value across networks that operate continuously.

However, stablecoins do not remove the fundamental economic and regulatory constraints associated with international money transfers.

You still need foreign exchange liquidity. You still need compliant entry and exit points into local currencies. You must comply with anti-money-laundering requirements, sanctions screening and applicable capital flow regulations.

For example, moving a dollar stablecoin between two wallets can happen very quickly. But if the recipient needs naira deposited into a Nigerian bank account, the quality of the local conversion and payout infrastructure becomes just as important as the blockchain transaction itself.

This is why I believe the winning proposition is not simply a stablecoin. It is the combination of liquidity, banking relationships, regulatory permissions and reliable settlement infrastructure.

Technology can make money move faster, but the surrounding financial infrastructure determines whether that movement creates real economic value.

Luno has largely been recognised as a consumer-focused cryptocurrency platform. What insights have you gained from operating in Nigeria that led you to identify greater opportunities in developing infrastructure to support other financial service providers?

One of the most important lessons from operating in Nigeria is that the demand for digital assets extends well beyond individuals looking to invest or trade.

Over time, we have seen increasing interest from businesses seeking solutions around liquidity, international settlement, treasury operations and access to digital asset markets.

We also realised that many financial institutions are interested in participating in the digital asset economy, but understandably do not want to build the entire infrastructure themselves.

Building a secure custody solution, establishing liquidity relationships, maintaining compliance controls and integrating blockchain networks requires substantial investment and specialist expertise.

Luno has spent more than a decade developing many of these capabilities.

The opportunity, therefore, is to make that infrastructure available to other businesses rather than limiting its usefulness to customers who transact directly on the Luno platform.

For me, that represents a natural evolution of our business. We are taking capabilities developed through years of serving retail customers and making them relevant to a much broader financial ecosystem.

Luno is expanding its engagement with banks, fintechs and payment companies through its B2B infrastructure strategy. How does this shift redefine its position in Nigeria’s financial ecosystem, from serving individual cryptocurrency users to providing the underlying infrastructure that other businesses can leverage?

It changes the nature of our relationship with the broader financial services industry quite significantly.

Historically, the typical relationship with Luno involved a customer coming onto our platform to buy, sell or hold a digital asset.

What we are now building is a model where another financial institution can integrate some of those capabilities into its own products and customer experience.

For example, a bank or fintech may want to offer digital asset access, institutional custody or stablecoin-enabled settlement without building a cryptocurrency exchange or managing the technical complexity of blockchain infrastructure.

Through propositions such as Crypto as a Service, we can provide components of that infrastructure while the institution maintains its own customer relationship.

Our broader ecosystem capabilities, including BlockTower’s stablecoin infrastructure and GTXN’s international payment and settlement capabilities, create opportunities to address more of the financial transaction lifecycle, subject to the appropriate regulatory permissions.

This moves Luno beyond being solely a platform customers transact on to potentially becoming an infrastructure partner for businesses serving much larger customer bases.

Importantly, this does not mean we are abandoning our retail business. It means we are extending the value of our existing capabilities into additional markets and customer segments.

If stablecoins become an integral part of financial infrastructure, how will this reshape the traditional banking sector? Will banks increasingly compete with cryptocurrency firms, collaborate with them or integrate the technology into their existing operations?

I believe partnership and integration will ultimately be much more important than competition.

Banks remain fundamental to the financial system. They provide deposit-taking, lending, access to domestic payment systems, regulatory oversight and established relationships with businesses and consumers.

What blockchain technology potentially introduces is a more efficient mechanism for transferring and settling value, particularly across borders.

I can envisage a financial system where a bank continues to provide the customer account, compliance framework and banking relationship, while integrating digital asset infrastructure into the settlement process.

In that scenario, the customer does not necessarily need to leave their bank or maintain a separate cryptocurrency account to benefit from the technology.

Of course, there will be competition in certain areas, particularly around international payments and transaction costs. But competition is not inherently negative if it encourages efficiency and better customer outcomes.

I do not see the future as banks on one side and crypto companies on the other. I see a future where the distinction becomes less relevant as digital asset capabilities are increasingly incorporated into mainstream financial services.

Nigeria’s regulatory framework for digital assets continues to develop. As an operator in this sector, what additional regulatory clarity is required to move digital-asset infrastructure beyond experimentation and towards widespread adoption in mainstream financial services?

Nigeria has made meaningful progress, particularly through the SEC’s regulatory framework for digital assets and the growing engagement between industry participants and financial regulators.

However, for digital asset infrastructure to achieve mainstream institutional adoption, there needs to be greater clarity around the intersection of capital markets regulation, banking, payments and foreign exchange.

For example, a digital asset exchange, a stablecoin issuer and a company providing international settlement infrastructure may all use blockchain technology, but they perform fundamentally different economic functions and present different regulatory risks.

It is important that the framework recognises those distinctions.

We also need clear rules around institutional participation, stablecoin issuance and redemption, reserve management, access to banking services and permissible use cases for digital assets in cross-border financial transactions.

I am particularly encouraged by the move towards greater coordination between the SEC, CBN and other relevant authorities.

Ultimately, businesses need regulatory certainty to make long-term investments, while financial institutions need confidence that the infrastructure they are integrating is properly supervised.

The objective should be a framework that protects the financial system without unnecessarily limiting responsible innovation.

Luno recently joined the SEC’s Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme. How does participation in the initiative change the way the company operates, and what insights have you gained so far about the requirements for responsible digital-asset innovation in Nigeria?

Our admission into the SEC’s Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme is an important milestone for Luno Nigeria and reflects years of engagement with regulators around the responsible development of the digital asset industry.

Importantly, admission into the programme provides an Approval in Principle, not an unrestricted or final operating licence. It allows us to operate within the scope and conditions established by the Commission while progressing through the applicable regulatory requirements.

What I particularly value is the opportunity for more structured engagement with the regulator.

It creates an environment in which regulators can better understand the technology, assess our operational controls and evaluate how these products function in practice.

One thing our experience has reinforced is that responsible innovation cannot be an afterthought.

You need strong corporate governance, effective compliance systems, appropriate custody arrangements, sound risk management and clear accountability from the outset.

For Luno, regulation and innovation are not opposing objectives. In fact, I believe regulatory credibility will become one of the strongest competitive advantages for businesses seeking to serve institutional customers.

If digital assets are going to form part of mainstream financial infrastructure, they must meet the standards of trust, security and accountability expected of any serious financial institution.

Stablecoins are frequently touted as a means of easing foreign exchange and settlement challenges. However, Nigeria must also consider its domestic currency and monetary policy objectives. What factors should policymakers and financial institutions consider as stablecoins become more widely integrated into financial transactions?

I think policymakers need to approach this from two perspectives: the efficiency benefits of the technology and the broader implications for monetary and financial stability.

Stablecoins can help facilitate international settlement, but we must recognise that the widespread use of foreign currency-denominated instruments can have implications for currency substitution, capital flows and the transmission of monetary policy.

For a country like Nigeria, those considerations are particularly important.

The objective should not be to create an alternative monetary system operating outside established safeguards. Rather, it should be to determine how digital settlement infrastructure can support legitimate economic activity while remaining consistent with Nigeria’s monetary and foreign exchange framework.

This means paying attention to transparency of flows, reserve quality, redemption arrangements, regulatory reporting and the institutions permitted to facilitate conversion between digital assets and local currency.

I also believe there is an important conversation to be had around properly regulated local currency stablecoins and other forms of tokenised money, although their usefulness will ultimately depend on adoption, liquidity and trust.

We should not confuse the benefits of blockchain settlement with the need to encourage foreign currency dependence.

A well-designed framework should allow Nigeria to benefit from technological innovation while preserving the authority of its monetary institutions.

The growing adoption of stablecoins also raises concerns around consumer protection, cybersecurity, reliance on private issuers and emerging forms of financial concentration. What are the major risks the industry must address as this infrastructure evolves?

I would group the major risks into three broad areas: financial integrity, operational resilience and trust.

First, a stablecoin is only as credible as the assets and governance arrangements supporting it. If an issuer cannot demonstrate adequate reserves, transparent redemption arrangements and sound financial management, the technology underlying the token becomes almost irrelevant.

Second, there are operational and cybersecurity risks. Blockchain transactions may settle quickly, but that also means mistakes, compromised credentials and unauthorised transfers can be difficult to reverse.

Third, as financial institutions increasingly depend on a smaller number of infrastructure providers, we must be conscious of concentration risk and the consequences of operational failures across interconnected systems.

There are also legitimate concerns around illicit finance, consumer understanding and the responsibilities of the institutions offering these products.

My view is that the industry should be held to rigorous standards, particularly where its infrastructure begins to support critical financial activity.

At Luno, our experience has taught us that trust is built through consistent investment in security, compliance, governance and transparency.

The industry will not achieve sustainable adoption simply by demonstrating that the technology works. It must demonstrate that the entire financial proposition is safe, reliable and accountable.

How do you envision Nigeria’s financial system evolving with widespread adoption of blockchain-based infrastructure, and how could this transform cross-border transactions for individuals and businesses in the country?

I think the most meaningful change would be that the experience of moving money internationally begins to resemble the experience Nigerians already enjoy when making domestic transfers.

Imagine a Nigerian business paying a supplier in Kenya, South Africa or Europe with greater visibility over the exchange rate, transaction costs and expected settlement time, without having to understand the complexities of the underlying financial infrastructure.

Imagine Nigerian fintechs and banks being able to offer international payment services through interoperable networks rather than having to establish separate arrangements across every market.

That would have important implications for trade, business competitiveness and the ability of African companies to participate in the global economy.

But I do not believe this future will be built by blockchain companies acting in isolation. It will require collaboration between banks, fintechs, payment providers, liquidity providers and regulators.

For me, the real measure of success will not be how many Nigerians own cryptocurrencies. It will be whether the technology helps businesses transact more efficiently, lowers the cost of financial services and makes our financial system better connected to global markets.

That is the opportunity we are pursuing at Luno, and I believe it is one of the most consequential developments in the next phase of Africa’s financial evolution.

title: Odu’a targets N1tn assets, N30bn profit by 2030
description:
Odu’a Investment Company Limited has set a target of N1tn total assets, N30bn cash-backed Profit Before Tax and N50bn group revenue by 2030.
The Group Chairman, Dr. Tola  Kasali, stated on Monday, at a press conference held at the Boardroom of the Cocoa House, Ibadan, as part of activities marking t
content:
Odu’a Investment Company Limited has set a target of N1tn total assets, N30bn cash-backed Profit Before Tax and N50bn group revenue by 2030.

The Group Chairman, Dr. Tola  Kasali, stated on Monday, at a press conference held at the Boardroom of the Cocoa House, Ibadan, as part of activities marking the company’s 50th anniversary.

“Our target is clear. By 2030, we want N30bn cash-backed profit before tax,  N1tn total assets and N50bn group revenue,” Kasali said.

The anniversary theme is, ‘Celebrating our Legacy, Embracing the Future.’

Kasali added that the target is anchored on the SRC 2.0 plan, which began in January 2026, to reposition Odu’a as a professionally managed and commercially- focused holding company.

“Odu’a was founded to preserve our regional assets and create wealth. For 50 years, we have endured, but longevity alone does not guarantee success,” he said.

Kasali admitted that some investments lost competitiveness while some subsidiaries struggled, adding, “Our performance did not fully reflect our asset base.”

“We are repositioning OICL as a professionally managed, commercially focused, strategy-driven investment holding company, through stronger governance, financial discipline, subsidiary accountability, investment rationalisation and rigorous performance monitoring,” Kasali said.

He said the company had paid dividends for 11 consecutive years since 2015, totalling about N1.53bn to its six shareholder states, and recorded N23.58bn PBT in 2025.

“Since 2015, dividends have been paid to our six shareholder states for eleven consecutive years, totalling approximately ₦1.53 billion. The Group recorded a profit before tax of 23.58bn in 2025,” he said.

Kasali said the Group was driving growth through real estate, hospitality, agriculture, and agro-allied businesses, infrastructure- related investments and other promising sectors.

“We are pursuing opportunities in real estate, hospitality, agriculture and agro-allied businesses, infrastructure-related investments and other promising sectors, in collaboration with the private sector, institutional investors and development partners,” he added.

The post Odu’a targets N1tn assets, N30bn profit by 2030 appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Pension crisis: NAMA retirees threaten mass protest
description:
Retirees under the Contributory Pensioners Union of Nigeria, Nigerian Airspace Management Agency branch, have threatened to stage a two-day peaceful protest over alleged unpaid pension increases and arrears accumulated over the past 20 years.
The union said the protest would hold from 25-26 November
content:
Retirees under the Contributory Pensioners Union of Nigeria, Nigerian Airspace Management Agency branch, have threatened to stage a two-day peaceful protest over alleged unpaid pension increases and arrears accumulated over the past 20 years.

The union said the protest would hold from 25-26 November, 2026, in Lagos and the agency’s headquarters in Abuja.

This was contained in a statement made available to The PUNCH on Monday and signed by the union’s branch Chairman, Olopha Steven, and Secretary, Lawal Wasiu.

The planned action is aimed at demanding the payment of outstanding pension increases and arrears allegedly approved by the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission.

The union said the decision followed the failure of NAMA management to respond to several letters sent on 30 September, 12 October and 17 November, 2026, seeking the resolution of the outstanding payments.

The statement read, “We refer to our letters dated 30th September, 12th October and 17th November, 2026, which regrettably remained unanswered.

“The Contributory Pensioners Union of Nigeria,  NAMA Branch, hereby gives notice to embark on a two-day peaceful protest from 25th to 26th November, 2026, at the NAMA Pension Office, Lagos, and Headquarters, Abuja, to demand for the payment of the accumulated 20 years pension increases and arrears approved by the Salary, Incomes and Wages Commission.”

The latest development comes amid a lingering disagreement between the retirees and the agency over the payment of their outstanding entitlements and the channel of communication between both parties.

In October, the union had rejected a meeting proposed by the agency for 3 November, 2026, insisting that NAMA management should meet with its leadership by October 21 and settle the outstanding arrears before the end of the month.

In a message to pensioners, Wasiu told The PUNCH that the agency responded to the planned industrial action, initially scheduled for 22 October, with a letter dated 19 October.

He, however, alleged that the correspondence was an attempt to mislead the retirees, arguing that it was addressed to NAMA Contributory Pension Scheme retirees rather than the Contributory Pensioners Union of Nigeria, which he described as the recognised body representing their interests.

Wasiu also accused NAMA management of deliberately refusing to communicate with the union since a meeting held on 10 June, 2026, while allegedly continuing to engage with the elders’ forum.

However, responding to the planned protest, NAMA Managing Director, Umar Farouq, said the agency had approved a payment schedule for the outstanding pension arrears and had commenced disbursements to the retirees.

Farouq disclosed that the agency had made provision for about N6bn to settle the payments, adding that the money would be released in batches.

He said, “I have approved their payment schedule and we have started paying them. We came up with about N6bn and we have started paying in batches. I got the paper in November and I immediately approved. I have told the DFA that we should do between N400m-N500m on monthly basis to off set the said money.”

The Managing Director also questioned the union representative’s awareness of the ongoing payments, insisting that the agency was engaging with what he described as the authentic leadership of the retirees.

“Meanwhile, this particular man speaking is not even aware that we have started paying because retirees are not refining with him. We are dealing with the authentic leaders of the retirees and they are cooperating with us,” he said.

The post Pension crisis: NAMA retirees threaten mass protest appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Greenwich Bank expands South-South footprint
description:
Greenwich Bank Limited has intensified its national expansion drive with the opening of branches in Warri, Delta State, and Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, as it targets five additional cities in its quest to establish a stronger presence in Nigeria’s commercial banking sector.
A statement signed by Head, Cor
content:
Greenwich Bank Limited has intensified its national expansion drive with the opening of branches in Warri, Delta State, and Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, as it targets five additional cities in its quest to establish a stronger presence in Nigeria’s commercial banking sector.

A statement signed by Head, Corporate Communications of Greenwich Holdings, Ozena Utulu, said the new outlets would bring the bank’s physical network to seven, following the opening of five branches in Lagos, Ondo and Ekiti States in October.

The bank plans to extend its operations to Asaba, Port Harcourt, Abuja, Benin and Ibadan in the coming months.

Speaking at the commissioning of the Warri branch, Group Chairman of Greenwich Holdings, Kayode Falowo, described the Niger Delta as a strategic market, citing its economic importance, entrepreneurial potential and concentration of business activities across oil and gas, maritime services and logistics.

He said Warri’s economic prospects extended beyond its natural resources to the entrepreneurs, traders, contractors, service providers and other businesses driving commercial activities in the region.

According to Falowo, Greenwich’s more than three decades of financial services experience, combined with its commercial banking mandate, positions it to provide a wider range of financial solutions to individuals, small businesses and corporate customers.

At the Uyo branch commissioning, Chairman of Greenwich Bank, Segun Oloketuyi, said the commercial banking licence would enable the institution to extend its 32 years of financial services expertise to a broader customer base, including farmers, traders, civil servants, students and entrepreneurs.

He identified credit facilities, agricultural and SME financing, trade and treasury services, salary solutions and digital banking as some of the services through which the bank intends to support businesses and individuals.

Oloketuyi added that the bank would leverage the resources and expertise of the Greenwich Group to help local enterprises access financial services beyond conventional lending.

Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, represented by the Commissioner for Finance, Fidelis Telije, who commissioned the Warri branch, welcomed the bank’s entry into the state, describing it as an opportunity to strengthen financial services and support economic development.

He urged residents and businesses to take advantage of the new outlet, particularly small businesses, young entrepreneurs and women-owned enterprises that require financial support to expand operations and create jobs.

Similarly, Akwa Ibom State Governor, Pastor Umo Eno, represented by the Commissioner for Finance, Emem Almond Bob, described the Uyo branch as a significant development that would improve access to banking services and credit, support business growth and potentially enhance the state’s internally generated revenue.

The Oruesen of Okere-Urhobo, Warri, His Royal Majesty (Dr.) Ogheneochuko Morris, also welcomed the bank’s establishment in the community, expressing confidence that its presence would create opportunities for businesses and residents.

Group Managing Director of Greenwich Holdings, Oyewale Ariyibi, said the bank’s entry into the region would support the emergence of new businesses and strengthen existing enterprises through specialised financial services.

He noted that the Group’s long-standing experience in the financial services industry had provided valuable insights into regional business dynamics, which would inform its approach to supporting enterprises across different sectors.

Managing Director of Greenwich Bank, Benson Ogundeji, said the Warri and Uyo branches would deepen customer engagement and bring financial solutions closer to businesses and individuals in the South-South.

He identified oil and gas, maritime services, agriculture, manufacturing, trade, logistics and small and medium-sized enterprises as priority sectors requiring responsive financial support.

Ogundeji stressed that the bank’s expansion strategy went beyond physical branch openings to building lasting customer relationships and deploying technology-driven solutions that promote enterprise growth and financial inclusion.

The post Greenwich Bank expands South-South footprint appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Siemens project delivers 1,080MW, may miss 5,540MW target
description:
The Federal Government has delivered 1,080 megawatts of additional electricity transmission capacity under its Presidential Power Initiative, popularly known as the Siemens power project.
This leaves 4,460 megawatts outstanding against the government’s target of adding 5,540MW to the national grid b
content:
The Federal Government has delivered 1,080 megawatts of additional electricity transmission capacity under its Presidential Power Initiative, popularly known as the Siemens power project.

This leaves 4,460 megawatts outstanding against the government’s target of adding 5,540MW to the national grid by 2028, The PUNCH reports.

The 1,080MW transmission capacity was delivered through the installation of 10 mobile substations and 10 power transformers across 10 locations in the country.

This comes eight years after the deal was conceptualised in August 2018 during the visit of former German Chancellor Angela Merkel to Nigeria. The Federal Government and Siemens signed the implementation agreement in July 2019, formally setting the project in motion.

The delivery represents about 19.5 per cent of the programme’s targeted additional transmission wheeling capacity, while another 984MW is under implementation through the first batch of transmission substation upgrades.

It said stations to deliver 3,376MW are in the pipeline, comprising the second batch of 12 substations and special projects, including the expansion of transmission infrastructure at Epe and Omotosho.

This means that although the Federal Government has completed its pilot phase, the bulk of the additional transmission capacity promised under the programme is still awaiting implementation, financing and other project approvals.

Details contained in a programme status document obtained from the FGN Power Company by our correspondent on Monday showed that the completed pilot phase involved the delivery of 10 power transformers and 10 mobile substations by Siemens Energy, providing 1,080MW of additional transmission wheeling capacity.

The equipment was deployed across 10 locations, including Ajah in Lagos, Ibadan in Oyo State, Sapade in Ogun State, Potiskum in Yobe State, Kwanar Dan-gora in Kano State, Jebba in Niger State, Okene in Kogi State, Apo in Abuja, Ihovbor in Edo State and Amukpe in Delta State.

As of November 2026, the initiative has lasted approximately eight years from conception and seven years since the formal implementation agreement was signed.

However, its execution has suffered repeated delays, with the original targets of increasing the country’s operational grid capacity to 7,000MW by 2021 and 11,000MW by 2023 not achieved.

The Federal Government subsequently signed an accelerated performance agreement with Siemens Energy in December 2023 to fast-track implementation.

The company said €60.4m in financing was secured for the pilot phase.

The document identified the pilot as the completed component of the programme, distinguishing it from the first batch of five substations currently being implemented and the second batch and other special projects still in the pipeline.

Under the first batch, the government plans to add another 984MW through the rehabilitation and upgrading of five existing transmission substations at New Abeokuta in Ogun State, Ayede in Ibadan, Oyo State, Offa in Kwara State, Onitsha in Anambra State and Sokoto in Sokoto State.

Siemens Energy is the engineering, procurement and construction contractor for the substation projects.

The programme also includes 16 transmission lines covering 606.5 kilometres of 330kV and 132kV networks, with a cumulative throughput capacity of 7,140MW.

The transmission lines comprise 399.5 kilometres of 132kV infrastructure and 207 kilometres of 330kV lines.

According to the document, the transmission line projects are expected to address bottlenecks preventing electricity generated by power plants from being efficiently evacuated through the national grid.

Two priority projects are the 38-kilometre 132kV Ajah-Shapaati transmission line and the five-kilometre 330kV Ayede-New Abeokuta line.

The government is targeting the completion of these priority lines by May 2027, subject to the conclusion of financing arrangements and other implementation requirements.

The document stated that the Federal Government had paid its 15 per cent counterpart funding for the transmission line programme, while negotiations on the facility agreement were ongoing.

Financial close is expected in the first quarter of 2027, with delivery of the 16 lines scheduled between the first quarter of 2027 and the fourth quarter of 2028.

The document further stated that the government is planning another 3,376MW through the second batch of the Siemens substation programme and special interventions.

The second batch involves 12 substations expected to contribute 2,400MW, while the Epe and Omotosho special projects are expected to provide another 976MW.

Other planned interventions include a dedicated transmission line for the State House, voltage-control equipment through the supply of shunt reactors and additional mobile substations at Okigwe and Ila-Orangun.

The document also listed projects at Jebba and Ganmo as part of the planned interventions.

However, the proposed projects are still at different stages of preparation, with the FGN Power Company identifying contract execution, financing, regulatory approvals and environmental assessments as outstanding requirements.

On financing, the programme is structured around 85 per cent funding from export credit agencies and development finance institutions, while the Federal Government provides the remaining 15 per cent as counterpart funding.

The Federal Ministry of Finance serves as the borrower and guarantor, with the funds expected to be on-lent to the Transmission Company of Nigeria and electricity distribution companies for repayment.

The financing partners include Sinosure, China Exim Bank, KfW IPEX-Bank, Commerzbank, Bpifrance, Standard Chartered and Deutsche Bank.

The document indicated that counterpart funding had been paid, while a €155.9m facility agreement was awaiting execution.

The post Siemens project delivers 1,080MW, may miss 5,540MW target appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Universities tasked to train students on antimicrobial stewardship
description:
Universities have been urged to equip pharmacy students with the knowledge and practical skills to promote responsible antimicrobial use, identify drug misuse and educate patients on the dangers of antimicrobial resistance.
The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Victory Drugs, Folasade
content:
Universities have been urged to equip pharmacy students with the knowledge and practical skills to promote responsible antimicrobial use, identify drug misuse and educate patients on the dangers of antimicrobial resistance.

The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Victory Drugs, Folasade Lawal, made the call while delivering the ninth Ladipo Mobolaji Abisogun-Afodu Annual Lecture in Pharmacy, organised in collaboration with the Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Lagos, on Thursday.

Speaking on the topic, “Addressing Microbial Stewardship in Nigeria: Current Perspectives and Future Imperatives,” at the College of Medicine, UNILAG, Lawal said pharmacy students needed to be adequately trained to understand the appropriate use of antimicrobial medicines and help prevent their misuse.

She said antimicrobial stewardship should be incorporated into pharmacy education to prepare future pharmacists to educate patients, promote responsible prescribing and dispensing, and strengthen efforts to tackle drug resistance at the community level.

Lawal identified self-medication, indiscriminate use of antibiotics, failure to complete prescribed doses, weak regulatory enforcement, poor-quality medicines and the misuse of antimicrobials in farming and fishing as factors driving resistance.

She said pharmacists, particularly those working in communities, had a critical role in checking the trend by educating patients, asking appropriate questions before dispensing medicines and refusing to sell antibiotics without prescriptions.

The drug executive noted that poverty contributed to self-medication and the use of different drug combinations, stressing the need for pharmacists to help patients understand the consequences of inappropriate antimicrobial use.

She called for stronger community-level antimicrobial stewardship, urging universities to prepare students to participate in public awareness campaigns, patient education, surveillance and referral systems.

Lawal also advocated student-led campaigns and research to strengthen public understanding of antimicrobial resistance, adding that responsible antimicrobial use should become part of professional and community culture.

She warned that antimicrobial resistance was making infections more difficult to treat, prolonging hospital stays, increasing healthcare costs and contributing to preventable deaths.

She cited figures showing that bacterial antimicrobial resistance was directly responsible for 50,500 deaths in Nigeria in 2021, while 1.14 million deaths were attributable to it globally in the same year.

Lawal said Nigeria needed to move beyond awareness of the problem to effective implementation of measures to contain it.

Among the measures she proposed were stronger enforcement of regulations governing antimicrobial sales, sustainable funding for stewardship activities at federal, state and healthcare facility levels, improved diagnostic services and mandatory antimicrobial stewardship programmes in healthcare facilities.

She also called for a One Health approach that recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health, warning that indiscriminate antimicrobial use in agriculture and fishing was contributing to resistance.

Lawal urged healthcare professionals, researchers, policymakers, students, the media and members of the public to take responsibility for preserving the effectiveness of antimicrobial medicines for future generations.

In her remarks, the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Lagos, Prof Folasade Ogunsola, represented by the Dean of Basic Medical Sciences, Prof Niyi Osuntoki, said resistance was growing as microbes continued to develop ways to survive.

She warned against irrational use of antibiotics, including indiscriminate consumption and failure to complete prescribed doses, and called for the promotion of their appropriate use.

The Special Guest of Honour, Olayioye Abidoye, urged individuals to pursue legacies that would contribute to improving humanity.

The event was attended by the host, Prof Oluwole Familoni; the Dean, Faculty of Pharmacy, UNILAG, Prof Sunday Adesegun; and the Chairman of the occasion, Olumide Akintayo, among other academics and stakeholders.

The post Universities tasked to train students on antimicrobial stewardship appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Poor primary results spurred my academic turnaround – YABATECH best student
description:
Best Overall Higher National Diploma student at the 38th convocation of Yaba College of Technology, Lagos, Momoh David, has narrated how his poor academic performance in primary school and the desire to overcome low self-esteem inspired him to work harder and pursue academic excellence.
Momoh, of th
content:
Best Overall Higher National Diploma student at the 38th convocation of Yaba College of Technology, Lagos, Momoh David, has narrated how his poor academic performance in primary school and the desire to overcome low self-esteem inspired him to work harder and pursue academic excellence.

Momoh, of the Electrical Engineering Department (Power option), graduated with a Cumulative Grade Point Average of 3.96 to emerge the college’s Best Overall Student at the HND level.

Momoh was one of 10,886 students of the 2024/2025 academic session who graduated on Thursday, with 361 of them earning distinctions.

Speaking in an interview with The PUNCH on Monday, Momoh said he was not an outstanding pupil in primary school and often felt ashamed of his results, adding that his determination to improve began when he prepared for admission into secondary school.

Momoh said, “In primary school, I wasn’t really outstanding. In most cases, I was ashamed of my results because I used to feel like people who were doing well were special, and God just had this special love for them.

“Even the result that I graduated from primary school with wasn’t good at all, and I felt really bad. I was at home preparing to go for a tutorial because I wanted to enter SS1, and I was so unhappy. I prayed and asked God to help me.”

Momoh said he resumed secondary school late but came ninth in his first term, an improvement that encouraged him to work harder.

He said his academic performance continued to improve, adding that he became determined to distinguish himself academically.

Momoh said his ambition to become the best student at YABATECH took shape during his National Diploma convocation, where he was inspired by the valedictory speech.

Momoh said, “From the very first day I attended my National Diploma convocation, I had that goal. I was really inspired by the valedictory speech. When I got home, I made up my mind that I would be the next valedictorian or the next best graduating student.”

He said he wrote down his goal, surrounded himself with friends who shared similar aspirations and made regular attendance at lectures a priority.

According to him, he developed the habit of revising lessons immediately after classes to ensure he understood what lecturers had taught before moving to another topic.

“I ensured that I did not miss class for any reason. I was always punctual and made sure I got to class on time. After every class, I would go back to the material and quickly go through it before the next lecturer came in.

“I would ask myself, ‘What did this lecturer teach me just now?’ I would identify what I did not understand and quickly go through it to ensure that I had a good grasp of what had been taught,” he said.

Momoh said his commitment to studying extended to weekends, adding that he often returned to his books after church services and used available opportunities, including transit time, to revise his materials.

He also disclosed that he sometimes woke up at 3 am to study before resuming lectures at 8 am.

He said he combined his lecture notes with textbooks and online resources, including YouTube tutorials, to deepen his understanding of engineering concepts.

Momoh also said he used artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT, to simplify difficult concepts and improve his understanding of engineering subjects.

“If I find a concept difficult to understand, I can just go to ChatGPT and ask it to explain it to me like I am a five-year-old. It breaks it down and gives me the ability to connect the dots,” he said.

Momoh said he avoided parties and other social distractions to remain focused on his academic goal, adding that he also abstained from examination malpractice because of its implications for his integrity and learning.

He said cheating would have prevented him from identifying areas where he needed to improve.

“If I had involved myself in malpractice at any level, whether during a test, it would have affected how I built my integrity. If I did it at the test level, I would not be able to understand or identify where I made a mistake so I could correct myself,” he said.

Momoh, who said his parents financed his education, disclosed that he hoped to pursue a degree programme and was exploring scholarship opportunities abroad.

He also said he was considering developing an application that would help engineering students learn and retain technical concepts through short, accessible lessons.

He expressed interest in operational technology and industrial control systems, particularly as Nigeria’s electricity grid becomes increasingly digitalised and exposed to cybersecurity threats.

On the challenges facing Nigerian students, Momoh identified unreliable electricity supply as a major obstacle, recalling that he sometimes had to study with torch lights because of power outages at home.

Momoh urged the government to improve electricity supply, invest in community libraries and equip laboratories to encourage innovation among students.

He advised students to remain disciplined and persistent, surround themselves with people who shared their academic goals and combine hard work with faith.

“My principle is: pray like you didn’t read and read like you didn’t pray,” Momoh said.

title: I sought AI’s guidance when existing theories didn’t fit –  89-year-old Nwagwu
description:
Eighty-nine-year-old Professor Mark Nwagwu has disclosed how he turned to artificial intelligence when existing social theories failed to provide a suitable framework for his doctoral research, leading to the development of what he described as the Cultural Stem Cell Theory.
Nwagwu, who recently ear
content:
Eighty-nine-year-old Professor Mark Nwagwu has disclosed how he turned to artificial intelligence when existing social theories failed to provide a suitable framework for his doctoral research, leading to the development of what he described as the Cultural Stem Cell Theory.

Nwagwu, who recently earned another PhD from the University of Ibadan, said AI suggested that he could develop a speculative theory after he struggled to find an existing social theory that adequately explained his research.

The professor, who began the doctoral programme at the age of 86, disclosed this in an interview with The PUNCH.

He said, “I went to social theories, one by one, but not one of them suited my work. Eventually, I went to AI to ask, ‘I don’t have a theory for my work, what do I do?’ It said I could develop a speculative theory. It’s in my thesis.”

According to him, AI also contributed to some of the justifications for his research, particularly as he explored how his findings could be applied to society.

“If you read my thesis, there are four or five justifications for this. Why did I do this? A lot of those justifications come from AI,” he said.

Nwagwu, however, maintained that the Cultural Stem Cell Theory was an original contribution arising from his research, explaining that the artificial intelligence system had not previously encountered the particular work.

He said the theory, which brings together biology, sociology and the humanities, was developed from his study of Nsibidi, an indigenous African system of communication through gestures, signs, movements and other non-verbal expressions.

The professor explained that his research examined how the interaction between different elements could produce new forms of understanding and transformation, drawing an analogy from the biological functions of stem cells.

He said, “The important point in the stem cell theory is communication, interaction and change. You are no longer what you once were because you are now interacting and you produce something innovative.”

Nwagwu explained that his interest in Nsibidi developed following a conversation with former Nigeria’s Ambassador to Brazil, Bolivia and Paraguay, Christopher Okeke, who challenged him to consider the importance of understanding one’s cultural origins.

He said Okeke’s observation that people needed to understand where they were coming from to know where they were going inspired him to undertake research into Nsibidi.

Although he initially intended to write a book on the subject, he decided to pursue a doctoral degree because he considered Nsibidi a specialised social discipline that required proper academic investigation.

He subsequently approached Professor Sola Olorunyomi of the University of Ibadan to supervise the research, while Okeke supported the project with a monthly stipend.

Nwagwu said the research eventually produced the Cultural Stem Cell Theory, which he hoped to apply to communities to promote interaction, understanding and unity across cultural and social boundaries.

He added that his examiner described the thesis as innovative and multidisciplinary, recommending that the postgraduate college recognise the work for bringing different academic disciplines together and proposing a theory with potential applications in society.

He described the decision to undertake the doctorate as unexpected, saying, “I did not set out to do a PhD. Fortunately, I have done it. And a theory has come out of it: Cultural Stem Cell Theory.”

The professor explained that Nsibidi was a non-verbal system of communication involving gestures, eye movements, dances and other forms of expression through which people conveyed meanings without spoken words.

“Nsibidi is the heart of a culture in which the human mind comes out not in words but in gestures, in eye movements, in dances, in every possible way of expression except words,” he said.

He argued that the interaction between Nsibidi and biological concepts provided the foundation for his theory, which draws on the ability of stem cells to develop into different forms depending on their environment.

“The stem cell is that part of embryology, that part of development that can grow into anything depending on where it finds its location,” he said.

According to him, the theory is built around communication, interaction and transformation, with the potential to explain how different individuals and communities can interact and produce new forms of social understanding.

“The important point in the stem cell theory is communication, interaction and change. You are no longer what you once were because you are now interacting and you produce something innovative,” he said.

On concerns about the growing influence of artificial intelligence, Nwagwu said knowledge could be dangerous depending on how it was used, comparing AI’s potential benefits and risks with the development of nuclear weapons and drones.

He argued that the same knowledge that produced weapons could also be deployed for beneficial purposes, adding that the challenge was ensuring that technological advancements were properly guided.

“Knowledge is dangerous. In itself, it’s wonderful. If we use it, that’s what we are using,” he said.

The professor, however, acknowledged that AI had made complex tasks easier, particularly in analysis, but questioned whether it could ultimately be regarded as the highest expression of wisdom.

He said, “AI has made complex things simple. How it can analyse, et cetera. We can ask the question, where are human beings going? Is AI the ultimate scope of wisdom? Is AI wisdom? You can say, well, we do not know until we put it to use properly.”

Nwagwu also warned that the technology could influence language and moral values, stressing the need to guide its applications.

On the commercialisation of research findings, he supported efforts to translate academic discoveries into products and services but cautioned against allowing the pursuit of money, wealth and professional recognition to undermine the broader benefits of research.

Citing the development of the COVID-19 vaccine and the discovery of insulin, he argued that researchers should be willing to make useful discoveries available for the benefit of humanity rather than prioritising personal financial gains.

Turning to the Nigerian education sector, the professor identified declining discipline as one of its major challenges, arguing that the country’s education system had deteriorated from the standards he experienced in the 1950s and 1960s.

He attributed much of the decline to the military’s intervention in governance following the 1966 coup, saying the period marked a turning point in the country’s institutions, including its schools.

According to him, discipline and academic standards were once central to educational institutions, with students who failed examinations facing the possibility of being withdrawn.

He lamented the deterioration of infrastructure and standards in public schools and universities, adding that the increasing preference for foreign education reflected declining confidence in Nigeria’s educational system.

Nwagwu called for a restoration of discipline and order in schools, arguing that academic qualifications alone were insufficient to produce responsible leaders.

Despite his latest academic achievement, the professor said he did not set out to pursue another PhD, describing the decision to study Nsibidi as a development that unfolded through divine direction.

He said he began the programme at 86 and was delighted to have completed the research and produced what he considered a significant contribution to knowledge.

Nwagwu also said he was not interested in ranking his achievements, stressing that cooperation, interaction and the ability to contribute positively to society were more important than personal recognition.

He said he hoped to take the Cultural Stem Cell Theory beyond academic research by applying its principles to different communities to encourage mutual understanding and social transformation.

“My cultural stem cell theory is big and will take me places. But those places will be the work of the Holy Spirit. How I do it will be the work of the Holy Spirit,” he said.

The post I sought AI’s guidance when existing theories didn’t fit – 89-year-old Nwagwu appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Alkamba Times Raises Concern Over Intimidation Of Court Journalist, Demands Probe
description: Gambiaj.com – (BANJUL, THE GAMBIA) – The Alkamba Times has raised concerns over the treatment of its court correspondent, Sainabou Sambou, at the Bundung High Court, calling on judicial and prison authorities to ensure journalists can carry out their professional duties without intimidation or inter
content:
Gambiaj.com – (BANJUL, THE GAMBIA) – The Alkamba Times has raised concerns over the treatment of its court correspondent, Sainabou Sambou, at the Bundung High Court, calling on judicial and prison authorities to ensure journalists can carry out their professional duties without intimidation or interference.

In a statement issued on Monday, 23 November, the media organization said Sambou was involved in a confrontation with a prison officer while covering court proceedings and attempting to photograph an accused person outside the courtroom.

According to the account provided by the journalist, a prison officer approached her and attempted to seize her phone, triggering a verbal confrontation. A colleague reportedly intervened to prevent the situation from escalating into physical contact.

The incident was subsequently brought before Justice M.S. Jallow, who, according to The Alkamba Times, accused Sambou of using foul language, threatened to send her to Mile 2 Central Prison and directed her to remain silent without giving her a fair opportunity to explain her version of events.

Media Organisation Defends Journalists’ Right To Newsgathering

The Alkamba Times described photographing accused persons in public spaces outside courtrooms as a legitimate journalistic activity, arguing that journalists should not face harassment or restrictions while carrying out their responsibilities.

It maintained that no law in The Gambia prohibits the practice and recalled that similar incidents involving journalists and security personnel had previously attracted condemnation from the Gambia Press Union (GPU).

The organization stressed that prison officers and other security personnel have a responsibility to respect journalists and members of the public, warning that attempts to seize journalists’ equipment or subject them to intimidation undermine the ability of the media to perform its watchdog role.

It also questioned the manner in which the matter was handled by the presiding judge, arguing that courts, as institutions of justice, must uphold fairness by allowing all parties to present their accounts before reaching conclusions.

“The perception that a journalist was judged without being heard undermines public confidence in the judicial process,” the statement said.

Calls For Investigation And Clear Guidelines

The Alkamba Times called on the Gambia Prison Service to investigate the conduct of the officer involved and establish clear guidelines to ensure journalists can cover court proceedings and undertake legitimate newsgathering activities without harassment.

It also urged the Judiciary to ensure that members of the press are treated with the respect their constitutional role demands.

The organization reaffirmed its support for Sambou, saying it would continue to stand by her in carrying out her professional responsibilities and report any further developments transparently.

“Press freedom is not a privilege granted by officials; it is a constitutional right essential to accountability and democracy,” said Sainey M.K. Marenah, the organization’s Founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief.

The incident raises broader questions about the working relationship between journalists, security personnel and judicial authorities, particularly the need to protect legitimate newsgathering activities within and around court premises.

While maintaining order and security in court facilities is essential, such responsibilities should not become grounds for arbitrarily restricting journalists from documenting events of public interest. The protection of press freedom requires public institutions to respect journalists’ professional responsibilities while ensuring that any restrictions are grounded in law and applied fairly.
