title: 2027: Nigeria needs reset, not political insults –Makinde, APM
description:
From Ndubuisi Orji, Abuja and Oluseye Ojo, Ibadan
The presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Seyi Makinde, has declared that Nigeria needs a fundamental reset to overcome insecurity, poverty, hunger and infrastructural deficiencies, as his party challenged President Bola Tinubu
content:
From Ndubuisi Orji, Abuja and Oluseye Ojo, Ibadan

The presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Seyi Makinde, has declared that Nigeria needs a fundamental reset to overcome insecurity, poverty, hunger and infrastructural deficiencies, as his party challenged President Bola Tinubu to defend his administration’s record rather than resort to political insults ahead of the January 16, 2027 presidential election.

Makinde, who spoke in Abuja on Sunday, said Nigerians dissatisfied with the prevailing economic and security situation should embrace his Reset Nigeria Agenda, while urging citizens to pray for divine intervention in the country’s affairs rather than his personal victory at the polls.

His remarks coincided with a statement by the APM condemning Tinubu’s reported use of the Yoruba expression, “Egbe palemo,” at Saturday’s All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally at Mapo Hall Arcade, Ibadan, which the opposition party interpreted as a disparaging reference to its political platform.

Speaking to journalists after attending a service at the headquarters of Dunamis International Gospel Centre, Makinde maintained that Nigeria was no longer providing the opportunities and benefits of governance that citizens deserved, insisting that a change in direction had become necessary.

“My message still is, if Nigeria is not working for you, then join me to press the reset button.

“Or if it’s working for you, okay, keep doing what you are doing, but I know Nigeria is not working,” he said.

The Oyo State governor explained that his presidential ambition was informed by the desire to restore public confidence in governance and recreate the opportunities that once enabled Nigerians to pursue their aspirations across the country.

He, however, maintained that the outcome of the election should ultimately reflect God’s will, stressing that his appeal for prayers was not intended to secure personal political advantage.

“When I came out to declare to run for president, what I asked people for was to pray that God should show mercy onto this country.

“I don’t even pray for me to be president of Nigeria, but pray that God’s will and God’s will alone be done.” Makinde said the spiritual dimension of national development could not be separated from the physical challenges confronting the country, urging Nigerians to remain committed to prayers while participating in efforts to improve governance.

“You can’t take this spiritual aspect away from the physical,” he said.

Makinde, who also attended a service at the Nongo u Kristu u i Ser u sha Tar (NKST), the Universal Reformed Christian Church, in Mabushi, Abuja, recalled his experience of moving from Oyo State to Rivers State as a young man in the 1990s before returning home and eventually becoming governor in 2019.

He cited the experience as an example of the opportunities he believed Nigeria should once again provide for its citizens.

Receiving him at the church, the resident pastor, Basil Orkpe, encouraged Makinde to remain committed to his presidential ambition, describing it as an opportunity to serve the country and alleviate the suffering of Nigerians.

“Without a shadow of a doubt, this great movement that God Himself has orchestrated has a purpose.

“Many people may have said, ‘Stop this, concentrate on something else’, but your heart’s desire and your cry to Jesus Christ have been that you would be able to serve this nation and, by extension, the rest of the world, and bring relief to the suffering of the people of this great land,” Orkpe said.

The cleric urged him not to be discouraged by opposition to his aspiration but to remain focused on what he described as the task of salvaging the country.

Meanwhile, the APM accused Tinubu of attempting to divert attention from the performance of his administration through political name-calling, arguing that Nigerians were more concerned about economic hardship, unemployment and insecurity than exchanges between rival political parties.

In a statement issued by the Director of Communication and spokesperson of the Oyo State APM Campaign Council, Yinka Oladoyinbo, the party said the President should explain what his administration had achieved since assuming office on May 29, 2023, rather than ridicule political opponents.

“We consider the expression a curious choice of words from a President whose administration has become synonymous with economic hardship, public frustration, political manoeuvring and an increasingly desperate search for electoral validation,” the statement said.

The party explained that the Yoruba word palemo could suggest hurriedly gathering or packing belongings, sometimes in preparation for departure, and questioned the President’s choice of expression.

“Mr President may wish to explain why such vocabulary comes so readily to him. As the saying goes, it takes a master of a craft to recognise the language of fellow practitioners. And when an accuser points one finger at another, the remaining four are invariably directed at himself,” it stated.

APM insisted that the challenges confronting Nigerians demanded concrete policy responses rather than political exchanges, maintaining that the rising cost of essential commodities, declining purchasing power and insecurity should dominate public debate ahead of the election.

“The APM will not be distracted by presidential name-calling. Nigerians are far more concerned about the cost of living, the purchasing power of their incomes, insecurity, unemployment, collapsing economic confidence and the daily struggle to survive than the linguistic theatrics of a campaign podium.

“A President seeking another mandate should be explaining what he has done with the first, not trading taunts with political opponents,” the party declared.

It further argued that Tinubu should have used his visit to Oyo State to address the economic difficulties confronting Nigerians and explain how his administration intended to improve living conditions.

The opposition party also rejected suggestions that the reception accorded Tinubu by the Olubadan of Ibadanland, Rashidi Ladoja, and the Soun of Ogbomoso, Ghandi Afolabi Olaoye, amounted to an endorsement of his re-election bid by the monarchs or their communities.

According to APM, traditional rulers are custodians of culture, history and communal harmony whose institutions should remain accessible to citizens irrespective of their political affiliations.

“A royal handshake does not constitute a ballot. A palace audience does not confer electoral authority. Political choreography cannot manufacture the consent of the people,” the statement said.

The party maintained that traditional institutions should preserve their neutrality and continue to provide platforms for dialogue, mediation and reconciliation rather than become instruments of partisan mobilisation.

“Their palaces must remain places where the ruling party, the opposition, the undecided and the politically disenchanted can find counsel, mediation and a sense of belonging. They are not campaign surrogates, electoral assets or instruments for manufacturing political legitimacy,” it added.

Invoking the Yoruba proverb, “Bi ikun lo ni oko, bi pakute, ipade d’ojo ibo,” APM maintained that neither presidential visits nor public appearances with traditional rulers could substitute for the freely expressed choices of voters.

It insisted that the January 16 presidential election would provide Nigerians an opportunity to assess the records and promises of the competing candidates and determine the country’s political direction.

title: Tinubu: Water stopped flowing while I was shaving in Villa
description:
• Admits electricity, water supply challenges, promises solutions
• Lagos must deliver maximum votes in 2027, says 200,000 out of 7m unacceptable
From Juliana Taiwo-Obalonye, Abuja
President Bola Tinubu has revealed that water supply was interrupted at the Presidential Villa in Abuja while he was sh
content:
• Admits electricity, water supply challenges, promises solutions

• Lagos must deliver maximum votes in 2027, says 200,000 out of 7m unacceptable

From Juliana Taiwo-Obalonye, Abuja

President Bola Tinubu has revealed that water supply was interrupted at the Presidential Villa in Abuja while he was shaving last Wednesday, acknowledging that the country’s electricity and water supply challenges persist even within the seat of power.

The President, who promised to address the infrastructure deficiencies, said his administration remained determined to improve essential services across the country, insisting that Nigeria had the capacity to overcome its development challenges.

Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at the Tinubu Family Special Prayer for his second-term re-election bid, held at the Yoruba Tennis Club, Onikan, Lagos, where he also challenged leaders of the All Progressives Congress (APC) to intensify voter mobilisation ahead of the January 16, 2027 presidential election.

Recalling his experience at the Villa, the President said the interruption demonstrated the inconvenience Nigerians faced because of inadequate public utilities.

“Last Wednesday, I was shaving when the water supply went off in the Villa o. You would not know the inconvenience that caused there, too.

“We will correct all these problems. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have only just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.

Tinubu maintained that the difficulties confronting the country were surmountable, citing ongoing infrastructure development in Abuja and Lagos as evidence of what could be achieved through determination and sustained investment.

“There is nothing we cannot achieve. Look at Abuja; we have moved mountains. In Lagos, we have tamed the Atlantic. In Abuja, we have moved mountains to make way for development.

“There is nothing we cannot achieve if we put our hearts into it,” he declared.

Turning to preparations for the 2027 general election, the President expressed dissatisfaction with the level of voter mobilisation in Lagos, warning that the APC could not afford to record low turnout in a state with millions of registered voters.

He challenged party leaders and supporters to work towards securing the maximum possible votes for his re-election, arguing that winning with only a fraction of the state’s registered voters would fall short of expectations.

“To me, Lagos is the big deal. How can you have seven million registered voters and produce only 100,000 or 200,000? That is failure.

“Even if you win and say a win is a win, no. You have to generate the maximum number of votes,” Tinubu said.

He urged party members to set aside personal grievances, reconcile with aggrieved supporters and encourage eligible voters to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), stressing that internal disagreements should not undermine the party’s electoral preparations.

“It is not about anger. Anger will not do it. You may be angry with Silva or Mulika. Put that anger aside and call Mulika to go and vote.

“Call Mulika and let her go and vote. We finish the anger that day, and you can go back to it the next day. Do you get my message? We must generate enough votes to overwhelm them,” he said.

The President also directed his Special Adviser on Political Matters, Ibrahim Masari, to begin reconciliation efforts among aggrieved APC members, starting from Katsina State before extending the exercise to Jigawa and other parts of the country.

Describing Masari as his political confidant and bulldozer, Tinubu said the party needed to resolve internal differences and restore unity ahead of the election.

“To my confidant and bulldozer, Alhaji Masari, go back home and reconcile with everybody. That is the order of the President, and when you finish, move to Jigawa and other places and reconcile them, beg them. Badaru, you get what I said. We have to reconcile. Every anger must evaporate,” he declared.

Tinubu recalled his political disagreements in 2021 and 2022, saying he had to put aside personal grievances when former President Muhammadu Buhari invited him to serve as coordinator and co-chairman of the campaign.

He said political differences should not prevent party members from working together towards common objectives, urging them to embrace forgiveness and reconciliation.

“The first thing we ask from Allah is forgiveness. If you cannot give it, why are you asking Allah to forgive you? What you want from Him, you must be able to give to humanity,” he said.

The President also thanked members of the Tinubu family for their prayers and support throughout his political career, recalling their involvement during his governorship contests in Lagos and subsequent presidential ambition.

He said their continued encouragement had accompanied him through successive political challenges and campaigns.

Reflecting on the economic difficulties experienced during the 2022 and 2023 political transition, Tinubu recalled the cash scarcity and fuel shortages that affected Nigerians, maintaining that the challenges confronting the country today were less severe than those of the previous period.

“The challenges we face today are much easier than those of yesterday, but we must not take that for granted,” he said.

He also urged young Nigerians to prepare for leadership responsibilities, stressing that the task of building and sustaining the country would increasingly rest on their shoulders.

The event was attended by Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu; Kwara State Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq; Lateef Femi Okunnu; Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila; and members of the Tinubu family, among other dignitaries.

title: Smart devices redefining music entertainment
description:
Smartphones, wireless earbuds, smart televisions and artificial intelligence are reshaping music production, distribution and consumption, creating new opportunities for artistes, producers and entertainment businesses globally, writes ANOZIE EGOLE
The music industry is experiencing a remarkable tec
content:
Smartphones, wireless earbuds, smart televisions and artificial intelligence are reshaping music production, distribution and consumption, creating new opportunities for artistes, producers and entertainment businesses globally, writes ANOZIE EGOLE

The music industry is experiencing a remarkable technological revolution, driven by the growing influence of modern electronic devices that are changing how music is created, recorded, distributed, promoted and consumed. From smartphones and smartwatches to wireless earbuds, tablets, smart televisions, Bluetooth speakers and virtual reality headsets, technological innovations are redefining the relationship between artistes, producers and music lovers.

What was once an industry largely dependent on recording studios, radio stations, physical music collections and conventional promotional channels has evolved into a digitally connected business where music can be produced, shared and accessed from virtually anywhere.

Today, a young musician can record a song with a smartphone, edit a music video on a tablet, promote a release through social media and distribute it to international audiences without necessarily engaging a traditional record label. Similarly, music lovers can access millions of songs through wireless devices, stream live performances and enjoy personalised listening experiences wherever they are.

These developments have not only improved convenience but have also created new commercial opportunities, expanded the industry’s audience base and encouraged innovative approaches to music production and entertainment.

In Nigeria, where Afrobeats and other contemporary genres continue to attract international attention, modern devices are becoming increasingly important to the industry’s growth. They are helping emerging artistes overcome traditional barriers, enabling established musicians to connect with global audiences and creating opportunities for technology companies, digital entrepreneurs and entertainment professionals.

Smartphones

The smartphone has arguably become the most transformative modern device in the music industry. Beyond its traditional communication functions, it now serves as a portable recording studio, music player, video camera, promotional platform and digital distribution tool.

With applications such as BandLab, GarageBand and FL Studio Mobile, musicians can compose melodies, record vocals, create beats and edit musical arrangements directly on their smartphones.

This has lowered the barriers to entry for aspiring artistes who may not have the financial resources to hire professional recording studios. Young musicians can develop musical ideas, produce demonstrations and share their work online without investing heavily in conventional equipment.

Smartphones have equally changed music promotion. Platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube enable artistes to release short performance videos, interact with fans and build audiences around their music.

A song can gain popularity through a viral social media video, dance challenge or user-generated content before receiving significant attention from conventional media outlets.

For Nigerian musicians, this development has created opportunities to reach audiences beyond the country’s borders. A song produced in Lagos can attract listeners in London, New York, Johannesburg and other international markets through digital platforms.

However, the growing dependence on smartphones also means artistes must understand digital marketing, content creation and online audience management to remain competitive.

Smartwatches

Smartwatches are gradually changing how people interact with music, particularly during exercise, travelling and other activities where carrying a smartphone may be inconvenient.

Modern smartwatches, including the Apple Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch, allow users to control music playback, adjust volume, skip tracks and access compatible streaming services.

Some models support offline music storage, enabling users to listen through Bluetooth headphones without carrying their smartphones.

This development has created a more convenient listening experience for people who exercise, jog, cycle or engage in outdoor activities.

For music streaming companies, smartwatches provide another platform through which subscribers can access their services. They also strengthen the relationship between wearable technology and digital entertainment.

Although smartwatches are not primarily designed for music production, their integration with smartphones and other connected devices illustrates how music consumption is becoming increasingly mobile.

Wireless earbuds, headphones

Wireless earbuds and headphones have transformed personal music consumption by eliminating the inconvenience of cables and providing listeners with greater mobility.

Devices such as Apple AirPods, Samsung Galaxy Buds and Sony wireless headphones have become popular among consumers who want to enjoy music while commuting, working, exercising or relaxing.

Modern models feature noise cancellation, improved sound quality, touch controls, voice assistants and other functions that enhance listening experiences.

Noise-cancelling technology is particularly useful in busy environments because it reduces unwanted background sounds, allowing users to concentrate on music.

Some advanced headphones also support spatial audio, which creates an immersive listening experience by making sounds appear to come from different directions.

This technology is changing how music producers and engineers approach audio production. As more consumers adopt sophisticated headphones, there is growing interest in producing music that takes advantage of immersive sound formats.

Wireless headphones have also become useful tools for musicians and entertainment professionals. They allow artistes to monitor audio, rehearse performances and communicate during certain production activities.

However, the increasing use of personal listening devices has raised concerns about hearing damage. Listening at excessive volumes for prolonged periods can affect hearing, making responsible use important.

Tablets

Tablets have emerged as valuable tools for musicians, producers, songwriters and other creative professionals.

Devices such as Apple’s iPad and Samsung Galaxy Tab combine portability with processing capabilities that support music production, video editing, songwriting and digital content creation.

Through applications such as GarageBand, Cubasis and other music production software, musicians can compose songs, arrange instruments, record audio and experiment with different sounds.

Tablets also provide digital interfaces for controlling compatible musical instruments and recording equipment.

For artistes who travel frequently, these devices offer an opportunity to develop musical ideas without depending on a fully equipped studio.

Beyond music production, tablets are useful for managing song lyrics, organising performances, reading digital sheet music and controlling stage equipment.

Their touchscreen interfaces also make certain creative activities more intuitive, particularly for younger musicians familiar with mobile technology.

As processing power and software capabilities improve, tablets are likely to become even more important in mobile music production.

Smart speakers

Smart speakers are changing how households access and enjoy music.

Devices such as Amazon Echo, Google Nest and Apple HomePod allow users to request songs, albums, playlists and radio stations through voice commands.

Instead of manually searching for music, listeners can simply ask their smart speakers to play a particular artiste, genre or song.

These devices are connected to digital music services, making extensive music libraries accessible through simple voice interactions.

Smart speakers also allow users to control volume, create playlists, set alarms and integrate music into broader smart-home systems.

For the music industry, this development represents another distribution channel through which streaming platforms can reach consumers.

It also creates opportunities for artistes to gain exposure through curated playlists and voice-based music discovery.

As smart-home technology becomes more widespread, the demand for connected entertainment devices is expected to grow.

Smart televisions

The modern television has evolved beyond a device for watching conventional broadcast programmes. Smart televisions now provide access to music videos, live concerts, documentaries, streaming platforms and other forms of digital entertainment.

Platforms such as YouTube, Apple Music and other streaming services allow users to watch performances and enjoy music-related content directly on their television screens.

This has changed how families and groups experience music. Instead of listening through individual headphones, people can enjoy music videos, concerts and performances together in their homes.

Smart televisions have also expanded opportunities for music marketers and content creators. Artistes can reach audiences through music videos, interviews, documentaries and live-streamed performances.

For Nigerian musicians, the growing availability of digital television platforms provides additional opportunities to showcase Afrobeats, gospel, hip-hop and other local genres to international audiences.

Bluetooth speakers

Portable Bluetooth speakers have made music more accessible in homes, offices, parties, beaches, outdoor events and other social environments.

Unlike conventional sound systems that require complicated wiring, these devices connect wirelessly to smartphones, tablets and laptops.

Their portability, rechargeable batteries and improved sound quality have made them popular among young people and music enthusiasts.

Manufacturers such as JBL, Sony, Bose and other audio technology companies continue to introduce devices with improved battery performance, water resistance and sound output.

For the entertainment industry, portable speakers have expanded the market for personal and group music consumption.

They are particularly useful for outdoor parties, small gatherings, fitness activities and informal performances.

Some advanced models also support multiple-speaker connections, allowing users to synchronise audio across different devices.

This demonstrates how relatively compact gadgets are changing the traditional concept of music entertainment.

Digital DJ devices

Modern DJ controllers and digital mixing equipment have changed how DJs organise, mix and deliver music at parties, concerts and other entertainment events.

Contemporary controllers allow DJs to access extensive digital music libraries, combine tracks, manipulate sound effects and create customised musical transitions.

When connected to laptops or compatible mobile devices, they provide access to software that simplifies music selection, beat matching and performance management.

This has reduced dependence on physical records and compact discs while giving DJs greater creative flexibility.

Digital equipment has also made it easier for emerging DJs to develop their skills and perform at events without investing in extensive traditional equipment.

In Nigeria, where nightlife, concerts, weddings and entertainment events provide important opportunities for DJs, these devices have become essential tools for professional performance.

Virtual, augmented reality

Virtual reality and augmented reality technologies are introducing new possibilities for music entertainment.

VR headsets allow users to experience simulated environments, including virtual concert venues where they can watch performances through immersive digital experiences.

Rather than physically attending a concert, music lovers can participate in selected virtual performances from their homes.

Augmented reality, meanwhile, combines digital elements with real-world environments. It can be used to create interactive music videos, enhance live performances and provide audiences with additional visual experiences.

These technologies could create new commercial opportunities for artistes, concert organisers, technology companies and entertainment platforms.

For international musicians, virtual performances can provide alternative ways of reaching audiences who cannot afford or access physical concerts.

Although the adoption of these devices remains limited by affordability, internet access and the availability of compelling content, their potential to reshape music entertainment is considerable.

AI-powered devices

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence into smartphones, computers, tablets and other modern devices is creating additional opportunities in music production.

AI-powered tools can assist musicians with songwriting ideas, melody generation, sound editing, vocal separation, mixing and mastering.

Some applications can analyse musical arrangements and suggest improvements, while others can help producers create instrumental sounds and experiment with different styles.

AI-enabled smartphones and computers can also assist content creators with video editing, promotional artwork and social media materials.

These capabilities are particularly useful to independent artistes who may lack the financial resources to employ large production and marketing teams.

However, AI has introduced concerns about copyright infringement, the unauthorised use of musicians’ voices and the potential misuse of existing musical works.

The industry will therefore need appropriate regulations and licensing arrangements to ensure that technological innovation does not undermine the rights of creative professionals.

Nigeria’s music landscape

The growing influence of modern devices presents significant opportunities for Nigeria’s music industry.

First, they are reducing the cost of entry for upcoming artistes. Smartphones, tablets and affordable computers allow young musicians to experiment with music production without necessarily establishing expensive studios.

Second, digital devices are expanding access to international markets. Through smartphones, smart televisions and streaming platforms, Nigerian music can reach listeners across continents.

Third, the devices are creating employment opportunities for software developers, video editors, sound engineers, digital marketers, equipment retailers and other professionals within the creative economy.

They are also encouraging new business models, including online music distribution, virtual performances, digital subscriptions and direct-to-fan engagement.

Nevertheless, challenges remain. The high cost of imported gadgets, foreign exchange fluctuations, unreliable electricity and limited access to affordable internet services can restrict the adoption of modern technology.

There are also concerns about digital piracy, intellectual property protection, unequal access to technology and the revenue artistes receive from streaming services.

sing these challenges will require investment in digital infrastructure, creative education, copyright enforcement and policies that support local innovation.

Conclusion

Modern electronic devices are no longer merely accessories to the music industry; they have become essential instruments shaping its development.

From smartphones that enable artistes to record and promote songs to wireless earbuds that provide personalised listening experiences, these innovations are transforming almost every aspect of the music business.

Smart televisions, Bluetooth speakers, smartwatches and virtual reality headsets are equally expanding how audiences experience music, while artificial intelligence is introducing new possibilities for creativity and production.

For Nigeria, the opportunity is particularly significant. As Afrobeats and other local genres continue to gain international recognition, greater adoption of modern technology could strengthen the country’s creative economy and improve the global competitiveness of its musicians.

Ultimately, technology alone does not make great music. Talent, originality, discipline and creativity remain essential. However, artistes and industry stakeholders who understand and effectively deploy modern devices will be better positioned to adapt to changing consumer preferences, explore new revenue opportunities and participate in the future of the global music industry.

title: Sima Pledges Jobs And Export-Led Growth, Vows To End Gambia’s Import Dependence
description: Gambiaj.com – (FASS NJAGA CHOI, THE GAMBIA) – Alliance of Progressive Citizens (APC) presidential candidate Modou Lamin Sima has pledged to reduce The Gambia’s dependence on imported goods through increased domestic production, export growth and support for local entrepreneurs, arguing that the coun
content:
Gambiaj.com – (FASS NJAGA CHOI, THE GAMBIA) – Alliance of Progressive Citizens (APC) presidential candidate Modou Lamin Sima has pledged to reduce The Gambia’s dependence on imported goods through increased domestic production, export growth and support for local entrepreneurs, arguing that the country cannot overcome rising living costs without transforming its economy.

Addressing supporters during a campaign rally in Fass Njaga Choi, Sima said economic recovery must begin with creating employment opportunities and making it easier for Gambian businesses to trade.

He argued that the country’s reliance on imports, particularly food products, was undermining its economic prospects and contributing to the hardship experienced by households.

“For a country to develop, there are two things involved: the creation of more jobs and easy trading. None of that can be achieved if we Gambians depend on imports,” he said.

Sima estimated that The Gambia imports between 90 and 95 per cent of the food it consumes, insisting that much of what the country purchases abroad could be produced locally with adequate investment and support for farmers and other productive sectors.

Imports, Foreign Exchange And Rising Prices

The APC flag bearer linked the country’s import dependence to pressure on foreign exchange reserves and the depreciation of the Dalasi, which he said ultimately contributes to rising market prices.

He argued that without expanding exports and generating foreign currency through international trade, the country would struggle to address the economic pressures facing ordinary Gambians.

“If we cannot export to other countries to earn foreign currency, the hardship will only increase,” Sima warned.

He said his proposed economic approach would prioritize local production while creating opportunities for farmers, gardeners, masons, traders and factory workers to contribute more directly to national development.

Sima also called for the establishment of dedicated financial institutions to provide funding for businesses owned by women and young people, describing access to finance as essential to expanding entrepreneurship and creating jobs.

Entrepreneurship Against Market Monopolies

Drawing on his decade-long experience working in business, investment and labor conditions, Sima argued that encouraging entrepreneurship and competition would help improve economic opportunities and the availability of goods and services.

He illustrated his argument with an experience near Esseu, along the road to Dakar, where he said women regularly queued outside a single pharmacy to purchase medicines.

According to Sima, facilitating the opening of a second pharmacy in the area helped ease the congestion and gave customers an alternative.

He presented the experience as an example of how encouraging more businesses to operate could break market bottlenecks while creating productive opportunities for individuals.

“What we need is entrepreneurship so that everyone can have something productive to do, creating healthy competition that will boost the country’s economy,” he told supporters.

“This is what I am an expert in, and I can help Gambians achieve it.”

Sima Takes Agricultural Message To North Bank

Sima continued his second day of nationwide campaigning on Sunday, November 22, with engagements across the North Bank Region, where he renewed his call for greater investment in agriculture and local production.

At a rally in Sunchu Sanjali village, in the Sabach Sanjal District, he outlined his party’s plans to reduce food imports, mechanize agriculture, empower farmers and strengthen domestic production.

Earlier, Sima had travelled from Farafenni towards Upper Badibu, making brief stops at Pallen Polo and the Pallen Wollof junction to interact with residents before proceeding through Sarakunda and Kunjata towards Bambali.

He also made a brief stop in Bambali, where he was unable to hold a full campaign rally because the village was reportedly mourning the death of a resident.

During his engagements, Sima appealed to voters to support the APC in the December 5 presidential election, pledging to address the country’s economic and agricultural challenges.

The APC candidate said his decision to contest the presidency followed growing calls from citizens who wanted him to move beyond public advocacy and take direct responsibility for implementing his economic proposals.

He explained that he had initially stepped back from public advocacy after becoming frustrated with what he perceived as a lack of attention to his ideas, but later reconsidered following appeals from people who believed he could contribute to addressing the country’s economic challenges.

Sima is among eight cleared candidates seeking to lead The Gambia in the December 5 election. His campaign has placed economic self-reliance, agricultural development, employment creation and private-sector entrepreneurship at the center of his proposed program.

title: Violence threatens election  voter turnout, credibility of polls
description:
From Fred Itua, Romanus Ugwu, Okwe Obi, Abuja; Scholastica Hir, Makurdi; John Adams, Minna; Emmanuel Adeyemi, Lokoja; Jude Owuamanam, Jos

Attacks on campaign gatherings, destruction of political offices and billboards and alleged restrictions on opposition activities are heightening tension across
content:
From Fred Itua, Romanus Ugwu, Okwe Obi, Abuja; Scholastica Hir, Makurdi; John Adams, Minna; Emmanuel Adeyemi, Lokoja; Jude Owuamanam, Jos

Attacks on campaign gatherings, destruction of political offices and billboards and alleged restrictions on opposition activities are heightening tension across the North Central, raising concerns about voter safety, participation and the credibility of the 2027 general elections.

Reports from Benue, Niger, Plateau, Kogi and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) show that supporters of both the ruling and opposition parties have suffered attacks, while disputes over access to venues and political advertising are deepening accusations of an uneven campaign environment.

In Niger State, armed youths stormed the Trade Fair Complex in Minna after Governor Umaru Bago’s governorship campaign flag-off, hurling stones and sending supporters fleeing. Several people were injured, while police said six suspects were arrested with cutlasses, knives and scissors.

The incident followed an earlier attack in which the windscreens of three campaign vehicles belonging to the African Democratic Congress (ADC) were smashed.

Supporters of Bago and the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate, Mohammed Nami, also allegedly clashed in Lapai in October, leaving several people hospitalised.

In Benue, the PDP alleged that its billboards, including those of senatorial candidate Eunice Ortom, were destroyed, while its Benue Northeast senatorial candidate, Thomas Unongo, was harassed by suspected All Progressives Congress (APC) supporters on his way to a burial in Vandeikya.

The party’s secretary, Fan Nyikwagh, said political intolerance had extended to places of worship.

The ADC also complained that it was denied access to the Buruku Youth Centre and a secondary school for a stakeholders’ meeting.

Governor Hyacinth Alia and the police have appealed for restraint following the signing of a peace accord.

In Kogi, President Bola Tinubu’s campaign office in Lokoja was vandalised and posters pulled down, but almost a month after the incident, no arrest had been made.

The ADC separately alleged that thugs loyal to the APC attacked and set fire to its office in Dekina, threatening members of the party.

APC campaign spokesperson, Kingsley Fanwo, denied the party’s involvement in attacks on the opposition.

Kogi PDP Chairman, Mohammed Gambo, also accused the authorities of using political advertising charges to weaken opposition parties, citing a signage fee of N150 million for presidential candidates.

In Plateau, billboards and posters of Tinubu and Governor Caleb Mutfwang were pulled down before and after the North Central APC rally in Jos.

The APC attributed the destruction to disgruntled elements, insisting that the attacks did not amount to a rejection of the President by residents.

Police, however, said they had received no official complaint.

In the FCT, the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and Action Democratic Party (ADP) accused the ruling party of restricting the opposition’s access to the political space.

SDP spokesperson, Rufus Aiyenigba, alleged that parties were asked to pay as much as N250 million per billboard, describing the charges as an obstacle to political participation.

“This is not the democracy we laboured for,” he said.

The APC, however, accused sections of the opposition, particularly elements within the Obidient Movement, of promoting hostility towards Tinubu and his supporters.

Its National Youth Leader, Dayo Israel, cited the reported attack on the President’s convoy at a mosque in Abuja and warned that further attacks “will not be condoned”.

Security chiefs and political leaders have called for issue-based campaigns and warned against thuggery, while opposition parties are demanding action against attackers and access to public venues.

content:
…Projects to open up rural communities, boost economic activities in four LGAs

By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe

The Gombe State Government has signed contract agreements with construction companies for the execution of seven road projects covering approximately 97 kilometres across four local government areas.

The projects, which span Balanga, Kaltungo, Shongom and Yamaltu-Deba Local Government Areas, are aimed at improving rural connectivity, facilitating the transportation of agricultural produce, enhancing access to markets and stimulating economic activities.

The contract agreements were signed at a ceremony organised by the Ministry of Works and Infrastructure, attended by government officials and representatives of the construction companies.

Speaking at the ceremony, the Commissioner for Works and Infrastructure, Hon. Shehu Yerima Abdullahi, said the projects were part of the infrastructure development agenda of Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya’s administration to connect underserved communities and promote socioeconomic growth.

He said the road projects demonstrated the government’s commitment to extending infrastructure development beyond urban centres and improving the living conditions of rural residents.

Abdullahi charged the contractors to justify the confidence reposed in them by adhering strictly to approved engineering specifications, quality standards and contractual obligations.

He stressed that timely completion and quality workmanship were non-negotiable, adding that the ministry would sustain monitoring and supervision to ensure the projects were delivered within the agreed timelines and required standards.

Earlier, the Permanent Secretary of the ministry, Danladi Adamu, said the contract-signing exercise was an important step towards ensuring effective implementation, supervision and delivery of the projects.

In their separate remarks, the Branch Manager of EEC International Limited, Mr Dong Jian; representative of the Managing Director of SWAS GRADE Limited, Engr. Christina Daniel; and Managing Director of DATUM Construction Nigeria Limited, Engr. Daher Kaworma, thanked the state government for awarding the contracts to their companies.

They pledged to deliver quality infrastructure in line with approved specifications and contractual provisions, assuring that the projects would be completed within the agreed periods.

The seven road projects were approved by the State Executive Council at its last meeting presided over by Governor Yahaya.

They include the 18.9-kilometre Talasse-Bangu-Boka Bundi-Walalunguda Road, with a spur to Dalawaja, and Phase One of the four-kilometre Degri-Sikam-Nyuwar Kindiyo Road.

Others are the 38-kilometre Lapan-Labariya-Lasanjan-Latatar-Lakunturum Road, with a spur to Burak; the 15-kilometre Bangunji-Dadiya-Yelwa-Gombe/Yola Road; and the nine-kilometre Kurjale-Pata Road.

The remaining projects are the 10.5-kilometre Dogon Ruwa-Kaltin Road and the 1.5-kilometre Kunuwal Road Network.

The latest contracts add to the administration’s ongoing efforts to expand the state’s road network, improve connectivity between rural and urban communities and enhance access to economic opportunities.

The projects are expected to ease transportation challenges, facilitate the movement of farm produce to markets, reduce travel difficulties and improve economic activities across the benefiting communities upon completion.

title: Tinubu’s insistence on fuel subsidy removal insensitive –ADC
description:
From Ndubuisi Orji, Abuja
The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has criticised President Bola Tinubu’s insistence on sustaining the removal of fuel subsidy, describing his position as insensitive to millions of Nigerians still grappling with rising living costs, hun
content:
From Ndubuisi Orji, Abuja

The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has criticised President Bola Tinubu’s insistence on sustaining the removal of fuel subsidy, describing his position as insensitive to millions of Nigerians still grappling with rising living costs, hunger and poverty.

The campaign council said the President’s remarks at the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally in Ibadan at the weekend suggested that his administration was unwilling to acknowledge the hardship which, it argued, had followed the implementation of its economic policies.

In a statement issued yesterday by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, the ADC-PCC accused Tinubu of displaying a lack of empathy for Nigerians whose purchasing power had been eroded by rising prices of food, transportation and other essential commodities.

It questioned the President’s reported suggestion that Nigerians should put the subsidy removal controversy behind them, arguing that the consequences of the policy remained evident in the daily struggles of households across the country.

“The President appears more interested in being addressed as Mr President than in tackling the crushing realities confronting the people. That explains his brash insistence that Nigerians should forget about fuel subsidy removal simply because, in his estimation, it belongs to the past.

“How can hardship, hunger and widespread poverty, which are direct consequences of the hurriedly imposed economic policies of the Tinubu administration, suddenly become things of the past when Nigerians continue to bear their devastating consequences every day?

“To ask Nigerians to forget a policy whose consequences they confront every waking moment is not only insensitive; it is an insult to their intelligence and a mockery of their suffering,” the council stated.

The opposition campaign council maintained that the administration’s continued defence of its economic reforms, despite complaints over their impact on household incomes, raised questions about its willingness to review policies that had imposed additional burdens on citizens.

It argued that responsible leadership required listening to public concerns, acknowledging shortcomings in policy implementation and making adjustments where necessary to alleviate hardship.

According to the council, the government’s approach had been characterised by a determination to defend its decisions rather than address the immediate difficulties confronting Nigerians.

The ADC-PCC further warned against allowing the debate over the administration’s economic policies to overshadow what it described as concerns about the state of democratic institutions and the welfare of citizens.

“Nigeria cannot afford a second term built on the ruins of its democratic institutions and the continued impoverishment of its citizens.

“Nigerians deserve a government that feels their pain, understands their struggles and takes deliberate steps to ease their burden, not one that dismisses their suffering or asks them to forget the circumstances that have made life increasingly unbearable.”

The campaign council maintained that the January 16, 2027 presidential election would provide Nigerians an opportunity to assess the administration’s performance and determine the country’s political direction.

“In 2027, Nigerians will have the opportunity to change this narrative. The power to rescue the country and restore hope rests firmly in their hands,” the statement added.

title: COP31: Onuigbo tasks legislators on climate laws, funding
description:
By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe



The President of GLOBE Legislators International, Rt. Hon. Sir Sam Ifeanyi Onuigbo, has urged parliamentarians across the world to translate international climate agreements into enforceable national laws, backed by adequate funding and effective oversight.







Onuigbo sa
content:
By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe

The President of GLOBE Legislators International, Rt. Hon. Sir Sam Ifeanyi Onuigbo, has urged parliamentarians across the world to translate international climate agreements into enforceable national laws, backed by adequate funding and effective oversight.

Onuigbo said international climate agreements would achieve little unless national parliaments incorporated decisions reached at United Nations climate conferences into domestic legislation and ensured their implementation.

He made the call at the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) COP31 Parliamentary Meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, where he highlighted the role of legislators in ensuring that commitments reached at the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Conferences of the Parties (COPs) produced tangible results at the national level.

In a statement made available to journalists in Gombe on Saturday, the former member of the House of Representatives said parliamentarians must deploy their constitutional powers of lawmaking, budgetary appropriation and oversight to ensure governments implement international climate commitments.

Drawing on his legislative experience, Onuigbo recalled that his participation in the GLOBE COP21 Legislators Summit in Paris influenced his decision to sponsor Nigeria’s Climate Change Act.

He argued that without the necessary legislative backing, negotiations and agreements reached at international climate conferences could fail to translate into practical outcomes.

“After all the contributions here, if they are not brought down into laws for implementation, it becomes an exercise in futility,” he said.

Onuigbo described parliamentary action as central to bridging the gap between international climate negotiations and domestic implementation.

He stressed that legislators must ensure that agreements reached at COP meetings were reflected in national laws, budgetary allocations and effective government oversight.

Describing the deliberations at the Antalya meeting as detailed and incisive, he said their impact would ultimately depend on the ability of parliamentarians to translate the discussions into actionable legislation.

The GLOBE Legislators president also commended the National Council on Climate Change, its leadership under Dr Majekodunmi, researchers and other stakeholders for their contributions to the development of the Host Country Approval Criteria for Carbon Market Activities in Nigeria and the country’s broader climate change efforts.

He also acknowledged President Bola Tinubu’s role in Nigeria’s climate change efforts.

“Above all, I want to thank President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, who has exercised admirable leadership in ensuring that the climate journey remains steady and very successful,” he said.

Onuigbo was inaugurated as President of GLOBE Legislators at the United Kingdom Parliament on June 24, 2026.

Established in 1991, GLOBE Legislators works to strengthen parliamentary engagement and international cooperation on environmental governance and climate change.

title: Borno youths develop affordable local foods to tackle child malnutrition
description:
From Timothy Olanrewaju, Maiduguri
Young innovators in Borno State have developed locally produced, ready-to-use nutritious foods aimed at combating child malnutrition, offering a potentially affordable and accessible alternative for vulnerable children suffering from nutritional deficiencies.
The f
content:
From Timothy Olanrewaju, Maiduguri

Young innovators in Borno State have developed locally produced, ready-to-use nutritious foods aimed at combating child malnutrition, offering a potentially affordable and accessible alternative for vulnerable children suffering from nutritional deficiencies.

The food products, made from locally sourced ingredients, were unveiled at a youth-led nutrition challenge organised by the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) in Maiduguri at the weekend to commemorate the 2026 World Children’s Day.

Health experts at the event described the innovations as nutritious and affordable, while UNICEF said the initiative demonstrated the potential of young people to develop practical solutions to malnutrition using resources available within their communities.

UNICEF Chief of Maiduguri Field Office, Francis Butichi, said the competition was designed not only to address acute malnutrition but also to encourage young people to collaborate, innovate and contribute directly to improving child nutrition.

“The youth-led nutrition challenge is more than an effort to address acute malnutrition. It is a platform for young people to collaborate and create local solutions to a global problem.”

Butichi explained that the participants sourced nutritious ingredients locally to develop food products that could be affordable and accessible to children affected by malnutrition, particularly in vulnerable communities.

He said the initiative reflected UNICEF’s commitment to supporting homegrown innovations capable of improving children’s health and wellbeing.

According to him, the commemoration of World Children’s Day provided an opportunity to celebrate children while renewing commitments to their rights, survival, development and protection from preventable illnesses.

He stressed that every child deserved the opportunity to grow up healthy and fulfil their potential, adding that tackling acute malnutrition remained essential to achieving that objective.

“We urge our young people to keep going. The world is waiting for your creative ideas for the nutrition of children right here in Borno. UNICEF will continue to support you,” Butichi said.

Director of Community and Family Health at the Borno State Primary Health Care Development Board, Abdulwahab Mala, commended UNICEF for its interventions in child health and nutrition across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states.

Mala, who represented the Borno State Government at the event, said the state recognised the progress recorded in efforts to prevent and manage malnutrition, describing the youth-led initiative as a demonstration of collective commitment to improving child health.

“Malnutrition is a scourge and it is possible to deal with it. This collective initiative is a reflection of our bold commitment to child health,” he said.

He also commended the state government for expanding access to healthcare services across several local government areas, maintaining that improved healthcare delivery and collaborative interventions were essential to addressing the nutritional needs of vulnerable children.

The post Borno youths develop affordable local foods to tackle child malnutrition appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Operators jostle for market share after Uber’s exit
description:
Uber’s withdrawal from Nigeria has intensified competition in the country’s ride-hailing market, putting renewed focus on transport fares, passenger safety and driver welfare as operators seek to retain and attract customers.
The global ride-hailing company discontinued its Nigerian operations on Se
content:
Uber’s withdrawal from Nigeria has intensified competition in the country’s ride-hailing market, putting renewed focus on transport fares, passenger safety and driver welfare as operators seek to retain and attract customers.

The global ride-hailing company discontinued its Nigerian operations on September 2, 2026, after 12 years in the market, creating opportunities for existing and emerging operators to strengthen their positions.

The exit has also heightened expectations around service reliability, affordability and the financial sustainability of app-based transportation, as commuters reassess their mobility options.

Ride-hailing services have become an increasingly important part of urban transportation, particularly in major cities where commuters depend on app-based platforms for convenience, predictable journeys and access to transport outside conventional public transport hours.

A 2025 Ride-Hailing Safety Index Report conducted by Ipsos and commissioned by Bolt found that 81 per cent of surveyed Nigerian passengers considered ride-hailing safer than other forms of transportation.

The survey, which covered Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt and Ibadan, also found that 96 per cent of respondents used ride-hailing services when public transport felt unsafe.

The findings highlight the importance of passenger confidence in a market where safety and reliability increasingly influence consumer decisions.

Onadipe Oluwafemi David, founder of Nigerian ride-hailing service Ona, said the industry’s next phase would depend on how effectively operators addressed the expectations of passengers and drivers.

“The opportunity in Nigeria’s ride-hailing market goes beyond filling the gap left by an existing operator. Commuters want a service they can depend on, while drivers need an operating structure that makes their participation worthwhile. Platforms that address both sides of the experience will be better positioned to compete in the long term,” he said.

Despite Uber’s departure, other operators, including Bolt and inDrive, remain active in the Nigerian market.

Their ability to retain existing customers and attract new users will depend partly on how they address transportation costs and service quality.

For passengers, affordability, waiting times, driver verification and access to customer support remain important considerations.

For drivers, rising fuel prices, vehicle maintenance costs and platform commissions continue to affect the financial viability of ride-hailing operations.

The situation presents a challenge for operators, as lower fares could attract more passengers, but driver earnings must remain sustainable to ensure service availability and encourage driver retention.

Safety infrastructure is also emerging as an important competitive factor. Features such as identity verification, trip monitoring, accessible emergency support and transparent driver information can strengthen accountability and build trust between platforms and users.

As the market adjusts to Uber’s exit, competition is expected to extend beyond the number of available platforms to the quality of their operating models.

For Nigeria’s ride-hailing industry, the immediate challenge is to absorb displaced demand while demonstrating that digital mobility services can deliver consistent value to passengers and support the livelihoods of drivers.

The post Operators jostle for market share after Uber’s exit appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Tinubu commits N450bn to agricultural financing, targets 2m farmers  –APC
description: The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has said President Bola Tinubu’s administration has committed N450 billion to agricultural financing programmes aimed at boosting domestic food production, improving food security and expanding access to credit for smallholder farmers
content:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has said President Bola Tinubu’s administration has committed N450 billion to agricultural financing programmes aimed at boosting domestic food production, improving food security and expanding access to credit for smallholder farmers across the country.

The council also disclosed that the President had approved a N1.5 trillion recapitalisation of the Bank of Agriculture (BOA) to strengthen its capacity to provide affordable financing to farmers, cooperatives, processors and other operators in the agricultural value chain.

In a statement issued by its spokesperson, Dele Alake, the campaign council said more than 500,000 smallholder farmers across 16 states, including over 70,000 women, had benefited from agricultural interventions under the Renewed Hope Agenda, while the government was targeting two million farmers through an expanded support programme.

According to the council, the N450 billion intervention comprises the N250 billion Renewed Hope Smallholder Support and Value Chain Fund and the N200 billion Guaranteed Minimum Price Programme, designed to address farmers’ financing challenges, improve access to agricultural inputs and reduce losses arising from unstable commodity prices.

It explained that the N250 billion fund was being implemented through Farmer Aggregation Companies responsible for coordinating farmer registration, input distribution, extension services and market linkages.

The programme, it said, had facilitated the distribution of approximately 2.5 million bags of fertiliser and 300,000 bags of certified seeds, with plans to expand coverage to two million farmers and distribute more than 10 million bags of fertiliser.

The council maintained that the interventions were particularly important in Northern Nigeria, where agriculture remained a major source of employment and household income.

It listed Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Niger, Borno, Gombe, Taraba, Adamawa, Yobe and Bauchi among states receiving attention under the agricultural financing programmes.

On efforts to protect farmers against price fluctuations and distress sales, the campaign council said the Bank of Agriculture was implementing the N200 billion Guaranteed Minimum Price Programme, under which approximately 170,000 metric tonnes of maize, rice, sorghum and cassava had been procured.

It explained that the initiative was intended to strengthen agricultural commodity markets and provide farmers with greater certainty over returns on their produce.

The council also highlighted a financing arrangement for onion farmers, developed by the Bank of Agriculture in partnership with the National Onion Producers, Processors and Marketers Association of Nigeria (NOPPMAN), representing more than 11,800 farmers.

Under the Onion Financing Programme, farmers are expected to receive support for improved seeds and fertiliser, while processors would have access to commodity purchase financing and facilities for storage and solar-powered cooling to reduce post-harvest losses.

The arrangement requires participating cooperatives to contribute 30 per cent of their input costs, with the Bank of Agriculture financing the remaining 70 per cent.

On the proposed N1.5 trillion recapitalisation, the APC campaign council said the intervention would strengthen the bank’s financial position and enable it to expand lending to underserved farming communities, agricultural cooperatives, processors and commercial producers.

It described the recapitalisation as part of Tinubu’s commitment to strengthening agricultural financing and transforming the sector into a major contributor to economic growth and employment.

The council further disclosed that the bank was working with the All Farmers Association of Nigeria on a dry-season financing programme targeting 400,000 farmers during the 2026 farming cycle.

The initiative covers a proposed 120,000 hectares of wheat cultivation and another 300,000 hectares for rice, maize, sorghum, millet, cassava and soybeans.

It also cited the Nigeria Ginger Recovery Programme, which it said had supported 3,200 farmers in Kachia, Kaduna State, with blight-free seeds and recovered more than 9,000 bags for multiplication, with plans to extend the intervention to 20,000 hectares across 16 states.

For women farmers, the council said the Bank of Agriculture was targeting at least 50,000 beneficiaries through insured cooperative production financing at an interest rate of nine per cent, in collaboration with the Federal Ministries of Women Affairs and Agriculture.

The statement also disclosed that 1,571 tractors had been deployed to 23 states under the Renewed Hope National Agricultural Mechanisation Programme, with a target of mechanising 1.2 million hectares of farmland through qualified mechanisation service providers.

Other interventions highlighted included a N385 billion productive-use-of-electricity programme involving 44,000 electric cargo tricycles and 100,000 solar irrigation pumps, intended to support approximately 500,000 farming families.

The campaign council maintained that the combined interventions demonstrated the administration’s commitment to addressing agricultural financing constraints, increasing domestic production and strengthening food security.

It said expanding access to credit, improved seeds, fertiliser, mechanisation, irrigation and reliable commodity markets would help farmers increase productivity and improve their incomes.

The post Tinubu commits N450bn to agricultural financing, targets 2m farmers –APC appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: NELFUND reviews structure as student loan beneficiaries hit 870,000
description:
The Nigerian Education Loan Fund has commenced a strategic organisational review to strengthen its institutional capacity following the expansion of its student loan scheme, which has recorded approximately 870,000 beneficiaries and over N375bn in disbursements.
The Fund said the exercise was aimed
content:
The Nigerian Education Loan Fund has commenced a strategic organisational review to strengthen its institutional capacity following the expansion of its student loan scheme, which has recorded approximately 870,000 beneficiaries and over N375bn in disbursements.

The Fund said the exercise was aimed at strengthening its institutional framework, improving operational efficiency and ensuring that its internal structures remained responsive to the growing demands of its national mandate.

NELFUND disclosed this in a statement signed by its Director of Strategic Communications, Oseyemi Oluwatuyi, on Sunday.

It said the expansion recorded since the commencement of the scheme had made it necessary to review its operational systems and processes to sustain its growing responsibilities.

The statement read, “Since the commencement of the Student Loan Scheme, NELFUND has experienced significant operational growth, recording approximately 870,000 unique beneficiaries and disbursing over ₦375 billion.

“This level of expansion represents a significant milestone for the Fund and reinforces the need for institutional systems, processes and structures that can effectively support its increasing responsibilities.”

The Fund explained that the review would assess existing operational arrangements, identify areas requiring improvement and develop recommendations to strengthen institutional effectiveness, clarify organisational responsibilities and improve service delivery.

It added that an independent professional consulting firm had been appointed to conduct the exercise, following procurement procedures prescribed by the Public Procurement Act 2007.

According to the statement, the consulting firm would undertake the assignment independently and provide recommendations based on its findings.

“NELFUND considers the integrity of this process essential and expects that the exercise will be guided by professional standards, evidence-based assessment and the broader institutional interests of the Fund,” it stated.

The Fund also assured students and tertiary institutions that the exercise would not disrupt its operations.

It said, “Importantly, the Fund assures all student beneficiaries, tertiary institutions and other stakeholders that this exercise is strictly an internal institutional development initiative and will not interrupt its core operations.

“The processing of applications, loan approvals, disbursements and other services under the Student Loan Scheme will continue without disruption.”

The review comes as the Federal Government continues to expand access to higher education financing through the student loan programme, established under the Student Loans (Access to Higher Education) Act, 2024.

The scheme, launched in May 2024, provides interest-free loans to eligible students in public tertiary institutions to reduce financial barriers to higher education.

NELFUND said the review was part of efforts to build a sustainable institution capable of responding to emerging challenges and meeting the expectations of millions of Nigerian students.

“The objective is clear: to build an institution whose capacity, systems and organisational effectiveness match the scale of its mandate and the expectations of the millions of Nigerian students it ultimately seeks to serve,” the statement added.

The post NELFUND reviews structure as student loan beneficiaries hit 870,000 appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Succession battle: Who authenticates the shepherd?
description: In my short time on earth, I have noticed common features in founder-led churches and independent ministries. Many of their founders are doing remarkably well in their ministries and making their mark. At some point, the immutable truth expressed in Psalm 89:48 (KJV: “What man is he that liveth, and
content:
In my short time on earth, I have noticed common features in founder-led churches and independent ministries. Many of their founders are doing remarkably well in their ministries and making their mark. At some point, the immutable truth expressed in Psalm 89:48 (KJV: “What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death? Shall he deliver his soul from the hand of the grave? Selah.”) catches up with every mortal; death comes, burial follows, and next is the succession contest among followers (disciples).

The same theme and pattern are now playing out at The Fountain of Life Church: who will succeed the late founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya.

In a video recorded in December 2021 (released by the Board of Trustees in November 2026), Pastor Taiwo explicitly named Pastor Kunle Areogun as his preferred helmsman (successor), while his son, Jimmy Odukoya, was to take charge of the youth church and serve as administrative assistant.

Then came the “Jimmy, it’s your story and laying on of hands” narrative, recounted by Rev. Wale Oke, who credited Jimmy Odukoya, Pastor Taiwo’s son, as the narrator.

These are two accounts of succession pointing to two different people but emanating from the same source.

On  November 17, 2026, a group identifying itself as the Board of Trustees announced that Jimmy Odukoya was no longer the ministry’s leader, citing a December 2021 video. The group appointed Rotimi Okpaise as interim leader.

The Fountain of Life Church countered: “For the avoidance of doubt, Pastor Jimmy Odukoya remains the duly appointed Senior Pastor and Chairman of the Board of Trustees of The Incorporated Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church.”

The claim and counterclaim bring to mind a Yoruba adage: “Agbo meji ko le mu omi ninu akoto kan náà.” Two rams cannot drink water from the same gourd. This is exactly what they are trying to do at The Fountain of Life Church. Such arrangements can only result in tension and conflict, as is presently being experienced.

Ordinarily, succession in churches should be as smooth as a hot knife through butter, because a biblical framework makes the issue of succession seamless. Though I am not a theologian, the little Sunday school I attended exposed me to some frameworks that, if followed, are likely to make succession seamless.

First, let’s look at Numbers 27:15–23. Here, Moses asked God for a successor to lead His people. The Lord said: “And the LORD said unto Moses, Take thee Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the spirit, and lay thine hand upon him; And set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and give him a charge in their sight. And thou shalt put some of thine honour upon him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may be obedient.”

From this story, we can see that the appointment was made by God. The appointee was presented to the priest, Moses laid hands on him, and he was presented to the community for recognition.

Placing this alongside The Fountain of Life Church’s approach raises some questions: Why was the December 2021 video not made public before now to the priests (clergy) in the church for onward recognition of the successors by the congregation?

Jimmy was reported by Church Times Nigeria to have told a meeting of 300 church workers that his father had instructed him to delete the video. So, who had custody of the video, and why was it not destroyed? Can a flock be left in the hands of a shepherd if he cherry-picks instructions?

The story of Elijah and Elisha, as recorded in the Bible, also shows succession through discipleship. Long after the cloak-throwing experience on the field, Elisha continued to follow Elijah throughout his ministry till he picked up the mantle when Elijah was no more. The two individuals in a contest for an exalted position, Kunle Areogun, thrown up by the December 2021 video, and Jimmy Odukoya, who got laying on of hands on his head from his father, were both disciples of the late founder, Taiwo Odukoya. This raises another question: Should succession be a cagey affair? Even when it is a cagey affair, is there no need for confirmation by the sons of prophets—in this case, the church?

In Nigeria, however, some denominations practise an emergent succession pattern: a prophetic declaration by a vessel (God’s channel) in a conclave. As novel as this method may sound, it is also not rancour-free. To better understand this method and its inherent issues, let me tell you a non-fiction story. I have only changed the church’s name and the dramatis personae, as I once attended the church.

In 1982, a church, here called CAAT, with missionary headquarters nestled between Aramoko and Igede in present-day Ekiti State, was on the verge of choosing its supreme head. The first head of the CAAT was Apostle Omotoso. Before he joined the saints, he instructed that Apostle Jagunlabi should succeed him. Unfortunately, Apostle Jagunlabi never gave any instruction before he joined the saints. Rev. Fakipe was second in hierarchy to Apostle Jagunlabi, with almost a cult followership.

The mission’s top echelon decided to hold a conclave in which God would anoint the next steersman through prophetic declaration.

According to an unconfirmed story, Fakipe and his followers had allegedly perfected clandestine plans to have him announced as the new leader through “prophetic declaration”. Alas, when the Spirit of God came upon Rev. Samori, the arrowhead who was supposed to declare, “Thus saith the Lord,” he did exactly that, but rather than announcing Rev. Fakipe, he said: “Thus saith the Lord, Rev. Jajiji is my chosen one.”

What happened next shocked CAAT to its pillars. Rev. Fakipe left the mission, taking many branches with him. Even today, CAAT has not recovered from the haemorrhage of years back caused by the issue of succession.

The “to your tents, O Israel” schism in CAAT has affected (and continues to affect) many founder-led ministries in Nigeria. The factionalisation of a prominent white-garment church, well known for using “Hallelujah” as a form of greeting, continues to rage more than 41 years after the death of its founder.

On the other hand, some founder-led ministries, such as the one in the Ikotun area of Lagos, where “Immanuel” is the signature buzzword, have experienced a relatively “smooth” succession, as the founder’s widow took charge. One can only wonder why the mantle never fell on any of his senior ministers!

The big question arising from the CAAT story is: who authenticates the prophetic declaration as truly coming from God’s throne?

The CAAT anecdote reveals something interesting, yet sad, about the reality of succession in churches. Even when prophetic declaration identifies a successor, there is still the issue of legitimacy and acceptance. Another challenge is the continuous existence and sustenance of the one-fold, one-shepherd mantra preached by many churches.

What happens when the others refuse to follow the person chosen through prophetic declaration? The tension at The Fountain of Life Church and the CAAT story shows that succession has taken on a different colouration from what it was in the biblical era. Now, being divinely chosen is not enough; there is also the issue of legitimacy, acceptance, and assured continuity of the church after the founder’s exit.

The Fountain of Life Church is currently playing with a Molotov cocktail. How soon they resolve the issue at hand determines whether the intended implosion would be manageable or the one that would destroy (God forbid) the pillars of the church.

From my crystal ball, I see a long, fractious fight that does nobody any good. To avert the impending cataclysm, the video needs authentication; private transfer of mantle must be openly questioned, and respected fathers of faith must separate the two rams drinking from the same gourd.

Let me end with a popular song by gospel artiste Evangelist Niyi Adedokun, sung during the succession-related crisis in a church often associated with “Baba Olomi Iye”. Thankfully, the raging dust eventually settled, but the song remains a homily for the recent happenings.

The song says: “Oyin Oyin Oyin Oyin… Oyin so adun nu, o di eni yeye.” Honey, honey, honey, honey… Honey has lost its sweetness; it has become a thing of ridicule (or worthless).

I have said my piece.

Shodunke, a media practitioner, writes via tolushodunke@yahoo.com

title: Enugu police launch manhunt for fleeing kidnappers
description:
The Commissioner for Police in Enugu State, Fidelis Ogarabe, has ordered a manhunt for the fleeing kidnappers of a 73-year-old man, Patrick Onyia.
Mr Onyia ‌‌‍‌‌‌regained his freedom last Thursday, following sustained rescue operations by the police, in collaboration with Forest Guards and th
content:
The Commissioner for Police in Enugu State, Fidelis Ogarabe, has ordered a manhunt for the fleeing kidnappers of a 73-year-old man, Patrick Onyia.

Mr Onyia ‌‌‍‌‌‌regained his freedom last Thursday, following sustained rescue operations by the police, in collaboration with Forest Guards and the Neighbourhood Watch personnel.

Spokesman of the Enugu State Police Command, Daniel Ndukwe,  said the directive was issued on Friday. He said that the victim was abducted at about 6pm last Wednesday, in the Umuabi community, Udi Local Council.

“Preliminary investigations revealed that the abductors allegedly used the victim’s ATM card to withdraw an unspecified sum of money from his bank account before fleeing.

“The commissioner directed operatives to intensify efforts to track down and arrest the perpetrators and bring them to justice,” he said.

The police chief reassured residents of the command’s commitment to protecting life and property.

Ndukwe said the commissioner urged members of the public to provide credible information that could help apprehend the fleeing suspects.

title: WHO chief calls for peace amid heavy fighting in Ebola-hit DR Congo region

title: NDC condemns 200-man vigilante in Ebonyi LG, urges investigation
description:
From Uchenna Inya, Abakaliki 
The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Ebonyi State has condemned the reported establishment and inauguration of a 200-member local security codenamed Neighbourhood Watch outfit by the Chairman, Ohaozara Local Government Area, Osborn Nweze Umahi.
