title: 26bn fraud: Court adjourns EFCC forfeiture case against ZNL
description: The Federal High Court in Abuja has adjourned proceedings in the final forfeiture case involving over ₦26bn linked to Ziklagsis Networks Limited, a company accused by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission of failing to execute a prepaid electricity meter contract awarded by the Federal Govern
content:
The Federal High Court in Abuja has adjourned proceedings in the final forfeiture case involving over ₦26bn linked to Ziklagsis Networks Limited, a company accused by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission of failing to execute a prepaid electricity meter contract awarded by the Federal Government.

Justice E. U. Akpan adjourned the matter until December 15, 2026, for hearing of pending applications after counsel for the company sought more time to complete the filing of processes.

The EFCC is seeking the final forfeiture of the funds to the Federal Government, alleging that the company failed to execute a mass metering contract awarded in 2003 through the defunct National Electric Power Authority.

However, Ziklagsis Networks Limited is opposing the forfeiture, insisting that the funds were released pursuant to court judgments and agreements with the Federal Government and constituted a loan secured by bank guarantees.

In a counter-affidavit filed by an EFCC operative, Naankus Panwal, on November 12, 2026, the commission alleged that the company, in connivance with some staff members of Polaris Bank Plc who are currently on the run, transferred N39bn from an account with the bank to Providus Bank Plc.

The EFCC alleged that the transfer was made despite the company’s failure to execute the contract for the installation of prepaid electricity meters in Yola Electricity Distribution Company.

“That rather than carry out the installation of prepaid meters in Yola Disco, ZNL surreptitiously and in connivance with staffers of Polaris Bank Plc who are on the run, moved the entire sum of N39 Billion in the account with Polaris Bank Plc to Providus Bank Plc, which lacked the capacity to hold such an amount in its custody,” the document read.

According to the commission, Providus Bank subsequently sought approval from the Central Bank of Nigeria to accommodate the funds, which exceeded its threshold.

The CBN reportedly directed that the funds, being public money, should be invested in Federal Government Treasury bills and bonds rather than left idle.

The EFCC, however, alleged that Ziklagsis Networks Limited continued to misappropriate the funds and the interest generated from the investments.

It further alleged that the company opened a separate account to receive interest accruing on the contract sum, contrary to banking practice.

The commission said between July 2021 and March 2024, the company received N22,642,666,970 through the account and allegedly diverted the money for personal use.

“That since the action in the paragraph above, the ZNL has continued to misappropriate the funds and the accrued interest the funds have generated.

“That to perpetuate this fraud and defraud the Government of Nigeria, ZNL opened a separate account for the interest that will be accrued on the said contract sum contrary to the usual banking practice.

“That between July 2021 and March 2024, ZNL, through the said account, received the sum of N22,642,666,970.00 and misappropriated the same for personal use,” the deponent stated.

The EFCC also accused the company’s management of refusing to refund the funds despite the termination of the contract by the Federal Ministry of Power.

It alleged that the continued retention of the money was intended to generate additional interest for the company and its alleged associates at the expense of the Federal Government.

The commission subsequently approached the court for an interim forfeiture order over the funds.

Justice Akpan granted the application, following which a notice was published in a national newspaper inviting interested parties to show cause why the funds should not be finally forfeited to the Federal Government.

In its affidavit to show cause dated 28th August 2026, deposed to by one Jones Listowel, Ziklagsis Networks Limited denied the allegations, describing the transaction as a commercial contractual arrangement and insisting that the funds were not proceeds of crime.

The company’s Managing Director, Jones O. Listowel, who deposed to the affidavit, said the company had a legal and equitable interest in the bank account and the funds subject to the interim forfeiture order.

He alleged that the EFCC deliberately misrepresented facts to obtain the interim forfeiture order, adding that the commission’s allegations were “substantially incorrect and misleading.”

The company said it entered into a tripartite agreement with the Federal Government and the defunct NEPA on December 5, 2003, for the manufacture, supply, installation and maintenance of three million prepaid electricity meters across 23 states.

It claimed that the contract was subsequently revalidated following negotiations with the Federal Government and that the project was approved under the Presidential Initiative to Supply Meters to Nigerians.

According to the affidavit, the company was to supply 3,315,820 prepaid meters under the revalidated agreement, with funding of $196,835,396.02 approved by the Federal Government.

Ziklagsis alleged that the government failed to release the approved funds for the execution of the project, despite the company’s efforts to meet its contractual obligations.

The company said it instituted arbitration proceedings in 2010 over outstanding payments and obtained an arbitral award in its favour, which was subsequently made enforceable by the Federal High Court.

It further claimed that the Federal Government later reached a settlement with it over outstanding payments and related contractual issues.

The company said the sum of N32bn was eventually released into its account with the then Skye Bank Plc, now Polaris Bank Plc, pursuant to a court judgment delivered on September 30, 2015.

In the judgment, the court reportedly directed the release of the funds for the immediate implementation of the revalidated tripartite agreement.

Ziklagsis quoted the court as ordering that the defendants should not “divert, convert or utilize” the funds for any purpose other than the prepaid meter contract.

The company alleged, however, that although the funds were transferred into its account, it was prevented from accessing them.

It said a subsequent compromise judgment agreement reached with the Federal Government in 2017 provided for the release of N39,171,985,233.95, comprising the N32bn awarded by the court and accrued interest.

According to the company, the funds were released as a loan for the execution of the tripartite agreement, with repayment terms agreed upon by the parties.

It maintained that the transaction was secured by bank guarantees and other instruments, arguing that the funds were not stolen or diverted.

Ziklagsis also cited a judgment delivered on July 17, 2025, which it said restrained the Federal Government from unilaterally revoking the compromise agreement.

The company quoted the court as holding that any attempt by the government to revoke the agreement without complying with the judgment would amount to “a wilful disobedience to a valid Judgment of the Court.”

It further alleged that the Ministry of Power terminated the agreement in September 2025, less than 12 days after the judgment, despite the court’s order.

The EFCC, however, maintained that the company failed to execute the metering contract and continued to retain the funds despite the termination of the agreement.

The commission said the source of the funds was the Federal Government and that their continued retention without executing the project amounted to criminal misappropriation.

Ziklagsis argued that the forfeiture proceedings would undermine pending litigation over the same funds, insisting that the transaction was contractual and should not be treated as a criminal matter.

The EFCC, on the other hand, said its investigation uncovered alleged illegal transactions involving the funds and urged the court to grant the final forfeiture application.

The company, through its counsel, Oladipo Okpeseyi, SAN, filed an affidavit claiming ownership of the funds and opposing the final forfeiture.

The EFCC, represented by J. N. Dogonyaro, filed a counter-affidavit urging the court to grant its application.

When the matter came up on Friday, November 20, 2026, for hearing and determination of the applications, counsel for the company informed the court that some processes were still being filed and sought an adjournment to enable him complete the filings.

Justice Akpan consequently adjourned the matter until December 15, 2026, for hearing of all pending applications.

The post 26bn fraud: Court adjourns EFCC forfeiture case against ZNL appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Tinubu donates N250m to families of Bayelsa boat victims
description:
President Bola Tinubu on Sunday donated N250m to families of victims of Friday’s boat mishap in Bayelsa State. He ordered stricter enforcement of safety standards on inland waterways as the death toll from the accident rose to 29, with more than 50 survivors.
Vice President Kashim Shettima conveyed
content:
President Bola Tinubu on Sunday donated N250m to families of victims of Friday’s boat mishap in Bayelsa State. He ordered stricter enforcement of safety standards on inland waterways as the death toll from the accident rose to 29, with more than 50 survivors.

Vice President Kashim Shettima conveyed the President’s position and the donation on Sunday during a condolence visit to Government House, Yenagoa, the Bayelsa State capital.

This is according to a statement signed on Sunday by the Senior Special Assistant to the Vice President on Media and Communications, Stanley Nkwocha, titled ‘Bayelsa Boat Mishap: President Tinubu Orders Stiffer Waterway Safety Measures.’

The accident occurred on Friday at the Oweikorogha/Otuan River Junction in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area, when a boat carrying scores of mourners travelling to a funeral capsized.

Governor Douye Diri, who briefed the Vice President at Government House, attributed the tragedy to an alleged failure by boat operators to observe established safety protocols, describing it as avoidable.

He said the state government had constituted a committee to investigate the immediate and remote causes of the accident.

Shettima said Tinubu had also demanded a thorough investigation into the circumstances of the mishap, including preliminary reports of a possible mechanical fault.

He stated, “We have received preliminary reports concerning the circumstances of this accident, including indications of a possible mechanical failure.

“These reports must be thoroughly investigated by the appropriate authorities. We must establish what happened, identify any failures in safety procedures and take the necessary steps to prevent a recurrence.”

The Vice President described the disaster as an equity issue, arguing that Nigerians who travel by water were entitled to the same standard of protection as those who travel by road or air.

“We cannot accept a situation in which citizens must gamble with their lives simply to move between communities. Geography may determine how people travel, but it must never determine how much protection their lives deserve.

“A Nigerian travelling by boat is entitled to the same concern for safety as one travelling by road or air,” he said.

The Vice President described the tragedy as carrying “a particular cruelty”, noting that the victims had set out to mourn the dead before death claimed them along the way.

Shettima stated, “Each person lost in those waters had a name, a history, relationships and responsibilities. Somewhere, a family is struggling to understand how someone who left home for a funeral will never walk through that door again.”

He assured the bereaved families that they would receive lasting support from the Federal Government.

“To the families who have lost their loved ones, I will not pretend that time alone will make this pain disappear.

“Our responsibility is to stand with you beyond this visit, beyond these condolences and beyond the days when this tragedy dominates the news,” he said.

Before proceeding to Government House, the Vice President visited survivors receiving treatment at the Bayelsa Medical University Teaching Hospital, where he consoled patients and assured them of adequate medical care.

Shettima commended Governor Diri for visiting the accident scene and coordinating the state’s response, and acknowledged the efforts of the National Emergency Management Agency, the Bayelsa State Emergency Management Agency, the Nigerian Red Cross Society, the Nigeria Police Force, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, local divers and community volunteers.

Governor Diri announced that the state government had taken responsibility for the medical bills of all survivors and assured bereaved families that they would not be abandoned.

On arrival in Yenagoa, the Vice President was received by Governor Diri, Minister of State for Petroleum Resources, Senator Heineken Lokpobiri; Niger Delta Development Commission Managing Director, Dr Samuel Ogbuku; Bayelsa State APC Chairman, Dr Dennis Otiotio; and Niger Delta River Basin Development Authority Managing Director, Prince Ebitimi Amgbare.

Members of the National Assembly, the Bayelsa State House of Assembly and the State Executive Council were also present.

The post Tinubu donates N250m to families of Bayelsa boat victims appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Fountain: Okonkwo preaches unity, Jimmy insists court order not served
description: The Fountain of Life Church, Ilupeju, Lagos, on Sunday received an intervention from one of Nigeria’s prominent Pentecostal leaders, Bishop Mike Okonkwo, who, amid the escalating leadership crisis rocking the church, urged members not to take sides but to protect an institution he said was built on
content:
The Fountain of Life Church, Ilupeju, Lagos, on Sunday received an intervention from one of Nigeria’s prominent Pentecostal leaders, Bishop Mike Okonkwo, who, amid the escalating leadership crisis rocking the church, urged members not to take sides but to protect an institution he said was built on the blood, sacrifices and lives of its founders.

Okonkwo, founder of The Redeemed Evangelical Mission, said he had been prompted by the Holy Spirit to visit the church and bless its congregation after his telephone was inundated with calls over the preceding week, with people demanding to know why he had remained silent as the dispute between Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and his sister, Tolu, threatened the church’s unity.

But Jimmy, who also spoke during the service, addressed the interim court order restraining him from presenting himself as the church’s Senior Pastor and Spiritual Head, saying he had heard about the injunction but had not been formally served.

Okonkwo, in his sermon, said, “I have not slept since 1.30 am.

The Holy Spirit said to me, son, go to the Fountain and bless them. That’s why I am here,” he told the congregation.

His appearance and sermon, titled The Glory of the Church, were an attempt to redirect attention from the personalities at the centre of the dispute to the institution they inherited from their late parents, Pastor Taiwo and Pastor Bimbo Odukoya.

But beneath his generally conciliatory message were pointed admonitions that appeared to address the warring parties, the congregation and a wider public that has followed the controversy, cautioning against turning a leadership disagreement into a battle capable of destroying the church.

Opening with an assurance that “all is well”, Okonkwo recalled the traumatic period following Taiwo’s death, when he had addressed the congregation and urged members to preserve the legacy of the deceased founder.

“I remember when Pastor Taiwo passed, it was a traumatic time and experience. We cried, we wailed, we blew our noses and dried our tears, and the responsibility fell on me to come here to talk to us,” he said.

He said he had reminded the congregation at the time that the greatest honour it could pay the late pastor was to ensure that his life’s work continued.

“And I know one of the things I said that day is, please, the only honour we can do for the sacrifice, the price, the pains and everything… that the only thing is that the legacy must continue. And I told you that day that Fountain will never die.”

The bishop said he remained personally invested in the church and could not be indifferent to developments there.

“For the past one or two weeks, we have been literally battered on social media. There’s nothing that has not been said, both the ones that are true and the ones that are not true. Phone calls from far and near: ‘Bishop Mike, where are you?’” he said.

“You can’t separate me from Fountain because it is a covenant that God himself created by himself, so what happens to Fountain affects me. So don’t think that I am just aloof.”

However, the central thrust of his message was that the church was bigger than the individuals currently fighting over its leadership.

Drawing extensively from biblical passages on redemption, the value of the church and the sacrifices behind its establishment, Okonkwo argued that the institution could not be reduced to a human organisation whose survival depended on the fortunes of particular individuals.

“The church is not a human institution. It is God’s house. It belongs to him. Think of the price that God had to pay for his church,” he said.

He subsequently made one of the most direct references to the leadership dispute, telling members that their allegiance should not be to either of the Odukoya siblings or the church’s governing board.

“Every one of us, from myself downwards, should know: you are not for Tolu or for Jimmy or for the board. None of them died for you. Church is not a political party. The blood. Life was involved. The church is not an ordinary thing. God could not redeem the church with anything other than his life,” he said.

“We must be careful so that none of us will be an instrument of destroying the church of Christ.”

The appeal appeared directed not only at the two sides in the dispute but also at members whose public declarations of support, social media exchanges and competing narratives have increasingly made the crisis a subject of wider controversy.

Okonkwo’s emphasis on the sacrifices of the founders also appeared intended to remind the contending parties of the responsibility attached to the institution they inherited. He insisted that the present difficulties were not evidence that God had abandoned the church, arguing that its challenges had already been anticipated in God’s plan.

Using Jesus Christ’s illustration in Luke 14:28 of a builder who must first calculate the cost of constructing a tower, Okonkwo questioned why members would allow the present crisis to unsettle their faith in the church’s future.

“Question, Fountaineers, are you saying that Jesus did not factor in the challenges you will go through? He is saying that if I want to build a house, I will first of all be sure that I have all that is necessary, and he is the builder of the house, we are the building. Are you saying that all the crises, all the gossips, all that is happening to you individually is taking you by surprise?” he asked.

“He has already factored all those in even before you were called. He has already taken care of business. That is why I know without shadow of doubt whatever the devil does, he is already a failure. The believer never ever ends in shame.”

But while assuring the congregation that the church would survive, the bishop also warned against reactions that could aggravate its problems.

“Do you know the challenges of the believers? When trials come, temptations come, difficulties come, we fall apart, we forget what he told us, we begin to run helter-skelter, and many times we do the things we are not supposed to do and further arm the devil,” he said.

“If there was a time Fountaineers needed to chill, it is this time. Let God perfect what he has started.”

He declared that the church would eventually surpass the achievements of its late founder. “This church is going to do seven times more than Taiwo left it,” he said.

“The game is not over. You are still in the will of God. You are still in his hands. God has not left this church. And can I tell you, he will never leave this church; the glory of God remains in this house.”

He ended with a call for collective responsibility, assuring members that the church would not be destroyed by the present controversy.

“Be assured. No matter what anyone says, that is not your business. We will build this church. Together we will build this church.”

Jimmy’s personal battle

But the atmosphere that followed Okonkwo’s sermon suggested that the bishop’s appeal for a collective response to the crisis might not have entirely displaced the personal dimension of the dispute.

Jimmy, who addressed the congregation after Okonkwo, appeared to frame the unfolding controversy more directly around his own predicament, a departure from the senior bishop’s sustained emphasis on the survival of the institution beyond its current leadership.

He mounted the pulpit and sang the popular hymn It Is Well with My Soul before moving to gospel musician Dunsin Oyekan’s My Worship Is My Weapon, whose refrain declares worship as a means of winning personal battles.

The choice of songs, coming immediately after Okonkwo had urged members not to identify with either of the contending parties, shifted the emotional emphasis towards a personal struggle and appeared to reinforce the perception among his supporters that he was fighting an unjust campaign against him.

Jimmy was the only party to the leadership dispute who addressed the congregation during the service.

He subsequently addressed the interim court order restraining him from presenting himself as the church’s Senior Pastor and Spiritual Head, saying he had heard about the injunction but had not been formally served.

“I heard that there was an injunction against me. I heard. I’ve not seen it. But I heard. But I’ve not been served. So, legally, I’ve not been served,” he said.

He also thanked members for remaining at the church despite the controversy and assured them of his continued commitment to their interests.

“In spite of everything, you are still here,” he said. “There is no Fountain without you. You are Fountain of Life. And as long as you are with me, I will continue to speak for you. I will continue to stand with you.”

While the remarks were likely to reassure his supporters, they offered little indication of an immediate willingness to de-escalate the dispute or pursue reconciliation with the opposing side.

Towards the end of the service, as the choir continued singing, Jimmy walked up to the choir leader at least twice to whisper instructions. On one occasion, the choir subsequently sang the popular gospel song in Pidgin by Bidemi Olaoba, Who Dey Talk Wetin God No Talk, a primarily individualistic chorus that became the closing song.

The choice of song, with its message about disregarding declarations contrary to God’s will, added another layer to the service’s underlying contest of narratives.

Jimmy also appeared determined to maintain his position as the church’s leader despite the legal challenge, leaving the question of reconciliation unresolved.

The Odukoya legacy

The controversy has also revived questions about the personality, public conduct and religious identity of the Odukoya family, particularly as Jimmy’s unconventional appearance and style of ministry continue to attract criticism from sections of the Christian community.

Tattooed, dreadlocked, fond of swaggering dance routines and wearing earrings, Jimmy has attracted considerable attention for a public persona that departs from the conventional image of a Pentecostal pastor in Nigeria.

But the apple did not fall far from the tree.

His late mother and co-founder of The Fountain of Life Church, Bimbo Odukoya, also faced considerable criticism during her lifetime for challenging the conservative social conventions and strict codes of appearance that characterised much of Nigeria’s expanding Pentecostal movement in the 1990s and early 2000s.

At the time, many Pentecostal churches maintained restrictive expectations around dressing, hairstyles, jewellery and other forms of personal adornment, reflecting a broader doctrine of separation from worldly influences.

Pastors’ wives were generally expected to dress in long skirts and modest clothing, often complemented by church hats and restrained accessories.

Bimbo, however, cultivated a considerably different public image. Her fashionable outfits, shorter skirts, wigs and jewellery attracted criticism from conservative Christians who considered her appearance inconsistent with the standards expected of a pastor’s wife.

Yet, her appearance was accompanied by a formidable preaching ministry. Her sermons, which frequently focused on purpose, relationships, leadership and personal development, established her as one of the more recognisable female Christian voices of her generation.

She was also known for her forceful, scripture-based responses to criticism, challenging interpretations of biblical doctrines that she considered unnecessarily restrictive.

Her ability to combine an unconventional public image with an intellectually engaging preaching style helped distinguish her from many of her contemporaries.

Jimmy’s public persona, however, has generated a different kind of debate. While his appearance and contemporary style have endeared him to a section of younger Christians, questions have persisted over whether his public responses and conduct consistently reflect the temperament, depth and intellectual maturity expected of someone leading a large congregation.

The distinction is particularly evident in the way both generations have approached public criticism.

During Sunday’s service, Okonkwo used a football analogy, drawing on the nature of a Manchester United match, to explain that conceding a goal did not mean the referee would immediately end the game. The match would continue until the allotted time elapsed before the final result was determined.

The analogy was a measured attempt to contextualise the reputational damage the church might have suffered, reminding members that the present controversy was not the end of its institutional story.

It contrasted with Jimmy’s own much-discussed social media engagement with Manchester United, in which he adapted a popular Christian song, invoked the name of Christ while praying for the club’s victory, and danced before the camera.

The performance attracted criticism from social media users who considered it unbecoming of a pastor of his stature.

The criticism raises a broader question about the boundaries between contemporary Christian expression, personal branding, and the public responsibilities attached to pastoral leadership. While younger audiences may appreciate Jimmy’s informality and entertainment-oriented presentation, the same approach can be received differently by members of a religious institution whose identity was shaped by more conventional standards of pastoral conduct.

Indeed, Nigerian Pentecostal churches are increasingly confronting the challenge of negotiating these competing expectations.

The country’s large youth population is growing up in an environment shaped by the internet, international entertainment, social media and cultural influences that increasingly challenge traditional assumptions about dressing, music, personal expression and religious identity.

Tattoos, dreadlocks, earrings and contemporary dance styles, once widely regarded with suspicion in conservative Christian circles, have become increasingly common forms of expression among younger generations.

Some Pentecostal leaders have argued that these practices are not inherently sinful and should not be confused with a person’s spiritual disposition.

Even traditionally conservative denominations, including the Deeper Christian Life Ministry, have over time deemphasised or relaxed some of their earlier positions on aspects of dressing, hair covering, jewellery and contemporary music.

The challenge for churches is how to accommodate a changing generation without losing the doctrinal identity and institutional traditions that defined their establishment.

For The Fountain of Life Church, this generational transition is history re-unfolding alongside a particularly sensitive leadership dispute involving the children of its founders.

The immediate legal battle remains unresolved. The Lagos State High Court, presided over by Justice O.O. Adewunmi-Oshin, issued an interim order on Wednesday, November 18, restraining Jimmy from presenting himself as the church’s Senior Pastor and Spiritual Head.

The order followed an application by the Incorporated Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church. The court also restrained him, either personally or through proxies, from interfering with or disrupting the church’s activities, governance and other business.

The matter was adjourned until December 1 for mention.

Sunday’s service offered little indication that the dispute was nearing a resolution. While Okonkwo sought to redirect the congregation’s attention to the church’s founding vision and collective future, Jimmy’s address placed his own position and relationship with members at the centre of the unfolding controversy.

For a church founded on the ministry and public identities of Taiwo and Bimbo Odukoya, the crisis is now testing not only the succession arrangements but also the meaning of the legacy they left behind.

Okonkwo’s message was that the church must survive its present troubles and become greater than it was under its founders. Whether those now contesting its leadership can subordinate their differences to that vision remains the more immediate test.

The post Fountain: Okonkwo preaches unity, Jimmy insists court order not served appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Anosike plans industrial clusters, housing estates for Osisioma
description:
The governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party in Abia State, Kelechi Anosike, has promised to establish industrial clusters and government-backed housing estates in Osisioma Local Government Area, saying the development would ease pressure on Aba and expand the council’s revenue base.
A
content:
The governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party in Abia State, Kelechi Anosike, has promised to establish industrial clusters and government-backed housing estates in Osisioma Local Government Area, saying the development would ease pressure on Aba and expand the council’s revenue base.

Anosike unveiled the proposal at a PDP campaign rally in Osisioma, where he presented what he described as strategic development plans for each of the state’s 17 local government areas ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

He said Osisioma would be developed as a satellite town to accommodate residents and businesses spilling over from Aba, the commercial centre of the South-East, which he argued had become congested.

“Aba is already filled up. As part of the decongestion plan, government will build several housing estates in Osisioma where people can live and go to work in Aba. Also, industrial clusters will spring up in Osisioma to service Aba,” he said.

The candidate said the council’s landmass made it suitable for the proposed expansion, which he claimed would improve its internally generated revenue and make it one of the wealthiest local governments in the state within months of his administration taking office.

“Osisioma has the landmass suitable for our development plans and when we assume power, the economy of the council will be turned around and its internally-generated revenue improved. It will become one of the richest local governments in Abia in a matter of months,” Anosike said.

He said his decision to contest the governorship election was driven by what he described as the suffering of Abia residents, accusing the incumbent administration of failing to provide adequate economic support and welfare programmes.

“A government that didn’t provide empowerment, subsidy, grant, palliative and other incentives to improve the welfare of her citizens, should be changed because people need to be alive to enjoy the infrastructure built by government,” he said.

Anosike promised that his administration would introduce regular empowerment programmes, arguing that infrastructure development alone would not address the hardship facing residents.

He also blamed the high cost of living in the state partly on what he described as the government’s failure to prioritise agriculture, promising to introduce a state-backed food production programme called Operation Feed Abia.

Other proposals he outlined included establishing a traders’ microfinance bank to provide soft loans to women, youths, traders and artisans; free multiple-skills training for young people; and a N90,000 minimum wage.

He also promised to sponsor more than 30 talented footballers abroad annually and introduce health insurance and subsidised healthcare to reduce the cost of medical services.

“For a government minded to improve the welfare of the people, these programmes are possible. The money to do it is there; it is Abia money and should be spent on the people,” he said.

The candidate urged residents to support his ambition, saying his administration would focus on economic development and giving people the resources to improve their livelihoods.

At the rally, he also approved a request by Osisioma stakeholders for the council to receive more than one commissioner in his proposed administration, citing its special status.

Earlier, the Director-General of the PDP Governorship Campaign Council, Obinna Nwachukwu, had asked Anosike to consider allocating about three commissioner positions to the local government if elected.

Nwachukwu also drew attention to the condition of roads in the area, saying several had deteriorated and required urgent attention.

The Abia PDP Chairman and deputy governorship candidate, Amah Abraham, and the Chairman of the campaign council, Empire Kanu, urged party supporters to back Anosike, describing him as committed to improving the welfare of residents.

Other PDP candidates at the rally included the Abia South senatorial candidate, Chinyere Onuoha; Aba North/Aba South Federal Constituency candidate, Bob Chiedozie Ogu; Obingwa/Osisioma/Ugwunagbo Federal Constituency candidate, Solomon Akpulonu; Osisioma South State Constituency candidate, Ahamefula Young Onyike; and Obingwa West State Constituency candidate, Enyinnaya Appolos.

The Osisioma PDP Chairman, Emeka Onyenso, the local government woman leader, Blessing Ahaiwe, and youth leader, Ahamefula Ogidi, pledged the area’s support for the party in the 2027 elections.

title: Gambia’s Genocide Case Against Myanmar Sets to Trigger Precedent for International Justice
description: Gambiaj.com – (BANJUL, THE GAMBIA) – The Gambia’s successful genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) could have far-reaching implications for international law, particularly as the court faces growing scrutiny over allegations of genocide in other parts of the world
content:
Gambiaj.com – (BANJUL, THE GAMBIA) – The Gambia’s successful genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) could have far-reaching implications for international law, particularly as the court faces growing scrutiny over allegations of genocide in other parts of the world, including Gaza.

In a landmark ruling on Thursday, November 19, the United Nations’ highest court found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority in northern Rakhine State, marking the first time in its 80-year history that the court has established that a state committed what is widely described as “the crime of crimes”.

The ruling, adopted by nine votes to six, also found Myanmar in breach of its obligation to prevent genocide under the 1948 UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

Reading the judgment, ICJ President Judge Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar’s security forces had killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence, carried out extreme violence against children and attacked people fleeing the violence.

The court also upheld estimates by an independent UN fact-finding mission that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the 2017 military crackdown, finding that the figure was supported by the evidence before it.

At the time, approximately 815,000 Rohingya were living in Rakhine State, with hundreds of thousands subsequently fleeing across the border into neighbouring Bangladesh.

The Question Of Genocidal Intent

Beyond the scale of the killings, the ruling carries particular legal significance because genocide is defined not simply by the number of people killed, but by the intention to destroy, in whole or in part, a protected national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The 1948 Genocide Convention identifies five categories of acts that can constitute genocide, including killing members of a protected group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately imposing conditions calculated to bring about its physical destruction, preventing births and forcibly transferring children.

The ICJ concluded that the only reasonable inference from the evidence was that Myanmar intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population.

International lawyer Johann Soufi explained that the court had clarified an important principle: genocidal intent can exist alongside other military or political objectives.

A state may claim to be pursuing legitimate security objectives or fighting an armed group, he said, while simultaneously committing acts intended to destroy a protected population.

The existence of other objectives does not automatically exclude the possibility of genocide.

The judgment therefore reinforces the importance of examining the overall pattern of conduct, rather than accepting a state’s stated military or security justification at face value.

Why The Gambia’s Case Matters Beyond Myanmar

The ruling is also significant because it reinforces the principle that states have an obligation to prevent and punish genocide, even when the alleged crimes are committed outside their own territories.

Under the 1948 convention, countries must take all measures within their power to prevent genocide and hold those responsible accountable.

The Gambia invoked that obligation when it brought proceedings against Myanmar before the ICJ in 2019, seeking to hold the Asian country accountable for its treatment of the Rohingya.

For the Rohingya community, the decision represents a major recognition of years of suffering.

Wai Wai Nu, a former political prisoner and director of the Women’s Peace Network, told Reuters that the ruling had ended what she described as Myanmar’s longstanding denial of the community’s existence and suffering.

She welcomed the court’s recognition of genocide and its demands for guarantees against a repetition of the crimes, as well as restitution and compensation.

However, despite the binding nature of ICJ decisions, the court has no independent enforcement mechanism to compel states to implement its judgments.

Whether Myanmar’s authorities will comply with the ruling, including measures to facilitate the safe return of Rohingya refugees who wish to go home and provide compensation, remains uncertain.

Implications For Israel’s Case At The ICJ

The ruling has also drawn attention to the ongoing genocide proceedings brought by South Africa against Israel over its military operations in Gaza.

South Africa filed its case before the ICJ in December 2023, arguing that Israel had violated the Genocide Convention.

In January 2024, the court found that Palestinians in Gaza faced a serious and imminent risk of genocide and ordered Israel to take measures to prevent acts prohibited under the convention, including direct and public incitement to genocide.

The ICJ has yet to deliver a final judgment in the case, which could take several more years.

Meanwhile, a UN independent commission of inquiry concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in the Palestinian territory, a finding strongly rejected by the Israeli government, which accused the commission of bias and relying on what it called Hamas propaganda.

Although the Myanmar and Israel cases are different in several respects, legal experts have identified similarities in the arguments advanced by both governments.

Both have invoked national security and military objectives to defend their actions.

For international law professor Rafaëlle Maison of Paris-Saclay University, the question of genocidal intent can be established through patterns of conduct or explicit statements by political and military leaders.

She argued that statements by Israeli officials could be relevant to the court’s assessment of intent in the South African case.

Soufi also pointed to the importance of examining the cumulative impact of military operations, including the killing of children and the destruction of civilian communities.

He said the evidence documented by UN investigative mechanisms in Gaza contained elements similar to those considered relevant by the ICJ in the Myanmar case.

A Test For International Justice

Beyond its immediate implications for the Rohingya, the judgment comes at a time when international judicial institutions face increasing political pressure, particularly from powerful countries.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said the ruling sent a strong message that those responsible for genocide must be held accountable.

Gambian President Adama Barrow described it as a historic day for international justice.

However, the court’s decision also comes amid growing criticism of international judicial institutions from governments that have challenged their authority.

The United States, which officially recognised the atrocities against the Rohingya as genocide in 2022 under then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken, has increasingly criticised international courts over their actions involving Israel.

In November, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio attacked the International Criminal Court (ICC), describing it as illegitimate and threatening to dismantle it.

Washington has also expressed concern about the potential implications of the ICJ’s approach to establishing genocidal intent in the Myanmar case.

US Ambassador to the United Nations Michael Waltz had previously warned against what he viewed as a possible lowering of the evidentiary threshold for establishing genocide.

For Soufi, the broader challenge is whether states, including established democracies, will continue to respect international judicial institutions when their decisions affect powerful political and military allies.

He warned that international justice rests on a fundamental principle: no state, however powerful, should be above the law.

The Gambia’s legal victory has therefore established an important precedent in the fight against genocide. But whether it signals a stronger era of international accountability will depend not only on the decisions of judges in The Hague, but also on the willingness of governments to respect and implement them.

title: ‘Stablecoins ease cross-border payment burden’
description:
Timon CEO Oluwatomi Ayorinde tells JUSTICE OKAMGBA how stablecoins and local partnerships are streamlining African cross-border payments and reducing dollar dependence through local settlements and PAPSS
What key challenges in Africa’s cross-border payment systems is Timon addressing through stablec
content:
Timon CEO Oluwatomi Ayorinde tells JUSTICE OKAMGBA how stablecoins and local partnerships are streamlining African cross-border payments and reducing dollar dependence through local settlements and PAPSS

What key challenges in Africa’s cross-border payment systems is Timon addressing through stablecoins, and what gaps remain in existing platforms such as PAPSS?

The core problem in African cross-border payments is convertibility. Too often, a business or individual holding one African currency can’t easily exchange it for another, so the payment has to go through the US dollar first. That extra step adds cost and delay, and for many people the dollars are hard to access in the first place. Today, USD stablecoins are the most practical fix. They give people a way to hold value and move it across borders without waiting on scarce dollar liquidity, and Timon uses them to help customers access and spend their money across borders, including through card payments. However, this still leaves African currencies dependent on the dollar as the bridge between them. Local-currency stablecoins could reduce that dependence by enabling direct exchange between African currencies. PAPSS, created by Afreximbank, is already laying the groundwork, with its payment rail connecting African markets and its African Currency Marketplace enabling direct exchange between their currencies. Timon was part of the first cohort of the Afreximbank Accelerator Programme, and we actually plan to build with PAPSS as this infrastructure develops, bringing those benefits to individuals and businesses through the cards, accounts and payment methods they already use. We see our work as complementary to the broader infrastructure being developed across Africa, with partnerships helping to make cross-border financial services more accessible and practical for customers.

Can you illustrate with an actual transaction how Timon’s stablecoin infrastructure has improved the speed, cost and efficiency of cross-border payments compared with conventional channels?

I travel to Kenya often for business, and my own experience is the simplest example. Most businesses there prefer M-Pesa, so before Timon, I had to exchange my naira for physical US dollars, get a Kenyan SIM, and set up an M-Pesa account. Topping it up meant finding an agent each time and took about 30 minutes because of the physical interaction. When I used Kenyan ATMs to withdraw cash with my international card, each transaction could cost as much as KSh 1,000, depending on the bank. Today, I top up from my Nigerian account and send directly to M-Pesa accounts whenever I need to. It takes less than three minutes and costs far less than those card fees. Behind the scenes, Timon uses USD stablecoins to move the value between the two markets, so I no longer have to carry cash, withdraw from ATMs or rely on an agent. The next step is to remove the dollar from the middle of that journey. USD stablecoins still have to be converted into Kenyan shillings, but a shilling-backed stablecoin could allow settlement into M-Pesa without that extra conversion, which is where we see this heading.

How does the settlement process work when a business in one African country pays another across the continent? What role does the stablecoin play, and at what stage are local currencies introduced?

Timon is currently focused primarily on consumers rather than operating as a business-to-business settlement network, so it is important to distinguish our existing product from the broader possibilities for cross-border payments. Conceptually, a stablecoin can serve as an intermediate settlement asset in a cross-border transaction.

A sender could initiate a payment using an available local currency or payment method, value could move between providers using a stablecoin, and the recipient could receive funds in their preferred local currency. Whether this approach is suitable depends on the markets involved, available liquidity, the participating providers, and applicable regulatory requirements. We see potential for different payment and settlement mechanisms to work together, but the specific arrangements depend on the infrastructure and partnerships supporting each transaction. Our current focus remains on making cross-border financial services more accessible and convenient for individual users.

You have highlighted stablecoins as a solution to liquidity challenges among African currencies. What are the major constraints in the current system, and how does Timon’s model address them?

The specific problem is that there is very little direct liquidity between most pairs of African currencies.

 For example, not many people actively trade naira for Kenyan shillings at any given moment, so providers usually convert through the US dollar. That adds cost and exposes the payment to dollar shortages, and providers often have to keep money pre-funded in each market, which ties up capital. Timon uses what’s often called a stablecoin sandwich, which means we don’t have to hold balances in each market ourselves. When I send money from Nigeria to M-Pesa, the naira is converted into USD stablecoins, which move across the border at any hour. A local liquidity provider in Kenya then accepts those stablecoins and pays out in shillings. Because we work with multiple providers on an ongoing basis, we can get the best available rate and avoid relying on any single one, and connecting each market to the same stablecoin bridge means we don’t need a deep direct market for every currency pair. That structure makes the liquidity problem far easier to manage. Without pre-funded balances to maintain, we can open new corridors faster and avoid locking up capital in every market we serve. Rates still depend on how deep local liquidity provider markets are, and regulatory requirements still apply in each market, but that is a much lighter constraint than funding each market ourselves. The next stage is direct exchange between African currencies, which is why we’re interested in local-currency stablecoins and in PAPSS’s African Currency Marketplace. As those markets deepen, more transactions can settle without going through the dollar.

How does Timon intend to complement PAPSS rather than compete with it? Could stablecoins serve as an underlying settlement mechanism for local-currency transactions processed through platforms such as PAPSS?

PAPSS and Timon work at different layers, so there’s little to compete over. PAPSS, created by Afreximbank, is building the rails and the currency marketplace that let African markets pay and exchange directly with each other. Timon builds the customer-facing products on top, the cards, accounts, and transfers that let individuals and businesses actually use their money across borders. Our approach is to plug into infrastructure like PAPSS rather than duplicate it, just as we work with local liquidity providers in each market instead of holding balances ourselves. On the second question, yes, we believe stablecoins could become that settlement layer. Today, we use USD stablecoins to bridge markets, which works but still keeps the dollar in the middle of every transaction. Local-currency stablecoins, such as naira- or shilling-backed ones, could let value settle directly between African currencies, and PAPSS’s African Currency Marketplace is already moving in that direction with stablecoin-based exchange. If those two develop together, a payment from Lagos to Nairobi could settle end to end in local currencies, with PAPSS providing the rails and Timon delivering it to the customer. Our time in the first cohort of the Afreximbank Accelerator Programme reinforced that view, and we plan to build alongside PAPSS as this infrastructure matures.

Which African currencies and markets does Timon currently cover, and what volume of cross-border transactions has the platform handled to date?

Timon has more than 100,000 users across 16 African countries, with Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa among our strongest markets. Our platform offers multi-currency settlement, cross-border transfers, virtual and physical cards, and other services designed to help customers access and use their money across markets. To date, we have processed approximately $50m in transaction volume, with monthly transaction volume currently exceeding $4m. We are focused on making our services useful to customers whose financial needs extend beyond a single market, while continuing to develop the product and infrastructure needed to support them.

What are the major regulatory challenges facing stablecoin-based cross-border payments in Africa, particularly regarding licensing, foreign exchange regulations, consumer protection and anti-money laundering compliance?

Honestly, the hardest part is that every market plays by different rules. Some countries have clear stablecoin regulation, some are still figuring it out, and one payment from Lagos to Nairobi can touch both. So you can’t build one model and copy it across the continent. What works in Nigeria might need a different licence or a different partner in Kenya. FX controls are the other big one. Many African countries keep a close eye on money going in and out, and stablecoins don’t get a pass, so every conversion and payout has to fit each country’s rules. KYC and consumer protection are similar. Customers want the same experience wherever they are, but the requirements change from market to market, which is why we do dedicated local KYC for local top-ups. If you’re funding your account in a market, you’re verified to that market’s standard. We handle this by working with licensed merchants of record and local partners in each market, including the liquidity providers who pay out in local currency. Every part of the transaction sits with someone properly licensed to do it. It’s slower than pretending one set of rules applies everywhere, but it’s the only way to build something that lasts. I do think the rules will get clearer and more aligned over time, and that’s what local-currency stablecoins and systems like PAPSS will need to really take off.

Given that stablecoins are largely dollar-backed and may deepen dollar dependence, how do you address concerns that their adoption could weaken African currencies instead of strengthening local currency markets?

It’s a fair concern, and I don’t think anyone building in this space should dismiss it. But it helps to separate the demand for dollars from the tools people use to get them. That demand was here long before stablecoins. When a currency loses value quickly, people look for ways to protect what they’ve earned, and they’ll find one whether it’s cash under the mattress, a domiciliary account or a stablecoin. Stablecoins didn’t create that need, and they can’t fix the conditions behind it. Where I think we can genuinely help African currencies is in how they relate to each other. Right now, many intra-African payments go through the dollar simply because there’s no better bridge, even when neither side wants dollars. We use USD stablecoins for that today because they’re the most practical option available, but we see them as the bridge, not the destination. Local-currency stablecoins, alongside systems like PAPSS, could let a naira settle directly into the West African CFA franc without the dollar in the middle, which would reduce reliance on the dollar for trade within Africa. So, the effect really depends on how these tools are used and how each market’s policy develops. We’d rather be part of that conversation with regulators than build around it, because the version that lasts supports African currencies rather than replacing them.

What key changes are needed in Africa’s financial infrastructure to create a unified payments market across the continent, and which major challenge should be addressed first?

There’s an old economic idea that explains a lot of this. The economist Williams Stanley Jevons called it the “double coincidence of wants”: the problem that trade happens only when both sides want what the other has at the same moment. Very few people want to swap naira for Malawian kwacha directly at any given time, so the market is thin, and everyone routes through the dollar. Krugman showed in 1980 that this is how a vehicle currency locks in, because the more people trade through it, the cheaper it gets. So the bottleneck to solve first is convertibility, and Asia offers a useful lesson. After the 1997 crisis, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand appointed specific banks to quote direct rates between their currencies, deliberately creating market makers for pairs the market wasn’t serving. They also built local-currency bond markets, which gave investors a reason to hold those currencies. Connecting their payment systems came later. What might work in Africa is a similar approach, with designated liquidity providers quoting direct rates on corridors like naira to kwacha, supported by central banks and institutions like Afreximbank. PAPSS pairing its payment system with the African Currency Marketplace is an important step in that direction, and local-currency stablecoins could make that exchange cheaper still. None of it works without stable macro policy, but once direct pairs beat the detour, the same loop that locked in the dollar can start working for African currencies.

Since joining Afreximbank’s Flagship Accelerator Programme, what progress has Timon made in securing partnerships, engaging regulators, attracting funding and advancing its pan-African expansion plans?

The biggest shift has been in who we’re talking to. Before the programme, most of our conversations were with card networks, liquidity providers and fintech partners. Afreximbank opened doors to a different tier, including trade finance institutions, central banks and regulatory contacts across several markets, and the wider Afreximbank ecosystem, including PAPSS. Those relationships take years to build on your own, and the programme compressed that. It also changed how we think about expansion. We support payments in 16+ African countries today and were planning to reach 40 soon, but the programme pushed us to focus on trade corridors rather than just adding countries. That’s a big part of why we’re looking to build more for businesses soon, aimed at SMEs moving money between African markets every day. Afreximbank is also investing in Timon, which matters beyond the capital itself. Having the continent’s trade bank behind us gives partners and regulators more confidence in what we’re building. Our priority now is turning these relationships into live products and growing market by market as customer demand and each regulator’s requirements allow.

The post ‘Stablecoins ease cross-border payment burden’ appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: FG targets wider health insurance coverage
description:
The Federal Government is seeking to expand health insurance coverage beyond 24 million Nigerians through increased government funding, compulsory enrolment for public sector workers and the extension of state-backed insurance schemes.
The Director of Health Planning, Research and Statistics at the
content:
The Federal Government is seeking to expand health insurance coverage beyond 24 million Nigerians through increased government funding, compulsory enrolment for public sector workers and the extension of state-backed insurance schemes.

The Director of Health Planning, Research and Statistics at the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Dr John Ovuoraye, said the government was working to address funding and awareness gaps that had limited the expansion of health insurance in the country.

Speaking during an interview on Arise News on Friday, Ovuoraye disclosed that the number of Nigerians covered by health insurance had increased from approximately 16 million to 24 million, attributing the growth to interventions introduced by the current administration.

He said the government was also working with state governors to increase financial commitments to healthcare financing and expand insurance coverage across the country.

According to him, President Bola Tinubu and the Nigeria Governors’ Forum had secured commitments from federal and state governments to contribute to healthcare funding.

“By that compact, it simply means that the Federal Government will be contributing to health, and the states will also be bringing in their money,” he said.

Ovuoraye explained that states were expected to establish their own health insurance schemes alongside the national programme following the establishment of the National Health Insurance Authority.

He, however, acknowledged that expanding coverage to more Nigerians would depend largely on the availability of funding, noting that insurance programmes required adequate financial backing to meet the healthcare needs of enrollees.

“Every insurance has a cash backing, which is financing at the back end,” he said.

He said the government was gradually moving towards compulsory health insurance enrolment for civil servants and public sector workers, with plans to extend the arrangement to other organised groups.

The government is also relying on the Basic Health Care Provision Fund to strengthen healthcare delivery and improve access to insurance services.

Ovuoraye said the fund receives one per cent of the Federation’s Consolidated Revenue Fund and is being deployed to support the rehabilitation and revitalisation of primary healthcare centres.

He explained that strengthening primary healthcare facilities was central to the government’s insurance expansion strategy because it would enable more enrollees to access medical services without making direct payments at the point of care.

The programme also includes free healthcare and delivery services for women at participating health facilities.

Ovuoraye disclosed that 172 local government areas were currently benefiting from the intervention, but said the government planned to extend it to additional communities, particularly those with high populations and significant maternal and newborn health challenges.

“We should not stop at 172. The country is large,” he said.

He added that the government was also working to extend health insurance coverage to vulnerable groups, including inmates in correctional facilities, as part of efforts to make healthcare more accessible.

Despite the increase in enrolment, Ovuoraye acknowledged that Nigeria remained far from achieving its desired level of health insurance coverage, given its population of more than 240 million.

He identified population growth, large household sizes and inadequate public awareness as factors that had previously slowed enrolment.

The government, he said, was introducing additional measures to reduce out-of-pocket healthcare expenditure and ensure more Nigerians could access medical services through insurance.

“We are making efforts, but we are not there yet,” he said.

title: Senegal: Alioune Ndao Warns Against Court Challenge To Faye’s Decree Over Risk Of Legal Precedent
description: Gambiaj.com – (DAKAR, SENEGAL) – A member of Senegal’s ruling PASTEF coalition, Alioune Ndao, has urged against challenging President Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye’s decree on the implementation of the 2026 Supplementary Finance Law before the Supreme Court, warning that an unsuccessful legal challe
content:
Gambiaj.com – (DAKAR, SENEGAL) – A member of Senegal’s ruling PASTEF coalition, Alioune Ndao, has urged against challenging President Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye’s decree on the implementation of the 2026 Supplementary Finance Law before the Supreme Court, warning that an unsuccessful legal challenge could establish a precedent strengthening the president’s authority.

Ndao, a former special prosecutor at the Court for the Repression of Illicit Enrichment (CREI) under former President Macky Sall, described the presidential decree as “manifestly illegal and unconstitutional” in a social media post.

Despite his criticism, the lawmaker argued that taking the matter to the Supreme Court would be counterproductive, as he believes the chances of the court overturning the decree are slim.

“Above all, do not file an appeal before the Supreme Court,” he cautioned.

His concern is that if the court upholds the decree, its decision could provide President Faye with legal jurisprudence that he could invoke to defend similar actions in the future, potentially expanding the executive’s room for manoeuvre in its dealings with the legislature.

“We must absolutely avoid giving the President the opportunity to have jurisprudence that he can brandish whenever necessary, as is already the case with the date of local elections,” Ndao wrote.

Rather than pursue a judicial challenge, the MP believes the president should be left to bear the political and social consequences of the decree.

He argued that responsibility for the decision rests exclusively with Faye, while defending the National Assembly’s handling of the supplementary budget.

“The National Assembly did its job correctly, in accordance with the law and the Constitution. That is what matters. Let us leave it at that,” he concluded.

Ndao’s position places particular emphasis on the potential long-term legal consequences of challenging the decree, rather than simply its immediate constitutionality, highlighting the institutional implications of the dispute within Senegal’s ruling camp.

title: NELFUND considers increase in ₦20,000 student upkeep
description:
…Sawyer says allowance under review, hints at possible changes



By Joseph Erunke, Abuja



The Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) is considering an increase in its ₦20,000 monthly upkeep allowance for students amid concerns that rising living costs have reduced its purchasing power.







The
content:
…Sawyer says allowance under review, hints at possible changes

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

The Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) is considering an increase in its ₦20,000 monthly upkeep allowance for students amid concerns that rising living costs have reduced its purchasing power.

The Managing Director of NELFUND, Akintunde Sawyer, disclosed this during an interview on TVC’s Beyond the Headlines, saying the allowance was under constant review.

Although he did not announce a new amount or timeline for any adjustment, Sawyer confirmed that the possibility of an increase was being considered.

“Are we considering it? Yes, of course. It’s under constant review,” he said.

The proposed review comes amid complaints by students that the current allowance is inadequate to meet the rising costs of feeding, transportation, accommodation and other basic needs.

Sawyer, however, said any increase would have to take into account the fund’s financial capacity and the need to sustain support for all eligible beneficiaries.

“What we need to do is plan it in such a way that it doesn’t put us in a situation where we can’t cater for the totality of the people that we need to cater for,” he said.

Beyond the proposed review, the NELFUND chief disclosed that President Bola Tinubu was considering an intervention to provide students with more substantial financial support to help them complete their academic programmes.

He did not provide details of the proposed intervention, including its scope, funding or implementation timeline.

“I know the President certainly is looking at intervening in a way that helps the students have more meaningful sustenance so that they can get through their courses,” Sawyer said.

He also hinted that changes could be introduced in the future, although he gave no definite commitment on when the review would be concluded.

“I suspect that if you watch this space, you’ll see some changes coming up in the future,” he added.

NELFUND’s proposed review comes as the Federal Government’s student loan scheme continues to expand, with millions of applications received from students seeking financial assistance for tertiary education.

According to figures provided by the fund, it has disbursed ₦180.5 billion in upkeep allowances since the scheme commenced in May 2024, while another ₦194.7 billion has been paid to tertiary institutions to cover tuition fees.

The combined disbursement of approximately ₦375.2 billion underscores the scale of the programme, which is intended to reduce financial barriers to tertiary education and help students remain in school.

The fund has also recorded more than 2.5 million applications and about 1.6 million loan transactions across 320 beneficiary institutions.

Despite the programme’s expansion, the adequacy of the monthly upkeep allowance remains a concern for beneficiaries who depend on it to meet their daily expenses.

For now, the ₦20,000 monthly allowance remains unchanged, pending any formal announcement by NELFUND or the Federal Government on a possible increase or additional intervention.

The post NELFUND considers increase in ₦20,000 student upkeep appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: S’African golfer, Kenyan chef arrested with 50kg cannabis in Lagos
description:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency has arrested a 37-year-old South African professional golfer, Grobler Henlo, and a 25-year-old Kenyan chef, Abubakar Njambi, over an alleged attempt to smuggle 50.40kg of a potent cannabis strain known as Loud into Nigeria.
The suspects were arrested at the M
content:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency has arrested a 37-year-old South African professional golfer, Grobler Henlo, and a 25-year-old Kenyan chef, Abubakar Njambi, over an alleged attempt to smuggle 50.40kg of a potent cannabis strain known as Loud into Nigeria.

The suspects were arrested at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Ikeja, Lagos, in October, according to a statement issued on Sunday by the NDLEA spokesperson, Femi Babafemi.

The agency said Henlo arrived in Lagos from South Africa aboard a South African Airways flight on October 11 and was intercepted at the Terminal 2 arrival hall.

A search of two travelling boxes in his possession reportedly led to the recovery of 46 parcels of Loud weighing 50.40kg.

The NDLEA said investigations revealed that although the boxes were with Henlo, they bore the luggage tags of Njambi, who had collected two other boxes bearing her tags from the airport conveyor belt and left.

“The swap of luggage tags was a deliberate ploy by the syndicate to frustrate the identification of ownership so that each courier could deny the boxes bearing his or her name if intercepted.

“During a preliminary interview, the golfer, who travelled in business class while his accomplice flew economy, said he was recruited by a South African associate identified as Shanel, who linked him with other members of the syndicate he never met in person.

“He said a driver picked him up from his home in South Africa, handed him four travelling boxes and took him to the airport, where he was instructed to meet the Kenyan lady and swap luggage tags with her. He claimed he was promised 5,000 South African rand upon successful delivery,” the statement read.

It added, “Further examination revealed that tracking devices had been installed on the travelling boxes as well as on his mobile phone, a feature also found in the bags abandoned by the American basketballer a month later, which shows how closely the cartels monitor their couriers and consignments.

“The passport biodata page of Abubakar Faiza Njambi, recovered from the golfer’s phone, was profiled and placed on the NDLEA watchlist, leading to her arrest at the departure boarding gate of the Lagos airport on Thursday, October 15, 2026, as she attempted to board a South African Airways flight to return to Kenya.

“The 25-year-old private chef told NDLEA operatives she was recruited by a man, adding that a friend in Kenya persuaded her to accept the offer of US$8,000 upon successful delivery of the consignment.

“She said she left Kenya for South Africa on October 4, stayed in a hotel for about a week, and met the golfer at the airport in South Africa on October 11, where he handed her two of the four boxes before they checked them in under their respective luggage tags.

“She claimed that on arrival in Lagos, she collected the two boxes bearing the golfer’s tags before a driver took her to a hotel in the Lekki area of Lagos.

“The claim tag of the two boxes bearing her name, which she abandoned at the airport, was recovered from her hand luggage, while both suspects identified each other during an identification parade.”

In a separate operation at the Lagos airport, NDLEA operatives on November 13 intercepted a consolidated consignment from the United Kingdom aboard an Allied Air flight.

The agency said the shipment contained 10 parcels of synthetic cannabinoids weighing 10.10kg, 27 packs of marshmallow weighing 318.80kg and precursor chemicals weighing a combined 34.55kg.

A freight agent, Sobowale Oladayo, was arrested when he presented himself to clear the consignment.

The consignee, identified as Kareem Issa, 35, also known as Ola, was arrested the following day when he arrived to collect the shipment at a logistics company’s premises in a grey Lexus 460 SUV.

The agency said Issa, a plumber who lives on Lagos Island, allegedly posed as a senior security official and routinely used a siren fitted to his vehicle when visiting the logistics company to collect consignments.

In Kaduna State, operatives arrested two men, Lawali Muhammad, 35, and Aliyu Mohammed, 30, in connection with 160 pieces of explosives intercepted along the Abuja-Kaduna Expressway at Jere on November 17.

The intended recipient, Mohammed, was arrested in a follow-up operation in Gusau, Zamfara State, the agency said.

Two other suspects were arrested along the same route with 6,900 tablets of tramadol, 20,000 tablets of diazepam and 25,000 tablets of Exol-5.

NDLEA operatives also recovered 627,500 capsules of tramadol weighing 21.50kg from a Hummer bus along the Zaria-Kano Expressway. The driver reportedly abandoned the vehicle and fled.

In Ogun State, a woman, Esther Ogundipe, was arrested on November 19 during a raid on a suspected drug joint at Eleweran, Abeokuta, with two locally made firearms and five live cartridges.

Two other women were arrested in Ilaro on November 17 with 7.4g of cocaine, 638g of cannabis and 5.9g of methamphetamine.

In Osun State, a 43-year-old man, Francis Oduke, was arrested along the Ikire-Ibadan Expressway with 359 bags of skunk weighing 4,627.7kg, allegedly concealed beneath a load of granite in a truck.

In neighbouring Ondo State, operatives intercepted a truck carrying 93 bags of cannabis weighing 1,045kg and heading to Kano State. The seizure was made along the Zango-Ado Expressway, Akure, on November 16.

Four suspects, Adamu Yerima, 19; Mohammed Mohammed, 19; Nura Mohammed, 25; and Usman Mohammed, were arrested in connection with the seizure.

The agency also reported arrests and drug recoveries in Edo, Katsina, Abia and Rivers states.

In Edo, Emmanuel Eze, 48, was arrested with 11 and a half bags of cannabis weighing 156kg at Aduwawa community, Benin City, on November 20.

In Katsina, Abbas Bello, 39, was arrested in the Gafai area on November 17 with 148 blocks of cannabis weighing 72kg, allegedly concealed in the boot of his white Honda Accord.

In Abia, operatives recovered 2kg of cannabis from a hole beneath the tiled floor of a shop belonging to a 25-year-old woman, Oluebube Innocent, at Amankwa Street, Obingwa Local Government Area, on November 18.

In Rivers, a 46-year-old physically challenged man, Peter Sunday, was arrested with 300g of cannabis during a raid in Eneka on November 17.

The agency also said its commands and formations across the country continued to conduct their War Against Drug Abuse sensitisation activities in schools, worship centres, workplaces and communities.

The activities included lectures for students and staff of Local Government Primary School, Ebute Ikorodu, Lagos; Government Girls Unity College, Birnin Kebbi; and Community Secondary School, Usa, Enugu Ezike.

The Ondo State Command also paid an advocacy visit to the Deji of Akure, Oba Aladetoyinbo Ogunlade Adelusi.

Commending officers of the affected commands, the NDLEA Chairman, Brig. Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa (retd.), said the arrests of the South African golfer and Kenyan chef, coming within the same period as that of the American basketballer, showed that international drug cartels were changing their couriers but retaining their methods.

“The two cases show a trend in which international drug cartels now recruit sportsmen and other professionals as couriers, in the hope that their profiles will shield them from scrutiny.

“The NDLEA has a clear message for such syndicates: no profession, passport or travel class will provide cover for drug trafficking through Nigeria’s ports of entry,” Marwa warned.

He urged officers at all ports of entry to remain vigilant and professional, while charging personnel across all commands to sustain the balance between drug supply reduction and demand reduction efforts, particularly the War Against Drug Abuse sensitisation campaigns in schools, workplaces, worship centres and communities.

title: One dies in three-truck crash on Lagos-Ibadan Expressway
description:
One person has died in a road accident after three trucks collided on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway in Ogun State.
The crash occurred at about 7.12am on Sunday in front of Ashabi Police Station, along the BHN axis, inbound to Lagos.
The spokesperson for the Ogun State Traffic Compliance and Enforcemen
content:
One person has died in a road accident after three trucks collided on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway in Ogun State.

The crash occurred at about 7.12am on Sunday in front of Ashabi Police Station, along the BHN axis, inbound to Lagos.

The spokesperson for the Ogun State Traffic Compliance and Enforcement Agency, Babatunde Akinbiyi, disclosed this in an accident report on Sunday.

Akinbiyi said the vehicles involved included a red FAW container truck with registration number AAA 150 YM, a white HOWO granite truck with registration number LSR 59 YN and another truck, which had been evacuated before TRACE operatives arrived.

He noted that four persons were involved in the accident, adding that one person died while no injuries were recorded.

“Four people were involved; one adult male died while no injuries were recorded,” he stated.

According to him, eyewitnesses attributed the crash to overspeeding.

“TRACE operatives controlled and managed traffic during the evacuation exercise to prevent secondary accidents,” Akinbiyi said.

He added that the victim’s corpse was evacuated to the Idera Hospital morgue, while the affected trucks were taken to the Motor Traffic Division of the police in Mowe.

Akinbiyi concluded that the road had been cleared and normal traffic movement restored.
