title: Relief as Lagos firefighters rescue 70-year-old woman from well
description:
The Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service has rescued a 70-year-old woman who fell into a 60-foot-deep well at Oworonshoki, in the Kosofe Local Government Area of the state.
The septuagenarian was rescued alive by firefighters from the Oworonshoki Fire Station following a distress call in the early ho
content:
The Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service has rescued a 70-year-old woman who fell into a 60-foot-deep well at Oworonshoki, in the Kosofe Local Government Area of the state.

The septuagenarian was rescued alive by firefighters from the Oworonshoki Fire Station following a distress call in the early hours of Sunday.

The Controller-General of the service, Margaret Adeseye, disclosed this in a statement on Sunday.

Adeseye stated that the incident occurred at 37 Abiola Street, Oworonshoki, adding that firefighters promptly responded to the distress call and successfully brought the woman out of the well.

She stated, “The Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service has rescued a 70-year-old woman who accidentally fell into a well about 60 feet deep at 37 Abiola Street, Oworonshoki, Kosofe LGA, Lagos.

“The Oworonshoki Fire Station promptly responded to the distress call in the early hours of Sunday, successfully rescuing the victim alive.”

She concluded that the victim was stabilised and handed over to her family.

“The operation was concluded after the septuagenarian was stabilised and handed over to her family,” Adeseye stated.

This is not the first time an open well accident has occurred in Lagos.

PUNCH Metro reported on October 20 that a man died while attempting to rescue a two-year-old child who fell into a domestic well at Abule Egba, Lagos State.

The Lagos State Emergency Management Agency, in a statement by its Permanent Secretary, Dr Olufemi Oke-Osanyintolu, said that the incident occurred at Paul Street, inward Agbe Road, Abule Egba.

Oke-Osanyintolu noted that the toddler, whose mother worked as a cleaner in the compound, accidentally fell into the well, prompting a resident from the community to descend in an attempt to save the child.

title: Beyond publications, Nigeria pushes university research commercialisation
description:
Nigeria’s universities are rich in research and innovation, but can fresh government funding, commercialisation initiatives and industry partnerships turn academic discoveries into market-ready products, jobs and solutions to national challenges, writes DEBORAH TOLU-KOLAWOLE
From medical technologie
content:
Nigeria’s universities are rich in research and innovation, but can fresh government funding, commercialisation initiatives and industry partnerships turn academic discoveries into market-ready products, jobs and solutions to national challenges, writes DEBORAH TOLU-KOLAWOLE

From medical technologies and agricultural innovations to artificial intelligence, engineering, and renewable energy, researchers across Nigerian institutions continue to explore solutions to the country’s challenges.

Yet, many of these discoveries struggle to move beyond academic publications, exhibitions and research competitions into commercial products capable of attracting investment, creating employment and improving people’s lives.

The gap between research and commercialisation has remained one of the longstanding weaknesses of Nigeria’s higher education and innovation ecosystem, raising questions about the ability of universities to translate intellectual capital into economic value.

Recognising the issue, the Federal Ministry of Education has renewed efforts to promote research commercialisation, innovation funding and stronger collaboration between tertiary institutions and industry.

In January 2026, Alausa inaugurated the Steering Committee and Policy Drafting Committee for the National Research-to-Commercialisation Policy, designed to establish a structured pathway for converting research conducted in universities, research institutes and specialised agencies into commercially viable products and services.

The initiative was informed by concerns that substantial investments in research had not translated into corresponding industrial and economic benefits.

According to the minister, too many research outcomes remained on university shelves instead of becoming solutions to national problems.

The proposed framework is expected to institutionalise collaboration among government, universities, industries and financing institutions, while strengthening incentives for innovation, entrepreneurship and intellectual property protection.

Alausa announced a N2bn provision in the 2026 budget to support the work of the Research, Innovation and Commercialisation Committee, alongside a N3bn operational budget for its activities. The government also announced a N50m Student Grant Venture Capital Initiative to support student-led enterprises in tertiary institutions, as well as institutional innovation grants for universities and research centres seeking to develop market-ready solutions.

The financial commitments are significant because research commercialisation often requires a different funding structure from conventional academic research.

While traditional research grants may support literature reviews, data collection, laboratory experiments and publication, commercialisation requires additional resources for product development, testing, intellectual property registration, regulatory compliance, manufacturing and market entry.

A researcher who develops a promising medical device, for instance, may need access to specialised laboratories, clinical testing facilities, engineering support and regulatory expertise before the technology can be deployed in hospitals.

Similarly, an agricultural innovation may require field trials, production facilities, distribution networks and partnerships with farmers and agro-processing companies before it can become commercially sustainable.

Without these additional investments, promising research may remain confined to prototypes, irrespective of its potential value to society.

Speaking on the issue, the Vice-Chancellor of Ahmadu Bello University, Prof Adamu Ahmed, said universities were increasingly being assessed not only by their academic publications but also by their ability to apply research, commercialise discoveries and translate knowledge into measurable impact.

“Our research must begin to generate income for our researchers, for the university, and for the wider society,” Ahmed said.

He described commercialisation as “not a distraction from scholarship but a higher expression of it”, arguing that universities needed practical frameworks to move their research patents and outputs into the marketplace.

Ahmed also identified what he called the “valley of death” – the difficult gap between invention and adoption – as a major challenge the university’s committee was expected to address.

A similar position was expressed by the then Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Administration) of the University of Ibadan, now Vice-Chancellor, Prof Peter Olapegba, in May 2026, when he urged Nigerian universities to prioritise entrepreneurship-driven research capable of solving societal problems and boosting the economy.

Olapegba, who spoke at a TETFund capacity-building workshop for early-career researchers, said research findings should address problems in host communities, while patented university innovations should move from laboratories to local markets.

He encouraged researchers to design projects around societal and industrial needs, develop intellectual property literacy and integrate entrepreneurship into teaching and learning.

Olapegba clarified that an entrepreneurial mindset did not mean every professor should become a trader. Rather, he urged researchers to see “the laboratory as a prototype factory, the department as an innovation hub, and the students as potential employers of labour and not just job seekers.”

At Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, a similar conversation took place in June 2026, when professors, research leaders and industry practitioners examined how academic work could be connected more directly to industry and national development.

Niran Oluwaranti, a Professor of Computer Science and Engineering and Director of Partnerships at the university, said the traditional emphasis on publications and academic points needed to give greater consideration to whether research was being adopted.

Oluwaranti said, “It should no longer be only about publishing papers and accumulating points. The question should increasingly become: who is adopting your research, and what value is it creating?”

He added that rigorous research did not automatically translate into usable products, stressing the need for continued engagement between universities and industry.

Christianah Elusiyan, a Professor of Natural Product Chemistry and Senior Research Fellow at OAU, also called for a change in the traditional orientation of academic work.

“The traditional orientation has largely been research, publication, citations and recognition,” she said. “This is a fundamental shift to let our research impact society, which is where it is needed. We need that reorientation.”

The university’s Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Research, Innovation and Development), Prof Akanni Akinyemi, said researchers should increasingly be challenged to explain how their work improved lives, solved problems and created value beyond the university.

“The future of universities will depend not only on rigour, but on their ability to connect knowledge to impact,” he said. “Research becomes more powerful when the marketplace, policymakers and society can actually use it.”

An industry practitioner, Akin Monehin, who addressed the OAU researchers, similarly warned that researchers should not focus only on publications, awards and citations.

“Organisations are struggling with problems whose solutions may already exist somewhere on your shelf,” he said, arguing that the challenge was often connecting existing knowledge with the people and organisations that needed it.

Recent initiatives announced by the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, suggest an attempt to change the relationship between academic research and national development.

One of the government’s strategies is the Research, Innovation and Commercialisation Committee, established by the Federal Ministry of Education in collaboration with the Tertiary Education Trust Fund.

The committee is intended to promote the uptake of research outputs, encourage collaboration between universities and private-sector organisations, and create pathways for moving discoveries from laboratories into the marketplace.

Its membership includes representatives of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group, Bank of Industry, Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, vice-chancellors and TETFund.

The approach is designed to bring together institutions with different but complementary capabilities. The government is also exploring partnerships with the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure to strengthen the link between universities and industrial production.

In August 2026, Alausa urged NASENI to establish stronger partnerships with universities through its proposed NASENI Campus, which is expected to connect researchers to advanced laboratories, prototyping facilities, industries and investment opportunities.

The minister said NASENI could help bridge the gap between academic research and commercial success by supporting patenting, connecting researchers with venture capital and facilitating the creation of spin-off companies.

NASENI Chief Executive Officer, Khalil Suleiman, said the proposed campus, located within a 100-hectare free trade zone, was being developed as an integrated environment where researchers, professors, prototyping facilities, industries and commercialisation opportunities could operate together.

The Vice-Chancellor of Bayero University, Kano, Prof Haruna Musa, also disclosed that two research projects from the institution had reached the final stage of NASENI’s research commercialisation grant process.

They included a reusable sanitary pad project and the commercial production of sweet potato-based starch derivatives.

The projects illustrate the potential of university research to address practical needs in healthcare and agriculture, although their eventual success will depend on further development, financing, production and market adoption.

Another component of the government’s strategy is the introduction of the Tertiary Institutions National Laureate Prize, an annual N365m initiative announced by Alausa in August.

The award is designed to recognise outstanding undergraduate dissertations, master’s theses and doctoral research with commercial potential or clear industrial and developmental applications.

It covers six thematic areas: Engineering and Technology; Medicine and Health Sciences; Arts and Social Sciences; Agriculture; Law; and Teaching Innovation.

The government also announced the Dr Stella Adadevoh Prize for Medicine and Medical Innovation in honour of the late Nigerian physician who played a significant role in the country’s response to the 2014 Ebola outbreak.

Alausa said the prize was intended to establish a national platform for recognising academic excellence and encouraging young researchers to develop solutions to Nigeria’s challenges.

“Scholarship matters. Research matters. Innovation matters. Intellectual excellence deserves a prominent place in our national consciousness,” he said during the unveiling.

The minister added that the initiative was not simply about celebrating academic achievement but encouraging research that could translate into commercial ventures, industrial applications and practical solutions.

“We want Nigerian students to understand that there is honour in scholarship, opportunity in innovation and national recognition for intellectual excellence,” he said.

The selection process is expected to begin at the institutional level before progressing to regional and national assessments, with professional bodies and experts participating in the evaluation.

The prize is also expected to work with the Nigeria Education Repository and Databank, NERD, to strengthen the documentation, verification, preservation and accessibility of academic research.

The National Laureate Prize could encourage students to approach academic research differently, particularly if the selection process rewards originality, practical application and the potential to address identifiable societal problems.

The Nigeria Education Repository and Databank is another initiative expected to support the government’s research and innovation agenda.

Although primarily established as a national digital repository for academic records and research outputs, the platform could become an important part of the infrastructure required to identify, preserve and make Nigerian intellectual work accessible.

Its contribution, however, will depend on how effectively research records are connected to commercialisation institutions, intellectual property services and potential investors. A repository is not itself a commercialisation mechanism, and making research available does not automatically provide the financing, technical expertise or industrial partnerships needed to turn it into a product.

The government will also need to ensure that researchers’ intellectual property rights are protected when their work is made accessible through the platform.

The government’s commercialisation ambition is also receiving support through the University Innovation Pods (UniPods, being implemented in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme and TETFund.

The national rollout was flagged off on April 7, 2026, with the launch of an artificial intelligence-focused UniPod at the University of Lagos.

The first cohort, backed by more than N30bn in public investment, spans six geopolitical zones. The specialised facilities include agriculture and food systems at Benue State University; resilience and recovery at the University of Maiduguri; manufacturing and trade at Michael Okpara University of Agriculture; green and blue economy at the University of Uyo; mining technology and resource innovation at Nasarawa State University; and industrial and government technology at Ahmadu Bello University.

The facilities are intended to provide spaces where students, researchers, engineers, entrepreneurs and industry practitioners can work together to develop practical solutions.

Speaking at the launch, TETFund Executive Secretary, Sonny Echono, said, “These innovation Pods/Hubs are not just buildings, but they are collision spaces where scientists and innovators meet the engineers, where students meet the mentors, and where the raw idea meets the industrial transformation.”

UNDP Nigeria Resident Representative, Elsie Attafuah, said, “This is not about innovation hubs – it is about building a system.”

She added that Nigeria needed to move from fragmented interventions to coordinated, investment-backed platforms capable of supporting enterprise, jobs and long-term economic transformation.

The partnership has also set specific targets. Under a memorandum of understanding signed by TETFund and UNDP in December 2025, the two institutions aim to activate eight University Innovation Pods and one Polytechnic Pod, upgrade more than nine additional innovation facilities, establish or strengthen between 15 and 20 technology transfer offices, equip more than 500,000 students and researchers with digital and innovation skills, support between 1,500 and 2,000 university-linked start-ups, and commercialise 5,000 research outputs. These are programme targets, not completed achievements.

The facilities could be particularly important in addressing infrastructure limitations facing researchers in many Nigerian universities.

Access to specialised equipment, prototyping facilities, testing laboratories and technical mentors can determine whether an academic idea progresses beyond the experimental stage.

For instance, a researcher developing an agricultural processing machine may require access to engineering equipment to refine the prototype, while a student working on an artificial intelligence application may need computing infrastructure, technical mentorship and opportunities to test the product with potential users.

The UniPods could provide some of these opportunities within university environments.

Nevertheless, the government and its development partners will need to demonstrate that the facilities are adequately equipped, maintained and accessible to researchers beyond their immediate host institutions.

Their effectiveness should also be measured by the number of viable products developed, start-ups established, patents registered, industry partnerships secured and innovations adopted by consumers.

One of the issues that could determine the success of the government’s research agenda is intellectual property protection.

Researchers may develop valuable technologies but lack the legal and commercial knowledge required to protect their inventions or negotiate agreements with companies interested in using them.

In some cases, uncertainty over ownership can discourage researchers from collaborating with private-sector organisations or sharing their discoveries with potential investors.

Recognising this challenge, the Federal Government has also intensified engagement with the World Intellectual Property Organisation to strengthen Nigeria’s intellectual property ecosystem.

In June 2026, Vice-President Kashim Shettima met with a WIPO delegation led by its Director-General, Daren Tang, to discuss ways of converting Nigeria’s intellectual property into financial assets.

The engagement followed the Federal Executive Council’s approval of the National Intellectual Property Policy and Strategy in November 2025.

Shettima said Nigeria needed an intellectual property system that served both inventors and investors, researchers and entrepreneurs.

He stated, “The countries that will lead this century are those able to create, protect, commercialise, and scale intellectual assets.”

For the education sector, the implications are considerable.

Universities will need functional technology transfer offices, intellectual property specialists and clear guidelines governing the ownership and sharing of revenue generated from discoveries developed with public funding.

Researchers must also understand the difference between publishing their findings and protecting inventions that could have commercial value.

Without such safeguards, promising discoveries could be commercialised without adequate benefits accruing to their original developers or institutions.

Despite the various initiatives, the challenge of converting Nigerian research into commercial products remains considerable.

One major issue is the sustainability of funding.

Research commercialisation can take several years, particularly in sectors such as medicine, biotechnology, engineering and agriculture, where products may require extensive testing and regulatory approval.

Consequently, annual grants and research prizes may not be sufficient to support innovations through every stage of development.

The government will need to establish predictable financing arrangements that accommodate different stages of innovation, from initial research and prototyping to product testing, manufacturing and market expansion.

The N50m Student Grant Venture Capital Initiative, for example, could support early-stage student businesses, but its impact will depend on the number of beneficiaries, the size of individual grants and whether successful ventures can access further investment.

The N2bn and N3bn allocations announced for research commercialisation will also require transparent reporting to establish how much has actually been released, how it has been spent and what results have been achieved.

Another concern is the relationship between universities and private-sector organisations.

While Nigerian universities have researchers and intellectual resources, companies may be reluctant to invest in technologies that have not been sufficiently tested or whose commercial prospects remain uncertain.

This makes the roles of institutions such as NASENI, TETFund, the Bank of Industry and the Research, Innovation and Commercialisation Committee particularly important.

They could help reduce the risks associated with early-stage innovations by providing technical support, facilitating partnerships and connecting researchers with investors.

The Federal Government will also need to ensure that commercialisation does not undermine the academic responsibilities of universities or restrict access to research findings that have important public health, agricultural or social benefits.

The objective should be to establish a system in which commercial interests and public welfare can coexist.

One development drawing attention to this renewed push is the emergence of GenScan AI, an innovation by Nigerian researcher Mary-Brenda Akoda, which won the 2026 Nigeria Prize for Science and Innovation organised by Nigeria LNG.

The emergence of GenScan AI provides a useful starting point for understanding the opportunities and challenges confronting Nigeria’s research ecosystem.

Akoda’s innovation was selected as the winner of the 2026 Nigeria Prize for Science and Innovation after competing against 236 other entries.

GenScan AI’s recognition raises an important question about the future of locally developed technologies: how can Nigeria ensure that promising innovations do not end with awards and public recognition but progress into products and services that can be deployed at scale?

Meanwhile, it is worth pointing out that GenScan AI was not originally developed at a Nigerian university. Akoda’s research originated at Imperial College London, where she completed postgraduate research in artificial intelligence and machine learning. She disclosed that the work received support from Innovate UK and UK Research and Innovation, as well as the NHS Clinical Entrepreneur Programme.

Its recognition in Nigeria therefore demonstrates the potential of Nigerian innovators and the value of international research collaboration, rather than constituting evidence that the technology emerged from the country’s university research system.

At the public presentation of the prize, Akoda explained that the technology, known as GenScan AI, uses artificial intelligence to reconstruct diagnostic-quality magnetic resonance imaging pictures from a fraction of the data normally required.

She said it could reduce a 20-minute scan to about two minutes, while an hour-long scan could be completed in approximately six minutes, without requiring hospitals to purchase new scanners.

According to her, the technology was developed after a personal experience involving an elderly relative who suffered a stroke but encountered delays in accessing an MRI scan.

Akoda said the system had been evaluated using thousands of MRI images and that a blinded assessment by a consultant radiologist at Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust in the United Kingdom found the images diagnostically equivalent to conventional scans in the cases assessed.

For Nigeria’s research commercialisation agenda, the recognition of GenScan AI represents an opportunity to demonstrate what can happen when scientific discoveries receive institutional backing and access to international research and innovation networks.

However, the circumstances surrounding the technology also offer an important lesson. Although GenScan AI won Nigeria’s 2026 science prize, its research originated at Imperial College London and received support from UK research and innovation institutions. The experience illustrates the importance of sustained research support, international collaboration and access to specialised expertise.

It also shows why Nigeria’s universities need stronger connections with international research institutions, technology companies, healthcare providers and investors.

For GenScan AI, the immediate task will be to translate the recognition and government support into wider clinical validation, appropriate regulatory processes, investment and eventual deployment.

Ultimately, the success of Alausa’s research agenda will depend on whether the government can build an ecosystem that supports researchers long after their discoveries have attracted public attention.

The number of research papers published, prizes awarded, innovation hubs established and grants announced will provide useful indicators of activity, but they will not, on their own, demonstrate commercial success.

More meaningful measures will include the number of patents secured, products developed, technologies adopted by industries, start-ups established, private investments attracted, jobs created and public services improved through locally developed innovations.

Nigeria has considerable intellectual resources across its universities, polytechnics and research institutions. What has often been missing is a dependable system for connecting those resources with finance, industry, technology and markets.

From the National Laureate Prize and NERD to the Research, Innovation and Commercialisation Committee, NASENI partnerships and University Innovation Pods, the Federal Government is attempting to establish that connection.

But the real test will be whether discoveries such as GenScan AI can become the beginning of a sustained pipeline of Nigerian innovations that move from research laboratories into hospitals, factories, farms, businesses and other areas of everyday life.

If the initiatives are adequately funded, transparently implemented and supported by industry, Nigeria’s universities could become more than centres for producing graduates and academic publications. They could become important sources of technology, enterprise, employment and solutions to national development challenges.

The post Beyond publications, Nigeria pushes university research commercialisation appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Ex-FUTA VC donates books, cash to Lagos pupils
description:
A former Vice-Chancellor of the Federal University of Technology, Akure, Peter Adeniyi, has donated educational materials and N50,000 each to 10 indigent pupils in Lagos State to support their education.
The beneficiaries, selected from three public secondary schools in the Ojokoro area of the state
content:
A former Vice-Chancellor of the Federal University of Technology, Akure, Peter Adeniyi, has donated educational materials and N50,000 each to 10 indigent pupils in Lagos State to support their education.

The beneficiaries, selected from three public secondary schools in the Ojokoro area of the state, received the support on Wednesday during the Education Support Programme Presentation Day organised by the Professor Peter Olufemi Adeniyi Foundation.

The schools are Ijaiye Ojokoro Senior High School, Ijaiye Ojokoro Senior College and Ijaiye Housing Estate Senior College.

Other dignitaries at the event included the founder’s wife, Modupe Adeniyi; a Board of Trustees member, Ademola Ayodele; the Principal of Ijaiye Ojokoro Senior High School, Ogunleye; the Principal of Ijaiye Ojokoro Senior College, Oyefunke; and the Vice Principal of Ijaiye Ojokoro Senior High School, Otiniyi.

Speaking at the event, Adeniyi said the intervention was aimed at preventing poverty and other socioeconomic challenges from disrupting the education of pupils from financially disadvantaged backgrounds.

He noted that some pupils struggled to afford basic educational materials, transportation costs and other necessities required for regular school attendance.

According to him, such challenges could undermine academic performance, weaken pupils’ motivation and, in some cases, force promising pupils to abandon their education.

He said these concerns informed the foundation’s decision to establish the Education Support Programme to assist indigent pupils in public secondary schools.

The beneficiaries received textbooks, school supplies and cash to ease the financial burden on them and their families.

Adeniyi acknowledged that the number of beneficiaries was small compared with the scale of educational needs in society but expressed optimism that the intervention would make a meaningful difference.

“Every great journey begins with a step. We regard today’s intervention as one such step, and we hope that, with sustained support and stronger partnerships, the programme will grow to benefit many more deserving students,” he said.

He urged the beneficiaries to remain disciplined, hardworking and committed to their studies, stressing that education should go beyond passing examinations and obtaining certificates.

“Knowledge without character can become a danger rather than a blessing. Our society needs not only academically accomplished individuals, but also people of integrity, compassion, courage, humility and a genuine commitment to the common good,” he said.

The former vice-chancellor said the foundation’s broader mission included improving educational opportunities, strengthening learning environments, supporting teachers, developing school libraries and promoting community participation in education.

He added that the government alone could not meet every educational need, noting that families, communities, businesses, philanthropic organisations and individuals also had important roles to play.

Adeniyi said the foundation would continue to complement government efforts through targeted interventions, advocacy and partnerships aimed at achieving sustainable educational development.

He appreciated the Lagos State education authorities, school administrators, teachers, donors and partners for supporting the programme, particularly acknowledging Jana Heemskerk for her contributions to the foundation’s educational initiatives.

Also speaking, the foundation’s Programmes Manager, Temitope Odetoye, said the beneficiaries were selected from 29 nominated pupils through a rigorous process.

He explained that the final 10 were selected based on their Junior Secondary School qualifying examination results and verification of their parents’ or guardians’ financial status.

Odetoye said the foundation, which focuses on innovation, research advocacy and scholarships, designed the exercise as a pilot phase for Senior Secondary School 1 pupils, with plans to extend the sponsorship to the tertiary level.

Reacting on behalf of the state government, the Tutor-General/Permanent Secretary, Olufunke Oyetola, represented by the District Officer, Esther Oni, thanked the foundation for supporting the pupils.

She urged the beneficiaries to make effective use of the assistance for their academic growth and development.

The post Ex-FUTA VC donates books, cash to Lagos pupils appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: On food inflation and agriculture
description: Food, a major and the first basic need for human existence, remains one of the main items of concern in Nigeria’s developmental trajectory. Each time inflation figures are released by the National Bureau of Statistics, food inflation figures usually show up like a cancerous sore. But we move on as i
content:
Food, a major and the first basic need for human existence, remains one of the main items of concern in Nigeria’s developmental trajectory. Each time inflation figures are released by the National Bureau of Statistics, food inflation figures usually show up like a cancerous sore. But we move on as if it does not matter, yet it is one of the figures used in poverty calculation. The leadership of a country that cannot feed its populace should bury itself in shame, even though agriculture is better handled by the private sector.

Policy, design, and the push or commitment to food self-sufficiency should come from the government. The priority the government gives agriculture would serve as an impetus for the private sector to develop the agricultural sector. Nigeria is blessed with abundant human and non-human resources that can enable any serious, people-centred, and non-corrupt government to govern at an exceptional level. Beyond abundant mineral resources underground, the surface soil is rich in everything needed for all kinds of plants to grow. If an asphalt-laid road is abandoned for just three months, grass would emerge from any available crack and grow luxuriantly within weeks. How can a country with such blessings go hungry?

 It is time the government is intentional about agriculture. It is not going to be agricultural reform but agricultural revolution, as there seems to be no agricultural policy on the ground. Everything relating to agricultural production seems to be in the cooler. There are ministries that, if mentioned, the principal actor, the Minister, is immediately recognised; not so with agriculture. The “actor” seems not active. I listened to a television programme where students were asked to mention the names of ministers of “top” ministries like works, education, health and social welfare, finance, agriculture and labour. None of the students remembered the name of the Minister for Agriculture! One of the organisers said the Minister of Agriculture was probably a silent achiever. The ministry deserves an aggressive achiever.

 Whenever the government talked of releasing grains from the national reserves, I felt proud until I learnt that what we have in the reserves is imported grains. For many years, we have observed that concentration on oil production and financial rewards from the sector has diverted the attention of the government and the non-public sector away from other sectors that can equally provide income or revenues and, more importantly, generate employment, like agriculture, which was hitherto the mainstay of the Nigerian economy. Importation of food items into Nigeria should be limited to manufactured items; we do not have the raw materials, and that too should be a temporary issue.

 Just recently, a report emerged that the Republic of Benin has regained its top spot as a main producer and exporter of cotton.  Nigeria was a major exporter of cotton during the First Republic. Albeit the Nigerian government’s concern presently should be how to become self-sufficient in the production of agricultural produce we currently import. This is to reduce our dependence on other countries for food and industrial raw materials.

 The agricultural revolution required must be championed by the Federal Government through policy formulation, general coordination, and consistent/sustainable funding.

 The last time Nigeria had an agricultural revolution scheme, like President Shehu Shagari’s Green Revolution, it was more sloganeering than practical action. Now, we need to be practical in defining what we want to achieve; when, in terms of timeline; the modus operandi; and the deliverables. We may need to concentrate production firstly on some products, before moving to others and many others within the food crop gangre and the cash crop sector. Many models of agricultural revolution can be adopted or adapted around the world.

 India and China are the most populous countries in the world, with each boasting over one billion citizens. They are self-sufficient in food and also export food to other countries. Nigeria, with a population less than one-quarter of the population of these two giants, imports food from around the world. The Green Revolution of India in the mid-to-late 1960s helped India shift from food shortages and heavy grain imports to food grain self-sufficiency. High-yielding varieties of rice and wheat were introduced with the use of chemical fertilizers, irrigation and use of modern farming machinery.

 Other major agricultural revolutions in India are White Revolution, or Operation Flood, which boosted milk and dairy production through the establishment of dairy cooperatives. The Blue Revolution led to the expansion of fisheries and aquaculture, while the Yellow Revolution resulted in increased oilseed production, and the Golden Revolution focused on horticulture, fruits, and honey. The Silver and Pink Revolutions were carried out to take care of poultry (silver), pharmaceuticals, prawns, and onions (pink); and Evergreen Revolution was an omnibus action geared toward overall productivity, growth and ecological sustainability.

 China has less than 10 per cent arable land for agriculture but a massive population. The government’s programmes on food for all were taken by the jugular and executed with honest determination. The Maoist revolution involved land reform and collective farms, expanded irrigation, and double-cropping in the early 1950s. The post-1978 Household Responsibility System, which replaced communes with household contracts and market incentives, sparked rapid output growth in all aspects of agriculture and shifted diets towards more vegetables, meat, and dairy. China is now undergoing a modern high-tech transformation. This involves land consolidation, greenhouses, drones, mechanization, and high agrotechnology investments.

 Reports show that Israel’s agricultural revolution took the shape of necessity-driven, high-tech farming combined with cooperative organisation and strict water management. The model involved drip irrigation, wastewater reclamation, natural infrastructure, and desalination methods, as well as Cooperative Farming Models, the type that was introduced in the Western Region during Chief Obafemi Awolowo’s leadership.

 Agriculture accounted for over 60 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product and about 85 per cent of foreign exchange earnings of Nigeria at independence in 1960. These were derived from cash crops from the regions. Cocoa was from the Western Region, groundnut and cotton from the Northern Region, and Palm oil from the Eastern Region. The crude oil boom of the 1970s nearly eliminated agriculture’s importance in terms of income and job opportunities, as the sector’s dominance declined steeply.

 To reverse the decline, a number of Federal Government interventions were taken. National Accelerated Food Production Programme was launched in 1972; Operation Feed the Nation in 1976; the River Basin Development Authority in 1978; and the Green Revolution Programme in 1980. Some other minor initiatives also took place. The programmes could not succeed because of inconsistent funding, poor agricultural infrastructure, policy reversal and the main impediment to national progress – corruption. The recent framework, the National Agricultural Technology and Innovation Policy, which focuses on commercialisation of agriculture and boosting local production, does not carry the required revolutionary measures that the agricultural sector deserves today.

 Nigeria cannot continue to rely on food importation to feed itself or to stock its reserves. We have the land, we have the human resources, and the technology is available, but we are looking for sustainable financing and policy consistency. Nigeria can adopt the Indian model of sub-sector revolution. In this connection, the focus should first be on food production to bring down food inflation and reduce importation of those food items. There must be coordination among the three tiers of government, as State governments own the land while the federal government has the policy and funding. Coordination at the local government level is equally imperative.

The post On food inflation and agriculture appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Suspected cult clash leaves two dead in Osun
description:
The Osun State Police Command has confirmed the deaths of two persons in separate attacks involving suspected rival cult groups that occurred between Thursday and Saturday in Ilesa, Osun State.
But sources in the Isokun area of Ilesa, where the first killing occurred, told our correspondent on Sunda
content:
The Osun State Police Command has confirmed the deaths of two persons in separate attacks involving suspected rival cult groups that occurred between Thursday and Saturday in Ilesa, Osun State.

But sources in the Isokun area of Ilesa, where the first killing occurred, told our correspondent on Sunday, on condition of anonymity for security reasons, that two men were killed there.

They identified the deceased as Bobo and White.

They said the duo were suspected members of the Eiye confraternity, adding that the assailants rode on a motorcycle and arrived at the scene around 9:45pm on Thursday.

A resident, identified as Titi, said in a telephone interview with PUNCH Metro on Sunday that the assailants shot the deceased in the head and injured one other man.

“The incident happened at about 9:45pm on Thursday, very close to where one Alafin sells weed in Isokun, Ilesa. The deceased are popularly known as Bobo and White. Both are members of the Eiye Confraternity, and the other guy in critical condition does not belong to any cult group.

“Before the attackers arrived, there was a misunderstanding among some people around Alafin’s joint. Suddenly, some people came on a motorcycle and took advantage of the situation on the ground and hit their targets at close range. They shot the deceased in the head.

“The reason behind this attack is not clear. While some people said old rifts between the Eiye and KK confraternity in the town were the cause, some said it is politically motivated because the father of one of the two men killed is a serving councillor in one of the wards in Ilesa West,” Titi said.

In the second attack, two individuals identified as P. A and Omo Mummy were allegedly shot around Omi-Eran Atijo, in Ilesa, around 8:15pm on Saturday.

It was, however, learnt that one of them later died as a result of injuries sustained in the attack.

A source close to the scene said those who carried out the attack shot the duo at close range before fleeing the area.

The cause of the current rift could not be immediately established, as the return of hostilities involving suspected cultists, at a time when normalcy was gradually returning to different parts of the state ravaged by extrajudicial killings before the last August 15 governorship poll, has continued to raise concerns in security circles.

When contacted for confirmation, the Osun State Police Command Public Relations Officer, Abiodun Ojelabi, said one person each was killed in the Isokun and Omi-Eran incidents, blaming the development on rival cult groups.

“In the Isokun incident, one person was killed, not two. In the Omi-Eran incident, one life was also lost. Police operatives were informed about the incident at Omi-Eran around 7:10am this morning. Maybe it happened earlier.

“We have mobilised to the area. Normalcy has returned, and we are going after the perpetrators. The killings are cult-related,” Ojelabi said.

The post Suspected cult clash leaves two dead in Osun appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Moniepoint disburses $700m to MSMEs, targets six regional offices
description:
Moniepoint Microfinance Bank has disclosed that it disbursed over $700m in loans to micro, small and medium enterprises in 2025, as it unveiled plans to establish six regional offices across Nigeria to expand financial services and support business growth.
The bank disclosed this in a statement issu
content:
Moniepoint Microfinance Bank has disclosed that it disbursed over $700m in loans to micro, small and medium enterprises in 2025, as it unveiled plans to establish six regional offices across Nigeria to expand financial services and support business growth.

The bank disclosed this in a statement issued on Sunday following the inauguration of its North Central regional headquarters in Abuja, the first of six offices planned across the country.

The expansion comes amid persistent difficulties in accessing formal credit among Nigerian small businesses, despite their contribution to employment and economic activity.

In an October 2026 research report by the Development Bank of Nigeria, it was disclosed that commercial bank lending to small-scale enterprises accounted for just 0.38 per cent of total private sector credit in 2025, compared with 27.04 per cent in 1992.

According to the latest statement, Moniepoint disbursed more than $700m, equivalent to approximately N1tn, to MSMEs last year, with 75 per cent of the beneficiaries accessing formal business credit for the first time.

“In 2025, Moniepoint disbursed over $700m (about N1tn) in loans to micro, small and medium enterprises. For three out of four of those borrowers, it was the first formal business credit they had ever accessed,” the statement read.

The bank said the lending programme formed part of its efforts to address financing constraints facing small businesses and expand access to financial services.

It disclosed that the Abuja headquarters, located on Dar-es-Salaam Street, Wuse 2, would serve as the operational hub for the North Central region.

The facility was inaugurated by Vice-President, Kashim Shettima, represented by the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele.

Speaking at the ceremony, Shettima commended Moniepoint’s investment in Nigeria and its contribution to financial inclusion and business development.

“This investment aligns with the Federal Government’s priorities of financial and economic inclusion, agricultural development, and affordable financing for businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises,” the Vice-President said.

“These priorities are also connected. When a small business can receive payments reliably, keep proper records and obtain suitable financing, it has a better chance of expanding, employing more people and contributing to national prosperity.”

The bank disclosed that additional regional offices would be established in Kano, Kaduna, Port Harcourt, Ekiti and Ibadan.

It explained that the facilities would provide physical access to financial services, strengthen customer relationships and create employment opportunities in their host communities.

“With Abuja now open, regional offices in Kano, Kaduna, Port Harcourt, Ekiti and Ibadan are to follow. Each will serve as a base for its own region, and each will create new jobs within its host community.

“Together, the six offices will give Moniepoint a permanent physical footprint across key regions of the country, built on a network that already reaches all 774 local government areas,” the statement read.

The Managing Director of Moniepoint Microfinance Bank, Babatunde Olofin, said the expansion would complement the company’s digital banking infrastructure.

“Today, we are expanding beyond digital to give every Moniepoint customer a welcoming space to walk into for face-to-face support, and also to have contact with our business relationship managers,” Olofin said.

“By bringing our services closer to you, we are making banking more convenient, reliable and trustworthy than ever before. This is just the beginning. We plan to open more locations across additional states as we bring even better services closer to you.”

According to the bank, its services currently reach more than 30 million businesses and individuals, while its agency banking network and point-of-sale terminals cover all 774 local government areas.

It added that it had expanded its physical service network to more than 600 centres nationwide in 2026.

In a goodwill message, the Chairman of the Senate Committee on Banking, Insurance and Other Financial Institutions, Mukhail Abiru, commended the bank’s contribution to digital payments and MSME financing.

“Moniepoint has distinguished itself through its contribution to digital payments, financial inclusion and the growth of MSMEs,” Abiru said.

The post Moniepoint disburses $700m to MSMEs, targets six regional offices appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Plateau school burnt, residents suspect bandits
description:
The Government Secondary School, Masharkut, in the Butura District of the Bokkos Local Government Area of Plateau State, has been burnt down following a fire outbreak on Sunday afternoon.
The Chairman of Bokkos Local Government Area, Amalau Samuel Amalau, confirmed the incident to PUNCH Metro in Jos
content:
The Government Secondary School, Masharkut, in the Butura District of the Bokkos Local Government Area of Plateau State, has been burnt down following a fire outbreak on Sunday afternoon.

The Chairman of Bokkos Local Government Area, Amalau Samuel Amalau, confirmed the incident to PUNCH Metro in Jos, the state capital, when contacted on Sunday.

“It’s true that the school building was set ablaze. It happened today,” the chairman said.

Asked whether terrorists had set the building ablaze, Amalau said the cause of the fire and those responsible could not yet be ascertained.

“How will I know? We only saw the school on fire. We cannot ascertain for now what it is and who is responsible. It happened today,” he said.

The incident reportedly caused panic among residents of the community after smoke was sighted rising from the school premises shortly after church service.

Some members of the community have, however, blamed the fire incident on bandits, who they said had been operating in the area.

A resident, Daniel Bwehfa, said residents initially noticed smoke coming from the school before discovering, about 30 minutes later, that the building was on fire.

According to him, the incident raised concerns among residents, who reportedly suspected that the school premises had been used as a temporary shelter by some individuals.

Bwehfa alleged that some suspected bandits had been using the school premises as a sleeping place, claiming that people were often seen gathering within the compound in the evenings.

He, however, did not provide further details about the identities of those allegedly seen around the school or establish whether they were responsible for the fire.

“Some strangers whom we suspect to be bandits have been coming to that school. We don’t know their mission. This has been a source of concern to community members. If they are not the people who set the school on fire, who else might have done that?” Bwehfa wondered.

The latest incident has heightened concerns over the safety of public institutions and educational facilities in communities affected by insecurity in parts of Bokkos LGA.

Efforts to reach security operatives for confirmation, including the spokesperson for the Plateau State Police Command, Alabo Alfred, were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report.

The post Plateau school burnt, residents suspect bandits appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Ex-convict nabbed in Oyo over Lagos vehicle theft
description:
Operatives of the Lagos State Police Command have arrested a 34-year-old ex-convict, Adams Victor, in Ibadan, Oyo State, over alleged vehicle theft.
Two vehicles suspected to have been stolen were recovered in the process.
The command disclosed this in a statement by its Police Public Relations Offi
content:
Operatives of the Lagos State Police Command have arrested a 34-year-old ex-convict, Adams Victor, in Ibadan, Oyo State, over alleged vehicle theft.

Two vehicles suspected to have been stolen were recovered in the process.

The command disclosed this in a statement by its Police Public Relations Officer, Abimbola Adebisi, on Sunday.

Adebisi noted that the suspect was arrested following an investigation into a vehicle theft case reported in Lagos in May 2026.

She added that the operatives extended their investigation beyond Lagos to Ibadan, where Victor was apprehended.

The recovered vehicles were a 2008 Toyota Corolla, number plate EPE 594 KR, and a 1999 Toyota Sienna, number plate AGL 632 KU.

According to the statement, preliminary investigation revealed that the suspect had previously been convicted of offences relating to criminal activities.

“Undeterred by the complexities of the investigation, the operatives pursued available leads, intensified intelligence gathering and extended their operations beyond Lagos State to Ibadan, Oyo State, where the suspect, one Adams Victor, male, 34 years, was apprehended and two vehicles suspected to have been stolen were recovered,” the statement partly read.

The Commissioner of Police, Lagos State Command, Fatai Tijani, commended the operatives for their diligence and determination in pursuing the investigation across state boundaries.

Tijani assured residents that the command would sustain efforts to track down criminal networks, recover stolen property, and bring perpetrators to justice.

He urged members of the public to report suspicious activities and provide useful information to the police.

The post Ex-convict nabbed in Oyo over Lagos vehicle theft appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: CBN seeks stronger Nigerian influence ahead 2027 ECO launch
description: The Central Bank of Nigeria has called for greater Nigerian representation in the governance of the proposed Economic Community of West African States Monetary Union, insisting that countries making substantial financial contributions must have corresponding influence over decisions affecting the re
content:
The Central Bank of Nigeria has called for greater Nigerian representation in the governance of the proposed Economic Community of West African States Monetary Union, insisting that countries making substantial financial contributions must have corresponding influence over decisions affecting the regional currency.

The CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso, made the call on Friday at the ministerial session of the sixth Presidential Task Force Meeting on the ECOWAS Single Currency Programme in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire.

His position comes as West African countries intensify preparations for the phased introduction of the ECO single currency in 2027.

A statement issued by the CBN on Sunday read, “The Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Mr Olayemi Cardoso, has called for equity, fairness and proportional representation in the governance structure of the proposed ECOWAS Monetary Union.

“He stressed that while regional solidarity and respect for the sovereign equality of member states must remain fundamental principles of the Union, these should be appropriately balanced with the relative financial commitments, responsibilities and risks borne by individual member states, particularly in determining participation in decision-making and governance.”

Cardoso argued that the governance structure must reflect the economic importance, financial commitments and risks borne by participating countries.

“While bigger economies continue to take up the burden, they should also be considered to play a significant role because of the risk and systemic importance they have in the sub-region,” Cardoso said.

“Above all, such economies need to defend the huge contribution they make before their respective parliaments and the civil society. Where obligations are shared but influence is not, arrangements may be agreed, but their long-term sustainability may be difficult to guarantee.”

The governor maintained that regional solidarity and the sovereign equality of member states should remain fundamental principles of the proposed union but must be balanced against their financial responsibilities.

He explained that Nigeria’s position was not motivated by a desire to dominate other countries but by its responsibilities as the region’s largest economy and a major contributor to the monetary integration project.

According to him, Nigeria would commit substantial financial resources, foreign reserves and institutional capital to the proposed union, making it necessary to align governance participation with financial exposure.

Cardoso warned that decisions on the location of monetary institutions, leadership appointments and allocation of authority would have long-term implications for the credibility and sustainability of the ECO.

“The decisions we take today will shape the future of the Union for decades to come,” he told delegates.

“They will influence its credibility in the eyes of investors and development partners, its legitimacy in the eyes of our citizens, and the confidence of Member States that their commitments are being matched by a meaningful voice within the institutions they are helping to build.”

He reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to the ECOWAS Monetary Cooperation Programme, citing its financial contributions, technical support and compromises made to promote regional consensus.

“Nigeria has and will continue to demonstrate solidarity and fairness, respecting the sovereignty of other member states. We remain fully committed to the successful establishment of the ECO and to a Monetary Union that is credible, sustainable and beneficial to all Member States,” Cardoso said.

The post CBN seeks stronger Nigerian influence ahead 2027 ECO launch appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Single-digit: Test of dropping inflation
description:
NIGERIA’S inflation rate fell to 14.06 per cent in October, but this is no cause for celebration. Food, transport, rent, electricity and other essentials remain punishingly expensive. The real test of inflation is to achieve a single-digit rate.
Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele has rightly clarified t
content:
NIGERIA’S inflation rate fell to 14.06 per cent in October, but this is no cause for celebration. Food, transport, rent, electricity and other essentials remain punishingly expensive. The real test of inflation is to achieve a single-digit rate.

Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele has rightly clarified that falling inflation does not mean falling prices; it means prices are rising more slowly. But this explanation must not become an alibi. Families whose food bills have doubled are not comforted by a slower pace of increase. What matters is whether incomes can buy more.

The latest National Bureau of Statistics figures indicate headline inflation eased from 14.63 per cent in September to 14.06 per cent in October, and from 18.97 per cent a year earlier. Yet month-on-month inflation accelerated to 0.43 per cent from 0.06 per cent.

Food inflation remained 19.13 per cent year-on-year. Food prices fell 0.75 per cent in October, but that was a smaller monthly fall than September’s 1.55 per cent. The average price level continued to rise. Therefore, relief remains fragile.

The retreat over the past 12 months has been anything but steady. Annual inflation fell from 18.97 per cent in October 2025 to 17.33 per cent in November and 15.15 per cent in December. It hovered around 15 per cent in January and February 2026, then rose to 15.38 per cent in March, 15.69 per cent in April and 15.93 per cent in May, before easing to 14.06 per cent in October. This is progress, not a stable retreat.

The 2025 CPI rebasing reduced food’s weight from more than half to about 28 per cent; the IMF warns that this affects comparisons across the rebasing period. Therefore, the headline figure cannot capture the cost-of-living crisis.

Market prices paint a far more accurate picture of Nigerians’ lived realities. NBS data put the average national price of a kilogramme of local rice at N487.47 in October 2022, N819.42 in October 2023, N1,944.64 in October 2024 and N1,913.78 in October 2025, nearly four times the 2022 price.

A measure of brown beans rose from N564.69 in October 2022 to N2,798.50 in 2024, before falling to N1,760.53 in 2025, still more than three times the 2022 price. Boneless beef climbed from N,266.24 to N6,850.51 over the same period.

The NBS food price reports, October 2024 report and October 2025 figures document this disturbing trajectory. It shows that a fall from a peak does not restore purchasing power.

Nigeria must aim lower if the cost-of-living crisis is to abate. CBN Governor Olayemi Cardoso described single-digit inflation as the Bank’s medium-term goal in July 2026.

The United States Federal Reserve and European Central Bank both target 2.0 per cent inflation.

Nigeria’s situation and vulnerabilities differ, but a country seeking investment, deeper credit and productive growth cannot normalise inflation above 10 per cent. Single digits must become a credible, sustained objective.

The NESG chairman, Olaniyi Yusuf, made the economic case that inflation below 10 per cent would create room for interest rates to fall, improve access to credit for businesses and households, and support expansion and consumer spending. He warned against premature celebration and identified insecurity and logistics as barriers to moving goods. The NESG chairman’s observations are apt.

The CBN’s Monetary Policy Rate remained 23 per cent after its September decision. At this cost, many manufacturers, farmers and small businesses cannot borrow affordably to expand. High rates may restrain demand, but used alone against supply-driven inflation, they can suffocate the investment needed to bring prices down.

Inflation is not exclusively monetary or the result of traders’ greed. Petrol subsidy removal and sharp naira adjustments since 2023 raised the cost of transport, imported machinery, fertiliser, packaging and other inputs. The IMF identifies food supply shocks, exchange-rate depreciation, deficit financing and supply constraints as major drivers.

About 30 per cent of food consumed in Nigeria is imported; the 2022/23 drought and 2024 floods damaged domestic production. Transport accounts for roughly a quarter of retail food prices. Poor roads, storage gaps, expensive diesel and unreliable electricity compound costs between farm and market. Insecurity keeps farmers from their land and makes moving produce riskier and more costly.

External forces also matter. Global food, fuel and fertiliser prices, shipping costs and geopolitical disruptions feed into an economy dependent on imported food and production inputs.

But external shocks do not explain why local prices stay high after global prices ease. Domestic productivity deficits, fragmented markets and inconsistent policies magnify the effects.

Fiscal indiscipline and deficit financing can inject liquidity and undermine monetary restraint; unpredictable levies and abrupt trade restrictions add risk premiums.

The IMF says inflation has become less persistent and more responsive to monetary policy, but durable disinflation still requires credibility, fiscal discipline and coordination between monetary and fiscal authorities.

Market conduct also comes into play. Oyedele rightly observed that expectations can become self-fulfilling as traders anticipating further cost increases may mark up prices in advance. But the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission has warned that its surveillance detected conspiracy, price gouging, hoarding and other unfair practices in parts of the food chain.

True, not every high price is profiteering; sellers face real costs. But these must not cover collusion, artificial scarcity or opportunistic mark-ups.

Prices often rise quickly when costs rise, but fall reluctantly when costs recede. Competition enforcement, transparent price information and action against hoarding are essential rather than blunt price controls.

Still, a disinflation programme must go beyond monetary tightening and liquidity mop-ups.

The CBN withdrew over N90 trillion in the first 11 months of 2026, more than double the N40.90 trillion mopped up in all of 2025, but inflation eased by just 1.09 percentage points from 15.15 per cent in December 2025 to 14.06 per cent in October 2026.

The CBN must defend price stability, maintain a transparent foreign-exchange market, and ease rates only as inflation falls sustainably. Government must avoid monetary financing, restrain wasteful recurrent spending and prevent election-driven liquidity surges.

Food production must rise through secure farming communities, rural roads, irrigation, affordable inputs, storage and processing. Farmers must be able to plant, harvest and transport without paying a ransom to insecurity.

Nigeria must cut the energy and logistics costs embedded in every product. Reliable power, competitive gas, efficient ports, highways and rail freight can cut production and distribution costs.

Predictable tax and trade policies, local manufacturing and agro-processing, and stronger non-oil exports would reduce import dependence and earn foreign exchange.

Government policies such as targeted cash transfers, school feeding and other support, if well-governed, should cushion the poorest households, but broad, fiscally costly subsidies are no substitute for reform.

Genuine macroeconomic improvements are undeniable. The World Bank reports that the economy grew by 4.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, up from 3.9 per cent a year earlier, while external reserves reached $51.9 billion at the end of July. Yet the Bank also warns that growth remains insufficient to create enough productive jobs or materially reduce poverty.

Thus, reform cannot be judged only by reserves, exchange-rate stability or a lower CPI reading. It must be judged by whether workers can afford decent meals, businesses can move goods, factories can obtain reliable power, and families can meet rent, school and medical bills without sinking deeper into debt.

The NESG is right that single-digit inflation is necessary to consolidate recovery and unlock affordable credit. But the destination must be more than a number on an NBS chart.

The government must make food affordable, energy dependable, and transport cheaper; protect production, not just financial indicators; and ensure lower inflation translates into real relief.

Nigerians have endured years of rising prices. They cannot be asked to applaud because the pain is increasing more slowly. Elegant explanations of disinflation are not a testament to economic policy success. What counts is whether ordinary citizens can afford a decent life.

The post Single-digit: Test of dropping inflation appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
