title: Governors’ public endorsement of preferred successors undemocratic – Oduyoye, Makinde’s ex-aide
description: Babatunde Oduyoye, a former House of Representatives member and ex-Oyo State Advisory Council member, speaks on his fallout with Governor Seyi Makinde, the politics of succession in Oyo State and why he believes governors’ endorsement of preferred candidates undermines democracy. GABRIEL OSHOKHA bri
content:
Babatunde Oduyoye, a former House of Representatives member and ex-Oyo State Advisory Council member, speaks on his fallout with Governor Seyi Makinde, the politics of succession in Oyo State and why he believes governors’ endorsement of preferred candidates undermines democracy. GABRIEL OSHOKHA brings excerpts

In July, you resigned from the Oyo State Advisory Council. What actually informed that decision?

The Advisory Council is expected to advise the governor on policy, politics and administration. When I resigned, I cited personal reasons, including the need to improve myself in certain areas. Beyond that, I felt the council had outlived its usefulness. When a council is no longer functioning effectively, or the governor is no longer paying attention to its contributions, there is little reason to remain a member. That was why I decided to resign honourably.

In your resignation letter, you said you had not joined any political party other than the Alliance for Democracy. We know that the AD is no longer a registered political party. Where do you stand politically, at the moment?

I was never a card-carrying member of the Peoples Democratic Party, nor did I attend any of its local government or state meetings. All my activities within the party were carried out in my official capacity, first as Special Adviser on Strategy and Politics to the governor of Oyo State and later as a member of the Advisory Council. There were occasions when I represented the governor outside the state, particularly in Edo and Kogi states. However, I was never invited to meetings of PDP leaders in the South-West. On one occasion, I even sent out an invitation on behalf of the governor for a meeting of the party’s South-West chapter in Ibadan. I recall that a commissioner from Osun State questioned why someone who was not a PDP member was inviting them to a party meeting. What happened in 2019 was that, as members of the AD, we joined hands with Seyi Makinde to support his governorship ambition. Those involved included Tunde Tijani and Pastor Akinade Akanmu, who later became Chairman of the Teaching Service Commission and also joined me in the Advisory Council.

Before I left Makinde’s government, my good friend and brother, Oloye Dotun Sanusi, popularly known as Okanlomo Oodua, and I had been very close. It was also known to the government and several other people that we were pushing for him to succeed Seyi Makinde because I believed he had all it takes to govern Oyo State. However, the idea was not welcomed in some quarters. Besides, Sanusi is a very busy man. It was surprising that an idea that had not even crystallised became toxic in some quarters before it could take off, with some people already ganging up against him. As members of the Oyo State Advisory Council, we were given the responsibility of assisting the government in choosing the preferred candidate of the governor’s party. Governor Makinde wanted the Advisory Council to make recommendations, and we submitted a list of candidates. Att the top of the list was retired Commissioner of Police Fatai Owoseni, whom the council unanimously endorsed. Segun Ogunwuyi, who was then the Chief of Staff to the governor, came second. Some of us also pushed for Nureni Adeniran to be ranked third, but the chairman, Bolaji Ayorinde, and some other members favoured Bimbo Adekanmbi for that position.

However, weeks later, we were informed that our recommendations had been altered. We never saw the original report again. The chairman submitted a report, even though it was the committee’s responsibility to submit one. Some people have raised this issue, and I have read contradictory accounts in some publications. But I am saying authoritatively, as someone who participated in the meetings, that Owoseni was unanimously endorsed by members who were physically present and those who participated virtually via Zoom. That also contributed to my resignation from the Advisory Council. If we could spend almost two days deliberating and making recommendations, only for our efforts to amount to nothing, there was little point in continuing. Of course, the final decision rested with the governor, but our recommendations were eventually disregarded. That was one of the reasons I decided to leave. Let me also add that some governors are introducing practices that are strange to democracy. As we understand and practise democracy worldwide, I do not think it is normal or consistent with democratic principles for a sitting governor to publicly announce his preferred candidate. The governors of Nasarawa and Oyo states have introduced this into our political lexicon under the current political dispensation. If we want the best in politics, we should provide a level playing field for all aspirants to test their popularity and support. At the end of the day, whoever emerges as the candidate should have the necessary followership, with everyone in the state able to rally behind that person. Unfortunately, what we are witnessing is the reverse.

You referred to Governor Makinde as your friend and brother. He is aspiring to become president of Nigeria. Will you vote for him?

No.

Why is that?

When he wanted to become governor, he came to me, as he has acknowledged on several occasions, and we discussed his ambition. I was convinced and gave him my support. He recalled this at my 60th birthday lecture at the University of Ibadan. From the moment I said yes, I never looked back. There was a time I granted an interview to some journalists when rumours emerged that he wanted to become president of Nigeria. I cautioned him then that he knew what to do. Beyond that, I believe such an ambition is something he should discuss, or perhaps has discussed, with people close to him. However, I was never part of such discussions. So, why should I key into an agenda about which I know nothing? The same thing applies to the person he is supporting as his preferred governorship candidate. I have never met him. I was not part of the government of the late Senator Abiola Ajimobi. The understanding and responsibility I had with Seyi Makinde were to help him become governor of Oyo State and ensure that he performed well in office. That was where it ended.

Your ally, Dotun Sanusi, has declared support for the ambitions of APC candidates, particularly President Bola Tinubu and Senator Sharafadeen Alli. Were you consulted on this?

Yes, very much so. We are together. When Makinde first contested the governorship election, we approached Sanusi, and he supported us without conditions. In 2023, when Makinde sought re-election, Sanusi was initially reluctant. He had good reasons to be, having given so much, as he usually does during elections. Yet, the only road leading to his resort, which the governor had personally promised to fix, remained unattended to. The road is still in a bad state. Although some people may claim that work has commenced, the pace of construction is nothing to write home about.

Meanwhile, Dotun Sanusi has personally invested millions of naira in the road through his partnership with OYSTROMA. During the governor’s 2023 re-election campaign, Sanusi also connected more than 20 communities to the national grid. That was why the first official function Governor Makinde attended after winning the 2023 election was the commissioning of transformers donated by Sanusi to the communities during the campaign. So, I am with Dotun Sanusi. We consult, collaborate and have made several things work politically. I stand with him.

You are yet to formally declare for the APC. What is happening?

Well, the APC is an offshoot of the Alliance for Democracy. At a point, we had an internal crisis that produced two factions: the Moji Akinfenwa faction and the Baba Bisi Akande faction. I was close to Abdulkadir because he ensured my re-election in 2003, so I remained with his faction. While working with Makinde, I remained a member of the AD. So, what party am I expected to defect from? The AD? Remember, I was never a card-carrying member of the PDP.

So, we can say you are a progressive, as it is fondly called?

My relationships with people are not based on political alliances. My friends and political contacts cut across the APC. The President is also someone I have known for a long time. I had the privilege of hosting him in my house in 1998, after the D’Rovas AD primaries. He returned to my house before proceeding to his hotel. What I am saying is that I do not need to make any public declaration about defection. I have remained a progressive since the beginning of the Fourth Republic.

Some people have said that Governor Makinde’s ‘good work’ is enough for him to win both the February 6 and January 16 elections.

I have made up my mind not to comment on Governor Seyi Makinde’s administration in the run-up to the coming elections. However, I make bold to say that every candidate, depending on his background and political party, will campaign and present his case to the people. Ultimately, the people’s opinion will determine who wins the election.

Your ally, Dotun Sanusi, is championing the campaign for President Tinubu’s re-election in 2027. What is your take on those who argue that President Tinubu will win re-election and secure Oyo State, in the forthcoming elections?

In 2023, President Bola Tinubu won Oyo State, marking the first time the progressives would win a presidential election in the state. In 2027, the President is looking good. He is looking good because Pa Ayo Adebanjo, my respected leader in Afenifere, supported Peter Obi in 2023 while he was alive, for reasons of equity. He believed that the South-East had been denied the opportunity to govern Nigeria because of what happened during the Civil War. That sentiment still pervades our political landscape. A lot of things also happened during the 2023 election as a result of mutual understanding. For instance, President Bola Tinubu, in no small measure, assisted Governor Makinde in securing his re-election. I remember one of the governorship candidates who claimed he had been thrown under the bus.

What I am saying is that I see the Yoruba people rallying around their own this time. I will be working for President Bola Tinubu’s success in the next election, and I believe many other people will do the same. I listened attentively to an interview on Channels Television with former Lagos State Governor, Raji Fashola, in which he spoke about flipping Lagos back. I believe that with Obafemi Hamzat contesting the governorship election in Lagos State, a lot of good things will happen. Something worked in Obi’s favour during the 2023 election. The younger generation, who were very enthusiastic at the time, have lost some of that zeal, and the noise on social media has also waned. Because of the youth movement in 2023, many of our children across Yorubaland voted for Obi. However, a lot has happened since then, and I believe they are now wiser. That is why we are no longer seeing the same momentum. It is no longer the kind of movement we witnessed in 2023. I therefore believe President Tinubu will record resounding success at the polls in the South-West. Beyond that, the good infrastructural projects he is undertaking will also earn him votes across the country.

Are you saying thatTinubu’s re-election is almost a done deal?

I think he is looking good, and at the end of the day, he will succeed. However, a lot still needs to be done between now and the election. There are many misconceptions surrounding issues such as the removal of fuel subsidy and the President’s promise to provide electricity. People often overlook the qualification attached to his statement on electricity. He said, “If I don’t provide electricity, don’t vote for me.” However, there was a proviso that allowed for circumstances in which there might be legitimate reasons for not meeting the target. I think that, considering the performance of the power sector so far, the new person at the helm of affairs and the many items that had been lying fallow at the ports for 20 years, I share Babatunde Fashola’s views on that particular statement by the President.

Do you view the 2027 governorship election in Oyo State as a two- or three-horse race?

I know there are many candidates in the race. However, my projection, as a political analyst, is that there will be a coalition, which will turn the contest into a two-horse race. Whoever the coalition backs will most likely emerge victorious. You can look at the role coalitions played in the 2019 and 2023 elections. As an advocate of coalition-building, I believe the alliances that shaped the elections in 2019 and 2023 will also play a significant role in 2027. Ultimately, that will turn the contest into a two-horse race.

In 2023, there was a group formed by you and some other stakeholders, called the Rescue Mission. Are we likely to see something similar this time?

At that time, somebody needed to be rescued, and the mission succeeded in rescuing that person. This time, however, the objective is to rescue Oyo State and ensure that it is placed on the path of progress.

You said part of the reason you resigned from Governor Makinde’s government was the way retired Commissioner of Police Fatai Owoseni was treated. Now, Owoseni has launched a group called Oyo Lagba Forum. Is this a political vehicle you are aware of?

Well, CP Fatai Owoseni is a fine gentleman and an epitome of a disciplined police officer. I know many young officers who joined the police force because of the way and manner he conducted himself while in service. Having said that, I never personally pushed his candidacy during our meetings at the Advisory Council. I remained neutral. However, several influential members of the council, for good reasons, urged other members to support and recommend Owoseni. Some members reminded us of the understanding between the two dominant faiths and the advantage he had, politically, as someone from Ibadan. However, I believe such an arrangement should not be permanent. As for the Oyo Lagba Forum, I am part of it. I am an integral member, and I believe in its ideals, ethos and values. It is a noble group that places emphasis on mentorship- something that is lacking in this part of the country. It seeks to mentor young people and organise seminars and discussions. These are issues I have consistently advocated for through my annual birthday lectures.

So, I am fully involved in Oyo Lagba. At the initial stage, we wanted Owoseni to be the face of the organisation, and we deliberately positioned him that way. Given the respect he commands across the country, the group has attracted a large membership. You cannot imagine how successful the membership drive has been. I am therefore part and parcel of the Oyo Lagba Movement and fully involved in its activities. The Oyo Lagba Movement will also play a prominent role politically. We are already playing a role behind the scenes, and when the time comes, or when the necessary resolutions have been passed in accordance with the group’s constitution, appropriate pronouncements will be made.

Is it not getting late, considering how close the elections are?

Let me say this, although I do not yet have the authority to speak on behalf of Oyo Lagba: I have an inkling that the group will gravitate towards the noble and popular choice in Oyo State. I have a good feeling about that. I may not have its mandate to speak on the matter yet, but some of the group’s subsidiaries are already putting structures in place across the state. So, time will tell.

Governor Seyi Makinde has been campaigning strongly against President Bola Tinubu in the presidential race. Again, what do you think of his presidential ambition?

Let me state clearly that Governor Seyi Makinde has a constitutional right, an inherent right enshrined in the Constitution, to contest for the highest political office in the country. We should also recall that Governor Makinde, under the G5, worked closely with others, although at the expense of his own party. The President, in turn, reciprocated by supporting his re-election. I also listened to Governor Makinde’s recent interview on Arise TV, and I think he has left the door open. He said he would be willing to discuss with the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike.

The post Governors’ public endorsement of preferred successors undemocratic – Oduyoye, Makinde’s ex-aide appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
author: Gabriel Oshokha

title: LASG targets 6,000km fibre network, 10% startup procurement
description:
The Lagos State Government is targeting an expansion of its fibre-optic network from 2,400 kilometres to 6,000 kilometres and plans to reserve 10 per cent of public procurement for startups as part of efforts to attract investment and accelerate the state’s digital economy.
Deputy Governor Obafemi H
content:
The Lagos State Government is targeting an expansion of its fibre-optic network from 2,400 kilometres to 6,000 kilometres and plans to reserve 10 per cent of public procurement for startups as part of efforts to attract investment and accelerate the state’s digital economy.

Deputy Governor Obafemi Hamzat disclosed the plans at a fintech town hall in Lagos on Friday, where he urged technology companies, financial institutions and investors to work with the government to develop the state’s digital infrastructure and innovation ecosystem.

Hamzat said the proposed fibre expansion would be pursued through partnerships with telecommunications companies and other private-sector stakeholders, while the startup procurement initiative would give smaller businesses access to government contracts and improve their ability to grow.

He said the government was also working towards ensuring that startups engaged through the procurement programme received payment within 15 days, reducing the cash-flow difficulties that often constrain small businesses.

The deputy governor added that women accounted for about 54 per cent of startups that had undertaken work under the initiative.

The town hall, themed “The Lagos Digital Economy Blueprint: Co-Authoring the Lagos Digital Economy Agenda”, brought together fintech operators, technology companies, investors and government representatives to discuss the policies and infrastructure required to strengthen Lagos’s position as a technology and financial services hub.

Hamzat challenged businesses to help bridge the gap between research and commercial investment, arguing that many innovations developed by young Nigerians failed to reach the market because of inadequate funding and weak connections with industry.

“We have seen a lot of ideas and young people bringing innovations, but how do we bring them to capital? How do we ensure that we understand the needs of the private sector and connect them to research?” he asked.

The former Commissioner for Science and Technology urged companies to identify challenges within their operations that could be addressed through academic research, and to fund universities and researchers to develop practical solutions.

He cited his doctoral research, which he said was funded by an oil company in the United Kingdom and resulted in a reported 33 per cent reduction in energy consumption in oil production, as an example of the benefits of industry-backed research.

On digital infrastructure, Hamzat said 680 of Lagos’s 1,028 public schools were connected to the internet, with the government working to extend connectivity to the remaining 348 schools.

He also outlined plans to integrate government databases through Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) to allow agencies to share information and reduce repeated requests for documents already held by the government.

According to him, an integrated data system would reduce duplication, improve public service delivery and make interactions with government agencies easier for residents.

The deputy governor urged fintech operators and technology companies to identify areas where their expertise could support the government’s digital agenda, rather than wait for the government to develop solutions independently.

Earlier, the convener of the town hall and Executive Director of MyCard Global, Aderemi Fagbemi, said the meeting was designed to bring government and industry stakeholders together to shape policies for the state’s financial technology and digital innovation sectors.

She said sustainable innovation required cooperation between public institutions and private businesses, adding that the town hall was intended to move discussions beyond individual corporate interests to a shared digital economy agenda.

“As someone proudly serving on Your Excellency’s Formal Sector Campaign Council, I see firsthand the immense passion and dedication driving this vision. We gathered because Lagos means business,” Fagbemi said.

She identified tax harmonisation, the integration of digital payment infrastructure into municipal systems and the development of innovation corridors as issues requiring attention if Lagos were to compete effectively as a global technology hub.

Also speaking, the co-founder of Flutterwave, Gbenga Agboola, said predictable policies and regulatory stability were essential to attracting investment and enabling fintech companies to expand.

He called for better coordination among regulatory agencies, particularly in licensing and approval processes, arguing that businesses should not have to navigate duplicative procedures to secure authorisation from different regulators.

Agboola said approvals granted by one relevant agency should, where applicable, help facilitate requirements from other regulators, reducing the time and cost of compliance for businesses.

He also urged the government to create room for startups to test new ideas and develop products without unnecessary regulatory obstacles, while operating within established legal frameworks.

The Flutterwave co-founder said more efficient regulation, consistent policies and tax-efficient business operations would encourage entrepreneurship, attract investment and support the growth of Nigeria’s fintech sector.

The town hall was organised by MyCard Global in collaboration with the Fintech Association of Nigeria, also known as FintechNGR. Participating organisations included Flutterwave, Paystack, PiggyVest, Kuda, PalmPay, Mastercard, Visa, Oracle, Interswitch, OPay, Moniepoint, Paga and Meristem.

title: PETROAN opposes petrol import curbs, cites cheaper foreign supplies
description: The Petroleum Products Retail Outlets Owners Association of Nigeria has urged the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority to sustain the issuance of petroleum import permits to qualified marketers, warning that restricting imports could weaken competition and expose consumer
content:
The Petroleum Products Retail Outlets Owners Association of Nigeria has urged the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority to sustain the issuance of petroleum import permits to qualified marketers, warning that restricting imports could weaken competition and expose consumers to higher petrol prices.

The association’s National Public Relations Officer, Joseph Obele, said multiple supply sources remained necessary to guarantee adequate petroleum products and affordable prices, despite increasing contributions from domestic refineries.

Obele, an energy expert and lecturer at Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, Port Harcourt, made the call in a statement on Sunday, citing the October 2026 industry statistics released by the NMDPRA.

The figures showed that daily petrol imports increased by approximately 47.1 per cent to 15 million litres in October from 10.2 million litres in September, representing an additional 4.8 million litres daily.

The statement read, “The Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority should sustain the issuance of petroleum import permits to qualified marketers, insisting that healthy competition remains essential to achieving affordable fuel prices and protecting Nigerian consumers.”

He said the increase demonstrated the continuing importance of imported petroleum products in meeting domestic demand, arguing that Nigeria’s evolving refining capacity should not be protected from competition through restrictions on imports.

According to him, the estimated landing cost of imported petrol stood at N1,056.79 per litre, compared with Dangote Petroleum Refinery’s reported gantry price of N1,159 per litre as of 16 November, leaving a difference of N102.21 per litre in favour of imported supplies.

Obele argued that the price difference reinforced the need for a competitive market where suppliers could compete on pricing, product quality and operational efficiency.

He warned that restricting import permits while domestic refining capacity was still developing could limit supply options and create conditions for higher prices.

The PETROAN spokesman also called on the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited to accelerate the proposed equity partnership with two Chinese companies interested in investing in Nigeria’s refining industry.

He said the entry of the Chinese investors could introduce additional competition into the downstream sector, noting that their business models were often associated with large-scale production, aggressive pricing and relatively low profit margins.

Obele expressed optimism that the proposed investments could eventually push petrol prices below N700 per litre, although he acknowledged that achieving such a price would depend on investment costs, crude oil supply arrangements, production efficiency, exchange rates and prevailing market conditions.

He urged the NNPC to move beyond announcements and translate the proposed partnership into concrete investment commitments, operational refineries and increased domestic petroleum production.

The energy expert also maintained that existing domestic refiners, including Dangote Refinery, should be encouraged to compete through efficiency, affordable pricing, product quality and reliable supply rather than protection from other market participants.

He said, “Competition is not the enemy of local refining; it is the foundation of efficiency. Nigeria must open its petroleum market to credible investors, sustain import permits where necessary and encourage strategic partnerships that will expand refining capacity. Our ultimate objective should be to make petrol affordable, guarantee adequate supply and ensure that Nigerians benefit from the gains of deregulation.”

He urged the NMDPRA and NNPC to take deliberate steps to build a competitive, investment-friendly and consumer-focused petroleum industry.

title: State police in Nigeria: Not so fast!
description: Last Wednesday, November 18, 2026, was a red-letter day for me. The reason is that on that day, news broke that, in an unprecedented move, the entire 36 State Houses of Assembly formally approved the creation of state police. Recall that in June, the House of Representatives and Senate have likewise
content:
Last Wednesday, November 18, 2026, was a red-letter day for me. The reason is that on that day, news broke that, in an unprecedented move, the entire 36 State Houses of Assembly formally approved the creation of state police. Recall that in June, the House of Representatives and Senate have likewise passed the 6th constitution alteration bill overwhelmingly.

 According to a press statement by the Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on State Police, Femi Gbajabiamila, the bill was formally transmitted to the President on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, by Basheer Lado and Wasiu Olanrewaju-Smart, his special advisers on Senate and House of Representatives matters, respectively.  President Tinubu would review the bill in consultation with Lateef Fagbemi, Attorney-General of the Federation and the Minister of Justice, before appending his signature.

 I had thought the President would sign the bill by last Friday, but he’s yet to do so as at the time of writing this piece. Meanwhile, I had the privilege of discussing the passage of this constitution alteration bill, the very first under President Tinubu, last Wednesday on Radio Now 95.3 Lagos. I did say on the programme that it is not yet Uhuru for state police, as there are still several hurdles to cross.

 Many people, particularly opposition candidates and political parties, believe the state police is being rushed to be used as a political weapon against them during the forthcoming 2027 general elections, holding on January 16 and February 6. I have consistently disabused their mind that no state will be ready with a functional police system until long after the elections.

 For instance, even if President Tinubu signs the constitution alteration bill into law, a National Policing Bill is still needed to flesh out the guardrails and modus operandi for state police operations vis-à-vis the existing federal police.  The committee overseeing it is headed by the Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila. In his press statement last Wednesday, he gave an update on the work of his committee when he said: “Meanwhile, the Presidential Working Group on State Police, which I chair, with the support of the Policy Advisory Committee, has undertaken extensive stakeholder engagement and nationwide consultations towards developing a draft National Policing Bill.” He said the draft bill had been submitted to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting and validation and that the working group would review the validated version upon receipt and present it, alongside its report, to the President for consideration.

 The key highlights of the National Policing Bill drafted by Femi Gbajabiamila’s committee include: Establishment of a Dual-Policing Structure: The bill aims to create a dual policing system comprising the Federal Police Service and 36 State Police Services; Minimum Standards and Certification: It will set national minimum standards for recruitment, training, oversight, and funding, ensuring credible and accountable policing; Human Rights Safeguards: The bill will include provisions to protect citizens’ rights and ensure that state police do not become instruments of political intimidation.

How early will this National Policing Bill be passed and assented to by the President when the National Assembly is struggling to form a quorum at the peak of this campaign season?

 I reliably learnt that about 62 extant Acts of Parliament relating to Nigeria’s policing system must also be amended before state police are on full legal footing. Furthermore, each governor has to sponsor an executive bill establishing the state police for their respective states. Among other things, the bill will establish a State Police Service Commission, an autonomous body responsible for the recruitment, training, promotion and discipline of the officers and men of the state police. At the takeoff of the state police, some federal police personnel may transfer to their respective states or go on secondment to serve as foundational staff pending the actual takeoff of the state police. For instance, not all state police recruits will start as constables.

 Another sticky point is that the law establishing state police does not permit state governments to procure arms and ammunition. They must apply to the Office of the National Security Adviser to procure arms and ammunition for their respective state police. Even applications to establish state police must be routed through the National Security Adviser or another federal body or committee, which will certify that the state has met the minimum threshold and safety standards for state police operations. Fear has been expressed in some quarters that the NSA, being a political appointee, may turn down applications from opposition state governments. This is, however, speculative.

 The big elephant in the room is the funding for state police. I learnt that 80 per cent of operational costs must be ready at inception before approval for establishment can be given. Many have wondered how state police will be funded and whether each of the 36 states has enough resources to fund them adequately. Questions are being asked if governors will still be collecting security votes when they have state police, or if they will have to set up Police Equipment Trust Funds, as some states have done. Another proposition is saying that the federal government must give take-off grants or bailouts to states wanting to establish state police.

 Sincerely, establishing state police is not a tea party or a walk in the park. It’s going to be capital intensive. States will have to establish their respective training institutions, build police stations and perhaps barracks. The state will also have to build armouries and stores. Automatic weapons are not cheap, as they are not manufactured in Nigeria and have to be procured abroad. States will also need forensic laboratories and to deploy technology to fight crime at the state level. Enugu State has procured drones and established a command and control centre, while the Oyo State government has bought two jet fighters to help combat insecurity in the state. Given the artificial nature of interstate boundaries, it’s important to specify in law how to treat transborder crimes and jurisdictional overlaps between federal and state police.

 Interestingly, former President Muhammadu Buhari signed a constitutional alteration devolving prisons, now known as Correctional Centres, from the exclusive legislative list to the concurrent legislative list, as the State Police bill has just done. However, to the best of my knowledge, no state government has established its correctional services. Meanwhile, most of the crimes being committed are likely to fall under state police jurisdiction. Will the Federal Government continue to bear the burden of awaiting trials and convicts of state crimes under the new dispensation? Food for thought!

 I.G: @jideojong

The post State police in Nigeria: Not so fast! appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Osun marathon winners get N2.55m
description:
Winners of the 2026 10-kilometre Imole Marathon have received N2.55m in cash prizes, with Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, reaffirming his administration’s commitment to grassroots sports development and youth engagement.
The race, held on Saturday, attracted participants from different backgro
content:
Winners of the 2026 10-kilometre Imole Marathon have received N2.55m in cash prizes, with Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, reaffirming his administration’s commitment to grassroots sports development and youth engagement.

The race, held on Saturday, attracted participants from different backgrounds and featured male and female categories, with six runners sharing the prize money.

According to a statement made available to journalists in Osogbo on Sunday by the race facilitator, Joseph Adeyemi, who is the Special Assistant on Youth and Sports to the governor, the marathon started at Abere Roundabout and ended at Freedom Park, Osogbo.

In the men’s category, Odelana James emerged winner and received N750,000, while Adeyemi Tunde Segun finished second with N500,000. Adebayo Michael placed third and earned N300,000.

In the women’s category, Arinde Boluwatife claimed the top prize of N500,000, followed by Idowu Adesewa, who received N300,000. Popoola Omar finished third and received N200,000.

Speaking at the event, Adeleke, who was represented by the Commissioner for Political Affairs and Inter-Governmental Relations, Dr Biyi Odunlade, said the state government remained committed to creating opportunities for young people through sports and other productive engagements.

“Sports remain an important avenue for youth development, talent discovery and community engagement.

“The Governor believes in creating opportunities for young people to demonstrate their abilities, and initiatives such as the Imole Marathon provide a platform to achieve this,” Odunlade said on behalf of the governor.

The Deputy Governor, who also doubles as the Commissioner for Sports, Kola Adewusi, also reaffirmed the government’s commitment to supporting sporting talents and strengthening sports development across the state.

Adeyemi said the marathon was conceived to encourage more residents, particularly young people, to embrace sporting activities.

“The Imole Marathon is about taking sports closer to the people and encouraging participation beyond professional athletes. We want to make sporting activities accessible, discover new talents and promote a culture of fitness and healthy competition in Osun State,” he said.

Beyond the cash prizes awarded to the six podium finishers, consolation prizes were presented to all participants in recognition of their involvement in the race.

title: Adesina challenges insurers to disclose claims, governance records
description:
Former President of the African Development Bank Group, Akinwumi Adesina, has challenged Nigerian insurance companies to open their claims settlement and corporate governance records to public scrutiny, saying transparency is critical to rebuilding confidence in the industry.
Adesina said insurers s
content:
Former President of the African Development Bank Group, Akinwumi Adesina, has challenged Nigerian insurance companies to open their claims settlement and corporate governance records to public scrutiny, saying transparency is critical to rebuilding confidence in the industry.

Adesina said insurers should demonstrate their commitment to policyholders by publishing information on claims settlement, customer complaints, regulatory compliance and governance practices.

He made the call at the Nigeria Insurance Directors Conference, organised by the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria in collaboration with the National Insurance Commission in Lagos.

The former AfDB president proposed that NAICOM introduce an annual public accountability and performance report for the insurance industry, detailing claims received and settled, outstanding claims, average settlement timelines, customer complaints, financial soundness and corporate governance.

He said insurers should not expect Nigerians to trust them without providing evidence of their performance and accountability.

“When a policyholder pays an insurance premium, that policyholder deserves a premium service in return,” he said.

Adesina said the industry’s credibility depended largely on how insurers responded when customers suffered losses and needed the protection for which they had paid.

He also urged insurance boards to take greater responsibility for claims performance, customer complaints, corporate governance and management accountability, arguing that transparency should extend beyond regulatory compliance.

Nigeria’s insurance penetration, estimated at about 0.5 per cent of Gross Domestic Product, remains low, reflecting the industry’s limited reach and the country’s inadequate protection against financial losses, he said.

Adesina called on insurers to expand coverage across agriculture, infrastructure, manufacturing, energy, transportation, healthcare and housing, stressing that insurance was critical to protecting productive assets and supporting economic development.

He also cautioned that the ongoing recapitalisation exercise under the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 would not automatically produce stronger insurance companies.

“Recapitalisation is not the same as institutional transformation,” he said.

Adesina said higher capital requirements must be accompanied by sound corporate governance, disciplined underwriting, adequate technical reserves, effective risk management and stronger reinsurance arrangements.

He urged the National Insurance Commission to strengthen risk-based supervision and hold insurance companies accountable for measurable performance.

According to him, the industry’s success should be assessed by the value it delivers to policyholders and the confidence it builds among Nigerians, rather than the amount of capital raised or premiums collected.

“The measure of success must be outcomes, not announcements,” he said.

title: Sporting Lagos first club to partner LockerRoom Bonus
description:
Sporting Lagos have partnered with Locker Room Bonus, the direct-to-athlete reward programme supported by betPawa, in an agreement that makes the Nigeria Premier Football League side the scheme’s first individual club partner.
The deal follows the club’s promotion to the NPFL and will bring match-wi
content:
Sporting Lagos have partnered with Locker Room Bonus, the direct-to-athlete reward programme supported by betPawa, in an agreement that makes the Nigeria Premier Football League side the scheme’s first individual club partner.

The deal follows the club’s promotion to the NPFL and will bring match-win bonuses directly to eligible players and technical staff in the top flight.

Sporting Lagos experienced the Locker Room Bonus model during their 2025/26 Nigeria National League campaign, and the new agreement extends those payments into their NPFL season.

Under the terms of the partnership, every eligible player and technical backroom staff member will receive a fixed bonus for each competitive victory. Payouts are made directly into personal mobile-money wallets before the squad leaves the dressing room, bypassing administrative bottlenecks and linking on-pitch results to immediate compensation.

Head of Football at Sporting Lagos, Ayobami Animasahun, said the arrangement reflected the collective effort behind the club’s rise.

“Getting to the NPFL took more than the eleven players people saw on matchday. It took an entire group working together, week after week. We want to carry that respect for the whole team into this next chapter. When we win, the reward should reach the players and staff who made it happen while the moment is still theirs. This partnership makes that part of how we operate,” Animasahun said.

The Regional Manager for West and Central Africa at betPawa, Nii Armah Ashong-Katai, said the partnership underlined the company’s commitment to athlete welfare.

“Athlete welfare is central to betPawa. We aim to support athletes, help them improve, and boost their wellbeing wherever they compete. Extending the Locker Room Bonus to non-onboarded leagues ensures more athletes benefit directly.

“Partnering with Sporting Lagos (our first African club LRB signee) highlights our dedication to rewarding athletes everywhere,” Ashong-Katai said.

To ensure transparency and remove friction, the disbursements rely on verified digital identity and mobile-money systems powered by pawaPass and pawaPay.

Locker Room Bonus operates across football and basketball on the continent and maintains equal compensation rates for all eligible men’s and women’s rosters.

According to verified figures published on the programme’s official portal, lrb.betpawa.com, the expansion to Sporting Lagos reinforces a key operating principle that true sports development begins with transparent, immediate recognition for the athletes who earn it on the pitch.

The partnership comes as the programme reaches a landmark, with more than $2m now paid directly to players and coaches across nine African markets since it was launched in the 2022/23 season.

The post Sporting Lagos first club to partner LockerRoom Bonus appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: NAICOM urges insurers to improve claims settlement
description: The National Insurance Commission has urged insurance companies to deploy the stronger capital positions achieved through recapitalisation to drive technological innovation, improve claims settlement, and rebuild public confidence, warning that increased financial capacity alone will not guarantee t
content:
The National Insurance Commission has urged insurance companies to deploy the stronger capital positions achieved through recapitalisation to drive technological innovation, improve claims settlement, and rebuild public confidence, warning that increased financial capacity alone will not guarantee the industry’s growth.

According to the Commission, the next phase of the sector’s transformation must be measured by its ability to develop relevant products, improve customer experiences, and extend insurance services to underserved Nigerians.

Deputy Commissioner for Finance and Administration, Mr Ekerete Gam-Ikon, who represented the Commissioner for Insurance, Mr Ayo Omosehin, gave this charge at the fifth edition of the ‘Insurance Meets Tech conference’, where stakeholders examined technology’s role in expanding penetration and strengthening competitiveness.

Speaking on the theme, ‘Building Insurance That Connects,’ Omosehin described the conclusion of the recapitalisation exercise as a defining moment for the industry, stressing that insurers must demonstrate how their improved financial capacity will translate into tangible value for policyholders. He noted that the exercise should not be judged by the volume of capital raised, but by the strength of institutions, quality of products, and improvements in service delivery that follow.

“The measure of our success will therefore not be the amount of capital raised. The real measure will be the ability to translate stronger balance sheets into stronger institutions, better products, superior customer experiences and greater economic impact,” he said.

Warning that capital without innovation would have limited impact, he declared that “capital without innovation is dumb capital.”

He identified digital onboarding, embedded insurance, artificial intelligence, automation, and advanced risk modelling as key opportunities to improve efficiency, develop new distribution channels, and reach previously excluded customers.

However, he cautioned against adopting technology for its own sake, insisting its value must be determined by the improvements delivered to policyholders.

“Technology is not the destination. Technology is the enabler. The destination remains the customer,” he said.

Earlier, the Convener of IMT, Odion Aleobua, noted that the industry is entering a critical phase where the focus must shift from meeting regulatory thresholds to deploying capital to expand the market.

He identified poor customer experiences, claims settlement concerns, and persistent public distrust as major drivers of low insurance penetration in Nigeria, adding that meaningful transformation depends on operators’ willingness to collaborate and invest in practical solutions.

Echoing the need for customer-centricity, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Enterprise Life, Nelson Akerele, emphasised simplifying products during a pre-session presentation. Akerele stressed that customers should not have to struggle with technical jargon to understand policies, urging operators to clearly explain benefits, costs, exclusions, and claims procedures while leveraging data and artificial intelligence to build more relevant offerings.

The event took centre stage during a panel discussion titled ‘Capital, Code and the Race to Nigeria’s First Insurance Unicorn’, featuring Flutterwave and Andela co-founder Iyin Aboyeji, Tope Adeniyi, and Babatunde Fajemirokun, with Rasheedat Adebisi as moderator.

Aboyeji identified the industry’s credibility deficit as a fundamental obstacle to building a large-scale insurance business in Nigeria, arguing that operators must consistently honour their commitments.

“Insurance has a trust problem, a well-deserved, I can say so myself, trust problem,” he said, noting that customers often discover policy exclusions only when attempting to make a claim. He maintained that transparency and reliable claims settlement are essential to building lasting customer relationships.

title: FG supports 4,000 Ekiti farmers after devastating floods
description:
The All Farmers Association of Nigeria has praised the Federal Government for coming to the aid of 4,000 members whose farms were recently destroyed by floods.
 AFAN Chairman in Ekiti State, Mr Sunday Adekogbon, thanked the Federal Government, the National Agricultural Development Fund and the state
content:
The All Farmers Association of Nigeria has praised the Federal Government for coming to the aid of 4,000 members whose farms were recently destroyed by floods.

 AFAN Chairman in Ekiti State, Mr Sunday Adekogbon, thanked the Federal Government, the National Agricultural Development Fund and the state government for supporting the affected farmers with farm inputs to enable them to recover from the disaster.

 The Federal Government, through the agency, distributed emergency farm inputs to 4,000 smallholder farmers affected by flooding in the state at an event tagged ‘NADF Intervention for Flood-Affected Farmers in Ekiti State’ on Saturday to help restore their farms and improve food production.

 Items distributed to the affected farmers by the agency included 4,000 bags of NPK fertiliser, 4,000 bags of urea, 2,800 bags of rice seeds, 1,200 bags of maize seeds, 4,000 bottles of pre-plant chemicals, 4,000 bottles of pre-emergency chemicals, 4,000 bottles of early post-emergency chemicals and 4,000 bottles of insecticide.

 Adekogbon, while appreciating NADF for the gesture, said, “The support will enable farmers to contribute more effectively to food security”.

 The AFAN chairman urged beneficiaries not to sell the inputs but to use them for their intended agricultural purposes.

 The affected farmers, represented by Mr Ojo Falana, expressed appreciation to the Federal Government, NADF, the Ekiti State Government and other stakeholders for the intervention.

 Falana said, “We appreciate the NADF for this gesture, and we promise to use the agricultural inputs judiciously to improve our farming activities and achieve the programme’s objectives”.

 Speaking earlier, NADF Executive Secretary and Chief Executive Officer, Mr Muhammed Ibrahim, urged the beneficiaries to “use the materials for the purpose meant to justify government’s investment”, saying the gesture was intended to ensure recovery.

 Ibrahim, represented by the Head of Strategy, Planning, Evaluation, Monitoring and Learning, Mrs Adebanke Fajana, said, “We want you to see renewed opportunity. We encourage you to see farms being restored to productivity. We encourage you to see families regaining their livelihoods, and we see communities strengthened against failure shocks. Above all, we see a pathway towards a more resilient and food-secure Nigeria. “

 The NADF boss said the intervention aligned with President Bola Tinubu’s vision “to protect livelihoods, strengthen food security and build a resilient agricultural economy under the Renewed Hope Agenda”.

 Speaking on the essence of the intervention, Ibrahim said, “For many farmers, this loss is threatening not only the current production cycle, but also the ability to prepare for the next production cycle. Without timely intervention, this disaster can easily become a crisis that lasts for seasons. We are here to ensure that recovery is done.”

 The Special Adviser to Ekiti State Governor Biodun Oyebanji on Agriculture, Boluwade Ebenezer, said the intervention would restore the affected farmers’ confidence, boost agricultural production and strengthen food security in Ekiti State and Nigeria.

The post FG supports 4,000 Ekiti farmers after devastating floods appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Gumel calls for transparency in global volleyball governance
description:
NOC President Habu Gumel has called for greater transparency and financial accountability in world volleyball, stressing the need for sound governance to sustain the sport’s development.
Gumel, also a member of the Finance Commission of the International Volleyball Federation, made the call during t
content:
NOC President Habu Gumel has called for greater transparency and financial accountability in world volleyball, stressing the need for sound governance to sustain the sport’s development.

Gumel, also a member of the Finance Commission of the International Volleyball Federation, made the call during the presentation of the body’s financial reports at its 40th World Congress in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic.

The congress, which was held from November 20 to 22, brought together representatives of national federations to deliberate on the administration and future of the sport

Speaking during the presentation, Gumel commended members of the Finance Commission for their commitment to responsible and transparent financial management.

He said stronger financial governance structures were necessary to support the FIVB’s development plans and ensure that the organisation remained accountable to national federations and other stakeholders.

Gumel also congratulated FIVB president Fabio Azevedo and his team, praising their leadership and efforts to modernise the international governing body.

Beyond financial management, the Nigerian administrator highlighted volleyball’s contribution to the Olympic movement, particularly in promoting unity, sporting excellence and cooperation among nations.

He urged stakeholders to strengthen their collaboration to create more opportunities for athletes, support national federations and widen participation in the sport.

The call aligns with the FIVB’s Vision 2032, which seeks to expand access to volleyball and increase its global reach.

Gumel’s role in the Finance Commission also places a Nigerian representative within an important structure responsible for overseeing the federation’s financial affairs and supporting its strategic direction.

The 40th Congress provided a platform for national federations to discuss governance, development, and the growth of volleyball worldwide.

title: Cornerstone splits insurance businesses to comply with new law
description:
Cornerstone Insurance Plc is reorganising its insurance operations into separate life and non-life businesses as it aligns its corporate structure with the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025.
The restructuring will see the insurer become Cornerstone Plc, a holding company overseeing three s
content:
Cornerstone Insurance Plc is reorganising its insurance operations into separate life and non-life businesses as it aligns its corporate structure with the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025.

The restructuring will see the insurer become Cornerstone Plc, a holding company overseeing three subsidiaries responsible for life insurance, general insurance and Takaful operations.

The company disclosed in a notification to the Nigerian Exchange Limited on Wednesday that it had secured approval from the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission, sanction from the Federal High Court and approval-in-principle from the National Insurance Commission for the restructuring.

Under the new structure, Cornerstone Life Assurance Limited will handle life insurance operations, while Cornerstone General Insurance Limited will take over general insurance business. Hilal Takaful Insurance Limited will continue to operate the group’s Takaful business.

The restructuring involves transferring the assets, liabilities and undertakings of the existing life and general insurance businesses to their respective subsidiaries.

The move comes as insurers adjust their corporate structures to comply with the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025, which mandates the separation of life and non-life insurance operations.

Cornerstone said the new arrangement would allow each subsidiary to operate with dedicated management, capital and resources, giving the businesses greater operational focus and flexibility in pursuing growth opportunities.

The holding company will oversee the three subsidiaries, while existing shareholders will retain their shares and current holdings in Cornerstone Plc.

The company will also remain listed on the Nigerian Exchange under its existing ticker symbol, CORNERST.

Cornerstone said the restructuring would not affect policyholders, with existing insurance policies remaining valid under their current terms and conditions.

Premiums, benefits, policy periods and claims rights will remain unchanged, and customers will not be required to take any action.

Customers of former FIN Insurance Company Limited will continue to receive services from Cornerstone General Insurance Limited, with their coverage, contractual benefits and outstanding claims preserved.

The company said the restructuring was subject to NAICOM’s final approval and would position the group for its next phase of growth through a simplified corporate structure and stronger operating businesses.

The post Cornerstone splits insurance businesses to comply with new law appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Women groups push 35% leadership quota for firms
description:
Women in Successful Careers is advocating reforms to raise female representation on corporate boards and executive management teams to 35 per cent.
The push forms the core agenda at a press conference hearalding the organisation’s 18th Annual Leadership and Mentoring Conference scheduled to hold on
content:
Women in Successful Careers is advocating reforms to raise female representation on corporate boards and executive management teams to 35 per cent.

The push forms the core agenda at a press conference hearalding the organisation’s 18th Annual Leadership and Mentoring Conference scheduled to hold on Saturday, 28 November, 2026, in Lagos, under the theme, ‘Courage in Action: Shaping Policies and Structures for Inclusive Progress.’

According to the organisers, the gathering will examine how policies, institutional frameworks and governance structures can create more equitable pathways for women to access leadership, influence decision-making and contribute meaningfully to national economic development.

WISCAR noted that conversations around women’s representation must move beyond advocacy and commitments to tangible institutional change. While developing capable women through mentoring and professional development remains essential, the group maintained that sustainable economic progress depends on institutions creating the enabling environment for women’s capabilities to translate into leadership and impact.

Speaking at a pre-conference press briefing in Lagos, the Founder and Chairperson of WISCAR, Mrs Amina Oyagbola, stated that the organisation’s experience over nearly two decades had reinforced the urgency of dismantling institutional barriers alongside individual capacity building.

“Developing capable women is essential, but institutions must also create the conditions and environment in which the capabilities of these talented women translate into leadership, influence and impact. We will not be able to move the needle until the systems and institutions within which women operate are redesigned to enable their full participation and contribution,” she said.

As part of its policy drive, WISCAR is collaborating through the Women in Leadership Coalition alongside the Women in Leadership Advancement Network, Women in Management, Business and Public Service, and the Nigeria Governors’ Forum to advance workplace and governance reforms.

Beyond the 35 per cent private-sector board and executive target, the coalition is pushing for improved female representation in public-sector leadership and family-friendly workplace policies, including 16 weeks of fully paid maternity leave and 14 days of paid paternity leave for new fathers.

The initiatives align with WISCAR’s 2026–2030 strategic plan to consolidate impact and scale for systemic change by prioritising leadership pipelines, institutional partnerships and policy influence.

A major highlight of the conference will be the conferment of the Distinguished WISCAR Award on a social impact and leadership executive, Dr Ndidi Nwuneli, who will also deliver the keynote address. Nwuneli is the former President and Chief Executive Officer of the ONE Campaign, Founder of LEAP Africa and African Food Changemakers, and Co-Founder of Sahel Consulting, AACE Foods and Wealth4Impact.

The conference, the organisers said, would convene leaders from government, the private sector, professional bodies and civil society. Expected speakers include the President of the Nigerian Bar Association, Mrs Oyinkansola Badejo-Okusanya, SAN; Group Chairman of the Nigerian Exchange Group, Alhaji Umaru Kwairanga; Director-General of the Maryam Babangida National Centre for Women Development, Dr Adedayo Benjamins-Laniyi; President of the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management, Mallam Ahmed Gobir; and Partner at Templars and Chairperson of the Chartered Institute of Directors Women’s Group, Mrs Ronke Sokefun.

The post Women groups push 35% leadership quota for firms appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: UAE-West Africa trade hits $61.3bn in 2026
description:
Trade between the United Arab Emirates and West Africa rose by 40.3 per cent to $61.3bn between January and September 2026, nearly matching the $62.1bn recorded for the whole of 2025.
 The UAE Minister of Foreign Trade, Dr Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, disclosed this at the West Africa Integration and
content:
Trade between the United Arab Emirates and West Africa rose by 40.3 per cent to $61.3bn between January and September 2026, nearly matching the $62.1bn recorded for the whole of 2025.

 The UAE Minister of Foreign Trade, Dr Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, disclosed this at the West Africa Integration and Investment Summit (WAIIS 2026), held on November 17 and 18 at the Julius Maada Bio International Conference Centre in Lungi, Sierra Leone, according to a statement on Sunday.

 The summit, inaugurated by Sierra Leone’s President, Julius Maada Bio, brought together heads of state and government, ministers, investors, development finance institutions and private sector leaders to discuss regional economic priorities, investment partnerships and the implementation of strategic projects.

 Al Zeyoudi participated in the summit on behalf of the UAE President, His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. During the event, he conveyed the UAE President’s greetings to Maada Bio and other West African leaders and representatives, alongside his wishes for the success of the summit and the continued progress and prosperity of the region.

 He also expressed the UAE’s appreciation to the Sierra Leonean President, government and people for hosting the summit and supporting regional integration, investment and sustainable development.

 Speaking on behalf of the UAE, Al Zeyoudi said West Africa’s economic prospects were supported by its large population, economic growth and investment opportunities.

 “West Africa is entering a new phase of economic integration, underpinned by a market of more than 450 million people, regional growth of 4.7 percent, and a portfolio of investment projects valued at more than $180bn.

 “The UAE views West Africa as a trade, investment and strategic partner of considerable potential, and we are committed to building long-term, mutually beneficial partnerships founded on the exchange of expertise and the development of projects that deliver sustainable economic impact.”

 He said the region’s investment opportunities were concentrated in four strategic areas: energy, industry and mineral resources, food security, and regional connectivity.

 According to him, these sectors offer opportunities to attract investment, expand productive capacity, develop infrastructure and strengthen West Africa’s participation in global supply chains and international trade.

 The UAE has invested or made investment commitments exceeding $118bn across Africa between 2020 and 2024, establishing itself as the continent’s leading investment partner.

 The investments cover energy, logistics, infrastructure, food systems and the digital economy. West African countries account for more than 6.1 per cent of the UAE’s total non-oil foreign trade and approximately 40 per cent of its non-oil trade with Africa.

 Non-oil trade between the UAE and Sierra Leone stood at $152.3m in 2025, while transactions reached $113.4m between January and October 2026.

 Al Zeyoudi identified the UAE-Sierra Leone Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, signed in Abu Dhabi in February 2026, as a major step towards expanding trade and investment cooperation between the two countries.

 He said the agreement would strengthen private sector participation and create new opportunities for partnerships in priority sectors.

 The minister also identified energy, infrastructure, industry, food security, agriculture, minerals and natural resources, trade, logistics and digital transformation as areas with significant potential for cooperation between the UAE and West African countries.

 He stressed the need to channel investments into projects that create jobs, add value, facilitate knowledge transfer and strengthen local capacity.

 Al Zeyoudi also emphasised the importance of private sector participation and the role of financial and investment institutions in converting economic opportunities into viable projects.

 He called for stronger coordination among governments, improved regulatory frameworks and measures to facilitate trade and investment flows across the region.

 He added that a transparent, stable and competitive business environment was necessary to attract investors and accelerate regional economic integration.

 “The success of regional economic integration depends on moving from dialogue to implementation, and from identifying opportunities to launching projects. This requires clear mechanisms to monitor commitments and measure economic and developmental impact, so that the peoples of the region see tangible and sustainable results.”

 Al Zeyoudi reaffirmed the UAE’s commitment to working with Sierra Leone, other West African countries, regional and international organisations and the private sector to establish economic and development partnerships that promote shared prosperity.

 The WAIIS 2026 focused on four major areas: energy and green manufacturing; strategic minerals and natural resource development; agribusiness and food systems; and digital transformation and regional connectivity.

 The summit also featured an investment deals platform designed to connect projects with investors, financial institutions and development partners to translate investment opportunities into concrete projects and commitments.

The post UAE-West Africa trade hits $61.3bn in 2026 appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Jensen Huang and the future of Nvidia
description: I have never met Jensen Huang. Yet his departure from Nvidia has left me with an unexpected sense of personal loss. For those of us who advocate the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence, he represented something increasingly valuable: an engineer who could explain the machinery of the fut
content:
I have never met Jensen Huang. Yet his departure from Nvidia has left me with an unexpected sense of personal loss. For those of us who advocate the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence, he represented something increasingly valuable: an engineer who could explain the machinery of the future and make its possibilities seem tangible. His fall forces an uncomfortable question upon his admirers. How much of our confidence in a technology have we invested in one man’s character?

On November 12, 2026, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. It was an abrupt end to the leadership of a company he had co-founded 33 years earlier. The board appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and Harvey C. Jones as chair. The company will seek a permanent successor from within and outside the company.

The circumstances demand precision. On November 8, Huang publicly acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues. Separately, the board announced an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. At that stage, it said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised. That statement is neither a completed investigation nor proof of wrongdoing beyond what Huang admitted.

Reuters has reported on his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, and the suspicions of US authorities about her intelligence connections. Beijing has denied that she is a spy. The two Huangs are unrelated. Espionage allegations must remain allegations unless established by evidence and the appropriate proceedings. His resignation does not, by itself, prove that he knowingly assisted a foreign power.

None of those distinctions diminishes the seriousness of the crisis. A chief executive responsible for strategically important technology must exercise judgement that protects the institution as well as himself. But responsible commentary requires us to resist the temptation to turn a personal admission, a corporate investigation and national-security suspicions into a single, settled verdict.

Huang’s achievement remains extraordinary. Born in Taiwan in 1963, he spent part of his childhood in Thailand before moving to the United States as a boy. He studied electrical engineering at Oregon State University and later earned a master’s degree at Stanford. Before Nvidia, he worked at AMD and LSI Logic. His ascent was rooted in technical training and semiconductor experience, rather than celebrity.

In 1993, he founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The discussions at a Denny’s restaurant have become part of Silicon Valley folklore. Their ambition concerned computer graphics, especially gaming and multimedia. The company that would supply essential machinery for the AI revolution began by pursuing a more immediate challenge: making images on computer screens more compelling.

The important insight was that graphics required enormous numbers of calculations to be performed in parallel. The architecture developed for that purpose could serve other demanding computational tasks. Nvidia’s GPU milestone in 1999, followed by its introduction of CUDA in 2006, helped turn graphics hardware into a platform for scientific computing. CUDA gave programmers a practical route to using that processing power beyond graphics.

The significance became unmistakable in 2012, when AlexNet demonstrated the power of deep learning in image recognition using Nvidia GPUs. Huang did not invent neural networks or single-handedly create modern AI. His distinction was recognising the commercial and scientific importance of a computing approach, sustaining investment in it, and building an organisation capable of supplying it at scale.

That is a more substantial achievement than the familiar description of a man who sold chips during a gold rush. Nvidia built a platform around its processors. The combination of hardware, software and developer familiarity made it useful to customers and increasingly difficult to replace. Its subsequent rise to the world’s most valuable listed company reflected investors’ belief that it occupied a commanding position in the new computing economy.

Huang also became its most effective interpreter. The leather jacket, the stagecraft and the expansive keynotes gave a recognisable human face to an industry of bewildering complexity. He could connect engineers’ work with the ambitions of investors and governments. The advantage was considerable. So was the danger of allowing a corporation’s identity to become inseparable from its founder.

As recently as October  21, he was addressing Nvidia’s GTC conference in Berlin. There he presented an account of AI infrastructure that stretched from energy and computing systems to models and applications, while emphasising the need to secure increasingly autonomous AI agents.

This last point matters particularly to me. I took encouragement from the prospect that the industry supplying AI’s computational power was also investing in its control. Yet that hope requires technical accuracy. The announcement concerned Nvidia’s OpenShell Reference Architecture for Safe AI Agents, rather than a single GPU capable of guaranteeing that AI would never go rogue.

Nvidia describes a combination of software and hardware that can isolate agents, restrict their permissions and monitor their behaviour. Its Sentry framework runs on BlueField data-processing units, providing monitoring outside the agent’s own execution environment. Such architecture aims to make dangerous actions harder to carry out and easier to detect or stop.

These are vendor-described capabilities whose effectiveness must be tested in deployment.

Containment is valuable, but it is not a universal solution to AI safety. A system might remain within its technical permissions while producing misleading advice or pursuing a poorly specified objective. Security controls must therefore sit alongside evaluation, human accountability and careful decisions about where autonomy is appropriate. No product announcement should be mistaken for proof that humanity’s long-term risks have been resolved.

Nvidia now faces a related challenge in corporate form: demonstrating that its controls and capabilities survive the departure of the individual most closely associated with them. Kress, who joined in 2013, brings deep knowledge of its finances and operations. Jones brings technology-industry experience. Their immediate task should be to preserve execution while making the investigation credible. The public announcement establishes an interim arrangement and a search; it does not identify a permanent heir.

The board should resist the pressure to recruit a celebrity merely to reassure the market. Nvidia needs leadership able to retain exceptional engineers, coordinate complex production, sustain customer confidence and navigate geopolitical scrutiny. Investors should seek evidence that those responsibilities are shared across a capable team. Whether a suitable internal candidate or an outsider offers the better answer remains open.

The market reaction illustrates the cost of uncertainty. Reuters reported that Nvidia shares fell more than 12 per cent in early trading after the announcement, putting roughly $500bn of market value at risk at that point. That was an intraday indication, not a verified closing loss. The same report recorded gains in AMD and Broadcom, suggesting that some investors were considering competitive beneficiaries as well as wider industry risk.

A lasting global market shock is possible, but it is not inevitable. The transmission channels are straightforward. A fall in a heavily weighted company can depress equity indices and funds that track them. Customers might postpone commitments while they assess continuity. Suppliers could face uncertainty over orders. Tighter export restrictions, if imposed, could change the economics of access to major markets. These are scenarios, not outcomes that can already be attributed to the resignation.

The distinction between a loss of confidence and a loss of productive capacity is essential. A leadership crisis does not erase engineering knowledge, installed equipment or customers’ computing requirements. Equally, those assets cannot guarantee flawless execution. Nvidia’s vulnerability lies in the possibility that uncertainty will disrupt decisions, relationships and recruitment long enough for competitors to benefit.

The company’s future will turn on questions more useful than speculation about its next charismatic figurehead. Can it deliver its products reliably? Can it demonstrate disciplined oversight of sensitive commercial relationships? Will its customers continue to find its platform worth the price? Can the investigation proceed independently, with findings communicated responsibly? A convincing answer would allow Nvidia to emerge as a more durable institution. A defensive or evasive response would deepen the damage.

For Africa, this is also a lesson in technological dependence. Our universities, businesses and public institutions should build AI strategies around skills, suitable infrastructure and clear accountability. Admiration for a foreign technology leader is no substitute for the ability to evaluate suppliers, understand limitations and maintain control over consequential decisions. Sovereignty begins with competence.

In my work advocating responsible AI, I have stressed the importance of responsible human oversight. That principle must apply to the people governing technology companies as firmly as it applies to the systems those companies produce. A board cannot treat commercial success as an exemption from scrutiny. Nor should an admirer confuse technical brilliance with infallible personal judgement.

I remain grateful for what Huang and his colleagues have contributed to computing. Recognising that contribution does not require excusing his admitted conduct. Concern for his family need not become public intrusion. Respect for the investigation requires withholding conclusions it has not yet reached. A serious assessment of his legacy must hold all these thoughts together.

Do we need another hero? We need talented people with the courage to pursue difficult ideas. We also need institutions that can challenge them, constrain their mistakes and continue their work when they leave. The most reassuring future for AI is one in which responsibility is distributed, independently tested and enforceable.

My disappointment is real. So is my hope. It now rests more firmly on a demanding proposition: the institutions entrusted with powerful technology must be strong enough to outlast the people who made us believe in it.

Iroche is an Oxford-trained Artificial Intelligence Specialist and Researcher, and the founder and CEO of GenAI Learning Concepts Ltd

The post Jensen Huang and the future of Nvidia appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: APM fires back at Tinubu over Ibadan remarks
description:
The Allied Peoples’ Movement in Oyo State on Sunday slammed President Bola Tinubu for attacking the APM during the All Progressives Congress rally held at Mapo Hall in Ibadan, saying, “what the people of the country need is better living conditions and not grandstanding.”
