title: Trouble in House of God: Single-founder churches spark succession storm
description:
By Ebunoluwa Sessou & Nnamdi Ojiego 



The leadership dispute at the Fountain of Life Church, Lagos, following the death of its founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, has brought a difficult question facing many founder-led churches into public focus: Who takes charge when the person around whom a ministry
content:
By Ebunoluwa Sessou & Nnamdi Ojiego 

The leadership dispute at the Fountain of Life Church, Lagos, following the death of its founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, has brought a difficult question facing many founder-led churches into public focus: Who takes charge when the person around whom a ministry was built is no longer there?

The disagreement over the position of his son, Pastor Jimmy Odukoya, has moved from the church’s internal leadership structure to the courts, with competing claims over the late founder’s wishes, the church’s constitution and the authority of its Board of Trustees.

On November 17, a faction of the church’s trustees announced that Jimmy was no longer recognised as senior pastor.

The trustees said their decision followed a review of the church’s succession arrangements and a video recording made by the late Taiwo Odukoya in December 2021, in which he allegedly named Pastor Kunle Areogun as his preferred successor.

Odukoya’s wife, Pastor Bimbo, a co-founder of the church, had earlier died in a plane crash.

According to the trustees, the late founder proposed that Jimmy serve as Areogun’s administrative assistant and head of the church’s youth ministry.

They said the recording was made available to them in December 2025 and was not presented when Jimmy was appointed senior pastor in September 2023.

The trustees subsequently named Pastor Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader, pending consultations and the establishment of a substantive leadership structure.

Controversy over remarriage

The dispute came on the heels of Jimmy’s recent remarriage, which the trustees identified as one of their concerns about his continued leadership of the church.

Jimmy introduced his new wife, Mo Jasyme, to the congregation during a Sunday service on November 1, 2026, describing her as his wife and the church’s new first lady. The union was publicly blessed by Pastor Tunde Bakare, founder of the Citadel Global Community Church, who prayed for the couple during the service.

The marriage followed the end of Jimmy’s previous union with Oluwakemi Banjoko, whom he married in London in March 2013. The couple have two children. The circumstances surrounding the breakdown of that marriage have not been publicly established. During the introduction of his new wife, Jimmy said his first marriage had ended before he became senior pastor in September 2023.

The trustees, however, described the remarriage and its public blessing as contrary to the church’s teachings, the values of its founders and the standards expected of its spiritual leadership. They said the development had caused distress among members and brought the church into public controversy and disrepute. Their statement placed the marriage alongside the disagreement over the succession recording as grounds for their action against him.

The trustees subsequently named Pastor Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader, pending consultations and the establishment of a substantive leadership structure.

Jimmy and the church’s opposing leadership position rejected the announcement, insisting that his appointment in September 2023 was unanimously approved by the Board of Trustees and that those who announced his removal lacked the constitutional authority to do so.

The disagreement escalated when the Lagos State High Court, on Wednesday issued an interim order restraining Jimmy from presenting himself as the church’s senior pastor and spiritual head, and from interfering with its governance and activities.

The order was made ex parte while the case was adjourned until December 1.

Sealed

Meanwhile, the church, on Friday, dismissed reports that its premises had been sealed and announced that its regular Sunday service would hold at 9am, although its 2026 Thanksgiving Service had been postponed.

At the centre of the dispute are questions that extend beyond the personalities involved.

How should a church founded and led by one individual determine who succeeds that person?

Does a founder’s recorded preference override a later appointment made under the church’s constitution?

What role should family members, trustees, elders and other senior ministers play?

And how can a ministry preserve its identity while ensuring that leadership is transferred through a process accepted by its members?

For churches whose growth, public identity and authority have been closely associated with their founders, succession can involve spiritual, administrative, legal and family considerations.

Pattern

The experiences of other Nigerian churches show that there is no single pattern.

The Church of God Mission International, founded by Archbishop Benson Idahosa, offers an example of a founder’s widow taking over leadership.

Following his death in March 1998, his wife, Margaret Idahosa, succeeded him as presiding bishop.

She had been actively involved in the ministry before his death.

Their son, Bishop Faith Benson Idahosa, has also held leadership positions within the church’s institutions.

The transition at the Synagogue Church of All Nations (SCOAN) also brought a founder’s widow to the forefront.

After the death of Prophet T.B. Joshua in June 2021, his wife, Evelyn Joshua, emerged as the church’s leader.

The transition attracted public attention amid reports of disagreements over the church’s future.

The church denied that there was a succession battle and said it would follow its founder’s instructions.

In September 2021, the Federal High Court in Lagos affirmed Evelyn Joshua as a trustee of SCOAN after a petition to fill the vacancy created by her husband’s death.

A similar family transition occurred at New Anointing Ministries in Makurdi, founded by the late Rev. Godwin Ikyernum. Following his death in an automobile accident in March 1997, his wife, Hannah Ikyernum, assumed leadership.

The ministry is now led by their son, Pastor Joshua Ikyernum.

Accounts of the transition have also documented dissatisfaction among some of the founder’s former associates, with some reportedly leaving the ministry.

Succession without spouses, children as beneficiaries

Other churches have followed succession arrangements that did not depend on a founder’s spouse or children.

The leadership of the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG), founded by the late Rev. Josiah Akindayomi, passed to Pastor Enoch Adeboye in 1981.

The church’s account of the transition says Akindayomi communicated his choice of successor in a sealed pronouncement that was read after his burial.

Adeboye, who was not the founder’s biological son, subsequently became General Overseer.

At the Foursquare Gospel Church in Nigeria, leadership has also changed through an electoral process.

In July 2019, delegates elected Rev. Sam Aboyeji as the church’s fifth General Overseer, succeeding Rev. Felix Meduoye, who had completed an eight-year tenure. Aboyeji emerged through a contest involving other candidates, including Rev. Isaac Komolafe.

The Upper Room Baptist Church provides another example of an institutionally managed transition.

The church, which began in 1987 with 17 founding families, operates a governance structure involving a General Council, Trustees and a General Assembly. Pastor Oluleke Akinola succeeded its first General Overseer, Pastor Abiodun Longe, in 2004. After 21 years in office, Akinola handed over to Pastor Rufus Dada on December 31, 2024.

The Apostolic Church Nigeria also experienced a leadership transition through an election in February 2025, when Pastor Lawrence Oladele emerged as National Leader.

These examples illustrate the range of arrangements available to churches: Succession by a spouse or child, appointment of a designated successor, election by delegates and leadership transitions managed through established institutional structures.

 What Oyedepo, Adeboye, Kumuyi, others say

Some of Nigeria’s prominent church leaders have publicly addressed the question of succession.

Bishop David Oyedepo, founder of Living Faith Church Worldwide, popularly known as Winners’ Chapel, has said the church should not become a family inheritance.

In a 2020 sermon, he reportedly referred to succession provisions in the church’s governing document, The Mandate, which outlines a process for selecting a successor.

Under the procedure he described, when the presiding bishop reaches 70, he is expected to present three names to the Council of Priests for consideration.

The nominees are assessed against specified qualifications, with fresh names to be presented if none is found suitable.

Oyedepo’s sons, David Oyedepo Jnr and Isaac Oyedepo, have both held pastoral positions in the ministry.

Isaac later left to establish his own ministry in 2023.

Pastor Enoch Adeboye of RCCG also spoke about the issue in 2018, saying he was waiting for God to reveal his successor.

He drew comparisons with the biblical transitions from Elijah to Elisha and Moses to Joshua.

Pastor William Kumuyi, founder of Deeper Christian Life Ministry, dismissed speculation in June 2026 that he intended to hand the ministry to his biological children. He said the church belonged to Jesus Christ and was not a family inheritance.

The different positions show that succession remains a subject of concern even among living founders.

Some refer to formal procedures, others speak of divine direction, while some have publicly rejected the idea that their children should automatically take over.

 Why founders delay succession plans

To Rev. Toyin Kehinde, Senior Pastor of Agape Generation International Church, the difficulty surrounding succession in some churches goes beyond the identification of a replacement.

It touches on power, identity, spiritual authority, family interests and the survival of the institution.

He said some founders regard their ministries as assignments received directly from God, making discussions about succession emotionally difficult.

“Some founders may find it difficult to contemplate another person exercising the authority they have personally held for decades”, he added.

“Succession may therefore be interpreted as surrendering control rather than preparing the institution for continuity”.

Kehinde observed that the identity of some churches had become closely associated with their founders, from their names and doctrines to their public image and achievements.

In such circumstances, allowing another person to assume leadership could become a personal challenge for the founder.

“Another challenge is that founders may avoid naming successors because they fear that doing so could create competition among senior pastors, family members and other influential church leaders. Ironically, postponing the decision may create the very rivalry they are trying to prevent,” he said.

According to him, some founders possess exceptional preaching and evangelistic abilities but may not have the institutional management skills required to establish a sustainable leadership structure.

He said some also expect that God would raise a successor after their death.

While spiritual guidance remains important, he argued that relying entirely on an eventual emergence without a clear process could expose a church to avoidable disagreements.

 Automatically inherited leadership

Kehinde said a founder’s wife or children should not automatically inherit leadership simply because of their family relationship. The successor, he argued, should emerge through a credible process that takes account of spiritual maturity, competence and the church’s established procedures.

The question of whether a founder’s anointing or spiritual authority can pass to a child by birth is central to the debate.

Favour Amako, a pastor with Deeper Christian Life Ministry, said spiritual succession should not be confused with inheritance of property or family name.

“You can inherit property, you can inherit a name, you can even inherit a building. You cannot inherit anointing,” he said.

Amako argued that a church is not the personal property of its founder and should not automatically become a family inheritance.

He cited biblical examples of leaders who did not transfer their responsibilities to their biological children simply because of family ties.

However, he said there was nothing inherently wrong with a founder’s child or spouse succeeding them if that person had the calling, qualifications and support of the church’s recognised leadership structure.”A founder can have a preference, and we respect that. But once a church has a constitution, once it has trustees and a governance structure, that constitution is supreme. Nobody is above it, not even the founder,” he said.

On the Fountain of Life dispute, he maintained that the church’s constitution and established procedures should guide the resolution of the competing claims, rather than personal preference alone.

Amako also cautioned against assuming that a church has no succession arrangement simply because it has not made one public. He said some churches handle such matters among elders, trustees, spiritual fathers and other people entrusted with the ministry’s vision.

He nevertheless called for clear procedures that members and senior leaders could understand.

“No success without a successor. That is the truth. If we want Pentecostal churches to outlive their founders, we must stop running them like personal shops. We need clearly defined ways successors emerge. We need governing councils that actually govern, and procedures for selecting successors that everybody understands,” he said.

He pointed to the Catholic, Anglican and Methodist churches as examples of religious institutions whose leadership structures are not dependent on the continued presence of one founding personality.

 The place of constitutions and trustees

Pastor Olukayode Oyedepo, Lead Pastor of LoveSquad Church, Lagos, also called for clear succession plans backed by church constitutions and functioning governing bodies.

He identified ignorance of church administration, personal interests and fear of exposing alleged wrongdoing as some reasons founders may avoid putting succession arrangements in place.

According to him, some founders lack the administrative knowledge required to build structures that can operate independently of their personal authority.

Others, he said, may want to retain control because of family or personal interests.

He added that some founders regard their churches as personal businesses that should eventually pass to their children, while others may fear that a successor could uncover questionable decisions made under their leadership.

Oyedepo said churches should have constitutions, boards of trustees and management teams with clearly defined responsibilities.

Such structures, he argued, would help prevent disputes when a founder dies or becomes unable to continue leading.

He urged founders to identify and prepare successors early, rather than wait until old age or ill health makes the question urgent. He cited the Catholic Church’s established process for choosing its leaders as an example of institutional succession.

Vanguard News

The post Trouble in House of God: Single-founder churches spark succession storm appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: 2027: Tinubu slams ‘mediocre’ party in Oyo
description:

President Bola Tinubu yesterday took a swipe at Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, urging the people of the state to disregard opposition politicians and vote for the All Progressives Congress (APC) from top to bottom in the 2027 general elections.



Tinubu, who spo
content:
By Omeiza Ajayi & Adeola Badru

President Bola Tinubu yesterday took a swipe at Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, urging the people of the state to disregard opposition politicians and vote for the All Progressives Congress (APC) from top to bottom in the 2027 general elections.

Tinubu, who spoke at the APC presidential campaign rally at the historic Mapo Hall in Ibadan, also endorsed Senator Sharafadeen Alli as the party’s governorship candidate in the state.

The President, apparently referring to Makinde, who is the presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), dismissed opposition parties as incapable of providing effective leadership, describing them as mediocre.

He cautioned residents against being swayed by opposition parties, which he accused of seeking to take away what the people had.

“There is a party out there parading themselves. Please don’t mind them and don’t listen to them. They are only interested in clearing what you have. Vote for APC from top to bottom.

“And there is a party around that cannot hold anything; please don’t look at them; they are mediocre. Please don’t mind them and don’t listen to them. They are only interested in clearing what you have. Vote for APC from top to bottom,” he said.

The President urged the people to sustain their support for the APC, recalling that they had voted overwhelmingly for the party in the previous election.

“You voted overwhelmingly for APC last time. You must stay the course for the sake of progress, the prosperity of our country and the development of your children and great-grandchildren,” he said.

He described the APC as the people’s political platform, thanking them for their previous support and urging them to remain committed to the party.

“I just want to say thank you. Thank you for all you have been doing and all the support you have given to APC. APC is our party. It’s your party. Is it clear?”, he asked.

“Our future children must benefit from the hope of Nigeria,” he said, stressing the need to prioritise education and agriculture.

“We must give them the right education, invest in agriculture,” he added.

The President also assured residents of improved electricity supply, commending the Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, and his team for their efforts.

“You will see, and I guarantee you an improvement in electricity. Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe is really working hard with his team,” he said.

He further announced that the Federal Government had signed an agreement with China’s Yutong to reopen the old Leyland factory in Ibadan for the production of public transport vehicles and the establishment of an automobile assembly plant.

According to him, the initiative would revive industrial activities in the state and create opportunities for economic growth.

“For Oyo State, we have just signed an agreement with China’s Yutong to reopen the old Leyland factory in Ibadan. We are reopening it to produce public transport vehicles and establish an automobile assembly plant there. We will continue to bring industries. You will see progress and development,” he said.

“Now it is time to say thank you to all the elders, starting from Aremo Olusegun Osoba, Chief Bisi Akande, and others who have been holding the flag and supporting the party ever since. I salute sincerely,” he said.

He acknowledged the support of traditional rulers in Oyo State, including the Olubadan of Ibadanland, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, and the Soun of Ogbomoso, expressing confidence in their continued cooperation with the party.

The President also called on traditional rulers to encourage their subjects to participate in the forthcoming election, stressing the importance of mass turnout.

Oshiomhole tackles Makinde

Meanwhile, former Edo State Governor and Senator representing Edo North, Adams Oshiomhole, challenged Makinde to reconsider his political position and support Tinubu’s re-election bid, arguing that Nigeria needed leaders committed to sustaining the administration’s policies.

Speaking at the rally, Oshiomhole questioned Makinde’s call for a political reset, asking whether the governor intended to reverse what he described as beneficial policies of the Tinubu administration.

content:
South Korea’s education minister resigned Sunday over an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted ahead of the country’s key college entrance exams last week.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial college entrance exam known as the Suneung.

The annual nine-hour Suneung is widely seen as a ticket to prestigious universities, well-paid jobs and even better marriage prospects in the highly competitive country.

The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures — including blocking public Wi-Fi in testing areas and placing stickers over clothing buttons but Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin struggled to reassure the public, particularly after remarks he made three days before the exam.

“The exam concluded without any major incidents… However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X.

“Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.

President Lee Jae Myung has accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.

Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.”

His response quickly drew public backlash.

Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, where a vice minister instead announced the preventive measures.

Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through three emergency alerts sent by the government to identify smartphones that test takers had failed to hand over.

title: 55 Days to Polls: Opposition parties, APC at war over political attacks
description:
•Stakeholders warn of threat to democracy, ask candidates to rein in supporters



By Henry Umoru, John Alechenu, Luminous Jannamike & Deola Badru



In the build up to the 2027 general elections increasingly characterised by attacks on supporters of political parties, destruction of campaign materi
content:
•Stakeholders warn of threat to democracy, ask candidates to rein in supporters

By Henry Umoru, John Alechenu, Luminous Jannamike & Deola Badru

In the build up to the 2027 general elections increasingly characterised by attacks on supporters of political parties, destruction of campaign materials, intimidation and allegations of political thuggery, opposition parties and the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, have traded accusations over who is responsible for the growing violence.

The political atmosphere across the country 55 days to the polls is becoming increasingly charged, with fears that the situation could deteriorate further in the coming days if political leaders fail to rein in their supporters and caution their members against inflammatory statements and actions.

The APC had accused opposition parties of sponsoring violence and hiring thugs to disrupt political activities, particularly following the incident involving President Bola Tinubu during his visit to a mosque in Abuja for prayers.

Sponsoring violence

It claimed the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) are sponsoring violence, spreading misinformation and recruiting young Nigerians to disrupt its presidential campaign activities ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Dr Dele Alake, spokesperson for the APC Presidential Campaign Council, made the allegations in a statement against the backdrop of recent attacks and confrontations involving political parties and their supporters nationwide.

The statement came days after suspected political thugs disrupted an NDC town hall meeting in Ikeja, Lagos, on November 12, where the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, was expected to address supporters.

“To create the false narrative of citizens’ discontent against the President, the ADC and NDC now sponsor hoodlums, arm them with cudgels and banners, and commandeer them to chant ‘Bamaiyi’ at APC campaign rallies,” the statement said.

“The latest instance of this abhorrent and anti-democratic stunt was the desecration of an Abuja Mosque last Friday, where these thugs were mobilised to pelt the presidential motorcade with stones.

“Also concerning is how our party’s campaign billboards are being destroyed under cover of night by opposition-sponsored agents. This is unacceptable and antithetical to democratic ideals,” the campaign council added.

“Again, we call on the ADC and NDC leaders to stop the dangerous conscription of ignorant young Nigerians for unwholesome political activities that put their lives at risk, while those leaders’ own children luxuriate in splendour abroad”.

Violence

However, opposition parties, including the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC; Social Democratic Party, SDP; New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP; Action Democratic Party, ADP; Peoples Democratic Party, PDP; African Democratic Congress, ADC; and Labour Party, LP, in chats with Sunday Vanguard, have rejected the allegations, with some accusing the ruling party of encouraging violence through its rhetoric and actions.

While some parties have urged President Tinubu to call APC governors and other party chieftains to order, others have warned that reckless political statements, poverty, hunger and intolerance among political leaders are worsening the situation.

The National Publicity Secretary of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Osa Director, said the ruling party was looking for scapegoats rather than accepting responsibility for the atmosphere of violence allegedly created by its members.

Director said: “The APC led by President Tinubu said all is fair in politics. The APC members across the country saw this as a clarion call to arms. Evidence abound everywhere about their rhetoric of violence. Why turn around to blame the opposition parties. We think and know that the APC is clueless and rudderless, therefore they are looking for scapegoat to blame for their monumental failures.

“The NDC will continue to explore all legal and constitutional means to carry out its campaigns. Those who engage in violence are those who have nothing to campaign with.”

Threats to democracy

Similarly, the Social Democratic Party, SDP, described political violence as a serious threat to democracy, insisting that political actors must embrace peaceful campaigns and respect the rule of law.

The National Publicity Secretary of the SDP and Chairman, Media and Publicity Committee of the party’s National Campaign Council, Araba Rufus Aiyenigba, said political violence, whether during campaigns or at any other stage of the electoral process, was unacceptable.

He said: “Political violence during campaigns or in any form in the course of the electoral processes is highly condemnable and is considered a threat to democracy.

“Every Nigerian owes it a duty to the true interest of the nation and the good of our polity, to strongly promote and champion violence-free politicking and elections.

“As a nation, irrespective of tribe, religion, and region, we all gain more when an atmosphere of peace is engendered in our democracy and order pervades our political landscapes.

“The SDP is a frontline political party that prioritises discipline and code of conduct in our political operations and activities. We are reputed to have always been at the forefront of the promotion of the rule of law, as evident in the plethora of legal cases we have pursued and won, rather than treading the ignoble path of inciting violence or promoting breakdown of law and order.

“The SDP is acclaimed as a national political party that thrives on the supremacy of nationalistic ideas over the strength of might and the brute force to snatch power.

“Our campaigns have always been conducted on the higher pedestal of civilised and democratic orientation that thrives on winning power by the free will of the people, social justice, and not jungle justice.”

Intimidation

Aiyenigba called for stiffer sanctions against political actors and parties found promoting violence, warning that Nigerians must be allowed to exercise their democratic rights without intimidation.

“The SDP, therefore, calls for strong legislations and stiff sanctions against every political actor or any political party found to promote violence in whatever form.

“Our democracy must be truly democratic in form and practice. Nigerian people must have the freedom to exercise their fundamental rights, free of any form of intimidation or harassment.

“That is what guarantees the survival of our democracy and enhances national stability, particularly as we enter the 2027 general elections,” he said.

Intolerance

For the New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP, the growing violence is partly a consequence of intolerance among political leaders and the worsening economic situation in the country.

The National Chairman of the party, Dr Agbo Major, said political parties must exercise restraint, particularly at a time when the country was already divided along ethnic and religious lines.

Major said: “It’s an unfortunate situation but we can only insist that the political parties exercise restraint. We are at trying moments dangerously divided along ethnic and religious lines.

‘Political leaders must be careful’

“The so-called bigger political parties must be careful and desist from encouraging violence. My party, the New Nigeria Peoples Party is for peaceful election.

“Violence is increasing due to intolerance from political leaders and the large scale poverty that is on the increase on daily basis. The people are angry, there is hunger everywhere.

“We are aggressively talking to our members to be peaceful and orderly as the election activities unfold. We must have a country that we will call ours.”

Also blaming the ruling party for the worsening political atmosphere, the Action Democratic Party, ADP, said the APC must accept responsibility for the consequences of its political rhetoric and alleged misuse of public resources.

Remarks

The National Publicity Secretary of the ADP, Dr Sani Dawop, argued that the President’s earlier remark that all was fair in politics had contributed to the atmosphere of hostility.

Dawop said: “If you remember, it is the President that said all is fair in politics so how can it turn around that it is the opposition that is doing that. The opposition political parties have very clear position they want to wrest power from the ruling party at whatever level whether at the state level or in the assemblies or at the presidency level.

“You don’t also forget that the ruling party has been using government resources to inaugurate campaign council of APC, using government property, government offices, government resources in government houses which is an anathema, this is very wrong. If it is a political gathering, it shouldn’t be sponsored with public funds, members of the party should contribute money to do that.

“And in this case we have seen where even the opposition party has been denied facilities, denied even space for campaign, the kind of exorbitant fees that are charged and refusing opposition parties space to even mount their billboards, space in media organisations owned by governments in the ruling parties they are denied even media coverage. This is not democracy.

“I mean for God’s sake let’s call a spade a spade, I don’t think the opposition is the one that is doing it, it is really the ruling party and I think the hardship that Nigerians are going through is what is making Nigerians to hate the APC, so terribly. These people are living on government funds, they don’t know what Nigerians are going through.”

Campaigns

He also expressed concern over the alleged expenditure on campaign vehicles at a time when public institutions, particularly hospitals, were facing serious shortages of essential equipment.

Dawop said: “Can you imagine launching campaigns, buying brand new vehicles when even government departments, government offices lack these vehicles, N120 million, N150 million SUV whereas our hospitals lack ambulances and you think Nigerians will be happy. I think Nigerians are venting their anger on the ruling party.”

On the measures being taken by his party to prevent violence, the ADP spokesman said the party was law-abiding and did not support violence from any political camp.

He, however, warned that no political party had a monopoly of violence, stressing the need for all parties to avoid actions that could provoke retaliation.

“I generally do not support violence whether violence against the ruling party or the ruling party unleashing violence against the opposition party and as a political party, we do not also support this position. We want peaceful democracy, we want peaceful campaigns and elections. After all, why do we sign the peace agreement when we know we are going to violate it,” he said.

Dawop further recalled the peaceful transfer of power by former President Goodluck Jonathan in 2015, urging Tinubu to demonstrate similar democratic commitment.

He said: “I have said it before that the moment President Tinubu and former Vice President Atiku refused to sign, refused to show up at the signing ceremony for the peace agreement, I sensed that there was going to be danger because even President Goodluck was personally present with then President Buhari, the major opposition candidate, they were all around and signed the agreement.

“And after the elections Goodluck has set his world record in Nigeria for a peaceful handover and this has given former President Goodluck tremendous respect within Nigerians and within the Committee of nations.

“And I hope that President Tinubu will do the same thing, that when he loses this election, he should hand over peacefully, go and rest so that Nigerians can respect him, despite the challenges he has had in running an administration that has caused a lot of hardship for Nigerians.”

Inflammatory rhetoric

He appealed to political parties to focus on issues rather than personalities, insisting that the country should not be sacrificed on the altar of political ambition.

The Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, on its part, warned that reckless political statements, inflammatory rhetoric and retaliatory actions by politicians were contributing significantly to the growing tension ahead of the elections.

The National Publicity Secretary of the party, Mr Jungudo Haruna Mohammed, said political leaders must stop trading accusations and accept responsibility for the worsening political atmosphere.

Mohammed said: “Our utterances, actions, retaliations, speeches and statements are contributing to the tensions we are witnessing.

“Apportioning blame, as I said, is not the way out. Rather, political leaders across party lines must take responsibility for what is happening.

“We must do everything possible to ensure that these elections are conducted in a peaceful atmosphere.

“We must look back at history and remember that situations like this are often what invite military intervention. I do not think this is a good time for Nigeria’s democracy to be truncated again.

“If we fail to act responsibly, become more patriotic and stop treating elections as a do-or-die affair, we will be doing ourselves a great disservice.” The PDP spokesman urged political parties to caution their candidates and supporters against violence, while calling on security agencies to remain professional and impartial.

He said: “Every political actor and party must call their supporters and candidates to order and encourage them to preach and promote peace. That is the only way we can reduce some of these tensions.

“Security agencies, on their part, must be professional, very professional, in the discharge of their duties.

“For our part, as the PDP, we have been doing very well. We have made concerted efforts to promote peace and urge our supporters not to resort to violence in their quest for political mandates, relevance and support.”

However, the African Democratic Congress, ADC, accused President Tinubu of fuelling political tension by allegedly failing to call APC governors and party chieftains to order.

The party’s Presidential Campaign Council, ADC-PCC, questioned why the President’s condemnation of political violence appeared to be directed at opposition parties rather than members of his own party.

The council’s Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, said the President’s alleged failure to condemn inflammatory statements by APC governors and chieftains was worsening the situation.

Ologbondiyan said: “’All Is Fair in Politics’ is not the language of a Head of State. It is the language of political desperation and an open licence for thuggery, ballot snatching, intimidation and bloodshed.

“From Edo to Cross River, Gombe to Lagos, and Kebbi to Kaduna, Nigerians have witnessed attacks on opposition gatherings, destruction of campaign materials and the brutalisation of innocent supporters, allegedly by APC-sponsored thugs.

“Yet, Mr President has not considered it necessary to call his governors and party members to order.”

The ADC-PCC spokesman challenged Tinubu to explain why his administration had allegedly failed to condemn threats against opposition supporters and inflammatory statements by APC officials.

The council demanded that the President publicly retract his remark, call APC governors and party officials accused of inciting violence to order, and direct security agencies to protect Nigerians without political bias.

Commitment

It also urged Tinubu to make an unequivocal commitment to peaceful elections, recalling former President Goodluck Jonathan’s declaration that no political ambition was worth the blood of any Nigerian.

The council said: “Nigeria belongs to all of us. No political ambition is worth the blood of any Nigerian.

“If former President Goodluck Jonathan could make that profound declaration in 2015, President Tinubu has no excuse not to say so and demonstrate the sincerity of his commitment to peace in 2026.”

The Labour Party, LP, has also condemned the rising politically motivated violence, describing it as a direct threat to democracy and warning that failure to address the trend could derail the electoral process.

The National Publicity Secretary of the party, Ken Asogwa, urged political parties to exercise restraint in their conduct and utterances, noting that the political atmosphere was already charged.

Asogwa said the Labour Party would not be drawn into politics of bitterness, personal attacks and violence, adding that its candidates had been directed to focus on issue-based campaigns.

Personal attacks

He said: “For us in the Labour Party, all our candidates are bound by our code of ensuring issue-based campaigns devoid of personal attacks, insults and inflammatory rhetoric.”

He maintained that elections should be about competing ideas and programmes capable of addressing the country’s challenges, rather than insults, intimidation and violence.

According to him, candidates of the party have been directed to focus on issues affecting the daily lives of Nigerians, including the economy, security, education, health, jobs and good governance.

Asogwa said: “We need to first have a nation before we can contest for elective offices.”

He urged security agencies to be proactive, impartial and firm in dealing with anyone found promoting violence, regardless of political affiliation.

The LP spokesman also called on the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, civil society organisations, the media and other stakeholders to join efforts to promote peace and tolerance ahead of the elections.

With opposition parties increasingly accusing the ruling party of creating an atmosphere conducive to political violence, and the APC insisting that opposition elements are responsible for attacks and disruptions, concerns are mounting over the ability of political actors to sustain peaceful campaigns as the 2027 elections approach.

Prosecution

Meanwhile, the growing concern over political violence has also attracted the attention of prominent socio-political organisations, with the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, condemning the escalating attacks and demanding the arrest and prosecution of perpetrators and their sponsors.

In a statement issued by its National Publicity Secretary, Comrade Jare Ajayi, the organisation warned that the increasing resort to thuggery, intimidation and inflammatory political rhetoric ahead of the 2027 general elections posed a serious threat to Nigeria’s democratic process.

Supporters

Afenifere expressed concern over reported attacks on political figures, campaign convoys and supporters in different parts of the country, including the reported attack on President Bola Tinubu’s motorcade shortly after he observed Jumu’ah prayers at the Central Mosque, Abuja, on Friday, November 13, 2026.

The organisation also condemned the attack on supporters of the Accord Party governorship candidate in Oyo State, Alhaji Oriyomi Hamzat, around Molete, Ibadan, which reportedly claimed the life of a 40-year-old supporter, Azeez Tajudeen.

It further cited attacks on the convoy of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) vice-presidential candidate, Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso, in Bichi, Kano State; the reported assault on the convoy of the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, in Calabar, Cross River State; and disruptions of political gatherings in Sokoto, Kebbi and Lagos states.

Jonathan

Afenifere recalled former President Goodluck Jonathan’s warning at the 2026 Goodluck Jonathan Foundation Peace Conference in Abuja against political parties operating like rival cult groups, as well as his caution against recruiting young Nigerians to perpetrate political violence.

The organisation also referenced warnings by former Head of State, General Abdulsalami Abubakar, and the National Peace Committee’s Co-convener, Most Rev. Matthew Kukah, over inflammatory political campaigns, following reports of about 60 election-related incidents recorded across the country within a month.

Highlighting the legal implications of electoral violence, Afenifere reminded political parties, candidates and their sponsors that recruiting, organising or financing political thugs constituted a criminal offence under Nigerian law.

Citing Sections 227 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, and Sections 78, 92 and 93 of the Electoral Act, the organisation called for the strict enforcement of existing laws against political violence.

Desperate politicians

Ajayi said: “The provisions of the laws are quite clear. But impunity persists because sponsors of violence are rarely brought to book.”

He urged political leaders to immediately call their supporters to order, while appealing to Nigerian youths not to allow themselves to be used as instruments of violence by desperate politicians.

“Nigerian youths must refuse to be used as cannon fodders by desperate politicians whose own children are safely tucked away from harm,” he warned.

Afenifere called on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), the Nigeria Police Force and the judiciary to move beyond public condemnations and ensure the prompt arrest and prosecution of those responsible for electoral violence.

The organisation insisted that accountability must extend beyond foot soldiers to individuals and groups who finance, organise and deploy political thugs, warning that failure to decisively address the menace could undermine the credibility of the 2027 elections and Nigeria’s democratic stability.

content:
The Federal Government has announced 19 vacancies for Nigerians at the African Space Agency and the General Secretariat of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, with application deadlines running from November 25 to December 24, 2026.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs disclosed this in two separate vacancy announcements dated Friday, November 20, 2026, which were signed by the ministry’s spokesperson, Oluwafemi Adeniyi, and shared on its official Facebook page on Saturday.

In the announcement on the African Space Agency, the ministry said the organisation was recruiting for five positions at its headquarters in Cairo, Egypt.

It stated that “interested and qualified Nigerians are encouraged to visit the official website of the Agency at https://africanspaceagency.org for more information on eligibility criteria and application procedures.”

The five vacancies are:

Director, Corporate Services (D-1) – Deadline: December 10, 2026.

Director-General, African Space Agency (D-2) – Deadline: December 10, 2026.

Head of Legal Affairs (Grade P-5) – Deadline: December 10, 2026.

Senior Finance Officer (P3) – Deadline: November 25, 2026.

Senior Human Resources Officer (P3) – Deadline: November 25, 2026.

The ministry also announced 14 vacancies at the General Secretariat of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The positions are:

Director-General of Political Affairs.

Director, Administration Department.

Director, Information Department.

Director, Conference Department.

Director, Muslim Communities and Minorities.

Director, African Affairs.

Director, European Affairs and International Organisations.

Head of Human Resources (PP2).

Professional Officer, Human Resources (PP2).

Professional Officers, Administration Department (P2).

Director, Peace, Security and Mediation Unit.

Chief of HRC Office – IUT.

Registrar – IUT.

Deputy Internal Auditor – IUT.

The ministry said the deadlines for the OIC vacancies “range from 29 November to 24 December 2026.”

It added that “interested and qualified Nigerians are encouraged to visit the OIC’s official vacancy portal at https://www.oic-oci.org/en/vacancies for more information on eligibility criteria, application procedures, and specific deadlines.”

title: 2027: Fresh alarm over political violence
description:
•Economic experts list how violence drives more Nigerians into poverty, scares investors
•85 killed in October as political tension mounts

By Omoniyi Salaudeen
Nigeria is entering another election season in a familiar way — with skirmishes, threats and intimidation as political parties mobilise sup
content:
•Economic experts list how violence drives more Nigerians into poverty, scares investors

•85 killed in October as political tension mounts

By Omoniyi Salaudeen

Nigeria is entering another election season in a familiar way — with skirmishes, threats and intimidation as political parties mobilise supporters and prepare for the battle ahead. But election violence is not merely a threat to a peaceful vote. It strikes at the heart of democracy itself: the ability of the state to guarantee the freedom and security on which multiparty politics rests.

More troubling, however, is the growing realisation that political violence carries consequences far beyond the electoral arena. It can undermine investor confidence, trigger capital flight, weaken the national currency, disrupt economic activities and ultimately deepen the hardship confronting ordinary Nigerians.

The warning is no longer abstract. On November 15, the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE) warned that rising political violence could trigger capital flight and weaken the naira. In its policy brief, Political Violence and Institutional Neutrality: Safeguarding Investor Confidence Ahead of the 2027 Elections, the organisation said: “The growing incidence of politically induced violence, intimidation and inflammatory rhetoric raises serious concerns about the implications for economic stability and investor confidence.”

Investors do not necessarily wait for elections to turn bloody before reconsidering their exposure to a country. They respond to early warning signals that suggest political instability, uncertainty over government policies and the possibility of disruptions to economic activities.

CPPE put it bluntly: “Political violence is not merely a threat to democratic governance; it constitutes a significant economic risk with far-reaching consequences.”

That is the real cost of election skirmishes. A thug disrupting a political rally in one state does not merely frighten voters in that locality. He sends a troubling signal to a factory owner in Lagos, a farmer in Benue and a fund manager in London that Nigeria may be struggling to guarantee the stability required for productive investments.

Beyond the immediate threat of capital flight, the Chief Executive Officer of CPPE, Dr Muda Yusuf, explained in a telephone discussion with Sunday Sun how political uncertainty and election-induced violence could undermine macroeconomic stability and worsen the living conditions of ordinary Nigerians.

According to him, although it may be difficult to establish a direct causal relationship between the current exchange-rate pressure and political developments, electioneering expenditure and capital flight remain possible contributing factors. “There are a number of possible factors that can put pressure on the naira. If you look at what is happening to the exchange rate, there is already pressure on the naira. But it is difficult to say the exact cause. This may be as a result of capital flight, or as a result of electioneering spending. Those are the two possibilities,” he explained.

Yusuf’s argument goes beyond the immediate impact of violence. He noted that political transition periods are traditionally associated with uncertainty, particularly among investors who may be apprehensive about the direction of government policies after an election. Such uncertainty can encourage capital-flow reversals even before any actual breakdown of law and order.

“But the point I’m making is that usually, political transition periods normally come with some level of uncertainty. So those things normally increase the risk of capital flow reversals because people are not sure exactly how things will move. Capital flight is not only because of the issue of violence, but because they don’t know what will happen to government policy. Violence is a factor, policy risk is a factor, political risk is a factor,” he said.

His qualification is important. It would be misleading to attribute every movement in the exchange rate to political violence when several economic and external factors are at play. Nevertheless, the danger is that escalating political tension could compound existing vulnerabilities and undermine some of the gains recorded through ongoing economic reforms.

Yusuf acknowledged that investor confidence and macroeconomic stability are among the gains of the current reform programme, warning that an escalation of violence could jeopardise those gains.

The ultimate victims, however, would not necessarily be the political actors or wealthy investors who could move their resources elsewhere. They would be ordinary Nigerians whose purchasing power is already under pressure. “If the macroeconomic environment becomes unstable in terms of swirling inflation — there is a very strong relationship between the exchange rate and inflation rate. Inflation affects cost of living, it affects welfare, it affects purchasing power. So it will affect macroeconomic stability,” he warned.

To put it more succinctly, the consequences of political violence could travel from the campaign ground to the foreign-exchange market and eventually to the neighbourhood market where families struggle to afford food, transportation and other necessities. A weaker naira can increase the cost of imported inputs, production and distribution, with the resulting pressure eventually passed on to consumers.

Yusuf nevertheless believes that the extent and duration of the economic consequences would depend considerably on the credibility of the electoral process.

“If the electoral process is credible, free and fair, normalcy will return soon after the elections,” he said, urging all critical stakeholders to abide by the rules and ensure a credible electoral contest.

This is a significant point. Political uncertainty is not necessarily permanent. A transparent election, accepted by the contestants and supported by credible institutions, can restore confidence and encourage investors to maintain or expand their commitments. Conversely, a disputed election accompanied by violence and institutional manipulation could prolong uncertainty and make economic recovery more difficult.

Not everyone, however, shares the apprehension that the approaching general election could degenerate into widespread violence or trigger serious capital flight.

APC chieftain and former Ogun State Deputy Governor, Senator Gbenga Kaka, dismissed the fears, arguing that the present political atmosphere is considerably calmer than what the country experienced during previous election cycles.

“We have had more volatile election campaigns in this country than the current one. And I don’t foresee any serious violence, other than these skirmishes, ahead of the 2027 general election,” he said.

Kaka pointed to the relatively peaceful conduct of party primaries and what he described as the subdued nature of current electioneering activities as reasons for his optimism. “We have had primaries, and there was no bloodshed accompanying them. Even the ongoing electioneering has not assumed the momentum expected of it. Beyond some billboards here and there, there is not much activity going on as it used to be. Many of the opposition candidates have gone to bed to sleep,” he added.

He also dismissed the suggestion that the current political atmosphere had created sufficient grounds for investors to panic, arguing that the foreign-exchange market was stabilising and that security agencies remained capable of containing isolated incidents.

“I have not seen any serious violence recorded so far, and I don’t envisage any, talk less of one that would affect investors. Besides, foreign exchange is being stabilised. So there is nothing yet to warrant the anxiety people are trying to generate,” he added.

While acknowledging the existence of occasional skirmishes, Kaka maintained that they should be treated as warning signals rather than evidence of an impending breakdown of security. “If anybody refuses to campaign till the election comes and resorts to violence, he will face the music. By the time they make a scapegoat of one or two, others will refrain from violent activities,” he said, expressing confidence in the capacity of security operatives to contain potential threats.

His position provides a counterpoint to the concerns raised by CPPE. Yet, the absence of widespread violence at this stage should not be mistaken for a guarantee of peaceful elections. Campaign activities will intensify, political competition will become fiercer, and the stakes will rise as parties approach the actual voting period. The appropriate response, therefore, is neither to exaggerate the threat nor to dismiss the warning signs, but to ensure that security institutions are adequately prepared to prevent isolated incidents from escalating.

According to available reports, October alone recorded at least 835 security-related deaths — the highest monthly toll of this campaign season. For many communities, insecurity is not an abstract political argument. It means bandits on farm roads, kidnappers on highways and political thugs disrupting rallies. All of these developments reinforce the perception that the state is struggling to protect its citizens.

That is why the warning from Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele on November 17 matters. He said negative narratives about Nigeria have become an economic problem in themselves, pushing investors away and accelerating the Japa syndrome. He also acknowledged the disconnect between official inflation figures and the everyday experiences of Nigerians who continue to grapple with the high cost of bread, milk, transportation and other essentials.

When citizens do not believe that the state can protect their lives and property, it becomes increasingly difficult to convince them that the economy is on a sustainable path to recovery.

 CPPE warned that this cycle could become self-reinforcing: “Political competition is a legitimate feature of democracy. However, when it degenerates into violence, institutional manipulation and disregard for due process, the consequences extend beyond politics to investment decisions, business operations, employment and economic growth.”

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) did not specifically warn about election violence, but its assessment underscores the economic vulnerability that makes insecurity particularly dangerous. In its 2026 Article IV Consultation, the Fund said: “Insecurity takes a heavy human toll, and impacts investment, agriculture, and oil production.”

It also warned that reform momentum could slow as elections approach, as politicians face pressure for higher spending. Taken together, the CPPE and IMF assessments describe a country that is both politically vulnerable and economically exposed.

Electioneering promises

Against this background, security has inevitably become a major component of the political campaigns ahead of 2027. The leading presidential contenders agree on one fundamental issue: Nigeria cannot achieve sustainable economic growth without addressing its worsening security challenges. Where they differ is in their proposed approaches, priorities and capacity to deliver.

In his 109-page manifesto, From Reform to Prosperity: Agenda 2027–2031, launched on November 10, President Bola Tinubu promises 78,000 additional security personnel, comprising 50,000 police officers and 28,000 military recruits, alongside 30,150 NSCDC personnel. His proposals also include four new Army divisions in Makurdi, Ilorin, Jalingo and Benin City, body cameras and a police-to-citizen ratio of 1:400.

The strength of the proposal lies in its specificity and emphasis on expanding the country’s security architecture. However, the central question for voters is whether the administration can translate these promises into measurable improvements, having already spent a considerable part of its first term battling insecurity.

His manifesto itself concedes that the work is far from complete. Voters will therefore demand explanations about the gaps in the existing security framework and how the proposed recruitment and expansion will address them.

Peter Obi, running with Rabiu Kwankwaso, offers a different proposition. Rather than emphasising numerical targets for recruitment, his campaign places considerable emphasis on intelligence-driven operations, community-based security and decisive leadership. He has promised to declare a security emergency and personally visit conflict zones to assess situations and demonstrate leadership.

His recent visit to Yelewata in Benue State and promise of an agricultural emergency underscore his argument that security and economic productivity are inseparable. His proposition is that farmers must first be protected before the country can expect a meaningful improvement in food production and prices.

The strength of this approach is its recognition that insecurity is not simply a military problem but also a threat to livelihoods, food security and national development. Its weakness, however, is the need for greater clarity on the institutional arrangements, funding and operational framework required to translate the promises into results.

Atiku Abubakar makes perhaps the most ambitious promise: to end insecurity within one year. “I will not take more than one year to end it. We will recruit additional security personnel and provide them with the necessary equipment. We will also provide adequate funding to support youths to establish businesses,” he told BBC Hausa.

His argument is fundamentally economic: expanding employment opportunities and supporting young entrepreneurs would reduce the attraction of banditry and other criminal activities among vulnerable youths. He also advocates a regional security response through the revival of ECOMOG and efforts to bring Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso back into ECOWAS.

The strength of this proposition is its recognition that insecurity is both a security and an economic problem. Its weakness is the ambitious one-year deadline for resolving a crisis that has persisted for more than a decade. His proposal to restore fuel and electricity subsidies also raises questions about fiscal sustainability, particularly against the background of projections that debt servicing could consume as much as 72 per cent of government revenue by 2030.

On paper, Tinubu offers structure, Obi offers leadership, while Atiku offers speed. But voters in Benue, Zamfara and Plateau are unlikely to be persuaded by manifestos alone. Their most immediate concern is whether they can return to their farms without fear, travel safely on highways and receive protection from security agencies when threatened.

How violence makes hardship worse

The economic consequences of insecurity and political violence are not difficult to identify. CPPE explained that “political violence could create investment uncertainty, discourage new investments, delay expansion plans and increase the risk premiums demanded by investors.”

The first casualty is agricultural production. When rural roads become unsafe, farmers in Benue, Plateau, Zamfara, Kaduna, Niger and Borno are forced to reduce cultivation or abandon their farms altogether. This affects food supply, increases pressure on prices and deepens the hardship of households already struggling with the cost of living.

That is why the reported food inflation rate of 19.13 per cent in October, despite the decline in headline inflation to 14.06 per cent, remains a source of concern. The projection that 34.7 million Nigerians could face acute food insecurity in 2026 further underscores the urgency of addressing the security challenges affecting agricultural production.

Second, transportation and distribution networks suffer. Clashes, roadblocks and attacks on highways disrupt supply chains and market access. Traders and transport operators are compelled to spend more on security, take alternative routes or suspend operations altogether. These additional costs eventually find their way into the prices consumers pay.

Third, investor confidence suffers, with possible consequences for the foreign-exchange market. CPPE warned that “prolonged political instability can weaken investor sentiment, trigger portfolio outflows and intensify foreign-exchange volatility.”

This concern is particularly relevant given the structure of Nigeria’s capital inflows. Available figures indicate that 85 per cent of the country’s $23.22 billion capital inflows in 2025 came from portfolio investment rather than foreign direct investment. In the first quarter of 2026, portfolio investment reportedly accounted for 95.1 per cent of inflows, while foreign direct investment represented only 1.3 per cent.

Unlike investments in factories, infrastructure and other productive assets, portfolio investments can be withdrawn relatively quickly when investors perceive heightened risks. A combination of political uncertainty, policy unpredictability and insecurity could therefore expose the economy to sudden capital reversals.

This is where Yusuf’s warning about the relationship between exchange-rate instability and inflation becomes particularly relevant. When investors withdraw funds and foreign-exchange pressures intensify, the consequences can extend to the prices of imported goods, production inputs and essential commodities. The resulting inflation erodes household incomes and weakens purchasing power.

Thus, the economic burden of election violence is not confined to the wealthy investor who moves capital elsewhere. It is ultimately transferred to the ordinary citizen who must pay more for food, transportation, healthcare and other necessities.

Breaking the cycle

If 2027 is to be different, three things must happen before election day, not after. First, political parties must demonstrate a genuine commitment to peaceful campaigns by disowning violence in practice rather than merely issuing statements condemning it. A party that sponsors thugs to disrupt a rival’s rally has already communicated a troubling message about its attitude towards democratic competition and the rule of law.

Political leaders must also rein in their supporters, avoid inflammatory rhetoric and accept that the legitimacy of an electoral victory depends on the credibility of the process through which it is obtained.

Second, institutions must act proactively. INEC must demonstrate its capacity to conduct a credible election, while security agencies must show that their responsibility is to protect all citizens and political actors, irrespective of party affiliation. The police must be seen to protect voters rather than VIPs, while the courts must demonstrate their readiness to dispense electoral justice without unnecessary delays.

Swift investigation and prosecution of electoral offenders would send a stronger message than the numerous peace accords that political parties routinely sign ahead of elections but often disregard when the contest becomes intense.

Third, citizens must refuse to be divided along political and ethnic lines. The farmer in Benue, the trader in Onitsha, the technology worker in Lagos and the student in Sokoto are not enemies. They are all vulnerable to the consequences of insecurity, economic instability and poor governance.

Ultimately, the argument is not that every political disagreement will trigger capital flight or that every campaign skirmish will destabilise the naira. As Yusuf rightly observed, several factors influence exchange-rate movements, and it would be difficult to establish a direct connection between a particular political incident and a specific economic outcome. But that uncertainty should not diminish the importance of preventing violence. It should instead reinforce the need to manage political risks before they become economic liabilities.

Nigeria does not lack security proposals or economic reform programmes. What it urgently needs is institutional credibility, political responsibility and public trust. Trust is built not at campaign rallies but in the quieter moments when a policeman refuses a bribe, a court delivers a fair judgment, a political rally ends without violence and a farmer returns from his field alive. It is also built when electoral institutions demonstrate neutrality and political leaders accept the outcome of a credible contest.

If Nigeria can protect these moments, it will not merely have a peaceful election. It will have taken a significant step towards restoring investor confidence, strengthening democratic institutions and creating the conditions for the prosperity all the presidential candidates promise.

If it cannot, whoever emerges victorious in 2027 will inherit not just a country struggling with insecurity and economic hardship, but a deeper crisis of confidence. And no number of additional soldiers, new military divisions or elaborate campaign manifestos will be sufficient to resolve it.

title: UNICEF urges governments to act on children’s demands
description:
By Hadiza Yusuf



The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has urged governments to translate children’s recommendations into concrete actions through policies, budgetary allocations and programmes that protect their rights and improve their welfare.







The Chief of UNICEF Field Office, Kano
content:
By Hadiza Yusuf

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has urged governments to translate children’s recommendations into concrete actions through policies, budgetary allocations and programmes that protect their rights and improve their welfare.

The Chief of UNICEF Field Office, Kano, Shafeeq Ur-Rehman, made the call at the Zonal Children’s Summit organised to mark the 2026 World Children’s Day in Kano.

Ur-Rehman, who was represented by the Officer-in-Charge of the field office, Dr. Serekeberehan Seyoum Deres, said children from Kano, Jigawa and Katsina states had identified critical issues affecting their lives and well-being.

He urged commissioners and senior government officials from the three states to give serious consideration to the children’s concerns and ensure their recommendations informed decisions in their respective ministries and agencies.

“But I urge you to do more than listen today: Take the children’s recommendations back to your ministries and agencies, and let them shape your budgets, policies and programmes,” he said.

He added that the children would hold government officials accountable for commitments made at the summit.

The UNICEF official stressed that children’s rights must be protected at all times, noting that every child deserved equal opportunities to survive, learn, live in safety and have their voices heard.

“Every child deserves the right to survive, learn, be protected and have their voice heard, regardless of gender, ability or circumstance,” he said.

He said UNICEF would sustain its collaboration with governments, communities and young people in Kano, Jigawa and Katsina to ensure that no child was left behind, particularly girls, children with disabilities, out-of-school children and those living in hard-to-reach communities.

Also speaking, Hajiya Aisha Albasu, who represented the Chairman of the State Universal Basic Education Board (SUBEB), Alhaji Yusuf Kabir, said the Kano State Government remained committed to promoting and protecting children’s rights.

She said the government would continue to work with relevant agencies and development partners to ensure children had access to quality education, healthcare, protection and other essential services needed for their growth and development.

Speaking on behalf of the children, Alamin Umar and Asma’u Anka raised concerns over alleged cases of abuse involving pupils in schools.

They called for stronger measures to protect students from all forms of violence, urging the government and relevant authorities to provide safe learning environments where children could study without fear of abuse or intimidation.

The children also appealed to the government to provide school buses to ease transportation challenges faced by students, as well as more classroom seats and improved learning facilities to create a conducive environment for effective teaching and learning.

title: How Nigeria can shape global narrative – Ex-UN official
description:
Former United Nations Under-Secretary-General, Prof. Ibrahim Gambari, has urged the Federal Government to invest heavily in Nigeria’s media institutions, diplomatic infrastructure and cultural industries to shape its international image and counter foreign-defined narratives.
Gambari made the call o
content:
Former United Nations Under-Secretary-General, Prof. Ibrahim Gambari, has urged the Federal Government to invest heavily in Nigeria’s media institutions, diplomatic infrastructure and cultural industries to shape its international image and counter foreign-defined narratives.

Gambari made the call on Friday while delivering a keynote address at the inaugural Annual Diplomacy Day, held alongside the presentation of a book titled Weapons of Mass Manipulation: State Media, Global Influence and the New Diplomacy of Power, by Dr Mkpe Abang.

Gambari further warned that Nigeria and other African countries risked remaining on the margins of global decision-making if powerful Western countries and other international actors continued to determine how the continent is portrayed, understood and perceived worldwide.

He said the country could not aspire to global leadership while relying on other nations to tell its story.

The former Minister of External Affairs said the imbalance was also evident in the United Nations Security Council, where African countries often struggled to shape discussions on conflicts on the continent.

Recalling Nigeria’s membership of the council in 1994 and 1995, he said he had expected African members to lead the drafting of resolutions on African conflicts.

However, he said Britain and France frequently took on that role.

“Guess who holds the pen, who drafts the resolutions on Africa? It’s usually the British or the French, not the African members of the Council,” he said.

“Whoever holds the pen, they take the narrative. They decide what is important and what is not.”

He lamented that despite Nigeria’s population, cultural influence, natural resources and economic potential, its international image remained dominated by negative narratives.

He identified inadequate funding of foreign missions, weak foreign policy institutions, reactive diplomacy and poor coordination of diaspora resources as factors undermining the country’s global standing.

Gambari urged the Federal Government to turn the Nigerian Television Authority and other public broadcasters into credible international platforms, citing the BBC World Service, Deutsche Welle, France 24 and Japan’s NHK as examples.

He stressed that Nigeria’s state media should have adequate funding, professional independence, modern technology and international distribution networks rather than serve as instruments of government propaganda.

“They must build their editorial culture, professional standards, funding levels, digital capability and international distribution infrastructure, and transform them into genuine instruments of narrative power,” he said.

He also called for the strategic use of Nollywood, Afrobeats, Nigerian literature, fashion, cuisine and other creative industries to strengthen the country’s soft power.

On constitutional reforms at the United Nations, Gambari insisted that Africa deserved at least two permanent seats on the Security Council, warning that Nigeria could miss the chance if it failed to build diplomatic influence and continental support.

He proposed a 10-year plan ending in 2036 for Nigeria to establish a respected international broadcasting institution, strengthen its diplomatic capacity and build a more balanced international image.

He cautioned that the country could not gain international influence simply by complaining about negative coverage.

“The world is not waiting for Nigeria to get its narrative together. The contest for global influence is unfolding now, with or without us.”

Former Nigerian Ambassador to Russia, Prof. Abdullahi Shehu, who reviewed the book, described it as an important contribution to discussions on Nigeria’s international image and the strategic role of state media in diplomacy.

Shehu said the book made three key arguments: that state media act as diplomatic actors, that credibility determines their effectiveness and that media organisations in developing countries face structural disadvantages, including weak funding and technology.

He said, “In the absence of a credible voice, silence becomes a message. In the economy of perception, credibility operates as the principal currency.”

Representing the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, an Assistant Director in the Ministry’s Department of Planning, Research and Statistics, Oladile Adeleke, said strategic communication had become vital to modern diplomacy.

In his remarks as father of the day, former Cross River State Governor, Liyel Imoke, said the book should wake Nigerian policymakers to the need to improve the country’s international communication strategy.

Earlier, the National President of the Association of Retired Career Ambassadors of Nigeria—insert name—urged Nigerian broadcasters, especially the NTA and other television stations, to widen their international reach beyond Nigerians in the diaspora.

He argued that the country’s broadcasters would only meet their international goals when non-Nigerians also watched and trusted their content.

In his response, Abang said the book did not argue for propaganda but called on Nigeria and other African countries to develop the capacity to share their perspectives globally.

He maintained that countries that failed to tell their stories left others to define their identities and international reputations.

“If a nation does not use its own media, does not tell its own story, others will tell that story, and they will tell that story in a bad way,” he said.
