title: Mexico nabs notorious drug cartel leader
description:
Mexico’s military captured an alleged drug lord listed among the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, sparking violent exchanges of gunfire in Sinaloa state on Friday that sent fans fleeing from a baseball game.
According to CNN, Mexico’s defence ministry said Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chap
content:
Mexico’s military captured an alleged drug lord listed among the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, sparking violent exchanges of gunfire in Sinaloa state on Friday that sent fans fleeing from a baseball game.

According to CNN, Mexico’s defence ministry said Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” who leads the Sinaloa-based cartel Los Mazatlecos, was arrested with the help of the US.

CNN has approached US authorities for comment.

The operation was conducted by “elite military forces” using “stealth and surprise” to reach their target, the ministry posted on X, saying Meza-Flores was taken to Mexico City following his arrest.

Two other alleged members of the criminal organisation were arrested in the same operation, Mexico’s Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch said in a post on X. They include the group’s second-in-command, Germán “N,” alias “Serafín,” and José “N,” its alleged financial operator.

Meza-Flores is “allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States,” according to an FBI wanted poster offering a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest.

He was previously indicted in 2019 for drug trafficking violations and possession of a firearm, and in 2012 for drug trafficking charges, it said.

The US Drug Enforcement Administration called the arrest a “significant blow” to a violent criminal organisation and praised intelligence sharing between the two countries.

“(The) DEA commends the Mexican authorities who carried out this operation,” the agency said in a statement to CNN.

In a 2013 statement, the US Treasury Department said the Meza-Flores cartel had been involved in “an extremely violent turf war” with the rival Sinaloa Cartel – then led by notorious drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, who is now serving time in a US prison.

The operation to capture Meza-Flores sparked violent clashes on Friday between the Mexican military and armed militants in Guasave, an area known as the agricultural heart of Mexico.

The defence ministry said that authorities “came under attack with gunfire and explosives” upon initiating the operation, and that militants set up roadblocks in several municipalities near the arrest site.

Dramatic footage, verified by CNN, shows a barrage of rapid fire from what appear to be Mexican security force helicopters firing at the ground and circling over Guasave city.

Video captured by a surveillance camera shows an apparent exchange of gunfire between cartel members in the back of a truck and Mexican security force helicopters above in the city of Guasave in Mexico on Friday night.

title: Tinubu’s pardon of convoy attack suspects divides opposition
description:
Opposition parties have expressed divergent views over President Bola Tinubu’s decision to grant clemency to 78 suspects arrested over the alleged attack on his convoy in Abuja.
While some political parties condemned the incident and demanded prosecution, others faulted the President’s intervention,
content:
Opposition parties have expressed divergent views over President Bola Tinubu’s decision to grant clemency to 78 suspects arrested over the alleged attack on his convoy in Abuja.

While some political parties condemned the incident and demanded prosecution, others faulted the President’s intervention, describing it as politically motivated and a missed opportunity to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The parties stated their positions in separate interviews with Sunday PUNCH on Friday, following an attack on Tinubu’s motorcade shortly after he observed Jumu’ah prayers at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque in Abuja’s Garki District on November 13.

The incident initially generated conflicting accounts, with the Presidency disputing reports that the President’s convoy was attacked.

Tinubu’s Senior Special Assistant on Digital Engagement, Strategy, and New Media, O’tega Ogra, had dismissed the claims, describing them as an opposition narrative.

However, the Federal Capital Territory Police Command confirmed the incident on November 16, saying 78 suspects had been arrested following intelligence-led operations.

Police spokesperson for the FCT command, Josephine Adeh, said the suspects were being processed for release after the President extended clemency to them and directed that they be warned and freed.

Commenting on the development, the National Publicity Secretary of the Social Democratic Party, Rufus Aiyenigba, described the attack as unacceptable and an assault on democracy, saying those responsible for promoting political violence should be identified and prosecuted.

Aiyenigba said although the incident reflected growing public discontent over poverty and insecurity, citizens had a responsibility to respect the office of the President.

“The SDP condemns, in very strong terms, the recent attack on the convoy of President Tinubu. The party considers the incident, which was carried out by those unruly fellows, unacceptable, and it is considered not only a national embarrassment, but a major assault on our democracy.

“Although it undeniably speaks to the growing public discontent, particularly regarding the high and pervasive poverty level, and unabating insecurity that have enveloped a greater part of the nation, nonetheless, Nigerian citizens have a duty to protect and respect the office of our President, which is the symbol of the nation.

“Individuals and political figures who are found to be culpable in the act of promoting election violence have to be identified and prosecuted to serve as the much-needed deterrence. Crime and criminality in any form must be met with appropriate punitive measures,” he said.

Aiyenigba warned against the growing culture of political intimidation, threats, and violence, particularly as parties began preparations for the 2027 general elections.

He said political actors must promote peaceful campaigns and electoral processes, adding that the SDP believed political parties should seek power through popular support rather than violence.

The party called for stronger legislation and stiff sanctions against political actors and parties found culpable in promoting violence.

“Our democracy must be truly democratic in form and practice and be safeguarded. Nigerian people must have the freedom to exercise their fundamental rights, free of any form of intimidation or harassment. That is what guarantees the survival of our democracy and enhances national stability, particularly as we enter the 2027 general elections,” he said.

However, the National Publicity Secretary of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, Osa Director, questioned the circumstances surrounding the arrests and subsequent release of the suspects, accusing the ruling All Progressives Congress of double standards in its handling of attacks involving opposition figures.

Director said NDC was surprised that the APC had acknowledged the incident through the arrests after initially disputing reports that Tinubu’s convoy was attacked.

“It is surprising that the APC is claiming that they arrested some hoodlums who have now been set free on the order of the President. Was it not the same APC that said there was no incident where the President was pelted with stones by hungry Nigerians over his non-performance?

“When will APC ever learn to tell the truth and play straight? Why is it that it was only when the President’s convoy was stoned that they are suddenly arresting people? Peter Obi and the NDC have been attacked several times, but to date no one has been arrested. Atiku was attacked in Sokoto, but nobody was arrested.

“This double standard is uncalled for in a democracy,” he said.

Similarly, the Labour Party National Publicity Secretary, Ken Asogwa, questioned the legal basis for the President’s intervention, arguing that the decision to release the suspects could undermine the investigation.

Asogwa queried whether the President could exercise his constitutional power of pardon over suspects who had not been charged and convicted by a court.

“There are two salient questions to be asked here. First, does the President have the power to grant a pardon or clemency to someone who has not been charged and convicted by a court?

“Section 175 of the 1999 Constitution (as amended), which confers the power of prerogative of mercy or pardon on the President, as well as established legal practice and judicial interpretation, contemplates clemency as a post-conviction measure.

“So, the action of Mr President in ambushing the police investigation through his hasty pardon is not helpful to the intelligence community,” he said.

The LP spokesman also questioned the motive behind the attack, saying the police investigation could have provided answers to the circumstances surrounding the incident.

“Secondly, we need to understand why someone would suddenly defy the paraphernalia of security surrounding the President and Commander-in-Chief and decide to embark on a suicide mission by attacking the President’s convoy with stones.

“Is this a suicide mission borne out of frustration and despair? The investigation should have been able to reveal some of these motives. Unfortunately, the President has thwarted that opportunity.

“In all, I enjoin the President to engage in deep introspection and soul-searching. Why would someone decide to stone the convoy of the President of Nigeria in Abuja, not elsewhere? That is the deeper question,” he said.

The post Tinubu’s pardon of convoy attack suspects divides opposition appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
author: Adebayo Folorunsho-Francis

title: Becoming SAN remains my proudest professional moment – Ex-NBA president,  Osigwe
description:
Senior Advocate of Nigeria and former President of the Nigerian Bar Association, Afam Osigwe, speaks to PELUMI KAZEEM about his childhood, journey into the legal profession, challenges, personal interests and concerns about Nigeria’s judiciary and electoral system
What was growing up like for you?
I
content:
Senior Advocate of Nigeria and former President of the Nigerian Bar Association, Afam Osigwe, speaks to PELUMI KAZEEM about his childhood, journey into the legal profession, challenges, personal interests and concerns about Nigeria’s judiciary and electoral system

What was growing up like for you?

I grew up in Nnewi North Local Government Area of Anambra State. I come from a very large family. My mother had nine sons, while my stepmother had one, so it was a big family.

I grew up largely in a trading community. My father was a trader, while my mother was a housewife who also had a shop within our family premises. It was an environment where very few people went to school, and trading was one of the major occupations.

However, despite the importance of trading in the community, our parents wanted their children to be educated. Encouraging children to go to school and discouraging them from dropping out after primary or secondary school were important values in our community. Most of the schools were built through communal efforts. The only general hospital in my hometown at the time was also built through communal effort, as was the post office. There were churches belonging to the Catholic and Anglican denominations.

That was the kind of environment in which I grew up before proceeding to Dennis Memorial Grammar School, Onitsha, for my secondary education. From there, I went on to study Law at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka.

What values did your upbringing instil in you that shaped the person you are today?

My parents instilled in us the values of hard work, diligence and honesty. In fact, my father’s business motto was, “Honesty is the best policy.” Lies were not tolerated in our home, and we were always made to take responsibility for our actions.

We were also taught not to depend on other people but to work hard, become independent and be able to provide for ourselves and our families. Excelling in whatever we did was very important.

My father drove from Nnewi to Onitsha every weekday for his trading business. I remember him always quoting a portion of the Bible which says, “A little sleep, a little slumber, and a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come on you like a thief.” His message was that if you did not want to be poor, you had to work hard and take whatever you were doing seriously.

As a student, I always remembered those words. Even when I became a lawyer and started working, the importance of hard work and making good use of my time remained at the back of my mind.

When I was leaving for Abuja in 1999 to establish myself there, one of the pieces of advice I received was never to postpone what I could do that day until another time. I was also advised not to allow my plans or ideas to become stale, but to remain focused and do things that would not bring shame to my family or me.

These are some of the values from my upbringing that have influenced the person I am today and continue to guide me as I strive to improve in whatever I do.

Was becoming a lawyer something you had always dreamed of?

I never thought I would become a lawyer. In fact, I never wanted to be one. In a manner of speaking, I would say that law happened to me by accident because, when I ran out of course options to study, it became the only other choice available to me.

As a child, my dream was to become a medical doctor. However, when I got to secondary school, I struggled with Mathematics and the sciences. By the time I completed SS1, it had become obvious that I had no future in the sciences because I found it difficult to understand some of the subjects. On the other hand, I was doing very well in my arts subjects.

I sought advice, and it became clear that medicine was no longer an option. During my SS3 year, I took what we called Trial JAMB to prepare for the actual examination, and I chose Mass Communication. I did not tell my parents or siblings about my decision.

When the result arrived at the post office, my father collected and opened it. He was surprised by the subjects I had written because they were mainly arts subjects. I explained that I had struggled with the sciences and decided to switch to the arts.

I had developed a great admiration for journalism from an early age. I started reading newspapers quite early, enjoyed listening to the news and watching newscasters, particularly the older presenters. I thought journalism was something I would love to do, having given up on my initial dream of becoming a medical doctor.

However, my father was disappointed because he had been excited about my ambition to study medicine. He told me he would not dictate the course I should study, but he knew he would not pay for me to study Mass Communication. According to him, if I wanted to study any course, I should choose a professional one that would enable me to stand on my own after graduation.

At the time, my elder brother had graduated from the University of Jos and had been called to the Bar in 1987. He had returned to Nnewi to establish his legal practice and was doing quite well. I respected him and thought it would not be a bad idea to study Law after all.

That was how I gradually shifted my attention to Law. It had never featured in my plans, but when I gained admission and started attending lectures, I realised that I could not have studied anything else. I became increasingly convinced that Law was my calling.

Looking back, I believe God directed me to where I was meant to be, and I am grateful that I eventually chose to study Law.

Looking back at your journey, what would you describe as the biggest turning point in your career?

It is difficult to identify just one turning point, but I would say that getting the opportunity to work with the late Chief T.J. Onomigbo Okpoko, SAN, was a major starting point.

Although I worked with him for less than two years, the experience broadened my understanding of the opportunities available in the legal profession and the kind of services one could provide. It also exposed me to the importance of identifying specific areas of practice, developing expertise and striving to become excellent in them.

At the time, his practice was growing, and I had the opportunity to witness different aspects of commercial transactions, litigation and cross-border transactions. These experiences widened my horizons and gave me a better understanding of what I could achieve as a lawyer.

I also encountered several people who had distinguished themselves in the profession, and I learnt from their experiences. So, I would say that the different people I met and the opportunities I had along the way contributed to the turning points in my professional journey.

You established your law firm, LAW FORTE, in 2002. What inspired you to start your own practice?

After working with the late Chief T.J. Onomigbo Okpoko for some time, I decided it was time to establish my own practice.

It was not easy initially. Clients were not readily available, and there were times when I had the capacity to work but did not have enough work coming in. There were also situations where I had work to do, but the fees people were willing to pay were inadequate.

Interestingly, I got married in 2002, and on March 3, 2003, I became a father. So, I was also dealing with the responsibility of raising a young family while trying to establish my practice.

What challenges did you face?

Some of the initial challenges were inadequate capital, attracting clients, identifying the right areas of focus and building the right team. However, God was faithful, and we continued to grow gradually.

Like every business, establishing a law firm comes with challenges, but we were able to overcome them little by little. You must continue to build your client base, find the right people to work with and create an environment that encourages growth.

You also have to keep improving yourself through training, reading and seeking the opinions of others. Sometimes, you need to form partnerships with other law firms and collaborate with them to provide services to clients.

Life is a race, and there are times when you feel exhausted. However, you must keep going if you want to cross the finish line and succeed at whatever you have set out to do.

After many years in the legal profession and serving as NBA President, what has been your most fulfilling experience?

My most fulfilling professional experience was the day I was conferred with the rank of Senior Advocate of Nigeria.

When I first arrived in Abuja, I came in on a night bus and initially squatted with friends and colleagues in Gwarinpa before I was able to get my own accommodation in Karu. When I reflect on where I was coming from and the struggles involved in building my practice, becoming a Senior Advocate remains particularly significant to me.

When I started practising law, I never imagined that I would become a Senior Advocate. Initially, I just wanted to make a living from the profession, establish a law firm, attract enough clients to sustain myself and save something for the future.

Some people might expect me to say that becoming NBA President was my most fulfilling experience, but becoming a Senior Advocate remains the most important professional moment for me. It represented recognition of the efforts and sacrifices I had made in the profession.

What did the journey teach you about yourself?

When I worked with the late Chief T.J. Onomigbo Okpoko, I saw how hard he worked to attain the rank. I also encountered other lawyers who had distinguished themselves through hard work and excellence. That made me realise it was an achievement worth pursuing.

When it eventually happened, it reminded me that God had blessed me beyond my expectations.

It reminded me that every profession rewards those who work hard and strive for excellence.

What is one thing people often misunderstand about you because of your position and achievements?

It would be difficult to assume that people will never misunderstand you. Even people who have not achieved much in life will have others who misunderstand them. Sometimes, it may be about one’s attitude, as people might consider you arrogant or have other perceptions about you.

I remember people telling me that I was overambitious and asking whether I was not too young to aspire to become NBA President. When I contested for the position in 2018, I was disqualified. I tried to explain to some people that I did not consider myself too young for the position.

I pointed out that there had been people who became heads of state in their 30s and governors in Nigeria in their 40s. So, I did not understand why aspiring to become NBA President at my age should be considered overambitious.

There will always be people who misunderstand you, just as you may not always understand other people. I do not allow such perceptions to worry me.

What matters to me is remaining faithful to my moral standards, personal beliefs and principles. I am committed to doing what is right rather than acting out of self-interest or simply trying to please people.

I also believe in working for the greater good of society and whichever profession I find myself in.

Having achieved so much in your career, what are some of the things you still hope to accomplish?

I do not think I have achieved everything I want to achieve. I want to continue becoming a better person than I was the previous day and accomplish more, although I know that, at some point, I will have to retire.

Professionally, I have attained some of the highest positions in the legal profession. I am a Senior Advocate of Nigeria and a life member of the Body of Benchers. I also had the opportunity to serve as President of the Nigerian Bar Association.

I have no interest in contesting for another elective position in the profession. However, if an opportunity for a political appointment that I believe I can credibly discharge comes my way, I may consider it. I do not intend to contest for political office, and I do not belong to any political party.

Beyond personal achievements, I want to see Nigeria become stronger, the legal profession improve and the judiciary become an institution that enjoys the confidence and respect of the people who depend on it.

Some Nigerians believe that money and other interests sometimes influence court judgments. What is your response to these concerns?

I think there may be some truth to those concerns. We operate in a political environment where judges may sometimes feel compelled to consider the implications of their decisions, particularly when the government is involved. For instance, a judge may feel that he cannot make an order or deliver a judgment that could affect the government, even without anyone approaching or inducing him.

There have also been proven cases of judges receiving money to influence decisions in cases before them. The general perception among members of the public is that money and other interests play a role in the administration of justice.

However, we must recognise that perception can sometimes be greater than reality. People may hold certain beliefs without necessarily having evidence to support them. As I have mentioned, there have been cases where the National Judicial Council sanctioned judicial officers over allegations of corruption and misconduct.

There are also situations where a judgment appears to go against established judicial reasoning, the facts or the law. When I was NBA President, I consistently emphasised that when a judge delivers a judgment that is inconsistent with established judicial precedents, the facts and the applicable law, it could be a product of corruption or incompetence.

Whichever of the two it is, such a person has no business remaining on the Bench.

In recent years, some court judgments have affected the outcomes of elections. Do you think this has reduced Nigerians’ confidence in the judiciary and the electoral process?

I think so. There is an over-judicialisation of the political process, and I have always advocated reducing the involvement of courts in determining who becomes a candidate for a political party.

In my view, political parties should be allowed to decide who they want to field as candidates, and the choice of candidates should not be justiciable. One of the things that has contributed to the negative perception of the judiciary in Nigeria is the number of political cases that end up in court.

If we get the electoral process right and reduce the number of disputes that go before election tribunals, public perception of the judiciary will improve. Similarly, reducing the involvement of courts in determining election winners could help restore confidence in the system.

I also believe that some of these judicial decisions have contributed to the feeling among Nigerians that their votes do not count. When people begin to believe that election outcomes are already determined, they may see little reason to participate in the voting process.

There are other factors contributing to this problem. Politicians sometimes prevent opposition parties from freely participating in the electoral process. In several states, you find billboards belonging mainly to the ruling party, while members of the opposition face difficulties putting up theirs. The high charges for erecting billboards may also be used to discourage opposition activities, particularly where there is no evidence that members of the ruling party pay the same amounts.

We also have issues of electoral violence, intimidation, the high cost of acquiring political power and the monetisation of the electoral process. There is also the question of whether Nigerians have sufficient confidence in INEC as an independent umpire.

Another issue is the restriction of vehicular movement on election days. I do not think it makes sense to restrict people’s movements because an election is taking place. Imagine someone whose polling unit is two or three kilometres from their home being expected to walk that distance simply because they want to vote.

People should be allowed to go about their normal activities and vote if they choose to. Voting should not mean that people’s lives must come to a standstill. In many countries, people go about their daily activities while participating in elections.

Restricting movement does not necessarily prevent electoral malpractice, and it discourages some people who may not be willing or able to walk long distances from voting. When combined with a lack of confidence in the government and the electoral process, these factors contribute to low voter turnout.

Do you think there is a need to review Nigeria’s electoral laws to reduce the number of election disputes that end up in court?

I think pre-election matters should not be justiciable. If a political party decides that the least popular person is the candidate it wants to field, it should be allowed to do so without the courts determining who its candidate should be.

I believe the provisions of the Electoral Act that make these matters justiciable should be removed. Political parties should be allowed to succeed or fail based on their decisions.

When an electoral process is seen to be fair, people are more likely to accept its outcome without going to court. I recall attending the Osun governorship election, where the outcome was generally expected, and those who lost did not challenge it.

However, when people believe that the system can be manipulated or that the outcome does not reflect their will, they will continue to seek redress in court.

Nigeria may be one of the countries where electoral disputes are heavily litigated. That does not present us in a positive light because it suggests that we have not built an electoral system that is sufficiently transparent and credible.

As a former NBA President, what role can the association play in protecting the independence of the judiciary?

The NBA, like other civil society organisations, has a responsibility to hold institutions and public office holders accountable, speak truth to power, protect the independence of the judiciary and the legal profession, and insist that the rule of law prevails.

If the association consistently carries out these responsibilities, it will play an important role in protecting judicial independence.

It must also engage in advocacy, put pressure on the government and draw attention to the poor state of infrastructure in our courts. The NBA should insist on the financial autonomy of the judiciary so that Chief Judges and heads of courts do not have to approach the executive to beg for funding.

There is also a need to protect the appointment process for judicial officers from political interference and ensure that the right people are appointed. Those appointed as judges must equally maintain their independence and avoid surrendering themselves to political authorities.

Judges must deliver decisions that inspire confidence, not only by resolving disputes between parties but also by ensuring that justice is served.

When this happens, people will have greater confidence in the judiciary. Despite the interdependence of the arms of government, the judiciary must remain independent and be able to make decisions without fear or favour.

Away from work and professional responsibilities, how would you describe yourself?

When I am away from work, I enjoy reading and sightseeing. I also used to do photography, although I have not practised it in recent years.

I keep animals, particularly dogs, because I love them. I have a few dogs at home, and I enjoy feeding and grooming them and spending time with them.

What do you enjoy doing in your free time?

I enjoy being around nature. I do not drink or smoke, and I am not particularly a club-going person. I enjoy the company of friends and having intellectual discussions with them or my colleagues.

Sometimes, I simply lie in bed doing nothing or sit at home and watch a movie.

I am not particularly a music person, although I listen to music occasionally. Interestingly, I do not like working in a completely quiet environment. When I am working at home or in the office, I prefer having some background noise, either from the television or music playing on my laptop. I enjoy reading and watching movies more.

title: Elections not do-or-die contest – Akpabio
description:
The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, has warned politicians against turning the 2027 general elections into a do-or-die contest, urging political leaders to caution their supporters and avoid actions that could trigger tension ahead of the polls.
Akpabio gave the warning while reaffirming the Fed
content:
The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, has warned politicians against turning the 2027 general elections into a do-or-die contest, urging political leaders to caution their supporters and avoid actions that could trigger tension ahead of the polls.

Akpabio gave the warning while reaffirming the Federal Government’s commitment to conducting free, fair and credible elections amid growing political activities ahead of next year’s polls.

He spoke when he received the Speaker of Ghana’s Parliament, Rt. Hon. Alban Bagbin, who visited Nigeria, at his residence in Abuja, according to a statement issued on Saturday by Akpabio’s Special Assistant on Media, Jackson Udom.

“As we prepare for our general elections next year, let me once again use this opportunity to restate the commitment of the President Bola Tinubu-led administration to a free, fair and credible election.

“Let the political actors caution their supporters against creating political tensions, because elections should not be treated as a do-or-die affair.”

The 2027 polls are expected to draw intense political competition as parties and prospective candidates position themselves for the presidential, governorship and legislative contests.

Akpabio said, “Let me thank my brother and Speaker of the Parliament of Ghana for this visit to the residence of the Senate President after his official engagement in Nigeria.

“Let me also commend the people and government of Ghana for your exemplary record in democratic governance. Nigeria is very fortunate to have a partner committed to strengthening relations between the two countries.”

He used the meeting to call for stronger bilateral ties between Nigeria and Ghana, particularly in trade, commercial cooperation and democratic governance.

Akpabio described the relationship between the two West African countries as historic and deeply rooted.

He also thanked Bagbin for supporting his participation in the leadership of the Inter-Parliamentary Union, which led to his election to the organisation’s Executive Committee.

In his response, Bagbin said his visit was aimed at sustaining the longstanding relationship between the two countries and strengthening ties between their parliaments.

He said discussions during the visit focused on deepening democracy and promoting good governance, noting that developments in Nigeria affect the wider West African region.

According to him, Ghana closely monitors developments in Nigeria because of their potential impact on regional stability.

The Ghanaian Speaker also expressed concern over declining public confidence in democracy across the region, saying political leaders must show that democracy remains the best form of government.

He pledged his support for efforts to ensure that Nigeria’s 2027 general elections are peaceful, free, fair and credible, reaffirming Ghana’s solidarity with Nigeria and its democratic process.

Bagbin stressed the need for collective action by West African countries to protect democratic institutions and strengthen democratic governance across the region.

title: 2027: Voter register row sparks electoral manipulation fears
description:
The discovery of AI-generated photographs in the preliminary register of voters has raised fresh concerns about the integrity of 2027 general elections, Ismaeel UTHMAN writes

Over the years, political actors have been accused of exploiting weaknesses in voter registration to manipulate the electora
content:
The discovery of AI-generated photographs in the preliminary register of voters has raised fresh concerns about the integrity of 2027 general elections, Ismaeel UTHMAN writes

Over the years, political actors have been accused of exploiting weaknesses in voter registration to manipulate the electoral process. These alleged practices include mobilising people to register in areas where they do not ordinarily reside, facilitating the collection of PVCs by political intermediaries and attempting to influence who has access to voter cards.

Such practices raise concerns about the possibility of proxy voting, although the electoral system requires voters to undergo biometric accreditation and cast their ballots personally.

The integrity of an election, therefore, depends not only on what happens on election day but also on the accuracy and credibility of the register used to identify eligible voters.

This is why the discovery of AI-generated photographs in INEC’s preliminary register ahead of the 2027 general elections has attracted considerable attention.

According to the commission, questionable records were first identified and flagged during the nationwide physical display of the preliminary Register of Voters between October 9 and 15, 2026. The commission subsequently uploaded the preliminary register to its website on October 26, triggering wider public concerns over suspected irregularities in the voter database.

INEC’s Director of Information and Communication Technology, Dr Lawrence Bayode, explained that some registration officers across the country used their login details to introduce questionable records into the database but could not explain the reasons behind their actions.

Subsequently, the commission said it had removed a total of 1,609,553 invalid registrations following a nationwide clean-up, which also uncovered 873 verified deceased voters. No fewer than 54 persons across 10 states were also identified as complicit in the registration irregularities.

 

 Why the voter register matters

Pundits believe that these irregularities raise a fundamental question about the reliability of the voter register. The register is the basis for determining who is eligible to participate in an election. Its accuracy is, therefore, central to the credibility of the entire electoral process.

Political analysts say a register containing fictitious identities, duplicate entries or ineligible voters could undermine confidence in the number and identities of eligible voters. It could also create opportunities for manipulation if the weaknesses are not detected and addressed before election day.

The Executive Director of Yiaga Africa, Samson Itodo, underscored this concern, describing the voter register as the foundation of electoral credibility.

“The voter register is the foundation of every credible election. If citizens cannot trust the integrity of the register, their confidence in the entire electoral process is weakened,” he said in an interview with Sunday PUNCH.

The National Chairman of the Coalition of United Political Parties, Peter Ahmed, also described the register as the benchmark for credible elections.

“A voter register is the benchmark foundation for determining credible and reliable elections. If the voter register is faulty, the outcome of the election will be faulty,” he said.

For the Executive Chairman of the Centre for Anti-Corruption and Open Leadership, Debo Adeniran, INEC must produce a clean and credible register that reflects genuine and eligible voters. His concern is that the commission cannot convincingly assure Nigerians of the credibility of an election if it cannot establish the authenticity of the identities on which the voting process is based.

The importance of an accurate register is also reflected in the weaknesses identified by international observers during previous elections. In its final report on Nigeria’s 2023 general elections, the European Union Election Observation Mission identified significant weaknesses in the voters’ register.

The observers highlighted the presence of deceased and emigrated voters, internally migrated voters who had not transferred their registration, as well as acknowledged cases of underage registration. These concerns demonstrate that questions about the quality of the register predate the latest discovery and are not limited to the AI-generated photographs.

 

Questions over INEC’s integrity

INEC’s explanation that some registration officers used their official login details to introduce questionable records raises questions about the commission’s internal controls, supervision of field officers and the security of its registration database.

Itodo said the development raised concerns about the integrity of the voter register, the effectiveness of INEC’s internal controls and the security of its registration system. He noted that the incident exposed human vulnerabilities that could undermine electoral technology, stressing that the effectiveness of systems such as the ABIS depended on the people managing them.

According to him, the concerns should not be limited to the voter registration database, as the credibility of other election technology systems, including the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System and the INEC Result Viewing Portal, also depends on the officials who operate them.

Similarly, the Executive Director of the Socio-Economic and Civic Rights Advocacy, Emmanuel Olowu, said the development raised serious questions about the integrity of INEC’s voter registration system and the security of its database.

“If authorised officers could introduce AI-generated photographs and questionable records, it suggests weaknesses in internal controls and monitoring mechanisms. INEC must explain how this happened and demonstrate that the wider database remains secure. Nigerians deserve more than assurances; they deserve transparency and accountability,” Olowu said.

Ahmed also questioned the commission’s transparency and commitment to credible elections, insisting that those responsible for the irregularities must be brought to book.

“INEC is not transparent and has not been acting in the best direction that will show that they are sincere and committed to a credible election. They must sincerely prove to Nigeria beyond all reasonable doubt that they mean well and that they are committed to doing well by making sure that those who are behind the manipulation of data are brought to book,” he said.

 

A shadow over 2027

With the 2027 general elections approaching, the discovery has raised concerns about whether the electoral process could be compromised. Although the identification of questionable records does not establish that there is a coordinated plot to manipulate the election, the possibility that such irregularities could be exploited by political interests has become a major source of concern.

In Adeniran’s view, the development has heightened doubts about INEC’s ability to conduct credible and reliable elections in 2027. He argued that the commission’s credibility would be in doubt if it could not establish that the individuals listed in the register were real people and eligible voters. Adeniran suggested that the development could be part of an attempt to manipulate the 2027 election, arguing that whoever introduced fictitious identities into the register might have an interest in influencing the electoral process.

However, Olowu cautioned against concluding that the incident was part of a deliberate electoral manipulation plot without concrete evidence.

“We cannot conclude that it is part of a deliberate plot without concrete evidence. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that such irregularities could be exploited for electoral manipulation. INEC must investigate who was responsible, who might benefit and whether the acts were coordinated,” he said.

Ahmed described the incident as part of an alleged plot to manipulate the 2027 elections. He questioned why the commission’s ICT department failed to prevent the introduction of questionable records despite the resources committed to INEC.

The different positions reflect the political sensitivity of the controversy. While the concerns raised by the civil society representatives point to the need for an evidence-based investigation, the allegation of a possible plot by political interests shows how the discovery could deepen distrust among stakeholders ahead of the elections.

 

The call for an independent audit

Civil society groups and other stakeholders have also called for a wider examination of the voters’ register. Their argument is that identifying the affected entries and removing them may not be sufficient to establish the accuracy of the entire database.

Itodo and Olowu advocated an independent and comprehensive audit of the voter register, with safeguards to protect personal data. They said such an exercise would help establish the extent of the irregularities and strengthen public confidence in the electoral process.

“Electoral credibility begins with an accurate and credible voters’ register. I therefore call for an independent forensic audit of the affected database, public disclosure of the findings and adequate safeguards to protect legitimate voters from wrongful exclusion,” Olowu said.

The demand for an independent audit is also consistent with the recommendation of the EU Election Observation Mission on the 2023 general elections. The observers noted that Nigeria had never conducted an independent audit of its voters’ register and recommended an external exercise involving physical verification, sample analysis and an assessment of biometric data quality.

That recommendation has become particularly relevant following the latest discovery. Although INEC’s internal biometric checks can identify duplicate registrations and suspicious records, an independent audit would provide an additional layer of scrutiny and help determine whether the problem is limited to the identified cases or reflects wider weaknesses in the database.

INEC’s own records also show the scale of the challenge involved in maintaining an accurate voters’ register. In its report on the 2023 general elections, the commission disclosed that it registered 12,298,944 new voters during the Continuous Voter Registration exercise before subjecting the records to biometric deduplication and a clean-up process involving photographs, fingerprints and facial biometrics.

The exercise identified 2,780,756 records as duplicate or multiple registrations, which were subsequently invalidated. The number of valid new registrations consequently dropped to 9,518,188.

Political analysts say the discovery of AI-generated photographs in the preliminary voter register raises questions about whether INEC’s existing verification mechanisms are sufficient to prevent questionable records from entering the database and whether the commission can guarantee the accuracy of the register ahead of 2027.

For the stakeholders demanding an independent audit, the exercise would provide an opportunity to establish the extent of the problem, assess the effectiveness of INEC’s safeguards and determine whether legitimate voters are at risk of being wrongly excluded. It would also give the commission an opportunity to demonstrate that it is prepared to address the weaknesses before they become a bigger source of dispute during the elections.

However, INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna urged Nigerians to have trust and confidence in the commission, assuring them that the electoral body would do everything possible to ensure that the election was credible. He promised that INEC would pursue the AI-generated photographs matter to a logical conclusion.

“Nobody is manipulating. There are people who will attempt to influence this. That’s life. But, of course, our only responsibility is to make sure that they don’t succeed,” Haruna said. “We have to be transparent. Transparency is one of the core values of INEC. When we investigate, we will find anybody who is guilty, and they will be prosecuted.”

The post 2027: Voter register row sparks electoral manipulation fears appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: ABBACARE: How Kano is expanding healthcare access for the most vulnerable
description:
By Hassan A. Karofi



Access to affordable healthcare remains a major challenge for millions of Nigerians, particularly low-income households and vulnerable groups who often delay or forgo treatment because of the cost. In Kano State, the ABBACARE Initiative is one of the interventions aimed at add
content:
By Hassan A. Karofi

Access to affordable healthcare remains a major challenge for millions of Nigerians, particularly low-income households and vulnerable groups who often delay or forgo treatment because of the cost. In Kano State, the ABBACARE Initiative is one of the interventions aimed at addressing this challenge through social health insurance.

Implemented by the Kano State Contributory Healthcare Management Agency (KSCHMA), ABBACARE is designed to provide healthcare coverage for vulnerable groups, including pregnant women, persons living with sickle cell disorder and emergency patients. Its focus is on reducing the financial barriers that prevent people from accessing essential medical services.

According to figures provided for the initiative, ABBACARE has enrolled 28,721 beneficiaries and extended service delivery to 13 hospitals across Kano State’s three senatorial zones. These figures point to an effort to widen access to healthcare, although the programme’s long-term impact will depend on the quality of services available, the regularity of funding and the ability to sustain coverage as more people are enrolled.

The initiative also highlights the role state governments can play in advancing Universal Health Coverage through social health insurance. While national policies provide an important framework, state-level programmes such as ABBACARE can help address local healthcare needs and extend financial protection to people who might otherwise struggle to pay for treatment.

The programme is part of a wider set of health interventions under Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf’s administration. Another is the Gida-Gida Lafiya Project, which focuses on hypertension and other non-communicable diseases through the distribution of customised digital blood pressure monitors.

The devices are intended to help beneficiaries monitor their blood pressure, identify possible health risks early and seek medical attention when necessary. Their adaptation to provide guidance in local languages also reflects the importance of making health information accessible to people in their communities.

Although ABBACARE and Gida-Gida Lafiya address different aspects of healthcare, they speak to two related challenges. The former seeks to reduce the financial burden of accessing treatment, while the latter encourages prevention, regular monitoring and early intervention. Both approaches are relevant in a health system where the cost of treatment and late presentation at hospitals can worsen health outcomes.

However, the success of such interventions should not be measured by enrolment figures or the number of devices distributed alone. Their value will ultimately depend on whether beneficiaries can consistently access the services promised, whether participating hospitals have the capacity to provide quality care and whether the programmes are adequately funded over time.

The Kano State Ministry of Health and the leadership of KSCHMA therefore have important roles to play in ensuring that the initiatives deliver their intended benefits. Dr Rahila Mukhtar, whose role in the agency’s operations and healthcare financing efforts has been noteworthy, is among the key figures associated with the implementation of approaches such as ABBACARE.

The agency’s work in administering the initiative underscores the importance of effective health insurance management. Enrolling vulnerable people is an important first step, but maintaining reliable access to care requires proper coordination with healthcare providers, transparent management of funds, regular monitoring and accountability to beneficiaries.

For Kano, the next task is to consolidate the gains made through ABBACARE and ensure that the programme remains accessible and sustainable. Expanding coverage will also require attention to the capacity of participating hospitals and the experiences of beneficiaries, particularly those who depend on the scheme for maternal care, treatment of sickle cell disorder and emergency services.

Other states can draw useful lessons from Kano’s experience, especially in using social health insurance to protect vulnerable populations. However, the model’s wider relevance will depend on evidence of its outcomes, affordability and sustainability.

As Nigeria pursues Universal Health Coverage, initiatives such as ABBACARE show why state-level action matters. The real measure of progress will not simply be the number of people enrolled, but whether they can obtain timely, affordable and quality healthcare when they need it.

•Karofi writes from Abuja and can be reached at hassankarofi@gmail.com.

title: Bandits threaten to stop 2027 elections in Zamfara communities
description:
Bandit leaders in Zamfara State told community leaders in the Anka Local Government Area that elections would not be allowed in their communities, according to a recent report by SARI Global, a US-registered risk intelligence firm.
The report says the warning came as armed groups tightened a blockad
content:
Bandit leaders in Zamfara State told community leaders in the Anka Local Government Area that elections would not be allowed in their communities, according to a recent report by SARI Global, a US-registered risk intelligence firm.

The report says the warning came as armed groups tightened a blockade on the state’s roads, burned vehicles, and imposed a N50m levy on communities in Dansadau District, displacing more than 300 residents.

The document, SARI Global’s Nigeria Monthly Security Overview for October 2026, obtained by Sunday PUNCH on Friday, said Zamfara replaced Borno as the country’s most incident-dense state, recording 69 incidents and 137 fatalities during the month.

“In Anka LGA, a bandit leader gathered community leaders in October and told them elections would not be allowed in their communities. If the blockades are not broken decisively, the risk is a permanent zone of prohibition and the depopulation of the affected districts,” the report stated.

It said the threat showed a trend in which banditry in Zamfara “moved from opportunistic ambush to the systematic control of roads.”

According to the report, a bandit group on October 13 released a video threatening to burn any vehicle travelling the Gusau–Dansadau road.

It said, a truck was burned on the Dansadau–Magami stretch the next day, and on October 16, bandits blocked the road, destroyed nine vehicles, and looted travellers.

More vehicles were reportedly burned on October 17.

The report added that the bandits also threatened attacks on communities that failed to pay the N50m levy, while two improvised explosive devices were found on the Magami–Hannutara–Dansadau road on October 8.

SARI Global said the blockade extended beyond one road as bandits also shut the Gurusu–Anka, Abare–Anka, Gusau–Magami, Kaura Namoda–Shinkafi, Mayanchi–Anka, Anka–Kuturu and Maradun–Danbaza roads, among others, abducting travellers and killing drivers and farmers.

According to the report, military escorts offered little protection as an ambush on October 11 near Gurusu killed at least 20 people in an escorted convoy of traders, including soldiers and police officers.

Troops reopened the Gusau–Dansadau road on October 21 and introduced regular escorts, however, bandits blocked it again on October 31.

“The strategy is economic strangulation. Cutting the roads that link Gusau to the Kuyambana Forest axis severs supply chains, cripples local markets and establishes the armed groups as the de facto authority over who moves and who pays,” the report said.

In its trajectory assessment, SARI Global said the armed groups were likely to consolidate control over the Kuyambana axis, with greater use of IEDs.

“Unless the blockades are broken decisively, the armed groups are likely to consolidate control over the Kuyambana axis, with greater use of IEDs and the depopulation of affected districts. The approach is likely to be copied on other corridors,” it added.

The report also noted that bandits attacked Kaura Namoda town directly on October 23, killing seven vigilantes and a boy and abducting at least 15 people.

Nationwide, abduction cases doubled to 55 in October from 27 in September, according to the firm.

SARI Global said the political environment hardened in parallel across the north, with about 46 incidents linked to parties, campaigns, or political thugs, and ruling-party campaigners stoned in at least five states.

The Independent National Electoral Commission revised its timetable in February, bringing forward the 2027 presidential and National Assembly elections to January 16, 2027, with governorship and state assembly elections scheduled for February 6, 2027. The dates were originally February 20 and March 6.

According to INEC, Zamfara has 14 local government areas and 3,529 polling units. The state had 1,952,060 registered voters at the 2023 general elections, with another 313,115 added through continuous voter registration as of August 2026.

Ahead of the 2023 governorship election, bandits reportedly imposed N2m levies on three communities in Zurmi LGA, at N200,000 per polling unit, before elections could be held there.

In October 2022, the then Matawalle administration announced a total lockdown in Anka, Bukkuyum and Gummi LGAs following a resurgence of bandit attacks, and also imposed an embargo on political activities.

In April 2025, bandits imposed a N60m levy on 12 communities in Maru LGA, which residents said was to punish them for allegedly giving information to the military.

Months earlier, bandits reportedly imposed a N172m protection levy on 25 villages in Tsafe West LGA in January 2025, forcing residents to flee.

The post Bandits threaten to stop 2027 elections in Zamfara communities appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Outrage as Kano court jails TikToker for ‘insulting’ Hisbah
description:
The arrest of a 19-year-old TikTok user, Zainab Abubakar, by the Kano State Hisbah and her subsequent conviction by a Sharia court over alleged insults against the agency and its Commander-General, Aminu Daurawa, have sparked outrage, with Amnesty International demanding her release.
Abubakar, an in
content:
The arrest of a 19-year-old TikTok user, Zainab Abubakar, by the Kano State Hisbah and her subsequent conviction by a Sharia court over alleged insults against the agency and its Commander-General, Aminu Daurawa, have sparked outrage, with Amnesty International demanding her release.

Abubakar, an indigene of Ogun State, was reportedly arrested alongside two others, Ahmad Usman and Muhammad Aliyu, after they featured in a video that went viral on social media, allegedly insulting Hisbah officials following the agency’s decision to stop them from organising an event along Zoo Road in Kano.

Abubakar was on Wednesday sentenced to five months imprisonment and 10 strokes of the cane by the state Sharia court.

Reacting to the conviction, Amnesty International described Abubakar’s sentence as an attack on freedom of expression and called for her “immediate and unconditional release.”

The human rights group also condemned the detention of Aliyu, who is currently being held in prison pending trial over an alleged offence.

In a statement on Friday, Amnesty International faulted the conviction, arguing that no one should be prosecuted or punished for expressing an opinion, even when such views are considered offensive.

“It is flabbergasting that someone can be made to appear before a court and stand trial, let alone serve a sentence and 10 strokes of cane for simply having expressed a strong opinion,” the organisation said.

The group described Abubakar’s trial and sentencing as the latest development in what it called the Kano authorities’ sustained repression of young people.

It said the five-month jail term was an indication of what it described as the increasing excesses of Hisbah officials against young people, particularly those from less privileged backgrounds.

The organisation maintained that the right to freely express one’s views, including opinions considered shocking or offensive, was protected under international human rights law.

It, therefore, called on the government to quash Zainab’s conviction and ensure her immediate and unconditional release.

In a separate statement on Saturday, Amnesty International also demanded Aliyu’s release, describing his detention as disproportionate and a violation of freedom of expression.

“Criticising public institutions or officials is not a criminal offence under international law, and no one should stand trial, let alone face imprisonment and strokes of cane for just doing that,” the group said.

When contacted, the Director-General of the board, Abba Sufi, declined to comment, saying, “I’m sorry, I cannot comment on the issue for now. I’m currently at the hospital and I can’t speak to you now.”

Efforts to get the state government’s reaction through the Commissioner for Information, Sunusi Bature, were also unsuccessful, as he did not respond to phone calls and messages sent to him.

Meanwhile, many netizens have criticised Hisbah and called for justice.

A Facebook user, Abdulkarim Ishiyaku, said freedom of expression was a fundamental human right, arguing that criticism or disagreement should not automatically attract criminal punishment.

He said, “No young person should face imprisonment or corporal punishment simply for expressing an opinion. Authorities must respect human dignity, fundamental rights and the rule of law. Zainab deserves justice.”

Similarly, a Facebook user, Hazmaf Arzet, described the punishment as excessive, arguing that the teenager needed guidance rather than imprisonment.

The user also questioned the basis for the five-month jail term, calling on the court to explain the Islamic provisions under which she was sentenced.

An X user identified as Abuja queen alleged that Abubakar’s identity as a non-indigene might have influenced her treatment.

Another user, WizkidEmpire, accused the Hisbah of selectively enforcing its rules, alleging that ordinary citizens were more likely to face punishment than the children of influential people.

Also reacting, an X user, belel_yusuf, called for the arrest of anyone involved in physically assaulting the teenager, describing her treatment as a violation of human rights and dignity.

The post Outrage as Kano court jails TikToker for ‘insulting’ Hisbah appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: ASIWAJU: Why I support 2nd term for President Tinubu

content:
By Moriamoh Ojikutu

A friend asked me recently, “Do you think Asiwaju is working?” My answer was simple: “Yes. He is doing his job.”

Let me be clear about where I stand. I strongly support President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and his administration, and I want him re-elected for a second term.

I believe in his leadership and the direction of his administration. I want him to complete the work he has started and deliver the lasting improvements I believe are possible.

That does not mean I think everything is perfect. It certainly does not mean I am unaware of the difficulties Nigerians are facing.

I live here. I run businesses here. I employ people, pay bills, buy fuel and deal with rising costs. I know what it means to reconsider spending, adjust plans and keep going when doing business becomes more difficult.

My support exists alongside that reality, not outside it.

When I say he is doing his job, I mean that I believe he is confronting difficult problems rather than leaving them for someone else.

But taking difficult decisions is not the finish line. Delivering results that Nigerians can see, touch and feel is.

Reform Is Rarely Comfortable: I do not believe Nigeria’s economic difficulties began with this administration, nor do I believe every problem can be resolved within a few years.

My view is that some difficult decisions had been postponed for too long.

President Tinubu’s administration has pursued major changes, including the removal of petrol subsidies and reforms to the foreign exchange system.

I support the decision to confront those structural problems. But I also recognise the hardship Nigerians have experienced during this period.

Families are making difficult choices. Businesses are adjusting their operations. People are working hard and still worrying about what they can afford.

Those experiences deserve to be heard, not dismissed with political slogans.

For me, acknowledging the pain does not mean rejecting the need for reform. It means asking how reform can be implemented more effectively and how people can be better protected through the transition.

A policy can have a sound objective and still need adjustments. I want the government to listen, respond and improve what needs to work better.

That is part of making reform succeed.

We Should Acknowledge Meaningful Interventions:

Alongside discussing the hardship, I believe we should recognise interventions intended to help people.

NELFUND provides interest-free loans to help eligible students overcome financial barriers to higher education, with support for institutional fees and/or upkeep. These are loans with repayment obligations, not grants.

For a student facing the possibility of leaving school because of money, access to financial support can make a meaningful difference. Education is one of the areas in which I want government intervention to open doors.

MAMII is another initiative I welcome. It focuses on reducing maternal and newborn deaths through measures that include improving access to care, strengthening referral systems and helping services respond to complications during pregnancy and childbirth.

As a country, we should care deeply about whether mothers can access care and whether students can continue their education.

These programmes deserve attention, alongside honest questions about whom they are reaching, how effectively they are operating and what results they are delivering.

I want them strengthened and delivered well. Recognising their value does not mean declaring the work complete. It means making room for a fair assessment of the administration.

Accountability at Every Level: I expect leadership from the president. I also expect governors, local government chairmen, legislators and ministers to fulfil their responsibilities.

Holding the presidency accountable should be the beginning of a wider demand for good governance, not the end of it.

When communities lack functioning schools, healthcare, drainage or clean water, citizens should ask which institutions are responsible, what resources they have received and what they have delivered.

We should ask these questions consistently, regardless of party affiliation. What is happening in our states? What is happening in our local governments? What are the people representing us doing with the responsibilities entrusted to them?

I want this presidency to succeed, and I want every other level of government to do its part.

Nigeria needs more than one office working. It needs public institutions and officials taking their responsibilities seriously.

Public Money Must Deliver Public Value: Government must be able to explain what citizens’ sacrifices are achieving. Where revenues and allocations increase, people deserve to know how those resources are being used.

How much was received? What was budgeted? What was spent? What was completed? And how has it improved people’s lives?

These should be normal questions, not uncomfortable ones. I want to see public money translate into better schools, accessible healthcare, reliable infrastructure and essential services.

I want clear reporting that allows citizens to judge performance beyond speeches and announcements.

Public funds are not personal gifts from politicians. They are resources held in trust for the people.

That trust must be respected at every level of government.

Security Must Remain a Priority: Security is central to the Nigeria I want to see.

Our farmers should be able to work without fear. Families should be able to travel safely. Communities should be protected, and businesses should be able to operate with confidence.

These are not partisan expectations. They are basic expectations of government.

I want the administration’s economic ambitions to be matched by sustained improvements in security.

Progress must be felt in people’s confidence that they can travel, earn a living and go about their daily lives safely.

That is an essential part of the success I want for this presidency.

Support Should Not Require Blindness: I sometimes find our political culture exhausting.

Apparently, you must either support everything a government does or oppose everything it does. There seems to be little room for thoughtful disagreement.

I reject that thinking.

I can support President Tinubu and question how a policy is being implemented. I can acknowledge progress and ask for greater urgency elsewhere. I can support the APC and still expect its public officials to explain their decisions and account for public resources.

There is no contradiction in that.

My questions do not come from uncertainty about where I stand. They come from wanting an administration I support to succeed.

Loyalty should not mean silence. Criticism should not automatically mean opposition.

We need room for honest conversations about what is working, what is not and what must happen next.

That is the kind of political participation I believe in: committed, constructive and willing to speak honestly.

Why I Support a Second Term: I want President Tinubu re-elected for a second term because I believe in his leadership and want him to complete the work he has begun.

I believe continuity offers an opportunity to build on these reforms, improve their implementation and turn policy changes into improvements people can feel.

That is my conviction, not a belief that time alone will solve our problems.

Nigerians need relief today. People need affordable food, access to healthcare, reliable electricity, security and opportunities for their children.

They need an economy in which hard work offers a reasonable chance of a decent living.

Those expectations are fair, and I want this administration to meet them with greater urgency.

For me, a second term should be an opportunity to build on what is working, correct what is not and deliver more widely.

I want stronger businesses, functioning institutions, better infrastructure and genuine opportunities for young Nigerians.

I want the sacrifices of this period to lead somewhere meaningful.

And I want a government that understands that the patience of the people must never be taken for granted.

Hope, With Its Eyes Open: So, why Asiwaju? Because I believe in President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s leadership, I support his administration, and I want him re-elected for a second term. I want him to complete the work he has started and turn the promise of these reforms into lasting improvements in the lives of Nigerians.

I do not dismiss the hardship people are facing, and my support does not mean silence when something needs to improve. I want this presidency to succeed and I want that success to be felt in our homes, our businesses and our communities.

That is where I stand: firmly in support, clear about my expectations, and hopeful for Nigeria.

Hope, with its eyes open.

The post ASIWAJU: Why I support 2nd term for President Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News.
