title: Dry season: Fear mounts over worsening power crisis
description: As the dry season approaches, millions of Nigerian households and businesses face the prospect of worsening electricity supply, with falling water inflows into hydroelectric reservoirs, gas supply constraints and persistent infrastructure challenges threatening to deepen the country’s power crisis.
content:
As the dry season approaches, millions of Nigerian households and businesses face the prospect of worsening electricity supply, with falling water inflows into hydroelectric reservoirs, gas supply constraints and persistent infrastructure challenges threatening to deepen the country’s power crisis.

The warning is coming amid an already declining electricity supply, with the national grid generating about 3,180 megawatts on November 19, leaving the 11 electricity distribution companies with a combined allocation of 2,885MW, according to data published by the Nigerian Independent System Operator.

The latest decline has renewed concerns about the ability of the power sector to sustain supply in the coming months, particularly as hydroelectric plants depend on water availability while gas-fired power stations continue to grapple with fuel supply constraints.

Although the dry season does not automatically translate into reduced electricity generation, the combination of declining water inflows, unreliable gas supply, ageing transmission infrastructure and distribution challenges could further limit the amount of electricity available to consumers.

Speaking in an interview with Saturday PUNCH, Professor of Energy, Dayo Ayoade, warned that declining water levels at hydroelectric dams, combined with unreliable gas supply to thermal power plants, could worsen electricity supply to Nigerian households.

The National Secretary of the Nigeria Electricity Consumer Advocacy Network, Uket Obanga, also expressed concern about the country’s preparedness for seasonal changes in water availability, stating that inadequate water management infrastructure could worsen electricity generation during periods of reduced rainfall.

Obanga also accused electricity distribution companies of concentrating available supply in urban centres and among customers considered more commercially viable, leaving residents of semi-urban communities struggling with inadequate electricity.

Supply already under pressure

On November 5, NISO attributed the decline in electricity generation to constraints in gas supply to thermal power plants and reduced water inflows into hydroelectric reservoirs.

The operator said limited gas availability had prevented affected thermal plants from operating at their available capacity, while reduced water inflows had affected hydroelectric generation.

The combined constraints, it said, had reduced electricity allocated to distribution companies, resulting in shorter hours of supply and increased load shedding across their networks.

The situation was reflected in the November 18 allocation figures, when the 11 distribution companies received a combined 2,885MW.

Abuja Electricity Distribution Company received 551MW, followed by Ikeja Electric with 366MW, Ibadan Disco with 340MW and Eko Disco with 339MW. Yola Disco received the lowest allocation of 74MW.

By the following morning, generation had fallen to about 3,180MW, according to a report published by The Guardian, indicating the extent of the supply constraints confronting the national grid.

The development has left households and businesses with fewer hours of electricity, forcing many to rely on generators, inverters and solar systems to meet their daily energy needs.

The power sector’s problems, however, extend beyond seasonal water levels. They involve the availability of fuel to generate electricity, the operational condition of generating plants, the capacity of the transmission grid to evacuate available power and the ability of distribution companies to deliver electricity to consumers.

Gas supply controversy

Gas supply constraints have remained a major challenge for Nigeria’s electricity generation, with thermal plants depending on adequate fuel deliveries to operate.The Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority’s September 2026 sector fact sheet showed that average daily gas utilisation by power plants fell by four per cent to 518 million standard cubic feet per day, compared with August.

The decline raised further concerns about the ability of gas-fired plants to sustain generation at a time when hydroelectric stations may also face seasonal pressure from reduced water inflows.

However, the gas supply situation has attracted conflicting explanations from operators.

In a November 7 statement, NNPC Limited disputed claims that its gas transportation network was responsible for the generation decline, saying the network operated by its subsidiary, NNPC Gas Infrastructure Company Limited, remained available to support deliveries to power plants without transportation constraints.

The national oil company said gas production had increased by about 10 per cent year-to-date in 2026, emphasising that the availability of gas transportation infrastructure was not the problem.

The NNPC, however, acknowledged that gas production, commercial supply arrangements and actual deliveries to individual power plants were separate issues that needed to be assessed alongside generating plant availability, maintenance schedules and gas offtake.

The financial challenges confronting the electricity market may also complicate gas supply.

Power generation companies and gas suppliers depend on payments for electricity and fuel delivered, while outstanding obligations within the electricity value chain have repeatedly raised concerns about the sustainability of supply.

Hydro generation and the weather factor

Nigeria’s generation mix makes the seasonal concern significant. Hydroelectric plants account for a substantial share of electricity supplied to the national grid, meaning reduced water inflows could affect their output.

The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission’s 2025 annual report showed that hydroelectric plants generated 12,804.18 gigawatt-hours, representing 32.66 per cent of total grid electricity generated during the year.

Historical figures also show that hydroelectric generation can fluctuate with seasonal conditions.

NERC’s second-quarter 2024 report recorded a 28.09 per cent decline in average hourly generation from Kainji, Jebba and Shiroro, from 1,030.88 megawatt-hours per hour in the first quarter to 741.28MWh/h in the second quarter.

The commission attributed the decline partly to seasonal variation, alongside operational constraints affecting some generating stations.

The Nigerian Meteorological Agency’s 2026 Seasonal Climate Prediction also identified potential implications of rainfall patterns for hydropower generation.

NiMet predicted that below-normal rainfall and shorter rainy seasons in parts of Borno, Yobe, Ogun, Oyo and Niger could reduce water levels in rivers Niger and Benue, potentially affecting water availability at Kainji Dam and hydropower generation, particularly towards the end of the rainy season.

The agency also warned that early cessation of rainfall in parts of Kogi, Niger and Rivers could shorten the operational hours of hydroelectric plants, create dry-season energy deficits and increase dependence on alternative sources of power.

It recommended climate-resilient energy planning, improved hydropower systems and increased investment in solar energy, particularly in areas with strong solar potential.

However, Professor of Energy and Electricity Law at the University of Lagos, Yemi Oke, disagreed with the suggestion that the dry season would necessarily worsen electricity supply, arguing that gas-fired plants should be able to sustain generation irrespective of rainfall, provided gas supply remained stable.

He said, “In the dry season, we should expect stabilised supply because most of the power plants are gas-fired and gas has nothing to do with whether there is a dry or wet season. So, if we have stable supply of gas, the DisCos should have something to distribute, provided they are able to get money.”

Oke said the dry season could affect hydroelectric plants because their operations depended on water flow, but stated that the impact should not automatically translate into reduced electricity supplied to homes and offices.

The professor also noted that transmission limitations, poor distribution infrastructure and commercial considerations could prevent consumers from receiving electricity even when generating plants have available capacity.

Oke added that affordability was another challenge, particularly in northern Nigeria, where some consumers struggled to pay for electricity despite government subsidies.

He also said distribution companies could prioritise customers who pay higher tariffs and generate better returns for their businesses over households whose consumption and payment capacity are lower.

Oke said, “The DisCos know how to segregate. For instance, DisCos that have 500 megawatts and, during the dry season, have like 250 megawatts, will serve the highest stakeholders.”

Oke said the dry season should also provide an opportunity for households, businesses and

communities, particularly in northern Nigeria, to expand their use of solar energy.

He stated that the country’s energy planning should reflect regional differences in electricity demand, geographical conditions and economic activities rather than relying on a uniform model of power supply.

According to him, northern communities with strong solar potential could benefit from mini-grids and standalone solar systems, particularly in rural areas where households may require electricity for lighting, small appliances and basic economic activities.

He said the South, with its concentration of industrial activities and businesses requiring substantial electricity, would continue to need a dependable grid supply.

Oke noted that electricity planning should be tailored to the needs of individual communities, with solar energy complementing the national grid rather than leaving all consumers dependent on centralised generation and transmission.

He also expressed optimism that the decentralisation of the electricity market under the Electricity Act 2023 could attract more investors and operators, allowing states and other participants to develop electricity systems suited to their local needs.

The post Dry season: Fear mounts over worsening power crisis appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
author: Daniel Ayantoye

title: 2027: Outrage over widespread billboard attacks
description:
Opposition parties in some states have expressed outrage over the widespread destruction of their campaign billboards, alleging deliberate attempts to stifle their political activities ahead of the 2027 general elections.
The parties, in separate interviews with Sunday PUNCH, also lamented the impos
content:
Opposition parties in some states have expressed outrage over the widespread destruction of their campaign billboards, alleging deliberate attempts to stifle their political activities ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The parties, in separate interviews with Sunday PUNCH, also lamented the imposition of exorbitant campaign fees, denial of access to public facilities for political rallies and restrictions on the erection of billboards.

They alleged that the destruction of their campaign materials, coupled with administrative restrictions and stringent conditions for accessing public spaces, had affected their campaign preparations and visibility.

However, the concerned state governments dismissed the allegations of political intimidation and discrimination, insisting that opposition parties were free to conduct their activities.

The African Democratic Congress and some northern state governments have, in recent weeks, traded accusations over the destruction of campaign billboards and the denial of access to venues for political activities.

In Benue State, the Chairman of the ADC, Adikwu Elias, accused the state government of denying opposition parties access to public facilities and using its agents to destroy their campaign billboards.

Speaking with Sunday PUNCH on Friday, Elias described the destruction of campaign materials across the state as a deliberate attack on the opposition, adding that the development had become a source of concern to the coalition of political parties’ chairmen in the state.

He called for a level playing field for all political parties, irrespective of their affiliations.

Elias said, “The state government has been depriving the opposition parties of venues for their programmes. If you have a political occasion and ask for a space, the government will tell you it is not available.

“If you paste posters, they will remove them. Their agents are all over the state, destroying opposition billboards. The coalition of political parties’ chairmen have met on this because we are concerned about it. We must be given a level playing field.

“Why is it called democracy if the government is not allowing the opposition to live? I must say that the All Progressives Congress, which is in government, is even fighting itself. A faction of the APC is not allowing the other faction to hold programmes in the state. It is as bad as that.”

Reacting, the Benue State Commissioner for Information and Orientation, Solomon Iorpev, dismissed the allegations that the government was restricting the campaign activities of opposition parties.

The commissioner disclosed that campaign billboards belonging to the ruling party were also being destroyed across the state, stressing that members of the opposition were not the only victims of vandalism.

Iorpev said the government was taking steps to constitute a task force in collaboration with security agencies to apprehend those responsible for destroying billboards and tearing campaign posters.

“We are trying to set up a task force because our own billboards are being torn and pulled down at every point. We see this as a nuisance, and it is something to take seriously.

“The officer in charge has been told to meet with the security agencies to set up a task force and see how to apprehend those responsible for pulling down billboards and tearing posters in the state,” he said.

The commissioner maintained that the state government had no reason to gag opposition parties, noting that the electorate had the exclusive right to determine who would emerge victorious at the polls.

“The Benue State Government is not afraid of anyone, so we have no reason to gag anyone seeking the votes of our people. Electioneering has nothing to do with government; we are all seeking the votes of our people, and voters have the exclusive right to decide on who they will vote for.

“Whether you gag people or not, the electorate has the decision on who to vote for. We cannot be seen fighting those who are seeking votes from the same people we are also seeking votes from.

“It will amount to making the people have sympathy for the opposition because they would think that they (opposition parties) have something better to offer. Whereas no one has a better offer than our governor.”

Iorpev, however, urged opposition parties seeking to use public facilities for political rallies and campaigns to follow due process.

Kaduna ADC alleges sabotage

In Kaduna State, the ADC accused the state government of frustrating its preparations for the 2027 general elections through the denial of access to public facilities and the alleged destruction of its campaign materials.

Abdulwaheed Adubi, the spokesperson for the ADC governorship candidate, Isa Ashiru, told Sunday PUNCH on Saturday that suspected political thugs linked to the ruling APC had been vandalising and removing the party’s campaign signposts and publicity materials.

He lamented that even small signposts bearing the party’s logo or the image of its governorship candidate were not spared.

“Even the small signposts we put up, whether carrying the ADC logo or the picture of our candidate, are either vandalised or removed. That is the situation in Kaduna State,” he alleged.

Adubi further accused the state government of denying the party permission to use the Ranchers Bees Stadium for a political event, despite what he described as compliance with the necessary application procedures.

According to him, the ADC had formally submitted its request to use the facility through the appropriate government office but was denied access.

“Interestingly, the commissioner later claimed that we did not apply, adding that if we had applied, the facility would have been made available to us. But the same facility was used for another event two days after we were denied access,” he said.

Adubi described the denial of access to the stadium as a deliberate attempt to frustrate the growing activities of the ADC in the state.

The spokesperson said the alleged restrictions and destruction of campaign materials had affected the party’s preparations for the forthcoming elections, particularly its outdoor publicity and public engagements.

When contacted, the Kaduna State Commissioner for Information and Culture, Ahmed Maiyaki, who is also the spokesperson for the APC Campaign Council, promised to call back.

However, he had yet to do so as of the time of filing this report.

Kano ADC petitions police, DSS

The Kano State chapter of the ADC also accused the state government of frustrating its campaign activities by preventing it from erecting billboards.

The state chairman of the party, Alhaji Musa Ungogo, alleged that the few campaign billboards erected by the ADC had been removed on the orders of the state government.

Ungogo said the party had formally complained to security agencies about the destruction of its campaign materials in September, regretting that the situation had persisted despite the petition.

The ADC had submitted the petition, dated September 24, to the Department of State Services and the police, condemning what it described as the illegal removal and destruction of its campaign billboards in the state.

A copy of the petition obtained by Sunday PUNCH read in part, “We write to formally petition your respective agencies regarding the illegal removal, vandalism, and destruction of our legally erected campaign billboards in Kano State. This act is not only a criminal offence but a direct assault on the democratic process and the fundamental rights of our candidates and supporters.”

The opposition party further alleged that the Kano State Agency for Social Intervention was acting on a directive to ensure that “no billboard belonging to the opposition should be allowed” in the state.

Efforts to obtain the reaction of the Kano State Government to the allegations were unsuccessful.

The Commissioner for Information, Sunusi Bature, neither answered phone calls nor responded to messages sent to him as of the time of filing this report.

Zamfara ADC protests hike in charges

In Zamfara State, the ADC alleged that the destruction of its campaign billboards and the imposition of charges on political activities had forced the party to resort to grassroots mobilisation.

The state chairman of the ADC, Kabiru Garba, told Sunday PUNCH that the government had introduced charges for campaign activities, including political rallies, the erection of billboards and the placement of banners.

Garba alleged that the government was unwilling to allow opposition parties to campaign freely in the state.

He disclosed that the ADC had written to the government protesting against the charges and demanding a reduction, but its request had not been granted.

“The state government sent a notification letter to us, asking us to pay some money before we could hold rallies, campaigns or erect billboards. We have written a letter in protest, asking the government to reduce the charges, but it did not.

“As I am talking to you, our billboards are being destroyed across the state. Even the billboards, banners and flags that we put up at our campaign office were removed.

“The government increased the signage charges by 70 per cent. We have to pay before we can hold a rally and before our vehicles can move from one place to another, while our billboards are being destroyed. They are targeting the opposition; the government doesn’t want us to campaign,” Garba said.

But the Special Assistant to the Zamfara State Governor on Media and Communication, Mustafa Kaura, dismissed the allegations of political persecution, challenging the opposition party to provide evidence to substantiate its claims.

Kaura described Governor Dauda Lawal as a liberal leader, maintaining that Zamfara State practised advanced democracy and that opposition parties were allowed to use government facilities for their activities.

“The state government has never witch-hunted any opposition party. They are allowed to use government facilities. Freedom Square is given to them to do whatever they want there,” Kaura stated.

Sokoto ADC decries vandalism

Similarly, the Chairman of the ADC in Sokoto State, Bello Yabo, lamented the destruction of the party’s campaign billboards across the state.

Yabo, who spoke with Sunday PUNCH on Friday, alleged that the party had been denied space to erect its billboards, while the few it managed to install had been vandalised.

He attributed the absence of the party’s campaign billboards in parts of the state to the alleged widespread destruction of its publicity materials.

“Our campaign billboards have been vandalised across the state. That’s why you have not been seeing them around,” he said.

Efforts to obtain a reaction from the Sokoto State Governor’s spokesperson, Abubakar Bawa, were unsuccessful, as he neither answered calls nor replied to messages sent to his phone.

Parties lament exorbitant campaign fees

In Gombe State, the Chairman of the New Nigeria Congress, Badingada Alkali, lamented the difficulties experienced by the party in erecting campaign billboards owing to what he described as high charges.

Alkali also complained about the difficulties associated with securing venues for political activities, alleging that even the use of privately owned facilities attracted scrutiny from government officials.

He said, “To even get a space for political activities is hell unless it is your own property. Even at that, the government would send people to verify if you are paying taxes for that property.”

However, the Publicity Secretary of the APC in Gombe State, Murtala Usman, dismissed the allegations, describing the state as one of the most receptive environments for opposition political parties.

Usman maintained that opposition parties were not being intimidated in the state and were free to conduct their campaigns.

Also, the Kogi State chapter of the NDC decried what it described as exorbitant charges imposed by the state government on billboard placements and other campaign materials.

The state chairman of the party, Monday Onate, told Sunday PUNCH that the charges were not restricted to billboards but extended to other materials used by political parties and their candidates to publicise their activities.

According to Onate, the government had imposed fees on campaign materials, including branded vehicles, T-shirts and face caps.

“The government has imposed fees on all campaign materials, including vehicle branding, T-shirts and others,” he said.

Anambra NDC turns to churches, community facilities

In Anambra State, the NDC lamented the destruction of campaign billboards erected by its candidates despite paying for the spaces.

The state chairman of the party, Ikemefuna Uzoezie, told Sunday PUNCH that the NDC was experiencing difficulties securing billboard spaces for its campaign activities.

He said even when candidates of the party succeeded in securing and paying for billboard spaces, their campaign billboards were subsequently removed or damaged.

Uzoezie also complained about restrictions on the use of government-owned facilities for political activities.

He disclosed that the party had resorted to using churches and community facilities for its programmes because of the restrictions imposed by the state government on access to public facilities.

Enugu defends N150m billboard charge

Meanwhile, the Enugu State chapter of the ADC lamented the reported imposition of a N150m fee on opposition parties for billboard placement in the state.

The state chairman of the ADC, Stella Chukwuma, disclosed this in a telephone interview with one of our correspondents on Saturday.

Chukwuma attributed the absence of opposition campaign billboards in the state to the charge.

She, however, explained that the party had yet to formally apply to the state government for permission to use public facilities for its political activities.

She said, “That is why you have not seen any billboards belonging to opposition parties in Enugu State.

“As for public spaces, we have yet to write an application to the state government to find out if we will be granted permission to use them.”

Reacting to the complaint, the Senior Special Assistant to the Enugu State Governor on Strategic Communications, Dr Collins Ogbu, described the N150m fee as a billboard permit charge.

Ogbu maintained that such charges were not peculiar to Enugu State, citing what he said was the amount charged in Lagos State.

He said, “We have it in Lagos, where it is N700m, and in other states as well.”

The post 2027: Outrage over widespread billboard attacks appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: IPC seeks citizen-focused  election coverage
description:
The International Press Centre has urged journalists and media organisations to prioritise citizens’ concerns, scrutinise political promises and hold elected officials accountable ahead of the 2027 elections, rather than focusing primarily on rallies, party defections and campaign activities.
The Ex
content:
The International Press Centre has urged journalists and media organisations to prioritise citizens’ concerns, scrutinise political promises and hold elected officials accountable ahead of the 2027 elections, rather than focusing primarily on rallies, party defections and campaign activities.

The Executive Director of the IPC, Lanre Arogundade, made the call in Abuja during an interface with the Nigeria Union of Journalists on Professional and Democratic Accountability Journalism ahead of the 2027 elections.

Arogundade said the media must strengthen its capacity to provide credible, balanced, inclusive and public-interest information as the country approaches another election cycle.

He said elections should not be reduced to political campaigns, rallies, candidates and the eventual announcement of results, stressing that citizens’ aspirations, concerns and expectations of leadership must occupy a central position in electoral reporting.

According to him, journalists have a responsibility to facilitate informed public discourse, interrogate campaign promises and ensure that the voices of ordinary Nigerians are adequately represented.

He said, “This is why we must begin to look beyond event-driven electoral coverage towards more substantive, issue-based, and citizen-centred reporting.

“The question before us is not simply how well the media can cover the activities of political parties and candidates. It is also how effectively the media can interrogate campaign promises, document citizens’ priority concerns, verify political claims, monitor the performance of elected officials, and provide the public with the information necessary to assess governance.”

The IPC director challenged journalists to examine whether their reports adequately reflected Nigerians’ concerns about the economy, education, healthcare, security, employment and infrastructure.

He also called for greater visibility for women, young people, persons with disabilities and other underrepresented groups in electoral reporting.

Arogundade warned that sensationalism, unverified claims, inflammatory rhetoric and the unchecked spread of misinformation and disinformation could undermine public confidence, deepen social divisions and weaken democratic institutions.

He said, “Conversely, a media environment that prioritises accuracy, fairness, verification, conflict-sensitive reporting, and accountability can strengthen public trust and contribute to peaceful, credible, and inclusive elections.”

He further urged journalists to strengthen their verification skills and resist pressure to prioritise speed over accuracy, noting that fact-checking must become an integral part of responsible electoral reporting.

The IPC executive director also expressed concerns about the safety and professional independence of journalists, insisting that they should be able to discharge their duties without intimidation, harassment or unlawful interference.

Similarly, the Chairman of the NUJ, FCT Council, Grace Ike, urged journalists to place citizens at the centre of electoral discourse rather than allow politicians to dictate the direction of election coverage.

She said democracy could not thrive where citizens were misinformed, while accountability would remain elusive if the media merely reported events without interrogating promises, policies and performance.

Ike said, “As we approach 2027, our reporting must go beyond rallies, defections, press statements and the drama of politics. We must ask the harder questions:

“What do citizens truly want? What are their priority concerns on security, the economy, jobs, education, healthcare, infrastructure, and the cost of living? Are candidates offering real solutions, or mere slogans? Are promises being kept, or broken?”

She described accountability journalism as putting citizens, rather than politicians, at the centre of electoral conversations.

The NUJ chairman identified misinformation, disinformation, hate speech, online manipulation, growing public distrust and safety threats to journalists as challenges confronting the media ahead of the elections.

She said verification must take precedence over speed and accuracy over sensationalism, urging journalists to resist being used as instruments of political propaganda.

Ike reaffirmed the council’s commitment to professional and ethical journalism, press freedom, fact-checking and the protection of journalists.

She added, “Let us give voice to the voiceless — the women, the young people, persons with disabilities, and ordinary Nigerians in communities whose concerns are often ignored until election season.”

title: NUPRC opens bidding for 40 oil, gas blocks
description:
The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission has opened its portal for the 2026 oil and gas licensing round, offering 40 blocks to investors as the Federal Government steps up efforts to attract fresh capital into the upstream petroleum sector.
The registration portal, br2026.gov.ng, went l
content:
The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission has opened its portal for the 2026 oil and gas licensing round, offering 40 blocks to investors as the Federal Government steps up efforts to attract fresh capital into the upstream petroleum sector.

The registration portal, br2026.gov.ng, went live on Friday, 20 November, with interested companies given until 15 January, 2027, to complete their registration and prequalification processes.

The 40 blocks are spread across three categories, comprising 17 onshore blocks, 14 shallow water blocks and nine deep offshore blocks.

The Commission disclosed this in a statement issued by its Head of Corporate Communications and Media, Eniola Akinkuotu, on Saturday, urging prospective investors to visit the portal to access the full list of available blocks, bidding guidelines and frequently asked questions.

It said the website had been designed to provide users with a seamless experience throughout the licensing exercise.

The statement read, “The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission wishes to inform the general public that the 2026 licensing round portal is now live. On offer are 40 oil and gas blocks across three terrains. The blocks are grouped as follows: Onshore (17), shallow water (14) and deep offshore (9). Interested bidders are urged to visit the site to view the full list of the 40 blocks, as well as the guidelines and frequently asked questions.”

The 2026 licensing round will be conducted in five stages, beginning with registration and prequalification, followed by access to data, submission of technical and commercial bids, technical evaluation and a commercial conference.

The opening of the portal marks the transition from the announcement and publicity phase of the exercise to the formal participation of prospective investors.

According to the commission, the next major activity will be the pre-bid conference scheduled to be held in Lagos on 16 December, 2026. The conference is expected to provide prospective bidders with an opportunity to obtain further information about the available assets, the bidding process and the requirements for participation.

The commission said the licensing round was first announced by its Chief Executive, Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, on 6 October, 2026, following approval by President Bola Tinubu, who is also the Minister of Petroleum Resources.

It added that the announcement was accompanied by statutory advertisements in local and international newspapers in accordance with the provisions of the Petroleum Industry Act.

The commission said, “Registration on the portal, br2026.gov.ng, began on November 20, 2026 and will close on January 15, 2027.”

It further stated that, “On offer are 40 oil and gas blocks across three terrains. The blocks are grouped as follows: Onshore (17), shallow water (14) and deep offshore (9).”

The latest exercise comes as Nigeria seeks to increase crude oil and gas production, attract investment into its petroleum industry and improve the country’s competitiveness in the global energy market.

The licensing round also follows the 2025 oil and gas licensing exercise, which offered 50 blocks and attracted interest from 143 companies. The exercise recorded 200 bids, with 31 companies emerging as successful bidders for 37 blocks, while 13 blocks did not receive bids.

The 2026 round provides another opportunity for indigenous and international oil companies to secure petroleum assets and expand exploration and development activities in Nigeria.

The availability of blocks across onshore, shallow water and deep offshore terrains is expected to provide investment opportunities for companies with different technical and financial capacities.

The exercise is particularly significant as Nigeria continues to grapple with production challenges, including crude oil theft, pipeline vandalism, underinvestment and declining output from some mature oilfields.

The government has repeatedly identified increased exploration, field development and private-sector investment as critical to achieving its production ambitions and improving revenue from the petroleum industry.

The post NUPRC opens bidding for 40 oil, gas blocks appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: PSHAN, WHO urge increased private investment to rescue Nigeria’s healthcare system
description:
By Matthew Johnson







The Private Sector Health Alliance of Nigeria (PSHAN) and the World Health Organisation (WHO) have called for increased private sector investment and stronger public-private partnerships to address persistent challenges confronting Nigeria’s healthcare system.







The or
content:
By Matthew Johnson

The Private Sector Health Alliance of Nigeria (PSHAN) and the World Health Organisation (WHO) have called for increased private sector investment and stronger public-private partnerships to address persistent challenges confronting Nigeria’s healthcare system.

The organisations said government alone could not shoulder the responsibility of transforming the health sector, stressing that sustained private sector investment was critical to improving healthcare delivery, strengthening infrastructure and achieving universal health coverage.

The call was made at the 2026 PSHAN Annual Gala and Awards Night held in Lagos on November 20, with the theme, “Legacy Builders: Honouring the Visionaries of the Nigerian Healthcare System.”

Speaking at the event, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of PSHAN, Dr. Tinuola Akinbolagbe, said the alliance was working to position the private sector at the centre of Nigeria’s health development through strategic partnerships, investment, innovation and institutional strengthening.

She said PSHAN was seeking to move beyond fragmented private sector interventions towards coordinated investments capable of strengthening health systems and delivering measurable and sustainable outcomes.

According to her, meaningful progress in healthcare requires shared responsibility and collaboration across different sectors.

“As we look towards 2027 and beyond, our ambition is to move from fragmented contributions by the private sector to coordinated investment, from isolated interventions to stronger health systems, and from good intentions to measurable, sustainable outcomes,” she said.

Akinbolagbe explained that the theme of the event was designed to celebrate individuals, institutions and organisations whose courage, leadership, innovation and commitment had contributed to shaping the future of healthcare in Nigeria.

In his keynote address, former President of the African Development Bank Group and Executive Chairman of the Global Africa Investment Summit, Dr. Akinwumi Adesina, described healthcare as an investment in human capital and essential economic infrastructure rather than merely social sector expenditure.

Speaking on the theme, “Health as Wealth: Mobilising African Leadership and Capital to Build Sustainable Health Systems,” Adesina said a healthy population was fundamental to productivity, innovation, economic competitiveness and national prosperity.

He maintained that no country could achieve sustainable wealth without a healthy population, insisting that investment in healthcare was essential to building a productive workforce and inclusive economy.

Adesina called for stronger partnerships between government and the private sector, noting that government alone could not finance and deliver the transformation required in the country’s healthcare system.

He urged businesses to move beyond philanthropy and corporate social responsibility initiatives to embrace healthcare as a strategic investment priority.

“I urge businesses to move beyond philanthropy and corporate social responsibility initiatives to regard healthcare as a strategic investment priority.

“Investments should be directed towards strengthening primary healthcare, training and supporting health workers, local production of essential medicines and vaccines, digital healthcare infrastructure, reliable diagnostics and sustainable health financing,” he said.

The former AfDB president said Nigeria must build a healthcare system where women did not die during childbirth because of lack of access to quality medical services and families were not pushed into poverty by illness.

He urged stakeholders to prioritise women, children and vulnerable communities, stressing that access to quality healthcare should not depend on an individual’s income or circumstances.

“Nigeria must reduce its dependence on imported essential medicines, vaccines and diagnostic products by strengthening local manufacturing, promoting health innovation and developing resilient healthcare supply chains,” he added.

Also speaking, Dr. Pavel Ursu, representing the World Health Organisation, warned that Nigeria and other African countries risked losing the benefits of their growing youthful populations without deliberate investments in healthcare.

He identified high maternal and child mortality, inadequate healthcare funding, shortages of health workers and poor infrastructure as major challenges undermining the continent’s healthcare ambitions.

Ursu stressed that healthcare facilities required essential infrastructure, including reliable electricity and water supply, to deliver quality services.

He cited Nigeria’s Universal Health Coverage Compact, signed in December 2023 and expanded in 2025 to include the private sector, as an example of the importance of involving businesses in health policy development and implementation.

He also identified the incorporation of the private sector into the implementation of the Basic Health Care Provision Fund as an opportunity to strengthen collaboration.

“Government policies must encourage private sector participation. The responsibility of developing the health sector cannot be left to government alone,” he said.

Ursu maintained that Africa’s demographic advantage could translate into a productive workforce and economic growth only if governments and other stakeholders took practical steps to improve health outcomes.

Similarly, the Special Adviser to the President on Health, Dr. Salma Ibrahim-Anas, said the Federal Government had urged the organised private sector to deepen collaboration with public health institutions to translate national health policies into measurable improvements in the lives of Nigerians.

She outlined six priority areas for private sector alignment under the Nigerian Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative. These include primary healthcare revitalisation, expansion of national health insurance enrolment, domestic manufacturing of pharmaceuticals and medical equipment, digital health deployment in underserved communities, maternal and child survival, and health workforce training.

Citing 2026 Federal Ministry of Health statistics, Ibrahim-Anas disclosed that the private sector already contributed over N5 trillion to healthcare delivery, owned 82 per cent of secondary health facilities and had revamped more than 5,400 primary healthcare centres.

She called on corporate organisations to move beyond isolated corporate social responsibility projects towards integrated investments aligned with state and local government priorities under the sector-wide approach.

She warned against abandoned and poorly equipped healthcare projects, stressing that renovated facilities must be adequately staffed and supplied with essential medicines, electricity and water.

“Private sector healthcare spending should be viewed as a strategic investment in human capital, workforce productivity and national economic growth rather than mere charity,” she said.

The United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Special Adviser on Africa, Dr. Ahunna Eziakonwa, also urged private sector leaders and policymakers to move beyond isolated health interventions and build enduring partnerships capable of strengthening public healthcare delivery for future generations.

Eziakonwa said the theme, “Legacy Builders: Honouring the Visionaries of Nigerian Healthcare,” represented the importance of building sustainable institutions that continuously improve lives rather than measuring legacies merely by physical structures or accumulated wealth.

She noted that governments had the primary responsibility of setting standards, financing public services and protecting equity, but maintained that private sector capital, technology and operational expertise could achieve greater impact when aligned with national, state and local health priorities.

“Cross-sector partnerships remain critical to Africa’s broader economic transformation, food security and climate resilience. Corporate and public leaders must sustain long-term alliances that deliver quality healthcare across generations,” she said.

The awards ceremony featured 125 public nominations across five major categories and 25 subcategories, which were subsequently reduced to 75 through public voting.

The organisers said the awards were designed to celebrate excellence across Nigeria’s healthcare ecosystem while encouraging greater commitment to sustainable healthcare development.

The post PSHAN, WHO urge increased private investment to rescue Nigeria’s healthcare system appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: French cops convicted in Black producer assault
description:
The lawyer for a Black man who was beaten up by three French police officers hailed a “historic ruling” on Saturday after a court acknowledged the racist nature of the violence and sentenced them to between one and two years in prison.
According to CNN, the assault on Michel Zecler, a music producer
content:
The lawyer for a Black man who was beaten up by three French police officers hailed a “historic ruling” on Saturday after a court acknowledged the racist nature of the violence and sentenced them to between one and two years in prison.

According to CNN, the assault on Michel Zecler, a music producer, took place six years ago during the coronavirus pandemic and was caught on camera. It showed the officers repeatedly punching him, using a truncheon and tear gas against him for no apparent reason.

Zecler told The Associated Press after the incident that the officers hurled repeated insults at him, including a very strong racist epithet.

“What is very important is that the racist nature of the violence he suffered has been recognised,” Zecler’s lawyer, Serge Money, told France Info. “As a legal professional, one can only be satisfied. This is a first.”

Money said that from the very beginning of the proceedings, Zecler maintained that he had been racially insulted, whereas the defendants’ accounts were somewhat inconsistent.

“Ultimately, they were convicted of lying, as the falsification of written records was established,” he said. The verdict was issued late Friday in Paris.

Videos published showed the violent arrest of Zecler in the 17th arrondissement of the French capital. The three officers intended to stop him for not wearing a face mask during the restrictions imposed because of the pandemic.

The video images, obtained by the AP, both from a security camera inside the studio and filmed by neighbours outside, showed officers following Zecler inside his music studio, where they could be seen repeatedly punching him and beating him with a truncheon.

“I want to understand why I have been assaulted by people who were wearing a police uniform,” Zecler told AP at the time. “I want justice actually, because I believe in the justice of my country.”

Zecler suffered injuries to his head, forearms and legs.

French law enforcement agencies have long faced complaints of excessive force. After Zecler was taken into custody for violence against public authority, then-Justice Minister Eric Dupond-Moretti said in a television interview that he was scandalised by the images.

He admitted that some officers were racists, but denied systemic racism within the force.

Money said that without the video, Zecler would have ended up in prison. He added that the officers apologised.

“This ruling should set a precedent for all those who have not been believed,” he said. “There has to be a first, a starting point. It is now up to the justice system to make use of this ruling. I have no doubt that everyone will recognise its significance. This is no small matter, particularly given that the investigating judges had initially dismissed the racist dimension of the case.”

Rap artist Stomy Bugsy said, “This is a victory for all victims. If it can help curb, reduce and ultimately put an end to this kind of police misconduct and abuse, then it is a victory.”

The post French cops convicted in Black producer assault appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Food inflation exceeds 20% in 19 Nigerian states
description:
Food inflation exceeded 20 per cent in 19 Nigerian states in October 2026, despite a decline in the national annual food inflation rate, according to an analysis of the latest Consumer Price Index data by The PUNCH.
The affected states represent 52.8 per cent of Nigeria’s 36 states, indicating that
content:
Food inflation exceeded 20 per cent in 19 Nigerian states in October 2026, despite a decline in the national annual food inflation rate, according to an analysis of the latest Consumer Price Index data by The PUNCH.

The affected states represent 52.8 per cent of Nigeria’s 36 states, indicating that more than half experienced annual food price increases exceeding 20 per cent, even as the national rate moderated from 19.59 per cent in September to 19.13 per cent in October.

The findings were contained in the September and October 2026 CPI reports and accompanying statistical tables obtained by The PUNCH from the National Bureau of Statistics website on Friday.

Ondo recorded the highest annual food inflation at 31.74 per cent, up from 31.49 per cent in September, while Lagos recorded 31.43 per cent, down from 34.40 per cent.

Imo followed with 29.75 per cent, declining from 33.79 per cent, while Oyo recorded 28.81 per cent against 24.50 per cent in September.

According to the October report, “Food inflation on a Year-on-Year basis was highest in Ondo (31.74 per cent), Lagos (31.43 per cent), and Imo (29.75 per cent).”

Ebonyi’s rate increased from approximately 22.0 per cent to 27.96 per cent, while Rivers recorded 25.33 per cent, compared with about 28 per cent previously.

Other affected states included Abia at 24.22 per cent, Delta at 23.91 per cent, Enugu at 23.48 per cent, Zamfara at 22.88 per cent, Ogun at 22.47 per cent, Yobe at 22.26 per cent, Anambra at 22.23 per cent and Kebbi at 22.21 per cent.

Akwa Ibom recorded 21.56 per cent; Edo, 21.52 per cent; Sokoto, 21.40 per cent; Ekiti, 20.61 per cent, and Kaduna, 20.32 per cent.

The figures showed that two states recorded food inflation above 30 per cent, while six exceeded 25 per cent.

However, the monthly figures revealed a different pattern, with food prices declining in several states despite their high annual inflation rates.

Nationally, food prices declined by 0.75 per cent in October, following a steeper 1.55 per cent reduction in September.

This represented a 0.80 percentage-point increase in the monthly inflation rate, indicating that food prices were still falling nationally, but at a slower pace.

The NBS explained, “On a month-on-month basis, the Food inflation rate in October 2026 was -0.75 per cent, up by 0.80 percentage points from September 2026 (-1.55 per cent).”

The September report showed that monthly food inflation had fallen from a positive 1.02 per cent in August to -1.55 per cent in September, a decline of 2.57 percentage points.

Consequently, the October figures marked the second consecutive month of declining national food prices, although the pace of reduction weakened.

At the state level, Yobe recorded the most significant reversal, with monthly food inflation rising to 18.41 per cent in October from -7.0 per cent in September, a 25.41 percentage-point increase.

Kebbi followed with 16.45 per cent, compared with minus 4.9 per cent previously, while Sokoto rose to 13.0 per cent from minus 1.7 per cent.

Zamfara’s monthly rate increased to 8.7 per cent from 6.0 per cent, while Anambra rose to 4.3 per cent from minus 0.3 per cent.

Enugu recorded 4.9 per cent against 14.5 per cent previously, Abia increased to 2.6 per cent from 0.4 per cent, and Ebonyi rose to 2.4 per cent from -2.1 per cent.

Ogun’s monthly food inflation increased to 1.5 per cent from -0.4 per cent, Edo rose to 0.9 per cent from -2.8 per cent, and Imo slowed to 0.6 per cent from 5.2 per cent.

Ondo moderated to 0.6 per cent from 2.6 per cent, while Kaduna’s food prices declined by 4.7 per cent, reversing September’s 3.2 per cent increase.

In contrast, Lagos recorded a monthly decline of 5.93 per cent, compared with a 0.4 per cent increase in September. Rivers recorded -4.3 per cent against -2.0 per cent previously.

Delta recorded minus 3.8 per cent compared with a 2.2 per cent increase, Oyo recorded -2.6 per cent against 3.8 per cent, and Akwa Ibom recorded -1.5 per cent against -0.4 per cent.

Ekiti’s monthly food inflation improved to -0.4 per cent from -1.5 per cent.

Overall, 11 of the 19 states recorded monthly food price increases in October, while eight experienced declines, highlighting the uneven distribution of food price pressures.

The NBS attributed national food price movements to changes in the prices of vegetable oil, sardines, green peas, frozen fish, local rice, fresh catfish, beef tripe, palm oil and millet flour.

However, the NBS cautioned against drawing direct conclusions from comparisons between states because consumption patterns and the weights assigned to food items differ across locations.

The post Food inflation exceeds 20% in 19 Nigerian states appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: US: Judge approves $7.25bn Roundup cancer settlement
description:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved a $7.25bn settlement stemming from lawsuits alleging that Bayer’s weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.
According to the BBC, Judge Timothy Boyer said the settlement was “fair, reasonable, and adequate.”
Bayer, the German biotech giant, had proposed paying the $7.25bn
content:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved a $7.25bn settlement stemming from lawsuits alleging that Bayer’s weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.

According to the BBC, Judge Timothy Boyer said the settlement was “fair, reasonable, and adequate.”

Bayer, the German biotech giant, had proposed paying the $7.25bn to definitively resolve a legal battle in the US.

The nationwide settlement will be paid to Roundup users who are already sick with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.

The company had already paid roughly $10bn to resolve litigation related to Roundup.

The settlements to participants range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on how frequently they used the product, when they were diagnosed with the cancer and how severe their illness was.

“[Friday’s] final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice,” said Christopher Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case.

Bayer will make annual payments into a fund for up to 21 years, providing as much as $7.25bn.

Some attorneys had objected to the settlement funds, arguing they were not enough, but the judge said he did not want to delay payouts to sick victims.

Bayer denies that its Roundup product causes cancer.

The settlement comes after the Supreme Court in June ruled in favour of Bayer, overturning a $1.25m settlement for a Missouri man who said Roundup and its ingredient glyphosate were to blame for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

The court ruled 7-2, saying Bayer cannot be sued in state courts because federal regulations do not mandate a cancer warning label.

The company has faced thousands of claims in US state and federal courts from people alleging they developed cancer after using the product.

Roundup was developed by Monsanto in the 1970s. Its active ingredient, glyphosate, was identified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, a unit of the World Health Organisation, in 2015 as a probable human carcinogen.

Bayer and some other regulators, including the US Environmental Protection Agency, have disputed those findings.

But the issue has forced the company through years of costly litigation in the US, as juries in several states opt to award billions of dollars to users of the herbicide.

The post US: Judge approves $7.25bn Roundup cancer settlement appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Access Holdings chief urges graduates on AI skills
description:
The Group Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Access Holdings Plc, Innocent Ike, has urged graduates of the Federal University of Technology, Akure, Ondo State, to acquire artificial intelligence and digital skills to remain relevant in a rapidly changing job market.
Ike said technological
content:
The Group Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Access Holdings Plc, Innocent Ike, has urged graduates of the Federal University of Technology, Akure, Ondo State, to acquire artificial intelligence and digital skills to remain relevant in a rapidly changing job market.

Ike said technological advancement was transforming industries and redefining career opportunities, making continuous learning, adaptability and innovation essential for young professionals seeking to compete in the global economy.

He spoke at the combined convocation ceremony of FUTA on Friday, where he challenged the graduates to see their certificates as the beginning of their professional journeys and not the end of their pursuit of knowledge.

“Your certificate is a ticket, not a destination. Much of what you learned in your first year may already be out of date.

“Master artificial intelligence and digital tools in whatever field you choose, but also build the human skills machines cannot replace: creativity, clear communication, sound judgement, teamwork, and integrity,” he said.

The Access Holdings chief urged the graduates to build meaningful professional relationships, seize available opportunities and avoid waiting for perfect conditions before pursuing their ambitions.

He noted that their university classmates and professional contacts could become future business partners, executives, public servants and investors, stressing the importance of building reputations that would attract recommendations and career opportunities.

“Do not wait for the perfect job or the perfect moment. Seize the opportunity in front of you, make the most of it, and let it lead to the next. Start something, learn from it, and improve. Always be ready for the next opportunity,” he said.

Ike also cautioned the graduates against measuring their progress against the achievements of others, particularly through social media, urging them to prioritise their mental and physical well-being.

He further encouraged those whose careers might take them outside Nigeria to maintain connections with the country and contribute to its development through investments, ideas and expertise.

“Whether your career takes you to Lagos, London, or Lusaka, find ways to put your skills, ideas, and resources to work for Nigeria,” he said.

Earlier, the Vice-Chancellor of FUTA, Prof Adenike Oladiji, urged the graduates to become problem-solvers and contribute meaningfully to their communities and the country.

She said the university had equipped them with the knowledge and skills to become innovative thinkers, critical problem-solvers and responsible citizens capable of making meaningful contributions beyond the institution.

Oladiji noted that technological advancements, particularly artificial intelligence and digital transformation, were reshaping industries, redefining careers and creating new opportunities.

She urged the graduates to embrace continuous learning and innovation, adding that their certificates should mark the beginning of a lifelong commitment to knowledge, personal development and service to society.

title: FG to service $500m World Bank loan until 2050
description:
The Federal Government will repay a $500m World Bank agricultural loan over 20 years, beginning in May 2031 and ending in November 2050, under a financing agreement signed with the International Development Association.
The agreement obtained by Sunday PUNCH from the World Bank’s website on Friday p
content:
The Federal Government will repay a $500m World Bank agricultural loan over 20 years, beginning in May 2031 and ending in November 2050, under a financing agreement signed with the International Development Association.

The agreement obtained by Sunday PUNCH from the World Bank’s website on Friday provides that the country will make 40 semi-annual principal repayments of 2.5 per cent each, equivalent to $12.5m per instalment if the entire credit is drawn.

According to Schedule 3 of the agreement, “the Recipient shall repay the principal amount of the credit” on May 15 and November 15 each year, beginning May 15, 2031, and ending November 15, 2050.

This means the country will remain responsible for servicing the agricultural credit until 2050, although the project itself is scheduled to close on July 30, 2032.

The PUNCH earlier reported in April that the World Bank approved a $500m International Development Association credit to boost Nigeria’s agricultural sector under a new programme targeting smallholder farmers, value chains, and food security.

The funding will support the Nigeria Sustainable Agricultural Value-Chains for Growth project, also known as AGROW, which aims to improve productivity, strengthen market linkages, and create jobs across the country.

The 29-page financing agreement obtained by Sunday PUNCH covers the AGROW loan project.

It was signed by the Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, on October 29, 2026, while the World Bank Country Director, Mathew Verghis, signed on September 16, 2026.

Under Article II, the IDA agreed to provide “a credit, which is deemed as Concessional Financing” amounting to $500m to support agricultural development.

The agreement imposes a maximum commitment charge of 0.5 per cent annually on the undisbursed financing balance.

It also provides that the interest charge will be calculated using the reference rate plus a variable spread, less 250 basis points, subject to applicable ceilings and floors.

The project seeks to increase smallholder productivity and strengthen agricultural value chains in participating Nigerian states.

Of the total financing, $230m, representing 46 per cent, is allocated to performance-based matching grants for agribusiness investments.

Another $229.5m, or 45.9 per cent, will finance goods, works, consultancy services, operating costs, and training, while $40.5m is reserved for expenditure linked to performance-based conditions.

The document explains that the matching grants will support investments in agricultural aggregation, storage, processing, logistics, post-harvest handling, and market connections between farmers and buyers.

It provides for agricultural research, improved seeds, extension services, digital farmer registration, and artificial intelligence-powered weather forecasting.

The agreement also requires improvements in seed certification, fertiliser quality regulation, and responsible land-based agricultural investment.

However, participating states must satisfy several conditions before accessing the financing.

According to Annex 2, states must adopt a responsible land investment framework through an executive order and establish regulations supporting a common digital farmer registry.

They must also publish “a consolidated schedule of trade-related fees and levies for inter-state movement of goods” and reports detailing traders’ complaints and remedial actions.

States must also publish policies linking support for agricultural cooperatives to verified commercial relationships with buyers.

Failure to meet these requirements could prevent participating states from receiving project funds.

The agreement provides that no withdrawal shall be made for payments to participating states until the Federal Government presents satisfactory evidence of compliance and executes the required subsidiary agreements.

The World Bank may also withhold, reallocate, or cancel financing linked to performance targets that are not achieved.

Among the targets is the registration of farmers in a national digital registry, with basic and enhanced coverage targets of 40 per cent and 70 per cent, respectively.

The agreement allocates $16m to this condition, with payments capped at $1m per participating state.

Other performance-linked allocations include $5m each for improved seed availability and private investment in seed production, $2.5m for fertiliser quality compliance, and $12m for responsible land investments.

The agreement requires the Federal Government to establish a national steering committee and a project coordination unit within three months of the project becoming effective.

It also mandates independent verification of performance targets, environmental and social safeguards, and periodic implementation reports.

For artificial intelligence applications, the agreement requires risk assessments before deployment and prohibits uses involving mass surveillance, social scoring, and discriminatory practices.

The financing agreement sets an effectiveness deadline of 90 days after the October 29 signature date, subject to the required implementation arrangements.

Although the credit is intended to strengthen agricultural productivity and private investment, its repayment schedule creates a long-term dollar-denominated obligation extending nearly two decades beyond the project’s scheduled closing date.

An analysis of figures published by the Debt Management Office showed that Nigeria’s outstanding debt to the World Bank rose from $14.34bn in March 2023, shortly before President Bola Tinubu assumed office, to $20.73bn as of June 30, 2026.

This represents an increase of approximately $6.39bn, or 44.6 per cent, within the period.

The latest debt stock comprised $19.12bn owed to the International Development Association and $1.61bn to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

Consequently, the World Bank accounted for approximately 38.02 per cent of Nigeria’s total external debt stock of $54.52bn at the end of June 2026, making it the country’s largest multilateral creditor.

Sunday PUNCH further observed that Nigeria’s external debt increased from N33.25tn ($43.16bn) in June 2023, shortly after President Bola Tinubu assumed office, to N75.20tn ($54.52bn) in June 2026, according to data from the DMO.

The figures represent an increase of N41.95tn, or 126.17 per cent, in naira terms, while the dollar-denominated debt rose by $11.36bn, or 26.32 per cent, over the three years.

The increase reflects additional external borrowing and the impact of exchange rate movements on the naira value of foreign debt, with external obligations accounting for 45.09 per cent of Nigeria’s N166.79tn total public debt as of June 2026.

Meanwhile, the World Bank’s International Debt Report 2026 has raised concerns about rising borrowing costs and debt servicing obligations among developing countries, warning that increased access to international financing does not necessarily translate into economic development.

The report stated, “Low- and middle-income countries are borrowing more, paying more, and, in many cases, leaving less for long-term development.”

It warned that rising debt servicing obligations could limit government spending on infrastructure, education, healthcare, and employment, particularly in countries already facing substantial financing needs.

The post FG to service $500m World Bank loan until 2050 appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: CJN faults weak enforcement of child protection laws
description:
The Chief Justice of Nigeria, Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, has said the country’s failure to effectively enforce child protection laws continues to expose children to abuse, exploitation and neglect, despite the existence of legal safeguards.
She stressed that legislation alone could not guarantee c
content:
The Chief Justice of Nigeria, Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, has said the country’s failure to effectively enforce child protection laws continues to expose children to abuse, exploitation and neglect, despite the existence of legal safeguards.

She stressed that legislation alone could not guarantee children’s safety, insisting that stronger institutional commitment and coordinated enforcement were necessary to translate the provisions of the law into tangible protection.

The CJN spoke on Friday at the inaugural conference of the Nigerian Association of Family Court Judicial Officers, Magistrates and Other Practitioners, organised to commemorate the 2026 United Nations World Children’s Day in Abuja.

Represented by a Supreme Court Justice, Jummai Sanke, Kekere-Ekun said the Child Rights Act 2003 provided an important legal framework for protecting children but required effective implementation by relevant institutions.

“In Nigeria, the Child Rights Act 2003 provides an important legal framework for the protection and advancement of children’s rights. Its recognition of the best interests of the child as a primary consideration in all actions concerning children establishes a principle that must guide our laws, policies, institutions and decisions.

“However, the existence of legislation, important as it is, does not by itself guarantee the protection of children. The real measure of our commitment lies in how effectively these rights are respected, protected and enforced in the daily lives of children,” she said.

The CJN listed child abuse, neglect, sexual exploitation, trafficking, child labour, early and forced marriage, abandonment and denial of access to education and healthcare among the persistent threats to children’s welfare.

She said the judiciary had a responsibility to ensure that children appearing before courts as victims, witnesses or children in conflict with the law were treated with dignity and sensitivity.

Kekere-Ekun called for child-friendly judicial proceedings that protected children’s privacy, allowed them to participate and took account of their age, maturity and emotional circumstances.

She added that children in conflict with the law should, where appropriate, be rehabilitated and reintegrated into society rather than subjected to measures capable of permanently undermining their future.

The CJN also advocated regular training for judicial officers on trauma-informed approaches, handling child witnesses and emerging forms of exploitation, including those involving digital technology.

She urged government institutions, law enforcement agencies, social welfare services, schools, healthcare providers, families and civil society organisations to work together to strengthen child protection.

“A child who has suffered abuse should not have to navigate a fragmented system in search of help,” she said.

Meanwhile, the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, disclosed that the Federal Government was reviewing the Child Rights Act 2003 to address emerging challenges in child protection.

Fagbemi said the review had produced a draft amendment bill scheduled for stakeholder validation on November 24, ahead of further steps towards its finalisation and enactment.

He said the country’s major challenge was not the absence of laws but the failure to implement them effectively.

“The pressing challenge before us is not the absence of laws, but the gap in their implementation. Across the country, too many children still face realities that threaten their safety and stifle their potential.

“Bridging this gap demands sustained political will, coordinated institutional action, and a readiness to adapt our systems to the evolving vulnerabilities of our children,” he said.

The minister said the Federal Ministry of Justice was also working to strengthen the child justice system through Legal Aid Guidelines and Prosecutors’ Guidelines for Handling Cases of Children in Contact with the Law.

He said the guidelines were intended to ensure quality legal representation and child-sensitive prosecution standards nationwide.

Fagbemi also called for stronger safeguards against cyberbullying, digital exploitation, harmful online content and breaches of children’s privacy.

He urged participants to ensure that the conference produced practical recommendations capable of improving court proceedings, policies and frontline child protection services.

Earlier, the President of NAFCJOMP, Justice Eberechi Suzette Nyesom-Wike, said the association was committed to advancing children’s rights and welfare through improved family court practice and a child-sensitive justice system.

She said the association, registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission in January 2026, brought together judicial officers, magistrates, prosecutors, social welfare officers, advocates, law enforcement personnel and other child protection practitioners from the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

Nyesom-Wike said its objectives included promoting compliance with child protection laws, advocating policies on education, healthcare and social security, and supporting the implementation of the Child Rights Act and corresponding state laws.

She added that the association, working with partners, had facilitated access to counselling, legal aid and medical support through a referral system.

The Speaker of the Children’s Parliament, Miss Progress Umoh, also made a case for children’s rights, while pupils from secondary schools across the FCT spoke on issues affecting their welfare.

The post CJN faults weak enforcement of child protection laws appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Who wants Odegbami dead? By Segun Odegbami
description:
The Bible told us that the Jebusites were descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham. An ancient Canaanite tribe who inhabited the hill country and fortified stronghold of Jebus, later known as Jerusalem.



They were among the peoples inhabiting the land God promised to Abraham’s descendants and Moses.
content:
The Bible told us that the Jebusites were descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham. An ancient Canaanite tribe who inhabited the hill country and fortified stronghold of Jebus, later known as Jerusalem.

They were among the peoples inhabiting the land God promised to Abraham’s descendants and Moses. They derive their name from a Hebrew root meaning “thresher,” “to trample down,” or “to tread on”.

Breaking this further down spiritually, “the name denotes a force that “stomps” or grinds down others, attempting to minimize, humiliate, or crush a person’s potential and authority”.

I have used the above to explain the situation we have in the administration of football in Nigeria since a certain group of human hyenas took control of the running of the game by ‘forcefully’ truncating the second term of one of Nigeria’s renowned sports administrators, Alhaji Ibrahim Galadima in 2006.

Alhaji Galadima, now late, wanted a reform of the Nigeria Football Association’s (NFA ) laws that excluded the majority of football’s key stakeholders.

After successfully getting the Kano-born administrator out of their way, the football ‘Jebusites’ changed NFA into NFF (Nigeria Football Federation) and manipulated the statutes to give more voting powers to the State FA Chairmen.

One stakeholder who would not rest until a proper reform was carried out for an inclusive Congress that would allow other stakeholders an opportunity to help change the face of football in Nigeria is Chief Segun Odegbami.

He used his weekly Column syndicated in some Nigerian newspapers for the campaign. He made speeches at seminars and sports workshops to spread his message for the reform of the NFF to no avail.

Nigerians carried on as if all was well with our football. A handful of Nigerians, sports journalists and passionate fans, joined in the crusade but their ‘cries’ seemed not to make any impact as the football Jebusites who seemed to enjoy the support of the government carried on.

Still Odegbami would not be deterred. His campaign intensified and went wide when he established a radio station, Eagle7 FM based in his little rustic town of Mosimi in Ogun State of Nigeria.

He talked about the rot in football and assembled analysts regularly to talk about why a reform is desirable before it causes Nigeria’s football to go into the ICU- Intensive Care Unit.

Odegbami is not a prophet of doom like Jeremiah and Ezekiel in the Bible who predicted gloom for Israel if the leaders didn’t do the right things, but his fears for football eventually came to pass.

Nigeria’s football prospects declined and all her teams, from ‘top to bottom’, apologies late President Muhammad Buhari, began to crash, surprisingly against minnows of yesterday.

Despite this, the Jebusites were climbing on both CAF and FIFA profile ladders and smiling.

At this stage, Odegbami’s campaign began to make sense to Nigerian fans who depended on the success of our football teams to console themselves in the midst of the unending economic crunch that had put them under physical and emotional stress.

And at last the government thought it was high time it looked into the simmering crisis in football and how it could be stemmed.

When the Jebusites saw the stand of the government, they talked to themselves and step aside. Although some people still believe that they were forced to throw in the towel.

Their mass resignation led to the decision by CAF and FIFA to step in and today a 5-man Normalisation Committee has been appointed to start the process of repositioning football with a reform that would allow a level playing field for all stakeholders.

With the Committee in place, it has become clear to the Jebusites that the end to their vice-grip on football has come to an end and that the era of deciding who could be elected into the NFF Board and become the president has gone.

Not quite a week after FIFA announced the Normalisation Committee, armed men invaded the Abeokuta home of the champion for the reform process in football, Chief Odegbami and nearly snuffed life out of him.

I don’t want to believe that those who are not happy that they lost their juicy positions in the NFF because of Odegbami’s consistent campaigns are behind this dastardly act.

An African adage which says, ‘the witch cried last night and the child died today’ that has kept me thinking since the news of the attack on Odegbami broke.

Odegbami has been a very easy going man, living for his former teammates, creating opportunities for them whenever he has a sports or football project to carry out for the good of the country.

They were involved in the Shell Cup for secondary schools he coordinated with the support of Shell Petroleum and Development Company as sponsor and the Nigeria School Sports Federation, NSSF as the organising body.

He still involves them to run his Segun Odegbami International College & Sports Academy (SOCA). They are among analysts he features frequently on the Eagle7 FM radio to dissect the problems of sports and proffer solutions that could make Nigerian athletes excel.

Would anyone say that the man, who uses his money and connections to assist his colleagues and help make things work for the progress of our athletes, hates Nigeria?

That is why I ask today, who wants Odegbami dead? The police must get to the root of the assassination attempt on him, fish out the culprits and bring them to justice.

A man like Odegbami who has had sleepless nights thinking of how the Super Eagles could be great again with a proper running of the NFF should not be the target of wicked people and must be protected by the country.

Chief Odegbami, here is wishing you a quick recovery from that deadly machete cut which could have snuffed life out of you.

The post Who wants Odegbami dead? By Segun Odegbami appeared first on Vanguard News.
