title: Geometric Power model can transform Nigeria’s electricity sector — Nnaji
description:
Geometric Power Group’s Managing Director, Agatha Nnaji, discusses how the Aba Integrated Power Project is improving electricity supply, plans to expand generation capacity, financing challenges and lessons for Nigeria’s power sector in this chat with SAMI TUNJI

How has the Aba Integrated Power Pro
content:
Geometric Power Group’s Managing Director, Agatha Nnaji, discusses how the Aba Integrated Power Project is improving electricity supply, plans to expand generation capacity, financing challenges and lessons for Nigeria’s power sector in this chat with SAMI TUNJI

How has the Aba Integrated Power Project impacted Nigeria’s electricity sector, particularly in Aba?

I would say that the Aba Integrated Power Project is a model that should make a difference in the Nigerian power sector because we believe it is a workable model that would enable people to get power at an affordable rate, provided it is implemented properly by whoever the sponsors are.

What we have been able to achieve in Aba is to prove that it is possible for Nigerians to have an affordable and sustainable power supply on a 24/7 basis.

We have a vision as Geometric Power. Our goal here is to provide power that will enable the people to grow economically, socially and environmentally.

From an environmental perspective, we make sure that we do not have noise pollution. We also want to ensure that, regardless of their status, whether they are wealthy or not, traders or students, people have access to electricity all the time. It is then up to them to determine how much electricity they want to use.

Because it is available all the time, people’s lifestyles have been positively impacted. As a young person, you can go home, find electricity available and do your homework. You do not have to light candles, which create health and environmental challenges and risks in family homes and businesses.

Before our arrival, a survey was conducted to assess the potential environmental impact that this project would have on Aba. We took note of the number of generators in the city. By the time the power plant was built, those generators had been displaced, thereby protecting the environment and the health of people who were inhaling fumes from generators, especially in marketplaces and other public places.

Economically, consider what is happening with the cost of diesel. A couple of weeks ago, we experienced gas supply challenges and, for a few days, had issues with power supply. We informed our customers, but when the disruption occurred and they had to buy diesel for those three or four days, their reaction was, “What has happened?”

Once people get used to a 24/7 power supply and experience an interruption, everything seems to have gone wrong. People get used to comfort and are able to plan around it.

How have manufacturers and businesses in Aba benefited from the improved power supply?

Businesses in Aba have been very happy and supportive. We actually made them our priority by ensuring that the power supply to them is reliable.

That meant that some of the equipment and infrastructure we inherited from EEDC and NEPA, which were about 60 years old in some cases, had to be replaced to ensure that areas where we had factories and industries received reliable power.

When we were redesigning the network, we made sure that we included brand-new substations in strategic locations around Aba so that those industries would be able to receive reliable, stable and good-quality power supply through their own substations.

If anything goes wrong in one location, we can loop them through another. That is how the network has been redesigned.

We examined the four or five substations we inherited, which were very old and dilapidated, and rehabilitated them completely, almost as if we were building brand-new substations.

The idea is that our people in Aba should not have to worry about the infrastructure that has been established for the next 50 or 100 years.

Securing funding for a project of this magnitude can be challenging. How instrumental were financial institutions in its completion?

Afreximbank provided the funding that enabled us to complete and commission the project.

Politics and human error got in the way, and the project was delayed when we were just about to commission it. For seven years, we maintained facilities that were already in place. We had staff who had to be paid to continue maintaining those facilities.

When the issues were eventually resolved and we determined the amount needed to complete the project, we were very happy that Afreximbank came in because it saw the vision and understood the impact it would have on the people we were going to serve.

When it saw Aba’s potential as an industrial city in Africa, I believe that made it more willing to find a way to make the project work.

I must also commend Diamond Bank and its late founder, Pascal Dozie, because he saw the vision. At a time when banks were mostly giving short-term loans to traders to import containers, turn over the money and repay their loans, he saw the value of a strategic project like this and the impact it would have on customers in Aba, who are largely traders.

He bought into that long-term vision and provided the initial funds that got us started. We subsequently faced challenges that made the project take much longer to complete, and Afreximbank came to the rescue.

At the time we approached Afreximbank, we needed $50m, and it provided the funding.

Typically, a bank or financier would run away when approached with a project that had the kind of challenges we faced.

There was not much we could offer to give them comfort other than the fact that our boss was a very determined investor. It was not just about investing to make money. The determination to see the project through was largely driven by the desire to make a sustainable impact that would touch lives.

Afreximbank eventually brought in technical advisers and financial experts. We examined the figures and went into the city to speak with customers, especially industrialists, to understand their level of need, commitment and willingness to pay.

We engaged an independent organisation to conduct that survey, and I think the outcome reinforced its belief that this project would make the kind of impact it wanted to make in Africa.

Geometric Power demonstrates the potential of private investment in electricity. What accounts for the shortcomings of Nigeria’s power sector privatisation?

It is a pity that the privatisation ended the way it did. If it had gone according to the original plan, and if we had selected investors, especially at the DisCo level, who had the technical know-how and financial muscle to invest in infrastructure, things could have been different.

For the DisCos, it was not simply about how much you could pay for the asset. It was about how much you could reduce aggregate technical, commercial and collection losses.

If you are able to reduce those losses, it means you would have made substantial investments in infrastructure.

The only way you can achieve that is by building substations, as we have done, and constructing new power lines at the appropriate voltage levels.

If we had stuck to that approach, we would not be in the mess we are in today.

But the answer remains that it is doable. There are things that need to unwind themselves, and that is already happening, although it is taking a lot of time.

How severely have recent gas supply disruptions affected your operations?

Our gas suppliers are dealing with a major challenge because they inherited gas infrastructure that was built in the 1960s.

Imagine having a Volkswagen that was built in the 1960s. Where would you get the spare parts? They have to struggle to find spare parts whenever anything goes wrong. They need to make huge investments, and the government probably needs to do something to help them upgrade the existing infrastructure.

Recently, something went wrong with one of their pieces of equipment. They checked for the part in Nigeria, but it was not available. They mobilised, found it in the United States and flew it in at enormous cost. They took it to the site, tested it, fixed it and immediately started supplying gas to us.

We also have an arrangement with NDPHC. Whenever we have such an emergency, we buy emergency power from NDPHC for that interim period so that we can maintain supply to our customers.

In light of the gas supply challenges, are you exploring renewable energy sources to diversify your power generation?

Yes. Part of our plan is to supply reliable power through gas-fired as well as steam-fired power.

We are also in discussions with people promoting alternative sources of power, including waste and solar energy. One or two people have talked about water, although we do not have a water source close by to test it.

In a nutshell, we are open to innovative ideas that can help us supplement the power supply from here.

What measures should the government take to ease gas supply constraints and attract greater investment in the power sector?

The gas infrastructure is ageing. Some of the infrastructure around here was installed decades ago. That is what suppliers are struggling with because spare parts are not easily available.

We need to figure out how we can engage and support gas providers to produce more gas. A lot of operators focus on extracting oil, but if they can produce more gas, it will help organisations that want to invest in power, as well as industries that want to use gas to drive their machines.

Having installed 141MW, what are Geometric Power’s plans for the next phase of expansion?

It is not just the South-East that will benefit from what we are doing. The power we are supplying here has displaced what used to be supplied to Aba from the national grid, and that power can go to other parts of the country. The more power we provide as we expand our geographical footprint, the more the rest of the country benefits.

At the moment, we have installed 141 megawatts. We have three LM6000 GE turbines, each generating 47 megawatts. We have also built the foundation for the fourth turbine, which will take us to 188 megawatts.

To put it in perspective, Aba currently consumes an average of about 50 megawatts. At one time, consumption was as high as 90 megawatts when we had not metered customers because people were doing all sorts of things.

Since we metered our customers, consumption has changed. People who used to leave their lights on when going to work now switch them off because they know that when they return in the evening, they can turn them back on and nothing in their refrigerators or freezers would have spoilt.

We have also provided electricity to some underserved communities in Rivers State that had been without power for years. We had to liaise with Port Harcourt DisCo because they are its customers and then approach the regulator for permission to serve them.

Going forward, when we designed the power plant, we planned the entire value chain, from gas supply to the power plant, substations, distribution transformers and end users.

Our 12-inch gas pipeline, which runs about 27 kilometres from Owaza to here, was designed to provide enough gas for up to 500 megawatts within this footprint.

So, in addition to the next phase, which would take us to 188 megawatts, if demand grows sufficiently, we can install more turbines and eventually increase capacity to 500 megawatts. That means we can continue to grow the business, and Discos in the South-East and South-South can get power from us more easily.

How practical would it be to replicate the Geometric Power model across other parts of Nigeria?

We have been the guinea pig for the power sector. Anybody else coming to replicate this model, by God’s grace, would never have to go through one-tenth of the challenges we have experienced.

Can the model work? Yes. I would say we should start with cities and locations that are commercially viable, especially places we want to industrialise. Cities such as Kaduna, Kano and Onitsha, as well as industrial corridors in Enugu and Aba, are examples.

If private investors can work with a DisCo, agree on the terms and raise the money, it can work. The money can only be raised if you have willing and capable buyers who can pay for the power and, of course, you have your source of fuel.

It could take up to two years to get a project from financial close to commissioning, but the devil is in the details of the negotiations.

The post Geometric Power model can transform Nigeria’s electricity sector — Nnaji appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Abuja thrash Akwa Ibom 6-0 to win Flag Football tourney
description:
Team Abuja defeated Akwa Ibom 6-0 to emerge champions in the male category of the fourth edition of the Aketi Bowl National Championship of the Nigerian Secondary Schools Flag Football League.
Abuja secured the six points early in the encounter and held on to their advantage despite a determined eff
content:
Team Abuja defeated Akwa Ibom 6-0 to emerge champions in the male category of the fourth edition of the Aketi Bowl National Championship of the Nigerian Secondary Schools Flag Football League.

Abuja secured the six points early in the encounter and held on to their advantage despite a determined effort by team Akwa Ibom to overturn the deficit.

In the female category, however, Akwa Ibom defeated Abuja 12-0 after recovering from a slow start to claim victory.

The championship featured eight states and marked the culmination of state preliminaries held between September and October.

The winners would receive N1m, while the second- and third-placed teams would get N700,000 and N350,000, respectively, in both categories.

The winning team would also benefit from a scholarship award worth N150m at JOF University in Ondo State.

Speaking on the growth of the competition, the League Coordinator of the Nigerian Secondary Schools Flag Football League, Oluwatobi Abe, said the event was the fourth edition of the Aketi Bowl but the fifth season of the secondary schools league.

Abe, who is also the Grassroots Programmes Lead of the Nigerian American Football Association, said the league had expanded through state activations and reinforcement programmes aimed at introducing the sport to new schools and strengthening existing teams.

He said, “We’ve come a long way if you look at where we started a few years ago, 2022, 2021, when we started in Lagos, to now. The game, overall gameplay, between what you saw back then and what you see now is so different because these kids are playing like people who have been playing for years.

“Meanwhile, some of them just started playing this year or a few months back.”

Abe attributed the improvement to former players returning to their schools to train younger students and sustain the development of the sport.

He said the winners would receive N1m, while the second- and third-placed teams would get N700,000 and N350,000 respectively in both categories.

He added that the winning team would also benefit from a scholarship award worth N150m at JOF University in Ondo State.

On efforts to address the challenge of equipment, Abe said the association, in partnership with Draft Nigeria and NFL Flag, had distributed more than 2,000 balls and 5,000 flags to schools under its One Ball, One Flag, One Future initiative.

Also speaking, the Director of School Sport at the Lagos State Sports Commission and Chairperson of Education and Grassroots Sport of the Nigeria American Football Federation, Dr Oluyomi Oluwasanmi, said the competition was important for the all-round development of students.

Oluwasanmi, who recalled being involved in the programme from its inception in Lagos in 2021, said combining education with sports would help develop children’s talents and reduce social vices.

“There is no way we can separate education and sport if we want all-round development of our children, which we need to raise the total child.

“And if you give them this platform to exhibit their inherent talents, you see that social vices, juvenile delinquency, will be reduced to the barest minimum,” she said.

She disclosed that some students discovered during the pilot edition in 2022 had gone on to represent Nigeria at the World Cup qualifiers in Egypt in 2025 in both male and female categories.

Oluwasanmi called for stronger collaboration among sports authorities, school administrators and the league organisers to identify young talents and provide them with opportunities to develop.

content:
By Vincent Ujumadu

The Anambra State Executive Council has fixed November 27, 2026, for the formal commissioning and opening of the Ekwulobia flyover constructed by the administration of Governor Chukwuma Soludo.

The flyover is strategically located at a junction that previously experienced serious traffic challenges, particularly during festive periods when vehicular movement increases significantly.

Rising from its meeting in Awka, the State Executive Council directed that all necessary arrangements be made to ensure a successful and hitch-free commissioning. However, it did not disclose who would perform the ceremony.

The state Commissioner for Information and Value Reorientation, Dr Law Mefor, described the flyover as one of the flagship urban regeneration projects of the Soludo administration.

He said the project stood alongside the transformation of Okpoko, formerly regarded as the biggest urban slum in the South-East, into an area characterised by improved infrastructure, order and human dignity.

“These projects underscore Governor Soludo’s irreversible commitment to building a liveable, prosperous and smart mega-city in Anambra State,” Mefor said.

Meanwhile, the Council resolved to move the state’s Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) drive from moral suasion to full enforcement, including the prosecution of tax evaders, to maximise the state’s revenue potential.

It consequently urged residents, business owners and other taxpayers to pay their taxes and levies promptly to avoid the consequences of enforcement, particularly prosecution.

According to the Council, no modern state can be built on voluntary compliance alone, stressing that payment of taxes is a civic responsibility.

“Anambra will enforce it fairly and firmly,” the Council said.

The Council also disclosed that it had concluded work on the state’s 2027 budget, which Governor Soludo is expected to present to the Anambra State House of Assembly on Tuesday.

Mefor described the proposed budget as a consolidation budget designed to deepen the gains of Solution 2.0 in infrastructure, security, education, healthcare, youth empowerment and economic transformation.

title: How costly tests, poor equipment delay patients’ treatment
description: Patients seeking care at public hospitals across the country face an impossible choice: pay exorbitant fees for diagnostic tests at private facilities or forgo essential investigations because of the lack of functional diagnostic equipment in public hospitals. content:
Patients seeking care at public hospitals across the country face an impossible choice: pay exorbitant fees for diagnostic tests at private facilities or forgo essential investigations because of the lack of functional diagnostic equipment in public hospitals. For those unable to afford the costs, abandoning tests often means delayed diagnosis and treatment, with potentially devastating consequences. Experts are calling for dedicated government funding, functional equipment and subsidised tests to ensure timely diagnosis and treatment. JANET OGUNDEPO reports

With several bouts of persistent chest pain and constant discomfort, a retiree and mother of four, Mrs Comfort Uwana, decided to seek medical attention at a public hospital in Lagos State, hoping to get medication that would relieve her symptoms.

After listening to her complaints and reviewing her medical history, the doctor issued a referral requesting five diagnostic tests deemed necessary to establish an accurate diagnosis and determine the appropriate course of treatment.

Uwana said she was surprised that she had been asked to undergo several tests rather than being given a prescription for medication. Although the doctor explained why the investigations were necessary, her concern deepened when she enquired about the cost of the tests that were available at the facility.

“I was asked to do five tests; one of the tests at the facility costs N65,000, another costs N12,000, and one costs N32,000. The other ones were not available at the hospital, so I asked to go to a private facility, which was more expensive. Where do I get the money to do these tests?” she asked.

The retiree, who said she depended on her pension and the goodwill of her children, told PUNCH Healthwise that she left the laboratory and returned home, where she has been managing her pain with painkillers.

Uwana recalled another instance where a relative who was advised to undergo an abdominal computed tomography scan at a private facility and was asked to pay N175,000 returned home without undergoing the investigation because of the cost.

For Titilayo Aina, a student of Lagos State University, Ojo, the financial burden began even before she could establish what was wrong with her.

After paying N15,000 for a consultation with a dermatologist at the Lagos State University Teaching Hospital, Ikeja, Aina said she was given requests for about six investigations.

Having already spent money on the consultation, the third-year student began thinking about the additional costs she would incur before obtaining a diagnosis and receiving the appropriate treatment.

She told PUNCH Healthwise that she did not proceed to the hospital’s diagnostic centre to enquire about the prices of the tests but returned home without knowing how much they would cost or how she would pay for them.

As a student paying out of pocket for healthcare, Aina said the prospect of financing several investigations at once was a source of concern.

For a resident of Ibadan, Oyo State, identified only as Deborah, the financial strain of several medical tests has drained her so much, leaving her with little to begin the much-needed treatment.

The middle-aged lady told PUNCH Healthwise that an accident over 10 years ago and increasingly intense pain led her to the hospital, where she was diagnosed with osteoarthritis in 2025 after several tests.

Deborah said she was asked to undergo X-rays of her waist and knee, including other tests, and, having already spent considerable money on medical investigations, she has yet to raise the funds needed to begin the recommended physiotherapy.

The Ibadan resident, who works in a small firm and earns below the minimum wage, says while she has made enquiries about the cost of the treatment, she has been unable to afford treatment.

Deborah said she currently lives with the constant pain and manages it with painkillers while trying to find the money to proceed with physiotherapy.

 

Postponing tests due to cost

When an entrepreneur and resident of Alimosho, Lagos, Sabirat Murtala, was pregnant in 2023, she was required to undergo several investigations, such as blood and urine tests, HIV screening, blood group and genotype tests, as well as several ultrasound scans to monitor her baby’s growth and development.

Murtala, who received antenatal care at a private hospital, said the cost of investigations varied by test and scan.

While the mother of three said she could afford the cheaper tests, she admitted that she delayed doing some of the ultrasounds until she could raise the money.

During the periods when she delayed the tests, she could only hope nothing would go wrong with her baby.

While Aina, Deborah and Murtala, as well as Uwana and her relative, represent different experiences, their stories reflect the delays and financial difficulties many Nigerian patients face when accessing diagnostic services, especially those without health insurance or whose insurance plans do not cover the required investigations.

 

Why patients need medical investigations

An epidemiologist, Professor Adebayo Onajole, said medical investigations were central to effective treatment because they helped doctors identify diseases early and make decisions based on evidence rather than assumptions.

Onajole, a public health physician and Professor of Community Health and Primary Care at the University of Lagos and the Lagos University Teaching Hospital, said treating patients based only on symptoms could lead to wrong diagnoses because different diseases sometimes present with similar signs.

He cited fever as an example, noting that patients should not automatically be treated for malaria without first confirming the infection through testing.

“Today we do agree that you must not start treating for malaria unless you have done the test to confirm that the individual actually has malaria. Because so many other features might present you with fever,” he said.

The physician warned that treating patients without establishing the actual cause of their symptoms could expose them to inappropriate use of medicines, which could contribute to drug resistance, adverse drug reactions and additional expenses.

 

Private versus public diagnostic centres

To compare the prices of medical investigations in hospitals and private laboratories, PUNCH Healthwise visited some tertiary healthcare facilities and private diagnostic centres. The prices of an abdominal CT scan and a brain MRI at these facilities were obtained to achieve a direct comparison.

According to the Cleveland Clinic, MRI scans provide detailed images that can help identify conditions that may not be visible through other imaging methods, including soft tissue injuries, spinal cord abnormalities and brain conditions such as tumours or strokes. The scans can help doctors establish accurate diagnoses and determine appropriate treatment.

A CT scan, on the other hand, combines X-rays with computer processing to produce detailed images of structures inside the body.

Findings from a private laboratory in Lagos showed that a brain MRI scan cost N133,150, while a CT abdomen and pelvis scan cost N117,500. The facility also charged an additional N10,000 for patients who wanted a hard copy of the scan film.

At another private laboratory in Lagos, a CT abdomen scan cost N110,000, while a brain MRI was priced at N170,000.

PUNCH Healthwise gathered that the average private-sector prices of the CT abdomen and brain MRI scans were between N120,000 and N160,000, respectively.

A visit to the BT Health and Diagnostic Centre at LASUTH, Ikeja, revealed that the centre charged N110,000 for a brain MRI and N160,000 for an abdominal CT scan.

Patients were also required to pay an additional N3,000 for a creatinine test before the scans could be conducted.

Further findings from staff members at the facility showed that its diagnostic services operated under a public-private partnership arrangement with the hospital.

At the Lagos University Teaching Hospital, a source informed PUNCH Healthwise that an abdominal CT scan cost between N130,000 and N150,000, however, the cost of the brain MRI could not be obtained as the MRI machine at the hospital was not functional.

In 2025, PUNCH Healthwise reported that, among eight state and federal teaching hospitals in the South-West, only LUTH had a functional MRI machine. A year and several months later, however, the hospital’s machine was no longer operational.

Findings by PUNCH Healthwise also reveal that many tertiary hospitals across the country do not have specialised diagnostic equipment.

For example, it was gathered that there were only three MRI machines in Enugu State. Also, in selected federal and teaching hospitals across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones, PUNCH Healthwise found that many had either unreliable, non-functional, or no CT scanners and MRI machines.

A 2017 study by the Association of Radiographers of Nigeria paints a worrying picture of persistent disparities in the availability and functionality of these critical diagnostic tools.

According to the study, 68 per cent of the CT scanners in Nigeria were privately owned, leaving only 32 per cent spread across federal and state facilities or operated through public-private partnerships.

Further research published in 2018 showed that three states in Northern Nigeria had no CT scanners at all, and of the scanners installed nationwide, only 83 per cent were functional at the time.

Unarguably, the unavailability of this life-saving equipment leaves many patients paying more in private facilities, with some having to travel to other states to have the tests done.

The challenges also extend beyond the availability of equipment to the additional expenses patients incur when they have to repeat investigations or pay for tests that could not be carried out at their usual hospitals.

A report from the Nigerian Health Continuity Survey showed that at least two in five Nigerian patients had paid more than once for the same laboratory test or medical scan because their previous results could not be retrieved.

The survey also found that 73.4 per cent of respondents spent at least two hours from leaving home until the end of their hospital visits, while 17.6 per cent said the process took a full day or longer.

Financially, 41.8 per cent of respondents spent more than N50,000 out of pocket on their most recent healthcare journey, including transportation and medicines, while 25.3 per cent spent more than N100,000.

An analysis of the 2023/24 General Household Survey found that 45.5 per cent of Nigerian households faced catastrophic health expenditure at the 10 per cent budget-share threshold, with rural households, female-headed households and those with elderly members particularly affected.

The report also revealed that out-of-pocket payments accounted for about 72 per cent of Nigeria’s current health expenditure.

Need for medical investigations in pregnancy

A Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Ernest Orji, said routine investigations during pregnancy were important for identifying conditions that could put mothers and babies at risk.

Orji, an Honorary Consultant at the Obafemi Awolowo University Teaching Hospitals Complex, identified urinalysis, blood tests and ultrasound scans as important investigations during antenatal care.

He said urinalysis could help detect abnormalities, including sugar or protein in the urine, which might point to underlying health problems requiring further investigation.

The gynaecologist also advised pregnant women to undergo ultrasound scans within the first three months of pregnancy to confirm and date the pregnancy, establish the baby’s position and monitor its development and the placenta.

He said scans were particularly important for women with underlying conditions such as diabetes and sickle cell disease, those with a history of delivering babies with abnormalities, and older pregnant women, who might have a higher risk of foetal abnormalities. Such women might require more detailed investigations to assess the development of the baby’s organs.

Orji identified the cost of investigations as a major reason some pregnant women failed to undergo recommended tests, noting that doctors could advise and appeal to patients but could not force them to pay for investigations.

He said government support could make pregnancy care and essential investigations more accessible to women who could not afford them, but warned that poor management of public funds could undermine such interventions.

Why diagnostic tests are expensive

The Lagos State Chairman of the Association of Radiologists of Nigeria, Dr Raymond Kuti, attributed the high cost of medical investigations to the rising prices of imported consumables, expensive diagnostic equipment, increasing operational costs and the fees paid to specialists.

Kuti said most consumables used in diagnostic medicine were imported and priced in foreign currency, making them vulnerable to exchange rate fluctuations.

He cited the cost of contrast medium, a substance used during some CT and MRI examinations, which he said had risen significantly over the years.

“Five years ago, one bottle of contrast medium was about N4,000. As of today, it’s about N15,000. So, it has increased to about 400 per cent. To buy a brand new CT machine now is N500m,” he said, explaining that borrowing such an amount at interest rates of between 32 and 35 per cent could make repayment almost double the original loan within three years.

The A.R.I.N Lagos chairman further identified electricity and diesel costs as major expenses involved in running diagnostic centres, saying facilities often had to rely on multiple sources of power, including the national grid, generators and solar energy.

The immediate past president of the Guild of Medical Directors argued that the cost of diagnostic investigations in government hospitals should be considered in the context of the financial support they received from the government.

He said public hospitals generally did not bear the same costs as private facilities in areas such as building rent, staff salaries, and equipment acquisition because the government provided these.

“If the government buys me N500 million CT, and they say I’m not using my money, of course, my price will come down,” he said.

He, however, argued that government hospitals did not always carry out the actual costing of diagnostic services, making it difficult to determine the true cost of providing investigations.

Kuti also explained that the growing use of public-private partnership arrangements for diagnostic services was partly because governments could no longer afford to purchase some of the expensive equipment.

He said an average 1.5 Tesla or 3.0 Tesla MRI machine could cost between N1bn and N1.4bn, making it difficult for many government hospitals to acquire the equipment without private-sector involvement.

Under the arrangement, he explained, a private investor provides the equipment in a government hospital and shares the revenue generated with the government.

He said private investors entered such arrangements to recover their investments within an agreed period, a consideration that could influence the charges for investigations.

Kuti also questioned the reimbursement rates proposed by the National Health Insurance Authority for some diagnostic investigations, arguing that the amounts were insufficient to cover the cost of providing the services.

He cited proposed payments of N50,000 for a CT brain scan, N62,000 for a CT chest scan and N65,000 for a CT abdomen scan, saying the rates were below the charges at diagnostic centres.

He maintained that the difference between charges under public-private partnership arrangements in government hospitals and those in private diagnostic centres could be between 20 and 30 per cent.

Beyond the cost of investigations, Kuti said diagnostic tests were important because they provided medical evidence to guide treatment, rather than leaving doctors to rely solely on patients’ symptoms.

“It’s better to measure ten times and cut once than to cut ten times and then measure once,” he said, using the expression to explain why doctors needed to establish what a patient was suffering from before commencing treatment.

Kuti said evidence-based medical practice was the current norm, adding that concerns about medico-legal consequences had also contributed to the increasing reliance on diagnostic tests.

On patients being asked to repeat investigations, he acknowledged that there were situations where another test might not be necessary.

He explained that doctors sometimes requested repeat investigations because they were not satisfied with the quality of images or reports obtained from a previous diagnostic centre. In other cases, repeat examinations were necessary for follow-up and monitoring of a patient’s condition.

He, however, advised doctors who had concerns about the quality of previous results to consider seeking another radiologist’s opinion before asking patients to pay for the same investigation again.

“What I usually encourage in that situation is to send it to another radiologist to evaluate, rather than tell the patient to go and repeat the test,” he said.

Need for tax waivers, dedicated diagnostic fund

The National First Vice-President of the Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists of Nigeria, Olusoji Billyrose, said the rising cost of diagnostic investigations was partly driven by heavy taxation, the high cost of imported medical supplies and equipment, and inadequate health insurance reimbursement rates.

Billyrose, who is also the Medical Director and Chief Executive Officer of Labcrest Laboratories Ltd, called on the government to consider removing or reducing taxes and import duties on medical equipment, reagents and other healthcare consumables to make diagnostic services more affordable.

He also identified inadequate reimbursement rates by Health Maintenance Organisations as a factor limiting patients’ access to laboratory investigations.

He said some HMO tariffs were far below the actual cost of conducting tests, making it difficult for laboratories to provide comprehensive investigations while maintaining quality standards.

“What you find is that most labs do not want to even work with the HMOs; they prefer people to pay out of pocket to them because the HMO tariff is not consistent and cannot even bear a quarter of the cost of doing that particular test,” he said.

He urged HMOs to involve medical laboratory scientists and laboratory directors in discussions on reimbursement rates to ensure that payments reflected the actual cost of providing quality investigations.

The laboratory scientist also proposed the establishment of a Bank of Health to provide low-interest loans to healthcare providers seeking to acquire diagnostic equipment and improve infrastructure.

He said the high cost of machines such as CT scanners and MRI equipment made it difficult for both private providers and government facilities to invest in diagnostic capacity without financial support.

Billyrose further called for a dedicated fund for medical diagnostics, describing diagnostic infrastructure as essential to the functioning of the health system.

He said strengthening laboratory accreditation and regulatory oversight was necessary to improve the quality and reliability of diagnostic services.

He urged hospitals to allow the Medical Laboratory Science Council of Nigeria to inspect their laboratories, saying such inspections would help assess their equipment, personnel and quality assurance systems.

Billyrose also advised members of the public to use laboratories licensed by the council and accredited to the ISO 15189 standard, noting that accreditation helped assure patients that laboratories operated according to recognised standards and produced reliable results.

“We should not just make the laboratories a ‘cash cow,’ a place where people must go to just because you want the money but rather to get good diagnostics,” he said.

Electronic sharing of results can reduce repeat tests

The National President of the Healthcare Providers Association of Nigeria, Dr Austine Aipoh, proposed an interoperable electronic health records system that would allow test results from one laboratory or hospital to be accessed by healthcare providers elsewhere.

He also advised that patients should be given soft copies of their results to share when they seek care at other facilities.

“If we get to the stage where all facilities, including diagnostic centres and hospitals, have electronic health records, then there will be interoperable results,” he said.

He warned that patients who could not afford requested investigations might delay treatment and resort to self-medication, including moving from one pharmacy to another in search of relief.

Aipoh advocated wider health insurance coverage, arguing that a larger pool of contributors would make it easier to finance expensive investigations. He said the country’s insurance coverage remained below 10 per cent and called for greater government investment in healthcare financing.

He also called for the establishment of a dedicated fund for diagnostic services and a health bank through which hospitals and healthcare providers could obtain loans to acquire equipment.

“If, for example, somebody brings in equipment for an MRI, and he is paying little for the equipment, he will not charge so much,” he said.

The post How costly tests, poor equipment delay patients’ treatment appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: How search for missing luggage led to Nigerian-Canadian’s death
description:
In this report, VICTOR AYENI examines how the recent death of a Nigerian-Canadian while attempting to cross the busy Airport Road in Lagos has reignited concerns over the persistent disregard for pedestrian bridges

When the late Abraham Osakpolor arrived from Canada at the Murtala Muhammed Internat
content:
In this report, VICTOR AYENI examines how the recent death of a Nigerian-Canadian while attempting to cross the busy Airport Road in Lagos has reignited concerns over the persistent disregard for pedestrian bridges

When the late Abraham Osakpolor arrived from Canada at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Ikeja, Lagos, on November 13, his immediate concern was retrieving his luggage.

On that sunny Friday afternoon, the 58-year-old was said to have made inquiries about where he could find and pick up his luggage.

Sunday PUNCH gathered that the Nigerian-Canadian citizen was directed to the Nigerian Aviation Handling Company, which is located near the MMIA along the Airport Road.

Osakpolor went to the place, hoping to find his luggage there, but was directed to return to the airport and make inquiries from the airlines.

Sadly, according to eyewitnesses, the middle-aged man was killed by a car while crossing the road.

In a statement signed by the Police Relations Officer of the Airport Police Command, Mohammed Adeola, on Wednesday, an appeal was made to the public for assistance in identifying Osakpolor’s family, relatives and friends.

Sharing photographs of his Nigerian and Canadian passports, the police said he died following a fatal motor accident that occurred along the expressway leading away from the MMIA towards the Oshodi axis.

Born in Benin City, Edo State, on September 1, 1968, Osakpolor was said to have been “hit by a moving vehicle and subsequently rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead.”

“His remains have been deposited in the hospital morgue. The motorist involved in the accident was immediately apprehended by the Airport Police Command and will be charged to court,” the statement said.

The police said that during an initial search of the deceased’s belongings, his Nigerian passport and a mobile device without a SIM card were recovered.

A further search by mortuary attendants revealed that his Canadian passport had also been discovered among his belongings.

Even though the incident had occurred about five days earlier, the police said efforts to establish contact with Osakpolor’s family or persons who might know him had been unsuccessful.

‘Not the first time’

As the statement and accompanying photographs went viral on social media, several individuals expressed sadness and shared additional details about the circumstances surrounding the incident.

A private jet charter operator, who goes by the name Jet Daniel (@LaceVine) on X, shared a photograph of the scene of the incident taken from his car.

In a photograph he took at about 2:19 pm on the fateful day, a crowd of people could be seen surrounding the victim, while a Toyota Camry, said to have been driven by the motorist, was parked on the other side of the road.

“The lawlessness that endangered the life of the deceased and the motorist happens right in front of the Airport Police Command on a daily basis, with a pedestrian bridge in place. On what grounds are you detaining and charging the motorist to court?” Daniel queried.

He urged the authorities to intervene, adding that accidents happened on the road frequently and that this was the second death he had heard of this year.

In another tweet posted at about 4:39 pm after the accident, an X user, Lexybabs (@Lexybabs), wrote in Pidgin English, “Omo, car jam person wey just land from abroad along the airport road.”

Another X user, Cherish Olufunke, said, “According to an eyewitness, they said he came to NAHCO gate to ask where he could pick up his luggage and was told to go to the International Airport. On his way crossing, he was knocked down by a car, just last week Friday. I’m so sure he just arrived in the country. What a sad loss.”

Other netizens shared their experiences along the road, alleging that many citizens abandoned the pedestrian bridges and chose to cross the busy airport highway instead.

“This reminds me of 2019, when a friend asked me to deliver some luggage to her colleagues at the MMIA, Ikeja. I almost got run over by a car that day. I’m still anxious about that area till date,” Remi Omotola said.

On Facebook, Dozie Noble commented, “People don’t use the footbridge on that road. There is no week that an accident doesn’t happen on that road. The road is very wide, yet people prefer to run instead of using the footbridge, especially at 7 and 8 Bus Stop.”

Also recounting her experience, Adichie Uche said, “I almost hit one woman on that road one day. She just entered my front absent-mindedly, and come and see the noise my brakes made that day. Our saving grace was that cars behind me were far; if not, it would have been multiple collisions. People should follow instructions on that road.”

In January, the Airport Police Command said it had arrested a driver responsible for a fatal hit-and-run accident that led to the death of a 19-year-old female pedestrian at Airport Bus Stop, Ikeja.

Preliminary findings revealed that the bus hit the victim shortly after she alighted at the Airport Bus Stop and was proceeding towards the airport.

“Following the occurrence of the fatal accident, concerned passers-by at the scene immediately rushed the victim to the Air Force Base Hospital for urgent medical attention.

“Upon receipt of information regarding the accident, police operatives of the Airport Police Command proceeded to the hospital, where medical personnel confirmed that the victim was dead on arrival due to the severe injuries sustained from the hit,” the statement said.

There have also been reports of vehicles hitting pedestrians in other areas of Lagos where pedestrian bridges are available.

Last month, the Lagos State Traffic Management Authority, on its X page, disclosed that a hit-and-run accident had claimed the life of a pedestrian crossing the main carriageway at Ojota inward Ketu.

“Pedestrians are advised to always make use of the pedestrian bridge to cross the expressway, as it is not meant for decoration,” the post said.

Family identified, driver in court

On Thursday, the Airport Police Command quoted its earlier statement on its X account and said contact had now been successfully established with Osakpolor’s family.

The statement quoted the Commissioner of Police, Airport Police Command, Dr Olufunke Ogunbode, who noted that “while effective policing thrives on mutual trust, cooperation and shared responsibility, [the command] reiterates its commitment to sustaining a cordial and productive relationship with the public.”

When Sunday PUNCH reached out to the Airport Police Command PRO, Adeola, he confirmed that the suspect had been arrested and declined further comments.

“The motorist who drove the car that hit him has been arrested, and the case is still in court,” he said.

However, a police source within the command said that, according to the information gathered by the authorities, the deceased was indeed looking for his missing luggage.

“The late Mr Osakpolor was just arriving in Nigeria and was coming to claim his luggage. He had luggage he hadn’t got, so he went to the NAHCO axis, which is the cargo area, hoping to get his luggage, but he was redirected, since that is where people who ship cargo materials go.

“He was told to go back to the airport and meet with the airline so that he could get his luggage. So, it was while trying to get to the other side to find his way into the airport that he was hit by a vehicle,” the source disclosed.

The source further stated that Osakpolor’s family members were currently meeting to finalise how the deceased’s body would be released to them for burial.

“He has some relatives here and others abroad, but we are trying to ensure that all parties involved have a unified front in terms of how they want the body to be released and how that is done. Once that is decided by the family, then the body will be released to them so that they can give him a befitting burial,” the source added.

An officer of the Lagos State Environmental Sanitation Corps who pleaded anonymity complained that, despite efforts to enforce the use of pedestrian bridges across roads in the state, many citizens still saw direct crossing as a waste of time.

“Under the Lagos State Environmental Management and Protection Law (2017), our operatives have the mandate to prevent pedestrians from crossing expressways and major highways, particularly in areas where pedestrian bridges are provided.

“But our people continue to shun these bridges, and that is why there have been people hit by cars along routes like Fadeyi, Onipanu, Ojota and the Airport Road,” the officer said.

Also commenting on the incident, a crime and forensic analyst, Damilola Benjamin, pointed out that, under the Criminal Law of Lagos State, “fatal gross negligence behind the wheel is not just a traffic slip. It can land a driver in court for involuntary manslaughter, subsections 224 and 229, carrying up to life imprisonment.”

Benjamin added that, “Reckless and Negligent Acts, Section 251, applies if rash driving endangered life. On federal highways, the FRSC Act 2007 steps in with Causing Death by Dangerous Driving, Section 20, and panicking and fleeing the scene only adds ‘Hit and Run/Failure to Report,’ Section 25, to the charge sheet.

“Even ignoring a pedestrian’s ‘right of way,’ under Regulations 161 and 173 of the NRTR 2012, is another evidence that ties into negligence. No one leaves home planning to take a life with a steering wheel, but drivers must drive like someone’s entire world is crossing a road.”

The post How search for missing luggage led to Nigerian-Canadian’s death appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: ‘A tray of locust beans’ come to the screen, by Bisi Adeleye-Fayemi
description: I watched the first cut of the 50-minute film at the Lufodo Productions office at Glover Hall in May. I cried. I wrote ‘A Tray of Locust Beans’ ten years ago. I have met many Mabels over the years and I have worked with others to ensure that they do not fall through the many cracks in our communitie
content:
I watched the first cut of the 50-minute film at the Lufodo Productions office at Glover Hall in May. I cried. I wrote ‘A Tray of Locust Beans’ ten years ago. I have met many Mabels over the years and I have worked with others to ensure that they do not fall through the many cracks in our communities. Sadly, demand always exceeds supply, and there are too many Mabels and not enough of a support system to break the cycle of poverty and oppression decisively. My dear friend and sister Ajoke Silva, founder of Lufodo Productions, persuaded me to look into making some of my stories or poems into short films.

I have always believed that advocacy efforts need to take many forms so that they can be relevant to as many spaces as possible. When I wrote ‘A Tray of Locust Beans’, I wanted to draw attention to the pervasive nature of sexual exploitation of poor young girls. By making this into a film, I hope that people can locate themselves somewhere along the spectrum of support required to enable us have better outcomes for young people around us. Lufodo Productions was commissioned by Amandla Institute for Policy and Leadership Advancement and Above Whispers Media Foundation to make the film, and it was directed by Orobosa Ikponmwen. ‘A Tray of Locust Beans’ was selected for screening at the African International Film Festival (AFRIFF), and it was shown on November 5th.

The response to the film has been overwhelmingly positive.  We were even shortlisted for Best Short Film at AFRIFF! There was a panel discussion after the screening on November 5th, which featured the production crew as well as sexual violence and child protection specialists. We have laws and policies in place, but more needs to be done to make the relevant institutions and duty bearers functional and accountable. There will be another screening in Abuja on December 1st, during the annual 16 Days of Activism against Gender Based Violence campaign, then it will be released for public viewing. I thank everyone who has been a part of making this project a success. My deep appreciation to The Ford Foundation for their support. We cannot continue to lose young girls just because they are poor and have limited choices. This means the next generation of potential Lawyers, Doctors, Engineers and Professors will end up with trays on their heads, while the boys and men who put them in this predicament go through life with minimal consequences. We all need to do more. For those who have not read the story before, here it is.

The person sitting next to Mabel nudged her. Her name was being called. She hadn’t been listening. Her mind was far away. Many years away. She had been thinking about the pain. She had often wondered how it was possible for any human being to survive that kind of pain. Then her mind wandered even further back to how she got to be in pain in the first place. A few weeks after her twelfth birthday, she noticed some blood on her panties. Her grandmother, Mama, had told her this would happen one day.She had been told, ‘Soon you will become a woman. You will bleed every month. This means you have to stay away from boys’. She was not told why she had to stay away from boys, and she did not want to ask because she did not want to upset Mama. She did not know when ‘soon’ would come, so she decided not to worry about it. Then her period came and she had to go and tell Mama. Mama and her older sister Mary, were the only relatives she was close to. The others were in distant places and like strangers. Mabel and Mary’s parents had died in a car accident, five years before. Mary was sent to live with a relative in Ibadan while Mabel lived with their paternal grandmother in Akure. Mama sold provisions as well as locust beans known locally as ‘Iru’. In the afternoon after shereturned from school, she hawked some of Mama’s locust beans. Then Mama fell ill and could not go to her shop.Mabel had to hawk the Irufor longer hours than she used to.

One day, Mr Felix, the tailor who lived two streets away, called her in to his room to sell him some Iru. He then pinned her down and forced himself on her. He covered her mouth to prevent her from screaming. When he was done, he gave her N200 and warned her not to tell anyone. Mabel was too scared to let anyone know, and besides Mama who was ill and had her own worries, there was no one to tell anything. Mary was not there. Mabel kept hawking her Iru after school, but made sure she did not pass by Mr Felix’s house.Soon, things got very bad for Mama and Mabel. Therewas no money in the house for them to buy food, and even when they had something to cook, Mabel had to do it because Mama was unable to. Mabel stopped going to school, so that she could look after Mama and sell Iru.Sinawas three years older than her. He was in her school as well and hawked bread for his mother. He was very kind to her. He gave her some of his bread to eat, and would lie to his mother that he lost one or two loaves when he tripped and fell with his tray, or a policeman had forcefully taken one from him. She liked being with Sina because he made her laugh and she looked forward to his company.

After what Mr Felix had done to her, she now understood what Mama had said about staying away from boys, but she thought to herself, ‘Sina is a good boy. He will never hurt me like Mr Felix’. When Sina kissed her, she did not push him away, and when he lifted her dress, she did not stop him. It felt good to be with him. He was her only friend and she did not want to hurt him. That meant he would stop talking to her, and she might even go hungry if he did not give her the bread she had become accustomed to.

A few weeks after she had started going to the abandoned house in their neighborhood with Sina, she was stopped by Mr Jasper, a policeman who always seemed to be in a bad mood. He asked her to follow him, and since she was too afraid to ask where to or why, she obediently went with him. He took her to his house and did the same thing Mr Felix had done. This time, she did not cry. When he allowed her to leave, she turned to him and said, ‘You need to give me N1,000’. ‘Why?’ he asked her. ‘That is what a full tray of Iru costs. I need to explain to Mama where I have been and why I have not sold my Iru.’ He gave her the money.  It became a routine. Locust beawns. Bread. Sina.Mr Jasper. Then she became pregnant. By now, Mama was feeling better, and was able to move about. Mama wailed and shouted for everyone to hear, ‘Who has impregnated a thirteen year old girl? What kind of monster has done this’? Mama asked her who was responsible, and after a lot of beating and threats, she named Mr Jasper as the culprit.  She was silent about Mr Felix and Sina.  When Mama went to see Mr Jasper about the matter, predictably, she was threatened with arrest, a beating, and even death.

One of their neighbours who was a teacher, Auntie Cecilia, advised Mama to go and see Lawyer Tina who usually helped with cases such as this. Lawyer Tina was a smart, immaculately dressed woman, who drove a shiningblack car. She spoke English as if she had been speaking it from the day she was born and she spoke so quickly, sometimes Mabel did not understand her. Mabel had never seen any woman like her, not even her teachers in school. Lawyer Tina responded quickly. She took her to the Ministry for Women. They declared that Mama was an ‘incompetent’ guardian. Mabel did not know what ‘incompetent’ meant. The Ministry said she would either have to go and live with another relative, or go to the government rehabilitation center.Mama did not want her sent to relatives far away, so she agreed when Lawyer Tina offered to look after her as a temporary guardian.

Mabel liked Lawyer Tina, because she talked to her about a lot of things and answered all her questions without scolding her like Mama. Lawyer Tina had told her that they would wait till after her baby was born, and then do a ‘DNA test’ to determine if Mr Jasper was the father. If he was, he would go to prison. This made Mabel nervous. What if it was not Mr Jasper? She however knew she needed to say something. The longer she waited, the more trouble she would be in. She eventually found the courage to confide in Lawyer Tina. Her reaction shocked her. She expected Lawyer Tina to scream at her and call her a prostitute,useless and wicked, and beat her like Mama had done.  Instead, Lawyer Tina burst into tears and hugged her tight. She called her a victim and said that that she had been ‘explooted’.

She had her baby after a lot of pain. That was the pain she was thinking about when she was nudged out of her reverie. She was in labour for many hours, till Lawyer Tina insisted that they perform an operation. ‘You can’t expect a thirteen year old to push a baby out’ she yelled at the Doctors. Lawyer Tina took her case to Mrs Kitara, the Governor’s Wife, who decided to adopt her. She would remain under the guardianship of Lawyer Tina, but all her expenses would be covered by her new benefactor. Her sister Mary was brought back from Ibadan to stay with her in a new apartment that was arranged by Mrs Kitara. Mabel was in awe of Mrs Kitara too, a kind lady who also spoke like Lawyer Tina – plenty of English and very fast. She also smelt very nice. Mabel day dreamed of how, one day, she would be like them.

The applause continued as Mabel stood up and walked towards the stage in the auditorium. The Vice-Chancellor shook her hand and presented her with a special plaque as Best Graduating Student, Faculty of Law. Even though she could not see them, Mabel knew that Lawyer Tina, Mrs Kitara, Mary and her son Emmanuel, were in the audience. Mama was still alive, but too old to make the trip to attend her graduation.Mabel never found out who Emmanuel’s father was. Mr Felix skipped town and Mr Jasper was transferred to a state in the North. She never spoke to Sina again. All this was ten years ago. Now her dream had come true. She was going to be like Lawyer Tina and Mrs Kitara. Knowledgeable, articulate and successful. ‘I am here because of them’, she thought. ‘Young girls are exploited and abused every day. They did not judge me. They gave me opportunities. They saved my life. I will dedicate my life to helping others ‘, she silently promised herself. As she walked back to her seat clutching the plaque, she no longer remembered the pain. Only the hope she had been given.

Bisi Adeleye-Fayemi is a Gender Specialist, Leadership Coach, Policy Advocate and Writer. She is the Founder of Abovewhispers.com, an online community for women. She can be reached at BAF@abovewhispers.com

title: Tinubu’s frog and the 36 scorpions

content:
​You likely know the old fable of the frog who agreed to ferry a scorpion across a flooded river. Hesitant at first, the frog relented only after the scorpion swore that stinging him would doom them both.

Halfway through the churning water, the scorpion struck anyway. As they sank into the depths, the dying frog gasped out a single question: Why? “Because,” the scorpion replied, “it is simply in my nature.”

​Today, President Bola Tinubu is that frog. The scorpions riding his back are Nigeria’s 36 state governors.

​For 15 years, I breathed the serene, orderly air of Abuja. Walking down broad avenues beneath working streetlights, insulated by relative security and federal infrastructure, it was easy to indulge a comforting illusion – that Nigeria was steadily finding its footing.

Step across the borders of the Federal Capital Territory into the states and 774 local government areas, however, and that illusion shatters. Out there, hunger is no abstract metric debated on television. It is a daily, grinding battle for survival.

​Like millions of my compatriots, my initial fury rushed straight toward the most visible target in the land: Aso Rock. When a bag of rice outstrips a civil servant’s monthly wage and petrol prices choke small businesses, public rage lands squarely at the presidential gates. Firm in the belief that the centre was starving the nation, I held the President personally to account.

​Then I stopped brooding and started reading – poring over the cold, unassailable ledgers of the National Bureau of Statistics, the Federation Account Allocation Committee, and BudgIT’s State of States report.

​What they reveal turns the popular narrative on its head. Blaming Abuja exclusively for grassroots misery is an elaborate alibi shielding the true architects of local poverty: our governors. When this administration scrapped the haemorrhaging petrol subsidy and floated the naira, it shut down decades of institutionalised leakage, tripling monthly distributable FAAC revenue.

The pool that once hovered between N700 billion and N900 billion now routinely breaches N2 trillion. States that scraped by on N5 billion to N8 billion a month suddenly saw N15 billion, N20 billion, even N30 billion land in their accounts every 30 days.

​We do not need forensic auditors to confirm this windfall; the governors have indicted themselves out of their own mouths.

During the Nigerian Governors’ Forum meeting in February 2024, Governor Dapo Abiodun of Ogun State candidly admitted that federal allocations had dramatically swelled, remarking that states were now receiving “almost double” what they got prior to subsidy removal, and adding pointedly that “we have no excuse not to perform.”

In Delta State, Governor Sheriff Oborevwori went further, telling residents openly that “we are receiving more money from Abuja now, so we cannot complain of lack of funds,” even boasting that his administration had avoided borrowing because the federal inflow was so substantial.

Across the country, from Bauchi’s Bala Mohammed to Anambra’s Chukwuma Soludo, governors have publicly acknowledged that Tinubu’s reforms rescued subnational treasuries from imminent insolvency.

​Yet if the coffers are overflowing by their own confession, why are hunger and decay worse at the state level than ever before? It’s simply because our governors have turned subnational administration into a fiscal black hole, sustained by the pathology of “feeding-bottle federalism.”

According to World Bank analyses, state reliance on federal transfers averages roughly 73 per cent of aggregate revenues outside Lagos. The feeding bottle has tripled in size, yet the appetite for economic self-reliance has flatly refused to grow.

​BudgIT’s State of States report lays this failure bare: an extraordinary surge in state revenues paired with deteriorating service delivery. Across the federation, states burned through nearly N2 trillion servicing debt while piling up massive contractor liabilities and choking arrears in pensions and gratuities.

Behind every delayed pension stands a retired public servant who gave their prime decades to the state, now reduced to begging for earned entitlements.

​Nowhere is this betrayal sharper than in the stranglehold on local governments. Constitutionally charged with primary healthcare, rural roads, and basic education, local councils now routinely attract upwards of N1 billion a month – more than enough to remake rural Nigeria.

Instead, governors have reduced council chairmen to errand boys who surrender their capital surplus to the governor’s office. Even after the landmark Supreme Court judgment of July 11, 2024, outlawed state tampering with joint accounts, governors engineered legal workarounds and captured state electoral commissions to keep local chairmen on a tight leash.

​There is a bitter historical irony here. As Governor of Lagos from 1999 to 2007, when President Olusegun Obasanjo withheld Lagos’s local council allocations, Tinubu did not wring his hands. He overhauled internal revenue collection, defended subnational autonomy, and proved a state could prosper without Abuja’s feeding bottle. Why, then, is the former Governor of Lagos allowing 36 governors to turn his painful reforms into a political tragedy?

​I suspect the answer lies in the cold arithmetic of 2027. Governors are regional barons who command party structures, convention delegates, and ballot machinery. Auditing their windfalls publicly and enforcing the Supreme Court ruling with real teeth would mean declaring war on the cartel required for re-election.

That silent bargain has turned the ruling coalition into a sanctuary for impunity, triggering a stampede of opposition defectors buying instant insulation from anti-graft scrutiny: pledge loyalty to the centre, and your local sins are washed clean.

​By shielding them, the President is ferrying scorpions across the river of 2027. None of this absolves Aso Rock – monetary policy, national security, and macroeconomic stability remains federal duties. Yet accusing the President of stalling the vehicle while governors slash the tyres and siphon the fuel is an intellectual failure.

​An ancient African proverb warns that a cat that cares about tomorrow does not eat a pregnant rat – the seed of continuity and future abundance. Driven by immediate appetite, our state capitals are devouring that pregnant rat today.

Through an obsession with ribbon-cutting infrastructure, governors pour billions into showpiece flyovers, airports, and imposing monuments because concrete is easy to photograph for campaign billboards, while education and healthcare budgets stagnate.

An eight-lane asphalt corridor cannot rescue a malnourished child or staff a dilapidated primary health clinic. Concrete is a vehicle for development, not development itself.

​It is time for the President to abandon quiet electoral appeasement and confront this sabotage head-on. Enforce direct local government disbursements without compromise. Publish itemised monthly breakdowns of every naira sent to every state and council. Unleash anti-corruption agencies on subnational diversions regardless of party badges.

And to our 36 governors – who have already confessed on record that Abuja has given them every naira they need to succeed: you cannot pocket triple what your predecessors received, suffocate local councils, splurge on vanity projects, and expect Aso Rock to serve forever as your human shield.

​The hunger is in the states. The money is in the states. Nigerians must stop gazing exclusively toward Aso Rock for salvation and march – intellectually, intentionally, and civically – to our state capitals to demand an accounting.

True wisdom in leadership is knowing what not to consume today so that tomorrow may live. It is time to stop measuring governance by the size of monthly federal cheques and start measuring it by the dignity of ordinary lives.

title: Mugu or not mugu: The livewire pledge
description:

content:
Suddenly, the Nigerian government is defending electricity: as supplied—or not—to the Nigerian people.

Because it is another election season, featuring a ballot box noose developed by the ruling party’s candidate exactly four years ago.

Officials and political party relatives are scrambling to rework the words and intentions of Mr Bola Tinubu, the APC flag-bearer, deployed in 2023 to take advantage of Nigerians’ desperation for electricity.

To the ruling party, the matter did not appear to be an important issue at the time. Its institutional promise on the matter, outlined on page 22 of the 2014 APC Manifesto, was simply to “Ensure Nigeria meets all its power needs within the next ten years.”

It was closing in on that 10 years later when candidate Tinubu arrived with his Emilokan (My Turn) philosophy.  It was not the most popular approach, and he knew it.

Perhaps that was why he looked for any dimensions that would haul in any hesitant votes. Electricity was one such fishing trip.

While his Renewed Hope agenda recognised that “the nation’s power problems cannot be solved overnight,” Tinubu wanted more.

And so, speaking during “Business Lunch with Asiwaju,” a meeting with the Organised Private Sector in Lagos in late 2022, he grabbed the national audience by the neck.

Here is the video of the event.  He commences his speech at about 1:43:43 on the video and gets to the defining BAMN promise at 2:09:50. I call it B-A-M-N—as in DAMN—By Any Means Necessary.

Here is the transcript: “Whichever way, by all means necessary, you must have electricity. And you will not pay for estimated billing anymore. A promise made will be a promise kept. If I couldn’t keep the promise and I come back for a second term, don’t vote for me. That’s the truth, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn’t deliver, and it is convincing enough.”

It was seductive. Powerful. Unforgettable.

An uncomplicated quid pro quo: A promise to be kept by all means, unless I give you convincing reasons. If not, please vote for someone else.

With the presidential contest just two months away, it is not surprising that this has become controversial. But it is a false controversy. Because while this matter masquerades as an election issue, what is really at stake is bigger: it is about who or what Nigeria is.

Did Candidate Tinubu make the B-A-M-N promise? I have quoted him in full. There is no hidden language in it. He provided a qualifier, to be sure: “…adequate reasons [that are] convincing enough.”

“You must have electricity.”

A direct, uncomplicated assertion with a three-year lifespan. Because the “second term” is campaigned for in the last year of the first. That is where we are now.

“You must have electricity”: a pledge that has now been breached, without the “convincing reasons” being tendered.

The truth is that it is impossible to manufacture an intelligent argument here in support of the man who is now President Tinubu.

That is attributable to who he has been as president, never matching his performance with the urgency and seriousness required of his office, even if he did not intend to run again.

Instead, he has acted like a man who arrived at the buffet and forgot that others were equally hungry, treating the public interest as background noise. In his first year, he advanced the rules for himself and his own:

  • A presidential jet for N150 billion
  • N40.6bn for the renovation and maintenance of the presidential palace
  • Foreign Exchange purchases of over N23bn in 2024 alone for international travel, and about N34bn in two years
  • A N5bn presidential yacht.
  • Acquisition, renovation, and rehabilitation of four EFCC fortified quarters in Mabushi and Guzape in the FCT, as “State House complexes,” for N3bn
  • Extensive acquisition of expensive SUVs and bulletproof tyres
  • Renovation of his official residence in Dodan Barracks, Lagos, for N4bn
  • Construction of an office complex within Aso Rock for N4bn;
  • N1.5 billion on cars for the nonexistent Office of the First Lady
  • Instituted the rock-star travel of his son, Seyi, and paid the private hotel bills of his daughter

He was only just the beginning.  Tinubu abandoned the elite State House Medical Centre—renovated and upgraded for over N21bn just days before he took office so it could care even for foreign leaders—for medical tourism abroad.

He commenced travelling in 100-car convoys, sometimes tying up roads for hours.  That was despite directing government officials in October 2024 to reduce their official convoys to three or less, citing the need to reduce the cost of governance. Most of all, that was despite his asking Nigerians to accept the hardship his “reforms” had emptied all over them.

The point, then, is that all of those who argue in favour of Mr Tinubu’s BAMN promise do not do him a favour.  He made the pledge to win an election but then ignored what was literally a live wire for a lifestyle that suggests it was a ruse.

What is repeatedly demonstrated to Nigerians is that the political elite is in it for itself.  Tinubu’s abandonment of his pledge is not accidental; it has been part of the APC game since taking office.  Remember: in the 2014 Manifesto, the party promised Nigerians not merely a change of government but a fundamental transformation of the country’s economic and social conditions. It expressly described the manifesto as a social contract and invited Nigerians to hold the party accountable for its delivery, a commitment from which it has continuously backed away since assuming control.

That manifesto was organised around three themes: Relief, Recovery and Reform, intended to produce immediate improvements in citizens’ lives, the rehabilitation of national institutions and a structural transformation of Nigeria’s political economy. In the Tinubu Years, APC has shifted the goalposts and diminished Nigerians by subverting those advertised goals.

They were going to conquer corruption, but they became corruption.  They were going to bring CHANGE, but they resisted change.  They were going to combat insecurity, but they became insecurity. They were going to lift 100m out of poverty, but they made us far poorer.

The mechanism of setting traps for the Nigerian voter reveals a self-centred leadership with no commitment to accountability, service, excellence, decency, compassion or merit.  Every “reform” emerges as a cover for official excess, and tokenism and speeches are substituted for performance.

No, this chicanery was always about power, not electricity, or insecurity, or education, or healthcare.  The government is spending billions not on programme delivery, but to win an election I have described as a survey where we learn who Nigerians really are.

Our country is poorer, hungrier, more insecure, less livable and less respected since APC arrived.  We have lost our way so thoroughly that only masochists and haters of true national progress can revel in this shame.

That is why the way we vote in 2027 will tell the world whether we are anything but mugus (pathetic fools).

BAMN and DAMN!
