title: From global blacklist to international recognition: Tinubu’s unprecedented aviation transformation
description:
By Seyi Bakare



91.45% ICAO safety rating breaks all previous records; five international airports achieve full certification; $850m trapped airline funds cleared; Emirates returns; indigenous airlines empowered as massive infrastructure renewal takes off.



Nigeria’s aviation industry is undergo
content:
By Seyi Bakare

91.45% ICAO safety rating breaks all previous records; five international airports achieve full certification; $850m trapped airline funds cleared; Emirates returns; indigenous airlines empowered as massive infrastructure renewal takes off.

Nigeria’s aviation industry is undergoing one of the most remarkable transformations in its history, with the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu recording unprecedented milestones in aviation safety, airport infrastructure, international relations, airline operations and the restoration of investor confidence.

What was once an industry struggling with international credibility, restricted access to aircraft financing, trapped foreign airline revenues, deteriorating infrastructure and regulatory deficiencies is gradually emerging as a more competitive and internationally respected aviation destination.

The transformation is not merely reflected in government announcements or policy pronouncements. It is increasingly evident in measurable improvements in safety oversight, the return of major international airlines, renewed access to aircraft leasing markets, the expansion of indigenous carriers and substantial investments in airport infrastructure across the country.

Perhaps the most compelling evidence of this turnaround is Nigeria’s historic 91.45 per cent Effective Implementation score in the International Civil Aviation Organisation’s (ICAO) safety oversight assessment conducted in April 2026.

The achievement represents Nigeria’s highest aviation safety rating in history, placing the country significantly above the global average of 70.4 per cent and the West African regional average of 61.1 per cent.

It is a remarkable departure from the approximately 70 per cent performance that had characterised previous assessments.

For an industry where safety standards determine international confidence, investment decisions and operational credibility, the improvement represents a significant national achievement.

The administration has also achieved full aerodrome certification of Nigeria’s five international airports in Lagos, Abuja, Kano, Port Harcourt and Enugu for the first time in the country’s history.

These accomplishments demonstrate the impact of deliberate regulatory reforms, institutional strengthening and investments in modern aviation infrastructure.

Rebuilding Nigeria’s aviation gateways

Beyond regulatory improvements, the Tinubu administration has embarked on an ambitious programme to modernise the country’s airport infrastructure.

The flagship project is the comprehensive reconstruction and modernisation of Terminal 1 at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, with a Federal Government commitment of N712.3 billion.

The project, which is more than 50 per cent complete as of November 2026, is designed to transform Nigeria’s busiest international gateway into a modern aviation facility capable of meeting contemporary international standards

The scope includes redesigned passenger movement systems, modern baggage handling facilities, a new overhead bridge and a skywalk connecting passengers to the departure halls of Terminals 1 and 2.

Significantly, the project is being financed through the Renewed Hope Infrastructure Development Fund, using savings from subsidy reforms rather than new external borrowing.

In Kano, N46 billion has been committed to the resurfacing of the runway at the Mallam Aminu Kano International Airport. The domestic terminal has also been completely remodelled, while a new Hajj terminal was commissioned in July 2026.

The administration has equally supported the upgrading of the Muhammadu Buhari Airport in Maiduguri to full international status, including a new international terminal and facilities for immigration, customs and other relevant agencies.

Other notable interventions include the upgrading of Victor Attah International Airport in Uyo to full international operations, the rehabilitation and expansion of the Benin Airport terminal, the provision of runway lighting at Osubi Airport, the construction of a new terminal at Akure Airport and the ongoing runway expansion programme at Sam Mbakwe International Cargo Airport, Owerri.

The Federal Government has also approved the development of a new international airport at Ubaha Nsulu in Abia State.

These projects reflect an emerging national aviation network in which more states can participate meaningfully in international commerce, tourism, cargo transportation and investment.

Restoring international confidence

One of the most significant achievements of the Tinubu administration has been its success in addressing the crisis of trapped airline funds that threatened Nigeria’s international aviation relationships.

At its peak in June 2023, foreign airlines had approximately $850 million in revenues trapped in Nigerian banks because of foreign exchange liquidity challenges.

The situation was so serious that some international airlines suspended operations, while others threatened to withdraw from the Nigerian market.

Through coordinated intervention by the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Ministry of Aviation and Aerospace Development, the backlog was substantially cleared by mid-2024.

The International Air Transport Association subsequently acknowledged the progress, while Nigeria was removed from the list of countries with blocked airline funds.

As of November 2026, Nigeria has emerged as Africa’s leading country in the repatriation of airline funds.

Another significant diplomatic and aviation milestone was the return of Emirates Airlines to Nigeria on October 1, 2024, after suspending operations in 2022.

The resumption followed high-level diplomatic engagements between Nigeria and the United Arab Emirates, culminating in a renewed bilateral aviation agreement.

The return of Emirates restored an important international connection and demonstrated renewed confidence in Nigeria’s aviation market

Breaking the aircraft leasing barrier

For years, Nigerian airlines faced enormous difficulties accessing aircraft through international leasing arrangements.

Nigeria’s poor compliance standing under the Cape Town Convention had placed the country on the Aviation Working Group’s non-compliance watchlist, making international lessors reluctant to expose their aircraft to the Nigerian market.

The Tinubu administration addressed this challenge through legal and regulatory reforms, including the signing of a Practice Direction by the Chief Judge of the Federal High Court in 2024 and the operationalisation of the Irrevocable De-registration and Export Request Authorisation (IDERA).

Consequently, Nigeria’s compliance score improved from 49.5 per cent to 75.5 per cent, leading to its removal from the Aviation Working Group’s watchlist.

The practical benefit became evident when Air Peace secured a Boeing 737-700 NG on dry lease from AerCap, one of the world’s leading aircraft leasing companies.

To consolidate this achievement, the Federal Executive Council approved the establishment of the Nigeria Aircraft Leasing Company in April 2026.

The initiative, which is fully privately funded, is projected to unlock more than $1 billion in aircraft financing capacity for Nigerian airlines through a locally based special-purpose vehicle supported by limited government guarantees.

This is a potentially transformative intervention for indigenous carriers that have historically paid significantly higher aircraft leasing costs than their international competitors.

Strengthening indigenous airlines

The administration has also demonstrated a clear commitment to strengthening Nigerian-owned airlines.

Rather than proceeding with the controversial inherited national carrier arrangement involving Ethiopian Airlines, which faced significant legal challenges, the government discontinued the proposed structure and redirected attention towards supporting existing indigenous operators.

Air Peace’s entry into the Lagos-London route in March 2024 was a significant demonstration of this policy direction.

The airline subsequently expanded its London operations to include Abuja, with services to Heathrow and Gatwick following diplomatic engagements with the United Kingdom.

Approval has also been secured for the proposed Owerri-Lagos-London and London-Owerri operations, further strengthening the international aviation prospects of the South-East.

In April 2026, President Tinubu also approved a 30 per cent discount on outstanding debts owed by domestic airlines to aviation agencies, following concerns over rising aviation fuel costs and threats of operational shutdowns.

These interventions, alongside engagements with major aircraft manufacturers including Boeing, Airbus, Embraer and Bombardier, are aimed at creating a more favourable operating environment for Nigerian carriers.

Ending two decades of legal uncertainty

Another major achievement is the resolution of the nearly two-decade dispute between the Federal Government and Bi-Courtney Aviation Services Limited over the operation of Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal 2.

The prolonged disagreement had denied the Federal Government expected revenue from the terminal for almost twenty years and created considerable uncertainty around the public-private partnership arrangement.

Following approval by the Federal Executive Council in April 2026, a negotiated settlement was finally signed in October 2026.

The resolution represents an important breakthrough in the management of aviation infrastructure and provides a clearer framework for investment and operational responsibilities.

Building aviation expertise and creating local value

The administration has also moved to strengthen Nigeria’s aviation human capital through

the commencement of full operations at the African Aviation and Aerospace University in Abuja.

The institution is expected to develop specialised manpower in aviation management, engineering and regulatory studies, reducing the country’s dependence on expensive foreign training institutions.

Similarly, the government’s policy requiring international airlines operating in Nigeria to source onboard meals for outbound flights from local caterers has created new opportunities for indigenous businesses.

The impact is becoming visible in the expansion of local aviation catering companies, including the opening of a N10 billion catering facility in Abuja in October 2026.

The administration has equally approved approximately N36 billion for the payment of pensions and severance benefits to more than 3,300 former employees of the defunct Nigeria Airways, with an initial N18 billion already released.

This represents a long-awaited resolution of an outstanding obligation that had lingered for more than two decades.

Nigeria’s rising international aviation profile

Perhaps one of the strongest indications of the country’s improved aviation standing is the growing international recognition of its leadership and regulatory achievements.

The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, SAN, was named among Africa’s top four aviation figures by the International Air Transport Association in April 2026.

He was also appointed Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the Banjul Accord Group, a regional aviation organisation promoting harmonised safety oversight and regulatory standards among West African countries.

Furthermore, the African Development Bank appointed him champion of its $7 billion Integrated Aviation Transformation Programme for Africa, with Nigeria as a pilot country.

Nigeria also hosted its first-ever International Airshow in December 2025, attracting international aircraft manufacturers, lessors, airlines and other aviation stakeholders.

For a country that had previously struggled with international aircraft leasing restrictions, hosting such an event was a powerful demonstration of its renewed ambition and growing relevance in the global aviation community.

A new chapter for Nigerian aviation

Taken together, these developments represent a significant departure from the challenges that confronted Nigeria’s aviation industry in 2023.

The record-breaking ICAO safety score, the certification of all five international airports, the return of Emirates, the clearance of trapped airline funds, improved aircraft leasing opportunities, support for indigenous carriers and the extensive airport modernisation programme constitute important milestones in the industry’s development.

While challenges relating to operating costs, passenger experience, infrastructure delivery and airline sustainability remain, the foundations for a more competitive and internationally respected aviation sector are increasingly being established.

The significance of President Tinubu’s intervention lies not simply in the number of projects undertaken, but in the deliberate effort to address structural weaknesses that had constrained the industry for years.

From regulatory credibility to international partnerships, from airport infrastructure to indigenous airline development, Nigeria’s aviation sector is witnessing a major institutional and operational reset.

The journey is far from complete, but one thing is increasingly evident: Nigeria is reclaiming its place in the international aviation community, and the Tinubu administration’s reforms are providing the foundation for that renewed ambition.

Bakare sent this piece through seyibakre@aol.com

title: Group plans school clubs to develop young leaders
description:
A grassroots youth development programme, Youth Arising Diplomatic and Leadership Initiative, has called for a reorientation of students to understand that leadership begins with small responsibilities, not political positions.
YADLI is an arm of a non-governmental organisation, Youth Arising Networ
content:
A grassroots youth development programme, Youth Arising Diplomatic and Leadership Initiative, has called for a reorientation of students to understand that leadership begins with small responsibilities, not political positions.

YADLI is an arm of a non-governmental organisation, Youth Arising Network. It teaches secondary school students about leadership, responsibility and positive contribution to society.

Its founder, Chigozie Onyegbula, said leadership should not be something young people think about only when they become adults.

According to him, positions such as class captain, head boy and head girl are already opportunities to learn and practise leadership.

“At that level, you are already a leader. You don’t necessarily need to have become a governor before you are a leader,” he said.

Onyegbula said the way students handle such roles could shape the kind of leaders they become.

He gave the example of a class captain asked to report an incident in class, who uses the opportunity to settle a personal score against a classmate.

“It might not sound like a big deal to you, but it’s showing the type of leader you are,” he added.

Our correspondent gathered that YADLI also works on students’ communication skills, critical thinking and understanding of their roles in society.

Its activities are linked to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly Goal 4 on quality education and Goal 16 on peace, justice and strong institutions.

In August 2026, the group held a three-week leadership training for 12 secondary school students in Bariga, Lagos. The programme covered leadership, communication, civic responsibility and personal development.

Onyegbula said workbooks were used so that the students could reflect on themselves instead of simply listening to facilitators.

To reach more students and give them a platform to express their views, YADLI organised an inter-school debate last Saturday, November 14, at the Greater Evangelism World Crusade, Bariga.

Eight schools had initially indicated interest, but three took part: Bright Hope College, Eben Noble College and Better Days College.

On the motion, “Leaders Are Made, Not Born,” Bright Hope College won. Eben Noble College came second and Better Days College third.

The Charter President of Energy Toastmasters Club, Israel Ekiko, who also spoke at the event, urged the students to develop their public speaking skills and make use of opportunities in school, church and other gatherings.

Onyegbula said YADLI plans to establish leadership clubs in schools so that students can keep learning beyond its programmes. He added that the organisation hoped to reach more schools and communities through partnerships and sponsorships.

“The responsibilities young people take on today could influence the kind of leaders they become in the future,” he said.

title: Eunisell boosts Warriors morale with MOTM, POTM awards
description:
In a major step to strengthen its relationship with Abia Warriors and motivate the players, the club’s shirt sponsor, Eunisell, has introduced the Man-of-the-Match and Player-of-the-Month awards for the players.
The gesture, which has been widely applauded by the players, technical crew, and support
content:
In a major step to strengthen its relationship with Abia Warriors and motivate the players, the club’s shirt sponsor, Eunisell, has introduced the Man-of-the-Match and Player-of-the-Month awards for the players.

The gesture, which has been widely applauded by the players, technical crew, and supporters of the club, is aimed at rewarding excellence, encouraging healthy competition, and spurring the team to greater heights on the pitch.

The awards come with additional cash prizes, which will see the Man-of-the-Match for each game going home with Fifty Thousand Naira (N50,000), while the Player-of-the-Month award attracts a One Hundred Thousand Naira (N100,000) reward.

While reacting to the development, Abia Warriors Chairman, Coach John Sam Obuh, expressed his gratitude to Eunisell for introducing such a laudable initiative, which he said will fire up the players as they navigate their way out of the murky waters of the relegation zone.

He reserved special praise for the Group Managing Director of Eunisell, Mr. Chika Ikenga, for his unwavering commitment, generosity, and continued support for the club, describing him as a true partner in the Abia Warriors project.

Coach Obuh further urged the players to reciprocate the kind gesture by giving their all in every match, fighting for the badge, and ensuring the club returns to winning ways.

Eunisell is a leading industrial solutions company providing specialised chemical products, technical services and engineering solutions to the oil and gas, manufacturing and other industrial sectors. With a strong commitment to innovation, quality and operational excellence, the company partners with businesses to address complex operational challenges, improve productivity and enhance operational efficiency.

title: I started writing children’s books to replace European stories – 96-year-old author, Ade-Ajayi
description:
Early childhood educator and children’s author, Chief (Mrs) Christie Ade-Ajayi, speaks with BIODUN BUSARI about her childhood, marriage, teaching career, passion for storytelling and the legacy she hopes to leave behind

What are your earliest childhood memories?
I was born in Ogbomoso, where my fat
content:
Early childhood educator and children’s author, Chief (Mrs) Christie Ade-Ajayi, speaks with BIODUN BUSARI about her childhood, marriage, teaching career, passion for storytelling and the legacy she hopes to leave behind

What are your earliest childhood memories?

I was born in Ogbomoso, where my father was a civil servant, but my family is from Ile-Oluji, Ondo State. My mother died when I was three years old, while my brother was one. My father did not want to remarry, so he handed us over to our grandmother, who was a chief in one of the Baptist churches. She looked after us until I was six, when I moved to Osogbo, where my father was then based.

Afterwards, I attended Kudeti Girls’ School in Ibadan, now St Anne’s School. Upon completing my education there, I proceeded to United Missionary College for teacher training. I have fond memories of my British missionary teachers, including Ms Brown and Ms Holmes, who were supported by a few trained Nigerian teachers.

We called our principal ‘Iya’ because she was like a mother to us. She was a strict but loving and caring British woman. She sometimes stayed in her office until about 3am. We heard stories that evil spirits occasionally visited her office in the middle of the night. She would tell them, ‘If you are in the Lord, come with me.’ The spirits would then disappear because they were not of the Lord.

We had many experiences of being taught, trained and mentored by British teachers. At the teacher training college, we had students from different parts of the country, including Igbo, Hausa and Efik students. We had a good time together.

How did your career progress after teacher training?

Teaching was one of the most common professions for women at the time. After our training, we were posted to different schools to teach. We had made friends during our time at the college and kept in touch during short holidays.

I enjoyed the primary teaching course we undertook. Some of us preferred teaching younger children, and I was transferred to Anglican Girls’ School in Ondo in 1952. After spending a few years in my hometown, I returned to Ibadan to continue teaching.

Later, I travelled to London, United Kingdom, and California, United States, where I obtained professional diplomas in child development and elementary school administration. I also worked briefly as a supply teacher in primary schools in London to learn different approaches to teaching young children.

What inspired your passion for children’s storytelling?

After completing our training at UMC and posted to different schools, we discovered that most of the books children read were written by English authors. They learnt about British culture through stories such as Janet and John. I told myself that something had to be done to promote indigenous stories and local experiences. That was how I started writing.

I remember that when I was in London, a young boy touched my skin and asked, ‘Do you bathe?’ He asked because of my skin colour. They had never seen Black people before. I was not offended, but the incident showed how limited their exposure was. Their books reflected their own environment and experiences.

It made me realise that Nigerian children also deserved stories that reflected their culture and experiences rather than relying solely on books written by English authors. I was not the only person who felt that way, but perhaps only two of us out of a hundred people took steps towards achieving that goal.

How did you feel when you began writing children’s books?

I feel very accomplished. There were not many publishers at the time, but some people ventured into publishing and began accepting my books. I felt it was a mission I had to pursue.

I started by drawing on my experiences with my children. For example, Ade, Our Naughty Little Brother was inspired by my only son, who had four sisters. He watched cartoons so much that he would say he wanted to be Superman. He would jump from one place to another and dress like the character. There was also a time when he wanted to dress like his sisters and follow them to parties.

Children enjoyed those kinds of storybooks, and I enjoyed writing them. The knowledge I acquired in London also enriched my teaching experience and improved my understanding of primary education and teaching methods in Nigeria. It contributed to what became a fulfilling career.

What inspired the popular book, Akin Goes to School?

The story was also drawn from my family history. It was based on my father, Akinleye Martins, who was the son of a chief in Ile-Oluji. My grandfather was a warrior who participated in the Yoruba wars. He said Europeans had beaten him, so he decided that his son, my father, would not go to school.

It was only after my uncle attended a college in Oyo and returned to persuade my grandfather that he agreed to allow my father to go to school. In those days, people trekked long distances to school because there were not many vehicles. After much deliberation, my grandfather enrolled my father in school. He later attended Ondo Boys’ High School.

Why did you draw on your family’s experiences to create stories for children?

They were fascinating experiences that could be used to educate and entertain children. I wanted to tell Nigerian stories rather than leave children to read only what English authors had written. We received feedback that children enjoyed the books.

They were real-life experiences adapted into fiction for Nigerian children to enjoy and learn from. I also wanted the stories to contribute to our educational system.

How did you meet your husband?

My husband, Prof J.F. Ade-Ajayi, was one of the foundation students at the University of Ibadan. He met me through my father’s friends. However, my father initially opposed the relationship because my husband wanted to travel to London for his PhD.

He assured my father that he intended to marry me, so I later joined him in London, where we had the opportunity to get to know each other better before getting married.

That was when I attended the Froebel Educational Institute. My husband encouraged me in my career. He taught history at the university and later became Vice-Chancellor of the University of Lagos in 1972. Whenever he was on sabbatical, he encouraged me to visit schools in England and the United States to learn more about early childhood education. Those experiences further strengthened my interest in writing.

Did any of your children develop an interest in your career?

None of them chose my profession. They each followed their own interests and have done well. One studied law, another studied medicine and is a surgeon in the UK. I also have a bank executive, an architect and estate manager, and an administrator who works as an admissions manager at a university in the United States.

I am happy that all of them are successful and fulfilled in their careers.

How would you describe your contributions to teaching and children’s literature beyond Nigeria?

In Nigeria, I held several positions at the University of Ibadan Staff School before my husband became a vice-chancellor. While we were at UNILAG, I served as president of the University of Lagos Women Society, where I introduced programmes to improve conditions for young children in the nursery section.

I also participated in several organisations focused on early childhood education. I attended conferences organised by the Organisation Mondiale pour l’Éducation Préscolaire in Japan, England and the United States. OMEP translates into English as the World Organisation for Early Childhood Education. It was established after some women went to war, leaving their children behind, but never returned. It was formed to ensure that those children received proper care and education.

I was also active in the International Board on Books for Young People, UNICEF, ZONTA and other organisations. I have continued to encourage women in Nigeria to pay more attention to early childhood education and women’s rights. It has been a fulfilling journey.

What legacy do you hope to leave for younger writers and Nigerian youths?

My husband left a library where people can study free of charge. It is also part of my legacy and that of our family. Researchers, undergraduates and other students visit to read and study without paying. His books, publications and other materials from his years at the university are kept there. I have also donated copies of my books for people to read and study.

We have a librarian who manages the facility, and we hope our children will sustain it. My husband and I believed that young people who read and study would make meaningful contributions to society and improve their lives.

I pray for young people and mentor them as much as I can. Since COVID-19, I have continued to pray for Nigeria and its youths, especially after seeing many young people leave the country.

What are the secrets to your good health and longevity at 96?

I believe we must remain close to God. I hold on to Him because He has kept me alive. I pray and try to do good to others. My husband and I have helped many young people by sponsoring their education through secondary school and university.

There are blessings that come from doing good to others. Love is the most important quality anyone can show towards others. We must care for people and avoid being selfish.

What values from your generation do you think are missing in society today?

Helping others is no longer as common as it used to be. In the past, people readily showed love and extended assistance to others, but that is not happening as much today.

Over the past two years, I have written to groups of women about how we can engage the government to support children and young people. Some of them asked whether the government would actually help. Such initiatives are not forthcoming.

There is a lack of love and support in society. If we fail to help people, some may turn to crime, including kidnapping. The government, parents and people in positions of authority must take responsibility for helping children and young people build better lives.

The Bible says that the love of money is the root of all evil. Many young people are desperate for money, and this can push some into criminal activities that endanger lives. What we should all focus on is showing love and care for others.

The post I started writing children’s books to replace European stories – 96-year-old author, Ade-Ajayi appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Praises provoke miracles, by Funmi Komolafe
description:

content:
Beloved, let’s thank God that we are gradually moving to the end of 2026. May the LORD see us to the end of the year joyfully in Jesus name.

We might have heard of the eleventh hour miracle which some have interpreted to mean the miracle that happens when hope is lost.

It is miracle when the benefactor does not expect it.

When a woman gets pregnant at age 63 or any age after 45, it is a last minute miracle.

It could also be miracle that one does not deserve but got one because of the mercy of God. An example is the labourer that was hired when work was almost completed but got the same pay as those that had worked their hearts out.

Matthew 16 vs. 8-11: (KJV)“ So when even was come, the lord of the vineyard saith unto his steward, Call the labourers, and give them their hire, beginning from the last unto the first.

And when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny.

But when the first came, they supposed that they should have received more; and they likewise received every man a penny.

And when they had received it, they murmured against the good man of the house”.

Brethren, when you receive an eleventh hour miracle, some people would grumble. They would express doubts, some might even be unhappy but they would be unable to stop the work of God.

The labourer in the above quoted passage, got an eleventh hour miracle by the mercy of the master of the vineyard.

You too can receive an eleventh hour miracle by the mercy of God.

You can also provoke yours with Praises.

How do I know? Psalm 22 vs. 3-4 gives me the answer. It states, “ But thou are holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel.

Our fathers trusted in thee: they trusted, and thou didst deliver them”.

When we praise God with faith, we should know that God would not watch you praise him and do nothing.

The LORD would definitely take an action on your behalf when you praise Him.

King David, the shepherd boy that God made a king also knew that God is moved to action when he is praised hence David wrote many Psalms of praise to God.

Psalm 34 vs. 1-3 is my witness. “ I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth. My soul shall make her boast in the LORD; the humble shall hear therof, and be glad. O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together”.

If you still have doubts, remember King Jehoshaphat used praises to provoke God to deal with enemies when three kings that were too strong for him rose against him.

Like any human being, Jehoshaphat feared. He cried to God in prayer but his last instrument was Praise.

2 Chronicles 20 vs. 21 &22 tells us what happened. “ And when he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army, and to say, Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever.

And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushments against the children of Ammon, Moab, and mount Seir, which were come against Judah; and they were smitten”.

In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whoever gangs up against God’s plans for you, the LORD will smite them as He did to the enemies of Jehoshaphat.

In the case of Jehoshaphat he raised a praise worship theme when he was confronted with enemies too strong for him to handle.

In the case of David, he formed the habit of praising God always and he always had victory. Even when he committed sins, God still had mercy on him. Perhaps because he had a habit of praising God almost on a daily basis.

2 Kings 6 vs. 21 tells us more about what happened when David was praising God after a victory over his enemies.

2 Samuel 6 vs. 20-21: “ Then David returned to bless his household. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, How glorious was the king of Israel today in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself!

And David said unto Michal, It was before the LORD, which chose me before thy father, and before all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the LORD, over Israel: therefore will I play before the LORD”.

For rebuking David for praising God without protocol, see what the LORD did to Michal in verse 23. “ Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death”.

This should tell us that the Almighty God takes Praises seriously. The question for us now, is when and how do we praise the LORD?

Human beings tend to praise God when we have a testimony. When God has done something that gladdens us or when he has delivered us from any form of pain, sorrow or accidents etc we find it easy to praise the Lord.

In such situations, praises flow from us freely. We begin to dance, shout , sing songs.

This is in order but we can also praise God when we acknowledge what he has done in the past like the sinking of Pharaoh and his horse riders and other miracles.

Brethren, the best time to praise God however is when we are expecting a miracle. That was the strategy of king Jehoshaphat and it worked for him.

However, it takes a higher level of faith to praise the LORD when you are still expecting a miracle. It is an action taken to demonstrate total faith and confidence in the ability of God to do the impossible and to reverse the irreversible.

It is a total demonstration of trust in God.

My prayer for you today, is that it doesn’t matter what you are still looking forward to, the Holy Spirit will open your mouth to praise the LORD at all times.

You need the Holy Spirit to help you because the flesh is bound to discourage you and give you the spiritual strength that you need to praise God in the time of need.

You may then ask, how do I praise God when I am in my office or not in a church? There are several ways to praise God.

For this article, we’ll discuss the names of God.

Brethren, you don’t need to shout when you call the Lord by His names when you are in a place that is not convenient to do so.

God has numerous names and each name, is for a purpose and all names are miracle working instrument.

You only need to repeat the names until your spirit man picks it up.

The numerous names of God, include, Jehovah El- Shadier, ( God Almighty), Jehovah Nissi, (Lord is my banner), the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, The God of all flesh, Jehovah Sabaoth ( The Lord of Hosts). Jehovah Jireh,( My Provider), Jehovah Rapha (The Lord that heals) , Jehovah Shalom ( The Lord is Peace),

Others include, Jehovah Elohim ( The Creator), Jehovah Rohi ( The Lord my shepherd), Yaweh ( I AM) and many more.

Brethren, whatever is your need, God can meet it.

Beloved as the year winds down, may the Lord open your mouth to praise the LORD.

God is good at all times.

The post Praises provoke miracles, by Funmi Komolafe appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Teaching hospital management can’t explain how my father’s corpse disappeared — Son
description: Three months after depositing the corpse of his late father, Chief Chukwunweike Okammelu, at the Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu Teaching Hospital mortuary in Awka, Anambra State, Onyebuchi Nwankwo was preparing for the burial when he discovered that the body had gone missing. He tells AYOOLA OLASUPO ab
content:
Three months after depositing the corpse of his late father, Chief Chukwunweike Okammelu, at the Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu Teaching Hospital mortuary in Awka, Anambra State, Onyebuchi Nwankwo was preparing for the burial when he discovered that the body had gone missing. He tells AYOOLA OLASUPO about discrepancies the family uncovered in the hospital’s records and efforts made to find the missing corpse

Can you recount the circumstances surrounding how your father’s body was deposited at the hospital mortuary?

I am the first son of the late Chief Chukwunweike Okammelu. My father died on December 30, 2025. According to the information provided by the hospital, he died of a heart attack.

I was at work when my stepmother called to inform me that he had taken ill and was being taken to the hospital. I was later told that he was moved from the initial hospital to the Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu Teaching Hospital in Awka, Anambra State.

By the time I arrived at the emergency ward, my father was already declared dead. We subsequently proceeded to the hospital mortuary to deposit his corpse.

My uncle made the payment, and the cashier issued us receipts and a tally card bearing the name Clement, the mortician assigned to attend to us whenever we visited. We were also given a form to complete.

My uncle’s in-law, a doctor who had previously worked at the hospital, helped us to fill it out because we were still grieving.

After completing the necessary procedures, my father’s body was taken into the mortuary, and we left.

When did you plan to bury him?

The burial was fixed for April 9, 2026. We had printed invitation cards, sewn our family uniforms and informed my father’s maternal and paternal relatives, as well as our in-laws. We were already making preparations when we discovered that his corpse was missing.

How did you discover that the corpse had disappeared?

My sister and I discovered the disappearance on March 1, 2026. We had travelled to Enugu, where we were staying with her husband, to meet our in-laws and formally inform them about the burial. On our way back, we decided to stop at the hospital so my sister could see our father, whom she had not seen since his death.

As usual, we called Clement, the mortician, and showed him our tally card. He went into the mortuary to locate the corpse. After about 35 to 40 minutes, he came out and asked whether I could remember where my father’s body had been kept. I said yes, and he asked me to accompany him inside.

We went to the particular section and opened the body bag, but my father’s corpse was not there. We searched other body bags in that section but could not find him. We also could not locate the tally number, 331, which was supposed to be on his wrist.

We proceeded to search every section of the mortuary, including the VIP section, where corpses were kept separately for a fee, and the section where the bodies of people shot or killed by the police were kept. Despite searching everywhere, we could not find my father’s body.

I immediately alerted my family, particularly my father’s eldest sister, and informed them that we could not find his corpse.

Did you check the mortuary records to establish whether his body was transferred or released?

Yes. I asked the mortician to bring out the register used to document incoming corpses. I believed that if there was a register for receiving bodies, there should also be one for recording corpses transferred or released.

We checked the records from January 1 to March 1, but my father’s name and tally number were not on the list of corpses that had been removed.

There was, however, an earlier incident that became significant after the disappearance.

On January 19, 2026, my elder sister, aunt and I visited the mortuary. When the mortician brought out my father’s body, we noticed that the tally number on his wrist was different from the one on the card issued to us. The number had also been written on a piece of cardboard instead of the proper identification card.

I pointed this out to the mortician, who removed the wrong number. We later went to check the register. Although my father’s name, the depositor’s name and phone number were recorded, the space for the tally number was blank. We asked him to enter the correct number, and he did so immediately.

We also gave him a white wrapper known as Kilikilista, which we had chosen to make identification easier. Other corpses had different wrappers, so we believed ours would help us recognise my father’s body whenever we visited. He assured us that he would keep it safe and correct the tally number.

Did the wrong tally number and missing entry in the register raise suspicions?

No. We considered them oversights that could be corrected. I never imagined that something like this could happen in real life. We believed the mortician had simply made a mistake and would rectify it.

If we suspected that something was wrong, we would have immediately alerted the hospital management.

What explanation did the hospital give when you reported the disappearance?

After leaving the hospital that evening, I called Clement around 3am to ask whether he had found the corpse. He said he had not but suggested that it might have been misplaced or transferred elsewhere.

I challenged him because we had checked the physical transfer register and found no record of my father’s movement. He then claimed that transfers were recorded electronically on the computer system in the Reverend Sister’s office, rather than in the mortuary register.

I asked him whether, as the mortician responsible for the corpse, he did not also have a record of such a transfer. He still could not tell me where my father’s body was supposedly taken.

I returned to the hospital on March 3, but Clement was absent. We were told that he had travelled to Enugu or Ebonyi State. I went to the Reverend Sister’s office and asked whether the hospital had any record of my father’s corpse being transferred. She said there was none and that she had been trying to reach the mortician.

When I eventually spoke to Clement, he claimed he travelled to search for the corpse and had obtained permission from one Mr Ozo. I questioned why he would leave the hospital when a corpse under his care was missing.

My uncle later accompanied us to meet the chief medical director. He asked us to remain calm, assuring us that the corpse could not have disappeared and must be somewhere in the mortuary. He suggested that the chemicals used in the facility might have affected our eyes and that the hospital would bring out all the male corpses for us to identify my father.

We expected the management to treat the matter more seriously. Instead, they appeared unwilling to accept that the corpse could actually be missing. Their position was that it must be somewhere in the mortuary. We found this frustrating.

We subsequently reported the matter to the police at Zone 13, Ukpo, Anambra State.

What happened after you petitioned the police?

The matter was also taken to the State Criminal Investigation Department in Awka. We made efforts to locate Clement and get him to return to the hospital. We traced some of his relatives, and two people were eventually arrested. Clement returned after one of his relatives, who worked in a bank, was arrested.

When the mortician was questioned, he gave a different explanation. He claimed that he released my father’s corpse to one of our relatives.

Did he identify the relative he claimed to have handed the corpse to?

No. He could not identify the person. The hospital management began relying on that claim to suggest that we collected the corpse and were now pretending it was missing.

But how could a hospital employee claim to have released a corpse to a relative whose name he could not provide?

There is a procedure for releasing corpses to families. We were told by the hospital management, including the Chief Medical Director, that certain steps had to be followed before a body could be released. We did not sign any document confirming that we collected my father’s corpse because we did not see any.

The Reverend Sister also confirmed that there was no record showing that corpse number 331 was released or transferred. We therefore questioned how the mortician could claim to have released it without any documentation or identifiable recipient.

What did the police investigation establish?

The initial investigation at Zone 13 was not progressing as we expected. My uncle, who lives in Abuja, subsequently moved the matter to the Intelligence Response Team in Abuja, which began a fresh investigation.

The IRT came to Anambra State and arrested several people connected with the hospital and the mortuary. These included the mortician, the Reverend Sister, Mr Ozo and some other staff members. Even the security personnel who were on duty when the corpse allegedly disappeared were picked up for questioning.

The investigators also obtained statements from my stepmother and one of the men who helped drive my father to the hospital on the day he died.

During the investigation, I learnt that the police traced the contact of a native doctor in Abakaliki through Clement’s phone records. I do not know the full details of that aspect of the investigation.

The investigation lasted about three months, but what disappointed my uncle and the rest of us was that almost everyone arrested was eventually released, leaving only Clement.

We could not understand why the hospital was not being held accountable. We paid the institution to preserve my father’s corpse. He was in its custody, and we had not signed any document indicating that we had collected him.

The mortician was employed by the hospital. Even if he was directly responsible for whatever happened, the institution should explain how a corpse under its care could disappear without a trace.

We were dissatisfied with the way the investigation was handled and subsequently petitioned the Inspector-General of Police.

What is the current status of the investigation, and has the whereabouts of your father’s corpse been established?

Unfortunately, the police have not been able to give us any positive information about the whereabouts of the corpse. We are still waiting for answers.

We want those involved to be brought back for further investigation so they can explain what happened and, most importantly, produce our father’s body.

We also believe that everyone involved in the process should be investigated. The Reverend Sister may not have physically released the corpse, but she was involved in the mortuary’s operations. She reportedly gave Clement permission to leave the hospital despite knowing that a corpse was missing.

The security personnel who were on duty should also explain how the body could have been taken out of the hospital without clearance. Unless it was moved in a vehicle or ambulance, how did it leave the premises without anyone noticing?

We want everyone involved to come forward and tell us the truth. Our family deserves to know what happened to our father and where his corpse is. We deposited his body in the hospital’s custody, paid for its preservation and expected to retrieve it for burial. Instead, we are left searching for a corpse that should never have gone missing in the first place.

title: Nigerian politicians preparing for war, not election, by Dele Sobowale
description:
“War is nothing more than the continuation of politics by other means” – Karl von Clausewitz, 1780-1831



The Prussian General and military theorist could not have had Nigeria in mind when he wrote several books on politics and war because Nigeria did not exist then. But, some of his theories, whic
content:
“War is nothing more than the continuation of politics by other means” – Karl von Clausewitz, 1780-1831

The Prussian General and military theorist could not have had Nigeria in mind when he wrote several books on politics and war because Nigeria did not exist then. But, some of his theories, which are still required reading in military academies worldwide, apply to the Nigerian political situation at the moment. Several Nigerian leading scholars have argued, with a great deal of conviction, that our country’s progress has been retarded by lack of institutions. That may be so. But, the nation is drifting towards war in January precisely because the most important institutions governing elections and which are supposed to be the guard-rails of democracy don’t appear to be doing their job. The institutions I have in mind are INEC, police, DSS, EFCC and the judiciary. No ranking is implied in the listing.

THE FIRST SHALL BE THE LAST– JUDICIARY

“We must not regard political consequences, how formidable so ever they might be. If rebellion was certain consequence, we are bound to say: ‘Fiat Justitia caelum’ (Latin), meaning, ‘Let justice be done even if the world perishes’” – Lord Mansfield, VANGUARD BOOK OF QUOTATIONS, VBQ, p 112.

One Federal High Court, FHC, Justice (name withheld), will serve proxy for what the Nigerian judiciary has become – even before retired Supreme Court Justice Augie informed us that the Nigerian court has become a cash and carry outfit. My Lord of the FHC has delivered at least two judgments which defy basic rules of justice. First, he made a pronouncement on a matter already before the Court of Appeal; and was roundly reprimanded. Second, he again made a contrary ruling on a matter on which another FHC had already given judgment. How else does one explain all these shenanigans on the Federal bench other than recalling what late Chief MKO Abiola once said: “No one stands all day in the rain for nothing.” The jurist knew in advance that his conduct would be publicly condemned. Yet, he went ahead with the breach of court processes each time. Furthermore, while the Justice, who has acquired notoriety, whether deserved or not, is not the only one on the bench pronouncing hair-raising verdicts concerning election issues – while the National Judicial Council, NJC, headed by the Chief Justice of Nigeria, apparently has done nothing to restrain rampant disregard for established court processes.

My colleague, Tony Iredia, summarized the situation last week in his must read column – Nigeria Today: “The other day, a respected retired justice of the Supreme Court asserted that our judiciary now operates like market stalls. Courts of coordinate jurisdiction have continued to give conflicting decisions in breach of warnings by the Chief Justice of the Federation.. In addition to this situation which greatly confuses our people, it has become the norm for parties to a case, to both claim to have won the case.”

Iredia has highlighted at least two issues which will render the judiciary a danger to Nigeria in 2027; and why losers might not go to court. First is economic. The market is a transactional institution – unlike what a court of justice should not be. If, as has been asserted, without refutation, Nigerian courts should be classified with Jankara, Monday Market, Utarko, Fegge or Ariara markets, it will serve no purpose for other political parties to go there. Markets sell scarce commodities to the highest bidder. The ruling party can outspend all the other political parties put together; and still have funds left to take the campaign committee to Umrah next year. Going to court will amount to a waste of time and money – which they don’t even have.

Second, with the fairness of the judiciary now in question, of what use are the various roles assigned to the Third Estate of the Realm by the Constitution and electoral laws when the verdicts of cases have already been written by the highest bidder?

I undertook a short exercise before writing this article. All the reported judgments by courts, in connection with political parties were tabulated. An astonishing 78 per cent went against opposition parties. Are these signs of things to come?

INEC: DOUBTFUL PREPAREDNESS AND QUESTIONABLE IMPARTIALITY

“Will the elections hold?” – Suleiman A Suleiman, Daily Trust, November 9, 2026.

Suleiman asked a question in that article; which should be concerning to every Nigerian. The consequences of the 2027 elections not holding or postponed are too calamitous to be contemplated. Yet, we must learn from a conqueror during the 19th century, Napoleon Bonaparte, 1769-1821, whose instruction to his commanders was: “Bring me the bad news quickly; the good news can wait.” Suleiman has brought us the bad news early in time for us to start thinking about how to manage a potential crisis before it transforms into a national disaster. Nigeria’s unity, always fragile, has never been more severely tested than now – a time when distrust is national and violence prevalent everywhere. Our country is like a room in which inflammable materials are stored – waiting for somebody to inadvertently or deliberately toss fire.

Right now, the single most potent match stick in the nation is the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC. To begin with, most people strongly doubt its independence or impartiality. “He who pays the piper dictates the tune” is an adage to which most Nigerians subscribe; and which they readily apply to INEC. The Commission has not done everything to dispel the suspicion of partisanship. Many people were surprised when INEC informed a court that it has no record of the certificates submitted by a presidential contender in 2023 and contesting again in 2027. Was it the truth or pre-meditated obstruction of justice? Either way, it stinks.

Suleiman, however, provided evidence which should frighten those who still care about Nigeria’s unity. I am one. One, he pointed out to us that the preliminary register of voters displayed by INEC in October, with promise to publish a final register of voters on December 15, 2026 have raised “a thousand and one legal problems with this release because nearly everything INEC says in this release is not only a direct violation of the Electoral Act 2026, but puts the entire election into a legal peril. By publishing the preliminary voters’ register on October 26, and promising to release the certified copy of the register on December 15, INEC has already breached the law twice.”

Let us pause here and consider the implications of what Suleiman has told us. He cited the Sections of the Electoral Act 2026 to support his assertions. The Chairman of INEC, Professor Joash Amupitan, SAN, does not need anybody to interpret the words of an Electoral Act to him. The obvious and troubling questions are: Why is he running INEC like a lawless organization? Is he aware of the repercussions of INEC conducting elections which are in breach of the law? Why is he doing it?

Free and fair elections don’t occur by accident. The entire world witnessed three recently – Brazil, Israel and the USA. Brazilians re-elected the incumbent government; Israelis rejected Benjamin Netanyahu and Americans delivered a dirty slap in the face to President Trump. The three elections have one thing in common – an impartial, incorruptible and well-prepared electoral body. Nobody went to court; because the umpire was truly independent. By contrast, INEC is exhibiting all the traits of the Nigerian Factor. Like a crooked referee, certain to award a penalty where none is earned, INEC had made a lot of decisions which negatively impacted opposition parties and not one against the APC; now it might be deliberately obstructing justice.

Meanwhile, the voters’ register released has exposed the Commission’s lack of integrity. Only a fool would believe that only the few names detected at first glance to have been cloned have bloated the register. When politicians whose states’ populations are less than 5 million – mostly people under 15 – boast of delivering 4 million votes, INEC should be aware that the votes have been counted in November 2026. More to the point; why is INEC reluctant to release the names of the criminals within its ranks who inflated the register? Are they “our boys” planted as moles to subvert the results if they turn out to be unfavourable? Hungry individuals who steal goats or phones are named and shamed. Those plotting to steal an election and the entire nation are shielded from the public.

INEC, except under late Professor Humphery Nwosu, who conducted the June 12, 1993 elections, has developed an unenviable reputation. Amupitan took over from a predecessor who was openly insulted after the 2023 elections. That was bad enough. I don’t condone violence any time, any place or against anybody. But, it is significant that this is the first time the Chairman of INEC would be mobbed long before the elections.

What will happen after?

· To be continued

Follow me on Facebook @ J Israel Biola

The post Nigerian politicians preparing for war, not election, by Dele Sobowale appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Being one step ahead of an opportunist
description:
By Bunmi Sofola



SYLVIA admitted that her parents’ marriage and the stoic way her mum yielded her position as the first wife to a much younger and ambitious woman prepared her for the way she handled her relationship with men.  Her story: “When a man suddenly discovers he’s scaled the ladder of su
content:
By Bunmi Sofola

SYLVIA admitted that her parents’ marriage and the stoic way her mum yielded her position as the first wife to a much younger and ambitious woman prepared her for the way she handled her relationship with men. Her story: “When a man suddenly discovers he’s scaled the ladder of success faster than he’d envisaged, what does he do when he gets to the top? Chuck his frumpy wife for a more sophisticated model that’s what! And it happened to my mother – a stark illiterate my father too couldn’t read or write, but he was a fairly successful cocoa farmer and although we weren’t exactly rolling in the lap of luxury, we were the envy of our small town – talk about big fish in a small pond indeed!

“My dad had been on the war-path with the leadership of the Pentecostal Church we attended. Things finally got to a head, and he broke away to found his own church. A chunk of the congregation from the former church went with him and in a couple of years, his church had ballooned into something he himself never envisaged. As donations kept on pouring in from far and wide, he built a mini estate, installed my mother and her children (four of us) in one of the chalets, then got married to a school certificate holder and made her his main wife. His excuse was that he needed an educated ally to go through the books of the church and welcome visitors in a presentable way.

“I don’t want to go through the rage and resentment we from my mother’s side felt as we witnessed this imposter parade herself as an intellectual. My poor father didn’t know that he was the laughing stock of the congregation who sniggered at the clumsy speeches his ‘educated’ wife always made, riddled with mistakes.

“I was lucky to have a sharp brain and qualified as a lawyer. But I wasn’t lucky in my choice of a husband. Eventually my marriage hit the rocks after five years and two children. The man I had my third child for wasn’t much better, but I was lucky to meet this influential projects director of a parastatal and my life changed for the better. He took care of all my financial needs and was almost twenty years older than I was.

“It is amazing what some women put up with for money. This man was fat and flabby. Whenever he slept over and I watched him asleep with his mouth so wide open I could see his missing teeth and the fillings in some of the rest snoring away without a care in the world. I felt really repulsed. He was definitely not a sight to light the fire in any virile woman’s loins, but he was kind and generous. Let’s face it, he was in his late fifties after all and it must be quite exhausting making love to his wife and God knows who else all the time!

“When he was retired and went into politics, I was often with him and through his contacts, I was able to land into the midst of the heavies. I was eventually appointed a special adviser to a top politician – my first class ticket to the gravy train.

“I’d reverted to my maiden name by this time and my ex-husband had remarried twice! But now that I was an important government official, I quickly changed back to my married name. He had by now burnt his finger in his business and was always broke, so when I sold him the idea of our coming together because of the kids, he jumped at the chance! His greedy eyes swept over my tastefully furnished quarters as he pretended to give our reunion a thought. He is no fool and his calculating brain must have told him that if he played his cards right, his poverty days were over!

“He moved into my official quarters at Abuja and my lover was livid. I re-assured him that my husband was the least of his problems and there was nothing stopping us from carrying on as before. It was an added bonus that he not only knew my husband, Ike, he’d given him a couple of contracts when he was in paid employment, just to shut him up. Not that he suspected anything anyway.

“Now my husband is a happy man. He drives new cars, wears designer clothes and shoes – and has his share of female admirers. That never bothers me – live and let live is my motto. Just a couple of months ago, he had to travel to the Far East on one of our projects. When he phoned, Lekan, my ‘benefactor’ was around and actually in bed with me. I told my husband he was around on a visit to Abuja and would be leaving soon, did he want to have a word with him? It gives you a sort of power getting away with a murder like that! My husband had no way of guessing that whenever he was out of town Lekan always sleeps over. I never bother to ask him what he was up to on his frequent jaunts!

“I don’t have any idea of what this ‘second chance’ marriage would last, but Ike is the least of my problems. He was a very violent and abusive man when we first got married. Now, with so much affluence around him he’s become a gentleman. I know he’s as calculating as I am and we know we’re both using each other, what we have, really is an open marriage and as long as both of us don’t rock the boat…

“Once in a while, I remember my poor mum and hw she suffered the humiliation of being relegated to the background because she didn’t have the financial clout to leave and I feel resentful. Yet, her courage encouraged me to seize happiness whenever I could – using what I have – money, power and position – to get what I want…”

Hugh Grant, the famous British international film star was once asked why he was so sure that women were attracted to money. His reply: “Be honest. Suppose you were unattached and some guy you adored were to walk through the door right now. If he could be cloned into one rich guy and one poor guy, who were otherwise exactly the same and were able to choose between the two, which one would you go for?” The same question should be put to men too, don’t you think?!

Are Men Really Getting Smaller?

These are certainly not the best of times for today’s men. Findings show they’re short, smelly and liars! The case of the shrinking penis! Let’s hope it really is what they do with it and not the size that matters because a recent study shows men’s penises are getting smaller!

This shocking discovery by the Life-style Condom Company (with a bit of help from latex-gloved nurses) is bound not to thrill either sexes. Previously, the Kinsey Sex Report put the average penis size at between 6.2 and 6.4 inches, but the condom poll claims it’s now 5.877 inches – with two thirds of the 1,000 men studied measuring between 5.1 and 6.2 inches. This discovery could answer two of our times most perplexing questions: Why vibrator sales are at a record high and why ex-girl-friends keep going back to their well endowed lovers.

Short-men Syndrome: It’s official; short men have less luck with the ladies. The discovery, set to shock vertically challenged men everywhere, comes from Southampton Hospital. After studying 3,500 medical records and comparing them to marital status, social class and income, the team claims small babies are programmed to be shy in the womb and small boys, who grow to be short adults, are less likely to marry early.

I love you, but … So there’s scientific excuse after all! The reason men have an urge for one-night stand is testosterone. Even though they may believe they have a huge attraction to a woman one night, when reality and or sobriety hits, the feelings disappear as quickly as they arrived. Men are different because the centres for emotion and reason are better connected in a woman’s brain. And, because women aren’t out of control on testosterone, they find it easier to evaluate whether a man is potentially the right partner.

Dirty, dirty boys! Despite years of cajoling from the girls and all the cosmetics firms spending hundreds of thousands of Naira to persuade them to use their grooming products, men still spend less than 15 minutes in the bathroom each morning. But, don’t despair! This trend is set to change – a recent Mintel survey found that the under-24 age group are now more likely to spend up to an hour making the effort to look and smell good.

The post Being one step ahead of an opportunist appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Don urges AI solutions for rural healthcare
description:
A Professor of AI and Applications, Prof. Abejide Ade-Ibijola, has urged governments to deploy artificial intelligence-powered solutions to improve agricultural productivity and healthcare delivery in rural communities, particularly through mobile applications and indigenous language technology.
Ade
content:
A Professor of AI and Applications, Prof. Abejide Ade-Ibijola, has urged governments to deploy artificial intelligence-powered solutions to improve agricultural productivity and healthcare delivery in rural communities, particularly through mobile applications and indigenous language technology.

Ade-Ibijola, made the call on Saturday during an interaction with journalists in Ado Ekiti, Ekiti State, where he advocated technology-driven interventions tailored to the needs of local populations.

He said AI should not be restricted to urban centres and educated technology enthusiasts but extended to rural communities where access to modern infrastructure and professional services remained limited.

According to him, AI applications could help farmers predict weather conditions, improve agricultural yields and access relevant farming information, while providing rural residents with easier access to basic healthcare guidance.

He said, “AI can help farmers predict weather conditions, improve agricultural yields and access relevant farming information and as well provide rural residents with easier access to basic healthcare guidance through mobile technology”.

The scholar, who said he had worked with governments and institutions across Africa and other parts of the world on developing AI-driven development frameworks, expressed willingness to collaborate with the Ekiti State Government to deploy such solutions.

He said he was particularly interested in contributing to the development of Ekiti, his home state, and grooming young people who could sustain technology-driven initiatives beyond the tenure of any administration.

Ade-Ibijola said the state’s peculiar demographic and geographical realities required an inclusive approach to AI adoption, adding that residents did not necessarily need formal technology education to benefit from its applications.

He said, “We don’t have to educate residents necessarily about technology. We just have to develop technology that helps them.

“Government can leverage the widespread availability of mobile phones in rural communities to introduce simple AI-powered applications that address everyday challenges. Such applications can provide farmers with information on weather patterns, support agricultural decision-making and help improve productivity, while similar tools could assist residents in accessing healthcare information”.

On making AI accessible to rural populations, the professor identified language as a major consideration, advocating the development of machine learning and language models capable of communicating in Nigerian languages and dialects.

He said, “We can develop machine learning models, language models, and they can speak in Yoruba, they can speak in Ekiti. Rural residents will find it easier to interact with technology if they can communicate with AI applications in their indigenous languages rather than being compelled to use English.”

He proposed collecting and recording thousands of audio samples from native speakers of the Ekiti dialect, which could be transcribed and used to train artificial intelligence models.

According to him, the initiative would enable residents to make enquiries, seek information and obtain responses through simple voice interactions on their mobile phones.

Ade-Ibijola also called for stronger collaboration between governments, private-sector operators, technology companies and other stakeholders to develop and deploy AI solutions capable of addressing the state’s development challenges.

He urged the state government to expose young technology entrepreneurs to international opportunities and established technology companies, including Microsoft and Huawei.

He said, “The state must create an environment where young people can develop technology products, establish startup companies, generate employment and attract investment”.
