title: Nigeria can’t achieve 70% local drug production by 2030 – Pharmacists
description:
Without enabling policies and structural conditions that make local drug manufacturing competitive and sustainable, pharmacists and pharmaceutical manufacturers said Nigeria is unlikely to produce 70 per cent of its essential medicines locally by 2030.
The pharmacists said manufacturers need a stabl
content:
Without enabling policies and structural conditions that make local drug manufacturing competitive and sustainable, pharmacists and pharmaceutical manufacturers said Nigeria is unlikely to produce 70 per cent of its essential medicines locally by 2030.

The pharmacists said manufacturers need a stable business environment, reliable energy supply, and access to affordable raw materials to expand production and compete with imported medicines.

They identified high energy and production costs, limited access to financing, and foreign exchange challenges undermining local pharmaceutical production.

The pharmaceutical stakeholders added that despite Federal Government initiatives to boost domestic production, local drug manufacturers continue to grapple with numerous challenges.

The pharmacists spoke exclusively with PUNCH Healthwise on challenges confronting local drug production as the World Health Organisation stated that Nigeria must produce 70 percent of medicines locally by 2030.

The Emir of Kano, Muhammadu Sanusi, in February 2026  declared that 70 percent of drugs Nigerians are consuming are being imported from other countries.

Sanusi, who was the keynote speaker at a conference organised by the Association of Industrial Pharmacists of Nigeria in Lagos, themed ‘Reimagining Nigeria’s Health Security: Local Production, Economic Sovereignty & Strategic Partnership ’, also said 80 percent of imported drugs come from India.

Speaking on the 2030 timeline, the President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria, Ayuba Tanko, said realities of the pharmaceutical manufacturing environment could make achieving the target impossible.

According to him, the target is desirable, necessary, and achievable as a national ambition, but we must be honest about the realities.

Tanko told PUNCH Healthwise that at the current pace, achieving 70 per cent local production by 2030 would be extremely challenging.

“I have previously made this position clear. Ambition without structural reform risks becoming another policy declaration that is not matched by measurable industrial capacity.

“Nigeria has the market, population, pharmaceutical professionals, entrepreneurial capacity and some established manufacturing companies to build a strong domestic pharmaceutical industry. What we have not adequately addressed are the structural conditions that make manufacturing competitive and sustainable,” he said.

WHO Country Representative in Nigeria, Dr Pavel Ursu, in a keynote address at the Academy’s 2026 Annual General Meeting and Investiture of New Fellows in Lagos, delivered on his behalf by the Coordinator, WHO Lagos State, Dr Akinola Fatiregun, stressed the need for Nigeria to reduce its dependence on imported medicines and build a resilient pharmaceutical sector.

He said, “Nigeria needs to strengthen local pharmaceutical manufacturing, reduce dependence on imported medicines and build a resilient pharmaceutical sector capable of safeguarding national health security. The Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain targets 70 per cent local production of pharmaceuticals by 2030.”

In June 2024, President Bola Tinubu signed an executive order to introduce zero tariffs, excise duties, and value-added tax on imported pharmaceutical products and inputs.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Ali Pate, who disclosed this, noted that the Executive Order also aims to increase local production of healthcare products.

According to him, the order is crucial to the success of the Presidential Initiative to Unlock the Healthcare Value Chain, approved in October 2023 by Tinubu, which aims to increase local manufacturing of pharmaceutical products in Nigeria to at least 70% by 2030.

While PVAC is designed to strengthen coordination across institutions and accelerate value chain transformation, the Executive Order provides direct incentives for local manufacturing of medicines, syringes, rapid diagnostic test kits and pharmaceutical inputs.

Giving reasons to back his position, the PSN president explained that the country remains heavily dependent on imported Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients, excipients, specialised machinery, packaging materials and other critical production inputs.

He added that manufacturers also contend with high energy costs, foreign exchange volatility, expensive financing, inadequate infrastructure and inconsistent policy implementation.

“We must therefore distinguish between manufacturing finished pharmaceutical formulations locally and achieving genuine pharmaceutical self-sufficiency. A country may manufacture tablets, capsules and syrups locally while importing almost all the critical ingredients required to produce them. That is an important level of industrial development, but it does not amount to complete pharmaceutical sovereignty.

“My position is that Nigeria can make substantial progress towards the 70 per cent target, but achieving it within the 2030 timeline requires a fundamental change in how we approach pharmaceutical industrialisation. We must move from policy pronouncements and isolated incentives to a coordinated national industrial strategy,” he said.

On what the country should do differently, he listed access to affordable and long-term financing, deliberate investment in local production of APIs and pharmaceutical raw materials, and reliable electricity and dedicated pharmaceutical manufacturing infrastructure.

Others, he said, include predictable government procurement and guaranteed market access, strengthened regulatory capacity and quality assurance, building a skilled pharmaceutical manufacturing workforce, establishing clear and consistent industrial policies, and the government coordinating the entire industrial ecosystem.

“The Presidential Executive Order for the pharmaceutical and allied sectors and PVAC are important interventions, but their success must be measured by actual investments, production capacity, product availability, and reduced import dependence.

“The government must coordinate the entire industrial ecosystem. The Ministries responsible for Health, Finance, Industry, Trade, Investment, Power, Science and Technology, alongside NAFDAC, PCN, CBN and development finance institutions, must work towards a common national objective.

“India and China did not build their pharmaceutical industries through isolated health-sector interventions. They pursued coordinated industrial policies that linked government, finance, research, infrastructure and private enterprise. Nigeria must adopt a similarly integrated approach,” Tanko said.

Also, the National Chairman of the Association of Community Pharmacists of Nigeria, Ambrose Ezeh, said the 2030 target was not realistic.

“How is it going to be feasible when the energy cost and forex rate remain high? With all these and other bottlenecks, how is it going to be achievable by 2030? Ask the people who made that pronouncement how it will happen,” he said.

Ezeh noted that the government knows what to do if the country was really interested in producing 70 per cent of its essential medicines locally.

“The government knows what to do. The government should support pharmaceutical companies. Right now, most pharmaceutical manufacturers use solar as their source of energy, which is not sustainable. Let’s even fix the basics first.

“The country has the Bank of Industry, and nothing is stopping the government from establishing a Bank of Health that can use soft loans to support pharmaceutical companies, so that they can go into mass production and achieve the target. The leadership of the country knows what to do if they really want to achieve that target by 2030,” he said.

The ACPN chairman added, “The exchange rate is high right now; what is the government doing in that regard for manufacturers?

“What of raw materials? Can we get all the raw materials to produce essential medicines here? Common starch, can we produce it locally? APIs are being imported at a high cost. If these things are looked into by the government and we begin to produce those raw materials locally, then it can be achievable.”

Meanwhile, the Executive Secretary and Chief Executive Officer of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Group of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, Frank Muonemeh, said the country’s pharmaceutical sector has recorded gains in the last five years.

“Anyway, the truth is that we have made a lot of progress in the last five years. We are transitioning, and we are making a lot of investments. We are improving our facilities, and we are closing the gap in access to medicines like no other before,” he said.

While commending President Bola Tinubu’s administration for the executive order and PVAC introduced to stimulate local production, he said implementing other favourable policies would help boost local production capacity.

“If we continue on this trajectory, achieving that goal will be a walkover. Today, we can probably say we are taking over 50 per cent of the essential medicines used in Nigeria. 50 per cent of essential medicines in Nigeria are now manufactured locally. It’s not from me; NAFDAC quoted that. It’s NAFDAC data and not mine.

With the right policies, he said the country can achieve the target by 2030.

“So, with the right policy and enabling environment, every other thing will fall into place. And about your question of whether we are going to achieve 70 per cent local manufacturing of essential medicines by 2030, it is a target that is achievable if we continue on this trajectory.

“The government should continue with its right policies, intensify incentives, and come up with more robust policies that will uptake what we manufacture locally,” he said.

Muonemeh urged the FG to optimise health insurance coverage, ensure access to finance at lower rates, and close the gap in infrastructural deficits.

“Everything falls under policy, and after policy, the next thing is access to finance. You cannot run any business with the kind of interest rates we are having.

“Also, about 40 per cent of our manufacturing cost is spent on energy costs, and when you compare with other countries in Asia, they don’t spend up to 10 per cent,” the PMG-MAN executive secretary said.

The post Nigeria can’t achieve 70% local drug production by 2030 – Pharmacists appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: CAF raises funding for member associations to $700,000 – Motsepe
description:
The Confederation of African Football has increased its financial support to member associations from $200,000 to $700,000, its President, Patrice Motsepe, has said.
Motsepe disclosed this on Saturday during a press conference after the 48th Ordinary General Assembly of CAF in Abuja.
He said the inc
content:
The Confederation of African Football has increased its financial support to member associations from $200,000 to $700,000, its President, Patrice Motsepe, has said.

Motsepe disclosed this on Saturday during a press conference after the 48th Ordinary General Assembly of CAF in Abuja.

He said the increase was part of efforts to strengthen the financial capacity of the 54 member associations and promote the development of football across the continent.

According to him, the governing body had initially set a target of providing $1m to each member association but was currently paying $700,000.

“Our million-dollar objective is paying very well. We’ve paid $700,000 without the money that was going to come from our commission,” he said.

Motsepe explained that the initial target of $1m was largely dependent on additional contributions from commercial partners.

“The $1m was mainly based on the commercial partners coming on board. We are now paying $700,000 from $200,000,” he added.

The CAF president also disclosed that the organisation had committed substantial resources to competitions, prize money and other football development programmes.

He said CAF had spent about $400m on its competitions and prize money.

Motsepe said the organisation’s financial support programmes were aimed at making African football more sustainable and reducing the dependence of member associations on external funding.

He added that increasing resources available to national football associations remained a priority for his administration.

“We need to increase the resources, financial resources, and the money that our member associations get, and the money from FIFA,” he said.

The CAF president said his administration was working towards leaving African football in a stronger financial position before the end of his tenure.

title: Abiola Dosunmu, Mo Abudu, others celebrate King Charles at 78
description:
Diplomats, captains of industry and prominent Nigerians gathered in Lagos to celebrate the 78th birthday of the British monarch, King Charles III, and the longstanding relationship between the United Kingdom and Nigeria.
The celebration, held at the residence of the British Deputy High Commissioner
content:
Diplomats, captains of industry and prominent Nigerians gathered in Lagos to celebrate the 78th birthday of the British monarch, King Charles III, and the longstanding relationship between the United Kingdom and Nigeria.

The celebration, held at the residence of the British Deputy High Commissioner in Ikoyi, Lagos, was hosted by the British High Commissioner to Nigeria, Pete Vowles, and the Deputy High Commissioner, Jonny Baxter.

Among the dignitaries at the event were the Yeye Oodua, Erelu Dr Abiola Dosunmu; Senior Pastor of House on the Rock, Pastor Paul Adefarasin; Lagos State Secretary to the State Government, Bimbola Salu-Hundeyin; and founder and Chief Executive Officer of EbonyLife Group, Mo Abudu.

Others included the founder and president of the Wellbeing Foundation Africa, Toyin Saraki, as well as members of the diplomatic community, business leaders and other distinguished guests.

The evening also featured musical performances by the Shuga Life Band, while cocktails and wines added to the festivities.

The gathering provided an opportunity to celebrate the longstanding friendship between the UK and Nigeria, as well as their shared interests and partnerships across various sectors.

title: State Police: Bravo to Tinubu, but…, by Tonnie Iredia
description: One of the most difficult ventures in Nigeria is the amendment of the Constitution of the Federal Republic. The major reason for this is the high threshold set by the constitution in its Section 9 which governs the subject. According to the section, a move to alter a constitutional provision must be
content:
One of the most difficult ventures in Nigeria is the amendment of the Constitution of the Federal Republic. The major reason for this is the high threshold set by the constitution in its Section 9 which governs the subject. According to the section, a move to alter a constitutional provision must be supported by at least a two-thirds majority of all members of both Houses of the National Assembly in addition to resolutions approving the alterations by at least 24 of the 36 State Houses of Assembly. A more difficult requirement is set for state creation/boundaries, local government areas or even the amendment procedure itself. In the latter case, a four-fifths majority of federal legislators plus approval from at least 24 State Houses of Assembly is required. But for this threshold, so many new states and local government areas would have for long been created following the unending agitations for such requests.

Consequently, several Bills were stalled in the past because of the said constitutional hurdles as well as a number of other factors which include legislative committee bottlenecks, intense political pushback and withheld presidential assent. One of the affected bills was the Social-Media and Online Speech Bills aimed at curbing online falsehood, hate speech, or regulating bloggers and social media platforms. Fierce opposition from civil society, media groups, and other articulate Nigerians had argued that the proposed bills and their subsequent versions could threaten free expression and press freedom. The Electoral Act Amendments especially on electronic transmission of results were similarly controversial attracting public protests and intermittent street demonstrations.

Against this backdrop, media reports a few days ago that all the 36 State Houses of Assembly had approved the state police bill must have come to many as an unprecedented achievement by the ruling party and its government. Indeed, nothing else has ever produced what many would call an inexplicable consensus on a volatile divisible subject. The passing of the bill was swift beginning with the Senate which acted on it on June 24, 2026, followed by the House of Representatives which approved it a month later. In less than 4 months, all the 36 state assemblies had approved the bill according to the Clerk to the National Assembly Kamoru Ogunlana thereby exceeding the two-thirds constitutional requirement of at least 24 states.

Exactly two days later, Femi Gbajabiamila, the Chief of Staff to the President announced that President Tinubu had received the bill for review with the Attorney-General of the Federation ahead of a formal signing ceremony. On this topic, even the most stringent political opponents of the President have no option than to accept his exceptional mobilization capacity. But then, the way all the relevant institutions and groups have either been lured, persuaded or cowed to follow a common line brings up a fresh fear. One of the reasons this column originally supported the state police issue was the expectation that it would help balance power in the nation. We had hoped that it would reduce the concept of the ‘federal might’ by which the Abuja politicians often overwhelmed state authorities that belonged to different political platforms.

It probably never occurred to some Nigerians that there could be a case where all politicians in search of a part of the national cake would generate a ‘consensus ad idem.’ Now that the state police bill has pointed to a direction where the presidency, state governors and every other political grouping could have a common mind, how will balancing be done? It would be recalled that in the past, state governors could not completely crush their political opponents; real or imagined, because the Commissioners of Police in their states declined to obey or were directed to act otherwise making it possible for such opponents to taste some relief. In the new scheme of things who would rescue the oppressed? Although these questions may provoke some fear, they do not evaporate the merits of a state police, they only remind us that there is much to be done before the state police service is operationalized.

The much that is to be done that we are harping upon is not the drafting of copious provisions to guide operatives; rather it is more about monitoring leadership. Let us not make the same mistake upon which our constitution was built. For example, although the drafters of our constitution belatedly realized that it is better to ask our media to make government accountable to the people than to leave everything to dispute resolution, Nigeria has no law that sufficiently empowers the media to do the prescribed job. Unlike other countries which appreciate the efficacy of empowering their media, Nigeria expects its media to which it gave an enormous task to derive its power from the general freedom of everyone who got no task. Consequently, our political office holders designed a strategy of doing whatever they wished by ensuring that law enforcement agencies are used to detain any media professional who tries to hold them accountable.

No one can stop a governor from using the power bestowed on him by the constitution to set up a police service commission to instead establish a kangaroo body and adorn it with the word ‘independent.’ Can we not perceive how our supposedly independent state electoral commissions count votes of local government elections from bedrooms of state governors? To stop a ruling party from taking over all societal institutions, each of the major political parties can be mandated to nominate one member of the governing council of each institution. In that way it becomes difficult for a governor to use state police against opposition politicians. But if that would politicize our state organs, a second option will be to let nominees to such institutions be made by reputable associations such as the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) or our Bar or Medical associations as well as apex Labour unions.

History should however teach us to exclude unions whose executives are forever visiting state governors to honour them with awards or to seek sponsorship of their annual professional meetings. In setting up a police service commission therefore, it would be wise to avoid a repeat of the type of traps which are usually hidden in our laws or arrangements under the guise of stating rules or laws that would further enhance proper running of institutions. Here, I like to recall a scenario which occurred in 1993 when an interim national government was set up to replace the government of President Ibrahim Babangida who was stepping aside. The enabling law of the regime was a provision that where the government is unwilling or unable to continue, the most senior minister shall take over. This gave room for General Sani Abacha to replace Chief Shonekan.

First, why did anyone imagine that Shonekan would not wish to continue? Second, what did the provision mean by the most senior minister? What eyewitnesses like this writer understood was that it was because some soldiers wanted a continuation of military rule that the famous June 12, 1993 elections internationally recognized as Nigeria’s best was annulled. If we relate this experience to the arrangements for state police, this is probably when to seriously ponder over a proposal that says ‘the federalpolice can temporarily intervene in a state during serious breakdowns of public order or rights violations with written presidential authorization and judicial review.’ The proposal does not only encourage people to organize breakdowns that the federal police will intervene in, it also makes the totally erroneous point that the federal police is itself impeccable!

A state police service in an emerging nation like Nigeria will have its challenges but because Nigeria runs the federal system of government, state institutions must be allowed to grow and develop to maturity. No room should be given to federal authorities to intervene in state institutions only because the central government appears stronger than the subnational. No matter the shortcomings of state institutions, local officers are better placed to act quickly on incidents and emergencies before they escalate. They also better understand community languages, customs, and terrain, that ably aid intelligence gathering and rural coverage. In addition, state officials are better than federal officials in coordinating security more directly with local residents and traditional institutions.

It is indeed an overstatement to argue that if state officials are allowed to do their own functions, the nation will enjoy a healthier growth. It would mean a reduction in federal workload which can ease pressure on federal agencies to have enough room to focus on rising federal crimes and interstate offences. There is therefore no better time than now to thank the current federal government for introducing state policing to Nigeria. Nothing also better underscores the reform than a deliberate arrangement that allows everyone to take control of issues within its jurisdiction.

The post State Police: Bravo to Tinubu, but…, by Tonnie Iredia appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Experts demand stronger immunisation as diphtheria kills 406
description:
As diphtheria claimed 406 lives in seven months, seasoned epidemiologists have called for the introduction of booster doses of diphtheria vaccines and expanded immunisation campaigns for children aged one to 14 years to curb the outbreak of the disease in Nigeria.
The experts said Nigeria needed to
content:
As diphtheria claimed 406 lives in seven months, seasoned epidemiologists have called for the introduction of booster doses of diphtheria vaccines and expanded immunisation campaigns for children aged one to 14 years to curb the outbreak of the disease in Nigeria.

The experts said Nigeria needed to strengthen routine immunisation, improve vaccine coverage and ensure adequate supplies of diphtheria antitoxin to prevent more infections and deaths.

They made the recommendations in separate interviews with PUNCH Healthwise while reacting to fatalities so far from diphtheria complications in 2026.

Reports show that there have been increased diphtheria cases over the past three to four years, with major surges recorded in 2024 and 2025.

More than 1,260 people have died from diphtheria in Nigeria since the disease outbreak started in late 2022, while suspected infections have surpassed 41,000, with the country recording more than 24,000 confirmed cases, according to Médecins Sans Frontières.

The MSF, known as Doctors Without Borders, also disclosed that between January and August 9, 2026, Nigeria recorded 12,977 suspected infections, 10,476 confirmed cases and 406 deaths.

Speaking with PUNCH Healthwise, the public health experts identified incomplete childhood immunisation, vaccine hesitancy, misinformation, poor access to healthcare and delayed diagnosis as factors contributing to the sustained resurgence of the vaccine-preventable disease.

The epidemiologists urged the government to extend vaccination campaigns beyond children under five, noting that a significant proportion of confirmed diphtheria cases occurred among children aged between two and 14 years.

A Public Health Physician and Epidemiologist at the Lagos University Teaching Hospital, Idia-Araba, Mushin, Prof Adebayo Onajole, said the availability of vaccines had not translated into adequate protection because many children were still missing routine immunisation.

Onajole said vaccination remained important in reducing the severity of the infection, adding that poor immunisation coverage, vaccine stock-outs and misinformation are some of the factors responsible for the continued spread of the disease.

“Why are we having an increase in diphtheria confirmed cases and deaths is straightforward. One, we have a failure of immunisation. That is, immunisation is not getting to the population, most especially children under five. Because diphtheria is more common among children under five,” he said.

The don urged the government at all levels to strengthen public awareness campaigns and ensure that healthcare workers reached communities that were difficult to access, particularly rural settlements and internally displaced persons’ camps.

Onajole also stressed the importance of maintaining the cold chain system to preserve vaccine potency.

“Health facilities also need to take care of the storage of their vaccines to increase their potency. Nowadays, electricity is not readily available and if that persists, storage is going to be a problem, and that means that the cold chain system might be hampered or affected.

“The government also needs to encourage healthcare providers to search for or go to difficult-to-reach terrains and immunise these populations that may need this support. Most of these populations are in rural areas and among the internally displaced population,” he said.

Furthermore, Onajole called for increased government funding and greater contributions from individuals and organisations to support immunisation and other preventive healthcare interventions.

“The government and the general population both need to support immunisation activities. When I say government and the general population, the government will support through funding. The general population may also need to fund indirectly.

“Rather than doing all these parties or owanbes, the people should support health interventions too, like Rotary has been doing with immunisation and supporting health activities; this is what I will call the hidden resources in health.

“Rather than spend so much money on activities that may not improve or protect life, people who can afford to donate or support these activities that can protect life or prolong life should channel funds into it,”

Similarly, a Consultant Epidemiologist and Professor of Community Medicine, Prof. Kabir Durowade, identified low routine immunisation coverage and incomplete vaccination as major drivers of diphtheria transmission in the country.

He said many children received the first dose of the pentavalent vaccine but failed to complete the recommended three-dose schedule.

The epidemiologist said available data indicated that only about half of children aged between one and two years were fully immunised against diphtheria, a situation he described as a major factor driving the outbreak.

He said, “People start the vaccine, take the first dose, and don’t complete all the doses. So, we have what is called dropouts. We have high dropouts. That is one major issue driving what we are beginning to see in Nigeria.”

He further identified inadequate supplies of diphtheria antitoxin as another major challenge, explaining that the medication was required to neutralise the toxin produced by the bacteria in patients with severe infections.

“We don’t have enough stockpiles of diphtheria antitoxin. Our stocks are very low, but it’s not peculiar to Nigeria alone. There are global shortages across the world,” he said.

On what should be done differently to curb outbreaks, he recommended increasing routine immunisation coverage to above 90 per cent to achieve herd immunity and reduce transmission within communities.

“We need to ensure that we improve our vaccination coverage to substantially above 90 per cent. When we do that, we’re going to have what is called herd immunity.

“Herd immunity means immunity of the entire community. When people are immunised, and an infection comes, the community can withstand the infection. It won’t spread because people are immunised against it. So, when we reach that level and scale up our coverage, we’re also going to drive up herd immunity in our locality,” the don said

Durowade, who is also the Dean of the Faculty of Clinical Sciences at the Federal University, Oye-Ekiti, also called for the procurement and strategic positioning of diphtheria antitoxin stockpiles to ensure that patients with severe infections could receive prompt treatment.

The epidemiologist stressed that mass vaccination campaigns should cover children between one and 14 years.

He said, “Now, we shouldn’t just limit mass campaigns to children under five because this outbreak affects children between one and 14 years old. We must extend the mass campaign to cover this age group, between one and 14, not just children under five.”

Furthermore, the don advocated the introduction of booster doses at school entry and adolescence to strengthen immunity beyond the three routine infant doses.

He said, “Again, I must add that there should also be booster doses. Apart from the three doses we give our infants, there should be a booster dose somewhere, maybe at school entry and adolescence stage, that can strengthen children’s immunity.”

Durowade also called for the training of primary healthcare workers to recognise the clinical signs of diphtheria, including the formation of membranes in the throat and enlarged lymph nodes.

He urged healthcare workers to recognise the condition and refer suspected cases to appropriately equipped hospitals without delay.

Durowade warned that delayed presentation or referral could allow the bacterial toxin to damage vital organs, including the heart, kidneys and nervous system.

The don added that public awareness campaigns should be intensified to address vaccine misinformation and hesitancy, with community and religious leaders enlisted to encourage acceptance of immunisation.

The World Health Organisation states that diphtheria vaccines are highly effective but recommends a three-dose primary series followed by three booster doses in childhood and adolescence to produce and sustain long-term immunity.

WHO also notes that booster doses strengthen and extend protection when immunity from the primary series weakens over time.

The post Experts demand stronger immunisation as diphtheria kills 406 appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Between boos, stones and seeking forgiveness
description:
Are we to venerate President Bola Tinubu as beneficent and merciful for freeing 78 people who booed and stoned his convoy at the Area 1 mosque on the Friday before last?
The young men struck on November 13, as the President’s motorcade left Juma’at prayers at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque in Gark
content:
Are we to venerate President Bola Tinubu as beneficent and merciful for freeing 78 people who booed and stoned his convoy at the Area 1 mosque on the Friday before last?

The young men struck on November 13, as the President’s motorcade left Juma’at prayers at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque in Garki. Police said several vehicles were damaged, some security personnel were injured, and 78 people were arrested.

By Monday, the President reportedly directed that the suspects be warned and released. Clemency is nobler than vengeance. But this could also be the fulfilment of a prophecy the President pronounced upon himself.

On April 16, while hosting his Renewed Hope Ambassadors at the Villa, Tinubu declared, “I took over from myself. The late Buhari is me.” If words mean anything, then anyone claiming to be Buhari, or an extension of him, should expect some of Buhari’s portion, including being stoned by the people. And 211 days later, that declaration materialised.

Were Buhari here, he might have drawn a shaken Tinubu under his comforting arm and whispered, “If they stoned me, they will stone you too. In this presidency, you shall have many tribulations…Nigerians are not easy to lead.” He has the experience to prove it.

On January 30, 2023, youths in Kano pelted Buhari’s convoy as he commissioned eight projects amid anger over fuel scarcity and the controversial new naira policy that left many Nigerians stranded. They set fires along the road and even threw pebbles at his helicopter as it hovered over them.

Buhari arrived at the Aminu Kano International Airport in the morning and was then flown by helicopter to the palace of the Emir of Kano, Aminu Bayero.

However, despite the heavy security presence mounted on the routes leading to Ahmadu Bello Way, where the President was to launch a Galaxy Backbone project, videos circulated online showed angry youths holding stones and sticks of various sizes, attacking his convoy and the helicopter believed to be conveying the President as it hovered above them.

That episode came only days after a similar outburst in his home state of Katsina, where youths stoned Buhari’s officials at the Kofar Kaura Underpass. They were chanting “Ba ma yi,” which literally means “We’re not doing,” and “Ba ma so,” meaning “We don’t want,” similar chants at the mosque that Friday before hailstones fell on Tinubu’s convoy.

Before Buhari, youths angry at the Boko Haram insurgency had stoned Goodluck Jonathan’s campaign convoy in 2015. Every president, it seems, gets his stones in one shape, form or velocity.

In August 2024, #EndBadGovernance protesters even lit a bonfire outside Buhari’s Daura home with the same chant, more than a year after he left office. Perhaps they too believed Buhari is Tinubu.

So that Friday, youths behind barriers shouted “Ba ma yi” and “Tinubu must go,” as they tore down APC posters across parts of Abuja. The President’s Senior Special Assistant on Digital/New Media Engagement, O’tega Ogra, denied that the President’s convoy was attacked, and dismissed the viral clips as misleading opposition propaganda involving “alleged paid thugs.” The aide posted short counter-footage of his principal waving at cheering worshippers from his vehicle. But the police later announced that stones actually flew and 78 arrests were made.

A day later in Jos, a section of the crowd at the APC North-Central rally booed the President’s convoy with the same chant. Video footage showed residents who lined the streets, pelting the president’s convoy with stones, shouting profanities and chanting, “Ba ma so.”

Other videos showed angry residents destroying billboards and campaign posters bearing Tinubu’s images. Residents were also filmed setting APC caps and brooms ablaze, with one woman saying she came only because she was paid N2,500. They asked for food items, not campaign caps and brooms, she said.

There at the Zaria Road Stadium, the President asked for forgiveness. Recalling his last visit, he admitted that he “was limited to the airport,” adding, “Forgive me if you didn’t see me in the hinterland.” Tinubu then promised to rebuild the ravaged communities and bring the displaced home. He also said the surveillance cameras promised to the state in April after the Palm Sunday killings had arrived in the country.

On April 2, days after gunmen killed at least 28 people in Angwan Rukuba on Palm Sunday, the President met bereaved families at the Yakubu Gowon Airport in Heipang, about a 40-minute drive from Jos. “You have no light at the airport, and I have to fly back within the next 10 minutes,” he had told them.

It was a neutral comment. And anyone could have said that to the people of Plateau. A local government chairman or a commissioner. But not a President. Understandably, his comments generated so much anger that some people rode with that anger to boo him in Jos.

You see, other presidents have faced worse than stones thrown at their convoys. President Emmanuel Macron, Tinubu’s close friend, has been slapped before and once had an egg plastered on his face.

In 2014, protesters pelted Czech President Miloš Zeman with eggs, tomatoes, and sandwiches. A year later, a woman threw a mango at former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro that struck him in the head. The mango had a message written on it asking for housing assistance, which Maduro later granted.

Now, nothing justifies throwing stones or any objects at anyone, let alone a president. And I will never advocate violence of any sort against the person of the President. What we cannot ignore is this: when people don’t feel heard or considered, they may resort to extreme measures to get your attention.

Think mangoes to the head with a message written on them. The President’s mercy to the youths at the Garki mosque is commendable. Booing the President is a manageable way to communicate disapproval. But throwing stones or any objects is where we must draw the line. Mr President, I am sure you never saw this part coming when you danced for this job. It is part of the job nonetheless. I warned about this day over two years ago.

In my column, ‘Mr President, while the pigeons are still flying,’ written after the 2024 Armed Forces Remembrance Day, I wrote about the pigeon release ritual: “While the pigeons are still flying for him, the President must take up the challenge to ensure that the nation follows their upward path, soaring towards real prosperity for the everyday Nigerian, [not merely a swelling foreign reserve and other distant statistics].

If he rests on the symbolic gesture of the birds, assuming their flight represents the current state of Nigeria, he is missing the message. Their flight is a call to action, not a sign that all is well. The potential for progress exists, but it is far from realised. There are many grounds to cover. He must cover some of those grounds before his next encounter with the pigeons.”

The post Between boos, stones and seeking forgiveness appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Lagos Theatre Festival attracts over 20,000 attendees
description:
The third edition of the Lagos International Theatre Festival attracted over 20,000 attendees, featuring more than 25 productions and international performances from four countries.
The seven-day festival, held from November 9 to 15, brought together Nigerian and international theatre practitioners,
content:
The third edition of the Lagos International Theatre Festival attracted over 20,000 attendees, featuring more than 25 productions and international performances from four countries.

The seven-day festival, held from November 9 to 15, brought together Nigerian and international theatre practitioners, creatives, diplomats and cultural enthusiasts, further strengthening Lagos’ position as a growing destination for theatre and the performing arts.

The festival opened with Theatre Meets Food at Kaly Restaurant, featuring celebrity chef Hilda Baci in a fusion of culinary artistry and live performance.

Speaking on the success of the festival, its Founder and Creative Producer, Bolanle Austen-Peters, said the vision was to establish a platform that would give African stories greater international recognition.

“Our ambition has always been to create more than a theatre festival. We want to build a platform that places Lagos firmly on the global cultural map, gives African stories the international visibility they deserve and creates meaningful opportunities for our artists,” she said.

Austen-Peters added that the turnout and international participation affirmed the festival’s vision, noting, “Theatre is not just entertainment; it is an instrument of cultural identity, economic opportunity and global influence.”

The festival featured performances from Kenya, Brazil, Norway and Canada, alongside diplomatic engagements, cultural exchanges and networking opportunities aimed at promoting collaboration within the global creative industry.

Other activities included diplomatic and cultural engagements hosted by the United States Consul General in Lagos and the British Embassy. The British Council also organised a networking reception for festival directors and participating production companies.

A major highlight was the Opening Night Gala, held on November 13 at Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, which attracted over 1,000 guests.

Among those in attendance were Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu; the Chargé d’Affaires of the US Mission in Nigeria; the US Consul General, Brandon Hudspeth; the British Deputy High Commissioner; and representatives of the Brazilian, South African and South Korean diplomatic missions.

Sanwo-Olu received an award in recognition of his support for the arts, while veteran theatre practitioner, Ben Tomoloju, was honoured with a Lifetime Achievement and Legacy Award for his contributions to the development of the arts in Nigeria.

The main performance programme took place from November 14 to 15 across the MUSON Centre, Ouida and KAP Hub, featuring more than 25 productions by established and emerging Nigerian creatives, as well as international performers.

The Festival Director, Vanessa Jev, described the achievement as a product of artistic vision, partnerships and collective commitment.

“We are proud to have created a platform where Nigerian and international artists could share their work, connect with new audiences and build lasting relationships,” she said.

Jev added that the success would provide a stronger foundation for expanding the festival’s reach and creating more opportunities for the creative community.

The festival was supported by sponsors and partners, including Afreximbank, Waltersmith, Pillar Oil, MTN, Wema Bank, the United States Consulate, British Council and Channels Television, among others.

The post Lagos Theatre Festival attracts over 20,000 attendees appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Cultism: A growing threat to lives
description:
CULTISM has become a deadly menace to public safety in Nigeria. Its alarming resurgence, geographical spread and increasingly violent character are compounding the country’s security crisis.
From university campuses to neighbourhoods, markets and rural communities, murderous gangs are holding innoce
content:
CULTISM has become a deadly menace to public safety in Nigeria. Its alarming resurgence, geographical spread and increasingly violent character are compounding the country’s security crisis.

From university campuses to neighbourhoods, markets and rural communities, murderous gangs are holding innocent citizens hostage. Government at all levels must stop treating this menace as youthful delinquency and confront it for what it has become: a serious threat to lives and social stability.

What began decades ago as campus-based confraternities, ostensibly established to promote intellectual development, solidarity and resistance against oppression, has degenerated into criminal networks responsible for killings, intimidation, extortion and other violent crimes. The transformation is as tragic as it is dangerous.

The growing spread of these groups beyond university campuses into secondary schools, neighbourhoods and rural communities demands urgent and coordinated intervention.

Recent incidents across the country paint a disturbing picture of the scale of the problem. Last Saturday, two people were killed and several others injured during a clash between suspected rival cult groups at a masquerade procession in the Okepopo area of Lagos Island.

The violence, reportedly triggered by an attack on a rival member, escalated into a reprisal that claimed another life and sent residents and business owners fleeing for safety.

Last Friday, a yet-to-be-identified barber was hacked to death by suspected cultists, who reportedly severed his manhood, around White House Bus Stop, Okokomaiko, Lagos.

 In Ogbomoso, Oyo State, police arrested 10 suspects following a violent clash between rival cult factions reportedly fighting over the sharing of money gifts. The recovery of large quantities of illicit drugs during the operation further underscores the disturbing links between cultism, substance abuse and other criminal activities.

Similarly, the killing of a young man in the Issele-Asagba area of Delta State, captured in a disturbing viral video, prompted police investigations and arrests.

On November 13, the Rivers State Police Command arrested two suspected cultists over the murder of a commercial motorcycle rider, Sani Musa, whose body was recovered from a forest in Ahoada West Local Government Area.

Osun and Imo states have also witnessed deadly confrontations involving suspected cult groups.

In Ogun State, cult-related activities remain entrenched in major towns, including Abeokuta, Ijebu-Ode, Ota and Sagamu. The police are, however, intensifying efforts against the notorious 7/7 cult gang, which has terrorised schoolchildren and other residents for years.

These are not isolated criminal disturbances. They point to a widening pattern of organised violence that threatens public safety, disrupts economic activities and undermines the stability of communities.

The statistics are equally alarming. The Nigeria Police Force’s performance report for September and October 2026 documented 73 cultism clashes nationwide within eight weeks. The Eons Intelligence Security Index also recorded 59 cult-related incidents in October, a 52 per cent increase over the previous month.

The death toll is grimmer still. SBM Intelligence tracked 1,686 deaths in 909 incidents between January 2020 and March 2025. Citing Nigeria Watch, the European Union Agency for Asylum reported 371 cult-related deaths in 2023 and 328 in 2024. Naija Confra, meanwhile, reported 581 fatalities from cult wars in 2024.

Behind these figures are hundreds of lives cut short, families shattered, and communities traumatised.

Worse, innocent citizens increasingly pay the price for the bloody rivalries of criminal gangs.

Traders, commuters, artisans, students and other ordinary residents face the danger of stray bullets, machete attacks and sudden outbreaks of violence. Markets and residential streets that should be safe spaces for economic and social activities have become potential battlegrounds.

It is particularly disturbing that cultural and religious gatherings, which should promote communal harmony, are increasingly being exploited by criminal elements to settle scores. When masquerade processions and other public events become theatres of bloodshed, the threat has clearly gone beyond the control of individual communities.

The roots of this menace must also be confronted. Youth unemployment, poverty, peer pressure, weak parental supervision and substance abuse have created fertile ground for recruitment.

Equally culpable is the apparent inability of security institutions to dismantle entrenched cult networks and bring their financiers and masterminds to justice.

Perhaps most troubling is the role of politicians who recruit, finance or deploy violent groups for electoral intimidation and other partisan interests.

Such relationships provide criminal elements with money, weapons and, in some instances, protection from prosecution.

It is sheer hypocrisy for political actors to publicly condemn cultism while privately cultivating the very networks that sustain it. Those who arm and sponsor these gangs must be regarded as accomplices in the violence they unleash.

The education sector must confront its failure to prevent the spread of cultism within its institutions. Universities and secondary schools must not become recruitment grounds for violent confraternities.

School authorities should strengthen security arrangements, establish functional counselling services and work closely with parents and law enforcement agencies to identify vulnerable students before they are drawn into criminal networks.

Student unionism, sports and legitimate extracurricular activities should be encouraged as alternative avenues for young people to develop leadership skills, build friendships and find a sense of belonging without resorting to violent associations.

Parents and guardians also have a critical responsibility. They must pay closer attention to their children’s associations, behavioural changes and unexplained sources of income.

Traditional rulers, community leaders and faith-based organisations should intensify efforts to discourage young people from embracing violence as a route to social recognition, protection or financial reward.

But moral appeals and public condemnations alone will not defeat organised criminality. The police and other security agencies must move beyond the familiar pattern of reacting to killings with arrests after the damage has been done.

Intelligence gathering must be strengthened to identify and dismantle cult networks, including their leaders, financiers, weapons suppliers and recruitment channels.

Arresting a handful of suspected members after every bloody confrontation, while the masterminds and sponsors remain untouched, is little more than a cosmetic response. It allows the networks to survive, regroup and strike again.

The real test of effective policing is not the number of suspects paraded before the cameras but the ability to dismantle these organisations and prevent further killings.

The prosecution of arrested suspects must also be pursued diligently. It is unacceptable for individuals apprehended with firearms and other dangerous weapons to return to their communities and continue terrorising residents.

State governments must ensure that anti-cultism laws are effectively enforced, while the judiciary should expedite the prosecution of cases involving violent crimes without compromising due process.

Governments must, at the same time, address the socioeconomic conditions that make vulnerable young people susceptible to recruitment. Job creation, vocational training, access to quality education and credible youth empowerment programmes are indispensable to a sustainable response.

However, such interventions must be properly targeted and implemented, rather than reduced to political slogans and poorly monitored spending.

With political activities gathering momentum ahead of the 2027 general elections, the danger of politicians mobilising cult groups for electoral violence cannot be ignored.

Security agencies must closely monitor this threat and investigate and prosecute anyone found financing or deploying criminal gangs, irrespective of political affiliation, influence or social standing. No politician should be above the law.

Ultimately, the protection of lives and property is a fundamental responsibility of government. Nigerians should not have to negotiate their safety with criminal gangs or abandon their homes and businesses whenever rival factions decide to settle scores.

Cultism has outgrown the campus indiscipline and youthful excesses with which it was once associated. It is now an organised security threat that demands sustained intelligence-led policing, uncompromising prosecution and political will.

Governments must act decisively before more communities are consumed by the violence. The right to life and the freedom to live, work and conduct legitimate business without fear must not be surrendered to cult gangs.

title: Late businessman’s family unveils scholarship for Osun students
description:
The family of late engineer and businessman, David Abiola, has launched a N10m education trust to sponsor university education for indigent but academically gifted students, particularly those from his state, Osun.
The initiative, unveiled on Friday at the 10th memorial lecture in his honour at the
content:
The family of late engineer and businessman, David Abiola, has launched a N10m education trust to sponsor university education for indigent but academically gifted students, particularly those from his state, Osun.

The initiative, unveiled on Friday at the 10th memorial lecture in his honour at the Metropolitan Club, Lagos, is aimed at extending the educational opportunities that helped shape Abiola’s life to disadvantaged young Nigerians.

Speaking at the event, his daughter, Yetunde Falore, said the trust would initially sponsor two students annually, covering their university education and providing mentorship and other support to help them build successful careers.

She explained that the family decided to establish the initiative because their father benefited from scholarships throughout his academic journey and strongly believed in the power of education.

“Our father was a product of the scholarships that he got, and we felt that it was time for us to pay it forward,” Falore said.

According to her, the family would provide an initial N10m to establish the fund, with the first beneficiaries expected to begin their academic programmes in 2027.

She said the scholarships would cover tuition and other academic expenses throughout the beneficiaries’ university education, subject to satisfactory academic performance and good conduct.

Falore added that beneficiaries would also receive mentorship from professionals and members of the family to improve their career prospects.

The deceased’s first son, Tolu Oni, described his father as a disciplined mentor whose commitment to education, intellectual development and personal integrity shaped his children’s lives.

“My father was a mechanical engineer by profession. He saw the world through the lens of precision, structure, and integrity. But at his true core, he was a master builder of human potential,” he said.

Oni recalled how his father personally supervised his education, ensuring that he developed strong analytical and communication skills while maintaining discipline.

According to him, Abiola’s passion for learning influenced his decision to study abroad, first at the University of Nottingham and later at the University of Oxford.

Oni explained that his father’s commitment to education was rooted in his humble background, noting that scholarships enabled him to attend prestigious institutions, including Niger Grammar School and King’s College, Lagos, before proceeding to the United Kingdom.

He said the deceased later earned an MPhil in Critical Management at Lancaster University, demonstrating that intellectual development should continue regardless of age.

“Age was never a barrier to his intellectual curiosity. At over 60 years old, at an age when most men were comfortably settling into quiet retirement, my father enrolled at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom,” he said.

Oni, a chartered accountant and entrepreneur, said the family hoped to extend the same opportunities to children who might otherwise be unable to pursue higher education because of financial constraints.

He also appealed to friends, corporate organisations and well-meaning Nigerians to support the trust, explaining that additional contributions would enable it to sponsor more students.

In his lecture, titled “The Lamp Kept Lit: Curiosity, Learning and the Making of a Nation,” immediate past Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of the Governing Council of Olabisi Onabanjo University, Professor Oluwatoyin Ashiru, called for a fundamental shift in Nigeria’s education system from certificate acquisition to practical knowledge and problem-solving.

He said the country had continued to produce talented individuals without adequately translating their intellectual abilities into national development.

“Our problem is not a shortage of intelligence; it is our difficulty in turning intelligence into broad national progress,” Ashiru said.

The don argued that educational institutions must prioritise critical thinking, technical competence, innovation and character development rather than concentrate on academic qualifications.

He also raised concerns about the country’s learning crisis, citing UNICEF estimates of millions of out-of-school children and poor mathematics proficiency among primary school pupils.

Ashiru said universities should be assessed not only by the number of graduates they produce but also by the practical problems their research and innovations solve.

“Learning must become capability and capacity. You can hold many certificates and still struggle to solve a practical problem,” he stated.

Ashiru also proposed a legacy-of-learning initiative to promote annual student problem-solving competitions, career counselling and mentorship for young Nigerians in memory of the deceased.

He described Abiola as a lifelong learner whose curiosity, humility, generosity and integrity remained important lessons for the younger generation.

Earlier, Chairman of the occasion and former Managing Director of Daily Times of Nigeria, Dr Yemi Ogunbiyi, described the deceased as a man whose life positively influenced many people.

He said celebrating Abiola’s legacy required examining the different areas of his life, particularly his commitment to education, professional excellence, friendship and service.

Ogunbiyi also acknowledged the support of the deceased’s friends, describing their continued commitment to his family over the past decade as a reflection of the relationships he built during his lifetime.

Also speaking, founder of Let It Shine Academy, Dami Fayide, shared her experience working with disadvantaged children and young people in correctional facilities, highlighting the importance of educational access, vocational training and rehabilitation.

The memorial lecture brought together family members, friends, associates and other dignitaries to celebrate Abiola’s life and renew their commitment to the values he represented.

title: The nationwide mock poll
description: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has fixed November 28, 2026, for a nationwide mock accreditation and voting exercise ahead of the 2027 general elections to test upgrades to its Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) and electronic results transmission.  INEC National Chairman
content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has fixed November 28, 2026, for a nationwide mock accreditation and voting exercise ahead of the 2027 general elections to test upgrades to its Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) and electronic results transmission.  INEC National Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, made the disclosure while speaking on the commission’s preparations for the 2027 general elections during a dialogue at Chatham House in London. The dialogue was held with the theme, “Nigeria’s 2027 Elections: Democratic Trajectory and Regional Stability Beyond the Ballot.”

According to Amupitan, the mock poll would simulate the presidential election and enable the commission assess the effectiveness of its accreditation and electronic transmission systems before the polls. “On the 28th of this month, we will conduct a mock accreditation and voting exercise across all states of the federation to simulate the presidential election and verify that we have gotten both accreditation and electronic result transmission right,” he said.

The INEC boss also disclosed that the commission had introduced technical safeguards to prevent inaccurate polling unit results and figures reflecting over-voting from being uploaded to its Result Viewing Portal. The commission assured Nigerians that only verified results from polling units will be uploaded to its Results Viewing Portal (IReV) ahead of the 2027 polls.

Amupitan added that INEC had identified polling centres as the major source of result-management problems during the 2023 elections and was introducing additional checks to ensure that figures were properly verified before transmission. The commission, he added, had learnt important lessons from the previous election and was determined to strengthen public confidence in the electoral process. To this effect, the electoral agency is introducing a new verification process to ensure polling unit results are verified by party agents before they are uploaded to IReV.

The mock poll arrangement by INEC is a step in the right direction. A mock election is a simulated voting exercise conducted to test electoral systems, educate voters, or demonstrate democratic procedures. Though the exercise does not produce legally binding results, the outcome will provide an opportunity to test-run the technological devices, security preparedness and assessment of the level of voter education. It also offers windows to test the equipment for the main election and assess its functionality.

The mock poll is a commendable move by the INEC chairman and his team. If not compromised, it will assist the commission in making assessments and taking decisions that will enable it deliver a free, fair and credible poll next year.

Instructively, INEC has done an audit of the 2023 elections and identified areas of challenges that need to be improved upon. According to the commission, the core problem of election result management and declaration in Nigeria is not even at the polling unit but at the collation centres. It has therefore devised a technical safeguard which ensures that if a result is not accurate at the polling unit, it will not go to IReV at all. He explained that the commission will upgrade its existing electoral technology rather than introduce an entirely new system, considering the limited time before the 2027 elections.

To guard against malfunctioning of BVAS, which occurred during the 2023 general elections, Amupitan said INEC was constructing climate-controlled storage facilities across the states to protect the devices from extreme temperatures. He said the commission had procured additional BVAS machines and reduced the maximum number of registered voters assigned to each device from 1,250 to 850. Under the revised arrangement, polling units with more than 850 registered voters would be provided with multiple devices.

The strategies announced by INEC are laudable. However, let the commission walk the talk and ensure that the adequate arrangements are put in place. The bane of Nigeria’s electoral system has been the corruption of the exercise which manifests in rigging, ballot-snatching, violence and manipulation of the voting processes. Some electoral agencies had promised delivering credible elections to Nigerians but failed to live up to their pledges.

The 2023 elections also fell below expectations. Before the polls, the then INEC Chairman, Prof. Mahmood Yakubu, had vowed that the days of election manipulation were over. The introduction of BVAS and IReV was particularly advertised as safeguards against rigging. However, at the presidential election of February 25, 2023, in particular, the systems failed to work. Similarly, the March 18, 2023 governorship election was characterised by rigging and violence. The outcome was not up to expectation. The pledge of free poll in 2027 by INEC is therefore timely and commendable. The voters do not expect anything less from Amupitan and his team.

The mock poll is good chance for INEC to assess its readiness for the daunting task ahead. The commission should ensure that the initiative is not sabotaged even from within. There is need for adequate public enlightenment on the nationwide exercise. Let all election logistics, including technology, security and others be tested during the mock poll. The lapses in the mock poll will be rectified before the general election. We urge eligible Nigerian voters to participate in the exercise.        

The post The nationwide mock poll appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Celebrated African writers converge in Lagos for Aké Festival
description:
African writers, including Nnedi Okorafor, Chika Unigwe, Wole Talabi and A. Igoni Barrett, have converged in Lagos for the 14th edition of the Aké Arts and Book Festival, which is exploring the relevance of indigenous African knowledge in an increasingly technology-driven world.
The three-day festiv
content:
African writers, including Nnedi Okorafor, Chika Unigwe, Wole Talabi and A. Igoni Barrett, have converged in Lagos for the 14th edition of the Aké Arts and Book Festival, which is exploring the relevance of indigenous African knowledge in an increasingly technology-driven world.

The three-day festival, which opened on Thursday, November 19, at the Silkwood Hotel, Ikeja GRA, will end on Saturday, November 21, with the theme, ‘Native Intelligence’.

Organised by the Book Buzz Foundation, the 2026 edition features 24 curated events, including book discussions, panel sessions, film screenings and the popular Palmwine and Poetry Night.

Speaking with Sunday Scoop, the festival’s founder and director, Lola Shoneyin, said the theme was inspired by the growing attention given to AI, which she believes has overshadowed the importance of indigenous knowledge.

She said, “There’s so much noise about AI, and to be honest, I didn’t think Native Intelligence was getting the kind of traction and celebration that it deserves.”

Shoneyin explained that the festival would provide a platform to examine different forms of intelligence, particularly knowledge passed down through generations and preserved in African cultures.

“There’s the intelligence that comes from education. Then there’s the intelligence from the people. This allows us to talk about that kind of intelligence.

“As you know, with the Aké Festival, we are not shy. We will have important conversations. We are constantly in pursuit of the unsayable. And that means we want to talk about the matters that are important to us, the things that we want people to take away and remember for months and years after leaving that festival,” she said.

Highlights of the festival include conversations on the future of creative work in the age of artificial intelligence, the relationship between memory and technology, and the global prospects of Nigerian comics and animation.

Ahead of the festival, the United States Consulate General in Lagos hosted a literary salon featuring Okorafor, who discussed her novel, Death of the Author.

Okorafor is also scheduled to discuss the novel at the festival, while Talabi will present The Fist of Memory. Unigwe will engage participants on her book, Grace.

Other writers and creatives featured include Fatima Bala, Oyin Olugbile, Bisi Adjapon, Suyi Davies Okungbowa, Nana Darkoa Sekyiamah, Wana Udobang and Dami Ajayi.

Shoneyin also reiterated her commitment to strengthening African publishing and literary institutions, stressing that writers on the continent should not depend on Western validation to establish their worth.

She commended the Lagos State Government for increasing its support for literary activities, particularly through an initiative offering N20,000 book grants and festival access to 100 residents below the age of 25.

The state government, through the Office of the Special Adviser on Sustainable Development Goals and the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture, partnered with the festival.

A representative of the state government reaffirmed Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu’s commitment to making Lagos a leading creative hub in Africa.

“Lagos remains the city where every heritage finds its place, and where creativity does not simply exist; it thrives,” the representative said.

The official added that the partnership and book grant initiative were designed to encourage young people to embrace indigenous stories, critical thinking and cultural identity.

Founded in 2013 by Shoneyin through the Book Buzz Foundation, the Aké Arts and Book Festival has grown into a gathering for writers, poets, filmmakers and cultural thinkers from Africa and the diaspora.

This year’s edition seeks to deepen conversations about African identity, heritage and creativity while examining how indigenous knowledge can remain relevant in a world increasingly shaped by technology.

The post Celebrated African writers converge in Lagos for Aké Festival appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Iwobi, Bassey rewrite Fulham records in City draw
description:
Super Eagles duo Alex Iwobi and Calvin Bassey set new Fulham landmarks as the Cottagers held Manchester City to a 1-1 draw at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
Iwobi made his 100th Premier League start for Fulham, becoming the first African player to reach that figure for t
content:
Super Eagles duo Alex Iwobi and Calvin Bassey set new Fulham landmarks as the Cottagers held Manchester City to a 1-1 draw at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.

Iwobi made his 100th Premier League start for Fulham, becoming the first African player to reach that figure for the London club, according to the Premier League. The former Everton midfielder, who joined in the summer of 2023, has made 122 league appearances for Fulham, scoring 20 goals and providing 12 assists.

The 30-year-old was booked in the first half and replaced by Antonee Robinson with 20 minutes remaining.

Bassey captained Fulham and played the full 90 minutes as they earned their first Premier League point at the Etihad in 13 visits. The result also ended City’s 17-match winning run against Fulham in the competition.

The defender had lost all four of his previous meetings with City since joining Fulham, conceding 15 goals in games that finished 4-0, 3-2, 5-4 and 3-0. Saturday’s draw ended that 924-day run.

Rodrigo Muniz put Fulham ahead in the 16th minute, and Bassey was booked six minutes later for halting a dangerous City counter-attack. Elliot Anderson levelled in the 57th minute.

Bassey, who has been linked with a move to Manchester United, helped limit City to two shots on target from 14 attempts.

He also forced a save from Gianluigi Donnarumma in the 69th minute after a forward run down the left, and almost turned Jérémy Doku’s cross into his own net in the 77th minute before Bernd Leno kept it out.

Fulham have now lost only one of their eight league games, and Alvaro Arbeloa’s side sit three points above the bottom three.

The post Iwobi, Bassey rewrite Fulham records in City draw appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Moses Bliss excites fans with romantic video amid divorce rumours
description:
Gospel singer Moses Bliss has shared a video featuring his wife, Marie Bliss, amid rumours of a marital crisis involving the couple.
The speculation began after blogs reported that the couple, who married in March 2024 and have a son, were considering divorce over undisclosed marital issues.
In what
content:
Gospel singer Moses Bliss has shared a video featuring his wife, Marie Bliss, amid rumours of a marital crisis involving the couple.

The speculation began after blogs reported that the couple, who married in March 2024 and have a son, were considering divorce over undisclosed marital issues.

In what appeared to be a response to the rumours, Moses Bliss took to his Instagram page on November 17, 2026, to share a video featuring himself and his wife.

In the clip, the couple were seen walking closely together and enjoying a night out at an upscale venue before the singer gently helped Marie into a waiting black SUV.

He accompanied the video with a brief caption: “Serenity.”

Marie also responded in the comments, writing that “nights like this with my husband are always my favourite”.

The post attracted significant attention after entertainment accounts interpreted it as a subtle response to the speculation about the couple’s marriage.

This is not the first time such rumours have surfaced. Similar speculation emerged in August 2026, and the couple’s previous response also involved sharing joint content rather than issuing direct public statements.

However, some celebrities criticised the singer’s approach to addressing the rumours.

Reacting to Moses Bliss’s Instagram video in a post on X on November 18, 2026, media personality and hype man Oladotun Kayode, popularly known as Do2dtun, criticised the singer for sharing a romantic video amid the breakup rumours.

He warned that trying to appease social media users could validate the speculation and make the singer appear guilty.

Do2dtun argued that rushing online to prove that a marriage was intact could achieve the opposite effect, cautioning that attempts to appease social media critics could create a slippery slope.

He wrote, “If he isn’t careful, he will slide into that net gradually. Whoever advised him to do this didn’t tell him; this makes him look more guilty to be honest.

“Nigerian entertainers need a good P.R, or social media manager. They don’t know how to kill a narrative or news. This move validates the rumour.”

Do2dtun’s argument was that the timing of the post worked against Bliss rather than in his favour, suggesting that engaging with unverified speculation, even indirectly, could inadvertently lend it credibility.

Some fans, however, supported the singer’s public display of affection and prayed for the couple’s marriage to remain intact.

One Instagram user, iam_jayni\_, wrote, “Best response ever. God won’t let their wish come to pass.”

Others echoed the prayer, while heron9010 added, “Father, we soak and cover this marriage with your precious blood.”

The post Moses Bliss excites fans with romantic video amid divorce rumours appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Osimhen, Orban, Iheanacho top scoring charts in Turkey
description:
Kelechi Iheanacho, Gift Orban and Victor Osimhen are leading the scoring charts in Turkey, with the trio combining for 37 goals this season, PETER AKINBO writes

Iheanacho (Bursaspor) – 17 goals
Iheanacho has 17 goals and three assists in 14 appearances for Bursaspor in the Turkish 1. Lig since join
content:
Kelechi Iheanacho, Gift Orban and Victor Osimhen are leading the scoring charts in Turkey, with the trio combining for 37 goals this season, PETER AKINBO writes

Iheanacho (Bursaspor) – 17 goals

Iheanacho has 17 goals and three assists in 14 appearances for Bursaspor in the Turkish 1. Lig since joining the club as a free agent after leaving Celtic. He scored in each of his first 12 games, but the run ended when he failed to find the net in the 3-0 win over Bandırmaspor on October 31.

He was back on the scoresheet in the 1-1 draw at Antalyaspor on November 6, and he has played 1,206 minutes in the league so far.

The 30-year-old has also picked up two yellow cards. His tally has long since passed the 12 league goals he scored for Leicester City in the 2020/21 season, his previous best, and Bursaspor are top of the table.

Osimhen (Galatasaray) – 10 goals

Osimhen has 10 goals and three assists in 11 appearances in all competitions for Galatasaray. Nine of the goals have come in eight Süper Lig games, while the other was in the 4-2 win at Lille, the club’s first victory of their Champions League campaign. He scored twice in the 2-1 win over Fenerbahçe on October 26 and added another in the 4-0 win at Konyaspor on October 30.

The striker has missed four of Galatasaray’s 12 league games, two of them with a groin strain and two more after arthroscopy. He was also absent for the 4-3 win over Amedspor on November 7 and the 2-1 victory over Samsunspor on Saturday.

Even without him, the reigning champions made it 10 wins from 12 league games and stayed top as they chase a fifth straight title. The win over Samsunspor also stretched their unbeaten home run in the Süper Lig to 42 games, a new club record that surpassed the 41 set between 2017 and 2019. The all-time league record is 90, set by Trabzonspor in 1981.

Orban (Amedspor) – 10 goals

Orban has 10 league goals and five assists in 12 appearances for newly promoted Amedspor, who are on loan from Hoffenheim. His goals include a hat-trick in the 5-0 win over Başakşehir, a brace in the 2-2 draw with Kasımpaşa and a strike in the 3-2 win over Beşiktaş. He also scored in the 5-1 win over Eyüpspor and the 2-1 win at Samsunspor.

He reached 10 goals in 11 games, a total that, according to Afrik-Foot, triggered an obligation-to-buy clause in his loan agreement. Amedspor are now set to pay Hoffenheim €3m to make the deal permanent, and they have reportedly ruled out letting him leave in January. Fenerbahçe, Trabzonspor and Istanbul Başakşehir have all been linked with interest.

The 24-year-old went goalless in the 2-0 home defeat to Çaykur Rizespor on Saturday, when a first-half effort went wide in the 33rd minute. He has said before that the Premier League is his “ultimate dream”. For now, he is one goal ahead of Osimhen in the Süper Lig scoring race.

Why Nigerians thrive in Turkey

Nigerian players have a long history in the Turkish top flight, and former Super Eagles midfielder Ogenyi Onazi believes the conditions suit them. Onazi, who played for Trabzonspor between 2016 and 2020, said culture, food, weather and passionate supporters make it easy for players to settle.

“Most Nigerian transfers to Turkey have been successful because the environment and culture help Nigerians settle in and do their best,” the 33-year-old told Footy-Africa.

Other Nigerians making their mark in the country include Paul Onuachu, Wilfred Ndidi and Ibrahim Olawoyin.

The post Osimhen, Orban, Iheanacho top scoring charts in Turkey appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
