title: Atiku, Obi, Tinubu: The race for Trump’s blessing, by Emmanuel Aziken
description: Despite his party’s bruising defeat in the US midterm elections a few weeks ago, President Donald Trump remains a powerful attraction in the political calculations of Nigeria’s leading presidential contenders, three of whom appear increasingly eager to secure Washington’s attention and goodwill ahea
content:
Despite his party’s bruising defeat in the US midterm elections a few weeks ago, President Donald Trump remains a powerful attraction in the political calculations of Nigeria’s leading presidential contenders, three of whom appear increasingly eager to secure Washington’s attention and goodwill ahead of the 2027 election.

The scramble for American recognition was particularly conspicuous this week, with President Bola Tinubu, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi engaging American political, media and policy circles in a determined effort to shape their international profiles.

The loudest signal came from the Tinubu camp, which released photographs of the President with American political strategist and media personality, Diana London. The encounter was initially presented as an interview but subsequently assumed a different character following criticism from Atiku’s camp, with London clarifying that it was intended to provide material for a documentary.

London had earlier taken to social media to praise the security partnership between Nigeria and the United States under Tinubu and Trump, describing the relationship as productive and capable of unlocking significant economic and trade opportunities. She also described Nigeria as America’s greatest ally in Africa.

But what appeared to be a publicity opportunity for the Presidency quickly became a political controversy when Atiku questioned the circumstances surrounding the engagement and demanded the release of the complete recording.

In a statement issued through his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, the former Vice-President questioned whether the engagement was connected to a $4.5 million lobbying arrangement involving the Nigerian government and American firm DCI Group AZ.

Atiku cited US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) filings identifying London as a consultant to the firm, reportedly engaged by the Nigerian government to enhance its image in America.

Although he acknowledged that the filings did not establish that Tinubu’s interview formed part of the services covered by the lobbying contract, he argued that the relationship raised questions requiring clarification.

He also questioned a large screen reportedly positioned within the President’s line of sight during the recording, suggesting that it might have contained prepared prompts. He challenged Tinubu to submit himself to a live, unscripted interview with Nigerian journalists, including Rufai Oseni, Ojy Okpe, Seun Okinbaloye and Reuben Abati.

London subsequently clarified the nature of her engagement with Tinubu, insisting that she had travelled to Nigeria to interview the President for portions of a documentary rather than for a conventional media assignment.

In a statement posted on her X account on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, she categorically denied receiving $4.5 million from the Nigerian government or anyone else in Nigeria.

“I unequivocally deny the claim that Nigeria’s government nor anyone else in Nigeria paid me $4.5 million. I went to Nigeria to interview President Tinubu @officialABAT for parts of a documentary and see Nigeria for myself,” she wrote.

She also dismissed the allegations surrounding her visit as a smear campaign.

Her clarification, however, has not entirely extinguished the controversy. While London denied personally receiving the alleged $4.5 million, FARA filings reportedly identify her as a consultant to DCI Group. Reports have also indicated that London Global Strategies, her company, received payments from the lobbying firm under the arrangement.

The distinction between payments to an individual and payments to a company is important. But it does not eliminate the need for transparency, particularly where a government-funded lobbying engagement and a presidential documentary interview appear in the same frame.

Yet, Atiku’s own relationship with Washington’s lobbying industry adds another dimension to the controversy.

In April 2026, reports based on US government filings revealed that he had engaged Washington-based lobbying firm Von Batten-Montague-York under a 12-month contract valued at $1.2 million.

The agreement provided for strategic advisory services, congressional and executive branch engagement, and efforts to strengthen his reputation among American policymakers. It also identified counterbalancing the Nigerian government’s lobbying narratives and advancing understanding of Atiku’s leadership posture and policy vision as objectives.

OBI’S WASHINGTON OUTREACH

Obi was equally active in the Washington theatre.

The former Anambra governor arrived in the American capital on Monday, November 16, for meetings with political figures, including members of the US House of Representatives and Senate.

He subsequently released photographs of his engagements, listing Congressman Marlin Stutzman, Congresswoman Beth Van Duyne, former Congressman Todd Tiahrt and other influential personalities among those he met.

According to Obi, the discussions focused on Nigeria’s development, security, economic prosperity, citizens’ welfare and democratic future. He also disclosed that he granted an interview to American television commentator Glenn Beck.

However, photographs and favourable remarks from some American personalities generated controversy, with suggestions in some quarters that Obi had secured congressional endorsement for his presidential ambition.

Karl Von Batten, the US-based representative of Atiku’s lobbying firm, challenged that interpretation, insisting that the gathering was a private engagement and did not constitute an endorsement by the US Congress.

Obi was quick to dismiss any suggestion that he had sought or secured an endorsement from the US government, Congress or individual American lawmakers.

He maintained that his visit was intended to discuss Nigeria’s development and democratic challenges.

THE WASHINGTON FACTOR

Taken together, the activities of Tinubu, Atiku and Obi reveal an emerging dimension of the 2027 presidential contest: the determination of leading political figures to shape perceptions of their leadership credentials beyond Nigeria’s borders.

For Tinubu, the priority appears to be projecting his administration as a strategic partner of the Trump government. Atiku is seeking to counter the government’s international narrative and present an alternative leadership proposition to American policymakers. Obi, meanwhile, is using political and media engagements to project his development-oriented message.

There is an irony in three presidential hopefuls competing for American attention while millions of Nigerians remain preoccupied with insecurity, unemployment, poverty, inflation and the rising cost of living.

Ultimately, the measure of presidential leadership will not be the warmth of its reception in Washington but its capacity to earn the confidence of Nigerians.

description:
From Adesuwa Tsan, Abuja 
Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, on Friday received a rousing welcome from supporters in Onitsha, Anambra State, ahead of a political event scheduled for the commercial city.
The reception, which attracted a large crowd of supporte
content:
From Adesuwa Tsan, Abuja

Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, on Friday received a rousing welcome from supporters in Onitsha, Anambra State, ahead of a political event scheduled for the commercial city.

The reception, which attracted a large crowd of supporters, brought parts of Onitsha to a standstill as residents and party loyalists turned out to welcome Obi on his homecoming visit.

A statement signed by the Spokesperson of the Nigeria Democratic Congress National Campaign Council (NDC-NCC), Dr. Constance Ikokwu, on Friday, described the reception as a demonstration of the growing support for Obi and the party. The Council said the crowd comprised youths, women and elderly supporters, whose presence reflected what it described as the people’s faith in Obi’s political vision.

“This was not just a political gathering; it was a profound family reunion,” the statement said, adding that the reception underscored the bond between Obi and the people of Anambra. It further described the turnout as evidence that the NDC’s ambition to rescue and rebuild the country was gaining momentum. “We are profoundly humbled by this breathtaking reception. To the incredible people of Onitsha and across Anambra, thank you for standing tall, for believing, and for showing the world what hope looks like,” the council said.

The council urged supporters to stay tuned for further developments, adding that the reception marked the beginning of what it called a march towards a new dawn.

title: LUTN to host 700 delegates at nation-building conference in Lagos

This was disclosed at a press briefing held in Lagos on Wednesday, where the Convener, Light Up the Na
content:
Light Up the Nation (LUTN), an inter-denominational Christian group, has urged Christians to take on their God-ordained assignment to build the nation and take active part in civic and public life.

This was disclosed at a press briefing held in Lagos on Wednesday, where the Convener, Light Up the Nation, Pastor Femi Obaweya, and speakers unveiled the programme for the group’s 7th conference, holding on Saturday, 21 and Sunday, 22 November 2026, in Lekki, Lagos.

Speaking at the briefing, Obaweya said the group was formed out of a conviction that faith must go beyond the pulpit and show up in the way the country is run.

“Beyond preaching salvation, we need to ask the question: What next? Our mandate is to shine before men, so that what we teach translates to actual transformation in our society,” Obaweya said.

Ideation Hub’s Programmes Director, Toyin Banjo, who represented Leadership Coach, Debola Deji-Kurunmi, said many citizens had withdrawn from national discourse because they believed their voices did not matter.

“Nation building is not just for politicians or policy leaders. It speaks to the entire citizenry. Many times we excuse ourselves and think our voices do not matter. It is in meetings like this that you grow in knowledge, strengthen your inspiration and take direct action on what truly matters,” she said.

Responding to why many Christians stay away from politics, Pastor Gerald Omo Osagie said that staying on the sidelines allows others to determine the outcome of elections.

“Your vote is your power. It is your voice. It is your birthright. We all have an obligation to get involved. We must stop complaining about the things we see and go out there to bring about change,” Osagie said.

The 2026 conference, themed, “The Assignment: Faith, Influence and Nation Building,” is expected to draw about 700 delegates, including ministers, church workers, young professionals, entrepreneurs, youth and families. Admission is free and open to the public.

The Saturday programme, which is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. to 2:40 p.m., will conclude with a panel discussion and question-and-answer session.

For some Nollywood stars, the spotlight extends beyond their performances on screen. They have ventured behind the camera, taking on the demanding roles of producers and directors, shaping narratives, bringing stories to life and creating films that have captivated audiences and made their mark at the box office. VERA ALKALI profiles some of the industry’s leading talents who have mastered the art of wearing many hats, both in front of and behind the camera

Funke Akindele

Olufunke Akindele, popularly known as Jenifa, has carved out a formidable place for herself in Nollywood, establishing a successful career that spans acting, producing, directing and screenwriting.

She first rose to prominence with her portrayal of the lead character in the television series I Need to Know and later cemented her popularity with Jenifa’s Diary. Her performance in I Need to Know earned her the Africa Movie Academy Award for Best Actress in a Leading Role. Since then, she has evolved from a celebrated screen actress into one of the industry’s most commercially successful filmmakers.

Her move into filmmaking has yielded a string of cinema successes, including Omo Ghetto: The Saga, Battle on Buka Street, A Tribe Called Judah and Everybody Loves Jenifa. The latter grossed about N1.88bn, while A Tribe Called Judah raked in approximately N1.4bn at the box office. With a reported cumulative box-office gross of over N4.7bn, Akindele has established herself as one of Nigeria’s highest-grossing filmmakers.

Her 2025 production, Behind the Scenes, further extended her impressive box-office run. Yet, despite her achievements behind the camera, Akindele has remained active as an actress, continuing to take on screen roles and demonstrating her versatility in both fields.

Toyin Abraham

Olutoyin Aimakhu, popularly known as Toyin Abraham, is another Nollywood actress who has successfully expanded her career into film production and directing while maintaining a strong presence on screen.

Known for her comic timing and ability to bring relatable characters to life, Abraham has built a film brand around stories that entertain and resonate with cinema audiences. She was nominated for Best Supporting Actress for her role in the Yoruba film Ebimi Ni.

Her popular Alakada franchise remains one of her major creative ventures, with instalments including Alakada Reloaded, Fate of Alakada and Alakada: Bad and Boujee. She has also produced films such as The Ghost and the Tout, Ijakumo, The Born Again Stripper and Malaika.

In 2025, she made her directorial debut with Oversabi Aunty, in which she also starred and served as producer. The comedy crossed the N1bn mark at the box office, marking a major milestone in her filmmaking career. Abraham has, however, continued to feature in other productions, balancing her work behind the camera with her acting career.

Femi Adebayo

Femi Adebayo has built a career that extends beyond his reputation as a lawyer and actor in Yoruba-language cinema. The son of veteran actor Adebayo Salami, popularly known as Oga Bello, he has established himself as an actor, producer and filmmaker, bringing ambitious stories to the screen.

Through his production outfit, Euphoria360 Media, Adebayo has been involved in notable productions, including King of Thieves and Jagun Jagun.

Released in 2022, King of Thieves grossed over N320m at the Nigerian box office, becoming one of the notable commercial successes in Yoruba cinema.

Adebayo also starred in the film as Agesinkole, combining his performance on screen with his responsibilities behind the scenes. His subsequent production, Jagun Jagun, further demonstrated his interest in large-scale storytelling. The film earned him the Africa Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role in 2024.

In 2025, his performance in Seven Doors earned him the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Award for Best Lead Actor. Despite his growing portfolio as a filmmaker, Adebayo remains active as an actor.

Odunlade Adekola

Odunlade Adekola is one of the familiar faces in Yoruba cinema whose career has grown beyond acting. Popular for his expressive performances, comic delivery and ability to interpret diverse characters, Adekola has taken on additional responsibilities in filmmaking, including directing and producing.

His involvement in productions such as Ajakaju: Beasts of Two Worlds and King of Thieves (Agesinkole) reflects his contribution to the industry beyond his performances on screen.

In Ajakaju: Beasts of Two Worlds, which he directed, Adekola also starred as an actor. The 2024 fantasy film grossed approximately N252.8m at the box office, making it one of the commercially successful productions of the year. His involvement in King of Thieves, another major Yoruba cinema production, further highlights his versatility.

While he continues to entertain audiences with his performances, Adekola has also demonstrated an interest in shaping the stories that make it to the screen.

Omoni Oboli

Omoni Oboli has successfully combined her career as an actress with filmmaking, directing and producing. After featuring in several Nollywood productions, she expanded her creative responsibilities, becoming one of the actresses actively involved in shaping the stories told on screen.

Her filmmaking credits include Being Mrs Elliot, The First Lady, Okafor’s Law and the Wives on Strike franchise. The franchise, which explores issues affecting women, marriage and family relationships, has become one of her notable contributions to Nigerian cinema.

The 2024 instalment, Wives on Strike: The Uprising, which she directed, recorded a reported domestic box-office gross of N127.1m. Beyond her work behind the camera, Oboli has continued to feature in films, maintaining her connection with audiences while pursuing her interests as a filmmaker.

Mercy Aigbe

Mercy Aigbe is another actress who has extended her career into film production and directing while maintaining her presence in front of the camera. Having built a strong following through her performances in Yoruba and English-language films, she has continued to explore other aspects of filmmaking.

One of her notable projects, Ada Omo Daddy, released in December 2023, featured her alongside actors such as Charles Okafor, Nkechi Blessing and Omowunmi Dada. The family drama, which she co-produced and directed, enjoyed an eight-week cinema run and grossed approximately N218.8m.

She followed it with other projects, including Thin Line, further demonstrating her commitment to developing stories for cinema audiences. Aigbe’s career reflects how established actors can draw on their experience and audience appeal to assume greater creative responsibilities without stepping away from acting.

The post Nollywood stars making waves on and off screen appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Help! My brother battling brain tumour hasn’t slept for over 95 days – Sibling
description: Ayomide, the younger brother of a Lagos-based executive assistant, Oluwagbemiga Olajide, who has been battling frequent seizures and severe headaches as a result of an aggressive brain tumour, tells AYOOLA OLASUPO about the family’s painful ordeal and urgent need for medical and financial interventi
content:
Ayomide, the younger brother of a Lagos-based executive assistant, Oluwagbemiga Olajide, who has been battling frequent seizures and severe headaches as a result of an aggressive brain tumour, tells AYOOLA OLASUPO about the family’s painful ordeal and urgent need for medical and financial intervention

Can you take us back to the last time you noticed that something was wrong with him?

It started with a constant headache. He used to complain about having headaches, but we usually dismissed them because we thought they were normal, perhaps due to work-related stress. It wasn’t until September, when one side of his eye started closing up, that we became seriously concerned. That was when we decided to go to the hospital for further examinations. It was in the hospital that we discovered that the situation was much more serious than we had thought.

What kind of work did he do before the ailment started?

My brother worked as an executive assistant.

Aside from the headache, were there any other symptoms or signs that you noticed before his eye started swelling?

No, it was only the severe headache.

What transpired at the hospital when you got there?

At first, they thought the problem was with his eyes. They believed that perhaps some of the nerves in his eyes were affected. However, when the condition persisted, they asked us to undergo MRI scans. One of the MRI scans revealed that there was fluid affecting his eyes. Since then, we have been moving from one hospital to another. They would refer us to one hospital, and when we got there, they would tell us to go to another hospital. It has been a continuous process of referrals.

Can you remember how much you have spent on the tests, drugs and treatment so far?

We have done several tests. For instance, the first MRI scan was done. We also conducted several other tests, although I cannot remember all their names. While carrying out these tests, we were also asked to get several other things. Altogether, we have spent more than N3 million before they were finally able to detect the location of the tumour.

We spent all that money just to get to that point. Now, the hospital where he is currently receiving treatment is asking us to pay N10 million for the surgery and post-surgery care. But we do not know how to get such an amount. We’ve really tried our best, and also spent a lot already. Right now, my brother cannot sleep because the headache and seizure are very constant. He has been unable to sleep properly for more than 95 days now.

Can you remember the last time he was able to sleep?

I think it was a long time ago. That was the last time he slept properly.

How has he been managing and coping with the situation?

Honestly, it is only God who has kept him alive until now because he experiences seizures, and they are very frequent. He can have seizures as many as 10 times a day. His entire body will start shaking, and he will be unable to do anything. He will just be screaming, but he is really strong. Some people in similar situations would have passed away, but he is still alive today. They have certain medications they administer when they notice that the seizures are becoming severe. I do not know the names of all the medications. Sometimes, after two or three hours, the seizure starts again. They have told us that the tumour is very aggressive. One side of his face is now paralysed.

Right now, his wife is pregnant and currently carrying his first child, and the entire family cannot sleep. As a pregnant woman, she should be getting enough rest, but she cannot. She has been trying, but it has not been easy. We are begging everybody to please help us. The financial stress, the pain he is going through, and the emotional stress are all overwhelming. Everything has been difficult. Whatever assistance anyone can offer, we sincerely appeal to them to please help us.

What other efforts have the family made towards his recovery?

We have made several efforts. We even travelled to Ibadan before coming to Lagos. We tried to seek help through different channels, but we were told that getting attention through those channels could take about a month. Considering the seriousness of his condition, and how quickly it was deteriorating, we could not afford to wait that long. We knew that we could not keep him at home because he needed immediate medical attention. That was why we decided to take him to a private hospital here in Ibadan. We were fortunate because there was a neurosurgeon available that day. We were told that getting access to the surgeon was not always easy, but we were lucky to meet him. We explained everything to the neurosurgeon. At that moment, my brother was emotional and started crying because of the condition he had found himself in.

But the neurosurgeon explained some things to us and mentioned that another appointment would be necessary. My brother was concerned and asked why there would need to be another appointment when his condition was so serious, and he needed to be admitted. The neurosurgeon also discussed the possibility of carrying out a procedure. He explained that there were different options, but the situation was very complicated. Since then, we have been spending money on his treatment, including injections and other medications. As his brother, I hardly sleep. I look at my brother and see the pain he is going through, and there is nothing I can do to take that pain away. Nobody should have to live in pain every single day, for 24 hours, and then wake up the following day only to experience the same thing again.

That is the kind of life he is living now. Honestly, I would not wish such a situation on anybody, not even my enemy. He is in pain almost every moment of the day. He takes several injections and medications, but sometimes they do not seem to provide lasting relief because the tumour is so aggressive. A few days ago, something happened that gave us a little hope. He sent me a message in the middle of the night, around 4:30 a.m. I was worried because whenever I do not hear from him, I become anxious. But this time, he told me that he had slept very well. He was so happy because he had managed to sleep for several hours, possibly about seven hours.

I was also very happy because I knew how much he had been struggling to sleep. When we saw him the following day, he was talking and was relatively calm. He was still experiencing some pain, but it was not as severe as before. He seemed a little relieved, and he was happy. Unfortunately, things changed again. I received a call the following morning. I had been trying to get some of his injections and medications, and I was informed that he had experienced another seizure. I was worried because I had thought he was getting better. When I eventually saw him, he was very weak. He was shaking, and his eyes were not responding normally. One of his eyes was partially shut, while the other one was just looking at a spot without blinking. I was scared, so I called his name several times, but he did not answer. He was just staring at the floor, so I became confused and frightened. I kept wondering what I was supposed to do. Should I go and call the doctor? My brother was no longer responding to me. I tried to get him to speak, but he could not. The doctor had already explained to us that the tumour was very aggressive and that his condition was serious.

Before that, there was a point when he sent me a message explaining how he was feeling. He said his brain felt like it was closing up and that his breathing was not normal. I showed the message to the doctor and explained what my brother was experiencing. The doctor explained that his condition was critical and that anything could happen at this moment. They also explained that they were still trying to arrange the necessary procedure, and that we needed to act urgently. We are also trying our best but the situation is now overwhelming for us. That is why we’ve come out to start begging people to come to our aid. I don’t want my brother to die. The doctor told us that a biopsy was necessary, but the hospital did not have the facility to carry it out at the time. I asked whether there was another way we could get it done, and they explained that we would have to pay for the procedure. The biopsy involves taking a sample of the tumour for examination. They need to carry out that procedure before deciding on the next steps in his treatment.

Even when the doctor gave my brother options, should they draw the tumour out from his nose or open up his head? He chose the latter instead because he cannot withstand the pain anymore. He prefers that they should just open up his head and take away the entire tumour once and for all. When I look at him sometimes I also pity him because of the kind of pain he passes through every time.

How much is needed for the surgery procedure?

To be honest, we have been trying everything possible. We have spent so much money. We have spent up to N4 million so far. The daily expenses involved in taking care of him are enormous. We buy drugs, injections, and other medical supplies, and we pay for different procedures and services. What I want to do now is appeal to Nigerians for help. This is my brother, who just got engaged, and the family had been looking forward to a happy future for him.

His introduction ceremony was only a few months ago, and everyone in the family was happy.

He is a young, intelligent, smart, and responsible man who has never deliberately hurt anyone. Now, his wife is pregnant, and they are expecting their first child. I do not want to find myself in a situation where I have to raise my brother’s child because he is no longer around. I want him and his wife to live happily together and raise their child.

I want Nigerians to hear our appeal and help us in whatever way they can. We need financial assistance to meet his medical needs and ensure that he gets the treatment he urgently requires. He is intelligent, hardworking, and responsible. He has worked with different organisations and has always tried to provide for his family. His family has also been looking out for him, but this situation has become overwhelming for us all. We are putting God first and trusting Him for a miracle. We sincerely appeal to Nigerians, individuals, organisations, and anyone who can help us to please come to our aid.

The post Help! My brother battling brain tumour hasn’t slept for over 95 days – Sibling appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: EFCC arraigns man for N450m fraud
description:
The Maiduguri Zonal Directorate of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission said it arraigned one Mohammed Yunus before Justice Adamu Shehu of the Federal High Court, Maiduguri, on Tuesday.
This was disclosed in a statement posted on the EFCC’s official X page on Friday, adding that the defendan
content:
The Maiduguri Zonal Directorate of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission said it arraigned one Mohammed Yunus before Justice Adamu Shehu of the Federal High Court, Maiduguri, on Tuesday.

This was disclosed in a statement posted on the EFCC’s official X page on Friday, adding that the defendant was arraigned on a two-count charge of money laundering to the tune of N450m.

Yunus was said to have been arrested for collecting N450m for a purported contract for the supply of goods to the World Food Programme, falsely presenting himself as having secured the contract and misappropriating the said funds for his personal use.

The statement said, “Count one reads: ‘That you, Mohammed Yunus, sometime in 2025 at Maiduguri, Borno State, within the jurisdiction of this honourable court, did commit an offence to wit: money laundering by converting the sum of N450,000,000, belonging to one Habu Tijjani Bolori under the guise that the said amount represent payment for the supply of goods to be made to World Food Programme where you falsely represented yourself to have secured the said purported contract from the World Food Programme, an NGO registered in Nigeria and thereby committed an offence contrary to Section 18 2(b) and punishable under Section 18(3) of the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022.’

“The defendant pleaded ‘not guilty’ to the charges when they were read to him, and counsel to the prosecution, Mukhtar Ali Ahmed, prayed the court for a trial date and to remand the defendant in a correctional centre.

“In the same vein, counsel to the defendant, B. Muhammad, through a motion for bail, informed the court that the defendant would not tamper with any of the prosecution witnesses and had undertaken not to commit any offence if released on bail.”

Justice Shehu thereafter admitted the defendant to bail in the sum of N50,000,000.00, with two sureties in like sum.

“He further ordered that the sureties must be residents of Maiduguri with properties having certificates of occupancy. The certificates and international passport of the defendant shall be deposited with the Registrar of the court,” according to the statement.

It added that the case was adjourned until December 1, 2026, for the commencement of trial.

title: Police nab serial rapist in Imo
description:
The Imo State Police Command has said a serial kidnapper, rapist and armed robber, Olisamaka Umah, who had been on its wanted list, has been arrested.
This was disclosed in a statement signed by the Force Public Relations Officer, Ani Iniedu, and posted on the Nigeria Police Force’s X page on Friday
content:
The Imo State Police Command has said a serial kidnapper, rapist and armed robber, Olisamaka Umah, who had been on its wanted list, has been arrested.

This was disclosed in a statement signed by the Force Public Relations Officer, Ani Iniedu, and posted on the Nigeria Police Force’s X page on Friday.

It read, “Operatives of the Anti-Kidnapping Unit, in synergy with Agwa Police Division, acted on credible intelligence to arrest a serial kidnapper, Olisamaka Umah (29), of Umuoma Irete, Owerri West LGA.

“The suspect, who had been on the command’s wanted list, confessed during interrogation to featuring prominently in several cases of kidnapping, armed robbery, and the rape of female victims.

“He has named fleeing gang members, whom operatives are actively tracking down to bring the entire syndicate to justice.”

The statement added that the case is currently being investigated by the State Criminal Investigation Department in Owerri, the state capital.

Similarly, four ex-convicts in Kwara State have been arrested by the Kwara State Police Command for suspected robbery.

According to a statement by the police, two firearms and other stolen items were recovered from the suspects.

The statement read, “Operatives on stop-and-search duty at NASFAT Area, EiyeKorin, intercepted a commercial bus, leading to the arrest of Abdulahi Olamilekan (20), who jumped out and attempted to flee.

“A ringing phone found on him revealed a robbery at Al-Hikmah University hostels. Further investigations led to the arrest of three accomplices: Jimoh Abdulfatai (28), Abdulahi Bashir (29), and Tunji Abel.

“The four suspects (all ex-convicts) confessed to robbing the university hostels three times in the past. Police recovered two locally crafted pistols, one live cartridge, eight mobile phones, and a laptop. They have been positively identified by the victims.”

title: Sokoto IDPs beg for home
description:
Months after fleeing their communities over bandit attacks, displaced families in Yabo Local Government Area of Sokoto State say they remain uncertain about where to settle, with their former homes and farmlands no longer accessible to them.
They have consequently appealed to the government to provi
content:
Months after fleeing their communities over bandit attacks, displaced families in Yabo Local Government Area of Sokoto State say they remain uncertain about where to settle, with their former homes and farmlands no longer accessible to them.

They have consequently appealed to the government to provide permanent accommodation and livelihood support to enable them to rebuild their lives after losing their homes and means of survival to insecurity.

They made the appeal on Friday during the distribution of dignity kits and other relief materials organised by ActionAid Nigeria, with support from the European Union, at the Yabo Local Government Secretariat.

Speaking on behalf of others, displaced resident Mukhtar Umar said farming, which was their major source of livelihood before the attacks, was no longer possible because bandits had taken over their communities and farmlands.

“Before now, we used to farm, but where we are now, we cannot do that. Our farms have been taken over by bandits, so we are desperately in need of help,” he said.

Umar acknowledged the assistance received from the government and humanitarian organisations but stressed that the displaced families urgently needed decent accommodation and regular food supplies.

He appealed for more sustainable interventions to enable them to rebuild their lives.

Another beneficiary, Modi Tuita, said displaced residents were experiencing serious hardship after leaving their communities in search of safety.

He commended ActionAid for the assistance but urged the government to do more to address their challenges.

Similarly, a representative of the displaced women, Hafsat Muhammad, appealed to the government and international organisations to assist them in securing decent homes.

Speaking at the event, ActionAid Nigeria’s Deputy Country Director, Suwaiba Dankabo, said the intervention was not merely about distributing relief materials but also about advocating safe housing and improved social protection for displaced persons.

She said displaced persons deserved protection and access to education, healthcare, security and other essential social services, regardless of where they were taking refuge.

Dankabo explained that the dignity kits were designed based on needs identified by beneficiaries, particularly women, and included sanitary pads and other essential items.

She disclosed that ActionAid had targeted 300 beneficiaries, with 100 expected to receive the items during the initial distribution, while the remaining beneficiaries would be reached subsequently.

On efforts to provide long-term support, Dankabo said the organisation was implementing a three-year partnership programme with the Sokoto State Government under its European Union-supported social protection initiative.

Meanwhile, the Vice Chairman of Yabo Local Government, Usman Na’Allah, disclosed that the council had been providing accommodation, foodstuffs and medications to displaced persons.

Speaking on behalf of the council chairman, Na’Allah said some displaced families had been accommodated in government-owned properties without paying rent.

“At a time, we had about 2,300 persons who came here from neighbouring villages in Shagari Local Government Area. Some of them were accommodated in government properties without collecting a kobo,” he said.

He added that the council had appealed to residents to accommodate displaced families where possible, while the local government chairman continued to support them with food and medical assistance.

Na’Allah commended ActionAid, the European Union and the federal and state governments for their interventions, urging beneficiaries not to sell the relief materials but to use them for their intended purposes.

He also expressed hope that lasting peace would enable the displaced persons to return to their communities and resume their normal lives.

The District Head of Yabo, Alhaji Muhammad Sani Bello, commended ActionAid for supporting displaced persons in the area.

The post Sokoto IDPs beg for home appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Nigerian lawyer reacts to fresh protest in S’Africa
description:
A Nigerian-born activist lawyer in Johannesburg, Austin Okeke, has reacted to a recent protest by the South Africans calling for a ban of Nigerians in their country.
Okeke, reacting on Friday, said the group that led the protest didn’t have the authority to ban Nigerians from entering South Africa.
content:
A Nigerian-born activist lawyer in Johannesburg, Austin Okeke, has reacted to a recent protest by the South Africans calling for a ban of Nigerians in their country.

Okeke, reacting on Friday, said the group that led the protest didn’t have the authority to ban Nigerians from entering South Africa.

“They are a vigilante group. It’s not in their place to say who or not enters South Africa,” he said.

Okeke dismissed claims that the fresh protest might have been connected to a diplomatic row between the Nigerian Ambassador to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode and President Cyril Ramaphosa’s officials after the former alleged that his letters of credence was removed from a livestream last week.

“It has nothing to do with FFK. He just arrived three weeks ago.  It couldn’t have been because of him. They have been saying it for over two years now. They sang it on the streets this year during the unending barbaric xenophobic show of shame on the streets of South Africa,” the lawyer added.

Newzroom Afrika reported that the protesters, organised by March and March, held placards during the anti-immigration demonstration in Durban, calling for tighter border controls and the deportation of undocumented migrants.

It was led by Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma to Sunnyside, a suburb home to a large Nigerian community nicknamed “Little Lagos.”

During the march, Ngobese-Zuma challenged residents over the name, “Who gave you permission to call this place Lagos or whatever you call it?”

“I am being told here that we’ve entered Sunnyside, the home of Nigerians. I am inviting Nigerians to come out, let’s talk to each other. We want to know who gave you this place and called it Nigeria,” she said.

title: Petrol imports jump 47% despite local refining
description:
Nigeria’s petrol imports rebounded by 47 per cent in October to 15 million litres per day, reversing the decline recorded in the previous month and raising fresh concerns about the country’s dependence on foreign supplies despite the expansion of domestic refining.
The latest figures released by the
content:
Nigeria’s petrol imports rebounded by 47 per cent in October to 15 million litres per day, reversing the decline recorded in the previous month and raising fresh concerns about the country’s dependence on foreign supplies despite the expansion of domestic refining.

The latest figures released by the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority on Friday showed that petrol imports increased from 10.2 million litres per day in September to 15 million litres in October, representing an additional 4.8 million litres daily.

Although domestic refineries remained the country’s largest source of petrol, their contribution also increased at a slower rate of 12 per cent, from 28.5 million litres per day in September to 31.9 million litres in October.

The October figures mean imported petrol accounted for approximately 32 per cent of the 46.9 million litres received daily, compared with 26.4 per cent in September. Domestic supply represented the remaining 68 per cent.

The development highlights the fragile nature of Nigeria’s emerging fuel self-sufficiency, as the recovery in domestic refining has not completely eliminated the need for imported petroleum products.

The NMDPRA disclosed the figures in its October 2026 fact sheet, which showed that total petrol receipts rose by 21 per cent from 38.7 million litres per day in September to 46.9 million litres in October.

The increase represented an additional 8.2 million litres daily, comprising 4.8 million litres from imports and 3.4 million litres from domestic refineries.

A month-by-month examination of the authority’s figures showed that petrol imports initially dominated supply in the final quarter of 2025 before domestic refining gained ground following the commissioning and expansion of local refining capacity.

In October 2025, domestic refineries supplied 17.1 million litres daily, while imports accounted for 28.9 million litres, bringing total receipts to 46 million litres per day.

In November 2025, domestic supply increased to 19.5 million litres, while imports rose to 32 million litres, pushing total receipts to 51.5 million litres daily.

The highest supply during the 13-month period was recorded in December 2025, when domestic refineries supplied 32 million litres and imports contributed 42.2 million litres, bringing total receipts to 74.2 million litres daily.

However, the pattern changed in January 2026 as domestic supply surged to 40.1 million litres daily, overtaking imports, which declined to 24.8 million litres. Total receipts stood at 64.9 million litres.

The decline in imports became more pronounced in February, when foreign supplies fell to just three million litres daily, compared with 29.4 million litres from domestic refineries. Total petrol receipts consequently dropped to 32.4 million litres per day.

In March, domestic supply recovered to 34.2 million litres, while imports increased slightly to 5.9 million litres, bringing total receipts to 40.1 million litres.

April recorded domestic supply of 40.7 million litres against imports of 3.7 million litres, with total receipts standing at 44.4 million litres daily.

The trend continued in May, when local refineries supplied 41.5 million litres, while imports contributed 5.9 million litres. Total receipts increased to 47.4 million litres.

However, imports began regaining ground in June, rising sharply to 18.1 million litres daily, while domestic supply declined to 32.5 million litres. Total receipts stood at 50.6 million litres.

In July, domestic supply fell further to 25.8 million litres, while imports increased to 19.7 million litres, bringing total receipts to 45.5 million litres.

August saw domestic supply recover to 35.9 million litres, while imports declined to 14.6 million litres. Total receipts rose to 50.5 million litres.

In September, domestic supply dropped to 28.5 million litres, while imports declined to 10.2 million litres, resulting in total receipts of 38.7 million litres.

The October figures subsequently showed a recovery in both supply channels, with domestic deliveries rising to 31.9 million litres and imports increasing to 15 million litres, bringing total receipts to 46.9 million litres daily.

The 13-month data showed that domestic refineries supplied an average of 31.5 million litres daily, representing 62.6 per cent of total petrol receipts, while imports averaged 18.8 million litres, accounting for 37.4 per cent.

Despite the October rebound, imported petrol volumes remained below the 13-month average of 18.8 million litres daily. Domestic supply, however, was slightly above its 13-month average of 31.5 million litres.

A year-on-year comparison also showed that domestic supply increased by 86.5 per cent, from 17.1 million litres daily in October 2025 to 31.9 million litres in October 2026.

Conversely, imports declined by 48.1 per cent from 28.9 million litres to 15 million litres over the same period. Total petrol receipts increased marginally by 1.96 per cent, from 46 million litres to 46.9 million litres daily.

The October recovery in imports was accompanied by deterioration in petrol stock sufficiency, which measures the number of days existing inventories can sustain consumption.

title: Nigeria’s crypto economy down 3%
description:
Nigeria’s cryptocurrency economy contracted by three per cent to $38.1bn or N51.44tn in the year to June 2026, despite remaining one of the largest digital asset markets in Sub-Saharan Africa, as activity on decentralised exchanges and cross-border peer-to-peer platforms declined.
The decline came a
content:
Nigeria’s cryptocurrency economy contracted by three per cent to $38.1bn or N51.44tn in the year to June 2026, despite remaining one of the largest digital asset markets in Sub-Saharan Africa, as activity on decentralised exchanges and cross-border peer-to-peer platforms declined.

The decline came amid efforts by Nigerian regulators to strengthen oversight of the cryptocurrency industry, with the Securities and Exchange Commission introducing tighter requirements for digital asset operators and the Central Bank of Nigeria moving to establish a licensing framework for stablecoins and other virtual assets.

According to the 2026 Geography of Cryptocurrency Report by blockchain analytics firm, Chainalysis, Nigeria’s cryptocurrency activity fell from its previous level, with a 45 per cent decline in decentralised exchange transactions and a 17 per cent drop in cross-border peer-to-peer flows outweighing growth in centralised exchanges and other cryptocurrency services.

The report measured cryptocurrency value received between 1 July, 2025 and 30 June, 2026. Nigeria ranked third globally in grassroots cryptocurrency adoption, indicating that digital assets continued to attract substantial participation from individuals and businesses despite the contraction in transaction activity.

Nigeria’s performance contrasted with that of South Africa, whose cryptocurrency economy expanded by 52 per cent to $39.3bn during the period. Together, the two countries accounted for more than three-quarters of cryptocurrency activity in Sub-Saharan Africa, where the market grew by 13.4 per cent to $101bn, making it the fastest-growing region globally.

The regulatory environment has also been changing as authorities seek to bring cryptocurrency businesses within a more defined supervisory framework following years of uncertainty over the industry’s operations.

In August 2026, the SEC admitted three additional virtual asset service providers, including Yellow Card Financial, Pisi Payments Solution and BC Access, into its Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme. The initiative allows eligible players to operate within specified conditions while the commission assesses their business models and compliance with regulatory requirements.

The commission subsequently proposed new rules covering digital asset exchanges, custodians, stablecoins, peer-to-peer trading and tokenisation platforms. The proposals include higher capital requirements and registration obligations for operators seeking to provide digital asset services in Nigeria.

In a further development, the Central Bank of Nigeria issued its regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria on 5 November, 2026. The framework provides for the licensing and supervision of stablecoin issuers and virtual asset service providers involved in payments, transfers, custody, remittances and settlement.

The regulations also introduce requirements covering capital, liquidity, customer protection and anti-money laundering compliance, while distinguishing the CBN’s oversight of non-security virtual assets from the SEC’s responsibility for digital assets classified as securities.

The developments followed President Bola Tinubu’s July 2026 Executive Order on Virtual Assets Coordination, which established a council chaired by the CBN, with the SEC and Nigeria Revenue Service as vice-chairs, to improve coordination among government agencies responsible for the sector.

Amid these regulatory changes, the Chainalysis report identified practical financial needs as a major driver of cryptocurrency adoption across Sub-Saharan Africa, particularly demand for cheaper cross-border payments, access to dollar-denominated value and alternative ways of managing personal finances.

For businesses, digital assets provide another channel for settling international transactions and moving money across markets, particularly where conventional payment systems are expensive or inefficient.

Stablecoin and Blockchain Commercial Lead at Nigerian fintech company Flutterwave, Mercy Emmanuel, said the commercial value of blockchain technology in African markets would depend on its ability to address existing financial challenges.

“For African markets, the most commercially relevant innovations will be those that reduce friction in existing financial activities rather than those that introduce complexity simply for the sake of using blockchain technology,” she said.

The report identified stablecoins, personal wallets and business-orientated transactions as important components of cryptocurrency adoption in the region, reflecting demand for greater control over funds, dollar-linked value and practical payment solutions.

South Africa’s growth was broad-based, with increases across every transaction category measured by Chainalysis. Cross-border peer-to-peer stablecoin flows and service-related transactions were among the leading contributors.

Nigeria, however, recorded a different pattern, as the decline in decentralised exchange activity and cross-border peer-to-peer flows outweighed gains in centralised exchange and other cryptocurrency services.

The post Nigeria’s crypto economy down 3% appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Customs suspend recruits’ training as FCC probes recruitment
description: The Nigeria Customs Service has suspended training activities for 3,852 newly recruited officers, nearly two years after it began the recruitment process, following concerns raised by the Federal Character Commission over alleged irregularities in the selection and invitation of successful candidate
content:
The Nigeria Customs Service has suspended training activities for 3,852 newly recruited officers, nearly two years after it began the recruitment process, following concerns raised by the Federal Character Commission over alleged irregularities in the selection and invitation of successful candidates.

The suspension, announced on Friday in a statement signed by the Deputy Comptroller of Customs and National Public Relations Officer, Abdullahi Maiwada, came after engagements between the management of the Customs Service and a delegation of the commission, with both institutions agreeing to further consultations to resolve the disagreement.

The statement read, “The Nigeria Customs Service has temporarily put on hold the ongoing training activities at its two training colleges to allow further consultations and dialogue with the Federal Character Commission towards the amicable resolution of concerns raised in connection with the ongoing recruitment exercise.

“The decision follows engagements between the Commission and a delegation of the NCS, during which both parties reaffirmed their commitment to resolving the issues through constructive dialogue, mutual understanding and continued institutional collaboration.”

Maiwada said the Service has suspended training activities at its two training colleges following concerns raised by the FCC over the ongoing recruitment exercise.

He said the suspension is aimed at allowing the two agencies to resolve the disagreements surrounding the recruitment process through further consultations and dialogue.

The development comes amid questions over the selection of successful candidates, following complaints by applicants who alleged that they were excluded from the training exercise despite appearing on the published final recruitment lists.

The Service said both institutions had reaffirmed their commitment to resolving the issues through constructive dialogue, mutual understanding and continued institutional collaboration.

It stated that the Comptroller-General of Customs, Bashir Adewale Adeniyi, had reiterated the agency’s commitment to working with relevant government institutions in the national interest.

According to the statement, “In consideration of the concerns raised by the Commission and in line with the series of engagements, the Comptroller-General of Customs, CGC Bashir Adewale Adeniyi, MFR, has reaffirmed the Service’s commitment to institutional collaboration and constructive engagement with relevant government institutions in the overall national interest.

“Furthermore, the CGC acknowledged the critical role of FCC in promoting national unity, fairness and equitable representation in public service appointments, noting the importance of its constitutional mandate in strengthening inclusiveness and ensuring that the principles of federal character are upheld across the Federation.”

The Customs Service added that it valued its longstanding relationship with the commission and was confident that the ongoing discussions would provide an opportunity to address the concerns raised.

“The NCS values its longstanding relationship with the FCC and remains confident that the ongoing dialogue will provide an opportunity to address the concerns raised in a mutually beneficial manner, while reinforcing the shared commitment of both institutions to fairness, national cohesion and effective public service delivery,” it stated.

The Service also pledged to maintain transparency and accountability throughout the process, stressing that it would continue to engage relevant government institutions to strengthen public confidence in its operations.

The dispute comes against the backdrop of a recruitment exercise that began with a newspaper advertisement on 27 December, 2024, when the Customs Service announced 3,927 vacancies across its Superintendent, Inspectorate and Customs Assistant cadres.

The exercise attracted more than 573,000 applications, with 286,697 candidates initially shortlisted for the next stage after the first round of documentary screening.

Following subsequent assessments, the Service published its final lists between 28 and 30 July, 2026, announcing 3,852 successful candidates comprising 1,275 officers in the Superintendent Cadre, 367 in the Inspectorate Cadre and 2,210 in the Customs Assistant Cadre.

The training exercise subsequently commenced on 9 October, 2026, with successful candidates reporting to the designated training colleges.

However, the recruitment process became contentious after some applicants complained that they had been excluded from training despite completing the required screening and documentation exercises and seeing their names on the published lists.

The Federal Character Commission subsequently raised concerns about the process, including allegations that some candidates whose names appeared on the final lists were not invited for training, while some individuals whose names were not published allegedly received invitations.

The commission also cited complaints from more than 500 applicants who claimed they had completed the necessary stages, including medical examinations, but were subsequently excluded.

In its position on the controversy, the FCC argued that the complaints required investigation to establish whether the recruitment process complied with the applicable federal character principles.

The commission called for the suspension of the training exercise pending an examination of the disputed recruitment process. It also said its 330th plenary session had resolved to suspend Customs recruitment activities indefinitely.

The latest decision by the Customs Service to put training activities on hold comes as both institutions seek an amicable resolution of the disagreement.

The post Customs suspend recruits’ training as FCC probes recruitment appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Inside Nigeria’s kidnap underworld: How terrorists organise abductions, launder ransom
description:
• Ex-NIA DG exposes network of terrorists, bandits, informants, financial facilitators
• Recounts how recovered Chibok girl sought to return to terrorist husband
• N7.78bn ransom paid from July 2025 to June 2026


By Beifoh Osewele
Former Director-General of the National Intelligence Agency (NIA), A
content:
• Ex-NIA DG exposes network of terrorists, bandits, informants, financial facilitators

• Recounts how recovered Chibok girl sought to return to terrorist husband

• N7.78bn ransom paid from July 2025 to June 2026

By Beifoh Osewele

Former Director-General of the National Intelligence Agency (NIA), Ahmed Rufai Abubakar, has blown the lid off the sprawling criminal machinery behind Nigeria’s multibillion-naira kidnapping industry, exposing how terrorists, bandit militias, informants and financial facilitators operate an intricate and elaborate network that identifies victims, tracks security operatives, coordinates mass abductions and launders huge ransom payments through cryptocurrencies and small financial outfits.

Abubakar revealed that behind the gunmen who storm communities, abduct schoolchildren and seize travellers lies a sophisticated web of collaborators whose activities have turned kidnapping into a major source of financing for terrorist operations, recruitment, propaganda and prisoner exchanges, with criminal gangs and extremist organisations increasingly pooling resources to sustain the deadly enterprise.

He disclosed that the scale of the illicit business extends to millions of dollars, citing the March 2022 Abuja–Kaduna train attack, during which kidnappers allegedly collected between $1 million and $2 million in ransom payments that he said were channelled to the terrorist organisation, Ansaru.

In another startling revelation, the former intelligence chief recounted how a Chibok schoolgirl rescued after years in terrorist captivity, during which she was married successively to three fighters, expressed a desire to return to her captors despite being brought to Abuja for medical examinations and debriefing.

Abubakar made the disclosures during a panel discussion at the eighth Global Security Forum in Doha, Qatar, held from October 19 to 21, 2026, under the theme: “The Future of Alliances,” where security and intelligence experts examined the growing convergence of terrorism, organised crime and hostage-taking.

Organised by The Soufan Centre and the Qatar International Academy for Security Studies, the forum brought together senior officials and security experts from more than 100 countries to examine international cooperation, emerging threats and the growing influence of non-state actors.

Informants identify victims, collaborators track security agents

Abubakar said the kidnapping network extended beyond the armed men who seized victims, with informants and other collaborators providing information essential to their operations.

“You have the perpetrators in three different categories. You have the motive behind, but you have a very strong network of logistics providers, and that is the informants.

“They use a lot of informants that tell them about their targets, their potential targets.”

Other collaborators, he said, provided logistical support, including intelligence on the movements of law enforcement personnel, enabling the perpetrators to evade security operations and sustain their activities.

“There are also other criminal support logistics that actually help them by informing them about the movement of law enforcement agents. So, this is what makes the ecosystem of kidnapping, hostage taking, mass abduction in Nigeria.”

How ransom is laundered

The former intelligence chief said the collection of substantial ransom payments had created a need for financial channels through which the perpetrators could conceal and move their proceeds.

“You collect ransom, huge ransoms, and you have to now launder the money,” he said, identifying cryptocurrencies and small financial outfits among the channels used. “Small financial outfits are used to launder this money.”

He placed the financial facilitators within the broader support structure sustaining terrorist organisations, bandit militias and other criminal gangs, whose objectives increasingly overlapped.

Abubakar cited the March 28, 2022, attack on the Abuja–Kaduna passenger train as an example of the financial benefits terrorist organisations derive from mass abductions.

He estimated that the kidnappers collected between $1 million and $2 million in ransom payments, which he said were channelled to Ansaru, a terrorist organisation with links to al-Qaeda.

Gunmen had attacked the Kaduna-bound passenger train after explosives were detonated on the railway track, killing passengers, injuring others and abducting dozens.

The hostages were subsequently released in batches, with the remaining 23 regaining their freedom on October 5, 2022, following efforts by security agencies.

The attack forced the suspension of passenger services on the route until December 5, 2022, when operations resumed under additional security arrangements.

Terrorists, bandits join forces

Abubakar identified terrorist organisations, bandit militias and other criminal gangs as the principal categories of perpetrators, explaining that their motives and methods had evolved over time.

According to him, terrorist groups such as Boko Haram abduct people for several purposes, including fundraising, recruiting young men as fighters and taking girls and women as spouses.

“They do targeted kidnappings individually. Initially, they did it to fundraise, and then, of course, also to recruit from the young men to fill their ranks of fighters, and then also recruit from young girls and women for purposes of having partners or spouses.

“And they go directly to communities and villages and then take what they want and then they go.”

Bandit militias, he explained, were principally driven by money, carrying out both targeted kidnappings and mass abductions. “They also do targeted kidnappings. They go directly into houses, to communities, and so on, and take victims.”

He added that the militias also engaged in cattle rustling and received support from gunrunners, distinguishing their financial motivations from the ideological objectives of terrorist organisations.

“They are not ideologically driven. They have no ideology. They want to enjoy life,” he said. “Their paradise is here.”

Despite their different motivations, Abubakar said terrorist groups and bandit militias increasingly collaborate to carry out mass kidnappings.

“Then we graduated to a situation where we now see alignment of, for instance, terrorist groups working with militia groups to conduct especially mass kidnapping.

“They do that for dual purposes: first of all to fundraise, to get money, and then, of course, also to serve as propaganda.

“So there is a political motive over there for them to be known, for the government to know that they are active, especially when the pushback from the government forces was very strong.”

JNIM, Ansaru and the Sahel connection

Abubakar identified Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and Ansaru among the terrorist organisations linked to kidnapping operations involving bandit militias.

JNIM, commonly translated as the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims, is an al-Qaeda-affiliated terrorist organisation operating across parts of the Sahel, including Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.

The organisation emerged in March 2017 following the merger of four extremist groups: Ansar al-Din, al-Murabitun, the Macina Liberation Front and the Sahara branch of al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM).

The United Nations placed JNIM on its sanctions list on October 4, 2018, following its involvement in terrorist attacks against military formations, international forces and civilian targets.

Ansaru, a separate Nigeria-based terrorist organisation, announced its existence in January 2012 after breaking away from Boko Haram. The United Nations identifies the group as having operational connections with AQIM, including training and attack planning, and placed it on its sanctions list on June 26, 2014.

A 2022 United Nations monitoring report recorded that Ansaru pledged allegiance to JNIM on December 31, 2021, although subsequent UN reporting indicated that the group had struggled to provide operational support to the Sahel-based organisation.

The report also raised concerns about possible operational connections involving terrorist organisations, criminal networks and former Boko Haram operatives in Kaduna, Katsina, Niger and Zamfara states.

Kidnapping for ransom has also been identified as a source of financing for JNIM. In April 2024, the United States Department of State announced sanctions against individuals linked to the organisation’s hostage-taking activities, identifying ransom payments, extortion and proceeds from smugglers and traffickers among its funding sources.

Abubakar further disclosed that terrorist organisations maintained links with sponsors outside Nigeria, enabling them to mobilise funds for their operations and expansion.

He identified Nigeria’s large population and economy as factors making the country attractive to terrorist organisations seeking financial resources.

N7.78bn ransom payments in one year

The scale of Nigeria’s kidnapping economy was further illustrated by findings from security consultancy, SBM Intelligence, which reported that at least N7.78 billion was paid in ransom between July 2025 and June 2026, compared with N2.56 billion in the preceding reporting period.

In its report, ‘The Economics of Nigeria’s Kidnap Industry, 2026’, the consultancy said 7,825 people were abducted in 1,713 kidnapping and related incidents during the period, while at least 1,142 people were killed.

According to the report, the Jama’atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda’awati Wal-Jihad faction of Boko Haram accounted for approximately 90 per cent of recorded ransom payments.

The consultancy called for stronger action against the financial networks sustaining insurgency and the economic conditions that continued to supply recruits to criminal organisations.

Schoolchildren, worshippers seized for prisoner exchanges

Abubakar said the objectives of mass abductions had increasingly extended beyond financial gain to securing the release of detained members of terrorist and criminal organisations.

“Now, currently, what we have is mass kidnapping of schoolchildren that is going on. Mass kidnapping of worshippers, either Muslims or Christians, is also going on.

“And in most cases perpetrated by bandits or terrorist groups, and the purpose now has evolved to prisoner exchange.

“So they do it because they have their friends, their comrades that have been arrested, and they want them freed.”

He explained that such demands often complicated negotiations, particularly where the abductors insisted on the release of associates who had already been killed during attacks or security operations.

“So that makes negotiation, hostage diplomacy very difficult,” he said.

Why negotiations go through back channels

Asked how diplomatic, legal and law enforcement tools could be applied to different hostage situations, Abubakar said the appropriate response depended on the identity of the abductors, their objectives and the circumstances surrounding each incident. “Different diagnosis, different medication,” he said.

He explained that while some terrorist abductions were principally intended to make political statements, others involved financial demands or attempts to secure prisoner exchanges, requiring different approaches to negotiations.

Where the captors communicated financial demands, he said, negotiations could require discreet engagement through trusted intermediaries.

“You have to use the hostage diplomacy. And it has to be through the back channel.

“There are groups, some of them foreign groups like the HD and others, and then internal groups, and some contact persons that the terrorists trust.”

He said such engagements were conducted quietly, without public disclosure of the details of negotiations or any ransom payments.

“This is a high level of hostage diplomacy negotiations,” he said.

Recovered Chibok girl wanted to return

Recounting the Chibok girl’s experience, Abubakar said security officials had continued tracking the abducted girls over the years, recovering them in small groups through liaison channels and security operations.

“There are also situations where they abduct people, intending to keep them, as happened with the Chibok girls, who were taken in 2014, relatively early in the group’s activities.

“They abduct people for several reasons, but in that case, a major objective was to make a statement. They entered a girls’ school and took the students. There was public outrage, but they kept the girls and remained silent.

“Some of the girls escaped, while some died. Many were retained and distributed among the groups, and they were married off to fighters.”

On efforts to recover the girls, he said: “We kept on all these years actually keeping track. And we got them in batches of two, three, four, depending on circumstances and situations, police, military raid and so on.

“But this particular case, we got across this lady. We brought her to Abuja, kept her for about two weeks, exposing her to medical checks and debriefing and so on. And what we found was very interesting.

“She went through three different husbands. The first two were killed in combat.”

He said the young woman was married to a third fighter when security officials recovered her.

According to him, a zonal commander within the terrorist organisation had adopted the young woman as a daughter and arranged successive marriages for her whenever her husband was killed.

“Now, the interesting thing is she had very good things to say about her godfather, that he was a very kind man.,” Abubakar said.

He said she wanted to see her parents but also expressed a desire to return to where she had been held.

He cited the experience to illustrate the complexities security officials encountered in recovering people who had spent prolonged periods in the custody of terrorist organisations.

The post Inside Nigeria’s kidnap underworld: How terrorists organise abductions, launder ransom appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Lagos renews campaign against open defecation
description:
…Calls for improved sanitation, gender-sensitive toilet facilities



By Olasunkanmi Akoni



The Lagos State Government has renewed its campaign for improved sanitation, proper hygiene practices and access to safe toilet facilities as part of efforts to eliminate open defecation and promote public
content:
…Calls for improved sanitation, gender-sensitive toilet facilities

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

The Lagos State Government has renewed its campaign for improved sanitation, proper hygiene practices and access to safe toilet facilities as part of efforts to eliminate open defecation and promote public health.

The Special Adviser to the Governor on Environment, Olakunle Akodu, and the Permanent Secretary, Office of Environmental Services, Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources, Tajudeen Gaji, made the call on Friday as the state joined the rest of the world to commemorate World Toilet Day at Alausa, Ikeja.

The 2026 celebration was held under the theme, “Sanitation and Gender Equality.”

Akodu said women and girls required toilet facilities that guaranteed adequate privacy, reliable water supply, handwashing stations and hygienic conditions.

He noted that Lagos’ growing population, rapid urbanisation and expanding commercial activities had placed enormous pressure on existing sanitation infrastructure.

According to him, addressing the challenges requires deliberate public policies, sustained capital investment, institutional discipline and collective civic responsibility.

He said the state government recognised that a clean, resilient and sustainable environment must guarantee every resident access to safe, dignified and functional sanitation facilities.

Earlier, Gaji, who was represented by the Director of Sanitation Services, Hassan Sanuth, said the commemoration underscored the importance of proper sanitation in preventing diseases, protecting public health and promoting a cleaner environment.

He described access to safe toilets as more than a basic necessity, saying it was fundamental to human dignity and public health.

Gaji said sanitation was closely linked to personal security, social equality and the fundamental right of every citizen to live in a healthy environment.

He warned that inadequate access to safe and private toilet facilities could undermine people’s health, security, dignity, education and participation in economic and social activities.

The permanent secretary therefore called for inclusive policies and investments that would address the sanitation needs of women, girls, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups.
