title: Protecting your device from hackers
description:
In plain terms, a hacker is someone who thoroughly studies computer systems, devices or networks to understand how they work, modify their behaviour and achieve specific goals.
These goals can either be for positive reasons or – as is common in many instances – for negative and even destructive purp
content:
In plain terms, a hacker is someone who thoroughly studies computer systems, devices or networks to understand how they work, modify their behaviour and achieve specific goals.

These goals can either be for positive reasons or – as is common in many instances – for negative and even destructive purposes.

Therefore, hackers are differentiated by the context that warrants their operations, the permissions given to them and the purpose behind the use of their skills.

Tech experts categorise hackers differently. White Hat Hackers (also called ethical hackers) are skilled security specialists who legally probe systems and software to find vulnerabilities and help organisations fix them to prevent malicious individuals from exploiting them.

Conversely, cybercriminals are generally known as Black Hat Hackers. These are individuals who gain unauthorised access to systems for malicious purposes.

They are known to disrupt networks or computer systems for illegal profit, steal financial data and hold data for ransom using malware – software or code they utilise to intercept or disrupt important information.

Last month, the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation, in collaboration with international partners, announced the arrest of nine suspects in Nigeria and the seizure of 53 electronic devices as part of an operation targeting international scam and cybercrime networks.

Similarly, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission and the Nigerian Police Force National Cybercrime Centre have carried out multiple stings (including arrests in Lagos and Delta states) targeting online impersonation, cryptocurrency investment scams and romance fraud networks, which often centre around Black Hat Hackers.

When hackers gain unauthorised access to your phone, computer or smart home appliance, they can perform a wide range of damaging actions, depending on the type of malware or exploit used.

They can hijack usernames, passwords and saved browser credentials. Some of them harvest credit card numbers, bank details, personal IDs, photos and private messages.

Using stolen data, cybercriminals can open fraudulent bank or credit card accounts, request new PINs, sell your information on the dark web or, worse, spy on you remotely.

“There are spyware or zero-click attacks that can secretly turn on your device’s camera and microphone to record you or snap photos without your knowledge. Hackers can also track your real-time GPS coordinates and movement history. They can log everything you type or take screenshots of your active apps.

“Many of these criminals can trick your mobile carrier into transferring your phone number to their SIM card, intercepting your calls, texts and two-factor authentication security codes from banks, and from there, they siphon funds from your account. There are also some who change your social media account passwords or lock your entire device and, in some cases, demand payment to restore access,” a cybersecurity expert, David Odes, explained.

Odes further stated that when these hackers gain access to devices, their activities can result in rapid battery drain, severe overheating, high data spikes and sluggish performance.

How to protect your device from hackers:

Be wary of suspicious messages

Posing as bankers, co-workers or tech brands, hackers can trick people into revealing their passwords, debit card numbers or personal identification details and use this information to install malware on their devices. This method is known as phishing.

“If you receive an unsolicited email or SMS, or a phone call from a bank asking you to send them a code, or you get a message on a messaging platform asking you to click on a link to claim some benefits, be very careful. You may be clicking on suspicious links or a malware file, which can cause your account to be compromised,” Odes advised.

Check your device

A regular audit of apps and devices will enable users to scrutinise third-party app permissions or notice if their phones begin to frequently overheat or become slow in operation.

“This can also happen to your laptop. If you notice that the camera lens is suddenly turned on without your permission, contact your tech support at work. Ensure you also remove any old accounts, unused apps or unfamiliar linked devices from your security dashboard,” a tech consultant, Solomon Nwadike, advised.

Stop reusing passwords

Nwadike advised that passwords for devices, bank apps, social media accounts and platforms used for online transactions should be varied and unique.

“You can use the password manager to generate and store long, unique passwords for every account. Avoid repeating passwords so a breach on one site doesn’t affect the others,” he said.

Enable multi-factor authentication

Adding a second verification step, which could include a code through an authenticator app or a security key, can help protect your device.

“This can safeguard your email, bank and social media accounts. This type of authentication will help block most unauthorised access even if your password leaks to hackers,” Odes said.

Update regularly

Consistently updating software on mobile apps, smart TVs and other devices will prevent them from becoming compromised and help safeguard them from hackers.

“When you regularly update software on your device, it will look for newly discovered security flaws and fix them before hackers can exploit them,” Nwadike advised.

The post Protecting your device from hackers appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
author: Victor Ayeni

title: When love meets genetics: The importance of genotype testing (2)
description: There is a misconception that genotype testing is only necessary when preparing for marriage. In reality, knowing your genotype is important regardless of your relationship status. It is valuable health information that everyone should have, rather than something to investigate only when wedding pla
content:
There is a misconception that genotype testing is only necessary when preparing for marriage. In reality, knowing your genotype is important regardless of your relationship status. It is valuable health information that everyone should have, rather than something to investigate only when wedding plans are underway.

Young people should be encouraged to establish their genotype early, instead of waiting until they are considering marriage or starting a family. Parents, schools, healthcare professionals and community organisations all have a role to play in improving awareness.

Genotype education should form part of wider conversations about health and inheritance, helping young people understand their genetic background before they reach the stage of making important family decisions.

In Nigeria, where family expectations, cultural traditions and religious beliefs can influence marriage decisions, conversations about genotype need to become more open.

Churches, mosques, schools and community leaders can help normalise screening without creating stigma around people living with sickle cell disease. These conversations should be approached with sensitivity and accurate information, rather than fear or condemnation.

It is equally important that genotype results are accurate. Testing should be conducted through reputable healthcare facilities. Anyone with uncertain or conflicting results should seek confirmation from an appropriate laboratory or specialist.

Genetic counselling can help individuals and couples understand their results, the way haemoglobin conditions are inherited and the possible implications for future pregnancies.

For couples who discover that they have a combination of genotypes that could result in a child being born with sickle cell disease, professional counselling is particularly important. They need an opportunity to ask questions, understand the risks and explore the reproductive options available to them.

Depending on their circumstances, these may include prenatal testing, IVF with preimplantation genetic testing, adoption or other family-building choices. Not every option will be suitable, affordable or accessible to every couple, but having accurate information allows them to consider their circumstances carefully.

These decisions can be emotionally challenging. Couples may face pressure from relatives, religious communities or society. Some may feel guilty, confused or frightened about what the future holds.

Others may struggle with the fear that a medical diagnosis could determine the direction of their relationship. This is why conversations about genotype should be handled with compassion. Couples need support and reliable advice, not condemnation.

As someone who lives with sickle cell disease, I understand that this is not simply a discussion about percentages, genetic combinations or medical terminology. Behind every statistic is a human being.

Living with SCD can involve recurrent pain, hospital admissions, fatigue and complications that disrupt education, employment, relationships and family life.

Some people experience relatively mild symptoms, while others face serious and life-changing complications. The condition can affect not only the individual but also parents, partners, children and other family members who provide support and care.

It is therefore important that discussions about genotype testing do not inadvertently suggest that people living with sickle cell disease are less deserving of love, marriage, parenthood or fulfilling lives.

People with SCD deserve the same opportunities to experience love, build families and pursue their ambitions.

They should not be defined solely by their diagnosis. The objective of genotype awareness is not to stigmatise anyone or make people feel that their worth as a potential partner depends on a laboratory result. It is to ensure that prospective parents understand the possibilities and can make informed reproductive choices.

Faith communities also have an important role to play. For many people, marriage is not simply a personal commitment; it is a spiritual and family decision.

Religious leaders can encourage couples to seek medical information and genetic counselling while reminding their congregations that people living with sickle cell disease deserve dignity, acceptance and compassion. Faith and medical knowledge do not have to compete. They can work alongside one another.

Parents should also avoid leaving these conversations until their children are old enough to contemplate marriage. Genotype awareness should be introduced as part of responsible health education.

Schools and youth organisations can help young people understand inheritance, testing and the importance of knowing their family health history. The earlier this knowledge is acquired, the less likely it is to become a source of panic or conflict later in life.

Genotype testing should not be treated as an afterthought or an administrative requirement to be completed shortly before a wedding. It should be part of responsible reproductive health education.

Couples need the opportunity to discuss their results honestly, understand the possible implications and make decisions without pressure from relatives or society.

Ultimately, love and genetic compatibility are two different things. Love may bring two people together, but knowledge helps them navigate the decisions that follow. Having a difficult conversation about genotype does not diminish love; it can demonstrate a willingness to approach the future with honesty and responsibility.

We cannot prevent every genetic condition, but we can improve awareness, access to reliable testing and opportunities for informed decision-making. We can also challenge the stigma that surrounds sickle cell disease and replace judgement with understanding.

The question, therefore, is not whether love can overcome genetics. It is whether we are prepared to combine love with knowledge, responsibility and informed choices.

Knowing your genotype does not determine whom you should love. It empowers you to understand the genetic implications of having children together. That knowledge, acquired early and used responsibly, can make a meaningful difference to the decisions we make about our future families.

title: Pay or park: Ogun motorcyclists allege N20,000 police extortion
description:

content:
For many residents of Ibafo, in the Obafemi Owode Local Government Area of Ogun State, returning home late from work has become a regular experience.

After spending several hours battling traffic on their way from Lagos, some commuters arrive at the Ibafo junction only to discover that commercial motorcyclists, popularly known as okada riders, are no longer readily available to take them to their destinations.

While some are left stranded at the junction, others resort to trekking for several minutes before finding a means of transportation to their homes.

The situation, Saturday PUNCH gathered, is linked to alleged repeated arrests and extortion of commercial motorcyclists by police officers attached to the Ibafo Police Station over their late-night operations.

Some of the affected riders alleged that officers, particularly those operating in plain clothes, seize their motorcycles and demand between N20,000 and N30,000 before releasing them.

They claimed that at least 10 motorcyclists fall victim to the alleged practice every night, forcing many riders to abandon their operations after certain hours for fear of being arrested.

The development, according to the riders, has not only affected their daily earnings but also made transportation difficult for residents who return from work late at night.

‘We pay to retrieve seized bikes’

One of the affected commercial motorcyclists, Haruna Sanni, told Saturday PUNCH that he paid N25,000 to retrieve his motorcycle after it was allegedly seized by police officers for operating at night.

“I paid N25,000 last week after my bike was seized,” he said.

Another rider, Mahmud Kebbi, said he paid N20,000 after he was arrested around 11 pm in the previous month.

According to him, retrieving his motorcycle was a frustrating experience, as he had to make several visits to the police station before he could secure its release.

“I paid N20,000 in cash. I was caught around 11 pm last month. I had to go with our chairman before I could retrieve the bike. If I had gone alone, I would not have been able to get it.

“I went there early in the morning, but I was told that the person who arrested me was not on site. Again, I went there around 12 pm, and I was told he was yet to arrive. It was not until 5 pm that I was able to get the bike.

“It was not easy at all. In fact, I only had N10,000 with me. I had to borrow another N10,000 from someone to complete the money,” he said.

Kebbi appealed to the state government and police authorities to intervene, arguing that commercial motorcyclists provided an important transportation service to residents who returned from Lagos late in the evening.

He said, “The government has to intervene because we are always out at night so that people returning from Lagos after work can find motorcycles to take them home.”

Similarly, another rider, Salisu Ahmed, alleged that the situation was peculiar to Ibafo, claiming that commercial motorcyclists operated at night without similar harassment in neighbouring communities such as Mowe, Arepo and Magboro.

He said his motorcycle was once taken to the Ibafo Police Station, where he paid N20,000 to secure its release.

“They carried my bike to Ibafo Police Station. I had to go there early in the morning, around 5 am, to retrieve it, and I paid N20,000. It was my people who contributed the money. It was not easy at all.

“Since then, I have been running away from them. Even now that you see me, I will not get to the junction. Even when I carried you, I had watched you for some time before approaching you because those policemen do not wear uniforms. They appear like civilians. You will not know they are police officers,” Ahmed alleged.

Ahmed said he had been arrested several times, with the amounts allegedly demanded from him varying on different occasions.

“I have been caught multiple times. The first time they caught me, I paid N5,000. Subsequently, I paid N10,000, N15,000 and now N20,000. They said it was because I was working at night,” he added.

He further alleged that his brother, Kabiru Mohammed, was arrested last Friday and also paid N20,000 before his motorcycle was released.

Two days in police custody

The alleged enforcement has also affected residents who use motorcycles for personal transportation rather than commercial activities.

A bricklayer, Sunday Ojo, who lives in Halleluyah Quarters, Ibafo, told Saturday PUNCH that he was arrested by police officers wearing jackets while travelling to pick up his wife from her shop last Friday.

Ojo said he explained to the officers that he was not a commercial motorcyclist but was allegedly ignored.

He added that his motorcycle was seized, forcing him to make several trips to the police station before it was eventually released on Tuesday night.

“I was going to pick my wife up from her shop when they stopped me and seized my bike, saying I was working at night. I told them I was not a commercial motorcyclist, but all my pleas fell on deaf ears.

“I visited the police station multiple times before I could get the bike on Tuesday night. I offered the officer who arrested me N15,000, but he rejected it, saying it had to be N20,000,” he alleged.

Ojo said the incident disrupted his work for several days, leaving him without his motorcycle and affecting his ability to move around.

Lagos workers stranded

Beyond the financial implications for the riders, residents say the alleged police operations have created transportation challenges for people who depend on commercial motorcycles to complete their journeys home after work.

Many residents of Ibafo work in Lagos and return to the community late at night after enduring heavy traffic on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway.

A civil servant in Lagos State, Taofeek Adedeji, said he had repeatedly struggled to find motorcycles at the Ibafo junction after returning from work.

According to him, the absence of riders on the roads at night has forced some commuters to trek considerable distances to their homes.

“There are many times when I will get stuck in traffic in Lagos and, on getting to Ibafo, I will find it difficult to get a bike because of their fear of being caught by the police.

“If you get to the junction past 10 pm, sometimes you will see people stranded, waiting for bikes, but the riders will not come because they are running away from the police. We will have to trek for about 10 minutes before finding one,” he said.

A petrol attendant at the Ibafo junction, who requested anonymity, also corroborated the account, saying he had made arrangements with a private motorcyclist to pick him up after work because of the difficulty in getting transportation late at night.

He said he had witnessed several motorcycles being seized by police officers on different occasions.

“Because of this issue, I have made efforts to get a private motorcyclist to pick me up after work because we close late.

“The police have arrested many motorcyclists in my presence on different occasions. I hope the government can intervene. The money they are demanding from these people is too much,” he said.

‘This has persisted for two years’

These allegations, according to the unit chairman of the Amalgamated Commercial Motorcycle, Tricycle Repairers, Owners and Riders Association of Nigeria, Sunday Idowu, are not new.

Idowu said the union had been dealing with complaints of motorcycle seizures and alleged extortion by police officers in the area for more than two years.

He disclosed that union officials frequently visited the police station to secure the release of motorcycles belonging to their members, adding that several complaints had been lodged with the authorities without any lasting solution.

Speaking with Saturday PUNCH, Idowu said the situation had become increasingly difficult for the union and its members.

“It is almost every day that we are visiting the police station to bail the bikes of our members. It is getting out of hand.

“Sometimes, they have to pay N30,000 before retrieving their bikes. It is only if you know someone in the station that your bike can be released with N20,000 or N15,000,” he alleged.

The union chairman’s account suggests that the alleged practice has become a recurring challenge for commercial motorcyclists operating in the community, with some riders depending on union officials and personal connections to retrieve their impounded motorcycles.

Police keep mum

Saturday PUNCH sought clarification from the state Police Public Relations Officer, Oluseyi Babaseyi, on whether the police were enforcing any directive prohibiting commercial motorcyclists from operating at night in the state.

A text message was sent to seek his reaction to the allegations of extortion and the reported demand for between N20,000 and N30,000 to release seized motorcycles, and whether there were legal provisions backing such enforcement.

However, Babaseyi had yet to respond to the enquiries as of the time of filing this report.

The post Pay or park: Ogun motorcyclists allege N20,000 police extortion appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: NUC approves medical university in Anambra, opens December 1
description:
…Tuition starts at N3m, says VC



By Vincent Ujumadu



The National Universities Commission (NUC) has approved the Transatlantic University of Medicine and Health Sciences, Umuchukwu, in Orumba South Local Government Area of Anambra State, with academic activities scheduled to commence on December
content:
…Tuition starts at N3m, says VC

By Vincent Ujumadu

The National Universities Commission (NUC) has approved the Transatlantic University of Medicine and Health Sciences, Umuchukwu, in Orumba South Local Government Area of Anambra State, with academic activities scheduled to commence on December 1, 2026.

The Vice-Chancellor, Prof. Charles Esimone, disclosed this while briefing journalists at the university, saying admissions began on October 1, while lectures were expected to commence on December 3.

Esimone said the NUC had formally communicated the university’s approval to the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB), which had subsequently issued the institution an identification code to enable prospective students to apply for admission.

He explained that candidates seeking to transfer to the university would be required to change their first-choice institution to Transatlantic University before accessing the platform for the post-UTME screening exercise.

“The students who transferred to our university will have to change their first choice to our university before they can access the platform for post-UTME. That process started in October.

“So we have started the admission process and verifying the students’ credentials before approving their admission letters. They will then get their admission numbers and pay the necessary fees before the commencement of lectures when we are sure the numbers are there. Orientation will then follow,” he said.

On tuition fees, the vice-chancellor described the university’s charges as affordable, despite the high cost of providing quality education.

He said students in programmes other than Medicine and Surgery would pay about N3 million annually, while those studying Medicine and Surgery would pay approximately N5.5 million.

Esimone explained that the university could not have commenced operations without securing the necessary NUC approval, adding that the commission had conducted physical inspections of its facilities, infrastructure, academic manpower and curriculum before granting the approval.

According to him, the NUC subsequently presented its findings to its board, which reviewed and approved the institution before recommending it to the Federal Executive Council for a provisional licence.

He said the provisional licence required the university to deposit N500 million as a financial guarantee to protect students and staff in the event of the institution’s failure to meet its obligations.

“If at any time the university fails to meet its obligations to them, they can petition the NUC and that money will be used to offset what they are owed,” he explained.

The vice-chancellor said the provisional licence was valid for three years, after which the institution’s operations would be reviewed.

He added that the university had successfully undergone resource verification and would invite the NUC for full accreditation after its first year of operation.

On the institution’s medical training facilities, Esimone said the founder planned to establish a teaching hospital to support clinical training and other medical programmes.

He disclosed that the teaching hospital was expected to take between two and three years to complete, while arrangements were already underway for the importation of medical equipment.

In the interim, he said the university had signed memoranda of understanding with some teaching hospitals to provide clinical training for its medical students.

Esimone also disclosed that some expatriate academics working with the university’s proprietor in the United States would periodically come to Nigeria to teach students.

He said the university would occupy the first to 11th floors of the building, while the proposed teaching hospital would occupy the 12th to 17th floors.

title: Waste crisis: LAWMA acting MD unveils 60-day action plan
description:
…Warns staff against laxity, promises operational overhaul



By Olasunkanmi Akoni



The newly appointed Acting Managing Director of the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA), Olajuwon Akinyemi, has unveiled a 60-day emergency action plan to tackle waste management challenges across Lagos State,
content:
…Warns staff against laxity, promises operational overhaul

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

The newly appointed Acting Managing Director of the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA), Olajuwon Akinyemi, has unveiled a 60-day emergency action plan to tackle waste management challenges across Lagos State, warning staff against indiscipline and poor performance.

Akinyemi, who has assumed office amid growing concerns over waste accumulation across the metropolis, said the plan was aimed at clearing waste backlogs, strengthening regulatory enforcement and restoring the agency’s operational efficiency.

He disclosed this on Friday while addressing management and staff at a workers’ forum held at LAWMA’s headquarters in Ijora-Olopa, Lagos.

Accompanied by the Acting Executive Director, Operations, Dr. Olorunwa Tijani, and the Executive Director, Finance, Kunle Adebiyi, the acting managing director called for renewed commitment, discipline and professionalism among workers.

He said repositioning the agency would require active participation and dedication from personnel at all levels.

“We are bringing in resilience and a new paradigm shift. It is a new wave in handling waste in Lagos.

“We already have the template to transform LAWMA positively. All we need to do is recreate, modernise and do better than in the past,” Akinyemi said.

Outlining the 60-day action plan, he said personnel would be redeployed across the state’s three operational districts based on their familiarity with the respective areas to strengthen field monitoring and improve response times.

He also announced plans to establish decentralised operational hubs to improve supervision, facilitate faster interventions and address waste disposal blackspots across the state.

On indiscriminate waste disposal, Akinyemi said the agency would intensify public enlightenment on waste sorting at source and responsible disposal practices.

He said traditional rulers, Community Development Association (CDA) leaders, market associations and artisans would be mobilised to promote compliance with proper waste management practices.

The acting managing director also called for stronger collaboration with Private Sector Participation (PSP) operators and urged residents to comply with approved waste collection tariffs to sustain service delivery.

On staff welfare, Akinyemi assured workers that their well-being remained a priority, disclosing that efforts were underway to procure Compressed Natural Gas (CNG)-powered buses to address transportation challenges.

Earlier, Tijani called for urgent action to revitalise LAWMA’s operational framework, saying the agency needed an immediate overhaul to improve field performance.

Similarly, Adebiyi said the success of the 60-day plan would depend on prudent financial management, accountability and effective collaboration across the agency’s directorates.

He urged workers to embrace professionalism and shared responsibility in implementing the proposed reforms.

Following the meeting, Akinyemi led members of the management team on an inspection tour of various departments at the headquarters to assess operations and identify immediate challenges requiring attention.

title: Akodo-Ise: Sea incursion threatens to wipe out Lagos coastal community
description:
Residents of Akodo-Ise in Ibeju-Lekki area of Lagos lament how advancing seawater is eroding their livelihoods, cultural identity and hopes of remaining on their ancestral land, DARE AKOGUN reports.
The Baale of Akoko-Ise, Lateef Temitope, no longer sees the sea as a source of livelihood for fisherm
content:
Residents of Akodo-Ise in Ibeju-Lekki area of Lagos lament how advancing seawater is eroding their livelihoods, cultural identity and hopes of remaining on their ancestral land, DARE AKOGUN reports.

The Baale of Akoko-Ise, Lateef Temitope, no longer sees the sea as a source of livelihood for fishermen.

It has become a threat to the community he inherited, the family home where he grew up and the ancestral land that connects generations of his family.

Located in Ibeju-Lekki Local Government Area of Lagos State, rising waters have swallowed the chief family’s house and coconut farmland, forcing him to move into a rented apartment.

Places that once defined his childhood have either disappeared beneath the water or become increasingly difficult to reach.

About 20 years ago, Temitope recalled, walking from the family’s coconut plantation to the ocean took roughly 30 minutes. His father’s house was only about five minutes from the farm.

The Baale said the community began noticing significant changes around 2016, as seawater increasingly encroached on the shoreline and threatened homes and farms.

By 2023, the situation had become so severe that about 40 palm and coconut trees were falling into the water daily for roughly a month.

Residents who depended on the land for food and income also lamented to Saturday PUNCH about the losses they have incurred and how their source of livelihood is gradually disappearing.

“We did not know what was happening until some environmental people came and explained it to us,” Temitope said, recalling how residents were introduced to the term ‘ocean surge’.

Since then, the community has watched the water claim homes, farmland and public infrastructure.

The Baale said the local primary school was also swallowed by the sea last year, leaving residents increasingly anxious about the future of their settlement.

Fishing under threat

For generations, fishing has sustained families in Akodo-Ise. The community’s proximity to the Atlantic Ocean and its network of waterways provided residents with access to fish and other aquatic resources, supporting fishermen, fish sellers and processors.

But residents say the changing coastline has made fishing increasingly difficult and expensive.

Temitope said the fishermen who once worked relatively close to the community now travel several kilometres into the lagoon in search of catches that are often smaller than what they used to bring home.

Women who buy fish for processing and trading also struggle to obtain enough fresh supplies locally. Some now travel to Epe to purchase fish, adding transport costs to already strained household businesses.

The threat is not limited to declining catches. Residents also recount incidents in which strong waves damaged or swept away fishing equipment, leaving fishermen with substantial replacement costs.

The Baale recalled an incident about two years ago in which waves reportedly dragged away approximately 15 fishing boats and nets. Some of the affected fishermen had to borrow money to replace their equipment.

A 35-year-old fisherman, Seun Rasaki, described the uncertainty which has now become part of his everyday life.

He said he now worries that his boat and equipment could be swept away whenever the water becomes turbulent. To reduce the risk, he moves his boat closer to his house and keeps its engine indoors.

Another fisherman, Femi Johnson, 42, said he was among those who lost a boat and fishing net during the incident involving about 15 fishermen. He subsequently took a cooperative loan to replace his boat, net and engine.

The financial burden has continued beyond the cost of replacing the equipment. Johnson said he now spends considerably more on fuel because he has to travel farther to find fish.

“Before, five litres of fuel could take me for a fishing trip, but now I use about 35 litres,” he said.

At the prevailing price of N1,400 per litre, that amounts to about N49,000 for fuel alone on a trip, before other operating expenses are considered.

For a fisherman whose income depends on the size of his catch, the additional cost leaves less money to support his family and repay loans.

Wale Mutiu, another fisherman, said his monthly earnings, which previously ranged between N300,000 and N500,000, had fallen sharply. He now struggles to make N100,000 in some months.

He also said he had lost about three boats within a year, with replacing one costing between N2.5m and N3m.

The women in the fish trade are also hit by the layers of hardship caused by the advancing seawater in the community.

A fisherwoman, Esther Fawole, 35, said her house was destroyed in August, leaving her and her family to cope with the loss of shelter while her husband’s fishing business also suffered.

She said her husband’s boat was damaged, while the reduced availability of fish made it difficult for her to sustain her trading business.

Fawole now smokes and sells fish around the Law School area of Ajah and sometimes joins friends travelling to Epe market to buy supplies.

Her husband, she said, has resorted to riding a commercial tricycle for another person while saving towards buying a replacement boat engine.

A widow, Wuraola Sanusi, said she had also lost an inherited coconut farm and could no longer depend on the community’s fishing activities for a steady supply of fish.

The 39-year-old now travels to Epe to buy fish, but transport expenses reduce her profit. With four children to support, she said the additional costs have made it increasingly difficult to meet household needs.

Ancestral land and graves disappearing

Beyond the loss of homes and livelihoods, residents say the advancing sea is threatening something that cannot easily be replaced – their ancestral heritage.

Speaking on how his family’s history is rooted in the community, Temitope, the Baale, said his forefathers are buried there, and the land holds memories that cannot simply be transferred to another settlement.

He said about 20 ancestral burial grounds had been relocated because of the advancing water. One of the affected graves belonged to his grandfather, who died in 1956.

The relocation of ancestral remains carries significance beyond the physical movement of a grave.

In Yoruba communities, burial grounds can represent family continuity, ancestral identity and spiritual connections between the living and the dead.

Relocating remains may also involve traditional rites and other cultural obligations, depending on the family and community.

Temitope said the community’s attachment to its ancestral territory makes relocation a difficult option, even as residents confront growing environmental risks.

“We have nowhere else to go. This is where our forefathers lived and where they were buried,” he said.

His concern is that, without meaningful intervention, residents could eventually be forced away from the place that defines their identity.

An uncertain future

Temitope estimated the population of Akodo-Ise at between 600 and 800 people; he said residents were increasingly worried about the safety of their homes, particularly at night, when the sound and movement of the water heighten fears that more land could be lost.

“We cry out to the government that time when Akodo-Ise and about 12 neighbouring settlements staged a protest in 2025, officials of the Lagos State Ministry of Waterfront Infrastructure Development visited the community about two years ago; we didn’t receive any clear feedback on what action would follow the visit,” he said.

The other communities he identified included Imedu, Akodo-Ise, Okun-Ise, Folu, Ikegun, Lekia, Oke Gelu, Oto Ilu, Ori Yanrin, Ita Maarun, Apaki and Ijekodo; their concerns, he said, were driven by the fear that the advancing water could eventually make several settlements uninhabitable.

The Baale said he hoped the government would consider interventions similar to coastal protection projects undertaken in parts of Lagos, including Victoria Island.

What is driving the sea inland?

Although residents describe the changes they have witnessed, establishing the precise causes of coastal retreat in Akodo-Ise requires scientific investigation.

According to scientists, coastal erosion, sea-level rise, storm surges and tidal flooding are related but distinct processes.

While erosion involves the removal of sediment from the shoreline, sea-level rise raises the baseline level of the ocean and storm surges produce temporary rises in water levels during storms.

Tidal flooding occurs when high tides inundate low-lying areas, and environmentalists have said these processes can interact, making vulnerable coastal settlements more exposed to flooding and land loss.

Checks by Saturday PUNCH showed that a 2026 study titled ‘Monitoring Coastal Erosion-Driven LULC and Shoreline Changes Along the Lagos Coastal Corridor with Sentinel-2 Imagery and DSAS’, published in the journal Geomatics, Natural Hazards and Risk, appears to provide a wider picture of the pressures affecting the Lagos coastline.

The researchers, Ahmed Abdulrahaman, Aqil Tariq,  Zuliehat Abdullahi, Oluwatosin, Abolaji Afolayan, Dmitry Kucher, Sajid Ullah, Hela Elmannai and Yahia Said, examined land-use and land-cover changes along a 180-kilometre coastal corridor between 2015 and 2025, using satellite imagery and the Digital Shoreline Analysis System.

The study found that built-up areas increased from 22 per cent, representing 283.61 square kilometres, in 2015 to 53 per cent, or 683.96 square kilometres, in 2025.

Vegetation cover declined from 31 per cent to 19 per cent, while the proportion classified as water bodies fell from 19 per cent to four per cent.

Wetlands, however, increased from nine per cent to 24 per cent, a change the researchers associated with factors including inundation and sediment redistribution, alongside the limitations of land-cover classification.

The analysis also used 3,658 shoreline transects to assess coastal movement. It recorded erosion rates of up to 25.1 metres per year in parts of the Okun-Ajah and Ibeju-Lekki axis, while some depositional areas recorded accretion of up to 32.29 metres per year.

The findings point to significant and uneven changes along the Lagos coastline.

Commenting on this, an environmental expert at the Greening Space Institute, Grace Adeyinka, said activities that disrupt the natural movement of sediment could destabilise shorelines.

She explained that dredging and major coastal developments could alter sediment flows, potentially leaving some sections of the coast more exposed to wave action.

“Where sand is no longer replenished naturally at the same rate it is removed, waves can exert greater pressure on the shoreline, increasing the risk of erosion,” Adeyinka said.

Vanishing natural protection

The mangroves that form part of the coastal ecosystem also matter to the future of communities such as Akodo-Ise.

Mangroves provide habitats for fish and other aquatic organisms; help stabilise shorelines and can reduce the force of waves. Their dense roots trap sediment and create sheltered environments where young fish, crabs and shrimp can develop.

The Managing Consultant of SmitBridge Consulting, Dr Samuel Babatunde, said mangroves play a critical role in sustaining fisheries.

“Mangroves are the nursery of the fishery. Many fish, shrimp and crab species spend their early life among those roots. Lose the nursery and catches fall, which hits the main livelihood in Ayetoro,” he said.

Although Babatunde, who is also a lead technical and consortium partner to the Ondo State Oil Producing Areas Development Commission, made the observation in reference to Ayetoro, the ecological function he described appear relevant to mangrove ecosystems elsewhere.

He further stated that mangrove restoration must be based on the conditions of the site, warning that planting seedlings along an actively eroding shoreline without measures to reduce wave energy and retain sediment could lead to failure.

Babatunde cited a mangrove-planting exercise undertaken at Akodo-Ise in May 2026 with Rotary and other partners, during which some seedlings reportedly survived while others were washed away.

The experience, he said, demonstrated the importance of understanding local hydrology and shoreline conditions before undertaking restoration.

A study conducted in 2026 by Senakpon Tcheton, a GreenSTEM scholar from the University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa, provided further insight into the relationship between mangroves and livelihoods in Lagos.

Working under the supervision of Professor Ismail Ibraheem, and Dr Temitope Sogbanmu of the University of Lagos Department of Zoology, Tcheton conducted field research between February and August 2026 on the ecological role of mangrove forests in the state.

One of the study’s important findings was that mangrove roots served as fish nurseries and were central to local livelihoods. The research also identified stronger grassroots conservation efforts in the community than those observed during the preliminary assessment in Epe.

Nigeria’s promises to protect its coastal communities are increasingly being tested by the reality confronting residents of Akodo-Ise, where advancing seawater is steadily eroding homes, livelihoods and ancestral heritage.

Plans by FG and Lagos

Over the years, the Federal Government has made ambitious commitments to protect marine ecosystems, restore mangroves and strengthen the resilience of vulnerable coastal settlements under its Third Nationally Determined Contribution.

Submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in September 2025, Nigeria’s NDC 3.0 sets out a range of measures that could make a difference to communities such as Akodo-Ise.

They include the conservation and restoration of 13,000 hectares of mangroves, the protection of coastal wetlands, the establishment of marine protected areas and measures to make fisheries more resilient to climate change.

The document also recognises that climate change threatens more than the physical environment.

It proposes insurance for vulnerable entrepreneurs, support for climate-affected livelihoods, disaster-risk management plans for frontline communities and mechanisms to address climate-induced displacement.

It further commits to identifying and protecting cultural heritage sites threatened by climate change.

Similarly, the Lagos State Government has acknowledged the severity of coastal erosion along its shoreline.

In May 2025, the state Commissioner for Waterfront Infrastructure Development, Yacoob Alebiosu, announced plans to strengthen coastal protection through partnerships and the possible deployment of groyne technology.

The commissioner also acknowledged the losses suffered by communities including Akodo-Ise, Itoke and Origanrigan.

In June 2026, the state government disclosed that it had engaged Dutch consultancy firm CDR International to undertake studies that would guide shoreline-protection interventions. It also said it was strengthening surveillance against illegal dredging and working with relevant stakeholders to address coastal degradation.

The funding question is equally important. Nigeria’s NDC 3.0 estimates that the country will require about $337bn between 2026 and 2035 to implement its climate commitments, including approximately $141.5bn for adaptation.

Financing required

Speaking to Saturday PUNCH, the Executive Director of the International Climate Change Development Initiative, Olumide Idowu, said that the national financing requirement is not the same as money released for vulnerable communities.

“Without clearly identified allocations, implementation timelines and accountable institutions, commitments to restore ecosystems and protect livelihoods risk remaining distant from the people who need them most.

“There is also the question of coordination. Protecting Akodo-Ise requires more than planting mangroves or constructing a coastal barrier. It involves scientific assessment of shoreline changes, regulation of dredging, monitoring of coastal developments, protection of fishing grounds, livelihood support and the preservation of cultural heritage.

“The challenge is particularly urgent because coastal interventions must be based on the physical characteristics of each location. Poorly designed groynes, seawalls or other structures can alter sediment movement and transfer erosion to neighbouring stretches of coastline,” Idowu said.

Lagos keeps mum

Saturday PUNCH learnt that the Lagos State Government divided responsibilities for addressing coastal and environmental challenges among relevant ministries.
While the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources, headed by Tokunbo Wahab, is responsible for flooding, ocean surges and climate adaptation, the Ministry of Waterfront Infrastructure Development, led by Dayo Bush-Alebiosu, oversees coastal erosion and shoreline protection projects, including the construction of groynes.

However, efforts to obtain Wahab’s reaction to the concerns raised by residents were unsuccessful. WhatsApp messages sent to his phone were not answered, while calls to his number did not connect as of the time of filing this report.

Also, attempts to reach the Commissioner for Physical Planning and Urban Development, Dr Oluyinka Abiodun Olumide, were unsuccessful. His ministry works with the Ministry of Waterfront Infrastructure Development on enforcement against illegal dredging and reclamation activities along the Lagos Lagoon.

title: What Nigeria must do to start making progress – Prof Yusufu Turaki
description:
•2027 campaigns more about character assassination than issues
Elder statesman, Prof Yusufu Turaki, has said the Middle Belt would not have a political voice and be politically recognised and respected by all Nigerians until the country constitutionally grants her a regional status as it was done to
content:
•2027 campaigns more about character assassination than issues

Elder statesman, Prof Yusufu Turaki, has said the Middle Belt would not have a political voice and be politically recognised and respected by all Nigerians until the country constitutionally grants her a regional status as it was done to Mid-West and Calabar Ogoja Rivers (COR).

The scholar noted that it is the debt that Nigeria owes the Middle Belt.

He spoke against the background of a recent visit of the Middle Belt elders led by Lt Gen T Y Danjuma (Retd) to President Bola Tinubu, which generated some remarks in the North. 

In an interview with VINCENT KALU, the Professor of Theology and Social Ethic who is also a Middle Belt leader, stressed that, ‘competence, capacity and integrity’ which are the universal determinants in choosing leadership don’t apply in Nigeria, because Nigerians, he said, use parochial and local language of their gods of ethnicity, religion and region to win elections.

The 2027 elections are around the corner. What are your expectations?

I pray that the elections would be peaceful, given the rising violence of political campaigns. 

What do you make out of the campaign messages?

The trend of the campaigns tends towards character assassination than political issues. We need issue-based campaigns and not demonising political fellows or parties.

The electioneering has been characterised by hostility, violent attacks, threats, and intolerance. Many of the contestants have had their convoys attacked. What is your take on this? And what should the authorities do before they escalate into anarchy?

The British Colonial Masters built Nigerian political philosophy and practice on three major pillars: ethnicity, religion and region. No one wins election in Nigeria without one, or two or three of these pillars. Nigeria’s political class have been schooled, trained, nurtured, groomed and conditioned in the arts and sciences of these three political pillars.  Politics in Nigeria is the battle of the gods of ethnicity, religion and region. The nature of Nigeria’s politics has turned these three political pillars into the battle of the gods of ethnicity, religion and region. Politics has turned good ethnicity into a god whom Nigerians’ worship. It has also turned religion into a god whom Nigerians’ worship, and as well as turning the region into a god whom Nigerians’ worship. The hostility, violent attacks, threat and intolerance are simply the outcome of the battle of the gods of ethnicity, religion and region. The third pillar to ethnicity and religion, which is region, is not going to come in 2027, but instituted right from the beginning.

The battle of the gods of ethnicity, religion and region has been charged by the sectional and divisive political rhetoric. The politicians are the pundits of these ethnic gods, religious gods and regional gods. The battle is converting Nigerians into their ethnic gods, religious gods and regional gods, hoping to win elections.

More than 60 years after independence, and 55 years after the civil war, why should ethnic and religious considerations be on the front burner in choosing Nigeria’s leadership, instead of competence, capacity and integrity?

The words, “competence, capacity and integrity” are of universal language, while Nigerians use parochial and local language of their gods of ethnicity, religion and region. Their languages could not transcend the boundary of their ethnicity, or the boundary of their religion, or the boundary of their region. Whenever political agreements are made across the board, that is universal, but after the communiqué signed or verbal or by consensus, the political pundits would turn to consult their tribal gods, or their religious gods, or their regional gods, and what ensues is always the battle of the gods in the field of politics. The game of politics is mathematical, rigging, manipulation and legalism.

For good 60 years of independence, Nigerians are yet to have learnt the ABC of the universal language of politics. Democracy can be turned into ‘Democrazy’

Last week Middle Belt leaders led by Lt. Gen. T. Y. Danjuma visited President Bola Tinubu, and endorsed his re-election. Does it mean a new dawn for the region, or political deals were cut?

Just prior to independence, the ethnic minorities in Western Nigeria, Eastern Nigeria and Northern Nigeria called upon the British Government to grant them regional autonomy before independence. The British Government rejected that. After independence, Nigeria’s Parliament created the Mid-West Region. During Nigeria’s Civil War of July 1967-January 1970, the military under General Yakubu Gowon carved out Calabar, Ogaja and Rivers (COR) provinces from Eastern Nigeria. But the British and their junior partners in the Anglo-Muslim Rule of Northern Nigeria refused to create the Middle Belt Region. Middle Belt was the only minority that was refused a region.

In spite of the concrete ethnic, cultural and religious reasons, the Middle Belt was appended against its will to Hausaland and Bornoland, thus giving it an inferior status and socio-political role in the racialised and hierarchical structure of the Northern Region of Nigeria.

In 1996, General Sani Abacha created Six Geo-Political Zones: South South, South East, South West, North East and North West. The Middle Belt was balkanised into three parts – One part was appended to North East; another part to North West and the rest was left as North Central.

Historically under British colonial rule, the Northern Region was fused into one political bloc because it was considered as one northern political bloc. The Middle Belt was classified as “Northern” politically, but excluded culturally and religiously in the affairs of Northern Nigeria. 

Lest Nigerians forget, when Lt. Gen T.Y. Danjuma (Retd), endorsed President Olusegun Obasanjo, there was no uproar; when he endorsed President Muhammadu Buhari, there was no uproar, now he has endorsed President Bola, and there is an uproar of some people of Hausaland origin. This reflects their desire to continue the subjugation and domination of the Middle Belt. If our brothers of Hausaland and Bornoland have treated the peoples of the Middle Belt as equal and humanely both historically and presently, such a visit would not have occurred.     

Public affairs analysts ask if the insecurity in the Middle Belt Region that escalated in the last three years has been tackled and the economy improved for the president’s support for a second term. What is your position on this?   

Insecurity in Nigeria is of long-term consequences of the colonial social values and social institutions that the colonial masters used to build Nigeria’s political social order. Herein lies the root of our problems and challenges.

Nigerians have focused too much on the social symptoms and talk much about them. Much time and resources are wasted in treating the symptoms, rather than finding the root causes. As it were, we climb on top of a tree cutting branches and leaves, while leaving the roots that feed the tree to bud branches and leaves. The root causes are in the history of making Nigeria by the empire builders.                                                           

How do you tackle insecurity successfully and effectively in the midst of the battle of the gods of ethnicity, religion and region? Nigeria is not like the USA that an economic downturn can cost elections. Put economy and insecurity aside, because Nigerians are steeped in the battle of the gods of ethnicity, religion and region. Nigerian political philosophy and practice are rooted in the manipulation and permutation of these three political pillars – ethnicity, religion and region.

A political pundit who knows the arts and sciences of these three could win elections, regardless of the state of economy or insecurity. Mark you, Nigerians by and large worship the gods of ethnicity, religion and region. Make no bones about it.    

Why is the Middle Belt always agitating?

Let me repeat your question. Why is the Middle Belt always agitating? I am sure you are asking about how they are always disturbed about their state and condition. Or why are they forceful in making their demands? Let me take you back to the era of Anglo-Muslim Rule in Northern Nigeria, between 1900 and1960.

Lugard and post-Lugardians used basically three mechanisms of British colonial rule in Northern Nigeria. The first instrument was Indirect Rule—ruling through native authority. The second instrument was proxy administration—using one group to govern others on behalf of the colonial administration. The third instrument was racialised hierarchies—classification of races into superior-inferior. These were the social tools that the British and the caliphates used to seal the inferior status and socio-political role of the non-Muslims in the hierarchical structure of colonial Northern Nigeria. This historical fact has never been changed or modified. It defines Government and religious policies, administrative practice, attitude of government officers and religious leaders in the Northern system. These are the historical social values and social structures that have kept the Middle Belt where they belong, where they were placed in the ladder of colonial human classification, having inferior status and socio-political role.

British colonial racial theory was like this in their classification of human races. The top is Anglo-Saxon (British and German Saxons: most civilised in world); the next is Teutonic races (the rest of Europeans); the next one is light skin and dark skin Arabs.

In Nigeria, it is the Fulani on top and the Hausa below, and at the bottom, you have Primitive Africans, Child Races (Middle Belt nationalities and other Nigerian ethnic groups).

Each race was treated according to the label attached to it. The Middle Belt peoples were placed at the very bottom. The consequences of this classification were: Pattern of superiority-inferiority relationships, dominance-subordination relationships, and politics of inequality, domination or exclusion. Stratified inequality and social and racial hierarchy, rivalry and antagonism abound in colonial policies, administrative practices and attitudes.

What would a human being joyfully and happily live in such a racialised hierarchical system of human servitude? Should the Middle Belt see a window of hope and emancipation in any Nigerian political leader, what would stop them from aligning with such a good Nigeria? The Middle Belters have watched the political dance of Nigerian politicians, and they know who dances best to them. 

When you talk about the Middle Belt, some Nigerians see it as Christians in the North. Even those that came from the Southern part of the North are still confused about it; their whole allegiance is still to the Fulani North. Why?

The cause is ignorance or bias. Let’s answer this state of ignorance or bias. I wrote a Memorandum to the 2014 National Conference of President Goodluck Jonathan, of which I was a member, representing Kaduna State. This is what I wrote and I quote: ‘Many analyses of Northern Nigeria, whether of its ethnicity, religion, culture, politics, economics, or geography, have always failed to address the political question of the Middle Belt in Nigerian politics. The Middle Belt of Nigeria consists mainly of the Traditionalists-Christian-Muslim Minorities.

‘The empire builders, the Sokoto Caliphate and the Sultanate of Kanem-Borno and the British Colonial Administration have all failed very woefully in creating a viable and conducive political and social environment for the well-being of the Traditionalists-Christian-Muslim Minorities (TCMM), who resides in the Middle Belt of Nigeria.

‘These Empire builders created artificial political, social, religious and economic boundaries that grossly denied the TCMM of the present northern states, political rights and freedom. When the British gave all Nigerians their political independence in 1960, in Northern Nigeria, the instruments of political power fell on the laps of the political class and elites. The TCMM of the northern states have been kept under a perpetual internal colonialism as the subordinate subjects of the ideology and idolatry of the North.

‘The time has come for all Nigerians to rise up and speak with one voice for the liberation of the peoples of the Middle Belt of Nigeria. This is one of the major tasks that awaits this long awaited National Conference.’

The population of the Middle Belt is more than that of the core north. Why is it that the region is always not considered for presidential running mate to a southern candidate? In 2023, the presidential front liners, President Bola Tinubu of APC picked a Muslim running mate of Kanuri extraction, while Peter Obi of Labour Party picked a Fulani man.

The colonial history of both the British and the Islamic Caliphates has both given them an inferior status and socio-political role. The Middle Belt had been annexed to Hausaland and Bornoland, whose rulers stood proxy to the British colonial masters. Since the Middle Belt has been fused and squeezed into Northern Nigeria, which had been made into one political bloc; an appendix becomes a second-fiddle.

For the Middle Belt to have a political voice and also be politically recognised and respected by all Nigerians, nothing would solve its political predicament unless Nigeria constitutionally grants the Middle Belt its Regional status as it was done to Mid-West and Calabar Ogoja Rivers (COR). This is the debt which Nigeria owes the Middle Belt.

The argument of some people – that the Middle Belt was conquered by the Fulani Jihad, and that for that reason, they must continue as the conquered – shouldn’t hold any water. Between 1900 and 1903, the British conquered the Sokoto Caliphate and the Sultanate of Kanem-Borno. The suzerainty of the caliphates was abolished by British conquest. The British gave political independence to all Nigerians regardless. No one and no institution can claim imperialism or colonialism over any free and independent Nigerian or region.

Assuming that you conquered somebody and you the conqueror were also conquered, you lack any form of jurisdiction or sovereignty over any one. Many Nigerians are ignorant of how colonialism and imperialism function.

After independence, the British have no political sovereignty over any old kingdom, chiefdom, caliphate, which they once conquered. So it is: No Nigerian, or old kingdom, or old chiefdom, or old caliphate can make a claim of conquest over any one in Nigeria.        

Based on the power rotation principle, in 2031, when political power rotates to the North, where should it berth?

This depends upon the dynamics, arbitration, consensus and arrangement of politics at the given time. The North-South political consensus about rotation in this political dispensation has been rejected by some regional politicians.

The Kanuri, unlike the Fulani, have not produced the presidency; they believe that they should succeed President Tinubu if he wins, since their son is the vice president. What is your position on this?

This also depends upon the dynamics, arbitration, consensus and arrangement of politics at the given time.

Mutual suspicion; hatred among ethnic groups in the country is palpable. Why has it remained so, and how can it be rested?

All these psychological issues are rooted in the colonial policies, administrative practices and attitudes towards Africans. I have already mentioned some of them, thus: the first is colonial racial views – the fundamental inequality of races or ethnic groups; classification of human races based upon superior-inferior status, and advocated separate development of people groups by highlighting that: Islam is better suited to Africans than Christianity; Western education and Christianity detribalise Africans, and applied the principles of dominance-subordination of ethnic groups.

The consequences of colonial policies, administrative practices, attitudes towards African groups have created a pattern of superiority-inferiority relationship; pattern of dominance-subordination relationships; pattern of the politics of inequality, domination or exclusion; stratified inequality and social hierarchy; rivalry and antagonism, and latent hostility.

Every group in Nigeria – from the North to the South is crying, which has brought about restiveness, insurgency etc. What are the reasons for these? And how can Nigeria be made comfortable for all its component units?

This is a very loaded question, which needs a very loaded answer.

In the first place, it has become necessary that we have a second look at all the hypotheses, assumptions, theories and models of political, economic, social and religious development that have been applied by various political regimes in Nigeria. Various nation-state builders have applied these, but Nigeria has perpetually become the worst of it.

For several decades, social scientists have formulated and developed theories and models for political and economic development, industrial take-off, modernisation, nation-state building and national integration, and of recent, religious theocracy (Sharia) and ethnic nationalism.

The art of statecraft has applied these models and theories, but what are the results? – Devastating and disappointing. Nigeria is yet to become politically stable. Nigeria is far from becoming industrialised. The emerging and powerful forces of ethnic nationalities, social chaos, moral decadence and religious bigotry have seriously questioned the unity and stability of Nigeria. What really went wrong?

Today, in the political sphere, one hardly hears of any rallying call for national unity and stability. Rather, ethnic nationalism cries only in ethnic tunes and dances only in ethnic rhythms. The agenda that one hears and reads in the national dailies are not national but ethnic, parochial and exclusivist. The Arewa Consultative Forum with its quest for a Northern president, which is revival of northernisation and Sharia. The Afenifere with its Oduduwa agenda and militant OPC, which is the creation of Egbe Omo Oduduwa. The Ohanaeze with its quest for an Igbo president and militant Bakassi Boys, which is the creation of Ndigbo. Other groups such as the MOSSOP—the creation of Delta Region and the Middle Belt Forum—the creation of the Middle Belt Region, have their own ethnic agenda. And presently, we have political parties versus INEC. All these point to a crisis of confidence, trust and legitimacy. By and large, political analysis has seriously taken the turn of ethnic nationalism, religious bigotry and parties’ feud.

Nigeria’s military strategists for the past few decades embarked upon massive political, economic and social engineering so as to stamp out poverty, tribalism, regionalism, ignorance, corruption and usher in political, economic and social growth and stability in Nigeria. But the results are devastating and disappointing.

The military strategists borrowed heavily from authoritarian bureaucratic military systems, especially from Latin America, Western political and economic theories and models and socialist statism. All of these resulted in producing only social, moral and institutional decay and chaos as it is being exhibited in contemporary Nigerian society. What went wrong with the political and military experiment at nation-state building and policy-making?

The people who would implement these had hidden programmes that governed their behaviour, practices and beliefs—their ethnic, religious and regional foundations. The politicians and military strategists have transformed Nigerian society into what? More corruption, resurgent ethnic and tribal nationalism, and fanned the embers of regional, sectional and religious and cultural sentiments, biases and prejudices; unleashed and uncontrollable social and moral chaos, indiscipline, insecurity, instability and forces of violence and conflict. Today, these unleashed and formidable forces of violence, chaos, and conflict confront Nigeria. What are the remedies? We must go back to the basics, our ethical and cultural foundations. The political, economic, social and religious answers and solutions given so far by Nigeria’s experts have all failed at correcting and rectifying the problems of Nigeria. Rather, Nigeria’s multitudes of problems have become more endemic and have also reached epidemic proportions. For this reason, I propose that we have a serious look at and a critical analysis of Nigeria’s obstacles to good governance, good leadership and stability.

Those Nigeria’s obstacles are not necessarily embedded in the political, economic, social and religious theories and models of development as proposed by the social scientists, policy-makers and nation-state builders, but are the fundamental ethical and cultural elements embedded within the Nigerian social environment. They are embedded in the hidden cultural and ethical codes and values of Nigeria’s ethnic, religious and regional groups. They govern the behaviour of ethnic, religious and regional groups, and individuals.

We need to identify those ethical and cultural foundations that have become obstacles to national development. My contention and charge is that these ethical and cultural foundations have been grossly ignored by policy-making and nation-state building in the history of Nigeria.

Today, we are reaping the results of ignoring our ethical and cultural foundations in unleashed corruption, moral decadence, indiscipline, insecurity and instability. These are the evil and wicked social forces that destroy our newfound social, economic and political structures.

Whatever new institutions and new values that we inject into the Nigerian society, they cannot withstand the negative social forces, such as, ethnic militias, religious bigotry, corruption, moral decadence, indiscipline, insecurity, and instability, and now the raging inter-party and intra-party feuds and ethno-regional nationalism.

The 36 Houses of Assembly have passed the State Police Bill, which is waiting for the President’s assent. What is your reaction to this development?

This is good news for Nigeria.

How can the State Police operate without the governors using it to oppress and hound perceived or real political foes?

The 36 states have spoken. This has laid to rest the phobia of State Police. The said governors’ use of state police is an opinion overruled by reason.

How can you rate the frontline presidential candidates – President Bola Tinubu (APC); Atiku Abubakar (ADC); Peter Obi (NDC); Seyi Makinde (APM); Sowore (AAC)?

Rating of political candidates lies within the realm of biased personal opinion. Facts or reality could be laid aside in favour of one’s political candidate. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is the incumbent president. He is the candidate to beat. Atiku Abubakar is currently under legal issues, whether the Supreme Court could clear him. Peter Obi is a Southern political candidate that could match politically with the incumbent president.

The last two, Seyi Makinde and Sowore add value to the political campaigns and competition.

Opposition parties have cried out over AI generated photographs in the INEC register, which the electoral umpire has admitted. What does this portend for the 2027 election?

Admission requires an act of rectification. If rectification has been done, can it be verified? Even if done, does this mean that INEC should be disbanded? I remember, several people and groups have protested against the appointment of the chairman and some have called for his removal or his resignation.

With this background, could some people who have opposed the appointment of the Chairman influence the AI generated photographs by some mischievous INEC officers? Would the INEC chairman order the AI issue? After all the debates on this matter, should INEC be disbanded?

Mistrust of the 2027 elections could come from many sources. Is this not a national problem? Right now, as it has always been, the battle of the gods of ethnicity, religion and region are raging fiercely. Some have used religion as a source of misgivings. Some have used ethnicity/tribalism as a source, while others have used region. There may be no solution as they are inherently divided. Which answer would satisfy whom? Thus, the mistrust would continue, while continuity would continue. This is our national predicament.

Don’t you think this may be a recipe for anarchy, as losers may not accept the result of the election?

Winning and losing elections is part of the political game. Losers do not readily accept the results. The battle of the courts is open for legal tussle. Anarchy after elections is never a new thing. It is part of political immaturity and the battle of the gods of ethnicity, religion and region. As a Nigerian, I have witnessed these battles often fought after elections. The cure of all of these is when we dethrone the influence of the gods of ethnicity/tribalism, religion and region.

The post What Nigeria must do to start making progress – Prof Yusufu Turaki appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.
